There is a risk that rural regional water service providers with smaller p opulations will struggle financially and continue to underinvest in three waters infrastructure. Smaller regions are also less likely to be able to take advantage of new technologies, or meet goals such as carbon neutrality. . The significant difference in t he size and scale of different regional water service providers would make benchmarking difficult. There are also likely to be higher regulatory costs due to the significant number of providers and the large variation between them. . The alternative option o f one, national water provider is also not a preferred option. This has a number of weaknesses, relative to the preferred multi regional provider model. In January , Cabinet Business Committee agreed that further work with local government on the design of new service arrangements would focus on multi regional and regional models for service delivery. This effectively ruled out a single provider as an option. Statutory entities . The preferred approach is that the new multi regional water providers would be statutory entities. This would require legislation. . Statutory entities have boards , but are not companies. Each statutory entity usually has its own establishing legislation that contains entity specific objectives that could be a mix of social, cultural, public policy, or commercial. Statutory entities can have noncommercial functions or commercial imperatives. . The main alternative to this approach would be for the new multi regional providers to be council controlled organisations (CCOs) . This is an organisational form that is provided for in the Local Government Act , and which is used regularly by local authorities. ) governs how objectionable content is to be dealt with in New Zealand. When an online content host becomes aware of objectionable content being stored on its platform by users, for example through a takedown notice, the online content host must remove, or prevent access by the public to, all copies of the online publication that is the subject of the notice to or over which it has access or control as soon as is reasonably practicable after receipt of the notice but no later than the end of the period specified in the notice. An online content host may also retain those files for evidential purposes in criminal investigations andor prosecutions.
) supports the retention by online content hosts of files relating to objectionable content for the purpose of supportingassisting the investigation and prosecution of criminal conduct as long as the relevant provisions of the FVPCA, including any takedown notices, are complied with.

Table : Objective priorities for action Objective : There is a reduction in gambling harm related inequities between population groups Priorities for action Short to medium term priorities Long term priorities Provide and monitor dedicated services for Mori, Pacific and Asian peoples where appropriate, including services for gamblers and their families , whanau and communities . Ensure that all services provided to prevent and minimise gambling harm are culturally appropriate and all services are health literate, high quality and effective. Continue monitoring gambling harm related inequities (eg, the disproportionate prevalence of harm within some populations) and identify factors that contribute to these inequities (eg, differences in the gambling environment by geographical area). Develop, pilot, evaluate and implement one or more initiatives specifically focused on reducing gambling harm related inequities, particularly among Mori , Pacific and Asian peoples Underlying principles: value and high performance te whinga hua me te tika o ng mahi We need to do better for the population groups that do not enjoy the same health as the general New Zealand population. In relation to gambling harm, these groups include Mori and Pacific peoples and the growing Asian population in particular. To achieve better outcomes, our focus must be on removing barriers to delivering high quality health services, including cultural, language, physical and financial barriers. The Ministry will consider tailoring services so that they are available in more accessible places or at more suitable times and are delivered in more culturally appropriate ways. The Health Quality Safety Commission s Triple Aim framework provides a systems approach to improving the quality of health services for individuals and populations. It can help us balance our goals to achieve the New Zealand Triple Aim of improved health and equity for all populations; improved quality, safety and experience of care; and best value for public resources. Objective : Mori have healthier futures Objective aims to improve Mori health through the prevention and minimisation of gambling harm. This objective reflects the rel ationship between the Crown and Mori under Te Tiriti o Waitangi. It aligns with objective and is supported by all the other objectives. This objective recognises gamblingharm related inequities both for Mori as a population and within the Mori popul ation group. For example, while the prevalence of moderaterisk (problem) gambling is relatively high for both Mori men and Mori women, Mori women are more likely than Mori men to experience harm from someone else s gambling. This second report back will also inform our appetite to release the earmarked investment stimulus beyond tranche one to the ()(f)(iv) sector. . One of the points we will need to consider is charging arrangements for water services . I am aware that councils currently use a variet y of approaches , including fixed rates, volumetric charges, and general rates . It will be important to ensure consumers experience minimal disrupt ion during the transition to, and implementation of, new multi regional water entities. I anticipate consumers would continue to be charged on a similar basis to their existing arrangements, at least in the initial years of the entities operations . Volu metric charging is something that could be consider ed in future , but only when it makes sense to do so . I note that Scott ish Water still raises its charges via local council rates notices. . We will also need to consider and address Treaty related rights and interests , including in the design of the new water entities . A preliminary analysis has been undertaken, ()(f)(iv) and is attached at Appendix C. I will report back with further advice in . This preliminary analysis has been informed by previous engagement with iwiMori, in relation to proposals for the new drinking water regulatory framework and creation of Taumata Arowai. During these engagement sessions, a number of comments were made that are relevant to reforms to service delivery arran gements. . The potential for reform of water service providers is likely to present a different range of Treaty interests, though, which will need to be identified and explored further . An engagement strategy will be prepared to inform this work. Engagemen t and analysis will be informed by guidance material that has been prepared through the Te Arawhiti portfolio, and intersections with our response to WAI and WAI . When engaging with iwiMori, we will seek to use existing platforms and relationsh ips, such as the National Iwi Chairs Forum, to minimise the consultation fatigue iwi may be experiencing. Finally, I am aware that several government agencies are facing significant costs to These sites are generally small and spread out. upgrade their water infrastructure . DOC has a significant number of sites around the country, many of which will require water infrastructure upgrades. ()(f)(iv) . ()(f)(iv) . The stimulus package in this paper is targeted at local government water infrastructure . I do not want to diminish the amount of investment that would be directed at improving local infrastructure and incentivising sector support for service delivery reform. This could happen if Crown owned water infrastructure was included in this stimulus package. . However, I recognise the challenges that DOC and other Crown water service providers , such as the Department of Corrections and New Zealand Defence Force , are facing and the implications this may h ave. Officials from the relevant agencies will do further work to explore the options for addressing these challenges. This could include the potential for the water investment stimulus package to be broadened, and options for Crown water supplies to be included within the scope of the new multi regional entities. I am advised that some agencies have expressed an interest in transferring responsibility for some of their water assets to the new water entities, if this was a ()(f)(iv) possibility . I will report back with further advice in I am proposing a three year reform programme and three tranches of investment but the substantive work would begin immediately . Maintaining momentum is critical. If my proposed approach is agreed, we will need to move quickly to develop and agree detailed policy proposals, engage with key stakeholders, and begin releasing the stimulus package . . With this in mind, I intend to seek policy decisions in view to legislation being introduc ed in early . . Overall, I consider that a three year programme is needed to design and implement the reforms effectively. This approach reflects that it will take time to : . engage meaningfully with local authorities, and for them to understand and com e on board with the reforms, and adapt their organisations ; . engage meaningfully with iwiMori, and consider Treaty of Waitangi rights and interests; . communicate and socialise the reforms with the public; . develop and enact the legislation needed to establish new water entities, and the associated regulatory framework ; , with a ()(f)(iv) Page of Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government UNCLASSIFIED . work through the complex transactional issues related to the aggregation of water services and assets from individual entities into a small number of multi regional entities, particularly as information about assets and revenue is poor. . I am proposing that investment is released in three tranches, broadly aligned with the investment waves of COVID recovery. This investment is a vital tool to incentivise buyin from the local government sector, and ensure support is maintain ed. A single tranche of funding , of a size that is able to be immediately deployed, is unlikely to achieve the desired structural reforms. . The diagram at Appendix A provides a high level indicative timeframe for th e proposed three year programme. . My officials have also been developing the work programme needed to develop and implement the service delivery reforms . An initial programme structure includes the followin g workstreams : . Stakeholder engagement and communications; . Policy, legislation, and sector guidance; . Structuring the new entities ; . Establishment and implementation; . Project management, reporting, and programme development. . The workstreams and structure are being designed to ensure that the programme can move at pace, is responsive (particularly to any further potential changes in the environment as a result of ongoing COVID impact), connected to the stimulus and regulatory reform activities, and suitably resourced. Commencing the front end work as soon as possible, to enable negotiations with local authorities and development of policy positions, will be key to enabling programme acceleration. . It will take significant resources to administer and implement a reform programme of this magnitude and complexity . The financial implications section of this paper sets out the funding being sought to resource the programme . . Subject to this funding being agreed , I am proposing the Department of Internal Affairs (DIA) leads the service delivery reform programme . The Department is the agency responsible for , and has primary relationship with , local government , and has been leading the Three Waters Review for the past three years . Officials would work closely with other key agencies, including The Treasury, Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment, Ministry of Health, and Ministry for the Environment, as they have been throughout the Review. . I am proposing that programme governance would continue to be provided by the group of Three Waters Ministers. These Ministers will meet regularly to guide the direction of this work, discuss policy options, and ensure momentum is being maintained and all aspects of the programme are on track. . The reform programme will have a close relationship with the oversight and release of the wider economic stimulus package. The detail of this work will need to be included in advice from The Treasury, Crown Infrast ructure Partners, and the Department of Internal Affairs, in the context of other stimulus approaches. Page of Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government UNCLASSIFIED . My officials would be involved in designing the stimulus package and deciding how it would be spent, given this relates to the local government sector and our water service reform objectives. Once agreement has been reached with local government about the specific reform and funding package that councils would be opting in to, I anticipate Crown Infrastructure Partners would have oversight of the alloca tion and use of the three waters stimulus funding in accordance with th e agreements . It is important to get support from local government, but there would be a deadline and agreed mechanisms for demonstrating that support . Support from local government is vital if we are to deliver the proposals in this paper, and achieve our short and long term goals. However, there is a need to move quickly to develop agreements with the sector, shape the broad reform agenda, and undertake detailed policy design work. It will not be helpful to our reform objectives, or community interests, to enter into protracted negotiations before the policy reform work can begin . . I have already had initial conversations with the Local Government New Zealand (LGNZ) National Council , and the Central Local Government Forum. It is clear that local government recognise s the opportunities of service delivery reform, and benefits of infrastructure investment. The sector has expressed a willingness to work with us to design a reform prog ramme , on a high trust and opt in basis . To achieve this, a joint working group will be formed between DIA, The Treasury, LGNZ and SOLGM. . I am proposing that the joint working group will prepare an initial high level agreement in June , on how loc al government will work with government on the reform agenda. This group would then work to prepare a more detailed agreement ( a memorandum of understanding) that councils across New Zealand would have the opportunity to opt in to . . Initial funding from th e economic stimulus package would be released to those councils that agree to the memorandum of understanding in August . Councils that do not opt in at this point would still be able to do so at a later , but would miss the first wave of stimulus investment. . In parallel, the joint working group will also explore the detailed policy reform matters referred to earlier in this paper, with a view to providing advice on these matters to Ministers by December . . I am planning further engagement with local government, both in this early, strategic phase, and on an ongoing basis as the reforms are developed and implemented. My approach to engagement will involve a combination of discussions with sector representati ve bodies and direct engagement with councils. . Officials will also engage with representative bodies and councils building on existing relationships between the Department of Internal Affairs and the sector, through the CentralLocal Government Partnerships team and Three Waters Review . A sector engagement strategy is being developed to guide this work. To support this process, I recommend that we immediately resource councils and their representative bodies, so they are able to engage in the reform programme . UNCLASSIFIED Office of the Minister of Local Government Chair Cabinet Economic Development Committee Investing in water infrastructure to accelerate reform and support economic recovery post COVID Proposal . T his paper proposes a three year programme for reforming three waters service delivery arrangements, which would be delivered in parallel with a n economic stimulus package of Crown investment in water infrastructure. . The proposed approach is designed to support economic recovery post COV ID, and address persistent systemic issues facing the three waters , through a combination of: . stimulating investment , to assist economic recovery through job creation, and maintain investment in water infrastructure renewals and maintenance ; and . fundamentally reforming the water service delivery sector, into large scale multi regional providers, to realise significant e conomic , public health, environmental, and other benefits over the medium to long term. We have an opportunity to achieve transformational changes to three waters services, to deliver significant long term benefits to consumers and the economy . Executive summary . A lot has changed in the past three months. COVID has exacerbated the three waters challenges already facing the local government sector. Many councils and communities will struggle to respond to these challenges. Without support, investment will not occur to the levels required, and the condition of infrastructure is expected to continue to decline as councils prioritise other areas of investment. Since late , we have considered a series of papers relating to the system for regulating and managing the three waters , and the response to the Havelock North drinking water contamination event . These papers highlighted that, in many parts of the country, communities cannot be confident that drinking water is safe, or that good environmental outcomes are being achieved. They also raised concerns about the regulation, sustainability, capacity and capability of a system with a large number of localised providers, many of which are funded by relatively small populations. . We have already made considerable progress with regulatory reform. Legislation to create Taumata Arowai is c urrently being considered by the Health Committee, and work to build this new Crown agent is underway. Drafting of a separate Water Services Bill is nearly completed, and will give effect to our decisions to significantly strengthen the drinking water reg ulatory framework. Analysis Local government three waters providers are facing significant challenges, whic h are being exacerbated due to COVID . Throughout t he Three Waters Review , we have heard about a number of systemic challenges facing the three waters sector , including : . significant investment requirements to address infrastructures deficits, and associated risks to public health and the environment; . capacity and capability issues relating to asset management and governance of water infrastructure, and service delivery ; The paper, Three waters service delivery and funding arrangements: approach to reform, was considered by the Cabinet Business Committee on January . Page of Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government UNCLASSIFIED . funding and affordability issues, particularly for smaller communities, driven by matters such as : .. community expectations and regulatory requirements relating to water quality, treatment and management; .. the need to replace ageing infrastructure , build re silience to climate change and natural hazards , and innovate; .. increasing demand for water infrastructure in high growth areas; .. delivering regional economic growth, including by sustaining local employment across distributed water networks; . the lack of alig nment between the development and operation of wastewater systems and a catchment based regulatory system; . the impact on local government of transition to new three waters service providers, particularly the reduction in operational budgets that would occu r if water assets were transferred . . The situation caused by COVID means the local government sector is facing a series of additional issues and challenges, many of which relate to the three waters. . Prior to COVID , territorial authorities were plannin g on spending up to . billion in capital over the next five years on water infrastructure . However, COVID is likely to cause significant decreases in revenue in territorial authorities over the short te rm. Revenues could declin e by between and per cent over the next financial year, and local authorities are facing increased cost pressures . As a result, borrowing will be constrained due to lower debt limits that flow from lower revenues , and opportunities to raise revenue through rates , fees a nd charges will be extremely limited . . Investment in water infrastructure has traditionally been an area where councils have constrained spending in response to financial pressure s. This is because investment in water infrastructure is long term, and has a less visible impact on communities than other forms of council expenditure. The Three Waters Review has highlighted that New Zealands water infrastructure already carries a burden of underinvestment. This is likely to worsen in response to COVID . . Officials have estimated that, in the absence of support from the Crown, territorial authorities will face pressure to reduce planned capital investment in three waters infrastructure by approximately . billion over the next three years . . Three waters providers will also be facing other pressures over the next few years , as our regulatory reforms begin to take effect, and communities increasingly experience the impact of climate change . For example, there will be more emphasis on compliance with drinking water regulatory requirements, and greater transparency about the environmental performance of wastewater and stormwater networks. The recent drought has demonstrated the significant issues, costs , and risks to public health associated with water short ages. Page of Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government UNCLASSIFIED I am proposing a combination of Crown investment and fundamental service delivery reform to address these challenges , and support short and long term economic recovery . Many councils and communities will struggle to respond to these challenges . Without support, investment will not occur to the levels required, the condition of infrastructure will continue to decline , and t here could be negative implications for public health and environmental outcomes . Sector capability and capacity issues will remain, and funding problems will progressively worsen . . The COVID situation has also affected progress with voluntary service delivery reforms. Understandably, councils and communities have other prioritie s. It appears unlikely that we will be able to regain momentum to achieve voluntary reforms in the shortmedium term, to the extent that is needed to deliver widespread improvements across the country . . We are presented with an opportunity to consider how to improve this situation , and to address a number of significant issues , both entrenched and new. We need to act now to respond to the immediate challenges , and to ensure current settings are not locked in for years to come, causing problems to re emerge . . Following discussions with other Three Waters Ministers, I am seeking agreement to proceed with a three year reform programme to address th e issues facing the three waters sector and support economic recovery post COVID . My proposed approach has two, inter related components, and is designed to : . stimulat e investment, to assist economic recovery through job creation, and maintain investment in water infrastructure renewals and maintenance; and . fundamentally reform the water service delivery sector, to realise significant economic, environmental, health, and other benefits over the medium to long term. (This would be an opt in reform programme, in which councils that choose to participate would be eligible for stimulus funding, provided there are sufficient numbers of councils to provide entity scale.) . This dual approach would be structured to achieve multiple objectives both in relation to economic recovery, and delivering the multiple benefits that are associated with three waters reform. . To support COVID recovery, we would be seeking to m aximis e the positive impact that any stimulus could provide to local economi es and jobs , and address the impact of the change process during transition. The i nvestment type and procurement support could be targeted at retaining local and lower skill jobs , prevent ing further deterioration in water infrastructure as council finances decrease, and avoid ing invest ment in assets that may become stranded in future entities . . Through this proposal, we can also achieve the objectives for reforming the three waters system that were outlined in my January paper: . significantly improving the safety and quality of drinking water services, and the environmental performance of wastewater and stormwater systems (whi ch are crucial to good public health and wellbeing , and achieving good environmental outcomes ); . ensuring all New Zealanders have equitable access to affordable three waters services; Page of Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government UNCLASSIFIED . improving the coordination of resources and unlocking strategic opportuni ties to consider New Zealands infrastructure needs at a larger scale; . increasing the resilience of three waters service provision to both short and long term risks and events, particularly climate change and natural hazards; . moving the supply of three wa ters services to a more financially sustainable footing, and addressing the affordability and capability challenges faced by small suppliers and councils; . improving transparency about, and accountability for, the delivery and costs of three waters services, including the ability to benchmark the performance of service providers CBC MIN refers. In the short term, t argeted fiscal stimulus would help councils to fund asset renewals, create jobs, and generate additional GDP . I am proposing a targeted stimulus package of up to to invest in water infrastructure and support service delivery reform. This package comprises: ()(f)(iv) . an early injection of to maintain planned investment and asset quality in the face of significant declines in council revenue; ()(f)(iv) . a second, more scalable stimulus of up to to support large scale asset replacements, and the bri nging forward of no regrets investment in the latter ()(f)(iv) half of the reform period . . The fiscal profile of the proposed investment is based on achievement of both stimulus and reform objectives. I propose that we progressively release funding to the local government sector, following demonstration of support for the reform programme and progress against well defined milestones. The mechanisms for demonstrating support will be discussed with the sector shortly . . To provide fiscal certainty and confidence tha t we can achieve the reform objectives, I ()(f)(iv) propose that a total funding envelope of is established to support this reform process. ()(f)(iv) In this paper, I am seeking agreement to an allocation for tranche one ()(f)(iv) of from the allocation , with delegation to the Minister of Finance , Minister of Local Government, Minister for Infrastructure, and Minister of Internal Affairs to release the funding to the sector, following demonstration of an agreed pathway to reform and subject to their satisfaction that the necessary conditions have been met. . Although this financial commitment from the Crown is substantial, this level of investment needs to be compared to the value of water assets that sit on council balance sheets. In total, councils have approximately billion in total assets, of which billion are three waters assets. Total depreciation expense on these three waters assets is million per annum. ()(f)(iv) Page of Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government UNCLASSIFIED part of my engagement in the next month. I note that the total quantum for subsequent tranches is scalable, and will need to be informed by our success with the ()(f)(iv). Commitment to proceed with subsequent tranches would be signalled to the sector as sector in meeting milestones and the size of incentive required to secure reform . . Analysis indicates that this fiscal stimulus would protect and create at least , jobs directly, and a total of , jobs once indirect effects are accounted for. It would also generate an estimated . billion in additional GDP . . This investment would achieve : . programme level support for major service delivery reforms across territorial authorities (and water related council controlled organisations) ; . renewals to core water infrastructure, such as wastewater treatment plants and drinking water, wastewater and stormwater pipes (including depreciation) , to prevent the further deterioration of assets particularly in response to COVID and declining council revenues ; . the best ideas from shovel worthy project initiatives, and new investments that emerge from combined multi region asset management plans ; . upgrad es to noncompliant drinking water supplies , with an appropriate amount of funding tagged to upgrade marae based water supplies (contributing to public health benefits associated with safe drinking water) . . Specifically, I am proposing that approximately of the stimulus would be set aside for rural drinking water supplies, to help to address the challenges these ()(f)(iv) suppliers are facing in delivering safe drinking water to consumers. There are a range of supply arrangements in rural and remote areas, including council and private providers, and further work is needed to establish how the funding would be targeted. I will explore how best to allocate the funding with the Minister for Infrastructure, and ()(f)(iv) report back with further details in . I have considered alternatives to targeted investment of this kind , but there are significant challenges associated with other approaches. . One alternative would be to ask councils to fund further investments on their balance sheets, by utilising further borrowing. Additional borrowing of around million per year was planned prior to COVID to fund capital investment. However, the decrease in revenues will severely constrain councils ability to take on more debt, and some councils (particularly in high growth areas) will quickly reach debt limits. . The reduction in revenue will mean most councils will need to curtail almost all of their borrowing programmes . It is estimated that, i n aggregate, councils will only be able to borrow an additional million per annum without breaching debt torevenue limits. ()(f)(iv) This is insufficient to bridge the expected investment gap. Page of Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government UNCLASSIFIED . A variation of this option would be to support council debt through issuing some form of government bond. This would provide councils with the ability to borrow at rates closer to the Crown cost of borrowing, rather than prevailing rates available to them through the Local Government Funding Agency. This option is only attractive if the differential is large and councils have a greater ability to take on debt than current circumstances allow. Overall, the likelihood of this occurring is low , and unlikely to be sufficiently attractive to the sector nor sufficient to prevent deterioration of the infrastructure . . Another option would be to use alternative funding or financing arrangements to support further investment in three waters assets, such a s Special Purpose Vehicles (SPVs). Th ese vehicles could seek up front capital from sources other than the Crown. . There are several challenges with this approach, particularly from an immediate response perspective, and they would not incentivise structural reform. The main issue is that SPVs and similar funding mechanisms are best suited to green field developments or new asset construction. SPVs are not well suited to brown field development or renewal of assets, which is what the bulk of this program me of work is looking to support in the short to medium term. . In addition, SPVs typically rely heavily on private or overseas equity investment to fund upfront capital costs. Due to the economic shock relating to COVID , it is likely that ready access to private equity and capital will be limited, and the Crown will need to step in to help fill this gap in the short term. Even in instances where private equity is available, borrowing costs are likely to escalate substantially for firms to access this form of capital. Provision of the stimulus would be conditional on local government opting in to service delivery reforms , to create multi regional water service providers . In April , Three Waters Ministers were asked to consider how water investment opportunities could support reform and be used to provide for economic stimulus in the context of COVID . . Ministers were presented with several options for providing investment, ranging from investment with no conditions, to investment that is condi tional on aggregation of water services. There was a strong preference for providing a f inancial contribution that is conditional on aggregation , and for the creation of four or five multi regional water service providers. . Our rationale for four or five entities relates to evidence about the size (population and customer density) over which scale efficiencies are likely to be achieved. This analysis has been supported by assistance from the Water Industry Commission for Scotland. Scotland is considered an exemplar in water reform internationally . . The preferred approach recognise s that fundamental reforms to the water service delivery sector are needed to address the challenges and achieve the objectives described earlier, and to ensure investment in infrastructure continues. This is an opportunity to deliver broader economic, health, environmental, and other benefits over the medium to long term, across the country . Page of Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government UNCLASSIFIED . The alternative options, such as unconditional investment, or investment that is conditional on best endeavours or on each individual council agreeing to a reform pathway, were not preferred. These options are unlikely to be effective, feasible, or have the desired level of impact. There is also a risk that unconditional investment would reduce sector interest in voluntary reform, may exacerbate regional inequities, and close the window of opportunity for many years . . It is important to recognise the significant amount of Crown investment that is proposed. We need to ensure the reforms are commensurate with the investment, value for money can be demonstrated, and the impacts are felt across the country . Without consistent and widespread service delive ry reform, it is likely that any infrastructure deficits will only be resolved temporarily , and entrenched structural and funding issues will remain in many places. . My proposal involves transformational structural reform and the creation of multi regional, asset owning water service providers. This would realise a number of economic and other benefits associated with large scale providers, address many of the systemic issues and infrastructure deficits facing the three waters system, and help us to deliver our reform objectives . Benefits include : . increased financial capacity and capability, with stronger, more flexible and resilient balance sheets, greater access to capital, and a more reliable investment pipeline; . opportunities to take a strategic and coordinated approach, to consider infrastructure needs at a larger scale and in the context of wider catchment outcomes ; . building technical capabilities, with access to a larger, more specialist workforce , and the ability to innovate and make use of new technology ; . enabling financial efficiencies and lower operating costs, by consolidating administration and overhead costs, and improving organisational capabilities; . enabling more consistent water charges, with the ability to harmonise tariffs across much larger areas . . Creating large scale providers with strong balance sheets should contribute positively to the supply of housing by enabl ing water infrastructure to be provided to new developments, which has been a big constraint for debt limited councils in high growth areas . The existing urban growth partnerships , and spatial planning, also provide an opportunity for integrating and coordinating large, multi regional water providers with priority development areas and other key projects . . From a regulatory perspective, this approach would be beneficial in terms of operating and funding Taumata Arowai, the new Water Services Regulator. It would significantly reduce the number of regulated parties, while increasing the capacity and expertise within those entities. This would mean Taumata Arowai would work with four or five large scale , dedicated water entities, instead of councils (some of which may need support to comply with the new drinking water regulatory system) . It also makes it feasible to cover a sizeable portion of the organisations costs through levying the new, wellresourced water entities . Page of Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government UNCLASSIFIED . The b enefits should not be overstated in the short term . While s ome benefits , such as stronger balance sheets, will be realisable immediately , others will take time . This is illustrated in Appendix B. We will need to support sustainable change, good long term investm ent decision making, and a supported transition for councils and consumers . . I have considered alternative options to structural reform , but these options have disadvantage s, do not deliver our reform objectives, or fail to address key challenges. For example, shared services models that do not involve asset ownership have a number of shortcomings, including the inability to access scale or scope efficiencies, and split accountabilities. The recent example of Wellington Water illustrates the need for new w ater entities to make their own funding and investment decisions, rather than relying on individual council owners for investment. The new service delivery model would include the safeguards and design objective s we have considered previously . I am p ropo sing the creation of a small number of multi regional water service providers. ()(f)(iv) . There will be further discussions with Ministers and local government about the exact number of new entities, and their boundaries . I am proposing that final decisions on these matters would be based on the following factors : . scale benefits including at least one very large urban centre within each entity, to en sure the full benefits of scale are achieved through a larger network and population base ; . communities of interest; . relationship s with other jurisdictional boundaries, including catchments . . Earlier in the Three Waters Review, we agreed that, if a new model for water service delivery is created , this must include certain high level design objectives: . financial sustainability, affordability, and resilience ; . effective, efficient, and reliable services ; . enable an effective, efficient regulatory system ; and . minimise the negative impact of reform, where possible . . We have also expressed a clear and consistent message that public ownership of water infrastructure must continue, and there must be protections against privatisation. This has always been, and will continue to be, a bottom line. There has a lso been an ongoing interest in mechanisms that provide for local community input and local service delivery , opportunities for iwiMori participation, and expectations around how new multi regional entities could better contribute to health and environme ntal outcomes . . If the approach in this paper is agreed, I am proposing that these design objectives and bottom lines would be an integral part of the policy development process, and would be reflected in legislation . Page of Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government UNCLASSIFIED . There are a number of options for pr otecting public ownership of water assets. This is already a feature of local government legislation, which prohibits the sale of water infrastructure and the divestment of ownership of water services . Similar protections would be carried into the legislation that creates new water entities. I would also expect officials to identify additional mechanisms for providing assurances about this important matter. This could be achieved through ownership arra ngements, andor forms of social outcome obligations (such as kiwishare, for example ). I am also seeking agreement to core components of the service delivery model . I am seeking in principle agreement to core components of the new water service delivery model, subject to detailed policy design work and discussions with local government. I am proposing that the new water entities would be: . statutory, asset owning entities, with commercial disciplines , and a competency based board; . owned by local authorities, as shareholders, but with sufficient legal separation to ensure there are no restrictions on the entities ability to borrow on similar lines to other utilities. . Establishing the new entities in statute is essential if we are going to create an effective, enduring ownership, governance, and service delivery model, and provide an appropriate regulatory framework (to protect the interests of consumers, for example) . I do not consider existi ng institutional arrangements , such as council controlled organisations , would be fit forpurpose in these circumstances. . Providing for local authorities to be shareholders in the new entities is also important. This would be structured in a way that main tains and protects community ownership, but enables assets to be transferred to the new public entities . The basis for shareholding will need careful consideration and financial analysis. It could be possible to apportion shares on the basis of the condi tion of the assets that are transferred, to reward previous investment and good asset maintenance. There could also be potential to provide for some form of annual return to shareholders councils . . If local authorities were to retain asset ownership, this would limit the new entities ability to borrow, as limits would be constrained by council debt limits or attitudes to debt. This could also result in sub optional investment decisions about assets that would benefit from a mu ltiregional (not district) solution. . Professional governance arrangements are essential to create some of the capability improvements that are required. This would separate the ownership and governance roles, and bring in specialist expertise. Further advice and decisions will follow in ()(f)(iv) . A number of highly complex matters would need to be explored further during policy development and design work for the new service delivery model. These include: . the nature of local government shareh olding arrangements; . the potential for the Crown to be a sharehold er (for example, in recognition of stimulus funding) , and for other investors to be party to financing (but not ownershipequity) arrangements ; Page of Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government I am proposing to report back with initial advice on these matters by , alongside progress with r eform discussions with local government, followed by ()(f)(iv)

Te Tari Taiwhenua Department of Internal Affairs Strengthening our Approach to Volunteering The volunteering sector makes a significant contribution to Aotearoa . Aotearoa is a volunteering nation almost half of the population volunteer with organisations or directly in their communities. . The economic value of volunteering is estimated at billion per year , but volunteering goes beyond financial impacts it connects c ommunities and strengthens peoples sense of belonging to an inclusive society where people can make a difference. The volunteering sector is experiencing workforce and funding issues . Volunteering numbers are reportedly falling, and the sector has concer ns about volunteer wellbeing and funding sustainability and access. For example , in a survey , difficulty recruiting new volunteers was reported as the biggest challenge for the sector , with almost per cent reporting they needed more volunteers. In another survey, only per cent of respondents reported having funding for more than one year. These issues have been exacerbated by COVID and related work force dynamics . There are opportunities for Gover nment to help address these issues . Govern ment has a role to play in helping to address these issu es as volunteering shoulder s civic responsibilities that sup port government services , which reduces the fiscal burden on tax payers. . I am considering how I can support existing sector initiatives and have developed a draft work programme that can be delivered within existing resources , including : . These actions will only go so far. These include : ()(f)(iv) ()(f)(iv). champion ing National Volunteer Week ( June ): ()(f)(iv) Proactively released by the Minister for the Community and Voluntary Sector . supporting the development of best practice guidance for volunteer management, pending confirmation that this is a priority for volunteering organisations; . reviewing the funding formula for the existing Support for Volunteering Fund to ensure that funding recognises the diversity of the volunteering sector; and . establish ing a cross agency steering group t o provide a strategic, joined up and practical approach to tackling volunteering problems . . targeting support to Mori, Pacific, ethnic and youth volunteers and communities, as government funding does not always meet the needs of these groups; . reimbursing outofpocket expenses for volunteers, to remove financial barriers and increase recognition of volunteering; State of Volunteering in New Zealand Report , Volunteering New Zealand. UNCLASSIFIED Investing in water infrastructure t o accelerate refor m and support economic recovery post COVID Supplementary informati on context and options analysis Overview o f proposed approach . The proposal involves the development and implementation of a three year programme for reforming three waters service delivery arrangements, which would be delivered in parallel with a ()(f)(iv) economic stimulus package of Crown invest ment in water infrastructure. . The proposed approach is designed to achieve dual goals: support ing economic recovery post COVID , and address ing persistent systemic issues facing three waters infrastructure and services. This would be done through a com bination of : . stimulating investment, to assist economic recovery through job creation, and maintain investment in water infrastructure renewals and maintenance; and . fundamentally reforming the water service delivery sector, into a small number of multi regional providers, to realise significant economic, environmental, and other benefits over the medium to long term. . Regarding the service delivery reform s, the proposed approach involves: . the creation of a small number of multi regional, asset owning water providers, which would be statutory entities; . protecting public ownership within the new service delivery models , and developing ownership arrangements that involve local government. . This supplementary information paper provides the context for these prop osals, and explains the alternative options that have been considered. It is informed by the work and stakeholder engagement undertaken to in the Three Waters Review , and previous decisions taken by Cabinet . . If the overall approach is agreed to, a large number of related matters would need to be explored further during policy development and design work . These matters would be the subject of further advice and report backs, following detailed options identification and analysis, and stakeholder en gagement. They are not considered in this document. Background . Rationale Existing contact tracing practices are resource intensive, slow, and often subject to recall bias (Kretzschmar, Rozhnova , van Boven, ). There are many areas digital solutions are required to improve existing contact tracing efforts. First, contact t racing for a single individual can take a team of contact tracers several days. These days to identify and infor m close contacts to selfisolate is a major concern for the COVID response as potentially infected people (both with and without symp toms) could be unknowingly infecting others. Second, there is currently no systematic way of prioritising close contacts outside of classifying close contacts by household and non household contacts (Verrall, ). Third, current systems are prone to reca ll bias as cases fail to recall every personal interaction during the period when they are likely to have been infectiou s (which may have been for up to two days before they developed clearly recognised symptoms (Ferretti et al., )). Fourth, there is a high degree of incomplete and out of contact information, even with possible National Health Index (NHI) integrati on in New Zealand (Verrall, ). In response, many software based digital contact tracing solutions are being developed to improve and supplement existing systems (Ferretti et al., ). However, software based solutions present major technological, p ublic uptake, and equity challenges. To support its bold elimination strategy (Baker, Kvalsvig, Verrall, Telfar Barnard, Wilson, ) , the New Zealand Government through the DIA is currently supporting the development of a Bluetooth enabled hardware solution, a CovidCard , for mass distribution (Wiltshire, ). Digital contact tracing using Bluetooth technology enables the identificat ion of close contacts (known or unknown) of cases and the automation of some contact tracing procedures (Ferretti et al., ). The CovidCard is a Bluetooth enabled card that automatically logs interactions with other cards based on hardwired proximity pa rameters (a close contact algorithm). Refined exposure parameters can be calculated during the post processing stage to enable flexibility in close contact definitions. Upon testing positive for COVID , the cases card data would be processed to yield al l close contacts within a predetermined amount of time prior to the onset of symptoms. These close contacts would be con tacted initially through an automated message to inform them to self isolate, drastically reducing the lag time in the current system. T hen, close contacts would be contacted via traditional public health contact tracing procedures using the contact number s of CovidCard owners stored in a secure, national level central registry. The CovidCard information could be used to create a risk prof ile based on the proximity information Proactively Released by the Department of Internal Affairs

Proactively released by the Minister for Digitising Government .Introduction Purpose The Department of Internal Affairs (the Department) seeks your views on the proposals outlined in this discussion paper for the development of regulations required to enable the establishment of the Digital Identity Services Trust Framework. Overview In a world where digital services are increasingly prevalent, it is important people can prove who they are online in a trusted, safe and consistent way. Digital identity services give people the ability to securely share information about themselves (for example , a persons name, age, of birth, qualifications, employment history or medical records) to access both online and face toface services . New Zealands digital identity environment currently lacks consistent standards. This makes it difficult to provide genuine and secure services people feel they can trust. To provide New Zealanders with more confidence in using online identity services, Parliament has passed the Digital Identity Services Trust Framework Act (the Act). The Act come s into force on July and enables the introduction of a new regulatory Trust Framework , which will establish rules and regulations for the provision of secure digital identity services. The Act provides for a Trust Framework Board (TF Board) and a Tru st Framework Authority (TF Authority) to administer the legislation. The Act also provides for a Mori Advisory Group to provide advice to the TF Board on issues that raise matters of tikanga M ori, and to jointl y establish with the TF Board an engagement p olicy covering how the two groups will work together and consult with iwi and hap when necessary . The Trust Framework will give people more control over their own data, including what they choose to share about themselves and who they share it with. We anticipate this will increase consumer confidence in digital identity services, as well as encourage innovation in the technol ogy industry more broadly. The rules will establish the technical service requirements that providers will need to meet when designing and delivering accredited services. The rules have already been the subject of early consultation with key stakeholders a nd will be the subject of a further final round of consultation , likely in the first quarter of . They cover identification management ; privacy and confidentiality ; security and risk ; information and data management ; and information sharing and facilit ating arrangements. The regulations will complement the rules by establishing broader legal and administrative process requirements that either need to be met by regulated parties or clarify how the TF Board and the TF Authority will manage aspects of the regulatory system. We propose establishing a Digital Identity Trust Framework to address regulatory gaps and accelerate the development of trusted and people centred digital identity services . A trust framework is a set of best practice standards based rules that ensure minimum requirements are met for security, privacy, identification management and interoperabil ity through accreditation and governance. Implementing a trust framework would support increased public trust (and uptake) of online services from both public and private sector providers and enable the wider use of trusted government information sources. . We propose a two phased approach to developing and implementing the Trust Framework, reflecting that there will likely be a sustained increase in demand for trusted digital identity services. As a first step, officials will develop an interim Trust Framew ork, which means that standards and rules can be developed and tested with providers in . Subject to Cabinet agreement, the development of a Bill will also occur, which will establish the Trust Framework and its core functions in legislation by . W e seek . million for and . million in to undertake this first phase. . Subject to Cabinets approval of this paper, we propose coming back to Cabinet with two further papers on digital identity: a detailed policy Cabinet paper to fo rm the basis for drafting instructions for a Trust Framework Bill, provided by the end of and led by the Minister of Government Digital Services; and a Cabinet paper focused on operational options for digital identity (including funding) for the imple mentation of the Trust Framework, and RealMe as a government owned and operated identity service. This paper would be provided early in and jointly led by the Minister for Government Digital Services and the Minister of Internal Affairs. The Cabinet p aper on operational response options will include options on the future of the RealMe services . Currently the main way people can assert their identity online is through the government provided RealMe service. RealMe is a centralised model of digital identi ty, which has been Crown funded since its inception. The number of people with a RealMe verified identity has been significantly boosted by initiatives such as Passport co apply and Studylink. Currently there are over , verified identities. . Since Re alMe was introduced, the digital identity environment has changed significantly. Globally and in New Zealand there has been an emergence of digital identity service providers, which are developing decentralised approaches that allow the customercitizen to have greater control of their information. These new approaches seek to realise the economic benefits of digital identity while minimising data transfer and enhancing security and privacy. . In this paper, we define digital identity as the user consented, digitally enabled sharing of personal and organisational information. This sharing of information allows people to assert their personal attributes , such as their income, qualifications, of birth, or proof of eligibility, online, in order to access services and entitlements. Focus area one: Embedding our regulatory foundations This focus area is all about ensuring each system has in place agreed foundational systems and processes such as a regulatory charter which demonstrates a clear and shared understanding of the regulatory system, and an assurance plan setting out how we will know if the system is effective. This starts the process of defining what RSG means by regulatory excellence. Strategic initiatives To be a system regulator, there needs to be a shared understanding of the system who is in it, what is their role, what are the risks and opportunities, etc. System groups have differing levels of information about this some systems are more straightforward to describe than others however, describing a system is just the beginning getting agreement to the scope and shared outcomes of a system by key participants is the real goal as that will enable the system participants to share information, collaborate on initiatives and share in the achievement of system outcomes. Likewise, the development of system group assurance plans is dependent on identifying what the most important performance measures are for the system and being able to answer the question, How will we know if our system groups are effective The initiative above, and the development of system groupspecific operating models, supports greater transparency of regulatory systems. Clearly articulated operating models also ensure that system groups have considered what capabilities (people, processes and systems) they need to achieve their objectives, who their stakeholders are, and what channels they will use to deliver their regulatory functions. Introduction Role of the Ministry of Health Since July , the Ministry has been responsible for developing and implementing the integrated problem gambling strategy focused on public health that is described in section of the Gambling Act . The Act states that the strategy must include: measures to promote public health by preventing and minimising the harm from gambling (see below for a definition of harm) services to treat and assist problem gamblers and their families and whnau independent scientific research associated with gambling, including (for example) longitudinal research on the social and economic impacts of gambling, particularly the impacts of gambling on different cultural groups evaluation. The Act defines a problem gambler as a person whose gambling causes harm or may cause harm. Its further states that harm : a) means harm or distress of any kind arising from, or caused or exacerbated by, a person s gambling; and b) includ es personal, social, or economic harm suffered i) by the person; or ii) by the person s spouse, civil union partner, de facto partner, family, whnau, or wider community; or iii) in the workplace; or iv) by society at large. The Ministry receives funding through Vote Health to develop and implement the strategy. The Crown then recovers the cost of this appropriation through a problem gambling levy paid by the main gambling operators. Role of the Department of Internal Affairs The Department of Internal Affairs (DIA) is the main gambling regulator and policy advisor to the Government on gambling regulatory issues. DIA administers the Act and its regulations, issues licences for gambling activities, ensures compliance with the legislation, works with the gambling sector to encourage best practice and publishes statistical and other information concerning gambling. It is also responsible for limiting the opportunities for crime and dishonesty associated with gambling and ensuring gambling proceeds benefit the community. DIAs role includes key regulatory aspects of gamblingharm prevention and minimisation. Local Government Portfolio Weekly Report Week ending ( August ) Recipient HON SIMEON BROWN MINISTER OF LOCAL GOVERNMENT M ichael Lovett Deputy Chief Executive, Local Government Ministers comments: Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs
Local Government Portfolio Weekly Report Week ending ( August ) Recipient HON SIMEON BROWN MINISTER OF LOCAL GOVERNMENT Hamiora Bowkett Executive Director , Water Services Policy Ministers comments: Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs
Local authorities have a partial income tax exemption. They are exempt from tax on income, e xcept for certain amounts of income earned from council controlled organisations (CCOs) such as interest or management fees . This policy setting prevents councils from profit shifting, i.e. a taxable CCO making tax deductible payments to a tax exempt council to reduce the CCOs tax liabilities. Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs The Department of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua INCONFIDENCE Page of a public purpose based income tax exemption, as this undermines the fairness and integrity of the tax system. . If a tax exempt water organisation has a taxable shareholder (e.g. a consumer trust that is not a registered charity ), and the organisation is making a taxable profit, there will be a strong incentive for income to be retained in the water organisation. This would result in a deferral benefit for the consumer trust because the water organisation can reinvest and accumulate income tax free. A later dividend will be taxable to the consumer trust , but it does not claw back the deferral benefit of the tax exemp tion. . There are no tax issues if the water organisation earns income and distributes that income to a taxable consumer trust within the same tax year . The distributions will be either subject to the trustee tax rate if retained in the consumer trust or subject to tax at the consumers personal tax rate s if distributed by the trust to consumers. There are no tax issues with either outcome . . Any income that is retained in the water organisation beyond the year it is earned, and then subsequently distributed to a taxable consumer trust , will result in a deferral benefit to the trust or consumers. It is not always feasible to distribute all income in the year it is earned . . To ensure that private individuals cannot obtain a deferral benefit from a water organisations income tax exemption , we recommend that income taxexempt status should be granted to water organisations that meet the minimum requirements, provided all of the shareholders are also income taxexempt . Tax status of water organisations that have an exemption from minimum requirements . Councils can apply for exemptions from three of the minimum requirements that apply to water organisations . The exemption can apply to the requirement that : . only councils or consumer trusts can be shareholders of a water organisation ; . the activities of water organisations are limited to the provision of water services, and directly related activities; and . water organisations must be companies . . The implications of each minimum requirement exemption on a water organisations tax status are discussed below. Exemption from the shareholder requirement . This exemption will allow water organisations to have shareholders other than councils and consumer trusts . As per the instruction from the Minister of Local Government the exemption will be limited to co operative companies wishing to have consumer shareholders. . These co operative companies serve a similar function to energy trusts in that they allow an amount of income earned by the company to be distributed back to the consumers, normally via a discount on services. This has the effect of using water organisation income to provide a private benefit to individuals. Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs The Department of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua INCONFIDENCE Page of . As such, we recommend that water organisations that are granted an exemption from the shareholder requirement should not be granted income taxexempt status. This is consistent with the tax settings for energy trusts, which are also subject to tax. Exemption from the limitation on activities requirement . This exemption will allow water organisation s to carry out activities other than the provision of water services and directly related activities. As discussed above , water services provide a public good in a monopoly market and fall within the policy intent of a tax exemption . . A water organisation that also undertak es other activities, such as general contracting or electricity network provision, would be competing with the taxable private sector entities . Allowing a tax exemption in these circumstances would provide the water organisation with an unfair advantage with respect to its non water activities. . We recommend that water organisation s that are granted an exemption from the limitation on activities requirement should not be granted income taxexempt status. Exemption from the company structure requirement . This exemption will allow water organisations to adopt a structure or form other than a company. There is nothing intrinsic about a structure other than a company which would suggest that it should or shouldnt be taxexempt . . However, consideration needs to be given to whether these different structures could allow distributions to be made to taxable entities. For example, a council may apply to set up a water organisation that uses a trust structure instead of a company. Under the trust deed it would be possible for individuals to be named as beneficiaries and to obtain a private benefit via a distribution. . Providing an income tax exemption for a water organisation that is structured as a trust would pose a significant risk to the tax base. Unlike companies, income can easily be extracted tax free as capital distributions from a tax exempt trust, regardless of who the beneficiaries of the trust are. The beneficiaries of a taxexempt water organisation trust would not be subject to tax on any capital distributions. . We recommend that water organisations that are not companies should be granted income taxexempt status provided the water organisation is restricted from making distributions to taxable persons . Financial implications . Agreeing to the recommendations in this briefing will not have any fiscal implications because it will only apply the tax exempt status to water organisations where the shareholders or beneficiaries of the organisation are already tax exempt. Consultation . The Treasury has been consulted on this briefing and agrees with the recommendations. Next steps . A copy of this briefing will be provided to the Minister of Finance for her information. Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs The Department of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua INCONFIDENCE Page of . The Department of Internal Affairs will consult with Inland Revenue to draft the necessary instructions for Bill to reflect the decisions made by Ministers. . Subject to your decisions on this briefing the necessary legislati ve provisions will be included in the Local Government (Water Services) Bill (Bill ) , planned for introduction in December . Recommendations . We recommend that you: a) agree that income taxexempt status should be granted to water organisations that meet the minimum requirements, provided all of the shareholders are also income taxexempt ; YesNo YesNo b) agree that water organisations that are granted an exemption from the shareholder requirement should not be granted income tax exempt status; YesNo YesNo c) agree that water organisations that are granted an exemption from the limitation on activities requirement should not be granted income tax exempt status; YesNo YesNo d) agree that water organisations that are not companies should be granted income taxexempt status provided the water organisation is restricted from making distributions to taxable persons ;

The Irish Citizens Assemblys ruling on the th Amendment to the Constitution (decriminalization of abortion) was thought to be overly liberal, but was confirmed when the public voted in favour during the referendum. Because the Assembly accurately captured pu blic opinion almost a year before the issue went to popular vote, the method is a valuable way for politicians to gauge p ublic opinion and to proper action before a decision is made. The money raised by Class operators goes towards worthy commun ity causes. The ability to fundraise will be more difficult once the exemption expires, and negatively impact an important revenue stream at a time when faced with rising operational costs . Class gambling is considered low risk . From a gambling harm pers pective, large scale lotteries present a low risk in terms of potential harm . This is because th is form of gambling is noncontinuous i.e. you cannot continue to play because there is a delay between purchasing a ticket and waiting for the result , and people cannot immediately reinvest any winnings. . The Department of Internal Affairs (the Department) regulates Class lotteries and has been monitoring activity since the temporary exemption came in to effect . There has been no noticeable increase in applications during this time . The exemption has resulted in less work for the regulator , as they have not had to enforce the old rules or educate applicants that they cannot take online or remote sales. This frees the regulator up to concentrate on the more harmful forms of gambling i.e. Class and casino gambling . . The regulator would continue to monitor activity in this class if the exemption became permanent . Licence holders would still have to apply for a licence for each individual lottery they wish to conduct , and comply with the Act s Lottery Game Rules , the rules by which lotteries and sweepstakes follow . . If appropriate , the regulator can place conditions on a Class licence if it has any concerns. As evidenced recently, the regulator has the power to deal with bad actors. There are limited options available to make the exemption permanent . The barrier for making this exemption permanent has been finding an appropriate vehicle to make the legislative change. The existing options are: . adopt the Gambling (Enabling Remote Interactive Gambling for Class Operators) Amendment Members Bill , which is sponsored by Hon Barbara Edmonds and not yet been drawn from the ballot , or . seek Cabinet approval prior to the expiry to make the exemption permanent when a suitable legislative vehicle becomes available i.e. Statutes Amendment Bill, online gambling , or the Regulatory Systems Amendment Bill . . Adopting the Members Bill is the best option in terms of legislative surety . However , it is unlikely it would be passed before the end of October unless you sought approval for it to be passed under urgency. Passing it under urgency would mean it is the most expedient option as well. . While it doesnt give immediate legislative surety, s eeking Cabinet approval under Option would enable us to act quickly when a legislative vehicle becomes available . Signall ing the Governments intention to change the policy when a suitable legislative vehicle becomes available will be helpful for both the regulator and Class operators . It would also help any further attempts to have the exemption included in the next Statutes Amendment Bill. Without a Cabinet decision, we consider it likely the exemption would be rejected again on the same grounds, furthe r delaying resolution of the issue.

Social bots automatically produce, share, and like content on media platforms. Fake profiles are operated manually, and in some cases by paid workers. Recommendation systems on online platforms refer to the ordering or visibility of content to users. Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua Department of Internal Affairs INCONFIDENCE Page of are more likely to be engaged with and therefore this type of content is given more visibility on platforms. Overseas Governments are considering more comprehensive regulatory frameworks for online content, in response to the risk this content poses . Against this backdrop of serious societal harm arising from online media content and greater insight into the online environment propensity to spread harmful media content, there have been several recent regulatory proposals for comprehensive frameworks for online content across Europe. Appendix B outlines and compares several international policy initiatives to regulate online content, which place greater accountability on online platforms. While these overseas policy initiatives offer learning opportunities, the success of these regulatory frameworks remains to be seen . Overseas online content policy initiatives provide useful models for considering greater regulatory and nonregulatory responses to the increase risk of harm online media content poses to New Zealanders . . Despite recent regulatory initiatives, comprehensive regulation of online content is still an unprecedented feat, and the effectiveness and unintended consequences of these overseas regulatory frameworks are still unknown. Regulating online content is complex: the borderless nature of the online environment poses compliance challenges; the scale of online content makes it administratively challenging to apply rules consistently and quickly; and online contentsharing platforms resemble public spheres they are the primary point of access to information, political discussion and political organisation for many people as a result there are intricate challenges to prohibiting certain types of content whilst preserving freedom of expression. . However, there is opportunity to manage these complexities through aligning any potential regulatory framework for online content with that of other jurisdictions, thereby increasing the efficiency and effectiveness of regulation. For example, aligning online content regulations with other jurisdictions existing regulations may increase compliance as regulated entities already have policies in place to adhere to similar regulatory requirements. . However, there is a tradeoff between the benefits of a more efficient regime through regulatory alignment and being able to tailor a response to New Zealand circumstances. For example, New Zealand values and norms differ to those held in other countries and as a result, aligning our regulatory framework for online content may mean compromises regarding normative decisions over what speech is permissible. Other jurisdictions approaches to regulating online content will be considered in the media content regulatory review . We will consider international regulatory frameworks for online content in our advice on the proposed media content regulatory review. As international proposals for Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua Department of Internal Affairs INCONFIDENCE Page of comprehensive regulatory frameworks progress, we will assess the desirability in copying and aligning our recommendations with these approaches. Recommendations . We recommend that you: a) Note that you requested information from officials on recent international proposal to regulate online content; b) note that other jurisdictions regulatory frameworks for online content offer opportunities for lessons in best practice and alignment; c) note that regulating online platforms is complex and there are intricate challenges to making online platforms accountable for the content they host while still protecting the freedom of expression of users; and d) note that international approaches to comprehensively regulating online content will be considered as part of the media content regulatory review.

There are a range of offences under the L GA (and the Act) to regulate activity in relation to water services and infrastructure (including a breach of a bylaw). Water services bylaws currently make up approximately percent of all bylaws. . The compliance, monitoring, and enforcement of those offences is currently undertaken by local authority officers, who have the necessary powers delegated to them through the LGA. These powers to operate bylaws can be delegated to water organisations under existing legislation. . However, i mportant context for any legislative provisions is the general principle that exercise of coercive powers requires democratic accountability. This implies limits for the use of some council powers by those water organisations which may be several steps rem oved from their elected owners. . There are a range of intended accountability mechanisms in the Local Water Done Well system which will supplement the ownership control of councils: . Councils contracting and commissioning arrangements ; . Requirements for competency based governance, including expertise in network infrastructure industries (particularly water), public health and environment, and perspectives of mana whenua, consumers and communities ; . Regulators Commerce Commission (economic); Taumata Arowai (water quality, national oversight of wastewater and stormwater systems) and regional councils (environmental) ; . Consumer contracts and protection mechanisms (MBIEs policy responsibility) ; . Transparency mechanisms including the Local Government Official Information and Meetings Act ; and . Office of the Auditor General oversight. . Further detailed design work will be undertaken during the legislation development stage to ensure the intent to allow councils to devolve powers to water organisations under the LGA will work effectively to achieve the Local Water Done Well objectives . This design work will also confirm other details regarding functioning water organisations , including regulatory functions and powers for joint council owners , and ensuring that water organisations will be required to uphold Treaty settlements where councils have existing obligations . .
