Command cannot normally be exercised outside an agency. Common Operating PictureA continuously overview compiled from local, regional and national data shared between integrated communication systems. Common Operating PlatformThe technological infrastructure or system used to support the creation, management, and dissemination of the common operating picture across different stakeholders involved in the response. Proactively Released by the Department of Internal Affairs APPENDIX : SERVERSIDE MACHINE LEARNING EVALUATION The serverside priorisation used probabilities from a Random Forest model to rank potential close contacts over casual contacts. During development different machine learning models were tested, and the Random Forest model produced the highest area under the Receiver Operating Characteristics (ROC) curve (AUC). The AUC is the probability that a randomly chosen true close contact will rank higher than a randomly chosen noncontact. AUC values are between . (random chance) and (perfect classification). A higher AUC value indicates that the model is more effective at prioritising close contacts over casual ones.

. Local authorities (councils) use ward systems to ensure that different communities of
. Many local authorities have been able to set up single and joint council owned CCOs for a variety of purposes under the current arrangements in the Act . (Appendix A provides a stocktake of current CCOs , other than Watercare, Wellington Water and Citycare , to demonstrate the diversity of existing CCOs .) However, w e understand the establishment of a joint CCO can be difficult and time consuming under the current arrangements. We have summarised the key issues and challenges below. . The proposed approach has been designed to address these issues. In developing our advice, we facilitated a workshop with the TAG to further explore the issues and options, and test the Departments understanding and approach . We also engaged with a small number of officials from councils which have attempted to set up a joint water services CCO in the past. Views from the TAG and council officials have informed the proposed approach . Issues that need to be addressed to help streamline the process for establishing water services CCOs Consultation processes can be time and resource intensive . To set up a CCO, councils must consult with their communities in accordance with the consultation principles set out in section of the Act. . Water services delivery is a significant activity. Under section of the Act, any decision to significantly alter the intended service level for any significant activity or to transfer the ownership or control of a strategic asset to or from the council cannot be made unless it is provided for in the councils long term plan (LTP). Therefore, councils would need to include the establishment of a water services CCO in their LTPs (via an LTP amendment , if out of cycle) and use the special consultative p rocedure when adopting the LTP . . We have heard that, for councils considering a joint CCO, it is likely to be more efficient and cost effective for them to undertake joint consultation potentially through a joint committee. T here do not appear to be any legislative barriers to this. Schedule , clause allows councils to delegate powers and responsibilities (with several exceptions named) to joint committees. Consultation powers are not named as an exception. . Instead, s ome of the council officials we engaged with indicated that it is the time and resources required to undertake the consultation process that presents the barrier . Some councils may consider they need to undertake multiple rounds of consultation before making the final decision to establish a water services CCO. This would likely ()(f)(iv) Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs The Department of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua IN CONFIDENCE Page of involve an early consultation round on alternative options, and then another consultation round on the necessary LTP amendment associated with the final decision. . This process could take several years , particularly if consultation involves multiple councils , and multiple rounds of consultation . Therefore, the current process is not optimal for those who are looking to swiftly set up a water services CCO to improve their water services provision. . The TAG has indicated that, while councils may be able to undertake joint consultation under the current requirements, the process would be slow and inefficient, especially if the intention is for swift establishment. Bill presents an opportunity to make much more explicit the ability of councils to undertake joint consultation and to use a joint committee for this purpose. Decision making processes can be onerous , and councils are concerned about the risks of legal challenge . Councils must, when making decisions, seek to identify all reasonably practicable options for the achievement of the objective of a decision . . They are also required by section A to review the cost effectiveness of current arrangements for meeting the needs of communities within their district for good quality local infrastructure, local public services, and performance of regulatory functions, in conjunction with consideration of any significant change to relevant service levels. This review must include a consideration of at least six listed options for the governance, funding, and delivery of infrastructure, services, and regulatory functions , including, but not limited to using CCOs , whether singly or jointly with other councils . . A council is also required to ensure prudent stewardship and the efficient and effective use of its resources in the interests of its district . Elected members swear an oath that reflects their responsibilities to their own district. . Some councils and TAG members noted that the consideration of all reasonably practicable options in relation to the establishment of a water services CCO can be unnecessarily onerous , as well as resource and time intensive. This could require analysis and consultation on a large number of options beyond a sole or joint CCO. . Similarly, the required review under section A also involves extensive analysis of a large number of options, which can be a significant undertaking. . Councils also indicated that a key barrier and disincentive to setting up a CCO is the possibility of judicial review. This mainly relates to the interpretation of what factors can be taken into consideration in a councils decision making including that they may not have fully considered all of the reasonably practicable options . . The establishment of a joint water services CCO will likely require consideration of the collective benefits and interests of the communities in the proposed CCO area. This is not currently explicitly allowed for in the Act . Doing so may be seen as a contravention to a councils obligation to perform its role in the interests of its own district . The risk that this may result in judicial review was emphasised by several council officials and confirmed in the workshop with the TAG. Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs The Department of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua IN CONFIDENCE Page of . A councils decision to set up a joint CCO can be contingent on the other councils decisions to go ahead with it. The potential for other councils to reject the proposal creates uncertainty and risk. It may also lead to further rounds of consultation (for example , if the timing of various council LTP decisions mean that some decisions to establish the joint CCO may need to be undone if other councils decide not to go ahead ). We recommend including bespoke arrangement s for establishing a water services CCO in the legislation . We recommend inserting into the Act a bespoke set of provisions for councils to use when considering establishing a water services CCO . Councils could choose to use the arrangements as an alternative to the current process es they are required to follow in the Act . These bespoke arrangements would achieve the objective of providing councils with a streamlined approach to consulting and deciding on whether to form a single or joint lyowned water services CCO . . The proposed arrangements, detailed further below , would include clarifying that councils can set up a joint committee , which could consult jointly and make recommendations to the participating councils. There would be clarity about minimum consultation requirements, modified information requirements , and modified considerations in the decision making process. . Providing for bespoke arrangement s in the legislation is the preferred approach . It would streamline the process for establishing a water services CCO, reduce time and resources put into consultation and decision making, and provide certainty to councils in terms of what they are able to factor in to their decision making . It would do this without u ndermin ing the importance of community consultation. This approach would also help to de risk this process and reduce the risk of legal challenge by providing a clear set of provisions in the legislation designed for this purpose. . Our engagement with the TAG and targeted engagement with several council officials supported this being the preferred option and potentially the only one that would lead to achieving the policy objective. . As these proposed bespoke arrangements would be optional for councils to use , the risk of any perception of reduced individual council autonomy would be limited . There could still be a perception of less focus on the interests of individual districts ; however, this will be mitigated through giving councils discretion as to how they weigh up various considerations in their decision making. . As part of our policy development, w e also considered other options that might address the identified challenges with the status quo. This included possible amendments to specific sections of the Act to make it explicit that councils could, for the purposes of considering forming a joint water services CCO, consult jointly and make a recommendation to the participating councils . However, we consider these options would not fully address the issues and challenges identified, and would also likely be more difficult to draft in the legislation. Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs The Department of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua IN CONFIDENCE Page of Key components of proposed approach Establishment of joint committee . Under Schedule , councils can set up joint committees with other councils , and delegate any of their responsibilities, duties or powers to the committee except for a number of specific powers outlined in the Act (such as the power to adopt a long term plan). As noted earlier, some council officials we engaged with thought that it is not entirely clear that councils can consult jointly , or use a joint committee for this purpose, and it would be beneficial if the legislation were clearer. . We are proposing to include a provision that clarif ies that councils who are wanting to form a joint water services CCO can set up a joint committee under the relevant provisions in Schedule . The joint committees scope would include being able to recommend a proposal to the councils , undertake consultation on the proposal (if approved by all councils ) in a joint manner, and make final recommendations to the participating councils. . The TAG members have suggested clarifying that councils would effectively have two decision points: () approving the preferred option proposed by the joint committee for consultation; and () approving the final proposal to be implemented (following consu ltation). Consultation process . We are proposing that if councils are thinking of establishing a water services CCO, they only need to undertake one round of consultation on the proposal. This consultation could be carried out by a joint committee, by other collective arrangements the councils choose, or individually. . We also propose that councils would not need to consult on subsequent LTP amendment s, provided they were satisfied they understood the views of their communities from the earlier consultation process. . If a joint committee is established for this purpose, it would have flexibility around how it wants to run its public hearings and manage the consultation process, including whether to use the special consultative procedure, providing it adheres to the consultation principles se t out in section () and the requirement to have processes in place for consulting with Mori in section () . . We propose the bespoke arrangements should be flexible enough to ensure that , if changes need to be made to the proposed model after consultation , this would not generally require another round of consultation unless the changes are extensive or have significant implications. Information requirements for consultation . Under section s and A , councils must undertake and provide for consultation information on an analysis of all reasonably practicable options for the achievement of the objective of a decision. This requirement places a large burden on them. . We are proposing that in this situation, councils, or the joint committee, are only required to analyse, provide information on, and consult on two options one being the current arrangements for delivery of water services (the status quo), and the other Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs The Department of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua IN CONFIDENCE Page of being the preferred option (relating to a water services CCO ). The proposal for consultation would have to provide a clear rationale for the preferred option . . This would not preclude councils or the joint committee from being able to consult on more than the two options . However, it minimises the range of options they would be required to analyse and present to their communities and clarifies this in the legislation . . We also propose that the proposal put out for consultation should have to include in sufficient detail the impacts (including financial) of each option on each of the districts included with the proposed CCO, as well as the collective impacts on the community as a whole within the total CCO area. This requirement would ensure that communities would have a good understanding of the impacts on their districts and would be able to genuinely engage in the proposal. This is particularly important because we are proposing that subsequent LTP amendments would not need to be consulted on. . Finally, w e propose that, if councils are considering establishing a single or joint water services CCO, they are not required to undertake a review under section A either as part of this decision, or in the time period afterwards (if a review would ordinarily be required in that period) . As previously noted, this review requires an extensive analysis of options , and is unnecessarily time consuming and resource intensive in these circumstances. Decision making considerations . As stated above, w e propose that a joint committee is able to make recommendation s to the participating councils about whether a water services CCO should be established . However, the final decision about joining the CCO rests with each council . This would protect local autonomy and accountability, and ensure that there is buy in from all councils involved. . We propose that in their decision making processes, both the joint committee (if used) and the councils are able to consider the collective impacts on the communities as a whole in the CCO area, as well as their usual considerations. It would be up to the joint committee and the councils as to how they weigh the various considerations. . We also propose that councils are able to factor into their decision making on the proposed CCO the considerations of the other participating authorities , and the views of people outside their own district (within the new CCO area) . . The above proposals help to address the concerns that have been raised by councils regarding judicial review of their decision making as they will be given authority by the new provisions to take these factors into consideration. Longterm plan ( LTP) amendments . We propose councils are still required to amend their LTPs to include their decision to establish or join a water services CCO and reflect the implications that will have . As above, we propose that the consultation requirements for these LTP amendment s be waived . Audit requirements would still apply. . The legislation would also explicitly enable council s to conditional ly approv e their LTP amendment s. This is so that, if another participating council subsequently decides against joining the CCO and that decision impacts on the other councils decision to Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs The Department of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua IN CONFIDENCE Page of join, that coun cil can pull out of the proposed arrangement without needing to make another LTP amendment. Possible risks associated with the proposed approach . Under this process, councils would only be able to establish a water services CCO that is currently allowed for under the Act, as the details about financially separate council owned organisations and any other models are intended to be included in Bill in mid . From our engagement with the TAG and several councils, we understand that those wishing to move early may prefer to be able to set up a financially independent council owned organisation. Therefore, it is unclear at this stage what the uptake of these bespoke arrangements might be . . However, if sufficient detail about the new model(s) is communicated following Cabinet decisions about Bill , some councils may feel they are able to start engaging with communities about establishing a water services CCO, and provide an indication about the new model they would like to move to in the future. Next steps . If you agree to the proposals amending the Act to provide bespoke arrangements for consulting and deciding on water services CCOs, we will include them in the Bill Cabinet paper. Proactively Released by the Department of Internal Affairs COMMERCIALINCONFIDENCE DTA Report A NR COVIDCARDTECHNOLOGYREVIEW Nathaniel de Lautour,Logan Small,AustinChamberlain, JohnHarris, Brent Martin, MattHopkins July ABSTRACT This report contains a DTA review of CovidCard, a digital contact tracing system proposed for COVID pandemic control in New Zealand. The system comprises a card with a Bluetooth Low Energy radio device that transmits pseudorandom numbers from a unique sequence, allowing other cards in range to detect and record its presence. In addition, there are multiple software service layers and a security architecture to enable the secure upload of contact data to a central server. We believe that CovidCard could provide benefit for contact tracing by reducing the time taken to identify close contacts, if there is sufficient user acceptance and the system proves reliable in practice. We also make some recommendations for modifications and additional testing, and finally highlight some potential security risks. COMMERCIALINCONFIDENCE Proactively Released by the Department of Internal Affairs COMMERCIALINCONFIDENCE DTA Report A Defence Technology Agency Private Bag Devonport Auckland New Zealand Crown Copyright COMMERCIALINCONFIDENCE Proactively Released by the Department of Internal Affairs COMMERCIALINCONFIDENCE EXECUTIVESUMMARY CovidCard is a digital contact tracing system designed to augment manual contact tracing for COVID pandemic control. The system comprises a card with a Bluetooth Low Energy radio device that transmits pseudorandom numbers from a unique sequence, allowing other cards in range to detect and record its presence. In addition, there are multiple software service layers and a security architecture to enable the secure upload of contact data to a central server. The server performs a process to match cards to serial numbers based on the pseudorandom number sequences emitted. This enables contact tracers to identify the owner of a card, and the identities of people the card has come into contact with. At the request of the Department of Internal Affairs (DIA), we have carried out a review of the technology underlying the CovidCard system based on documentation provided by the developer and prototype cards that were supplied for inspection and physical testing. The review was supplemented by a workshop at DTA that was attended by representatives of the CovidCard development team and DIA. In general, we were impressed with the quality of the effort put into the development of CovidCard, and in particular the attention paid to security and privacy considerations. We also note that the supplied documentation was of high quality, and that the development program has been informed by data collected during field trials. Following simulation exercises, physical tests and documentation review, we believe that memory, battery capacity, and robustness would be sufficient to meet the target design lifetime of at least one year. The security architecture of the card has been carefully designed and we believe it meets reasonable privacy expectations. However, to confirm our views we recommend that a professional security consultant be engaged to provide an additional review of the privacy and security aspects of the CovidCard system. We believe that CovidCard has the potential to detect and record close contacts to a level useful for contact tracing, but that an unknown and possibly significant number of false positive contacts will be . Increasing CovidCards detection thresholds to reduce the false positive rate is possible but this risks true positive contacts being lost. The true positive rates achieved in trials ranged from . to ., while false positive rates ranged from . to .. While it may be possible to improve card performance above what has been observed in trials, this would need to be demonstrated in a largescale trial. To mitigate possible false contacts from signal strength fluctuations we recommend that contact duration be stored along with the RPE, and we have proposed two possible modifications in contact record architecture to achieve this. When the firmware, including close contact detection thresholds, is finalized we recommend that CovidCard be run for an extended period (exceeding days) to verify software robustness and validate the battery life modelling. Given that cards may not always be worn on a lanyard, we recommend that additional tests be carried out to assess card performance when worn in alternative positions, such as a shirt pocket. Although these locations might not be ideal, it would enhance user acceptance and is likely to still provide a useful level of performance. DTAReport A COMMERCIALINCONFIDENCE vi Redacted consistent with (a) and ()(k) Proactively Released by the Department of Internal Affairs COMMERCIALINCONFIDENCE INTRODUCTION CovidCard is a digital contact tracing system designed to augment manual contact tracing for COVID pandemic control and to speed up the notification of atrisk individuals of possible exposure to SARSCoV. The system comprises a card with a Bluetooth Low Energy radio device that transmits pseudorandom numbers from a unique sequence, allowing other cards in range to detect and record its presence. In addition, there are multiple software service layers and a security architecture to enable the secure upload of contact data to a central server. The server performs a process to match cards to serial numbers based on the pseudorandom number sequences emitted. This enables contact tracers to identify the owner of a card, and the identities of people the card has come into contact with. At the request of the Department of Internal Affairs (DIA), we have carried out a technical review of the proposed CovidCard system. The primary purpose of the review was to provide independent advice as to whether CovidCard would be able to perform as represented under the assumption that a population wide distribution is achieved. DTA was provided specific terms of reference for the review which included the card system design, the security architecture, and ongoing support that we could provide to the project . The review was undertaken based on documentation provided by the developer, and non functional cards supplied for inspection and physical robustness testing. The material submitted for review was supplemented by a workshop at DTA that was attended by representatives of the CovidCard development team and DIA. The remainder of this report details the review covering the items listed in the terms of reference. Although we have provided feedback on the security architecture as requested we recommend that a professional security consultant be engaged to provide an additional review of these aspects of CovidCard. Note that there were a number of items specifically ruled out of scope for this review, including user acceptance, project cost, and alternative contact tracing solutions, and these issues are not considered here This report is an edited version of DTAReport which was releasedto DIAin July, . Parts of theoriginal report relatingto securityaresensitive andhave been removed. CARDPERFORMANCE . Overview CovidCard is designed to assist COVID contact tracing by recording Bluetooth Low Energy advertising signals emitted by nearby CovidCards. Each signal contains a random number known as the Ephemeral Advertising Identifier (EAI) which is drawn from a pseudorandom sequence that is unique to each card. The key and initial value needed to generate the pseudorandom sequence are uploaded from the card during production and stored on a central server. When contact records containing the EAIs are uploaded to the server, the cards can be identified by a partial reconstruction of the pseudorandom number sequences they emit. To decide whether a detection should be logged as a close contact an exposure risk metric based on the RSSI is calculated. It is based on the idea that exposure risk depends inversely on the distance, and that RSSI can be used to estimate distance. In free space conditions the signal strength varies inversely with the square of the distance. In this idealised case inferring distance from RSSI is straightforward, as long as the transmitter and receiver are calibrated. Here, CovidCard has an advantage over smartphone apps for RSSI based distance estimation DTAReport A COMMERCIALINCONFIDENCE Proactively Released by the Department of Internal Affairs COMMERCIALINCONFIDENCE because the Bluetooth radios in the cards are identical. However, there are additional factors that strongly influence signal strength multipath fading, antenna orientation, body attenuation and estimating distance based on RSSI data alone is an inherently difficult problem. . CardDetection Performance When CovidCards are in the active state, they cycle between advertising (transmitting) and scanning (receiving) modes. Assuming a Packet Error Rate (PER) of , the developers estimate that six detection opportunities a minute are needed to meet the criterion of chance of card detection in one minute (..., System Overview ). The PER assumption seems reasonable and we concur with the estimate of six detection opportunities per minute to meet the detection threshold. Scanning and advertising window durations intended to meet the six detectionsminute criterion are discussed in sections ... and ... of the SystemOverview . In advertising mode, the cards will transmit an advertising signal about every ms. The card remains in the advertising mode for seconds, after which it enters the scanning mode. In the scan mode the card listens for peer CovidCard packets for ms. We have checked and agree that these intervals enable detection of six advertising signals per minute and so meets the desired detection criterion. The performance of cards in high density environments (situations where large numbers of people are in close proximity) was considered in section .. of the System Overview by simulation. We have not been able to directly verify the results presented but the approach and underlying assumptions seem reasonable. The conclusions reached were that the CovidCard will cope with up to cards in receiver range without compromising detection performance with a ms advertising interval. Assuming a maximum density of about people per square metres, and the likely effects of body attenuation on the signal, a card density limit of is plausible. To further increase confidence in card performance a highdensity scenario could be tested as part of a field trial. . ExposureTrackingSubsystem The exposure tracking subsystem of CovidCard processes peak RSSI values, calculated over one minute intervals, for each entry in the watchlist. Exposure tracking is based on an internally calculated parameter called the Relative Proximity Estimate (RPE). The RPE is obtained by converting peak RSSI to a free space path loss estimate, and then calculating what is effectively a scaled inverse distance under the assumption of inverse square path loss. For the lifetime of a watchlist entry, the peak RPE is determined and the sum of the RPE values is accumulated. The total RPE is intended to be a measure of total exposure risk which can be used to prioritize contact tracing. Viral transmission risk is inversely dependent on the distance between two people and directly dependent on the contact duration. The exposure risk metric proposed for CovidCard seems a natural generalization of these criteria to the situation where the distance between people is varying with time. Note that this is a different approach to that taken in the GoogleApple Exposure Notification API, in which the exposure risk is dependent on attenuation, contact duration, number of days since exposure, and transmission risk . The intention is to convert the RPE into a fixedpoint representation, and scaling constants are to be defined to ensure that the range of RPE can be contained inside this value. These constants have not yet been defined, and the algorithmcode for calculation of RPE and accumulation of DTAReport A COMMERCIALINCONFIDENCE Proactively Released by the Department of Internal Affairs COMMERCIALINCONFIDENCE total RPE is not given. If intermediate calculations are performed in fixed point then the impact of round off error should be considered. The decision to record a watchlist entry in the contact log will be determined by thresholds on the peak and total RPE, but final values of these thresholds have not yet been set. The intention is to do this following final field trials to meet target performance requirements as stated in ..Firmware Specification . The setting of these threshold values carries the risk that either valid contacts (true positives) are missed, or the cards will record too many false positives. Since this is a critical aspect of card performance, we think that additional limited trials in a variety of environments should begin as soon as possible, and that the data on which the thresholds have been based should be released for independent review. . Effect of RSSIFluctuations We note an estimated range between two devices is implicit in the calculation of the RPE (it is proportional to the inverse of the range under the assumption of inverse square path loss). However, in real environments there are reflections of the signal that combine with the direct transmission path at the receiver, and this can result in extreme fluctuations in the RSSI. While on average the RSSI declines with range, when using the peak value there is risk that close and casual contacts may not be differentiated. To illustrate this, we collected RSSI readings from Bluetooth Low Energy packets exchanged between two Raspberry Pi devices in a meeting room at DTA. The devices were suspended at a height of about .mfrom two camera tripods One thousand packets each were collected at ranges from .mtombetween the devices, with a msinterval between transmissions. The data collection process took about two minutes at each position. The raw RSSI data is shown in the left hand plot of Figure . The raw RSSI data was then filtered to simulate the effect of a msscan interval repeated every seconds, combined with a one minute peak filter. The right hand plot in Figure shows the range of peak RSSI values that could be obtained with this processing approach. There is a range because the first scan interval on the CovidCard can start at a random time in the data series. This experiment shows that there can be considerable overlap in values of peak RSSI at different ranges. Hence any metric derived solely from peak RSSI may not be able to discriminate close and casual contacts. DTAReport A COMMERCIALINCONFIDENCE Proactively Released by the Department of Internal Affairs COMMERCIALINCONFIDENCE Figure : Left : Raw RSSI values measured at different distances between two Raspberry Pi devices. Right: The simulated range of peak RSSI values from CovidCard basedonthe Raspberry Pidata. We believe that providing contact duration information in the contact record may partially mitigate this issue. We suggest two possible approaches to incorporating contact duration in a contact record: a)Reduce the opcode to a bit field, introducing a new bit field containing the total contact duration in minutes (i.e. the number of minutes the EAI was visible), and reducing the size of the total RPE field to fit within the remaining bits. b)Replace the current bit field for total RPE with bit fields for both the time averaged RPE and contact duration. Saving the raw RSSI values and doing contact exposure processing on the server would be preferable. However, we recognize that this is not possible within the memory constraints of the device without severely impacting on the size of the watchlist. . Sensitivity andSpecificity CovidCard can be programmed to record an encounter if the received signal satisfies criteria based on duration and strength of the signal. For contact tracing the Ministry of Health defines seven scenarios with particularly high infection risk (close contacts). Two of these scenarios involve interpersonal contact within two metres for minutes or more, and these are targets for Bluetooth contact tracing systems like CovidCard. Implicit in these close contact definitions is that transmission occurs via inhalation of droplets from an infected person, and that a partition or barrier would block transmission. CovidCard can generate false positives by the same mechanisms as smartphone apps because it is also based on Bluetooth radio signals. False positive contacts fall into two categories: Acontact with correctly estimated range and duration where the signal was received through a physical barrier; A contact with an underestimated range due to Bluetooth signal strength variation. DTAReport A COMMERCIALINCONFIDENCE Proactively Released by the Department of Internal Affairs COMMERCIALINCONFIDENCE There is no way to mitigate the first of these on the card, and this is a problem inherent in all contact tracing systems based on radio signals. False contacts obtained through walls or partitions can only be resolved at the contact tracing interview stage, i.e. there is no technological solution to this problem at present. Estimating range using Bluetooth is an inherently difficult problem due to fluctuations in signal strength. Earlier this year we conducted a literature review of distance estimation using Bluetooth signals and concluded that this can be very unreliable . Our subsequent data collection exercises performed with Raspberry Pi devices have confirmed this view. An initial trial on an early CovidCard prototype was performed at Nelson Hospital The trial report recommended that further trials be held to refine the algorithm used to determine close contact. The report noted that an effective algorithm was essential to reduce false positives and conserve battery and memory. A number of additional trials on a CovidCard prototype were performed in May . These validation trials aimed to collect card data in a number of reallife situations and use this data to test and refine close contact detection algorithms. In this trial, a contact was recorded on a card if two or more detections with RSSI were received. Bluetooth data was downloaded from the cards and compared with ground truth data obtained by observer notes and video recordings, after applying a minute duration threshold to both data sets. The true positive rates for card contacts in these trials ranged from . to ., while the false positive rates ranged from . to . (Table of ). While it may be possible to improve card performance above what was observed in trials, this would need to be demonstrated in a largescale trial implementing an improved close contact detection algorithm. SERVERSIDEPROCESSING There are multiple aspects to the serverside processing that must be considered. The first step, after uploading readout data, is the identification of cards based on the received pseudorandom identifiers (the EAI values). The matching of EAI values with card serial numbers is performed by a search through a timelimited table of EAI values that is continuously by the server. The developers have not yet implemented or tested a specific algorithm for serverside card resolution. But, based on information provided at the DTA workshop, we believe that serverside card resolution is computationally tractable and could be scaled up or parallelised if needed using cloud computing resources. In the current design approach determination of exposure risk (measured by the RPE) is performed on the card. Only the total RPE is saved in a contact record, and this is very limited information with which to identify potential false positives. To give contact tracers more information that might help to identify false positives we recommend that contact duration be stored in the contact record log as well as the RPE. Two possible approaches to incorporating contact duration were described in section .. Neither of the modifications suggested change the contact record size, and would enable a more detailed exposure risk assessment on the server. This could take into account the the additional factors of transmission risk and time since exposure, as implemented in the GoogleApple Exposure Notification API . DTAReport A COMMERCIALINCONFIDENCE Proactively Released by the Department of Internal Affairs COMMERCIALINCONFIDENCE BATTERYLIFE . Overview It is clear from the supplied documentation that significant attention has been given to the power considerations of the CovidCard. The impact on instantaneous power consumption, battery duration and therefore indirectly, the usability of the CovidCard has been highlighted at all stages of the design. The need for such an ultralow power device has led many architectural decisions in the design of the CovidCard. It is important to note that this powerbattery assessment is based purely on a study of the CovidCard documentation since a device with fully operational firmware has not been submitted for testing. Empirical measurements have not been gathered. Given the potential consequences of mistaken power calculations, it is imperative that the power budget is accurately modelled. Such modelling commences in Section . of the System Overview with a description of the expected lifecycle of the CovidCard. Four distinct phases are considered: Production, Shelf life, Operation and Readout. Battery capacity is inherently determined by the form factor of the CovidCard and readily available battery chemistriescapacities. The limitations and realistic expectations of the selected battery are set out in Section ... and Table of the System Overview. Considering the mean annual temperatures in New Zealand, the CovidCard battery model is derated by due to temperature and manufacturing tolerances from mAh tomAh. A selfdischarge estimate of per annum is used throughout the usable life of the card For all phases the worstcase pessimistic view on battery capacity and power consumption is used in further modelling. These estimates are considered realistic. . Battery Life Modelling Production Given the high volume of manufacture, the production phase (specifically Initialisation) is very brief. The power model takes a worstcase consumption of mAh for this period. Shelf Life During storage the CovidCard is in a low power state awaiting activation. During this time, the power model assumes a maximum period of months consuming Aof current in order to maintain the realtime clock and RAM state. The quoted values of current are in line with the Apollo Blue MCU specifications stated in the device datasheet. Operation The battery model for this phase is the most complex and comprises three different states: Battery Level Check, Sleeping and ScanningAdvertising. Battery Level Check: To enable the user to check the battery of the CovidCard a button press will initiate a LED flash. This power consumption is estimated for an eager user to be no more than mAh during the month life cycle. In the current firmware version, the battery check procedure lights the red LED. This uses less power but is misleading to the user. Use of the green LED is far more intuitive and would not greatly impact power consumption. Sleep: To facilitate extended periods of low powered sleep during the Operation phase, the CovidCard utilises an accelerometer to detect card movement and wake the microprocessor. Section . of the FirmwareSpecification details the dutycycle and backoff procedure selected DTAReport A COMMERCIALINCONFIDENCE Proactively Released by the Department of Internal Affairs COMMERCIALINCONFIDENCE to enable accurate motion detection whilst minimizing accelerometer on time, even during long periods of inactivity. Given the ability to accurately detect user motion the power consumption model assumes hours of active use per day, days per week. A value of Ais predicted for the sleep state. The design of the accelerometer subsystem and assumptions stated are reasonable. ScanningAdvertising: Following subtraction of all above overheads the remaining battery capacity ofmAh can be assigned to scanning and advertising. Section .. in the SystemOverview presents a convincing model for parameter selection of scanning and advertising. This model can be used to prove that for the parameters selected, the remaining battery capacity is sufficient to obtain contact events. This statebased simulation boosts confidence in achieving a detection target with a ms advertising interval and ms scan window at an interval of seconds. Readout Reasonable estimates for power consumption are given in the readout phase considering the duration a readout is expected to take, the higher power BLE radio state and the LED flashing current. Net energy usage is estimated at mAh per readout cycle. . Conclusion Future changes to firmware design and a lack of empirical measurements makes a definitive answer on battery duration difficult, however based on the supplied documentation, we believe that the assumptions and values pertaining to battery duration are plausible and well modelled. The estimates given for current consumption and the time spent in each phasestate are reasonable and accurately described. NotesSuggestions It may be possible for a determined malicious user to frequently enter higher power states, such as battery checking or readout in order to reduce battery lifetime. This is considered unlikely given the effort required to do so. There may be other factors to consider such as battery internal resistance growth with age, however these ages are typically greater than the expected lifetime of the CovidCard. It is likely in mass roll out that defective batteries will be encountered, these cannot be predicted and must be overcome via a replacement programme. To enable a prediction of real battery and power consumption, a longterm programme of empirical power measurement could be undertaken on initial cards to prove expected performance. In the current firmware version the red LED appears to be used to signal Good battery state. If this is the case, we recommend changing to green to avoid user confusion. Note that the battery life projections depend on estimates of current drain by final production firmware, which does not yet exist and so has not been tested. But, based on the documentation provided, we believe the projected battery life and the modelling that underlies it is plausible. DTAReport A COMMERCIALINCONFIDENCE Proactively Released by the Department of Internal Affairs COMMERCIALINCONFIDENCE MEMORYCAPACITY The CovidCard is limited to the storage constraints of the included microcontroller unit (MCU). The CovidCard contains the Ambiq Micro Apollo Blue, specifically the part number AMABKKKBRB. This MCU has a total of MBavailable onboard storage (flash) and KBof available volatile memory (RAM). The MCU also contains KBof flash cache. The allocated storage for firmware and runtime is unknown as the firmware is not yet finalised. . Contact Log Design After activation, the CovidCard enters the Active state and the contact logging begins using the Bluetooth Low Energy Advertiser and Scanner. The size of the incoming data from the Bluetooth Scanner is variable depending on how many other cards are within Bluetooth range, unlike the Bluetooth Advertiser which transmits a static data size at a known frequency. Figure : CovidCardcontactlogdataflowfromScannertoReadoutasshownin section .ofthe FirmwareSpecification . During contact logging, the largest use of data is in managing incoming data from the Bluetooth Scanner subsystem (shown in blue in the figure above). The Tracker subsystem (shown in orange) receives all incoming data from the Scanner and must keep an ongoing watchlist for potential contacts (performed in RAM). The following Storage subsystem (shown in green) then takes confirmed contacts from the Tracker and stores them in the permanent contact log (in flash). . WatchlistMemoryCapacity The Tracker subsystem first mitigates against a flood of messages by limiting the incoming messages to per scan (in the FloodDoS protection block). The watchlist contains entries for every active unique temporary card ID (EAI) that is being received. kBof storage has been allocated in the RAM for the watchlist, an upper limit of entries (at octets per entry). We consider an extreme heavyusage scenario for the CovidCard as encountering new, unique EAIs per scan ( msevery seconds), which might occur when walking through a crowded area with many cardholders. watchlist entries would therefore be created every minute, resulting in new entries after minutes. This exceeds the maximum watchlist entries allocated in RAM. It is not specified when an EAI is considered inactive (at which point the entry is removed from the watchlist), but it is assumed this is at most minutes after the time that the EAI is first encountered (each EAI persists for to minutes). The Contact event detection block should therefore contain further logic to determine when a watchlist entry is DTAReport A COMMERCIALINCONFIDENCE Proactively Released by the Department of Internal Affairs COMMERCIALINCONFIDENCE considered inactive, rather than purely relying on a minute timer. If the inactivity threshold time were reduced to minutes (the current duration for the definition of a close contact), this extreme example would still create entries in that time. Although this extreme scenario can saturate the watchlist, we note that the entries with the oldest last seen time are deleted, which would minimise the risk that an active contact is removed. And the entries that are deleted are also assessed for exposure risk, meaning they may still be written to the contact log if the criteria are met. We consider a worstcase scenario for the CovidCard to be incoming messages with new and unique EAIs per scan. This represents a malicious attack that would create new watchlist entries per scan (one every seconds), or entries per minute, overwhelming the watchlist in just over two minutes. Mitigation against this type of attack may require further additions to the FloodDoS protection block, or stricter logic on when an EAI is considered inactive. . Contact Log MemoryCapacity The Storage subsystem takes watchlist entries that are potential close contacts and encrypts and stores them within the permanent contact log in flash. kBof flash storage has been allocated for the contact log, an upper limit of , entries (at octets per entry). Watchlist entries that are transferred to the contact log are first placed in a FIFO ring buffer in RAM, for batchwriting contacts to flash. The kBof flash storage allocated to the contact log is also designed as a ring buffer such that the oldest entry will be overwritten upon surpassing the memory limit. The extreme heavyusage example given in Section . of the System Overview assumes new contact events every minutes for hours every day. This would result in , new contact events every day, or , contact events over the days, which is just within the storage limit of , entries. Hence, we consider it is extremely unlikely that the memory capacity will be exceeded under normal operation. The CovidCard also records the times when the card enters a sleep state and wakes from a sleep state into the contact log. These entries take up the same amount of storage as an exposure entry ( octets). Continuing the extreme heavyusage example, the CovidCard could undergo minutes of inactivity to trigger a sleep state, followed by some motion or a button press to immediately trigger an active state. After hours of repeated sleepactive state cycling, sleepwake entries will have been written to the contact log. After days of hours cycling each day, , sleepwake contact events will have been written. In the extreme heavyuse example of , exposure events, this would overwrite the oldest exposure events in the contact log. This shows that the most extreme sleepwake cycling activity has the potential to cause exposure contact events to be lost (again, under the most extreme exposure activity). One mitigation may be to reduce the size of the sleepwake entries in flash. . Conclusion Based on the documentation provided, we believe the memory capacity of the CovidCard is sufficient to capture contact records over the period of interest (prior days from the start of the readout procedure). The current design can deal with extreme examples of use, however further thought may be needed on FloodDoS attacks and the conditions on declaring a watchlist entry to be inactive. Also, a limit on the frequency of wakesleep events being written to the contact log may guard against the overwriting of exposure events, which are more important data to be captured. PhysicalTestResults DTAhas been able to perform some of the physical tests suggested in section . of the Hardware Specification , which are intended to assess the cards robustness, usability, and to gauge whether it can meet its intended lifetime target of at least one year. Due to time constraints and lack of suitable equipment we were not able to perform all of these tests. The abrasion (alcohol) test described in section .. of the Hardware Specification was carried out using isopropanol and no deterioration of the printed label was observed. Three additional solvents were also trialled for interest: petroleum ether (hexanes), AVTUR (aviation kerosene), and acetone. Use of petroleum ether and AVTUR did not result in noticeable deterioration of the printed label but the acetone dissolved the card material resulting in a smearing of the etching. .. This method could give more useful results over the solely UV method proposed. Prescribing the exposure according to a known standard will give more weight to the results obtained. ASTM D (Standard Practice for XenonArc Exposure of Plastics Intended for Outdoor Applications) would be a good option as the card will be in use outdoors and polystyrene and its copolymers are susceptible to UV degradation. The use of recognised standards in the specifications will help to ensure that robust and relevant testing is undertaken. Where standards cannot be fully met or lack relevance then partial compliance or use of a subset of conditions or parameters would still be useful, if the deficiencies are noted. It is also recommended that a recognised standard of acceptance testing is used, such as the ISO or series . LanyardWearing The developers have proposed that the CovidCard be worn suspended by a lanyard on the front of the body. This aligns with the belief that maximum viral transmission risk is associated with facetoface contact. Worn in this position maximizes RSSI for facetoface contact, which is a key parameter in exposure risk calculation. Use of a lanyard would be precluded for machinery operators. But the card could be placed frontally in a shirt or overalls pocket, which should not significantly compromise performance. Surgeons and other health workers who perform procedures on patients may find lanyards too encumbering or dangerous to wear. Note also that lanyards have been identified as an infection control risk in hospitals and may not be appropriate for frontline medical workers for this reason alone Once again, in these situations the CovidCard could be placed in a pocket. Fitness instructors may find the lanyard inconvenient and uncomfortable to wear while taking classes. The nature of this work should not preclude the wearing of the card from a health safety aspect, but resistance to wearing the card on a lanyard may be encountered amongst this group. DTAReport A COMMERCIALINCONFIDENCE Proactively Released by the Department of Internal Affairs COMMERCIALINCONFIDENCE SECURITYARCHITECTURE . Specification and DesignAssurance Robust security is critical to protecting user privacy in the CovidCard system. Specific security elements needed to achieve this are described in Section . of the Security Specification (the primary security goals). Below we consider the security of CovidCard when in the active state, the secure download procedure, and the serverside security architecture. .. Card Operation The primary threat model considered in this section is the ability of an observer to track a specific CovidCard user. This tracking could be either following the user over time and distance or locating the user at a specific location. In both cases the attack is against the pseudonymous EAI can an attacker predict the EAI in order to persistently identify a given user The EAI has several measures which will make this a difficult attack, particularly with the limited range of the hardware. The random BDADDR, short and variable lifetime of each EAS, and destruction of previous EAS in the sequence, mean that an adversary does not have a predictable signal to attack. In most scenarios where the CovidCard is required where the CovidCard user is mingling with other users isolating a given card will be impractical at the software level. Another threat model is the ability of an attacker to determine the list of associates of a given CovidCard user. Given the difficulty of tracking a single user across the EAI changes, it would be substantially more difficult to attack multiple users. Afurther threat model is whether an attacker can overwhelm a given card or all cards at a specific location. This is explicitly addressed by the DoSFlood protection. An adversary could flood a target CovidCard with replay attacks (of valid advertisements) but this would only be effective against the target card(s) while the attack is maintained. This could have the effect of masking users in a group or blinding the contact system for a specific location. The usefulness of such an attack is questionable so it can be regarded as low risk. The use of the opcode in the contact log should be used with caution for other types of events. The standard exposure event is required, but any other type of event could present a privacy risk. Even simple card sleepwake events would be sufficient to develop a pattern of life for a given CovidCard user .. Secure Download Download of contact record data takes place over a Bluetooth connection with a tablet or smartphone that runs the Secure Download Application (SDA). When new contact records are first created they are placed in a circular buffer in RAM, and when the buffer becomes full the records are written to flash memory. Contact records are encrypted before they are stored in RAM or flash using AESCBC with a bit Log Encryption Key (LEK). The LEK and the associated Log Encryption Initialization Vector (LEIV) are by CovidCard when it is first activated by the cardholder, and remain on the card in RAM. The log manager process erases any contact records in either RAM or flash that are older than days. An attacker that gains access to the cards RAM may be able to decrypt the contact records that are stored on the card. To enable readout the card readout mode must be first enabled by pressing and holding the activation button, after which CovidCard acts as a Bluetooth Low Energy peripheral device. The SDA initiates connection to the CovidCard and communicates using the Readout GATT DTAReport A COMMERCIALINCONFIDENCE Proactively Released by the Department of Internal Affairs COMMERCIALINCONFIDENCE service. Before download can begin the SDA makes a Certificate Signing Request (CSR) to the CovidCard. The process of generating a CSR by the SDA and then submitting it to the Readout Authorisation Service is cryptographically very strong. It is normally applied on a lesser scale, for example in generating oneyear certificates for websites, but it scales well to the frequent use here. This cryptographic certificate request passed over a secure connection is a strong and fully tested process, fundamental to network security. The strongest protection against misuse of the download process is the required physical activation on the CovidCard itself. Unless the card has been maliciously modified during manufacture, there is no way to connect to the card without the physical activation. To target a given card would require theft or interference by the attacker, or subversion of the health care system by coercing a healthcare worker. The standalone Readout Authorisation Service (RAS) provides a degree of separation from the download process. This will make the RAS a target for any attacker attempting to subvert the download process, but also allows a zerotrust connection between the Secure Download Application and the RAS. The information passed to the RAS (the identity of the Healthcare Professional and the scope of the request) provides an auditable log. This will mitigate the risk of subverting the download process by persuading a healthcare worker to extract data. .. Serverside SecurityArchitecture The final design of the server components of the CovidCard system is still pending. These components consist of one mobile app (the Secure Download Application) and four serverbased systems: the Readout Authorisation Service, the Escrow Service, the Contact Analysis Service, and the Card Registry Service. The Readout Authorisation Service and the Escrow Service require some level of public access in order to allow access for the Secure DownloadApplication. Both should be designed with the key aim of limiting access solely to the SDA. The RAS already has a secure design for communication with the SDA. The Escrow Service should additionally minimise any communication back to the SDA. Since each upload instance requires coordination of the CovidCard user and a Healthcare Professional, the Escrow Service should confirm successful upload of the contact data (for Live Readout Mode) and this confirmation should be a minimal response with no further communication. Silently accepting the upload may provide marginally more security (particularly against an attacker probing the Escrow Service) but creates a significant service risk that failed uploads are lost. The remaining server components the Contact Analysis Service and the Card Registry Service are not directly exposed to public access and so can be designed according to standard system security principles. When registering cards, cardholder personal data and the CovidCard Serial Number (CSN) should be uploaded to the Card Registry Service by a oneway connection. The Card Registry Service is the most valuable target for an attacker seeking information from the CovidCard system, so there should not be any access to the public. There should be no way to check the details associated with a given card, apart from a COVID exposure alert. To minimise risk in this area, the CovidCard system should not allow cardholders to check or update their data. Users may withdraw from the system, or be issued a new card, as required. DTAReport A COMMERCIALINCONFIDENCE Proactively Released by the Department of Internal Affairs COMMERCIALINCONFIDENCE .. Conclusions We conclude that the primary security goals of the CovidCard System are sufficiently met by the security architecture. The CovidCard system separates the security operations at each stage of CovidCard use and uses dedicated encryption for each stage. This means separate encryption keys are used at each stage and so any successful cryptographic attack will only yield a fragment of the overall information. The ciphers in use are all current to accepted cryptographic standards with appropriate key lengths. Further security is provided by the use of ephemeral keys where possible, and the storage of keys in volatile memory to ensure their destruction in the case of most forms of tampering. DTA could also investigate use of the MANA computer model, or similar agentbased models, to simulate CovidCard interactions in a phase two trial. Combined with additional smallscale trials of real cards, the simulation modelling may partially substitute for a fullscale phase two trial. DTA could provide a second review of the exposure risk procedure if this is modified, either along the lines we have suggested or in another way, andor when exposure risk thresholds are finalized. We have considered the idea of a largescale field trial at a NZDF installation, for example, Linton military camp. This would be problematic for a number of reasons: a number of individuals would not be able to participate due to security issues; there are concerns that card data could reveal pattern of life behaviour; and that interactions of personnel in the trial would not be sufficiently representative of the population as a whole. There would also be frequent occasions where the cards would have to be placed in lockboxes, since they cannot be taken into classified environments. SUMMARY CONCLUSIONS We have carried out a review of the technology underlying the CovidCard system based on documentation provided by the developer and prototype cards that were supplied for physical testing. The review was supplemented by a workshop at DTAthat was attended by representatives of the CovidCard development team and the Department of Internal affairs (DIA). Following simulation exercises, physical tests and documentation review, we believe that memory, battery capacity, and robustness would be sufficient to meet the target design lifetime of at least one year. The security architecture of the card has been carefully designed and we believe it meets reasonable privacy expectations We believe that CovidCard has the potential to detect and record close contacts to a level useful for contact tracing, but that an unknown and possibly significant number of false positive contacts will be . Increasing CovidCards detection thresholds to reduce the false positive rate is possible but this risks true positive contacts being lost. The true positive rates achieved in trials ranged from . to ., while false positive rates ranged from . to .. While it may be possible to improve card performance above what has been observed in trials, this would need to be demonstrated in a largescale trial. To mitigate possible false contacts from signal strength fluctuations we recommend that contact duration be stored along with the RPE, and we have proposed two possible modifications in contact record architecture to achieve this. When the firmware, including close contact detection thresholds, is finalized we recommend that CovidCard be run for an extended period (exceeding days) to verify software robustness and validate the battery life modelling. Given that cards may not always be worn on a lanyard, we recommend that additional tests be carried out to assess card performance when worn in alternative positions, such as a shirt pocket. Although these locations might not be ideal, it would enhance user acceptance and is likely to still provide a useful level of performance. For convenience, they are itemized here: .The contact duration should be saved on the card along with RPE to reduce false positive risk from signal strength fluctuations. We suggested two possible approaches to incorporating contact duration in a contact record: a)Reduce the opcode to a bit field, introducing a new bit field containing the total contact duration in minutes (i.e. the number of minutes the EAI was visible), and reducing the size of the total RPE field to fit within the remaining bits. b)Replace the current bit field for total RPE with bit fields for both the time averaged RPE and contact duration. .For further physical testing it is recommended that a recognised standard of acceptance testing is used, such as the ISO or series In addition, theASTM D standard should be used for testing degradation in sunlight. .The Escrow Service should minimise communication back to the Secure Download Application. The Escrow Service should confirm successful upload of the contact data and this confirmation should be a minimal response with no further communication. .The Card Registry Service is the most valuable target for an attacker seeking information from the CovidCard system. There should be no way to check the personal data associated with a given card apart from a COVID exposure alert. To minimise risk in this area, the CovidCard system should not allow cardholders to check or update their data. .A professional security consultant should be engaged to provide additional review of the privacy and security aspects of CovidCard. .The performance of the CovidCard system should be conclusively demonstrated in a largescale controlled trial. This should be conducted by independent and experienced investigators, and subject to independent review. Under this process , the guardian applies on a young persons behalf but must have the young person s consent if the y are aged or over. It is also consistent with other legislation in New Zealand , for example , is the age at which you can apply for a learner driver licence , and consent to general medical procedures. It also aligns with other jurisdictions where selfidentification policies are often eased once a person turns , such as in Norway, Portugal , and Belgium. . Note , I propose to retain the existing provisions in the BDMRR Act that enable young people aged under to be treated as an adult where they are or have been in a marriage, civil union or de facto relationship. T hese young people will not need guardian consent or a letter of support from a third party.

TAB NZ partnership arrangement with Entain Group . On June , the partnership arrangement came into effect and allowed for TAB NZs daytoday operations to be run by a newly established New Zealand subsidiary, Entain New Zealand. This required Ministerial approval and the partnership took effect in June . The previous Government also agreed in principle to extend TAB NZs monopoly online in April DEV MIN refers. . The partnership between TAB NZ and Entain is a year contractual agreement, to operate TAB NZs day today functions (excluding governance, which includes deciding distributions to the racing codes). The partnership agreement provides no opportunity for government intervention in its details or operation. The agreement stipulates a revenue share between Entain and TAB NZ, with a million upfront payment from Entain in , and minimum guaranteed payments to TAB NZ of at least million per year for the first years totalling million in guaranteed funding. . This guaranteed funding has helped in the short term. It has contributed to an increase in prize money and allowed for more certainty to make investments into events such as racing carnivals as well as infrastructure improvements. Opex efficiency estimates are implausible Efficiency estimates derived from econometric studies in the UK are used in the Reform Scenario to drive a claimed . percent saving in opex. WICS use econometric models to claim that o pex efficiencies of percent are possible WICS has used an Ofwat econometric model to estimate that, after reform, larger New Zealand water entities can achieve up to a . percent efficiency impro vement to operating expenditure (opex) . To estimate the opex efficiencies, WICS combined data from the UK with recent data from N ew Zealand councils to estimate a performance baseline to measure New Zealand water entities against. To ensure comp atibility of the estimates with New Zealands operating environment, the gaps in efficiency between New Zealand entities and the benchmark w ere adjusted with special factors related to regulatory, geographic and environmental factors that were considered unique to New Zealand. Based on observed efficiency gains from UK water reforms, WICS assumes that New Zealand water reforms may achieve th e same operating efficiency results roughly a percent improvement. It is important to note that these estimates are an assumed benchmark that provide s a guide to what might be possible based on experiences in the UK water sector but, as peer reviewer Farrier Swier note s, care needs to be taken as it is not possible to conclude that those efficiencies can be realised . Guardian will mean all guardians jointly unless one guardian is unavailable, or one guardian has applied to the Family Court , and the Family Court consented to the child or yo ung persons sex marker being amended under section R of the Care of Children Act applications can be made to the Family Court to settle disputes between guardians. Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs INCONFIDENCE Page of I propose setting in regulations the third part ies who can provide the letter of support . The role of the third party would be to assess that the child or young person understands the amendment and that the decision is based on their own perceptions of their gender. It is important that the third party is suitably qualified to make this assessment but does not create a barrier by being difficult to access . Prescribing the third parties in regulations allows flexibility to experiment about how to achieve the right balance between prescribing third parties that can ensure a child and young person underst ands the decision and ensuring these third parties are accessible. . In develop ing the regulations target ed consultation will be completed with professional groups or people who may be suitable to act as the third party . These could include, for example, he alth professionals ; people outside of the health sector , such as counsellors ; or people who may know the child or young person well. The views of children and young people will also be sought on this matter. . As part of regulation development , consideration will be given to any training or guidance needed about the role of the third party. This is to mitigate the risks of transgender children and young people encountering professionals unwilling to support their transition for reasons unrelated to their cogn itive ability. I am aware that some guardians may not be accepting of their childs gender . I recognise that where there are concerns about guardians improperly influencing a child or young person to amend their registered sex , there are also concerns that guardians will prevent the amendment . Some guardians may not be accepting of their childs gender and will not consent to their child amending their registered sex . Some children and young people may not feel comfortable aski ng for their guardians consent , or may be estranged from their guardians . . The ability for and year olds to provide a letter of support from a third party instead of guardian consent should mitigate th e above risks to some extent. At this stage, I am not prepared to remove guardians from the process for those aged under years . This recognises a guardians responsibilities for their childs development and help ing their child determine important decisions. Any negative consequences of provisions requiring guardian consent can be considered as part of the proposed statutory review of the self identification provisions. . The need for a Family Court process to settle disputes between young people and guardians is likely to be a reduced if and year olds can apply with only a letter of support from a third party. However, there may still be scenarios where it is useful ( for example where the young person has trouble accessing a third party and their guardians refuse consent or disagree ). . I propose the Registrar General will be able to give effect to Family Court decisions on these matters made under the C are of Children Act . This will mitigate the risk of guardians , or disagreements between guardians , obstructing applications for children and young people.

Alcohol licensing trusts are community owned trusts that sell alcohol and provide other hospitality related services in their area. They then distribute their profits back to their communities and are accountable through the election of their trusteesmembers. Licensing trusts were first established in the s as part of the relaxing of prohibition in New Zealand. They were a new way of licensing the sale and consumption of alcohol. They were promoted as a more responsible and accountable alternative to the private licensed sale of alcohol.

Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs INCONFIDENCE Page of Regulation making powers are needed to give effect to my proposals . I propose a regulation making power to give full effect to the self identification proposals outlined above. This power will be to enable regulations that prescribe: . the sex marker options other than the binary; . the additional requirements where a person amend s their registered sex more than once ; . the third parties who can provide a letter of support for applications for children and young people ; and . any other matters required to give effect to a self identification process , which align with the overall intent of the proposals in this paper. There are further minor policy issues I intend to address . There are other, more minor, issues in the Bill to address. I am seeki ng Cabinets agreement that I can make decisions on the se issues . These issues include, but are not limited to: . a transition period for implementation of the self identification provisions up to months may be required to ensure the technical infrastru cture is in place to give effect to the changes with the birth register ; . how a persons previous re corded sex markers are treated on the birth register (eg are they closed or deleted); . clarify ing that section in the BDMRR Act means that birth certifica tes are not conclusive evidence of someones sex or gender ; and . clarifying that where a person has amended their registered sex , previous names and sex markers must not be shown on the amended birth certificate . . These changes will be included in the self identification SOP that I intend to bring to Cabinet in July . Minor technical and operational improvements to the wider Bill . I am also seeking Cabinet agreement that I can make decisions on minor and technical change s associated with a separate SOP unrelated to self identification. Other minor amendments will likely be needed to the Bill , which relate to the operation of and access to the Birth, Death and Marriage registers. These changes are needed to address operational issues that have been identi fied since the Bill was drafted in . These amendments will be made via a separate SOP later in the year. This SOP will not be referred to Select Committee and will be introduced at committee of the whole House stage. Addressing issues previously raised by Crown Law . The previous Minister of Internal Affairs cited and publicly released advice from Crown Law when they deferred the Bill in . Crown Law raised that section in the BDMRR Act, which states that a persons sex should be determined by the general law of New Zealand , is unclear. This provision means that birth certificates should not be the determining factor in decisions about a persons sex and that consideration should be given to other legislation and the common law. I intend for this provision to be re drafted, so its meaning is clarified. Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs INCONFIDENCE Page of . I believe that birth certificates should not be how a persons sex is determined. In practice birth certificates are not relied on to determine access to women only spaces (eg changing rooms or scho ols) or entitlements (eg sports teams or scholarships) and this should continue. . Related to this, Crown Law advised that clearer statutory guidance on how sex is determined could be beneficial (for example, what factors should be considered to determine a persons sex). While I agree this could be useful, the matter is broader in scope than the BDMRR Act and the Internal Affairs portfolio. Work on this matter would require a cross agency initiative as processes for determining sex are in place across numer ous institutions. Any further consideration of this matter should not delay the progress of introducing a self identification process. Crown Law also raised the placement of people in prisons . Birth certificates are rarely required in legislation to determi ne someones sex or gender. While sex is referred to across legislation, t here is only one instance where sex on a birth certificate determines a persons sex . This is the how the Department of Corrections (Corrections) determines the accommodation of peop le in male or female prisons. . Corrections determines placements in mens and womens prisons under the Corrections Regulations . These state that where there is doubt about if a person should be placed in a male or a female prison and a birth certificate is supplied, a person must be placed in accordance with the sex on the birth certificate . If a birth certificate is not provided, a review can be initiated where considerations include a persons gender, safety and wellbeing, and wider considerations. Where people have a history of prior serious sexual offending against their nominated sex, the placement cannot be reviewed. .
