. Digital identity is central to the secure, people centred digital delivery of services such as social prote ction, health care and finance. Digital identity has the potential to deliver significant economic and societal benefits in both the public and private sectors and through commercial market development. International studies have suggested that the potenti al benefit of enabling digital identity in a mature economy is between . and of GDP (approximately . to billion in NZD). . Developing the digital identity ecosystem is also a critical component of achieving the Prime Ministers commitment in th e Single Economic Market agenda towards mutual recognition of identity services with Australia. New Zealand and Australia are developing a roadmap for cross recognition of digital identities. This process can only commence once New Zealands requirements a re confirmed. . Digital identity can also enable digital trade and other cross border transactions. One example involves the recently concluded Digital Economic Partnership Agreement (DEPA) between New Zealand, Chile and Singapore. The development of the dig ital identity ecosystem and interoperability will enable New Zealand to advance discussions on digital identity in the DEPA and other contexts as appropriate.

Further work has identified the changes that need to be made in relation to enrolment for juvenile offenders. We propose that the Bill will match the current process for prisoners who are ye ars old or older, as far as possible . The only notable difference is that the responsibilities mentioned in paragraph above will sit with either the pris on manager, or the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki, depending on whether the or yearold is being held in prison or in a youth justice residence. The Electoral Act requires prison managers to communicate with a prisoner in a way that the prisoner can reasonab ly be expected to understand, when explaining electoral rights and collecti ng information for enrolment. The same requirement will apply to both prison managers and the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki when they are assisting youth electors.

The Office of the Privacy Commi ssioner understands the arguments about electoral roll information being publicly av ailable for the purposes of electoral integrity. However, the Office also encourages further consideration of whether any modifications to the exis ting settings for the electoral roll are needed for young electors, noting that their age may create particular vulnerabilities. The Office may choose to make a submission to the select committee on these matters.
The draft Bill introduces new age tiers where previously there was a single age of eligibility for all aspects of elections. This places new limits on the right to be free from discrimination on the basis of age (protected by section of NZBORA). It introduces differential treatment between people aged years and older, and people ag ed or yearsold, in relation to voting in alcohol licensing trust elections and candidacy for local elections.
The response notes that the Governm ent has decided that the best way forward is to introduce a bill to lo wer the voting age to in local elections. It also notes the other proposed age limits in the Bill (for example, a minimum age of for voting for, or being a member of, an alcohol licensing trust is to be retained).

Further work is required on the development of the TF Authoritys complaints and dispute resolution operating model, before we can determine whether regulations are required to support the establishment and implementation of accessible, fair, timely , and cost effective complaints and dispute resolution arrangements. This work will include considering what role, if any, an external alternative dispute resolution provider could play to support or complement the Authoritys compla ints investigation and compliance management functions. Complaints and dispute resolution process Figure highlights key elements of the complaints and dispute resolution process provided for in the Act. Complaints must be about breaches : Under the Act the TF Authority is charged with addressing complaints received from any person that believes a TF provider has breached the provisions of the Act, the rules, the regulations , or the terms of use for the accreditation mark . The Complainant must try and reso lve a complaint directly with the TF Provider before involving the TF Authority: Complainants are expected to make reasonable efforts to resolve a complaint directly with the TF provider concerned before involving the TF Authority. This should involve usi ng a TF providers internal complaints resolution process and utilise any disputes resolution scheme or process that the TF provider is a party to th rough their membership of a particular industry. Preliminary Assessment : When the TF Authority receives a c omplaint it will complete a preliminary assessment. The assessment process will include providing the TF provider with the opportunity to comment on the complaint. The preliminary assessment can result in the TF Authority: referring the complaint (in full or in part) to the Ombudsman, the Privacy Commissioner, the Inspector General of Intelligence and Security or another officeholder when, following consultation with those officeholders, the TF Authority determines the complaint falls within their jurisdi ction and would be more appropriately dealt with by them; informing the parties to the complaint that it will not consider the complaint further and explaining its reasons ( the reasons for not further considering a complaint are outlined in section of t he Act); or deciding that a breach appears to have occurred.

Intra ground discrimination is where there is differential treatment between peopl e who exhibit the same protected ground. In this case, there is differential treatment between people who are willing and able to undergo medical treatment and those unwilling or unable to do so. Authorised for lodgement Hon Jan Tinetti Minister of Internal Affairs Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs INCONFIDENCE Page of Appendix A: Risks and mitigations associated with introducing a self identification process Risk Likelihood Impact on introducing self identification Mitigations No broad public consultation on selfidentification High No broad public consultation has occurred. Low Broad public views have been canvased through other mediums. A good understanding of broad public views on selfidentification has been developed based on: submissions received at Select Committee in ; considerable public debate; and related work by other agencies (eg StatsNZs work updating the statistical standards for gender, sex and variations of sex ch aracteristics ). The views have been taken into account in developing the policy proposals. Referring the SOP to Select Committee will provide another opportunity for the public to provide feedback on the self identification provisions. Young people and Mori, Pacific and ethnic communities views on a self identification process have not been sought High No consultation with these communities has occurred . Medium These communities may express disappointment at not being involved in policy development , where their views would have been beneficial. Targeted efforts will be made to reach out to young people and Mori, Pacific and ethnic communities to support them to access and engage in the Select Committee process. Engagement will be undertaken with youn g people and Mori, Pacific, and ethnic communities as part of regulation development to explore options for culturally inclusive sex markers and appropriate third parties who can provide the letter of support . Opposition from some individuals and groups to a selfidentification model may affect the progression of the Bill High Opponents are critical that gender self identification: replaces a robust definition of sex; undermines sex based protections and will result in men accessing wom enonly spaces; and creates opportunities for predatory men to find ways to reach vulnerable women.Medium Groups opposed to selfidentification will likely organise public campaigns that will generate significant media interest. These could delay the progress of the Bill (eg through a substantial number of Select Committee submissions) and provide misinformation about the changes it makes. Debate on this issue is likely to be divisive and could negatively impact the wellbeing of some individuals. There is no evidence to suggest that a selfidentification process will affect how people access women only spaces (eg changing rooms) and entitlements (eg sports teams) as: o gender is already represented on passports without evidence of th is being abused; and o a birth certificate is not considered conclusive evidence of someones sex or gender and is not required to access women only spaces or entitlements. Any perceived risk that people would abuse the process is mitigated by: o the requirement to fill a statutory declaration form falsifying a statutory declaration form is a criminal offence and can lead to imprisonment for up to three years; and o making it clearer in the Bill that birth certif icates should not be taken as conclusive evidence of someones sex or gender. Communications material has been developed to manage expectations, likely questions and explain the rationale for a self identification process. Officials will be available to support Select Committee to make the submissions process safe for all parties and to support the wellbeing of those who want to submit. The Cabinet paper needs to be accompanied by a Regulatory Impact Statement . Attached to the Cabinet Paper at Appendix A is the accompanying Regulatory Impact statement (RIS). All policy proposals taken to Cabinet that include a government regulatory proposal must be accompanied by a RIS. A RIS is a government agency document that summarises the agencys best advice on the impact of a proposal. A RIS is approved by the responsible agency and must be independently assessed. . The Departments RIS on introducing a selfidentification process has been reviewed by the Departments Regulatory Impact Analysis Panel in accordance with the quality assurance criteria set out in the CabGuide. It has been assessed as partially meeting the quality assurance criteria. The RIS did not fully meet the criteria as there has not been full public consultation on introducing selfidentification. Partially meets is sufficient to allow for the Cabinet paper to be considered by SWC. The Cabinet paper is ready for consideration by SWC . Subject to your approval, the Cabinet paper should be lodged by on May with Cabinet Office for consideration at SWC on May . Officials will be available to support you at SWC. . A quick reference guide demonstrating the key changes between the Births, Deaths, Marriages and Relationship Registration (BDMRR) Act , the BDMRR Bill, and the SOP, and how the process would apply to children are attached as Appendix B . Suggested talking points to complement the quick reference guide are attached at Appendix C. We recommend that you announce your intention to introduce a selfidentification process and refer the changes to Select Committee . We consider that an announcement soon after Cabinet approval is important. Proactive communications clearly setting out the rationale for the changes and what they involve will help mitigate any opposition to selfidentification. Providing information on the changes early will also be important so interested individuals and communities can prepare to engage with the changes at Select Committee. . Early communication will also provide sufficient time to implement an engagement strategy encouraging more young people and people from Mori, Pacific and ethnic communities to participate in the select committee process. On May we will provide you with a briefing seeking your agreement to our recommended engagement strategy (briefing IA refers). . Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Regulatory Impact Statement What is the policy problem or opportunity . New Zealanders are spending almost a billion dollars every year at the pokies and t he level of harm associated with playing pokies is increasing and wi ll continue to do so without Government intervention. This gambling harm has a negative effect on individuals , t heir whnau, friends and the wider community. This harm is also disproportionately affecting Mori, Pacific peoples and other population groups. . The key reasons for harm are the time spent gambling and the money lost. These affect people differently. In , about . of New Zealand adults self reported some harm from their own gambling in the previous year. Gambling harm is widely believed to be underreported, in part due to the perceived stigma . . In addition, we know that people who have a problem with gambling on pokies are not usually identified in pubs and clubs. According to the Health and Lifestyles Survey , over of pokies reported that they had not any interaction with staff about their gambling. Interactions included: know my name or recognise me; monitor the pokie room; spoken to me with a concern about my gambling; given me a leaflet on gambling support services. . The current regulations do not ensure adequate use of some of the key levers for reducing pokies harm controls in the gam bling venue, restrictions on machine features, and enforcement tools to drive compliance. The research and practice advice, such as the guidance issued by Te Hiringa Hauora have evolved since the Regulations were created in and difference approaches are recommended as best practice in terms of venue management and game features. . S ome people are experiencing, or at risk of, a level of harm that could have been prevented or minimised. . A recent District Court decision has also identified that more prescriptive requirements are needed. A Christchurch patron with a n addiction to pokies , spent around , of earthquake insurance money on pokies over three years, before passing away suddenly. The manager of one of the venues he frequented was prosecuted for not identifying his problem. In a day period, hed spent over , there. On one single visit, he made EFTPOS withdrawals totalling ,. Towards the end, he was there every second day. The venue missed all the signs of his addiction. . The decision Department of Internal Affairs v Suppressed expendexpendNZDC has shown, the need to set more prescriptive requirements for identifying gambling harm in venues. To summarise: the venue manager was charged with failing to take reasonable steps to ensure that the venues harm minimisation policy was used to identify a problem gambler , the reasonable steps included having systems to track multiple cash withdrawals and regular long play durations , the Judge held that as these steps were not included in the harm minimisation policy, they were not self evident requirements, and the decision noted that these steps could be prescribed by regulations and that venue staff and gamblers would benefit from this. . The current light touch regulation model, where societies and venues have been expected to develop and apply strong harm minimisation measures, has not been successful . A more prescriptive approach to harm minimisation could reduce the harm New Zealanders experience from gambling on pokies. Advocates in the harm prevention and minimisation sector, as well as local authorities, have been asking for stronger measures for some time. . Preventing and minimising harm is one of the purposes of the Act and the sole purpose of the Regulations. The Act contemplates a substantially higher level of regulation in relation to Class gambling than is currently used. Detailed regulation making powers are provided for : harm prevention and minimisation (section ); gaming machines (section ); admission to, and exclusion from, gambling venues (section ); exclusion of problem gamblers (section ); and infringement offences for the breach of any regulations (section ). Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Regulatory Impact Statement . The range of regulation making powers provide an opportunity to create a stronger harm minimisation approach. Government intervention, by way of strengthening harm minimisation requirements, which could reduce the harm on individuals and their communities. In line with the scope, we could: set more explicit direction for venues and societies ; providing more player information on pokie games and make features less addictive; and providing supporting offences and penalties for the regulations. What objectives are sought in relation to th e policy problem . The core objective is to reduce the level of individual (and, by extension, second hand) gambling harm being experienced from pokies in venues. Our more specific objectives , in line with the Ministers scope decision s, are to: make it easier for venues and societies to reduce harm ; make pokie machines safer ; and creates consequences for breaches of the regulations . . The secondary objective, for the next stage of work post consultation, will be to ensure any proposed regulations are cost effective and not overburdening for the organisations impacted by them (societies, venues and the Regulator).

Page of the Select Committees response to Local Government Bill ( No ) faddafddcccdbbaef (www.parliament.nz) Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government Regulatory Impact Statement What are the poll provisions . Originally, the Act provided options for Mori wards to be established by: council resolution; or majority vote in a binding poll, initiated either by the council itself, or by a petition of electors. . A petition of electors could also be used to demand a poll on a council resolution to establish Mori wards. A valid petition needed to have signatures from at least of electors who were on the electoral roll for that council area at the last triennial election. If the petition was valid, the council was required to hold the poll, and the result was binding for two local government terms. . There is a similar binding poll mechanism in the Act that applies to council decisions about which electoral system will be used (STV or FPP). There is no binding poll mechanism for decisions on other parts of representation arrangements , such as decisions to establish new general wards. . The inclusion of the poll provisions was intended as a mechanism to allow Morielectors to seek Mori wards if the council did not consider it or decided against. However, in practice , the poll provisions were used to challenge council resolutions to establish Mori wards and proved to be an almost insurmountable barrier to their establishment . Between and only two councils established Mori wards using the pr evious process under the Act. Fourteen councils attempted to establish Mori wards, some more than once. Sixteen polls were held, and only one of these was in favour of establishing Mori wards (Wairoa District Council in ). One council (Waikato Regional Council) established Mori wards without a poll beingdemanded by electors. A summary of the outcomes of the processes under the Act is attached as Appendix A. . In an estimated of elected representatives on councils were of Mori descent , compared to a Mori population estimate of .. Over the period from to overall Mori representation on councils had improved, but there was still underrepresentation. For example, following the local elections an estimated . of elected members on councils were of Mori descent , compared to a Mori population estimate of .. These figures to do not reflect substantial variations in the Mori population by region. Mori wards and legislative changes . The previous G overnment amended the Act in to remove the ability for Mori ward decisions to be subject to polls. This meant that councils had the final decision on whether Mori wards were established. That decision would continue to apply for the next two electoral terms (six years) before a council could revisit the decision. . The policy rationale for the legislative changes was to remove the effective elector veto on Mori wards. Under these changes, final responsibility for balancing the various public interests, including minority interests, w ould sit with the councils elected representatives. . Another rationale was that Mori and general wards followed different processes for establishment . A petition followed by a binding poll allowed the public to challenge wards created to represent the Mori population of a district or region. Rural Supplies Technical Working Group ( ), Report to the Department of Internal Affairs , Rural Supplies Technical Working Group DRAFT report back May (dia.govt.nz) Proactively Released by the Department of Internal Affairs The Department of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua INCONFIDENCE Page of . the schemes supply of drinking water is usually a minute volume in comparison to their primary purpose of supplying water for agricultural or horticultural purposes; . there are practical compliance considerations, for example it is impractical to use chlorination for treatment and residual disinfection in rural water schemes which use open canals to transport water, as the chlorine is rapidly destroyed by sunlight; . if regulatory requirements are perceived to be too costly or resource intensive, a potential outcome is that owners or operators of these mixed use rural supplies may choose to cease supplying drinking water to human users, as the supply of drinking water is not their primary purpose. There would not necessarily be a viable alternative drinking water supply that can be readily or costeffectively used by people who lose access to drinking water in these situations. . The group recommended that council owned mixed use rural supplies should transfer to the previous governments water services entities, but there should be a process for consumers to opt by referendum to transfer mixed use supplies to their users. . Also under the previous government, the Department worked with Clutha District Council and farmer representatives to explore potential ownership options for mixed use rural water supply schemes in the Clutha District (under the previous governments water services entities). This work helped inform the Departments understanding of these schemes, their importance to farmers and rural economies, and the economic challenges associated with the operation of these schemes. Local Water Done Well will enable councils to work with their rural communities to determine the optimal management, governance and financing arrangements for mixed use schemes . Under Local Water Done Well, councils will have increased flexibility to work with local rural communities to determine the optimal management , governance and financing arrangements for these schemes. . When developing their Water Services Delivery Plans, councils will be required to consider how they plan to fund investment requirements, and how they will address infrastructure deficits and support growth in demand on these schemes . . Councils will need to give new consideration to: . investment requirements and how best to fund these, including possibly long term borrowing to spread the costs of long life infrastructure investments ; . how best to manage these schemes including their organisational form and the involvement of farmers in their governance and management oversight; . how best to charge for these schemes including the mix of variable and fixed charges to commercial and residential consumers ; and . how best to support the schemes to meet regulatory standards, for example work ing with Taumata Arowai to identify potential exemptions as necessary . . Some councils may decide to work together in their delivery of mixed use schemes, enabling efficiencies in their management and operation and associated funding and procurement arrangements. Proactively Released by the Department of Internal Affairs The Department of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua INCONFIDENCE Page of . Councils may choose to enter into a new water organisation that enables improved access to financing for water infrastructure, including by facilitating long term borrowing, so that the cost of infrastructure investments can be paid down over the life of the assets. . If councils choose to progress a standalone water organisation, the o rganisational and governance arrangements will be determined by councils in consultation with their communities . The governance arrangements could include existing or expanded roles for farmers in the governance and operation of mixed use rural schemes . . The new economic regulation regime for water services will result in strengthened incentives for councils to improve delivery of their local mixed use rural schemes. Local Water Done Well will reduce the regulatory burden for mixed use rural schemes . The proposed changes to the Water Services Act in your Cabinet paper Local Water Done Well Stage further decisions would help reduce regulatory compliance costs for these schemes. These changes include: . requir ing Taumata Arowai to explicitly consider the costs on suppliers as a key part of its regulatory approach ; . requiring Taumata Arowai to work proactively with suppliers to support them to meet r egulatory requirements ; . enabl ing Taumata Arowai to proactively issue exemptions where compliance with the Act is impractical, inefficient , unduly costly or burdensome; and . reducing regulatory burden for small supplies, such as lifting the threshold so that shared domestic supplies with under consumers would not be subject to regulation, enabling a small number of neighbouring properties who share water to be treated as domestic self suppliers . You may wish to consider further opportunities to reduce the regulatory burden for mixed use rural schemes . Mixed use rural water schemes are unique in that they provide large volumes of water across large areas for commercial farming purposes , and they also provide smaller volumes of water to rural residential properties for human drinking and sanitary purposes . . In their supply of water for human drinking and sanitary purposes, mixed use rural water schemes are required to operate to the same drinking water regulatory standards as those required of large urban schemes . Councils in their operation of mixed use schemes are also subject to the same regulatory requirements as those that apply to their operation of large urban schemes, including requirements for registration, drinking water safety plan ning , source water protection and various other testing, reporting and notification requirements. . There are existing and emerging challenges to safe supply of drinking water from mixed use rural schemes . These include known issues from animal contamination of water at source, within the distribution network and at the point of supply . Emerging issues include risks to human health from high levels of nitrates in soil and ground water . In some parts of New Zealand this is at levels close to or in excess of maximum acceptable values . Proactively Released by the Department of Internal Affairs The Department of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua INCONFIDENCE Page of . Small rural councils are constrained in their capacity to proactively address these challenges , especially emerging challenges, before they become problem atic. . The Water Services Act provides Taumata Arowai with a wide range of regulatory tools and instruments that it can tailor to the regulation of rural water supply schemes. Taumata Arowai has already developed a number of acceptable solutions tailored to the particular characteristics of rural water supply schemes, with the aim of making compliance easier and more cost effective for scheme operators. . More c an be done to develop cost effective regulatory approaches and compliance solutions for mixed use rural water schemes , and to recognise the ir particular characteristics and challenges in supplying safe drinking water. Potential areas of investigation could include : . Familiarisation with the characteristics, practicalities and challenges in operating mixed use rural schemes as a basis for their improved regulation . . Consideration of the various current and emerging risks to human health associated with operation of mixed use rural water supply schemes, and consideration of : .. how these risks should be assessed for purposes of regulation ; and .. whether the same risk tolerances should apply to schemes that serve very small populations to those that serve very large populations . . Consideration of the definition of what constitutes a water supply scheme for purposes of drinking water regulation, and at what point in the supply arrangements should regulatory requirements for treatment of drinking water apply to ensure the most cost effective approach to ensuring delivery of safe water for drinking . . How to best specify regulatory requirements and use the various regulatory tools and discretions available under the Water Services Act (such as acceptable solutions , authorisations and exemptions ) to make compliance as simple and low cost as possible for operators of mixed use schemes. . How to best support councils in their operation of mixed use rural schemes, with a focus on what Taumata Arowai can do in terms of direct support and what it can do to support council and industry organisations to support cost effective operation of mixed use schemes. You may wish to establish an independent advisory group to review the regulatory settings for mixed use rural schemes . You may wish to establish an expert advisory group to advise you and the refreshed board of Taumata Arowai on the above matters. We consider this is a s an important and practical step to improve regulation of mixed use rural water schemes . . The group could be appointed by you as Minister of Local Government and be tasked with advising you directly on these matters, with the Department as secretariat (similar to the Technical Advisory Group). Alternatively, the Group could be appointed by the Department and provide the D epartment with a report on their findings. The group would be available to advise you directly if you wished. . We consider the group should comprise a small number of persons with practical experience, recognised expertise and knowledge related to: Proactively Released by the Department of Internal Affairs The Department of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua INCONFIDENCE Page of . the practicalities of mixed use rural water supply schemes, their uses and importance to rural communities and the practicalities of their operation. This could be a farmer chairperson of a mixed use water supply committee , or a council officer with operational experience; . expert and practical understanding of the existing and emerging public health issues and risks associated with the operation of mixed use rural water supply schemes. This could be a public servant , for example from the Public Health Agency; . knowledge and practical understanding of industry structures, workforce capabilities and arrangements associated with the operation of mixed use rural water schemes; . expertise in the technical design and operation of mixed use rural schemes and the technologies and innovations available to ensure cost effective operation and safety of drinking from rural supply schemes; and . expertise in regulatory practice and regulatory economics with a focus on costeffective regulation. . ()(f)(iv) Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs The Department of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua INCONFIDENCE Page of Delegation of bylaw making power . The power to make bylaws is more complex. Currently, territorial authorities can transfer all or some of their bylaw making powers to a regional council that any part of their district falls within, or to any other territorial authority. Regional councils can transfer all or some of their bylaw making powers to a territorial authority in their region, or to any other regional council (s LGA). . Councils cannot delegate their bylaw making powers unless this is expressly provided for in legislation (Sch edule , LGA). There is not a specific provision allowing water bylaw making powers to be delegated this would need to be a new provision . . . If needed, there are several options to make any necessary new bylaws using current settings : . the council could make the bylaw then delegate associated powers to a water organisation (such as compliance, monitoring and enforcement); . Where councils are combining to provide water services (either as a joint CCO, shared services arrangements or as service agreements between councils) they could all transfer their water bylaw making powers to one of the councils, who could then make one bylaw covering all of the districts in the group ; or . Joint council owners could work together on a combinedconsolidated bylaw (e.g. the Wairarapa Consolidated Bylaw currently made by the South Wairarapa, Carterton and Masterton District Councils). . However, a simple legislative change would be to use the Watercare model (based on sections and of the Local Government (Auckland Council) Act ). This would allow water organisations to propose a bylaw to their owning councils which would then check the proposed bylaw against statutory criteria (such as cost effectiveness and consistency with existing strategies, policies, or plans). If agreed, the water organisation could then consult on the bylaw and, if the requirements are met, the owning councils mus t adopt the bylaw. This would be a useful model to adopt in the short term to enable new water organisations to operate it has good safeguards and has already been tested and found to work well . We are recommending this change for Bill because it is a simple, straightforward mechanism . Consultation with TAG and our response . The TAG indicated that while there is useful work to be done i n all the se policy areas, the majority did not see any as critical work for Bill . The highest immediate priority would be stormwater planning and management, in particular managing overland flow paths and watercourses. The TAG also noted a potential lack of clarity around the power to delegate infrastructure powers. However, t he TAG noted that Local Water Done Well is intended to be more flexible than the previous prescriptive ()(f)(iv) Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs The Department of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua INCONFIDENCE Page of approach. The TAG therefore generally preferred not introducing new requirements where existing tools are working adequately , including standard commercial practices . . The majority of TAG members concluded that, other than any minimum vital changes, most issues could be deferred for at least months. . We consider this is a viable strategy , given that most of the areas being considered in this briefing are ancillary to the basic functioning of water organisation s. It would also offer the advantage of opportunity to learn from the experience of the early innovators within the new regime, as well as not distracting from the highest priority needs for Bill . There are also various related policy development work programmes going on which will be more advanced by next year, allowing us to avoid unnecessary duplication. . Legislative design work for Bill will focus on ensuring that current powers are able to be used effectively in the medium term. This will avoid a further risk that the detailed work required to resolve all the complex policy and legislative design issues for significant improvements to regulatory and infrastructure powers will detract from the primary focus of Bill . Discussion and Comment on specific policy areas . The discussion covers a range of ancillary areas where legislative changes could be made to support the overall objective for Local Water Done Well: to deliver safe, resilient, reliable, environmentally sound, and customer responsive water services at the least cost . . We have set out our initial recommendations on these areas, following discussion with TAG , and review of wider work programmes. For each area recommendations are in the form: . Proposed minimum changes to enable water organisations to function, regardless of delivery vehicle. . Areas where desirable improvements which could be addressed in current or pending wider reviews . Functions and powers relating to infrastructure . The policy issues arising from water services infrastructure powers concern work on land and controls over connections to infrastructure. Current powers arise from the LGA, the Local Government Act and the Health Act . Powers to carry out work on land in relation to water services infrastructure . These powers enable councils to work on land for water services infrastructure, including install ing and maintain ing infrastructure on land they do not own. Immediate change is not required because c ouncils already have the ability to retain or delegate current powers, regardless of whatever delivery vehicle they adopt. Current legislation is outdated and hard to navigate which does lead to unnecessary compliance costs and c onsolidation and modernisation is desirable , but not essential . . A more concise and coherent approach is certainly possible , including alignment with the type of access powers other utilities have, including powers such as access to Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs The Department of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua INCONFIDENCE Page of road reserves, providing additional safeguards for landowners (such as escalation processes for disputes), and better recognition and protection for Mori land. . However, we recommend no significant change in this area in Bill , but rather that options for improvements be considered once the initial implementation stage of Local Water Done Well is completed so we can learn from early adopters . Legislative design will consider the question raised by TAG whether greater clarity for the delegation of existing powers is needed . Power to control connections . These powers enable councils to control connections to water services infrastructure, a critical aspect of new housing developments . Immediate change is not required for Local Water Done Well because c ouncils already have the ability to retain or delegate current powers, regardless of whatever delivery vehicle they adopt. . However, as with land works discussed abov e, current provisions are outdated and hard to navigate, resulting in high compliance costs. The TAG advised improvements were desirable but that the current legislation was adequate and was able to be supported with commercial practices . . Previous work proposed a clearer process which connected to the Building Act and the RMA . The key elements were a streamlined three stage approval process and a framework for Development Codes . . Local authority regulatory powers . Power to make controlled drinking water catchments . Power to control drinking water catchments is an important tool for ensuring drinking water quality. It enables the specification of catchments and control of access into the catchments, which might be requested for a range of purposes, such as predator control or tourismrecreation. Currently it derives from a mix of statutory provisions and bylaws (LGA ss ) which means there is some inconsistency and therefore uncertainty nationally . . The Water Services Entities Act provided a new streamlined system, modelled on Victoria, Australia, which allowed water services entities to specify land a controlled drinking water catchment area and govern that area via a catchment management plan. This approach was supported by many councils in their ()(f)(iv) ()(f)(iv) Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs The Department of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua INCONFIDENCE Page of submissions, but the transition will be complex and interim transitional arrangements would be needed . . We recommend that change is not an immediate priority for Local Water Done Well , because water organisations can be expected rely on the cooperation of their council owners . Again, after the initial implementation stage, the priority for change in this area will be clearer , including whether legislative change is needed at all . Trade waste regulation . Trade waste is any commercial and industrial liquid waste disposed of and discharged into the wastewater system, above what would be disposed of in a domestic household (e.g. from breweries, laundromats, food premises, dental surgeries ). It is distinct from major commercial and industrial liquid waste disposal and discharges which are controlled by requirements under RMA plans and consents. . Trade waste systems are currently largely controlled by local bylaws . There are large variations in approaches between councils and problems arising from lack of infringement powers. Relevant powers in the LGA would benefit from modernisation and standard requirements which would support a more consistent approach to case bycase decisions across the country . . Water supply and wastewater regulation . Both LGA and the Local Government Act are regarded as functioning adequately to enable water supplies and wastewater management, largely via bylaws . Water supply bylaws are mainly used to manage demand (e.g. during droughts) and set rules for doing things like filling or emptying swimming pools. . Compliance and enforcement for regulatory functions . LGA sets out a regime with enforcement officers who have a broad mandate over all bylaws, but it is out of and patchy. Bylaws vary between councils, so some will need to standardise their regimes to enable the smooth functioning of water organisations with combined council ownership . Such changes will be possible under the existing legislation, as well as necessary delegations for compliance, monitoring and enforcement functions by water organisations , so no immediate changes are necessary for Bill . Offence regimes are always needed to underpin statutory or regulatory requirements, and must accompany any new statutory powers or requirements. Therefore, new offences may be required as a consequence of any decisions about new substantive powers. . Next steps . Appendix A summarizes our recommendations, following discussion with TAG. Following your decisions, a draft Cabinet paper will be prepared for consultation with TAG and relevant agencies in time for consideration by Cabinet in July . . In the many areas where there are possible improvements that are not immediately needed for water organisations to function, the Department will ensure that lessons from the initial experience of water organisations , as well as relevant previous work with necessary modifications , is fed into wider work programmes, including inter agency work such as and RMA reform . Participation in gambling Most New Zealanders gamble at least occasionally. The most popular forms of gambling in were New Zealand Lotteries Commission products (), followed by informal gambling (), sports, dog or horserace betting (), gaming machines at a pub or club (), gaming machines at casinos (.) and table games at casinos (.). I propose prioritising limits on the rates of increase and some price stability, even if this means it takes l onger to remove distortions and cross subsidies from existing pricing structures. To avoid conflicts and tensions between different pricing objectives (particularly in the short term), there will be a clear hierarchy for the implementation of different pricing policies and levers. . Context Digital identity and online service delivery Many government and private sector services are now online. In keeping with this digital environment, New Zealanders expect to be able to access services and complete transactions remotely, rapidly , and with minimal paperwork. However, many online transactions that require the provision of digital identity information such as online banking, claiming a welfare payment , or opening a utili ties account online need high levels of security to ensure users personal information is safe and their privacy is protected. While the use of digital identity services is generally seen as being efficient and provides more opportunities for individuals than paper based identity systems, it also comes with risks. Unlike written or spoken information, digital information can be more easily accessed, copied and shared from anywhere in the world. Unfortunately, we are now facing increasing fraud and securit y risks because of the rapid evolution of global digital sharing. It is important for people to feel secure and confident in using digital identity services, including being in control of their information and who has access to it. A survey by Digital Identity N ew Zealand found of New Zealanders are concerned about the protection of their identity and use of personal data by organisations. Moreover, nine out of ten New Zealanders stated the idea of being more in control of their digital identity is appealing. This suggests there is a low level of confidence in the current state of the digital identity system. Trust Framework Purpose and b enefits The Trust Framework will help ensure the provision of more secure and trusted digital identity services for New Zealanders The Digital Identity Services Trust Framework Act will establish : a legal framework for the provision of secure and trusted digital identity services for individuals and organisations; and transparent governance and accreditation funct ions that incorporate te ao Mori approaches to identity. The Trust Framework will make it easier for individuals (users) to securely access and share information about themselv es with relying parties through regulated TF providers. It will also reduce transaction costs for relying parties that need verified identity and other personal information to provide their services.

The nature of gambling harm While most New Zealanders gamble without experiencing any apparent harm, a significant minority do experience harm from their gambling, including negative impacts on their own lives and the lives of others. Harm may include damage to relationships, emotional and psychological distress, disruptions to work or study, loss of income, the financial impacts of gambling, and potentially fraud and related crimes, which can also impact negatively on the gambler s family , whnau and community . It may also cause financial stress and anxiety and contribute to child neglect and family violence (Government Inquiry into Mental Health and Addiction ). Measurement of gambling harm We can measure gambling harm by various means. The Problem Gambling Severity Index (PGSI) differentiates between different types of harm and frequency of harm occurring, as reported by survey respondents. The PGSI is commonly used to screen and categorise three levels of harm: severe or high risk (problem gambling), moderate risk and low risk. While the proportion of the New Zealand population at risk of gambling harm as measured by the PGSI is currently at the lowest level seen for years, the level of harm in the overall population has remained relatively stable for the last five to seven years (at about ) (Abbott et al ; ThimasarnAnwar et al ). This plateau effect has also been observed overseas (Abbott ). Another measure of gambling harm is the burden of harm impact on healthrelated quality of life. Research shows that the total burden of harms gamblers experience, in terms of the decrease to healthrelated quality of life years , is greater than that people with common health conditions (such as diabetes and arthritis) experience, and approaches the levels seen with anxiety and depressive disorders. Importantly, the harm attributable to gamblers partaking in lowrisk gambling was significant, at nearly percent of all gambling harm. Recent research shows that one in five New Zealand adults () is affected some at time in their lives by their own gambling or the gambling of others. Estimates suggest that, in New Zealand in , , people aged years or older were at high risk of harm from gambling or are problem gamblers , about , were at moderate risk and a further , were at low risk but would experience gamblingrelated harm during their lifetime. Forms of gambling associated with gambling harm Some features andor modes of gambling are particularly associated with harm. Research both internationally and in New Zealand clearly shows that gambling harm is far more likely to be associated with continuous forms of gambling (in which a gambler can immediately reinvest winnings in further gambling, such as NCGMs and casino table games) than with any other mode of gambling. Online gambling and gaming The study Measuring the Burden of Gambling Harm in New Zealand estimated that years of life lost to incapacity as a result of harms from gambling was , in . Of this number, , were lost to gamblers themselves and , were lost to people effected by someone else s gambling. The review indicated that t here ar e a variety of rules that govern the use of personal and organisational information in New Zealand. These include : overarching legislation such as the Privacy Act which con trols how agencies collect, use, disclose, store and give access to personal information . identity related legislation such as the Electronic Identity Verification Act , which regulates the operation of the governments RealMe service , and the Identity Information Confirmation Act . sector specific legislation such as the AntiMoney Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act which aims to prevent money laundering and terrorist financing in New Zealand . standards like the Evidence of Identity standard which outlin es requirements for consistent identity establ ishment and confirmation by agencies (currently being ) . While this current regulatory environment enables some trust in the digital identity ecosystem, it does so in a restricted fashion, for example: The different legal requirements and definitio ns (e.g. for identity) for different sectors can result in a siloed approach to services. . Gambling harm needs assessment The Act requires the Ministry to undertake a needs assessment to inform the development of the strategy. The needs assessment looks at facts and figures about gamblingrelated harm in New Zealand to highlight any gaps between the research evidence, population needs, service provision and the strategy s goal. This helps to determine the most appropriate distribution of health services to promote better health outcomes for the population. To help prepare the needs assessment, the Ministry contracted an independent research organisation, Sapere Research Group, to review needs in the sector. The Sapere needs assessment report (Rook et al ) is available on the Ministry s website together with a table listing the report s recommendations and the Ministry s proposed response to them. Together, these documents form the Ministry s needs assessment that has informed the strategy s development. In summary, the needs assessment identifies that the key needs are much the same as they were when the Ministry developed the service plan for to in . There is provision for dedicated Mori, Pacific and Asian services and activities , as these are the most vulnerable populations. The needs assessment also suggests there is value in strengthening research and evaluation and in piloting new initiatives to address harm caused by persistent and relapsed moderate to highrisk gambling. It addresses concerns about the growth of internetbased gambling and the convergence between gambling and gaming: the Ministry proposes this as a research priority. Opportunities to learn Overall, Sapere found that: There are many opportunities to learn from best practice within New Zealand and create pilot service models to address service gaps. Work is needed to improve intersectorial relationships and make best use of the skills available within the industry as a whole to support those harmed by gambling (Rook et al ). In response, the Ministry notes the strategic goal for gambling harm reduction is Government, the gambling sector, communities, families and whnau working together to prevent and minimise gambling harm, and to reduce related health inequities (Ministry of Health ). The Ministry s statutory responsibility is to promote harm minimisation through an informed, resear chbased public health approach. www.health.govt.nzpublicationgamblingharmreductionneeds assessment (accessed November ). In this context, the gambling sector includes commercial and non commercial gambling operators (including NZRB and NZLC), member associations such as Clubs New Zealand Inc and Hospitality New Zealand, operators of gambling venues (including publicans and operators of retail outlets), providers of services to prevent and minimise gambling harm, and gambling researchers. . A populationbased public health approach The Act recognises the importance of prevention and a public health focus in addressing gambling harm. The Ministry proposes to continue using the continuum ofharm approach, which aligns a spectrum of gambling behaviour with a harm reduction framework, as first developed by Korn and Shaffer (). This approach recognises that people experience varying levels of harm from gambling. The framework, represented in Figure below, brings together the ideas of different levels of individual gambling behaviour, associated levels of harm and types of health intervention. The approach describes levels of gambling behaviour and associated harm as non problem (none), mild and moderate through to severe (problem) gambling. These categories can be overlaid with the three broad categories of population public health intervention s: primary , secondary and tertiary interventions. Figure also shows examples of the related types of activity that have been delivered through each current service plan. The categories of behaviour and harm have been aligned with the PGSI, which the Ministry uses to monitor the level of harmful gambling behaviour occurring in the New Zealand population. Figure includes the most robust estimates of the harm occurring for each category. The estimates are from a statistical metaanalysis of the pooled responses to the PGSI questions in the , and HLS. It is important to note that the PGSI measures the level of reported harm that is associated with the individual gambler and their immediately affected others (eg, family , whnau , employers and community groups ). While it is necessary to address the needs of those who have already developed a serious gambling problem and who need specialist help, early prevention interventions can help individuals and their family , whnau and communities avoid developing more risky gambling behaviours and associated har m. This approach aligns closely with other public health programmes in the mental health and addictions areas of alcohol, tobacco and drug use, and family, whnau and partner violence prevention. The estimates have been produced through the HLS Gambling module and the NGS, both of which the Ministry funds through the gambling levy. . Gambling harm inequality and inequity Improved health and equity for all New Zealand population groups is a government priority. To focus and prioritise gambling harm reduction activities in the next strategy period, the Ministry proposes to continue using a health inequality and inequity lens, which complements the public health approach by identifying areas where there are large differences in gambling harm experience between population groups. What the research tells us Gambling research shows there are inequalities and inequities attributable to gambling harm both in the New Zealand population and internationally (Canale et al ; KolandaiMatchett et al ; Rintoul et al ; Tu et al ; van der Maas ). An analysis of the responses to the HLS by a range of gambling predictors and population groups of interest (eg, ethnicity, gender, social deprivation) shows that inequalities and inequities have persisted for some time (ThimasarnAnwar et al ) . The HLS results for the period also show that while absolute levels of health inequ ality and inequity have reduced over time, relative levels of inequality and inequity between ethnic groups remain. In terms of overall gambling service u se, analysis indicates that there is substantive underu se of services by the Pacific and Asian groups. Similarly, an analysis using the social deprivation index shows significant inequality, disparity and inequity between New Zealand populations groups by socioeconomic status. Research also shows higher concentrations of class electronic gaming machines (NCGMs (ie, pokies) located in lower socioeconomic areas. Figure shows that approximately percent of all NCGMs (which is the source of the highest risk of harmful gambling activity) are located in the most socioeconomically deprived areas (ie, the poorest areas of the country). Economically, people in these areas can least afford financial losses from gambling. Based on NZDep census area units: University of Otago Wellington. Implementation No implementation planning has been done yet It has not been possible for the Electoral Commission to commence implementation scoping and planning as they have been occupied this year with implementing the changes to the Maori Electoral Option and preparations for the General Election. Also, policy decisions on the changes to be implemented are still being finalised. The proposed longer leadin time, for implementation by , will give the Electoral Commission the time to undertake the work required to design and secure funding for implementation. It will also allow enough time for local authorities and electoral service providers to carry out their implementation steps before the lower voting and candidacy ages apply for the first time. Civics education will be required We consider that lowering the voting age to needs to be supported by relevant civics education in schools. In its submission to the Justice Committee on the Declaration of Inconsistency, the Human Rights Commission noted the intrinsic link between the right to education and the right to participation in public and political life. The Taituara (Local Government Professionals) Electoral Reference Group also stressed the need for further, local government specific, civics education if these changes are implemented. The Ministry of Education has a fiveyear programme underway to refresh the New Zealand Curriculum, aimed at ensuring all students can contribute as active citizens now and in the future. The social sciences learning area is the first learning area to be refreshed and has been released. Social sciences is the primary learning area for civics and citizenship education , however, this will also be embedded across the reset of the curriculum as the remaining learning areas are refreshed over the next two years. Gambling Outcomes Monitoring Report (in publication) have all informed the development of the service plan set out below. The main changes in the service plan are to: expand the service mix to more closely match those available in the wider addiction and mental health sector (eg, peer support, residential care, consumer networks) foster codesign and establish a consumer (lived experience) network to inform services make greater use of pilot, evaluation and action research to inform service development. The service plan provides for the use of pilots to develop or trial new service models, particularly to address: gaps in current service provision public health , psychosocial and intervention services areas of systemic, persistent gambling harm, health inequities and gambling relapse technology to manage and mitigate gambling harm recovery services th at enhance the mana of service users and build their resilience. In addition, the service plan refocuses the mix of services for to: increase awareness of and engagement by those at risk (eg, by introducing a greater focus on health literacy, service responsiveness and gambling host responsibility) explore new intervention initiatives, based on learning about what works from the evaluation and research include an emphasis on addressing longstanding inequities for Mori and other ethnicities, through both culturally specific services and mainstream services maintain the emphasis on an outcomes and resultsbased approach to services, with a focus on achieving value for money alongside optimal service coverage. Strategic Intentions Ng Takune Rautaki Foreword from the Minister of Internal Affairs The Department of Internal Affairs (the Department) is dedicated to the effective delivery of its core services and its regulatory functions. From supporting key life events to preserving our nations heritage, supporting inquiries into matters of national significance and regulating charities services, their work impacts every New Zealander. Given the breadth of the Departments responsibilities, it is crucial that each component operates with efficiency and effectiveness while maintaining the integrity of services. As Minister, I am committed to ensuring that taxpayers funds are spent prudently, and they receive value for money. This involves identifying and managing fiscal risks, as well as finding areas where additional savings can be achieved. I have clearly communicated to the Department that our focus should remain on delivering the core functions that only the Government can provide. I am committed to working collaboratively with the Department, to ensure that the pursuit of efficiencies is an ongoing process, and that we continue to maintain a high standard of service delivery for the benefit of all New Zealanders. Statement of Responsibility I am satisfied that the information on strategic intentions prepared by the Department of Internal Affairs is consistent with the policies and performance expectations of the Government. During , we made a series of decisions to transform the three waters service delivery system through creation of four new water services entities. These decisions will be given effect through an initial piece of legislation the Water Services Entitie s Bill. . As signalled in my earlier papers, further policy decisions and legislation will be needed to fully develop the new system, operationalise the water services entities, and implement the reforms. These decisions are being sought through a further suite of papers, including this paper on pricing and charging arrangements for the new water services entities, an associated paper by the Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs, Economic regulation and consumer protection in the three waters sector , and a paper containing the remaining service delivery reform policy proposals Policy proposals for three waters service delivery legislative settings. . The first Bill is part of a broader, comprehensive suite of legislation, including a second Water Services Entities Amendment Bill, and a possible bill to provide for a new economic regulation and consumer protection framework for the three waters system. It is intended that this legislative programme will be fully enacted before the general election, to enable the water services entities to commence operation on July . . Three waters services are currently provided by territorial authorities, who charge for them through a combination of: . general rates (including uniform annual general charges); . targeted rates; . volumetric charges; . connection charges and other fees; and . development contributions. . The various charging mechanisms are applied in different ways by different territorial authorities. Some simply include water charges within general rates, others identify the water component of general rates, and others use targeted water r ates. Some territorial authorities use more utility type charging mechanisms based on the volumetric supply of water; and others a combination of the various mechanisms. . Moving to the delivery of three waters services by water services entities requires a shift away from the use of rates and other local government funding instruments to an approach based on direct billing. The proposals in this paper provide for this shift. Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government IN CONFIDENCE Page of Part A: Pricing objectives and relationship to economic regulation . The proposals in this paper relate closely to those of the Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs for the economic regulation of water services and should be considered alongside that paper. The proposals for economic regulation focus on ensuring that water services entities face regulatory disciplines and incentives to operate efficie ntly to minimise the long run costs of water service to consumers. The focus of this paper is on how water services entities distribute those costs between consumers. . In developing the two papers, I have worked closely with the Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs to ensure alignment across the various proposals. The companion paper proposes that the economic regulation regime will initially focus on ensuring the water services entities provide robust information to support the scrutiny and benchmarking of performance of those entities, supported by quality standards and performance requirements. . While legislation will provide for the economic regulator to set an entity specific revenue cap, this is not proposed to be put in place until commencement of the second economic regulatory period, around . In the period prior to implementation of economic regulation, this paper proposes pricing controls to limit increases in prices and price shocks. Similarly, this paper proposes using many o f the same types of tools and processes as the economic regulation paper, such as input methodologies and determinations. It also proposes roles for the economic regulator in the regulation of water services entity pricing and charging. . To ensure that pric ing and economic regulation work well together, they need to have similar objectives. If not designed well, pricing and economic regulation can pull in opposite directions. In Tasmania, for example, the politicised price setting process for water services has led to prices well below the maximum allowed under regulation. This under pricing means that they have a growing gap between the revenue from water services and the investment needed to deliver reasonable quality services.

. Reporting Overview The Act enables the regulations to establish TF provider reporting requirements. Proposed regulations Annual Reports : The regulations wi ll require every TF provider to deliver an annual report to the TF Authority that contributes to their ability to monitor and assess the performance of each TF provider and the overall regulatory system. Annual reports will need to include information in a form specified by the TF Authority on: Organisational Governance and Management: Organisational governance and management arrangements , and the personnel responsible for them . Service use: Service transaction volumes , and the types of parties accessing each accredited service . Service Delivery: Steps taken to ensure accredited services are delivered in accord ance with required service standards ; any breaches of service standards , and actions taken to remedy them ; and s teps taken to improve service delivery . Complaints and Disputes Resolution: Number and type of complaints made to the provider ; and the outcomes achieved by internal complaints and disputes resolution processes, including instances where the TF provider has upheld the complaint and implemented remed ies to ensure its service meets compliance requirements . Fraud: Any attempted fraud events , and the actions taken to address them . Financial Performance: The TF providers financial position and performance. This is a form of self assessment and reporting , which enables the TF Authority to provide oversight of TF providers without going through a full reaccreditation process each year. Other Reporting: We also propose that t he regulations will require every TF provider to submit separate reports with in working days covering any actual or suspected fraud events, or any other events that adversely affect confidentiality, the integrity or availability of the digital identity service , and has caused or present s a risk of serious harm. For the avoidance of doubt , the regulations will also refer to TF providers obligations under the Privacy Act to report privacy breaches that have caused serious harm to the Privacy Commission and require the provider to also inform the TF Authority. These reporting requirements are designed to ensure the TF Authority is aware of significant events , and is able to intervene or assist to resolve issues where appropriate. The regulations will also require TF providers to report to the TF Authority on any changes to the orga nisations people, operating policies, processes , or systems that have a material impact on their ability to meet accreditation requirements as specified in the Act, rules , or regulations. Estimates provided by TAB NZ in December . qwkdm ()(b)(ii) ()(b)(ii) ()(b)(ii) Regulatory Impact Assessment f) not require operators to make funding returns to the community; and g) require strong enforcement levers, including the ability for the regulator to take enforcement action against non licensed operators to maximise compliance. . The Minister of Internal Affairs is to report back to Cabinet in October on further details on these proposals. . These proposals however only cover online casino gambling (e.g. online casino table games and online pokies) and do not cover online sports and race wagering. . For TAB NZ to enter into the online casino market would require amendment to the Racing Act. The Minister for Racing has ruled out making such a change and consider s TAB NZ should only operate in its traditional wagering space. . While there will not be a direct impact on the way TAB NZ operates under the online casino proposal as licenced operators will not be able to offer or advertise sports or racing betting , the changes are still likely to strengthen the position of some of TABs closest competitors in New Zealand. This is due to the proposal for licensed operators to be able to advertise as part of licensing conditions. Most of the global operators, who currently are not permitted to advertise to New Zealanders, offer one stopshops (casino, sports and lottery products) so it is possible that sports and racing products offered by licensed casino operators may benefit from increased brand recognition, even if permitted advertising is limited to solely casino products (and licenced operators are not permitted to cross pollinate and use casino products to promote sports and race wagering in offshore related companies ). . These risks heighten the need to ensure legislative settings protect the financial sustainability of TAB NZ in order to improve the long term of the financial sustainability racing industry. What is the policy problem or opportunity . TAB NZ is increasingly under threat from the loss of revenue to offshore operators , which puts the longterm financial sustainability the New Zealand racing industry at risk from the period (when minimum guaranteed payments in the Entain agreement cease) . . The New Zealand racing industry is almost wholly reliant on TAB NZ for funding . Despite TAB NZs monopoly on land based sports and racing betting in New Zealand and the significant cash injection because of the recent TAB NZ Entain partnership, TAB NZ s distributions to the racing industry (and sporting organisations) are increasingly under threat from offshore operators which threatens the racing industrys ongoing financial sustainability. . Many of these offshore operators are larger than TAB NZ, with greater product range, better odds , and crucially, have no overall financial obligations to the racing industry (besides paying the Point of Consumption and Betting Information Use Charges ). There also will be other offshore operators offering sports and racing betting to New Zealanders, who are not paying GST or the POCC.

The consultation page can be accessed from the WSAs website. WSA are also notifying suppliers of the consultation through social media channels. Members of their Technical and Operations teams are presenting on the findings of our public reporting and will be available throughout the conference to engage with attendees. Department of Internal Affairs NG TAKUNE RAUTAKI STRATEGIC INTENTIONS Mtauranga Mori is respected and valued Developing our approach to Mtauranga Mori We recognise that we need to develop our own approach and understanding of mtauranga Mori. We want our engagement with Mori, their taonga and mtauranga to be genuine, meaningful and live up to the commitments under Te Tiriti o Waitangi. In the culture, heritage and information management sectors, we want to ensure that we understand what mtauranga Mori is, what it means for the work that we do, how we can see ourselves in this work, and what our collective contribution will be. This will inform the way that we partner with Mori to support them to reach their aspirations in caring for their mtauranga. We are also supporting the revitalisation of te reo Mori through our shared commitment under Maihi Karauna. We will be looking at ways to develop staf capability, enabling kura and iwi to engage with us in te reo me na tikanga Mori and having more resources available for learning. Te Ara Taonga and Treaty Settlement obligations To better support iwi, hap and Mori aspirations in the culture and heritage space, agencies in the sector made a commitment to approach Treaty settlements collectively through Te Ara Taonga (led by the Ministry for Culture and Heritage). As New Zealand begins to move towards an increasingly postsettlement world, we recognise the opportunity that Te Ara Taonga provides to be proactive in our future thinking on MoriCrown partnerships as a sector. We understand the barriers and frustrations that many hap, iwi and Mori face having to engage on the same kaupapa with a range of diferent ministries and departments within the same sector. As a sector we want to work beyond Treaty settlements to create an approach that focuses on fostering efective, practical and sustainable partnerships with Mori, and supports their future aspirations for their mtauranga and taonga. The interagency relationships created through Te Ara Taonga provide a significant platform for pursuing opportunities to support iwi researchers and students to engage in, and with, the culture and heritage sector. Together with Ng Taonga Sound Vision and Te Papa Tongarewa we will work together to design and develop a week experience for iwi researchersstudents that supports them to meet the culture and heritage aspirations of their iwi and tell their stories. , in June . Despite the decline in venue and machine numbers, total NCGM expenditure continues to increase. NZLC s annual report states that in that year there were , lottery outlets in its retail network and , registered MyLotto account holders. NZRB s annual report states that in that year there were retail TAB outlets, and that more than , TAB account holders plac ed a bet in . It also reports that of the TAB operated venues hosted gaming machines (compared with TAB venues hosting gaming machines in ). There are six casinos in New Zealand: one each in Auckland, Hamilton, Christchurch and Dunedin and two in Queenstown. They operate a total of just over , gaming machines and just under table games. The Christchurch Casino was the first to open, in . The Hamilton casino was the last, in . The Act prohibits any more casinos. The Auckland casino generates approximately threequarters of New Zealand s casino gambling expenditure. Since , several analyses have shown an association between numbers of NCGM venues, numbers of NCGMs and NCGM expenditure on the one hand and higher deprivation on the other. Most recently, the Gambling Harm Reduction Needs Assessment (Rook et al ) shows that gambling outlets tend to be located in areas with a higher social deprivation rating; for example, about percent of all NCGMs are located in areas with a high social deprivation rating. Section . discusses this further. Online gambling Significantly, as shown above, an increasing number of people in New Zealand purchase NZLC products or place bets on NZRB products online. There are concerns about the growing opportunities for online gambling, including those offered by overseasbased gambling operators, and their potential to increase harmful gambling behaviour. Submissions on the strategy from service providers and health groups expressed concerns about the ubiquitous nature of online gambling and gaming convergence (see below): particularly in terms of the potential impact on vulnerable groups including Mori and Pacific youth. Observation of patterns of online gambling in overseas jurisdictions has led to stakeholders expressing concerns that New Zealanders participation in online gambling may dramatically increase. An increase in online gambling overseas is attributed to the growth in online providers and products facilitated by rapid changes in technology, increasing ease of access to the internet, and the widespread prevalence of digital devices. Previous research into New Zealanders overseas gambling patterns has shown very low participation rates and low levels of reported expenditure.
