In September , the Australian G overnment announced investment of an additional . million into the governments digital identity programme. This is on top of previous investment of . million. s()(f)(iv) Proactively Released INCONFIDENCE Page of We propose g overnmen t investment aligns with the new digital identity approach underpinned by the Trust Framework . Government investment needs to support a fundamentally different approach to digital identity enabled by the Trust Framework to increase utility and realise benef its. We need to take advantage of the innovation offered by private sector providers . At the same time, we also need to consider the trust provided by a Government branded service as well as how the technical infrastructure that underpins RealMe services can be repurposed to support the new approach. . Future government provided digital identity services and technical infrastructure needs to be modernise d to ensure interoperability with other digital identity solutions operating under the upcoming Trust Framework . This will enable greater collaboration as well as wider choice for users, agencies and organisations about the digital identity services they use. As with private providers, future government digital identity services accredited under the Trust Framework will need to meet the rules currently being developed , including for security and information management. As part of this change , there would also be an opportunity to rebrand as well as reposition government provided RealMe serv ices. . Officials have engaged with stakeholders (including public agencies, Crown agents and entities, private digital service providers, financial institutions and academic institutions) and looked internationally to identify the infrastructure needed for the digital identity system to function effectively and to realise the benefits for people, government and the economy. A key change to increase utility is modifying the digital identity credentials issued by government to verifia ble identity credentials that will comply with future standards under the Trust Framework. . People that choose to use these verifiable identity credentials issued by government will be able to store the credentials on their personal device via an a pp or in an online account . They could then choose to share them to show who they are to access services. People will also be able to use a verifiable identity credential to identify and link other information about them held by agencies and organisations. This will provide a foundation to enable people to share more information about themselves in a safe and secure way. For example, a builder or electrician that needs to show their professional credentials to access a site could use the verifiable identity credential to establish who they are . They could then link their identity to other information such as their professional registration and share it using a digital tool, probably on a mobile phone, enabling them to start work on the sit e faster. . Further details about the verifiable identity credential and the other key technical components required, which include a common verification service as well as solutions to enable people to claim information about themselves and share it to access services (such as a digital wallet), are attached as Appendix C. Alternative directions have been considered and discounted . We consider that government has a continued role in providing digital identity services and infrastructure. The alternative of government exiting the provision of digital identity services has been discounted for the reasons set out below. Proactively Released Proactively Released Proactively Released Proactively Released INCONFIDENCE Page of . While initial investment would be required for the Department to develop services and for agencies to tr ansition to greater use of digital identity to improve their services, the re would be opportunities for cost saving in the long term from more efficient processes to verify identity and prove eligibility for services . Additionally, a ll three investment options could have significant benefits compared to costs . The Department has identified these benefits by working with a range of agencies to identify potential use cases where digital identity solutions could help deliver better services. The Department will work with early adopter agencies . To realise these benefits, regardless of the investment option chosen, organisations and agencies will need to make attributes they hold available and be ready to receive attributes digitally to provide services . We propose a staged approach based on what changes would add value to people and what agencies are ready to make a change. As a first step, the Department will work with the Accident Compensation Corporation, the Ministry of Education, the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment, the Ministry of Social Development, the Ministry of Health and Waka Kotahi NZ Transport Agency (Waka Kotahi) to investigate mak ing more attributes available by consent andor change how they receive information to provide better digital services. . Working with these early adopter agencies will help seed the digital identity system. This will then position the digital identity system to grow more rapidly in the future with a range of public and private organisations using the digital identity system to deliver more online services. . To support this transition, the Government Chief Digital Officer will also work with agencies to ensure that their digital investment plans support this change . In time a gencies will be expected to participate in the digital identity system underpinned by the Trust Framework to improve the services they provide to people. . This will be a significant transformation for agencies and different sectors, with funding and resources , and legislative changes in some instances required to enable this change. For example, Waka Kotahi could undertake a greater role in the digital identity system by providing greater access to driver licencing information while also relying on modernised digital identity services to improve its identity verification proc esses when issuing licences. This would involve significant changes to Waka Kotahis technology systems, application processes and the legislation that governs some of its services. This means that appropriate funding and prioritisation for related changes will be critical because the driver licensing regime is funded on a cost recovery basis through regulated driver licensing fees paid by licence applicants. Waka Kotahi has indicate d that it is not in a good position to pay for this transformation out of existing funding . . Given the impact on agencies, it will be important for them to actively participate in this system transformation . Cross agency governance arrangements will be impo rtant to ensuring that this is achieved.

Proactively Released by the Department of Internal Affairs Cafe The cafe trial (cafe, n) was performed on Friday th May, at a local cafe in Hamilton, New Zealand. This trial was a minute set of scripted interactions between nine participants, however, the cafe was also open to the public and there were customers present who were not participating in the trial. These customers did not affect the planned scripted interactions in any way. The scripted interactions included queuing to make an order, serving customers, bringing an order to a table, oneonone , passing by outside the restaurant. For example, the chef only interacted with the frontofhouse server, and none of the (participant) customers.

Results . Technical challenges Card firmware was one of the major challenges encountered during the study period. A full description of these issues can be seen in Appendix . The first major firmware issue was caused by putting the cards into sleep mode immediately after updating the f irmware (before seeing other cards), which caused the cards to not roll their card logging process. Consequently, all cards had to be re written before the study period, which delayed card distribution by sev eral hours on May . The second major firmware i ssue was a flash memory write exception that caused a card reset after the flash write, leading to cards capping their records at a certain point. All cards had to be recalled on the morning of May and re written with a new firmware v... Due to parti cipants working schedule, the last cards were not returned until May Consequently, all data before the rewrite was removed and the start time for each participant is staggered. UWB devices also had som e minor technical difficulties that lead to some initial data loss. One issue was the bespoke application sometimes crashed when a UWB device was attached. There was reoccurring problem with UWB device that was unable to write its data to a file. Finall y, on Day UWB device power buttons came loo se from the circuit board. For each problem, the research team provided timely troubleshooting that enabled all five UWB devices to stay in the field for the duration of the study. Additionally, in post proce ssing, the missing data was reconstructed using data from the other devices. With regards to the Qualtrics daily diary survey, there were two small technical problems encountered by participants on the Day survey. A University of Otago researcher addressed this by making the box free text so it would accept any response. The second technical problem arose from an error message not found and Qualtrics tech support suggested the link may have been cut off in a multi page SMS. As a result, we placed the link very early in the SMS message to avoid issues around page cut offscharacter limit per page. . However, the extent of the laws impact on freedom of expression is not yet clear. The United Kingdoms (UK) Online Safety Bill (proposed legislation) . On December , the UK released its Full Government Response to the Online Harms White Paper and has since announced an Online Safety Bill will be introduced in . The Response paper builds on the Online Harms White Paper in April , which proposed a comprehensive regulatory framework, addressing a spectrum of online harms from illegal to legal but harmful content. . The Bill proposes a new regulatory system for online content, which creates a duty of care on online platform operators to protect their users. Platforms in scope are hosts of usercontent which can be accessed by users in the UK; andor facilitate public or private online interaction between service users, one or more of whom is in the UK; and search engines. . The duty of care framework is aimed to be proportionate and risk based, ensuring companies in scope have the appropriate systems and processes in place to respond to harmful content and activity, while protecting users rights. The regulatory framework will be set out and overseen by its existing communications regulator (Ofcom), which will be given broad powers, including the ability to enforce fines of up to million or annual turnover. . The regulatory framework will have a twotiered approach, imposing additional requirements on the most highrisk, highreach services (category ), to the requirements of most services (category ). The European Union (EU) Digital Services Act (proposed legislation) . The EU Digital Services Act proposes to impose a uniform set of obligations on all online platform operators. These obligations are procedural rather than outcome focused, for example social media companies must have a complaints system. Platforms only have obligations to remove illegal content once they have knowledge of it on their platform. . Platforms with more than million EU users ( of the EU population) have additional requirements to smaller platforms. The Irish Online Safety and Media Regulation Bill (proposed legislation) . The Irish Online Safety and Media Regulation Bill proposes: to replace the existing broadcasting regulator with a new regulatory agency that will have responsibility for both traditional and new media; to update and align the way traditional television broadcasting and video on demand services are regulated; and to establish a regulatory framework to control the spread and amplification of defined categories of harmful online content. . The regulator will be given the power to set codes to govern the standards and practice of regulated entities.

Given the urgency, I consider there is a need to pass a standalone amendment to allow Class operators to continue to sell lottery tickets remotely and continue their important work in the community . A permanent provision would continue the arrangement that has been in place for the last four years , as well as being an appropriat e response to the change to the fundraising environment i.e. New Zealanders wanting to buy tickets without cash . It means there is no additional call on other community funding sources , for example, lottery grants, Class (pokies) gambling, and other phil anthropic sources, or on the Government to support these causes. Implementation My intention is for the permanent provision to be in place by October , before the temporary exemption expires. This is the only way to provide the most certainty for Class operators, who do not want to break the law and want to raise money in the most efficient and effective way possible . As the proposal simply makes the current arrangement permanent, there are no implementation implications for the regulator . Cost ofliving Implications There are no cost ofliving implications associated with this proposal. Buying lottery tickets from Class operators is a discretionary decision for individuals. Financial Impli cations There are no financial implications associate d with this proposal. Funding of the gambling regulator that grants Class licences is covered by fees from the operators. The Government response to the report of the Working Group for Reducing Barriers to Changing Registered Sex, approved by Cabinet on April , goes so me way to removing some of the access barriers. I have acknowledged, however, that that Working Group report was clear that its proposed improvements were not a substitute for law change in this area . An accessible process that works for transgender and intersex New Zealanders is important . Birth certificates are not intended to provide conclusive evidence of someones identity. However, they are often used by people to prove they are New Zealand citizen s with the right to work and study i n New Zealand. There are many p rocesses where birth certificate s can be requested , includ ing setting up a bank account or enrolling a child in school. While other documents can be used in man y of the same processes (such as a passport or driver licen ce), birth certificates are often more practical as they are low cost and do not expire. . Any situation where a birth certificate is requested can be distressing for transgender and intersex people if the sex recorded does not align with their gender. It can pla ce an extra administrative burden on transgender and intersex people to prove who they are. It creates a risk of people being outed as transgender or intersex or subject to discrimination. These experiences impact the wellbeing of transgender and interse x people , which contributes to higher rates of psychological distress, harmful substance use, and suicidal ideation and behaviour . . Being able to have their gender recognised on a birth certificate is likely to have symbolic importance to transgender and in tersex New Zealanders. It shows that the government recognises who they are, supporting their sense of belong ing and wider social cohesion. I have considered options to improve the process to amend registered sex . I have considered alternative options to improv ing the process to amend registered sex, such as: . removing the Family Court from the process but still requiring evidence of medical treatment ; or . making improvements to the existing process , while retaining the Family Court and medical evidence re quirements. . On assessment, my preferred approach is a self identification process. It best meets my objectives for improving the process, including: . better reflect ing societ ys changing views on gender diversity ; . improving peoples control of how their gender is recognised , a deeply personal part of how a person understands and perceive s themselves ; . improving peoples sense of social belonging and their general wellbeing ; and . maintain ing public trust and confidence in how birth register information is used and maintained .

. On December we provided you with a briefing seeking your decisions on
. Plans to achieve financially sustainable delivery to regulated quality standards, including, for
. Pricing and charging decisions are closely connected to economic regulation. This paper should be considered alongside an associated paper by the Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs, Economic regulation and consumer protection in the three waters sector . It is also accompanied by a further paper, Policy proposals for three waters service delivery legislative settings , which contains the remaining policy proposals needed to implement the service delivery reforms. Relation to government priorities . This Government has ambitions to significantly improve the safety, quality, resilience, accessibility, and performance of three waters services, in a manner that is efficient and affordable for New Zealanders. . This is critical for public health and wellbeing, environmental outcomes, economic growth and job creation, housing and urban development, adapting to the impacts of climate change, building resilience to natural hazards, and improving outcomes relating to water services for iwiMori. s ()(f)(iv) Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government IN CONFIDENCE Page of . The status quo (with three waters services provided by local authorities) has resulted in poor health and environmental standards, deteriorating infrastructure due to sustained underinvestment, and wide variation in service quality. It has also resulted in a wide range of different approaches to charging for water services, including historic cross subsidies between different classes of consumers. Maintaining the current service delivery arrangements no longer represents a financially sustainable option for funding significant infrastructure costs. This is recognised as a key challenge by the local government sector, which the reforms, set out in a suite of papers last year, are intended to address. . In April , it was agreed that the Three Waters Review is a Government priority. The Labour Party Manifesto committed to reforming New Zealands drinking water and wastewater system and upgrading water infrastructure to create jobs across the country. These reforms are anticipated to occur in parallel with reforms to the resource management system. Executive summary . During and early , we made a series of decisions on a comprehensive package of proposals to transform the three waters service delivery system. This involves the creation of four publicly owned water services entities, which would take over responsibilities for service delivery and infrastructure from local authorities from July . These decisions are due to be given effect through an initial piece of legislation the Water Services Entities Bill. . The Water Services Entities Bill also sets out the process for water services entities to develop their funding and pricing plans, in consultation with local communities. The entity boards will present these plans to their regional representative groups. . As signalled in my earlier papers, further policy decisions and legislation will be needed to fully develop the new system, operationalise the water services entities, and implement the reforms. I am now presenting additional papers to seek those policy decisions, and to obtain legislative drafting authority relating to a second piece of legislation the Water Services Entities Amendment Bill. . This paper sets out my proposals for pricing and charging by the new water services entities. The entities need legislative authority to charge for their services and this paper seeks agreement to that. I am also proposing high level legislative principles to guide the development of their funding and pricing plans. . I have also sought to create options to manage specific issues, such as protecting vulnerable consumers and minimising price shocks to consumers through the initial transition period before the implementation of economic regulation. These options could be given effect through regulation making powers andor the Government policy statement on water services. I am also proposing further work on whether and how we should use these tools. . The paper is set out in five parts. . Part A covers the objectives for pricing and charging and the relationship between pricing and the broader economic regulation framework. Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government IN CONFIDENCE Page of . I am proposing a set of objectives to inform our decisions on pricing and charging. These objectives relate to economic efficiency, affordability, price stability, cost sharing, horizontal equity, intergenerational equity, giving effect to Te Mana o te Wai, and consistency with other government goals. . Part B addresses who should be liable for water services bills and how the interests of financially distressed consumers will be protected. . Currently, the owner of a property pays rates, which include a component for three waters services, albeit that the water related component is not separately identified in many districts. I am proposing that property owners will continue to be liable for the payment of water services bills, with owners of residential properties able to continue to pass through any consumption based charges to tenants. More than half of New Zealand households currently pay some form of volumetric water charge. . I am recommending regulation making powers to protect vulnerable consumers, in situations where they pay a volumetric water charge. These include a discretionary power to set a limit on the ratio between fixed and volumetric water revenues, so the total amount to be rec overed through volumetric charges can be capped to remain affordable for most low income households. The regulations could also create a prohibition on the use of block tariffs or low user charges for residential households. I am not recommending that it be mandatory that these regulations be made. . I am also proposing changes to the Rates Rebate Scheme to take account of water charges after these are split out from rates bills; and to include water charges in the definition of accommodation cost, which is used to determine the level of Accommodation Supplement. . I propose to monitor the adequacy of these measures and, if they are deemed insufficient, to consider further changes to support vulnerable consumers to pay their water bills. However, I do not think this is necessary at this stage. . Part C covers the price setting process, including the statutory provisions necessary for the pricing and charging of water services and other types of direction and decision making that will influence pricing and charging. . I am proposing a statutory basis for c harging, tariff lists, and a price setting process. Water services entities will have a variety of charges and a general statutory authority to charge. Their funding and pricing plans will set out prices, and these will be detailed in an annual tariff list . The legislation will provide that the water services entities can either bill customers directly, or the territorial authority can collect water charges on behalf of the entities. . I am also proposing a set of pricing principles be included in the legislation, to guide price setting. These would include that tariffs should be simple, transparent and easy to understand for users, be non discriminatory, reflect full cost recovery, and promote resource efficiency. Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government IN CONFIDENCE Page of . I am recommending that the economic regulator would be able to issue guidance, input methodologies, andor determinations to the water services entities on how to implement the legislative pricing principles and any regulations. The economic regulator would also have the power to alter tariffs if an entity were not implementing the legislative pricing principles or regulations appropriately. . Ensuring that the investment required to maintain, and upgrade water infrastructure is affordable for small communities is an important objective of the reform, and the sharing of costs between communities has featured strongly in the case for change. Geographically averaged prices can be used to smooth and share costs across communities, thereby contributing to more affordable services for all. It is a feature of the approach to charging for a range of different utilities, such as ultra fast broadband. I am proposing that the legislation enable geographic averaging of prices by water services entities. I am also proposing that the Government policy statement can be used to provide direction to water services entities on geographic averaging. This geographic averaging would be within a water services entitys boundary and could only be applied to residential customers receiving a similar level of service. Moving to harmonised prices will inevitably take several years, to smooth the impact of changes on individual customers. For that reason, I do not anticipate that entities would operate geographic averaging of prices in the early years of operation. . Part D discusses issues that will arise from the shift to more standardised, principles based pricing, and reg ulation making powers that could be used to manage prices and smooth price shocks over this transition. . Currently there are high levels of cross subsidy between different user groups, such as households and commercial users. I am proposing that all drinking water supply and wastewater removal contracts that are transferred to the water services entities will have their current pricing provisions expire after five years. The decision to override preexisting contracts is likely to attract some scrutiny. . To mitigate the risk of price shocks in the first few years, I am proposing a regulation making power to enable the Minister to directly regulate the rate of price increase. These powers would expire when the proposed approach to economic regulation is fully implemented in . Ultimately, some price increases are likely to be necessary to address decades of underinvestment. Decisions on the possible use of these powers requires further work, informed by more detailed analysis of current prices, and would be subject to a report back by December .

Water quality regulation will improve the performance of WDC and other councils in s upplying water services . There will be greater clarity regarding what requirements WDC must fulfil and resour ces to assist WDC in meet ing these requirements. .. Possible improvements from e conomic regulation regime have been overlooked The proposed economic regulation regime could improve WDCs performance . Economic regulation, if well designed, can enable benchmar king between providers and incentivise water service providers to improve service quality and lower costs. The details of the economic regulation regime have not been designed, and only high level descriptions of the regime are available . However, t he government and WICS have assumed that the proposed economic regulation regime either cannot apply to councils that opt out of the Reform Scenario , or will have no material effect on the performance of those councils . This assumption is flawed. Even if WDC is not subjected to econo mic regulation, it is likely to make improvements based on benchmarking and performance comparisons . Governments assumption that economic regulation cannot apply to numerous council owned water services is seriously flawed The govern ment assume s that it i s not feasible to regulate water service providers. Climate Implications of Policy Assessment . The Climate Implications of Policy Assessment (CIPA) team has been consulted and confirms that the CIPA requirements do not apply to this proposal as the threshold for significance is not met. Population implications . Proposals in the suite of Local Water Done Well paper s are seeking to ensure there is greater transparency to local communities about the current state of local government water services and councils proposed arrangements for delivering and funding these services in a financially sustainable way. Human Rights . The proposals across the suite of papers are intended to improve water services and therefore the right to access safe drinking water and sanitation, and the right to a health y environment. . Further work on the specific proposals in this paper relating to land access powers would consider the rights to respect for property. As noted earlier, currently there are powers to access land , but they are outdated, spread across multiple Acts and therefore uncertain in their application . The proposed approach is to simplify and clarify these matters, which supports respect for property rights by making those powers more certain and predictable in their use . Councils all over the country have increased their rates significantly in recent times. In some Australian states, rates increases are controlled by caps on noncore council activities. I have investigated the rate peg mechanism used in New South Wales, which regulates the total income councils can raise through rates by: . allowing councils to automatically increase their rates each year to keep pace with the estimated change in the costs of providing their current services and service levels to households, businesses and the broader community (their base costs); and . limiting the impact of rates increases on ratepayers, by ensuring councils cannot increase their rates income by more than the estimated change in their base costs, and that they engage with their communities if they propose a change in their rates income to fund improvements in the scope, quantity or quality of their services. I want to investigate a similar system for New Zealand that will protect ratepayers from excessive rates increases. This will significantly change the funding system for councils, but it will take time to design it in a way that has a meaningful impact on New Zealand communities and avoids unintended consequences. For any new system to be effective, it needs to balance the longterm interests of ratepayers, by having a positive effect on rates affordability, with the financial sustainability of councils, so they can continue delivering for their communities. I will report back to Cabinet in Quarter of seeking policy approval to lay the foundation for a system to limit councils rates revenue. FFF The government and its advisors have overlooked the global evidence of effective regulation applied to multiple water service entities . Some examples include: In Florida, the Public Service Commission regulates investor owned water utilitie s FFF. In Victoria, the Essential Services Commission regulates businesses providing urban water and sewerage services to residential customers FFF. In Western Australia, the Economic Regulation Authority regulates licensed water service providers FFF. Columbia has a regulatory regime sp anning , municipalities that provide water services either directly or via public service companies . It is a much less developed country than New Zealand , with a GDP per capita of just over , US FFF and has experienced benefits of economic regulation. The resources available for investment in the water service provisions have increased significantly over the last years since regulation began FFF. New Zealands Commerce Commis sion already has experience regulating multiple electricity distribution businesses . The Commerce Commission regulates electricity distribution under Part of the Commerce Act . It sets price and quality controls for local lines companies and set s quality stand ards in the form of annual limits for the average number and duration of power outages across the region. The Commission applies information disclosure regulation to a further consumer owned lines companies, thus having oversight for entities. In the period following the electricity reforms of the late s until , the Commission undertook price regulation of all electricity distribution businesses (even consumer owned ones). The Commerce Commission is likely to be the institution t hat regulat es the water sector (adding to electricity distribution , gas pipelines , airports, dairy and telecommunications). It has demonstrated an ability to regulate more than four entities concurrently, and therefore the assumption that it could not regu late more t han the four proposed water entities is mistaken. Strategic context and government priorities Strategic Intentions Ng Takune Rautaki Our strategic context Our strategic context has an impact on what we need to do to develop and evolve the services and functions we provide. Changes to our context can happen quickly, so we need to anticipate as much as possible to ensure we are wellplaced to adjust our goals and objectives. The key features of our current strategic context include: Economy New Zealands economy has faced several challenges in recent years, including rising inflation, higher unemployment, increased costs and slower growth. Global geopolitical issues have also caused impacts. Many New Zealanders are currently facing tough times, and the public service needs to assist by delivering more efficient, effective and responsive services. Government expectations Government expects public service agencies to deliver highquality, efficient and responsive services while managing costs effectively. The Government has emphasised the importance of fiscal discipline, innovation and collaboration to achieve better outcomes for New Zealanders. These expectations aim to ensure that public services remain trusted, highperforming and capable of meeting the needs of all New Zealanders. Extreme weather changes Extreme weather events are becoming increasingly frequent and intense due to climate change. Rising global temperatures contribute to more severe heatwaves, prolonged droughts and wildfires. The atmospheres increased capacity to hold moisture leads to heavier rainfall and more severe flooding. These changes pose significant risks to infrastructure, agriculture, health and communities in general, necessitating strategic planning and adaptation measures to mitigate their impacts. Understanding these impact trends is crucial for developing resilient systems and policies to protect communities and economies from the growing threat of extreme weather.Central and local government cooperation Central and local government cooperation in New Zealand is crucial for effective governance and delivery of public services. Neither central nor local government can effectively meet current challenges (such as infrastructure investment, the changing economic environment and impacts of climate change) that New Zealand faces over the coming decades on their own. Joinedup solutions, greater partnership and system side approaches to deliver services and infrastructure of national significance will be a feature of the coming years. Cybersecurity Technology provides opportunities within government for innovation, efficiencies and productivity gains. However, the vulnerability of critical services and personal data to disruption is a growing issue, whether through deliberate or inadvertent actions. The number of cybersecurity incidents is growing, and they range in scale from localised, specific attacks to global incidents affecting multiple countries simultaneously. Protecting against, and responding to, cybersecurity incidents is a challenge for all businesses, organisations and government. Digitising government Digital technologies underpin our economy and are driving global change across society and government. They offer significant opportunities for innovation, stronger productivity and more efficient people focused customer services. New Zealanders want to have choice and engage as easily and efficiently with government as they do with the private sector. People also expect government services to be safe and secure. To maintain the publics trust and confidence in government services, a joinedup service delivery and a seamless customer service experience is needed. Strategic context and government priorities Strategic Intentions Ng Takune Rautaki How we support the Governments priorities As part of the New Zealand public service, the Department of Internal Affairs contributes towards the Governments outcomes and objectives. This means we focus our efforts to support the Government to achieve its priorities. The Governments priorities are to: Build a stronger, more productive economy that lifts real incomes and increases opportunities for New Zealanders Deliver more efficient, effective and responsive public services to all who need and use them in particular to restore law and order, and improve health outcomes and educational achievement Get the Governments books back in order and restore discipline to public spending Strengthen democracy in New Zealand. What this means for us Our outcomes are broad because of the diverse range of responsibilities we have and the variety of ways in which we contribute to and support government priorities. Strategic Intentions Ng Takune Rautaki Our outcomes framework He papa whinga Our outcomes framework Strategic Intentions Ng Takune Rautaki Our performance framework We use outcome indicators to demonstrate the impact of the work we do to benefit New Zealand and those who live here. We use statistical surveys and other research from local and international sources to see whether trends over time represent good progress towards achieving the outcomes. Our performance measures assess whether we have achieved the desired results in specific services or functions that collectively support the overall achievement of our outcomes. These performance measures are set out in the Estimates of Appropriations for Vote Internal Affairs and are reported on each year in our Annual Report. We regularly review our outcome indicators and performance measures to ensure they remain relevant and meaningful. This includes establishing and embedding appropriate rules and regulations, to ensure that participants in the digital identity services ecosystem can trust that the digital identity information they provide or receive is accurate and secure. Barriers to digital inclusion are reduced People can access our services through multiple channels, and we use plain language and test designs with a range of people. Services are designed for any device and forms show only the necessary information this makes it easier for everyone. For people using nondigital services we provide downloadable forms, print on demand and support via phone, email or at counters to guide customers. We use translation services when needed to support customers. This will include implementing a Roadmap for modernising services, along with a work programme and a new approach to digital investment. This work will improve how New Zealanders experience digital government services, and help people and businesses quickly and conveniently access government services and information Work with government agencies to improve customer digital identity onboarding processes across service channels Emerging technologies like AI have the potential to revolutionise public services for New Zealanders. We will support government agencies to trial and safely use these emerging technologies, in ways that build system capability and confidence, while maintaining public trust in the public service. Taonga tuku iho rights are protected Through the Departments Mana rite Relationship Agreement we aim to codevelop responsive and accessible digital public services for Mori, supporting data sovereignty and collaborating with other agencies on Mori data governance. Many factors influence peoples sense of belonging and connection. When people lack a sense of belonging and feel excluded there are high social costs for individuals, communities and society. A collective memory contributes to a sense of belonging through knowledge and understanding of our history and culture. Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua Department of Internal Affairs IN CONFIDENCE Page of . In considering the Bill, the Select Committee had separately heard a petition proposing a selfidentification process for changing sex on a birth certificate. The BDMRR Act allows people to change the sex on their birth certificate through the Family Court, but the Select Committee heard this process is inaccessible for many people. The Act requires a person undergo medical treatment that meets certain criteria and identify as male or female (there is no nonbinary option). The Select Committee agreed with the concerns raised in the petition and amended the Bill accordingly. . The BDMRR Bill was deferred in February because of the selfidentification provisions the Select Committee introduced to amend the process for changing the sex recorded on birth certificates . The previous Minister set up a Working Group to recommend operational improvements ahead of legislative reform . When the previous Minister of Internal Affairs deferred the BDMRR Bill, she announced work to make practical improvements to the current process to change the sex recorded on birth certificates . The Working Group for Reducing Barriers to Changing Registered Sex (the Working Group) was appointed to advise on non legislative improvements. . The Working Group delivered its report in early . A Government response to the report was drafted by the Department in consultation with the Ministries of Justice, Education and Health, the Public Service Commission, and SportNZ. Consideration of the report and proposed response by relevant Ministers was delayed by the response to COVID . . The Working Group do es not consider its changes to be an alternative to legislative reform. This is because operational changes cannot change the medical treatment requirements, introduce a non binary option, or make the process accessible to those unable to meet requirements due to poor access to treatment or legal resources . INCONFIDENCE Page of is governed by a body that will maintain and update the Trust Framework and ensure it continues to protect the user consented sharing of information. . The establishment of a governance body will also help to ensure that the Trust Framework will continue to evolve an d iterate over time, along with the needs and expectations of participants. For example, Australias Trusted Digital Identity Framework is currently undergoing its fourth iteration since its establishment in . . A Trust Framework will create an enablin g regulatory environment that will support better information sharing and management practices, by establishing commonly adhered to best practice rules and standards in New Zealand. Principles would guide the development of the Trust Framework . Eight princi ples would guide the development of the Trust Framework in New Zealand. They are: people centred, inclusive, secure, privacy enabling, enabling of Te Ao Mori approaches to identity, sustainable, interoperable, and open and transparent. These principles al ign with the principles in the Data Protection and Use Policy (DPUP), developed by the Social Wellbeing Agency and work will continue to ensure ongoing alignment between the DPUP and the Trust Framework. Accelerating the implementation of the Trust Framewo rk in response to Covid Phase : an interim Trust Framework to allow compliance testing of digital solutions and the development of legislation ( to ) . We propose the establishment of an interim Trust Framework to allow compliance testing of dig ital identity solutions to begin in , while Trust Framework legislation is developed. Officials will develop the Trust Framework rules (largely based on existing and developing standards and legislation) and work with a limited number of entities to test their systems against the rules. This will allow providers to align their systems with the Trust Framework and ensure they are well positioned to become formally accredited once the Trust Framework is established in legislation. This interim function w ould be established in the Department of Internal Affairs (the Department) with the Government Chief Digital Officer (GCDO) but could move to another agency or organisation once the Bill is passed. . The interim Trust Framework would provide government with the ability to assess existing and emerging digital identity solutions to ensure they are meeting best practice. RealMe is likely to be one of the first services to be subject to a compliance test under the interim Trust Framework. RealMe will provide a t est case for how effectively the interim Trust Frameworks rules work. An interim cross agency governance group will approve standards and the compliance testing process . The interim Trust Framework governance group will be supported by a team based in the Department of Internal Affairs, who will continue to engage closely with stakeholders to develop the rules and continue to build relationships with communities, industry and Mori. Government Inquiry into the Response to the North Island Severe Weather EventsPreface John Ombler CNZM, QSO, Julie Greene, Sir Jerry Mateparae GNZM, QSO, KStJ (Chair), Rangimarie Hunia . In early , three devastating weather events struck the North Island of New Zealand within a sixweek period. The impacts of Cyclone Hale, the Auckland Anniversary heavy rainfall, and Cyclone Gabrielle will be felt for years to come. Fifteen people died, one person is still missing, and the lives of many more were forever changed. We acknowledge the gravity of these events, and the seriousness of our task. . Over the past eight months, our role was to identify lessons from the severe weather events, and to make recommendations for the design of New Zealands emergency management system. The aim is to improve our countrys readiness for, and response to, future emergencies. . The Inquiry takes a highlevel view and does not seek to apportion blame to individuals or entities. Where necessary to identify lessons, we have made it clear where we found the actions of those involved fell below what was needed. In doing so, we equally acknowledge that many who had a role in the response did their job with the best of intentions. . Seen as a whole, the emergency management system did not enable people to prepare for and respond to the severe weather events as needed. In some places, it failed. Many communities and CDEM agencies were not adequately prepared, communication and warnings were nonexistent or insufficient, and the capability and capacity of people and infrastructure was overestimated or lacking. . There were some successful aspects of the response, particularly in the way communities courageously supported each other. Councils, communities, and organisations that had planned and prepared ahead of time were better placed to respond effectively under the challenging circumstances. . As a country, we are not ready to respond to largescale emergencies. Significant changes to the design, funding and operation of our emergency management system are needed. . The wideranging recommendations in this report are interconnected and should be considered as a package. We are frustrated that many of these recommendations are not new and are suggested in previous reviews. . Even if fully implemented, these recommendations alone will not result in a fitforpurpose emergency management system. Without adequate investment in risk reduction and readiness, the impacts of disasters will continue to be devastating. . We gratefully acknowledge the individuals, communities, businesses, and government agencies who contributed to the Inquiry and shared their experiences. For many, the conversations evoked deep hurt, grief, and frustration. Your contributions were open, honest, and insightful, and we appreciate your generosity. . We also thank the Inquirys secretariat led by Anita Balakrishnan, and Counsel Assisting Esther Watt, who supported us in our engagements and the preparation of this report. . It was a privilege to undertake this Inquiry. This report reflects the voices we heard, encourages the change that is needed, and proposes an approach to emergency management that puts people and their communities at its heart. John Ombler CNZM, QSOJulie Greene Rangimarie Hunia Sir Jerry Mateparae GNZM, QSO, KStJ (Chair) EXECUTIVE SUMMARY ABOUT THE INQUIRY PREFACE RECOMMENDATIONS Government Inquiry into the Response to the North Island Severe Weather EventsAbout the Inquiry . In July , the Minister for Emergency Management established the Government Inquiry into the Response to the North Island Severe Weather Events under section () of the Inquiries Act . . The Inquirys Terms of Reference state its purpose is to ensure that the design of New Zealands emergency management system is appropriate to support readiness for, and responses to, future emergency events by identifying lessons from the following three events: Cyclone Hale, to January heavy rainfall from January to February in the Northland, Auckland, Waikato and Bay of Plenty regions (hereafter referred to as the Auckland Anniversary heavy rainfall), and Cyclone Gabrielle, to February . . A copy of the Terms of Reference is attached as Appendix A. . As required by the Terms of Reference, interim recommendations were provided to the Minister for Emergency Management and Recovery by December . The recommendations in the final report are largely the same in their intent. Any changes improved clarity and accuracy following further considerations and fact checking processes. . The Inquirys findings are based on common or systemic themes. In places, this report comments on the common experiences, challenges or actions of groups or organisations involved in emergency management readiness and response activities. These comments should not be read as referring to all organisations or groups falling within the relevant category. Examples include councils, CDEM Groups, CDEM agencies or iwi. The Inquiry focused on readiness and response . New Zealands approach to emergency management is based on four areas of interconnected activity known as the Rs: (risk) reduction, readiness, response, and recovery. . While reduction and recovery are not within the scope of this Inquiry, we have commented on these areas where there is a compelling reason to do so. This reflects that the Rs are part of an integrated approach to emergency management, and improvements in one area can lift performance in other parts. N ew Zealand Gazette, Establishment of the Government Inquiry Into the Response to the North Island Severe Weather Events. July . https:gazette.govt.nznoticeidgo The Rs are: Reduction Identifying and analysing risks to life and property from hazards, taking steps to eliminate those risks if practicable, and, if not, reducing the magnitude of their impact and the likelihood of their occurrence to an acceptable level. For example, flood protection infrastructure such as stopbanks. Readiness Developing operational systems and capabilities before an emergency happens; including selfhelp and response programmes for the public, and specific programmes for emergency services, lifeline utilities and other agencies. For example, community plans. Response Actions taken immediately before, during or directly after an emergency to save lives and protect property. For example, swift water rescues. Recovery The coordinated efforts and processes used to bring about the immediate, mediumterm, and longterm holistic regeneration and enhancement of a community following an emergency. For example, rebuilding a bridge. Evidence was gathered through meetings and written information . The Inquiry started considering evidence on July , and presented its report to the Minister for Emergency Management and Recovery on March . . Between August and February , we considered over interviews and information requests, received submissions, and conducted desktop research. Appendix B provides a list of those who contributed to the Inquiry. . Engagement was a significant part of our process. We visited the regions most affected by the weather events and met with community groups, volunteers, iwi, hap, sector representatives, and businesses. We interviewed leaders, experts and other staff from the entities involved in the emergency management system, including government agencies, councils, and emergency services. National Civil Defence Emergency Management Plan Order , section , . If the Ministry of Justice reviews the Adoption Act, this could be leveraged to review and improve our legislation . In early the Ministry of Justice proposed a review of the Adoption Act . The Department strongly supports this. We administer the day today systems relating to registering adoptions and provide access to information about adoptees and their birth parents under the Adult Adoption Information Act provisions. . Changes to the Adoption Act may result in changes to the way adoptions are registered under the BDMRR Act. This could provide an opportunity to rethink what information is recorded on a birth record, and which information is available to whom and when (as an adult or a child). This could also include different ways to record and report parental, family and iwi relationships for children adopted or born of surrogacy in New Zealand or born or adopted to New Zealand from overseas. The way we record relationships is changing and our systems may need to change too In a child was registered with both her biological mother (who provided the egg) and her gestational mother (who gave birth to her) listed on the birth certificate. The child was conceived using assisted reproductive technologies. Current ly only two parents can be included on a birth certificate. If the above family intended for a third parent, for example the biological father, to be an active part of the childs life, there is currently no way he could be included on the birth certificat e. . If the Ministry of Justice includes a review of the Adoption Act in its work programme during this parliamentary term, we will provide you with advice regarding the implications for BDMRR Act reform. Timing for this would depend on the priority it is given in the Justice work programme. Impact Summary: Changes to the process for establishing Mori wards and constituencies LGNZ, Elected members census Amendments to the Local Electoral Act made through the the Local Government Electoral Legislation Act (the LGEL Act). Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government Regulatory Impact Statement have resolved to establish Mori wards have chosen to engage with the community on this topic before making the decision. . The additional consultation requirements will : require councils that do not already have Mori wards to, at least every six years, consider whether to establish specific Mori representation; and require councils to engage with Mori and other communities , and have regard to their views , before making the decision. . These changes are due to come into force from October . The enhanced consultation requirements do not apply to council decisions on Mori wards between the period of the legislative amendment and these sections of the Act coming into force. . Under the st atus quo, we would expect a small number of additional councils to resolve to establish Mori wards over the next years, and those resolutions would not be subject to binding polls. Some councils may choose to conduct non binding polls. It is also possible that some councils may choose to disestablish their Mori wards. . We would only expect a small number of additional councils to establish Mori wards because of the constraints of the formula in the Act for calculating the number of Mori ward councillor positions. This makes it unlikely that councils with a very low Mori electoral population, particularly in the South Island, will establish Mori wards. What is the policy problem or opportunity Government priorities . On March , the mechanism for councils to conduct binding polls on whether to establish Mori wards was removed through an amendment to the Local Electoral Act allowing councils discretion to resolve to establish a Mori ward. Following thesechanges, councils resolved to establish Mori wards for the first time, with of those councils implementing that change at the local elections. . Coalition agreements include a commitment to: restore the right to local referendums on the establishment or ongoing use of Mori wards, including requiring a referendum on any wards established without referendum at the next local body elections. . The Government considers that there is an imbalance between the ability for electors to determine their representation arrangements and Mori representation in local government. The proposed solution is that the community should be able to make the final decision on whether Mori wards are established, based on a majority vote, ratherthan the elected representatives making the final decision. This comes from a commitment to ensure that the public has a greater opportunity to have their views reflected in l ocal representation arrangements. . Current Mori wards legislation and the councils that have previously resolved to establish Mori wards under the amendment , without holding a poll, are inconsistent with Government objectives . . The coalition agreement indicates Government objectives for the councils to hold binding polls during the local elections. The Minister of Local Government has The Regulatory Impact Statements for these amendments are available on the Department of Internal Affairs website at https:www.dia.govt.nzdiawebsite.nsfFilesRegulatory Impa ct fileRegulatory Impact Statement Maori electoral representation.pdf Schedule A, Local Electoral Act Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government Regulatory Impact Statement further decided to consider holding standalone binding polls in so that the outcomes can apply from the local elections. The Minister has indicated that this is his preferred option. . The Government also intends to offer councils options to avoid the poll process, if they choose to. For councils that have resolved to create Mori wards but not yet implemented them, they will have the option to rescind these decisions, and forcouncils that have existing Mori wards, they will have the option to resolve todisestablish them. Removing the poll provisions has increased Mori representation on local authorities . Removing the poll provisions has enabled a significant number of councils to establishspecific Mori representation in their elected membership for the first time. . Feedback from councils indicates that the risk of triggering a poll, and the community division that the polls tended to create, act ed as a deterrent to promoting the option of Mori wards. Since the poll provisions were removed, council uptake of the Moriwards option increased by more than three times the number that had previously tried to establish Mori wards. There is very little time to conduct and implement polls before the local elections . Councils representation review processes for the current local government term are already under way. Some councils have already started early engagement with their communities prior to issuing their initial proposal s. There would be significant work needed, after legislation is enacted, for affected councils to carry out polls. Following that, if required, councils would implement changes through a truncated representation review. These steps need to be completed by April before pre election processes start. . The limited time available for polls and completing representation review process es may be challenging for councils to manage. T runcating the representation review involves effectively remov ing the role of the Local Government Commission in hearing appeals and objections. This could lead to poorer representation arrangements and or ongoing community dissatisfaction with council decision making. Stakeholders . There are a number of key stakeholders, including: Current and future electors of Mori descent (who are currently on the Mori electoral roll or may choose to be in the future) the Mori wards poll provisions affect the likelihood of this group having the option of specific Mori representation on their local councils, and they are likely to be affected if petitions and polls become a contentious issue within the local community. Mana whenua iwi and hap relationships with local authorities can be affected by decisions on Mori wards, and they tend to be the groups most affected ifpetitions and polls become a contentious issue within the local community . Current and future non Mori electors these electors have an interest in the general composition of the representation arrangements for their local councils, and may also be negatively affected by social division around contentious issues . Local authorities councils are responsible for delivering Mori ward polls and implementing the outcomes, including funding these processes. Councils also have responsibilities to consult with their communities on key decisions. The councils which have recently resolved to establish Mori wards, without holding a poll, are most immediately affected by the options in this analysis. The Local Government Commission has an appeal and determination function forall councils representation reviews. Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government Regulatory Impact Statement A number of other agencies and entities are involved in delivering the polls and supporting implementation of representation review outcomes , including the Electoral Commission, N ew Zealand Post and other postal service providers, election service providers, Stat istics New Zealand, and Land Information New Zealand. . Due to time constraints and confidentiality requirements , the Department of Internal Affairs has not consulted on options for implementing these changes outside government departments and Crown entities. The Department has had preliminarydiscussions with the Local Government Commission, the Electoral Commission,Statistics New Zealand, and Land Information New Zealand. Views on the poll provisions have been well canvassed previously . Although there has been no specific public consultation on the coalition agreement commitments, there have been other opportunities for public consultation on the topicof the Mori ward polls in the past, including: submissions on a petition by Andrew Judd that the House of Representatives consider a law change to make the establishment of Mori wards on district councils follow the same legal framework as establishing other wards on districtcouncils (which was considered as part of the Inquiry into the General Election and the Local Elections); the Tauranga Moana claim to the Waitangi Tribunal; and the Human Rights Commission report , Mori representation in local government. . Many of the arguments for and against polls on Mori wards were summed up in the Departmental Report to the Mori Affairs Committee on submissions on the Local Electoral (Mori Wards and Mori Constituencies) Amendment Bill , as summarised below : Support for removing the poll provisions Removing the polls provides for fairer electoral representation of Mori at local government. Removing the polls supports the Crowns obligations under te Tiriti o Waitangi the Treaty of Waitangi. Councillors are elected to make decisions, and as elected representatives theyshould be trusted with balancing the respective community interests involved. Removing the polls would avoid the community division that is heightened by Mori ward polls. Removing the polls addresses a discrepancy between the way that Mori wards and general wards are treated in law. Opposition to removing the poll provisions and to councils having Mori wards more generally The community should have a say on whether a council adopts Mori wards. Mori wards are undemocratic or divisive. There is already sufficient representation of Mori in local government. Petition Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government Regulatory Impact Statement If there is separate representation for Mori then there should be separate representation for other ethnicities. Previous Mori ward poll results have shown they are not wanted by communities. We lack i nformation on the implications of requiring polls in . As the Department has not had opportunity to consult with affected councils on these proposals, we have limited information about the impact of requiring councils that have resolved to establish Mori wards since to hold a binding poll to take effect for the term commencing in October . There are a number of implementation challenges to achieve the coalition agreement commitment s, however it is possible that unforeseen challenges to implementation can be resolved through future consultation with co uncils and affected parties . Conclusion . The policy problem is therefore determining the correct balance between public input in council representation decisions and facilitating Mori representation and participation in local government. What objectives are sought in relation to th e policy problem . The primary objective of the policy changes is to ensure the local community has a greater say about the shape of their representation arrangements, both on recent decisions and for decisions about Mori wards in future. Objectives for section A : Long term changes to the process for Mori wards . The objective for changes to the Mori wards poll provisions are to ensure that local communities have a greater say in decisions about council representation arrangements , while also supporting councils to facilitate Mori representation and participation in a way that is consistent with the Local Electoral Act and Local Government Act , and is consistent with other similar council decision making processes. . A secondary objective is to reflect New Zealands unique constitutional framework byconsidering how to maintain local democracy in a way that reflects the partnership between the Crown and Mori that is inherent in te Tiritithe Treaty. Mori wards are one way, but not the only way, that rights and responsibilities under te Tiritithe Treatycan be implemented. . Any changes should aim to ensure consistency in council decision making about representation arrangements as far as is practicable. Objecti ves for section B : Transitional changes for councils . Transitional changes will inevitably have an impact on councils. The objective of policyin this area should be to implement the long term changes around Mori wards legislation efficiently and inexpensively in a way that minimises disruption for affected councils while maintaining the integrity of local government processes . . The implementation should give effect to the objectives around balance between public input into representation arrangements and Mori representation in local government. Both of these should be consider ations in the implementation of policy objectives. Departmental Report to the Mori Affairs Committee on submissions on the Local Electoral (Mori Wards and Mori Constituencies) Amendment Bill , February , bafbffbabacc (www.parliament.nz) , pages Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government Regulatory Impact Statement Section : Deciding upon an option to address the policy problem For this section we have considered the two parts of the Governments preferred approach to the policy problem separately: Section A: Long term changes to the process for Mori wards . This section deals with options to make enduring changes to council decision making processes about Mori wards . Section B: Transitional changes for councils. This section deals with consistency for the councils that created a Mori ward while the poll provisions were not in place. A: Long term changes to the process for M ori wards What criteria will be used to compare options to the status quo . The criteria used to assess the options are to ask whether the policy : supports adequate public input into decisions about local representation; supports councils to facilitate Mori representation and participation in local government ; enables balancing of various community interests (including minority interests) ; support s consistency of council decision making about representation arrangements ; and minimise s fiscal andor compliance costs . . There is some tension between these criteria and the Governments objectives . Options that support the Governments objectives of ensuring the public has access to binding polls in response to council decisions to establish Mori wards are likely to conflict with the criteria of minimising costs, and facilitating increased Mori representation in local government . Supporting adequate public input into decisions about local representation . It is important that there is an opportunity for all members of councils communities to contribute to discussion and debate on decisions on Mori wards . While the decision primarily affects electors on the Mori electoral roll and mana whenua, all constituentshave an interest in council representation arrangements. A binding poll is one way for members of the public to have direct control over council decisions. Supporting councils to f acilitat e Mori representation and participation . The Crown requires local authorities to facilitate Mori participation in local governmentdecision making processes, to give effect to the Crowns TiritiTreaty obligations. Section of the Local Government Act gives explicit recognition to the Crowns obligations for local authorities in this respect. In the Waitangi Tribunal commented that, where the Crown has delegated functions to local authorities, it muststill ensure that the Crowns obligations of active protection under Ko te TuaruaArticle of te Tiritithe Treaty must be fulfilled. Levy rates for . Background Section () of the Act states that the purpose of the problem gambling levy is to recover the cost of developing, managing, and delivering the integrated problem gambling strategy . The levy rates are set by regulation at least every three years. The next levy period is from July to June to match the next strategy. Since the levy was first set in , it has applied to gambling operators in four sectors: NCGM operators, casinos , NZRB and NZLC. There have been suggestions for some years that spending on NCGMs in clubs or venues operated by NZRB should be levied separately from the rest of the NCGM sector. The consultation document indicated that the Ministry and DIA would consider changes to the number, size or composition of each gambling sector used to calculate the levy in the context of possible changes to the levy formula after decisions about the next levy period, which would be made using the current policy settings. Officials will inform stakeholders of potential changes to the levy formula in due course. . Process for setting the levy rates The Act sets out the process for developing and setting the levy rates needed to recover the cost of the strategy (refer to sections of the Act). As part of this process, the Ministry consulted extensively on its estimated annual funding requirements, and four alternative sets of estimated levy rates. After considering submissions, the Ministry revised its consultation document as it considered appropriate and submitted these proposals to the Gambling Commission a nd responsible Ministers. The Gambling Commission obtained its own advice and convened a consultation meeting on January . It submitted its report to responsible Ministers on February . After considering the Gambling Commission report, the responsible Ministers recommend ed new problem gambling levy rates and regulations to the Governor General . In , the definition of eligible person was amended to allow overseasborn citizens and permanent residents to apply for a Family Court declaration. The amendment responded to a recommendation in the HRCs report To be who I am on the rights of transgender individuals. At the time, overseasborn transgender individuals had no way to update the sex on official documentation to reflect their preferred gender identity. . Overseasborn New Zealanders now no longer need a Family Court declaration to update other official documentation, such as passports and driver licences, to reflect their preferred gender identity. . A selfidentification process does not produce a declaration like the Family Court process did. The outcome is a change reflect ed on a birth certificate. The Department does not support extending eligibility to someone whose birth is registered in another country. The Bill does not have extraterritorial jurisdiction . It would not be appropriate to legislate for a process that involves the Registrar General in births not registered in New Zealand (e.g. acting as an intermediary with an overseas authority). . In the Departments view, replacing the Family Court process w ith a self identification model that does not apply to overseasborn transgender or intersex New Zealanders will have limited implications for their existing rights and obligations. For example, it will not affect their ability to update their passport, or driver licence to reflect their preferred gender identity. .

. Data management and analysis One major issue for data management and analysis was the contact event structure provided by SafeDome for the Bluetooth card. This involved the Bluetooth cards registering every adverti sed card with no temporal or RSSI thresholds. Further, each contact event was recorded at the minute level so duration could not be distinguished between one and seconds. For example, a contact duration of seven mins with seven interactions could in re al terms be as little as seven seconds or as m uch as seven mins of contact time. The lack of granularity becomes more problematic with increases in contact frequencies relative to duration. It was possible participants left their cards at work which led t o recording false contact events. These false contacts could be corrected with real time working rosters. However, such rosters were not available to the research staff for this trial. The best alternative was a manual register recorded by the research coo rdinator on Day of the study. The lack of a realtime roster of participants observation time led to a slight loss of data and impacted the comparability between contact data. As noted earlier, there were a number of people in the medical unit that were not participants of the study but were record ed as close contacts by participants. This will be a continued problem in the full scale trial. To mitigate this, a new process for identifying close contacts and automating the process of de identifying survey data is required. One option would be to use the hospital staff details from the emailing system to create a drop down option for participants in the survey. Close contacts could be automatically de identifying by matching on first name and last initial. Recommendations: Create a data management and analysis strategy. Obtain a real time roster of participants observation time. Develop an automated system to de identify close contact survey data. . Concordance between data sources The low number of close co ntacts recorded in the survey data reinforces the weaknesses of self report data collection methods compared to technology based objective measures. However, it is possible the detail and changing structure of the surveys over the study period led to parti cipant fatigue. The research team w ill investigate ways to improve the user experience of the survey to reduce participant burden and encourage the reporting of more contacts. We want to retrieve self report contact data above and beyond what is possible w ith traditional contact tracing int erviewing to ensure the best possible self report results to compare against the Bluetooth card. The real world field trial did not permit the close surveillance of card interactions. As such, there was limited visibility of the environmental factors that could have be impacting the Bluetooth card and UWB device performance. However, the high proportion of cards detected each day suggests the Bluetooth cards were detecting most interactions. . The levy formula The formula in section of the Act provides a mechanism for allocating among gambling operators, and collecting from them, the approximate cost of the strategy. The formula is: Levy rate for each sector (A x W B x W x C) plus or minus R D where: A the estimated current expenditure in a sector divided by the total estimated current player expenditure in all sectors subject to the levy B the number of customer presentations to problem gambling services that can be attributed to gambling in a sector divided by the total number of customer presentations to problem gambling services in which a sector that is subject to the levy can be identified C the funding requirement for the period for which the levy is payable D the forecast player expenditure in a sector for the period for which the levy is payable R the estimated underrecovery or overrecovery of levy from a sector in the previous levy periods W and W are weights, the sum of which is . The top line of the formula determines the dollar amount to be paid by each sector as its share of the total levy amount, taking into account any over or underrecovery in previous levy periods. The bottom line of the formula ( D, forecast player expenditure in the sector) determines the levy rate that is necessary for a sector to pay its required contribution (the dollar amount) determined by the top line of the formula. All other things being equal, the higher the forecast player expenditure for a sector, the lower will be its levy rate. Player expenditure for each sector is defined in section () of the Act. Each levy rate is the amount per dollar of player expenditure a sector must pay. A rate of . means a sector must pay . cents per dollar for every dollar of player expenditure in the levy period to which the rate applies. Estimated current player expenditure (A) The formula in the Act requires the levy rate calculation to take into account the latest, most reliable and most appropriate sources of information on player expenditure. The figures used are DIA estimates of player expenditure for each sector for . The estimates for each sector take into account the latest, most reliable and most appropriate sources of information, including DIAs NCGM electronic monitoring R was added to the formula by section of the Gambling Amendment Act , which came into effect on March .
