Investigate how to continue electronic payments and provide cash: The Cash Industry Sector Coordination Entity could investigate how the banking sector can support business continuity through the provision of cash and the ability to continue to use electronic payments while power andor communications are down. Guidance to communities should include holding some cash in small denominations to purchase food, fuel and other necessities in emergencies if electronic payments arent available. Support infrastructure resilience Provide certainty of standards for infrastructure investment: Central government should provide certainty around infrastructure requirements and standards, so that companies can invest in more resilient infrastructure with confidence. For example, cell site battery standards. Preaccredit essential workers to access first responder routes: During the readiness phase, roll out an accreditation system for lifeline utility providers such as electricity companies, fuel truck drivers and other identified essential workers to access first responder routes. Support broadcasters to share information with communities Support broadcasters to share trusted information: Strengthen and formalise relationships between local broadcasters and CDEM so that there is clarity and consistency on how to operate during emergencies to ensure good trusted local information is broadcast. NEMA and CDEM groups and their PIM functions should provide accurate, verified information that is frequently as a proactive way to support broadcasters to provide trusted and critical information to communities and counter misinformation. They should involve broadcasters in regular scheduled briefings, nominate a point person to verify information and give advice on how to report safely in emergency situations. Chapter : Funding settings Overview . An effective emergency management funding system looks across all Rs and takes a longterm view to support communities to prepare for, and respond to, emergencies. While the Inquirys remit is funding settings for readiness and response, the emergency management funding system is much broader than this. . It is the Inquirys view that there needs to be greater focus and action on reducing New Zealands risk related to natural hazards and improving resilience. In the past decade, central government has spent billions on the response to and recovery from our most significant emergencies, but its investment in reduction pales in comparison. The approach is akin to the ambulance at the bottom of the cliff the funding comes too late to effectively minimise the impact of events. . Local councils are largely responsible for funding their own readiness activities. However, most councils have strained resources and competing priorities, making it difficult to invest in maintaining infrastructure and much needed activities like readiness planning, capability building and preparation of emergency centres. Councils have told us they cannot afford the cost of continual events. . The Inquiry considers the Government should proactively invest in reduction and readiness activities. This shift in focus will help reduce negative impacts for communities during and after emergencies and may also reduce future spending required on response and recovery. Across the funding system, change is needed to ensure money can be spent effectively during the critical first days of an emergency response. . Central government does fund councils for a range of activities related to response, and for readiness activities that take place immediately before an emergency event. The current funding system for these activities is outdated and not fitforpurpose, especially given the expected increase in the occurrence and severity of weather events in coming years. Councils are eligible for reimbursement of welfare costs, but the current process requires considerable time and effort by councils, it slows down action on the ground, and means some people making essential contributions to the response are unable to be reimbursed for costs incurred. CHAPTER : FUNDING SETTINGS CHAPTER : MANAGEMENT OF THE IMMEDIATE RESPONSE CHAPTER CHAPTER CHAPTER CHAPTER CHAPTER CHAPTER Government Inquiry into the Response to the North Island Severe Weather EventsImage: A section of SH between Napier and Wairoa was washed out. Source: NZTA Shift to a preventative model of funding emergency management . The Government needs to shift its focus to invest in the CDEM system before emergencies happen. As described throughout this report, the adverse impacts of underinvestment in reduction and readiness activities were very clear during the severe weather events. A shift in focus towards funding reduction and readiness would enable councils and communities to better prepare and build resilience with the aim of reducing negative impacts on people, property, and businesses. We note that while reduction is out of scope of this Inquiry, it is important we discuss the investment required in this area. Without it, the impacts of emergency events will continue to be devastating. . The costs of paying for emergency recovery activities are significant. IAG New Zealand, the countrys largest general insurer, estimates that Aotearoa New Zealand has spent more than of GDP per year for the past years recovering from natural disasters (due in large part to the Canterbury earthquakes). As IAG notes, this is almost as much as was spent on education, superannuation or purchasing health services. It therefore should be of national significance. . Risk reduction actions can have higher upfront costs than the other components of emergency management, but they tend to be more cost effective than disaster relief over the longer term. A range of studies suggest that on average, the benefits of resilience (broadly defined, and including aspects like risk reduction infrastructure) outweigh the costs fourfold. The diagram below illustrates a range of infrastructure resilience projects across the world, with the average benefit cost ratio significantly exceeding one. The New Zealand Lifelines Council notes that many of the damaged critical infrastructure assets were already known to be vulnerable. In addition, less well resourced regions tend to have poor infrastructure, making them more vulnerable in emergencies, for example the road networks in Northland and Tairwhiti. . The Inquiry heard from several infrastructure entities that the central government approach to infrastructure lacks coherence. The policy, regulatory, and operational responsibilities are scattered across core public service departments and Crown entities. This includes DPMC, NEMA, MBIE, Ministry of Transport, New Zealand Infrastructure Commission Te Waihanga, and the New Zealand Transport Agency (NZTA). The distributed nature of these responsibilities may be appropriate. However, at present, leadership is unclear, and the Inquiry heard that the sector has difficulty engaging with central government without a single point of contact.

Impact analysis requirements apply to some of the policies proposed in this paper. Two regulatory impact statements (RISs), on Refocusing the purpose of local government and Discrete Interventions , have been prepared and are attached. The Ministry for Regulation has determined the proposal relating to council performance measurement is exempt from the requirement to provide a RIS on the grounds that it has no or only minor impacts on businesses, individuals, and not forprofit entities. The Department of Internal Affairs regulatory impact analysis panel has reviewed the two RISs in accordance with the quality assurance criteria set out in the CabGuide. The panel considers that the information and analysis summarised in the Purpose RIS partially meets the quality assurance criteria. The panel stated that the RIS appropriately determines that refocusing the purpose of local government will likely have limited impact on its own and may complement planned work on council performance measurement and limiting council revenue from rates, but would be more convincing if it included evidence and analysis of issues driving rates increases and on the relationship between rates and other measures, such as the consumers price index. The panel considers that the information and analysis summarised in the Discrete Interventions RIS partially meets the quality assurance criteria. The panel noted that the RIS was developed within a tight timeframe. The panel stated that the RIS does an adequate job of explaining the nature and context of the proposed changes but, due to limited research, analysis and consultation, contains little evidence of the potential benefits, costs and risks associated with the proposals. Mitigations to these concerns include the role that Taituar has played in raising some of the issues that will be addressed, and the relatively modest and discrete nature of the proposals. Focus area five: Maximising our relationships We cannot work in isolation our system strategy is about partnering to achieve more. To do that, we need to understand who our key stakeholders and potential partners are and how we can work together. Strategic initiatives Our initiatives for this focus area are all about identifying our stakeholders and partners, understanding who they are, what their experience of us is, and determining what kind of relationship we want to have with them (including for some how we could work together). Prior to the development of the Bill, a legislative review programme would identify consequential amendments to other statutes needed to support the creation of the Trust Framework. Areas of focus are likely to include: Acts that prohibit the consented sharing of information (e.g. the Births, Deaths, Marriages and Relationships Registration Act ); Acts that relate to the conf irmation and sharing of identity information particularly through digital mechanisms (e.g. the Electronic Identity Verification Act ); Acts that contain overly prescriptive provisions that do not permit digital solutions (e.g. being required to send a physical letter and statutory declaration requirements under the Summary Proceedings Act ); and ensuring consistency in legal definitions of identity, information and other relevant terminology in the statute book. . The Climate Implications of Policy Ass essment (CIPA) team has been consulted and confirms that the CIPA requirements do not apply to this proposal as the threshold for significance is not met. While there are no significant climate implications from this paper there could be minor climate bene fits from digital identity enabling greater online interactions, including : . enabling people to access services remotely rather than in person; and . supporting the growth of the digital economy, including the trade of digital services and products, in propor tion to other more emission intensive industries. Te Tiriti o Waitangi . We recognise that work on digital identity will be of interest to Mori and we are committed to delivering digital identity services that are inclusive of Te Ao Mori perspectives , and support Mori to have control of their personal information and identity . The approach proposed in this paper will support a broader range of innovative and responsive digital identity services to be developed and will enable a wider range of identify ing attributes to be considered as part of a persons digital identity. If Cabinet agrees to the recommendations in this paper, officials will consult with Mori on the development of further proposals a s part of a Detailed Business Case. . Mori have partic ular interests and relationships with their data, and the concept of Mori data sovereignty seeks to enable Mori collective governance and agency over data. We recognise that Mori Data Governance is an approach that government is working towards. Therefo re, future development of investment options further to this paper will consider how to support Mori Data Governance. . Officials are also engaging with Mori at a programme level through the Data Iwi Leaders Group , with pan Iwi groups and development of th e Mana rite relationship between the Department and iwi. A partnership approach is being adopted for the development of Trust Framework rules, through the establishment of a Technical Working Group dedicated to reviewing draft rules and providing feedback to ensure Mori tikanga is recognised. Human Rights . There are no immediate impacts on human rights arising from the proposal outlined in this paper. However, it is important that any government digital identity services are implemented in alignment with ongoing work to improve digital inclusion across government and to support Article of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (everyone has the right of equal access to public service in his country). Other civil society frameworks include the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, the New Zealand Disability Strategy and the Disability Action Plan. These identify accessibility of information as a fundamental priority. Population implications . As the digital identity system evolves it will provide a variety of benefits through greater access to services, including to people who struggle with proving who they are online and in the real world. For example, enabling people to access services through widely used mobile devices could improve accessibility to services. Proactively Released INCONFIDENCE Page of . However, these may be inequitably realised due to variable levels of digital inclusion in New Zealand. Ensuring accessibility for groups that have been identified as most at risk of not being digitally included ( including Mori, Pacific peoples, seniors, a nd people with disabilities ) will be critical. For example, for people with disabilities, accessibility begins at the point of entry into any digital identity system, so it will be important to ensure there are accessible ways to obtain a digital identity. Additionally, many people living in rural areas will have limited broadband which will impact their access to digital services. . From th is wider Mahi Tahi (Inclusion) perspective, we will need to address four key barriers to inclusion: motivation, access through affordability and accessibility , skills and trust. This is important to ensure there is a just transition to a digital nation. . For the digital identity services outlined in this paper, accessibility will need to be considered in the design and implementation stages. Additionally, accessibility requirements , such as ease of access and opportunities to participate (inclusion) will be considered in the development of the framework rules, in collaboration with Mori partners, advisory groups and other stakeholders. . It will also be important to maintain trust by enabling safe and secure ways to access services. For example, privacy enhancing digital identity services will be important , particularly in circumstances such as when women need to access services as they are experiencing family violence. Passports have a self identification process for changing the gender printed in the passport. While gender is not displayed on a driver licence, this information can be changed on the driver licence record via a self identification process. Maintaining trust in and the integrity of the birth register is important. Other agencies and other parts of the Department of Internal Affairs rely on information contained in the birth register to confirm a persons identity and provide services. Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs INCONFIDENCE Page of . While other options considered may support public trust in the birth register better , this is at the expense of all other objectives and would result in a process that does not work for the transgender and intersex New Zealanders who need it . Selfidentification is the most inclusive and accessible process for amending registered sex . Under a self identification process a persons gender will be recognised based on their selfperception. This change will: . better enabl e transgende r and intersex New Zealanders to access services with less risk of being outed or experiencing discrimination; . demedicalise the experience of being transgender or intersex; . validate transgender and intersex people contributing to a greater sense of soc ial belonging and improving their wellbeing; . provide greater accessibility to a birth certificate that reflects a persons gender due to lower costs and reduced administration involved in an application ; and . enhances privacy as a person no longer must prov ide sensitive medical information to amend their registered sex. Selfidentification is increasingly supported internationally . International h uman rights discourse recommends that where sex and gender information is registered it should be based on an acce ssible self identification process with no eligibility criteria , such as medical treatment. Since , at least other countries have adopted a self identification process, as well as the Australian states of Tasmania and Victoria. There has not been ev idence found of any serious unmanageable consequences of introducing a self identification process. Decisions on a range of proposals are needed to enable a self identification process . To introduce a self identification process, I propose the removal of the requirement s to apply to the Family Court and to provide evidence of medical treatment . Instead people would apply to the Registrar General of Births, Deaths and Marriages to amend their registered sex to reflect their gender. Further decisions are re quired to enable a selfidentification process, which are discussed below. I propose a statutory declaration requirement to ensure people understand the decision . To achieve this the statutory declaration will require applicants to indicate that they : .. want the sex marker on their birth certificate to match their gender; .. intend to live as a person of this gender; and .. understand the consequences of the application . . Requiring applicants to verify the above requirements balances the interests of transgender and intersex individuals with the need to protect the integrity of the birth register . It will help ensure applications are treated consistently and fairly . It will also reduce the risk of fraudulent applications . Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs INCONFIDENCE Page of I propose that people can amend their registe red sex more than once, but that subsequent amendments may need to meet additional requirements . Gender can be fluid and how a person identifies may change over time. This may be particularly true for younger people as childhood and adolescence is a time o f development. I propose allowing a person to amend their registered sex multiple times in recognition that people may identify differently at different stages of life. . Allowing only one amendment would be out of step with a true self identification mode l. If a persons gender changes and they cannot amend their registered sex to reflect this, they no longer have control of how their gender is officially recognised. . People will be able to change their name at the same time as their registered sex if required. To accurately reflect their identity, where a person amends their registered sex, their previous sex and name are not displayed on their new birth certificate. This has the potential to increase the risk of identity fraud as a person cannot be easil y linked to their previous identity. This risk is exacerbated if people amend their registered sex multiple times, particularly as birth certificate s are fundamentally different to transactional documents , such as a passport or driver licences , which can be revoked and must be renewed periodically. Worst case scenarios of fraudulent behaviour include, for example, a person receiving multiple benefits or circumventing safe guards preventing money laundering and terrorism financing. . I propose t hat where a person makes subsequent amendments to their registered sex they may have to meet requirements to ensure their application is genuine. These will be in addition to the statutory declaration, which already acts to mitigate the risk of identity fr aud. False declarations are a criminal offence that can lead to imprisonment for up to three years. . Any requirements in addition to the statutory declaration will be set in regulations and designed to not be overly burdensome or reinstate the barriers th at the self identification process aims to remove. For example, extra requirements could include returning any previous birth certificates, provision of an identity referee or a letter of support from an adult who has known the applicant for over a year. M y officials will engage with other agencies in the development of the regulations, particularly agencies working in the justice sector, to ensure the extra requirements sufficiently mitigate the risk of identity fraud. . Changing registered sex multiple tim es relates to an existing issue with inaccuracy of information across justice sector agencies (such as the New Zealand Customs Service, New Zealand Police and Department of Corrections). There is already a risk of inaccurate information across this sector when name change information is not shared. This could result in a person having multiple identities and their offences not being linked. I am responsible for work developing a Justice Sector Identity Management Strategy to address this risk ; the impact of amending registered sex will be considered as part of this.

Effective screening environments: Individuals at risk of experiencing harm from gambling are identified as early as possible, and are made aware of where to access appropriate minimising gambling harm intervention services. Based on its current experience and the needs assessment, the Ministry intends to maintain funding for existing services at broadly the same level as in the previous funding period. However, it intends to explore the potential for innovation within that overall budget, particularly taking a community mobilisation approach, and drawing on successful models across the wider health system. Workforce development (public health) In the period, the Ministry s gambling harm public health workforce development provider identified the core competencies (including the cultural competencies) required for that workforce. In the most recent period, public health core competency assessment tools were developed to enable the public health workforce to assess their competency levels and associated training and development needs. The focus in the period will be increasing uptake of a training programme to help the workforce identify and achieve appropriate formal qualifications. In addition, submissions identified that there needs to be greater emphasis on understanding different worldviews in cultural competence training, including training for health support people working with Mori, Pacific and Asian communities. Awareness and behaviour change programme The Ministry expects that health promotion programmes will continue to raise awareness and educate about the signs and risks of harmful gambling, and how people can respond and seek help, by: promoting risk awareness and positive action messages that encourage positive behaviour change encouraging the development and promotion of selfhelp digital tools to improve access to relevant information, help and online support improving the reach of services to M ori, Pacific, Asian and other vulnerable groups , and the associated uptake of treatment and support. HPA will continue to actively promote the Gambling Helpline, Choice Not Chance (www.choicenotchance.org.nz ) and face toface services, with a renewed focus on Mori, Pacific and Asian audiences and other vulnerable groups, for the period. HPA will also develop and promote selfhelp digital tools to increase accessibility to help and provide online support information. It will also continue to work in partnership with DIA and the Ministry to promote safer gambling environments and host responsibility, including embedding work with class venues and expanding these activities to address other modes of gambling. Principal Advisor, Strategy and Business Planning The Principal Advisor, Strategy and Business Planning is responsible for the development and maintenance of the overall Regulatory Systems group annual strategic plan and the translation of the groups strategy into business plans that are measurable. This position will also support the development of accountability documents, lead the development of integrated performance reporting framework and cycle, and drive business planning activities. This includes development, implementation and monitoring of strategic initiatives in support of the overarching strategic direction of the group. Senior Advisor, Risk The Senior Advisor, Risk will work alongside the regulatory system, and provides intelligence and risk thought leadership, analysis, and advice to the intelligence function and Regulatory Services Group. Intelligence Coordinator The Intelligence Coordinator will support the Intelligence and Insights team through coordinating information for analysis and reporting purposes, helping Regulatory System improve their understanding of harm and risks. Head of Investigations and Prosecutions The Head of Investigations and Prosecutions leads the Groups investigation and prosecution function, setting its strategic direction and ensuring efficient management of the investigation and prosecution process that are strategically aligned to the Regulatory Services strategic outcomes and with the aim to protect New Zealand and prevent harm in communities. Investigations Coordinator The Investigations Coordinator will have responsibility and oversight for the coordination of investigation information for analysis and reporting purposes, administration, and support services to ensure the smooth functioning of the Investigations and Prosecutions function. Manager, Investigations AMLCFT The Manager, Investigations AMLCFT, is responsible for the dayto day management of a frontline investigation team, ensuring a strategically targeted, consistent, and outcome focused driven approach to serious, complex andor highrisk investigations and prosecutions under the AntiMoney Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism Act (AMLCFT Act). Senior Investigator AMLCFT The Senior Investigator AMLCFT is responsible for leading high quality investigations and prosecutions into serious, complex, and harmful noncompliance by businesses we supervise (our regulated sector) under the AntiMoney Laundering and Countering and Financing of Terrorism Act (AMLCFT Act). Head of Implementation The Head of Implementation leads the Groups operational policy and engagement function, setting its strategic direction and ensuring efficient management and successful implementation of existing and new policy and regulation changes, in an approach that is strategically aligned to the Regulatory Systems strategic outcomes and with the aim to protect New Zealand and prevent harm in communities. Section Five: Proposed change protocol Introduction This protocol sets out the proposed approach to managing the implementation of the structural changes arising from the Toi Hiranga l Regulation and Policy Organisational Change. This Protocol is consistent with all individual employment agreements and the Collective Agreement between the Public Service Association and the Department of Internal Affairs. Principles The process is designed to: ensure a fair and transparent process; maximise the placement of employees into available positions; ensure minimum disruption to business as usual; observe the provisions contained in the relevant employment agreements and organisational policy; and minimise uncertainty for employees. Who does this protocol apply to The protocol applies to all permanent employees of the department including: permanent fulltime and parttime employees employees currently on all forms of leave including leave without pay and parental leave For employees currently seconded to other positions the process will apply to their permanent substantive position. Fixed term (temporary) or casual staff are not covered by the protocol even though their position may be affected by any restructure. In this case the relevant provision of their employment agreement will apply. Overview Employees are affected if their current position is changing materially or is being disestablished. If there is no significant change to the position, and there are the same number, or fewer, employees than positions in the new structure, employees will be reconfirmed. Employees who are not reconfirmed will be considered for reassignment. This involves considering whether affected employees skills can be matched to alternative positions that require similar skills in the new structure. Released under the Official Information Act
Some Treaty of Waitangi settlement arrangements with councils have links to the four aspects of community well being currently in the Act. My officials advise me they do not consider that removing the four wellbeings from the Act will impact other legislation (including current and future settlement legislation), as the statutes are independent of one another. Removing the wellbeings from the purpose of local government in the Act does not change the responsibilities of local authorities under other legislation. Well being principles continued in, or were added to, other legislation during the previous period they were absent from the purpose statement for local government. Work on Local Government System Improvements will uphold existing Treaty settlement arrangements. Council participation in and obligations under Treaty settlement arrangements will be considered in the programme. Affected employees who are not reassigned will be consulted individually about other options. If no other options are identified, notice will be given and redundancy provisions apply. Affected employees Before final decisions are announced, all potentially affected employees will be notified individually. Employees may be informed that they: have been reconfirmed in a position and are no longer affected, or are affected and will be considered for reassignment. Reconfirmation process Prior to announcement of the final decisions, an assessment will be made to determine if employees meet the criteria for reconfirmation. This assessment will be made by the group General ManagerDirector, with support from HR, and approved by the Deputy Chief Executive, Toi Hiranga l Regulation and Policy. The reconfirmation process requires a comparison between existing positions and those in the new structure to determine if they are the same or nearly the same. The criteria for reconfirmation are: the new job description is the same or nearly the same as the job the affected employee currently does; the salary is the same; the terms and conditions, including career prospects are no less favourable; and the location is the same or in the same vicinity.

Reassignment process The purpose of the reassignment process is to place affected employees, who have not been reconfirmed into positions in the new structure, into suitable alternative positions. A suitable alternative position is one that involves duties that are not unreasonable taking into account the employees skills, knowledge, qualifications and experience, and where the employee could reasonably be expected to carry out those duties with a reasonable amount of training and development. A reassignment panel of the group General Manager or Director and a representative from Human Resources will consider all expressions of interest and seek to reassign employees based on a balance of: the employees preference(s) suitability for the position placing as many employees as possible.
. The consultation proposed in this paper is limited to the Mori ward changes because
. Affected employees may be invited to submit an Expression of Interest (EOI) for ringfenced vacancies. . A process for identifying the affected employees suitability for the ring fenced vacancy then takes place. This may include a range of selection activities for example, paperbased EOI form, or an interview. . The reassignment panel will assess the expression of interest against the reassignment options and to make recommendations to the Deputy Chief Executive, Toi Hiranga l Regulation and Policy. . Once approved, formal offers of reassignment will be made to individuals. Upon acceptance of reassignment, individuals are no longer affected by the review. An employee who declines reassignment to a suitable alternative position is deemed to have resigned. If an employee is reassigned to a position with a lower salary, an equalisation allowance will be paid. Reconfirmation or reassignment review process Employees have the right to seek a review of the reconfirmation decision where they do not consider that the criteria have been applied correctly. Employees who register a preference or preferences for reassignment also have the right to seek a review of the reassignment decision where they are not offered reassignment to any of the positions for which they registered a preference. Employees who do not register a preference for reassignment cannot seek a review of reassignment decisions. Any request for a review, including the grounds for the review, must be communicated in writing to the Deputy Chief Executive, Toi Hiranga l Regulation and Policy within working days of the reconfirmation or reassignment decision being communicated. If requested, employees will be provided with the documentation associated with the reconfirmation or reassignment decision under review that relates directly to them. They will not be provided with specific information or documentation regarding other affected employees. Reviewers will be independent of the original reconfirmation or reassignment panel and will be agreed by the Deputy Chief Executive, Toi Hiranga l Regulation and Policy and the employee andor their representative. Any recommendations made by the reviewer will be considered by the Deputy Chief Executive, Toi Hiranga l Regulation and Policy, who will decide whether any recommendations made by the reviewer will be implemented. Review decisions are final there is no internal appeal process. Released under the Official Information Act

A refreshed approach to funding during and immediately after an emergency . In addition to an overall shift in the investment approach to emergency management, there needs to be some specific changes to the way funds for response activities are administered and a reappraisal of which costs are eligible. The current state for funding response and immediate readiness activities . The current objectives of government financial support for local government during and immediately before an emergency focus on caring for directly affected people, and preventative actions to reduce immediate danger to human life or to reduce the potential consequences of an emergency. Current government policy is that councils can apply for reimbursement of of welfare costs they incur in caring for displaced people. Central government will fund of other eligible activities above a threshold based on the net capital value of the council. Eligible activities include the repair of essential infrastructure like water, storm water, electrical, sewerage and gas assets as well as other councilowned structures like retaining walls and tunnels upon which essential services depend. Both these funding functions (welfare, and other response costs) are administered by NEMA. . Councils are responsible for most other response costs, including for example repairs to local roads. In practice, government funding is made available to councils and communities to support this response spending through a range of government agencies. Increasingly, it is also provided through eventspecific bespoke government funds like the North Island Weather Events funding package. In addition, different government agencies provide funding for specific activities or sectors, ranging from support for farmers to silt removal following Cyclone Gabrielle. . Councils can also request reimbursement of funds that were incurred by iwi and other organisations with a formalised role in providing welfare services after an emergency. The Emergency Management Bill includes provisions for iwi and Mori organisations to be directly reimbursed for welfare costs within the criteria set at the time of the emergency. We support the intent of this provision, reflecting the key role of iwi Mori organisations in providing welfare services.

Remaining affected employees Employees who remain affected following the Branch reassignment process will be notified of this, and the Department will work with the employee to identify other potential reassignment opportunities elsewhere in the Department. Affected employees may then apply and be considered for any potentially suitable vacancies. Affected employees will have preferential right of appointment over nonaffected employees and external candidates in the event that their suitability for the position is assessed as being the same. Other options Employees not placed through reassignment are advised in writing that they are surplus and will be consulted individually about the potential for other options to be agreed. There may be vacancies within the wider Department which could be considered suitable for employees affected by this change process. Affected employees may apply and be considered for any potentially suitable vacancies. Affected employees will have preferential right of appointment over nonaffected employees and external candidates in the event that their suitability for the position is assessed as being the same. Upon acceptance of appointment to another position within the Department, employees are no longer affected by the review. Where another option is agreed with the affected employee, this will be confirmed in writing and the employee will no longer be considered affected. Notice If the Department determines that no other option can be agreed, the affected employee will be provided notice in line with their employment agreement. Where a longer notice period is preferred for operational transition reasons, this may be agreed between the Department and the affected employee. During the notice period, the Department and the employee may consider any opportunities for other options that may arise. If an affected employee is appointed to another position within the Department during the notice period, the notice is withdrawn in writing. The employees employment is not, therefore, severed. Revenue from usercharges arising from the classification of DVDs have also reduced. Over the last ten years, income from classifying commercial publications such as DVDs and films for release in theatres has reduced by percent. Due to the decreasing market for physical material, such as DVDs, increasing fees for the classification of physical media content may cause this classification activity to further decline. DVD distributers may not be able to sustain increased charges and there may be a flowon effect for consumers and viewers if less content is made available. Funding for OFLCs CVoD related activities is needed The classification of CVoD content is currently unregulated and there is no charging regime in place. This has created uneven business costs between distributors of media content such as DVDs and distributers of media content screened via online platforms. The Government is progressing an amendment to the Classification Act that will require CVoD content to be classified and allow CVoD providers to selfrate their content. The classification of CVoD content before screening will minimise the risk of harm to children and young people. It will support informed viewing choices by all New Zealanders by ensuring content has the appropriate classification, rating and advisory notes consistent with the New Zealand classification regime. The Amendment Bill is expected to be passed into law by mid. CVoD providers will be able to classify their material in three ways: using a selfclassification Rating Tool designed by OFLC and cocreated with industry; by using an OFLC approved and accredited system to selfrate content; and by submitting material to the FVLB. Further information about the Amendment Bill is available from the Departments website. OFLC will be undertaking new activities related to regulating CVoD content. The CVoD related activities are outlined in Table . Funding for the costs of these activities is needed. Review of options for funding the classification framework Consultation documentCostrecovery options Which OFLC costs are covered by the costrecovery options The costrecovery options discussed below refer only to the costs of Commercial classifications, including the costs of CVoD classifications. Classifications in this category make up approximately percent of OFLCs current annual budget (an estimated . million in ). For the purpose of this consultation and the setting of any subsequent charges, the following costs will be met by the Crown and are not included in the costrecovery options: Crown classifications; OFLCs information services, including a proportion of research costs; and fee waivers for the purposes of cultural benefits. The rationale for this approach is that the New Zealand community is the principal beneficiary of those activities not included in costrecovery proposals. Considerations of effectiveness, equity and fairness indicate that the Government should bear the costs involved, which make up approximately percent of OFLCs current annual budget (an estimated . million in , not including the funding agreed by the Government in September for OFLC to respond to increased demand for its services following the Christchurch terror attacks). Costrecovery for current Commercial classifications The current approach to funding Commercial classifications was established in . It involves the Crown and submitters sharing the costs. The options below step back from the current approach and ask: who should pay for current Commercial classifications, and how much each party should pay Who benefits from current Commercial classifications, and how much A key question in considering costrecovery options for classification is: who benefits Considerations of equity and fairness in particular suggest that the main beneficiaries should meet the costs, although a number of other factors (for example, ability to pay) may need to be taken into account. New Zealands classification system creates significant benefits for distributors, consumers, and the wider community. Rating systems are widely used by commercial distributors, whether or not there is any government involvement. Rating systems provide information which helps to define and promote the distributors products. By doing so, they help consumers make informed choices. Consumers value rating systems for the information they provide. The wider community benefits from rating systems, particularly because they help to protect individuals from the harm which arises from people viewing material that is inappropriate for their level of maturity. If the viewer doesnt have the psychological resources needed to take a healthy perspective on what they see, they may suffer personal harm or inflict harm on others. Government involvement in the provision of a New Zealand classification system reflects the fact that the community as a whole prefers a rating system that is different for example, more stringent, more informative, than what would be produced as a result of private arrangements between distributors and consumers. Review of options for funding the classification framework Consultation documentIncentives to keep costs low While equity and fairness may suggest that the Government and the sector should pay for the costs of classification, quantifying respective benefits can be challenging and may also be complicated by other considerations. The activities of distributors give rise to the risk of harm from media content, indicating that their share of the costs of classification should reflect this. Conversely, our classification system only exists in its present form because this is what the community wants, which supports the view that the Government should take responsibility for meeting the costs of the system. Any contribution to funding from the sector may produce benefits in terms of incentivising the provider to minimise costs. New Zealand distributors display a keen awareness of the cost of classification and a preference for those costs, or at least their contribution, being kept as low as possible. The degree of distributor influence on our systems cost efficiency will be enhanced by making the operations of OFLC as transparent as possible, through continued, regular review and setting of charges. Other evidence for different approaches to funding New Zealands classification system There is evidence that private distributors would prefer to use their own systems rather than participate in the official New Zealand system (suggesting that distributors may need to incur net costs to meet the requirements of the New Zealand system). However, this evidence is fragmented. Applications for CVoD classification fell significantly after a legal ruling which said that CVoD content was not covered by the Classification Act. Nevertheless, some distributors such as Google and Sony have continued to voluntarily submit CVoD items for classification. The fact that the sector and the community receive benefits from classification does not dictate what approach should be taken to costrecovery. For example, the federal Australian equivalent to our For example, a major distributor of CVoD material submitted items to OFLC for classification in the months leading up to August . The same distributor has submitted no items since the legal ruling.classification system is largely funded by the sector through classification fees and the British equivalent is percent sectorfunded. By comparison, the New Zealand sector is currently paying approximately percent of the costs of OFLC activities. Past patterns of funding for the New Zealand system also offer minimal guidance about how responsibility for the cost of the system should be divided between the Crown and the sector. Classification costs overall have varied over the years, as has income from the sector. Options for feedback Options discussed in Tables focus on the potential roles of the sector and the Government in funding current Commercial classifications. Comments on the advantages and disadvantages of individual options are principlesbased. The scenarios included in the tables are intended to be illustrative only. They do not represent a recommended approach, although all can be supported by principlesbased arguments. For example, a split of costs between the Crown and the sector can be justified as a pragmatic solution in the absence of evidence to support an alternative approach. In , for example, distributors paid for per cent of the cost of Australias National Classifications Board. The Board operates on a qualified full cost recovery basis, recognising that in some circumstances, for example because of a policy rationale, full cost recovery may not be appropriate. Current Regulations give the Chief Censor wide discretion to reduce or waive fees. For example, fees can be reduced for special interest groups and charitable organisations, and up to percent of the fee can be waived in situations where the charging of the full fee would be unreasonable, unfair or unduly burdensome. In terms of volume and income foregone, these provisions are mainly applied to film festivals and groupings of films and DVDs. Film festivals may have up to percent of classification fees waived on grounds of the cultural benefits to the community arising from their activities. Publications submitted as a group are required to pay only one classification fee, even though multiple items (for example, a box set of DVDs) are involved. The grouping provision recognises that classifying a group of similar items (for example, multiple episodes of a television series) takes less time than classifying the equivalent number of unrelated items such as films, and that the full fee applied to groups of DVDs and some films such as groups of short films would be unduly burdensome. The level of fee revenue forgone under current waiver and reductions provisions is projected as , in . Table Waivers and reductions Waivers and reductions Financial impact Waivers and reductions currently impact on the amount paid by submitters for classification services. A film festival, for example, may pay to have one film classified. This represents a reduction of from the standard fee. Projected income foregone in through cultural benefit waivers is approximately ,, or percent of the shortfall in revenue for that year. The operation of waiver and reduction provisions affect the quantum of costs that must be recovered either from those who dont qualify, or from the Crown. Advantages Waivers and reductions recognise that some media content provides significant cultural benefits and the cost of classifying some items are lower than for others or would otherwise be unduly burdensome for some providers. Disadvantages If the sector has to pick up the costs of concessions relating to cultural benefits, crosssubsidisation would be involved (crosssubsidisation can be associated with inefficiency, inequity and lack of transparency). Challenges in quantifying cultural benefits of media content, with associated risks of overpayment or underpayment. The current waivers and reductions system involves significant handling costs for OFLC, the FVLB and distributors. Implementation A system of concessionary rates could be developed for CVoD classification. If the present system of concessionary rates is retained no implementation issues. ()(f)(iv) Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Page of Further policy decisions are required, which we will provide advice on in April Determine the process for children and young people . Children and young people can change the sex on their birth certificate using the Family Court process. We recommend replacing the Family Court process with a selfidentification process for children and young people. Children and young people are high users of birth certificates as a form of identity as they often do not have entitlement or access to a driver license or passport. It is important that they can feel safe using their birth certificates and feel accepted for who they are as they grow up. . The policy changes required to introduce selfidentification for children and young people are more complex and potentially controversial. We have not had time to fully assess the implications and impacts of introducing a selfidentification process for children. We are still considering the requirements for: . parent al or guardian consent for example, ensuring we have policy around children or young people who are unable to gain consent, are wards of the state, or have multiple parents or guardians ; . differentiating requirements for different age groups the current drafting creates a separate category for or year olds that may add unnecessary complexity to the process ; and . requiring letters of support, for example from a health professional further work is required to determine what assurances we would be seeking through a letter of support and who would be best placed to provide that. . We are seeking an inprinciple agreement to introduce a selfidentification process for children and young people to change the sex on their birth certificates. We will provide further advice on the details set out above in April. Further consideration is needed on establishing a limit to the number of changes allowed . The select committee recommended only allowing for one change of gender (except under special circumstances). Agency feedback clearly argued against this, particularly for children, as gender is a deeply personal choice that can change over time. We will consider this issue further and provide advice in April. Selfidentification has implications for Corrections regulations . Birth certificates are rarely used to determine someones sex or gender. There is only one instance we have found where changing sex on a birth certificate would have implications for other legislation. Sex on a birth certificate will not override agency discretion to determine the accommodation of prisoners . The Department of Corrections makes decisions about the accommodation of male and female prisoners. Currently, if a birth certificate is supplied a placement must be made in accordance with the sex listed on the certificate (unless the person seeks a review of the determination). Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Page of . When the select committee considered the Bill, an issue was raised about the implications of a selfidentification process on accommodating transgender prisoners. There was a concern that removing judicial oversight could potentially enable prisoners to falsely claim a gender identity to change where they are placed. . We are working with officials at the Department of Corrections on this issue.

Councillors . The Inquiry heard councillors face some of the same challenges and confusion as mayors, including a lack of clarity around their role. Councillors can perform many of the same visible community leadership and communication tasks as mayors and need to have clarity about their governance role in an emergency. They are expected to provide reassurance to communities and dispel misinformation, as well as identify highlevel community needs, serve as a conduit between communities and emergency management, and liaise with other groups. Controllers . The operational response to an emergency is led by a controller. Controllers provide advice to the person responsible for declaring an emergency. Following a declaration, they become responsible for the operational response. This includes directing and coordinating the use of personnel, information, services, and other resources. They have powers of evacuation, requisition, tasking, entry, and transport control. . The roles and accountability lines of the local controllers and group controllers are confusing and convoluted, reflecting their multiple reporting lines and layers of accountability. For example, group and local controllers are appointed by a CDEM Group and employed by the relevant local authority. Group controllers are often employed by a regional council, while local controllers are usually a local council employee with controller responsibilities in addition to their substantive role. This means controllers are accountable to the CDEM Group for their emergency management responsibilities but also have an employment relationship with the local authority that employs them. In addition, the Director of Civil Defence Emergency Management has a role in monitoring the performance of group controllers. In a national state of emergency, the Director and the National Controller can set the priorities to be followed regionally and locally. . In general, controllers with senior management roles had more effective working relationships with mayors and the council. The Inquiry heard they were able to lead more effectively and exert sufficient authority with senior managers and elected officials. In addition, controllers need to take account of the management of future consequences of their decisions, which means they need to understand budgetary management and the ongoing responsibilities of elected officials. . The Inquiry recommends that council chief executives become their organisations primary controller, having overall responsibility and oversight for emergency management responses. Chief executives should set their response approach with the mayor or chair and retain overall accountability for the councils emergency response. However, they can delegate operational responsibility to other controllers. We saw this approach used by the Tararua District Council and consider this should be standard practice nationally. Along with additional clarity around roles and accountability, support pathways for controllers are needed to build their emergency management skill set, including command, crisis leadership, and operational training. Image: Search and Rescue and Surf Life Saving New Zealand carry out a rooftop rescue in Hawkes Bay. Source: NZ Police CHAPTER : LEADERSHIP, ROLES AND RESPONSIBILITIES CHAPTER CHAPTER CHAPTER CHAPTER CHAPTER CHAPTER Government Inquiry into the Response to the North Island Severe Weather EventsClarity of official roles helped the Tararua District The Mayor of the Tararua District, Tracey Collis, reflected that the councils clearly defined roles for staff and officials helped the district operate smoothly during Cyclone Gabrielle. Her role as Mayor and spokesperson remained unchanged from a nonemergency arrangement, while the Chief Executive took on the role of primary controller. The Chief Executive set up the arrangements for managing the emergency, before delegating to an experienced staff member to lead the ongoing emergency response. Relevant staff are trained in CIMS and use it on a regular basis on a range of incidents. This means they are familiar with roles and can move smoothly into an emergency management response. Elected councillors know they are responsible for ensuring twoway communication between communities and the emergency operations centre. During Cyclone Gabrielle, this helped communities to have accurate and regular updates on the emergency and response. Clarity of roles between local and regional tiers of response . There also needs to be clarity about roles and accountabilities between the regional and local levels, including group controllers, CDEM Groups, regional council chief executives and chairs. This lack of clarity reduced the regional oversight of hazards and muddled effective implementation of the emergency management system. Clear and empowered roles across the system . In addition to local governments responsibilities for emergency management, many other groups and organisations have vital roles to play to support the safety and wellbeing of people and communities. These include iwi, emergency services, health and disability services, lifeline utilities companies, search and rescue groups, government agencies, goods and services suppliers, and community organisations. . During the severe weather events, there was a lack of clarity about the specific roles of some groups and whether the response made best use of the expertise and resources available. Knowing where the key skills are in the community is essential to build readiness and trust. This includes having connections around food chain logistics, water infrastructure, engineering needs and equipment provision. . To ensure CDEM responses can draw on capability and capacity from groups and organisations around the country during an emergency, relationships and agreements should be set up ahead of time. Two specific areas where capability can be better recognised, and roles clarified, are set out below. More information about the role of iwi Mori in the system, and the need for this role to be better recognised and supported, is in Chapter . VOICES Utilise New Zealand Defence Force capability . The NZDF made a valuable contribution during Cyclone Gabrielle, carrying out a wide range of tasks including planning, and were also embedded in incident management teams. At the height of the emergency, the NZDF had over , personnel involved in the response. We heard from communities that these personnel were a reassuring presence. . The NZDF is recognised as a support agency in the National CDEM Plan. There are provisions for it to provide appropriate support to government authorities during an emergency, while maintaining its other operational outputs and missions. The NZDF has highly skilled personnel across a broad range of areas including intelligence, logistics, planning, operations, and aviation and temporary forward airbase coordination (see Chapter ). . The NZDF expressed frustration in relation to the lack of clarity about its roles in the response. It noted to the Inquiry, a lack of clarity in command and control in the locally led and nationally supported emergency response framework created confusion, at times it was unclear who was the lead and responsible. It also felt there was a mismatch between councils and communities expectations of the NZDF and what the NZDF had the capacity to provide. . The NZDF also told the Inquiry it received short notice requests for support when Emergency Coordination Centre (ECC) shifts were ending, as ECCs were not set up to be staffed for long duration operations. It noted this could have been mitigated through a formalised handover process that, after a predetermined period of time, staff could have seen staff deployed from around New Zealand to support the local response. . There needs to be greater clarity and agreement prior to an emergency about what roles and types of tasks the NZDF is equipped to carry out, and the process for making the most of the resources available. The Inquiry recommends the Government establishes a stronger mandate for the NZDF to provide emergency response specialist skill sets during severe weather events and other emergencies related to natural hazards and infrastructure failure. We also recommend establishing the NZDF as the agency responsible for temporary forward airbase coordination in severe emergencies. Shift leadership for the welfare function . Welfare services support individuals, whnau, and communities to be ready for, respond to, and recover from, emergencies. There are many groups that coordinate or deliver welfare services. Specific welfare responsibilities and processes are set out in the National Civil Defence Emergency Management Plan and CIMS. The provision of welfare services begins in response and continues into recovery. Welfare services are delivered at the local level and coordinated and supported at CDEM Group and national levels. At a national level, there are a range of agencies with a role to play. NEMA is responsible for leadership of the welfare function, supported by other agencies with specific areas of responsibility. For example, the Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI) is the support agency for animal welfare, and the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE) is the agency responsible for the coordination of the provision of temporary accommodation for people who must leave their homes as the result of an emergency. . It is currently confusing to understand which agencies and organisations are involved in undertaking welfare activities, both during and immediately after an emergency. In particular, it can be unclear how the leadership of the welfare function and delivery of welfare services fit together. There is an opportunity to strengthen national and local levels of service delivery, clarify interdependencies, and increase coordination to ensure the model for providing services is sustainable and coordinated. . There are some challenges with NEMA being the agency responsible for the coordination of all welfare services. It has a wide remit, making its capacity for carrying out this function limited. It currently takes a narrow view of welfare which does not include the wide range of welfare needs and considerations for communities. This means that gaps are filled by other agencies. . There is an opportunity to better utilise the expertise and capacity already in the public service to carry out leadership of welfare coordination. MSD already has a regional presence and memoranda of understanding with service providers across the country. The Inquiry heard that MSD has the capacity to respond at scale across multiple geographic regions using systems already in place. MSD also has strong links to government agencies and iwi and can distribute funds at speed in an accountable manner. . The Inquiry recommends that MSD is given responsibility for the leadership of welfare coordination. This responsibility would not replace the need for locally led provision of the welfare function but would support a joinedup approach and help to build system capability. With this shift of leadership responsibility to MSD, it may be appropriate that NEMA retains some specific areas of responsibility for welfare delivery. By removing leadership of welfare coordination from NEMA, capacity would be freed up for NEMA to focus on readiness and response, as outlined in Chapter . Embed health and disability services . Health and disability providers have a role at a local, regional, and national level before, during, and after emergencies. This role includes ensuring the continuity of care for patients, supporting surging demand for physical care, providing psychosocial and mental health services, and leading the response for secondary health impacts. The role of health and disability services continues into recovery and beyond. The health and wellbeing impacts of emergencies on people and their communities are longlasting. For example, in February , a year after the severe weather events, Hawkes Bay Health announced a million health and wellbeing package for Hawkes Bay residents affected by Cyclone Gabrielle. . Health and disability services have a legislated role in emergency management, but the Inquiry heard there is a need to strengthen the way this role is carried out and integrated into the wider system. The chief executive or a senior member of a provider of health and disability services is required to be a member of the CEG in each council or unitary authority. Relationships in the health and disability sector (including Health New Zealand) and other CDEM agencies need to be well established before an emergency event. This was not always the case during the severe weather events. The Inquiry heard there was a particular breakdown of the relationship between Health New Zealand and the Hawkes Bay CDEM Group Emergency Coordination Centre during Cyclone Gabrielle, which led to a critical gap in situational awareness for health officials. . We note at the time of the severe weather events, there was transitional change happening in the health sector, following the establishment of Health New Zealand in July . This meant some key national and regional roles were still being developed. This timing impacted the organisations ability to respond, and the relationships and communications with other organisations were not as strong as they should have been. In its postincident report, Health New Zealand noted to the Inquiry that, Participants were in new roles with new responsibilities, and it can be assumed that some internal and external relationships between individuals and departments were not as strong or as organised as they would have been otherwise. In some cases, relationships were formed during the emergency response itself. . We consider that the role of the health and disability sector needs to be strengthened and better integrated into the emergency management system prior to the next emergency event. This includes ensuring the roles and responsibilities of sector organisations are clarified ahead of time and they have strong relationships with local CDEM Groups. Systemwide leadership and stewardship . Emergency management is a complex system with many people and organisations, each with differing and intersecting roles and responsibilities. For it to work well, there needs to be a steward of the system that has line of sight across all CDEM agencies, can provide support for locally delivered approaches, and gives assurance that the different parts are all performing as they should. . NEMA has responsibility for monitoring and assurance that CDEM Groups and people with responsibilities under the CDEM Act, such as lifeline utilities, have the systems in place to carry out their emergency management responsibilities. However, this function is not currently being undertaken or resourced by NEMA due T e Whatu Ora Health New Zealand, Over m Of Health Funding For Hawkes Bay As Anniversary Looms, Scoop, February . https:m.scoop.co.nzstoriesGESovermofhealthfundingforhawkesbayas anniversarylooms.htm CHAPTER : LEADERSHIP, ROLES AND RESPONSIBILITIES CHAPTER CHAPTER CHAPTER CHAPTER CHAPTER CHAPTER Government Inquiry into the Response to the North Island Severe Weather Eventsto other priorities. . The Inquiry considers NEMA needs to significantly increase its focus on system assurance, including identifying improvements local councils, agencies, and other organisations can make to build their emergency management capability and fulfil their responsibilities. This will support NEMA to set standards and build a national picture of how well the emergency management system is working, and where there are gaps and good practice. The Inquiry considers NEMA should have sufficient authority and powers to enable it to fulfil its assurance function. Guidance to the sector CDEM Groups and councils should ensure they have internal clarity on how they manage their joint accountability responsibilities for controllers. A strong, effective CEG is critical to managing the response to an emergency. CDEM Groups need to ensure their CEG members are practised in large scale emergency scenarios and have a strong understanding of each others roles. The NEMA website contains useful guidance for mayors and councillors that helps clarify roles and expectations before, during and after emergencies. CIMS is the official framework for effective coordinated emergency management across all responding agencies, and its structure should be embedded into councils way of working. As part of readiness planning: CDEM Groups need to ensure all essential workers are identified during readiness, and systems are set up for their easy identification as essential workers once an event has happened. This includes residential care workers and utility repair crews, councils need to consider how they prioritise training for staff with emergency management responsibilities, and plan how to manage staff fatigue during an emergency, and relationships should be formalised (for example, through publicly available memoranda of understanding) between government agencies, local and regional councils, CDEM Groups, communities, iwi Mori, Sector Coordinating Entities, critical infrastructure entities, and local businesses. Chapter : Management of the immediate response Overview . The actions taken in the lead up to an emergency, and the first hours after it starts, are critical in establishing how effective the response will be. It is often in this window that decisions are made about declaring an emergency, warnings and information are sent to communities, emergency centres are activated to provide shelter and services, and evacuations and rescues take place. . Overall, a piecemeal approach was taken during the immediate response to the severe weather events many aspects lacked coordination and situational awareness was poor. The Inquiry found that some immediate response activities failed to perform as needed in Auckland for the Auckland Anniversary heavy rainfall, and in Hawkes Bay for Cyclone Gabrielle, exacerbating the trauma felt by communities. Many people we heard from, particularly in Auckland and Hawkes Bay, felt abandoned and let down by their council and the immediate CDEM response. Some councils pushed back against this perception. The Inquiry observed that there is a striking disconnect between communities and their councils in some places. . Councils and communities that had carried out effective readiness planning activities prior to the events were better able to respond under the challenging circumstances. To ensure an effective response to future emergencies, CDEM agencies need to make coordinated, timely decisions, supported by accurate information and common operating procedures. Communities need to be empowered to act based on clear, timely warnings and information and have resources to support themselves for days or weeks after an emergency. . Over the course of the Inquiry, most of our engagements with communities pertained to the immediate response. We heard repeatedly about the trauma people faced, especially in the first few days of the emergency. The disconnect described in Chapter between the views of some community members and those of many CDEM agencies, highlights the need for education, better relationships between communities and councils, and more focus on readiness throughout the system. . There is significant room for improvement of readiness activities to support the management of the immediate response to significant emergencies. However, it is important to note the severe weather events subject to this Inquiry happened at a speed and scale that would have resulted in significant damage and stress regardless of how well the immediate response went. CHAPTER : MANAGEMENT OF THE IMMEDIATE RESPONSE CHAPTER CHAPTER CHAPTER CHAPTER CHAPTER CHAPTER Government Inquiry into the Response to the North Island Severe Weather EventsDefinition of immediate response . For the purposes of this report, the immediate response to an emergency starts when notice is given that an event is likely and preparatory actions begin. The immediate response finishes when the threat to life has passed and the situation has reached the point of stability. Rescued from floodwaters in Pakowhai Pakowhai, between Napier and Hastings in Hawkes Bay, sits between the Tutaekuri and Ngaruroro rivers. When Cyclone Gabrielle hit, the rivers burst their banks, flooding the fertile plains and submerging houses. On the morning of February , Pakowhai resident Lynley Halpin checked the local Facebook page and saw the bridge on the Tutaekuri River at Vicarage Road in Puketapu had washed away at . Lynley and her husband, Dave, headed up the road to check on their horses, only to be faced by a wall of water. Having received no warning, Dave went to help his parents who lived nearby, while Lynley did what she could do to prepare their home for flooding. Dave soon found he was unable to return home through the flooded roads. With still no warnings issued, Lynley became aware that the opportunity to evacuate had likely gone, and her neighbours wouldnt know about the imminent risk. She alerted as many neighbours as she could and opened the gates to give her horses the best chance of survival. At , as floodwaters rose, Lynley and her teenage daughters made their way onto the roof of their twostorey shed and waited to be rescued. Just after , they saw the horses swim past them in the flooded waters below. Lynley and her daughters were finally rescued by a jet boat at .
