CABMIN, CAB MIN, CAB MIN (dia.govt.nz) qwkdm ()(b)(ii) ()(b)(ii) ()(b)(ii) ()(b)(ii) Regulatory Impact Assessment term, which is to be done by sustaining TAB NZs revenue stream (refer constraints section) . By long term sustainability we mean ensuring that the racing industry stays at least as big as it currently is in terms of economic contribution to the economy (adjusted for CPI) and numbers of industry employees; from the period (when minimum guaranteed payments in the Entain agreement cease) and onwards for the foreseeable future. To achieve this objective, the following options were considered: Option : Counterfactual TAB NZ remains the only authorised operator of betting products in New Zealand, the government s online casino regulation regime is put in place, but offshore online operators can continue to offer their sporting and racing products to New Zealanders, so long as they do not advertise . Option : TAB NZ hold an online monopoly TAB NZs land based betting monopoly is extended to the online environment. Offshore operators would be prohibited from offering betting products to New Zealanders ; alongside a package of measures to give the required oversight and monitoring of TAB NZ protections for customers in light of this monopoly to TAB NZ . Option : Wait and see while increasing POCC This option would delay immediate legislati ve change to gather more information on the partnerships performance and make an informed decision on a monopoly; potentially after an online casino regulation regime is established. However, in the interim, raise the POCC to address revenue concerns. This means offshore operators that take bets from New Zealanders, would be required to pay increased POCC charges . Our analysis shows that option (counterfactual) is not viable . Although TAB NZs financial situation is stable in the short term, there is uncertainty about what might happen after the guaranteed payments expire. The partnership has strengthened the financial position of the industry in the short term. However, the benefits of the partnership long term are untested at this early stage in the partnership. This means the risk of offshore competition eroding the revenue flow of the TAB NZ remains, thus a risk to future distributions. Option (wait and see), is preferable to doing nothing but still does not achieve objectives . This option means we can take the time to gather more information on how the partnership is working and can see what impact it is having on TAB NZs market share and revenue. Depending on when an online gambling regulatory system is implemented it would mean the online monopoly could be enforced via this regulator from the outset without an interim regulator step . This option would give more time which might enable Ministers to have access to better information when making decisions on some of t he settingssecond order policy decisions relating to a monopoly (or perhaps develop an alternative solution) . In the interim, the POCC could be raised to help boost revenue. This means offshore operators that take bets from New Zealanders, would be required to pay increased charges. The guaranteed payments to mean there is time to do the work and see what option is adopted in terms of regulating online gambling. However, it does mean if a monopoly was eventually implemented after , TAB NZ would miss out on the additional payments from Entain if the monopoly is not realised. Thus , this known benefit would be forgone for uncertain future potential benefit s. Option (online monopoly) is the preferred option as it is only option that could meet the objective of sustaining TAB NZ revenue, and in turn the racing industry , in the long term. In addition , this option , if implemented prior to June , should realise the immediate capital injection from the million payment and TAB NZ would also receive an uplift in the minimum guaranteed funding each month this guaranteed return period. qwkdm ()(b)(ii) Regulatory Impact Assessment likely require changes to the Gambling Act . However, due to the time constraints, the Minister for Racing does not intend to wait for that work to progress. This means any changes must be within the purview of the Racing Industry Act. Limited consultation on options the public and stakeholders were not consulted on the specific options in this RI A due to the time constraints discussed above. However, the issue of regulation of online gambling and sports and racing betting has been actively discussed for some years and the previous Government announced in May i t agreed in principle to TAB NZ having an online monopoly, subject to further work being undertaken. We anticipate there are likely to be a range of views on the options. For example, offshore operators are likely to be in favour of a regulated online gambling market they can legitimately enter and participate in and opposed to TAB NZ being given an online sports and racing betting monopoly andor a raised POCC rate. Conversely , TAB NZ and the racing codes are highly supportive of TAB NZ having an online monopoly. While not having been directly consulted on the overall package in Option , some other elements of the package have been signalled with them and we believe they will be generally supportive of the option package. In particular it should be noted that while we have consulted Sport NZ on extending TAB NZs online wagering monopoly , we have not consulted individual NSOs , hence their views and the financial impact on specific NSOs is uncertain. Quality of data and evidence there is a lot we do not know about the true nature and extent of existing betting by New Zealanders with offshore operators. We cannot identify exactly how many people are betting offshore and how many would return to betting with TAB NZ if an online monopoly was introduced. Analysis relies on data and forecasting provided by TAB NZ as well as other industry and government figures. Much of the data we have reviewed for this RI A predates the TABEntain partnership that came into effect in June . The estimates and forecasting provided by TAB NZ not been independently verified due to time constraints. We note that estimates provided by TAB NZ about the size of the offshore sports and racing betting market are not in line with our projections based on POCC. We have not been able to investigate the reasons for this difference, however a portion of this is like ly to be TAB NZ s estimate considering operators who do not pay the POCC (but this is unlikely to account for the full difference). The Entain deal is expected to result in a bigger market share and revenue for TAB NZ than what would have occurred without the partnership , through offering a better wagering product but, under current regulatory settings, revenue will continue to flow offshore and not contribute to racing and sporting industries (except through BIUC charges and relatively modest POCC takings). Analysis of options has been particularly impacted by these constraints and is based on several overall assumptions (summarised below). The racing industrys economic contribution to New Zealand was recently estimated at close to . billion. It employs approximately , full time equivalent positions, with , people participating in racing annually. . The racing industry comprises of racing codes: New Zealand Thoroughbred Racing, Harness Racing New Zealand , and Greyhound Racing New Zealand. Each code is responsible for its respective industry which includes race clubs, courses, trainers, jockeys, breeders , and owners. Racing New Zealand (Racing NZ) is the umbrella body that enables collaboration and collective decision making between the racing codes. TAB NZ, as the only domestic provider of landbased racing and sports betting, is a key funding source to the sector . Totalisator Agency Board (now known as TAB NZ ) was established in as the sole betting provider for racing in New Zealand (sport was included in the s). TAB NZ was intended to be the sole provider of sports and racing betting with a not forprofit funding model. Its purpose is to maximis e profits for the long term benefit of the New Zealand racing industry and New Zealand sports , as well as minimising gambling harm. . The racing industry relies heavily on TAB NZ for its income. The racing codes receive over of their income from TAB NZ. In TAB NZ returned approximately million to the racing codes from its betting revenue. . The racing c odes distribute the funds they receive from TAB NZ to the various racing clubs. The clubs in turn use these funds, to maintain their club and offer more prize money for example . Prize money plays a significant role as it supports owners, trainers, jockeys, stable hands, and the entire supply chain including breeders, vets, farriers , and feed merchants. A reduction in funding would reduce prizes, which in turn would limit the industrys ability to maintain (or grow) its size. . While participants in the racing industry may also have other income streams (e.g. owners who export horses), we expect a significant proportion of their income come s from participating in races. . The racing industry also receives a small amount (approximately million annually) from offshore operators who take bets from New Zealanders via the POCC (with a similar distribution going to sports).

This paper is that report back and takes into account feedback from consultation. Gambling harm The Act defines gambling harm broadly and includes harm from another persons gambling. Gambling harm can include depression, suicide , relationship breakdown, reduced work productivity, job loss, bankruptcy and crime. Harm can extend to family, wh nau, friends, employers, colleagues, and whole communities. He Ara Oranga noted Gambling was also seen as harmful due to its addictive nature and the financial stress and anxiety it causes families, contributing to neglect of children and family violence. Research shows that children in families affected by harmful gamb ling are more likely to develop risky gambling behaviours. While reported rates of gambling harm are at their lowest levels in years, the number of people affected has increased in line with population growth over the past seven years. Gambling harm a ffects percent of the New Zealand population, while one in five will be affected at some time in their lives by their own or someone elses gambling. A likely bigger deterrent to reputable providers than is the risk of losing their licences in larger more profitable jurisdictions by breaching New Zealands prohibition. This is because in some cases, licences in other jurisdictions, which are likely to have more profitable markets, are at risk if licence holders intentionally breach laws in other jurisdictions. . In addition, it is proposed that the criteria for an operator to gain a licence for an online casino will involve the operators track record of legislative compliance. Breaching the sporting and racing online monopoly would therefore jeopardise an operators chance of gaining an online casino licence and the significant financial benefits that would bring. . The enforcement powers are not expected to include internet blocking of offshore providers. This is an expensive and inefficient tool for enforcement. Internet filters are easily circumnavigated by consumers and less reputable providers, and are considered an intrusion on the principles of a free and open internet. Most reputable providers prohibited from operating in New Zealand will institute geoblocking on their platforms. . Enforcement action would be targeted at offshore operators. We do not propose banning or criminalising New Zealanders who gamble with offshore operators, as this could discourage people from seeking help if they are at risk of or experiencing gambling harm. The online monopoly, combined with the Entain partnership, will require greater oversight of TAB NZ and protections for customers . Expanding TAB NZs monopoly to online settings by prohibiting all other forms of online sports and racing betting is a significant consolidation of the revenue gathering channels for the sporting and racing industries. . There are some risks to providing a monopoly to TAB NZ without sufficient oversight and monitoring by Government, including the possibility that the mechanisms in place to support the racing industry continue to fail, following the guaranteed return period in the partnership with Entain.
. The Local Government Commission acts as a safeguard during the appeals and objections stage of the representation review process . The racing industry has been through a period of significant reforms since . In response to concerns about the racing industry declining , in April the Minister for Racing, Rt Hon Winston Peters appointed senior Australian racing expert John Messara to review the New Zealand racing industrys governance structures and provide recommendations on future directions for the industry. The Minister released the report on August which made a package of sweeping recommendation s for reform of the industry. . Following the release Messara report , a significant process of legislative reform was undertaken in to respond to the reports findings . These culminated with the enact ment of the new Racing Industry Act ( Racing Act ) which established a new industry structure . . A major change was to establish TAB NZ as a statutory entity focused on wagering and responsibility for running the industry was devolved to the racing codes. . The reforms also: progressively repealed the Gaming Duty on TAB NZ (redirecting funds to the racing industry); established offshore charges to provide additional sources of revenue to the racing industry (Betting Information Use Charges (BIUC) and POCC); and allowed TAB NZ to partner with offshore betting operators. . It should be noted that the Messara report; while making recommendation s on TAB NZ outsourcing its functions to an overseas provider, and introducing offshore changes did not make any specific recommendations around an online monopoly. . In the Government also provided a support package of .m to the racing industry to support its recovery from COVID . Due to pandemic restrictions limiting sporting and racing events in New Zealand and internationally, the industry (and TAB NZ) lost revenue. In early , TAB NZ was facing a rapid and ongoing drop in its revenue, which affected their distributions to racing industry . By early , TAB NZ was facing a rapid and ongoing decline in its revenue due to competition from offshore operators. From May to November , TAB NZ missed its betting profits target by an average of . million each month (the worst performance was a . million shortfall in just one month), meaning profits were running on average . below target .

A key consideration has been ensuring we can future proof the legislation. Gender theory and terminology evolves rapidly what was appropriate five years ago may not be what is used today . Setting the sex markers in regulations will mean they can be more easily reviewed and to ensure they meet the needs of transgender and intersex people. I propose amending the definition of eligible person to exclude people whose birth cannot be registered in New Zealand . . The Family Court process includes overseas born citizens and permanent residents whose birth cannot be registered in New Zealand in the definition of eligibl e person. This dates from when overseas born New Zealanders needed a Family Court declaration to update their gender on other official documentation, such as passports and driver licences. Overseas born New Zealanders now no longer need a Family Court declaration to update these documents in New Zealand . . The Bill does not have extra territorial jurisdiction. It would not be appropriate to legislate a process to amend information for births registered overseas. The impact of the change in definition on those born overseas but who reside in New Zealand is expected to be minimal. However, I am considering whether a process needs to be available to allow overseas born residents (including M ori) to have the ir gende r recognised on an official document . I propose a statutory review of the self identification provisions five years after enactment . The complexity of the policy and the sensitivity of this issue will make it important that the legislative settings are eva luated after enactment. A review would provide a transparent assessment of whether the policy settings supporting a self identification process are functioning well in practice. It would not include reviewing the basic change to a self identification proce ss. The statutory review would involve engagement with transgender and intersex communities and require developing a report to present to Parliament. The self identification process should apply to c hildren and young people . Children and young people unde r years can already access the Family Court process to amend their registered sex . Like adults, I want them to have access to a self identification process. It is important to ensure that children and young people can use their birth certificate without stress or discrimination and feel accepted for who they are as they grow up. A process for children and young people recognises that people are aware of their gender from a young age . . It is important that the process applies to children and young people as birth certificates may be one of the only forms of identification available to them and are used to enrol in education or apply for jobs . Other forms of identification are more expensive (eg passpor ts) or age restrictive (eg driver licences). As children and young people more frequently rely on birth certificates , they will face more daily stressors when th e sex recorded does not align with their gender, such as outing, invasive questions, discrimi nation or bullying.

If the implementation of the interim Trust Framework and development of the legislation is deferred, the problems with the current system will be perpetuated as new services arise. It will be harder to back fill compliance requirements after the services are built, and we may lose opportunities for innovation and collaboration if there are not ways for key information sources to be accessed appropriately. These risks, already present prior to Covid , are exacerbated by the current increase in use of digital services and the proliferation of new digital identity services. A Budget Bid will be made in for phase : the formal establishment of the Trust Framework in legislation . Indicative costings of implementing the formal Trust Framework amount to . million in total from to . This includes the co st of supporting and accrediting potential Trust Framework participants, providing governance and updating and maintaining the Trust Framework and supporting operational policies. The costs and funding sources will be refined to take into account the cost recovery model for the Trust Framework and detailed in a Budget bid, pending Cabinet agreement. A cost recovery model will be developed for the statutory Trust Framework, which will be in effect once the legislation is passed . A cost recovery model will be developed as part the legislative programme for the formal Trust Framework, and the Bill will p rovide the accreditation body with the power to charge for accreditation. The Department will first need to finalise the Trust Framework rules and accreditation processes before it can determine what kind of cost recovery model should be established. . Cost recovery will likely be nominal for participating agencies (to avoid the inefficiencies of government charging government) and actual for private sector entities. Work on potential cost recovery models for the formal Trust Framework will be progressed as part of the transitional policy and legislative development programme in the financial year. . Any system of cost recovery will need to consider the respective public and private benefits conferred by the Trust Framework. While some benefits may be f inancial and private in nature, many are not. The World Bank has stated that identification should be treated as a public good, provided to facilitate the rights and inclusion of individuals and to improve administration and service delivery. . A Trust Fra mework is critical infrastructure for the delivery of this public good, and will confer benefits to a wide range of system participants including regulators (e.g. by improving compliance monitoring, data collection and storage standards), the private secto r (through the provision of more valuable services, leading to increased revenue and greater compliance) and the public (e.g. through greater privacy, security and transparency around data use).

()(f)(iv) ()(g)(i) IN CONFIDENCE Page of Approach to consumer protection . The Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs and I have been developing an appropriate approach to consumer protection, to complement t he new economic regulation regime and local government water services delivery system. . We do not consider t here is a compelling case to introduce new, mandatory consumer protection measures into the primary legislation , particularly given the costs and bureaucracy that could be associated with such measures. It is currently unclear that there are problems with existing consumer protection measures, or whether any problems will emerge with the new local government service delivery arrangements. . Local government water service providers already have systems and processes in place for proposing and reporting on levels of service relating to water services, and for dealing with complaints about the services they provide. As drinking water suppliers, they are also subject to requirements to have complaints processes, under the Water Services Act. . If new water organisations are established, we expect these arrangements will apply. As owners of these organisations, councils will also be able to set any additional expectations that may be relevant locally such as requirements to have processes for collecting and responding to customer feedback on an organisations water services, or to undertake engagement with consumers. . We do not want to impose new statutory requirements on water service providers unless it is clear that further intervention is needed, and any costs can be justified. For example, if providers were required by the legislation to become members of an external dispute resolution bodyscheme, this would incur costs that would likely be passed on to consumers. These are identified as matters that ownersshareholders could include in a statement of expectations, referred to in the paper Local Water Done Well stage : water services delivery system . ()(g)(i) IN CONFIDENCE Page of . Instead, w e are proposing to take a pragmatic approach, which would leverage existing mechanisms, and enable further consumer protection measures to be considered later if these are needed to improve existing processes and settings. This approach is outlined below. Provision should be made for consumer protection measures to be included through regulations , if needed . As agreed through our joint paper, Local Water Done Well stage : water services regulatory system ECO MIN , information disclosure will be a key component of the new economic regulation regime that will apply to local government water service providers . . We consider information disclosure could be used to oversee aspects of the consumer experience, such as the number and themes arising in consumer complaints relating to local government water service providers . This would enable the Commerce Commission to learn more about how existing consumer protection settings are working in practice, and identify potential shortcomings. . To facilitate this, we are seeking a gree ment that the legislation clearly enable s the Commerce Commission to require public reporting from water service providers on consumer protection issues , and to publicly summarise and analyse the information disclosed. . We are also proposing the legislation includes the power for the Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs to make regulations relating to consumer protection measures. This will provide flexibility to consider what may be needed in the future particularly if information disclosure reveals that issues exist . The focus of these measures would be on providing protections for individual consumers primarily households and small businesses. . This power could be used to propose make regulations on any matters that relate to consumer protection measures. In particular , the provisions will allow for requirements that may be needed in the future relating to: . complaint processes, the provision of information, the recording of complaints, andor reporting ; andor . providing access to an external consumer dispute resolution process ; . other matters relating to consumer protections that the Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs considers necessary and appropriate . . The proposed approach does not affect or amend the consumer complaints provisions that apply to drinking water suppliers in the Water Services Act , or the role Taumata Arowai has in relation to those provisions. The Commerce Commissions role would be complementary, and put an additional and enhanced focus on local government water services providers providing transparency about all t heir services. The Commission and Taumata Arowai should be able to share information with each other on these matters , where relevant . . If regulations are made, we would expect them to be designed in a way that ensures there is no unnecessary duplication across the regulatory systems and local government water service providers are not covered in the scope of two different sets of requirements. IN CONFIDENCE Page of Service quality codes could be a useful addition, but should be sector led in the first instance . Service quality codes are common in other domestic and international markets, and may be a useful addition to the new water services system. These codes tend to cover matters such as customer service, billing transparency, and communication about network outages. . If it became clear that a service quality code was required for the water services system, we would expect it to be sector led in the first instance. This might be done by individual or group s of water service providers, or by an industrysector body. . To support this approach , we propos e the Commerce Commission should be able to issue guidelines to water service providers on matters relating to a service quality code. . We are also proposing t he legislation enable s the Commerce Commission to make a service quality code in relation to the provision of water services, where no sector developed code exists or , in the opinion of the Commission , the purpose of Part of the Commerce Act could be better met by a mandatory code . This would allow the Commission to specify minimum requirements in relation to consumer experience. . Before making a code, the Commission w ill be required to provide a report to the Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs containing the reasons for doing this . The legislation should also provide for appropriate mechanisms relating to enforcement and cost recovery . If the above proposals are agreed, the legislation will need to provide for associated compliance and enforcement provisions, to allow the Commerce Commission to take action should any consumer protections be brought into effect. We also need to consider how costs related to consumer protection s will be dealt with. . As noted in Local Water Done Well stage : water services regulatory system ECO MIN , the Commerce Act contains a range of compliance, enforcement and investigation powers for use under Part of that Act. . Through th at paper, i t was agreed similar mechanisms would be applied to the economic regulation of water services. I am proposing to extend these types of powers and tools to the enforcement of consumer protection regulation. The level of any penalties would be determined in consultation with the Ministry of Justice, and informed by similar requirements in other statutes. . It was also agreed recovery of costs for the economic regulation regime would be through levies, and that the legislation will include provisions that enable this. I am proposing to extend this recommendation so that costs related to consumer protections ma y also be recovered through levies (if needed) . Service quality codes are sometimes referred to as minimum service level standards or consumer care guidelines. IN CONFIDENCE Page of . The consumer protection proposals are designed to provide a scaled approach, so costs will only be imposed if there is evidence that a stronger means of regulation is justified. Initially, costs associated with consumer protection will be those incurred by the Commerce Commission when designing and monitoring consumer protection related information disclosure requirements . This will be part of the Commerce Commissions activities under the economic regulation regime. . If further consumer protection requirements are introduced through regulations, there would be costs associated with their implementation , and with compliance and monitoring activities carried out by the Commission. These costs w ill be considered as part of the analysis of costs and benefits when a decision is taken on their introduction. Amendments affecting Taumata Arowai and water quality regulat ion . As indicated in my previous paper ECOMIN , I have been exploring potential amendments to the water quality framework in the Water Services Act, and the legislation and practices relating to Taumata Arowai . . Decisions on an initial set of amendments were sought in th at paper, and a dditional proposals are set out below . I am proposing some changes relating to Taumata Arowai and how it operates Board appointments . Section of the Taumata Arowai the Water Services Regulator Act provides for the appointment of the board of Taumata Arowai. . Currently, under section (), the responsible Minister must appoint members to the board who, collectively, have knowledge and experience of, and capability in : . the compliance, monitoring, and enforcement activities of regulatory agencies; . public health; . the Treaty of Waitangi (Te Tiriti o Waitangi) and its principles; . perspectives of Mori and tikanga Mori; . performance monitoring and governance. . I consider this list is overly prescriptive and may hinder my ability to consider appointees who could make a valuable contribution to the board. I would prefer a more flexible approach, which would allow other attributes to be taken into account and provide access to a wider pool of potential members. . I am seeking agreement to amend section () to remove this list of specific attributes, and replace it with a more general provision to the effect that the Minister must only appoint people who, in the responsible Ministers opinion, have the appropriate knowledge, skills and experience to assis t the board to perform its role. IN CONFIDENCE Page of Ensuring cost considerations are more clearly incorporated into Taumata Arowais regulatory framework . Currently, consideration of cost is not explicitly mentioned in legislation, although it does form part of the p roportionate approach to regulat ion Taumata Arowai refers to in its regulatory documents. . As part of my focus on reducing the regulatory burden and the cost of compliance, I am seeking agreement to a mend the legislation to ensure consideration of cost is a clear part of Taumata Arowais legislative framework . This would need to be balanced alongside public health outcomes . . Section of t he Taumata Arowai the Water Services Regulator Act includes a list of operating principles that guide and inform Taumata Arowai in its performance and delivery of its objectives, functions, and duties . . I am proposing to include new operating principle s so that Taumata Arowai is expected to: . consider the cost of compliance on suppliers when performing and delivering its objectives, functions and duties , including an appropriate balance between public health outcomes and reasonable costs to suppliers. . ensure the regulatory framework is proportionate to the scale, complexity, and risk profile of each drinking water supply (and wastewater and stormwater networks, as the case may be), including the consideration of cost and affordability for the users of the supplies ; . proactively engage with suppliers and network operators to ensure that there is a path to compliance that takes into account the risk profile and capacity of the supplier or network operator itself. ()(f)(iv) IN CONFIDENCE Page of . This would provide Taumata Arowai with a clear legislative direction, which would then flow through into its operations, and the regulatory policy and guidance that it applies when regulating the sector. . I am also proposing to amend the operating principles of Taumata Arowai regarding Te Mana o te Wai to align with the proposed changes discussed later in this paper . Working pr oactively alongside Crown and local government suppliers . Currently, it is an express purpose of the Water Services Act that regulation is proportionate to the scale, complexity and risk profile of each drinking water supply. This has allowed Taumata Arowai to undertake targeted approaches to ensuring compliance with regulatory requirements wherever possible. . I want to ensure Taumata Arowai is directing its limited resources , and all available regulatory tools, to where they will have the most impact . I consider there should be a particular focus on larger drinking water suppliers (including Crown and local government suppliers), given the widespread consequences for public health if there is noncompliance and unsafe drinking water is supplied. . To help do this, I am propos ing to add a further operating principle into the Taumata Arowai the Water Services Regulator Act to ensure there is a clear legislative direction for Taumata Arowai to work proactively with suppliers, particularly larger suppliers, to ensure a path to regulatory compliance . I am also proposing some changes to the Water Services Act Ensuring it is clear Taumata Arowai can proactively issue exemptions , and improving alignment with other regulatory regimes . Section of the Water Services Act allow s the Chief Executive of Taumata Arowai to grant exemptions to any drinking water supplier or class of drinking water supplier from complying with nine requirements of the Act. This can be done if the exemption is consistent with the main purpose of the Act and , in the case of a class exemption, there has been public consult ation . . The Act is currently unclear about whether or not the Chief Executive can issue an exemption proactively that is, without the need for an application from a supplier. . I consider it is desirable to provide clarity about this, and am proposing the legislation enables exemptions to be issued proactively. This would provide flexibility to deal with situations where it is clear to the Chief Executive that an exemption is des irable and warranted . It would remove unnecessary costs and bureaucracy associated with submitting and assessing applications for exemptions. . I am also proposing to amend section () of the Act to allow exemptions to be granted for any one or more of the nine requirements that are currently specified. The current approach is all or nothing , which means the Chief Executive can only grant exemptions that apply to all nine of the listed regulatory requirements . IN CONFIDENCE Page of . Changing this approach would be consistent with other regulatory regimes that provide for exemptions, and provide additional flexibility. This is beneficial given the wide range of regulatory requirements listed in section ( ), and the fact that it may be appropriate to only provide exemptions relating to some of these requirements. . I am also seeking agreement to include a further item in the list in section ( ), so that exemption s may apply to requirements in section of the Act to notify Taumata Arowai of notifiable risk s or hazard s. Small suppliers , in particular , may benefit from an exemption from this duty. . My propos ed amendments w ill include additional statutory limitations and considerations that are found in other regimes . The amendments would provide for : . an express statement setting out the purpose of exemptions ; . flexibility to issue exemptions proactively, where compliance with th e relevant provisions referred to in section () of the Water Services Act is impractical, inefficient, unduly costly, or unduly burdensome (taking into account the nature of the specific issues ), or for matters that are minor or technical; . a requirement that the extent of the exemption granted cannot be broader than is reasonably necessary to address the matters that gave rise to the exemption. . Coupled with the existing requirement to publicly consult where class exemptions are being considered, and the need to publish the reasons for granting any exemption, the additional requirements should provide greater transparency , and safeguards for the Chief Executive and Taumata Arowai from perceptions of conflict of interests, inappropriate decision making , and industry capture . National engineering design standards . The provision of infrastructure is a key component of land use development. Councils develop and use Codes of Practice for Land Development to guide those people doing land developments on technical standards for network infrastructure. There are different standards in New Zealand providing information on how to design and construct water network infra structure. . Some work was undertaken during the previous governments reforms to develop national engineering design standards to provide the local government and the development sector with consistent national standard s. These would have been adopted on a voluntary basis. . I can see the potential benefits of national engineering design standards , which include consistent standards for design and construction of network infrastructure . This would support the Government s aim to increase standardisation to lower the costs on providing infrastructure. . Benefits are likely to include: For example, the list of requirements covered in section ( ) range from the duty to supply safe drinking water and comply with drinking water standards, to requirements to keep records and have consumer complaints processes. Similar to section B of the Overseas Investment Act , for example . IN CONFIDENCE Page of . greater efficiencies for the design, approval, procurement, construction , maintenance and renewal of network infrastructure; . the ability to use the national engineering design standards for construction and renewal contracts; . a common technical reference for the development of industry training and skills. accreditation programs for private sector suppliers. . National engineering design standards would provide regulatory engineers, design engineers, developers, and contractors servicing the land development industry with one common set of engineering design standards across New Zealand. They would not override any other regulatory requirements in relation to land development (such as Resource Management Act requirements ), but are intended to support the consenting process by providing the technical requirements for the planning, design, construction, and handove r of network infrastructure. . The primary purpose of these standards is to document technical best practice for design and construction of drinking water, wastewater and stormwater network or reticulation infrastructure. I anticipate they w ill include a mixture of mandatory minimum engineering design standards, and informative statements to provide context and enable better understanding of the mandatory requirements. They w ill be developed with appropriate technical and sector input, and reviewed regularly as new engineering methodolog y and products are developed. . I am proposing national engineering design standards are progressed and should be a mandatory requirement , provided for in legislation . However, further work is required to confirm the detailed scope, content and transitional arrangements needed to enable th is approach to be implemented. . To reflect the further work required, and the potential difficulties of providing for these matters in primary legislation, I am seeking agreement to include regulation making powers in the legislation relating to national engineering design standards . . The regulations would cover matters such as the detailed scope and content of these standards, the process for developing them, the relationship with other regulatory requirements, and any relevant transitional arrangements and timeframes. Extending the scope and transitional timeframes for an authorisation framework . The Water Services Act provi des for an authorisation framework to be developed and implemented through regulations . Once in place, th is framework will introduce requirements relating to the training, skills, or experience needed by operators of drinking water and wastewater networks , to help ensure these networks are operated safely. The Act provides discretion about how the framework should be designed and delivered, and details will be set out in the regulations. . Under transitional provisions in c lause of Schedule of the Act , all local authorit ies and CCOs that operate drinking water supplies are required to be authorised under the proposed authorisations framework within five years after the commencement of the Act (that is, by November ). IN CONFIDENCE Page of . I am seeking agreement to amend these transitional provisions, so councils and CCOs are required to be authorised within years after the commencement (November ). The provisions w ould also be to incorporate any new water organisations established by councils. . Work is currently underway to develop th e new authorisations framework, and no regulations have been made yet. This is a complex area , which includes a wide range of components and considerations including designing and putting in place mechanisms for delivering training and authorising particular operators. . Without this change to the statutory timeframes , there is a significant risk that the new requirements will be developed and introduced too quickly before the water sector is equipped to deliver and take up the necessary training . There may be unintended consequences , such as significant cost increases or difficulty maintaining safe staffing levels. . This longer timeframe w ill allow for essential collaborative work with the water sector on the design and implementation of an authorisations framework including the necessary training and support mechanisms . It will also ensure councils and CCOs that operate drinking water supplies and any new water organisations that councils may establish have sufficient time to become compliant with any new requirements . . I am also seeking agreement to expand the scope of the authorisation framework, and any regulations that may be made. The legislation currently refers to persons who operate, certify, test or assess drinking water supplies and wastewater networks. I consid er there should also be appropriate references to the work involved in the maintenance , repair or renewal of supplies andor networks (or parts, thereof ), and the Water Services Act should be amended to provide for this . . I want to ensure there is clarity that the new framework that will be developed and implemented can include persons such as plumbers who may be involved in working on these supplies and networks. . This will mean the qualifications and experience required for persons doing relevant work c an be provided for in a nationally consistent approach , through regulations which individual councils , water organisations , and other suppliers would then be expected to take into account at a local level. Requiring Taumata Arowai to provide acceptable solutions for suppliers . Under Section of the Water Services Act, Taumata Arowai may , by notice, issue a drinking water acceptable solution or verification method for use in establishing compliance with legislative requirements. . Acceptable solutions are a ready made option (template) to help drinking water suppliers meet standards. They apply to specific supply types and remove the need to submit a drinking water safety plan, if implemented in their entirety. Currently there are three acceptable solutions: Roof Water Supplies , Spring and Bore Drinking Water Supplies , and Mixed Use Rural Water Supplies. IN CONFIDENCE Page of . I am proposing to amend the Water Services Act to require Taumata Arowai to issue drinking water acceptable solutions (rather than this being a may in the legislation) . Ensuring these templates are readily available to a greater number of suppliers will help reduce the regulatory burden and costs for suppliers, by reducing the need for suppliers to develop their own bespoke solutions at cost to them . Changes relating to wastewater environmental performance standards . Taumata Arowai is currently developing national wastewater environmental performance standards under section of the Water Services Act. This provision empowers Taumata Arowai, following consultation, to make wastewater standards for the activities asso ciated with wastewater networks, like discharges to land or water. . Under current legislative settings, the standards are minimum standards. A regional council considering an application for a resource consent that relates to a wastewater network cannot grant a consent that has conditions that are less restrictive than the wastewater standards, but they may impose conditions that impose a higher standard. . I consider there should be a single standard, rather than a minimum or maximum. A single standard approach is consistent with international best practice. In other jurisdictions where a standard is set, plants are consented to a national standard. It is not a minimum standard it is just the standard. . I am proposing to amend the legislation to provide for a single standard approach. These amendments would be designed to ensure regional councils implement a single standard approach in resource consents, and cannot exceed the standard in consenting condit ions apart from on an exceptions basis. . This does not mean that th e environmental requirements for discharges to freshwater or coastal water will be lower. What it does mean is that we will enable a consistent approach for consenting the discharge of wastewater from treatment plants, which will reduce the regulatory burde n by ensuring environmental regulation in water services legislation is proportionate to risk and benefit. . This change will deliver much greater standardisation of treatment systems and related infrastructure, enable material cost efficiencies in the design, build and operation of wastewater systems , and provide councils greater certainty of costs. All of these outcomes are aligned with the objectives of Local Water Done Well. . Making this change is critical if we are going to support councils to address challenges in the reconsenting bow wave. Around percent of wastewater treatment plants will require reconsenting in the next years, with the most challenging issues arising where plants discharge to freshwater or low mixing environments like estuaries or bays close to the coast. . I note that around half of the wastewater treatment plants that will require reconsenting in the next decade provide services to populations of , people or fewer. These plants make up around percent of the total number of council owned wastewater pl ants in New Zealand. IN CONFIDENCE Page of . While there will be local differences, industry estimates of the costs of the design, consent and construction of these smaller plants are up to million and, in some cases, up to half of those costs relate to design and consenting issues. In contrast , a modular off theshelf wastewater treatment plant that was designed to meet the standard could be constructed and be operational for around million to million. . These proposals will require changes to the Water Services Act and the Resource Management Act, which could be progressed through the Local Government Water Services Bill. For example, these changes are needed to: . provide more directive provisions that ensure regional councils cannot set additional or higher requirements than the standard (allowing for some specific exceptions); . allow Taumata Arowai to be able to set infrastructure and operating requirements that, if implemented by a wastewater operator, will meet the treatment requirements in the standard; . allow an easier resource consenting path or pre consented option for lower risk small scale modular wastewater treatment plants that meet the wastewater environmental performance standard. . Further work is needed to develop and agree the appropriate policy approach and specific nature of the legislative changes. I am seeking delegated authority to work with and agree the correct approach with the Minister Responsible for RMA Reform and other Ministers as appropriate (such as the Minister for the Environment). . I am also seeking approval to issue drafting instructions once this group of Ministers has made decisions . I will include an update on this matter in the paper to the Cabinet Legislation Committee that seeks approval to introduce the Bill, in late . Process for making wastewater and stormwater environmental performance standards . Currently, Taumata Arowai is able to make wastewater andor stormwater environmental performance standards (under sections and A of the Water Services Act), through a process that includes public consultation but does not include Cabinet oversight. . I note that this is different from the approach to making drinking water standards in section of the Water Services Act, which are regulations made by Order in Council and do, therefore, involve Cabinet processes (as well as public consultation). . Given the importance of the wastewater and stormwater environmental performance standards, and the interest Cabinet is likely to have in the proposals, I consider these standards should be made through a process that includes Cabinet consideration and the associated requirements . This will ensure there is a regulatory impact analysis , which includes details about the costs, benefit s and risks of the proposals . . I am seeking agreement to amend the Water Services Act so that the power and process associated with making wastewater environmental performance standards and stormwater environmental performance standards is consistent with the power and process for makin g drinking water standards . IN CONFIDENCE Page of Mixed use rural water schemes . There are around mixed use rural water schemes across New Zealand. The se schemes are unique as they provide large volumes of water across large areas for commercial farming purposes, and they also provide smaller volumes of water to rural residential properties for human drinking and sanitary purposes. . While mixed use rural water schemes primarily supply water for agricultural or horticultural purposes, they are subject to the same regulatory requirements as other drinking water supplies including the supplies to large urban populations. . I am aware of concerns that complying with these requirements is driving up costs for mixed use rural water schemes , and can be burdensome and impractical . This was comment ed on by s ubmitters on the Local Government (Water Services Preliminary Arrangements) Bill , for example. . My recent paper, Local Water Done Well stage : water services regulatory system ECO MIN , include d proposals that are likely to reduce the costs for some of these schemes. In particular, the Water Services Act will be amended to exclude shared domestic drinking water supplies serving consumers or fewer from the regulation. Shared domestic supplies will include farm s that suppl y drinking water to a small number of nearby properties. . The additional proposals in this paper, outlined above, should provide further reduc tions to the compliance costs and regulatory burdens faced by mixed use rural water schemes. . I have also been considering other changes that could be made to ensure the unique characteristics of these schemes are reflected, both in the legislation and in the approach Taumata Arowai takes to regulation. My intention is that Taumata Arowai should support the se schemes to achieve compliance in a way that is appropriate and proportionate to their particular circumstances . . I am proposing to amend the operating principles that apply to Taumata Arowai (in section of the Taumata Arowai the Water Services Regulator Act) to specifically refer to mixed use rural schemes . These changes build on and supplement the other changes to the operating principles proposed earlier. . I am also proposing to amend sections and of the Water Services Act to require Taumata Arowai to: . include specific information on mixed use rural water schemes in its drinking water compliance, monitoring, and enforcement strategy; and . comment on mixed use rural water schemes in its annual drinking water regulation report. . In addition, I will be proceeding with some non legislative measures to ensure there is an appropriate focus on mixed use rural water schemes and affordability is being considered. They are often small, the risk is low, and they can find other ways to make water safe , which are cost effective for the small amount of water that is used by people . These measures include : IN CONFIDENCE Page of . communicating my expectations to the Taumata Arowai board that they ensure the regulatory response for mixed use rural water schemes is proportionate to the scale, complexity and risk profile of each supply and affordability is being given appropriate consideration ; and . encourag ing the board to consider establishing a technical advisory group to provide independent advice on the regulatory settings for mixed use rural water schemes . . I note that councils will be expected to include information on any mixed use rural water schemes that are part of their water services networks in the water services delivery plans that will be prepared under the Local Government (Water Services Preliminary Arrangements) Bill , once it is enacted . The guidance material provided by the Department of Internal Affairs will also encourage councils to include information in their plans on the schemes that are not part of their networks but where other support arrangements may be in place. I am proposing to amend the Water Services Act and Taumata Arowai Act relating to Te Mana o te Wai . I am proposing to amend the arrangements relating to Te Mana o te Wai in the Water Services Act and the Taumata Arowai the Water Services Regulator Act . . Section of the Water Services Act provides that when exercising or performing a function, power or duty under this Act, a person must give effect to Te Mana o te Wai, to the extent that Te Mana o te Wai applies to its functions, powers and duties. . The Taumata Arowai the Water Services Regulator Act requires Taumata Arowai to: . as one of its objectives, give effect to Te Mana o te Wai, to the extent that Te Mana o te Wai applies the functions and duties of Taumata Arowai (section (d)); and . as an operating principle, to partner and engaging early and meaningfully with Mori, including to inform how Taumata Arowai can give effect to Te Mana o te Wai (section ()(e)(i)). . These are general prov isions , and they apply to a broad range of parties who have a variety of differing roles under the legislation, including: . Taumata Arowai in relation to all of its functions under both Acts; . regional councils in relation to their source water risk management functions; . territorial authorities and Crown suppliers in their role as drinking water suppliers; and . a very broad range of private drinking water suppliers (includ ing, for example, farmers, bach communities, campgrounds , or cafes where they supply drinking water ). . One of the ongoing unresolved areas with the legislation is how these parties are expected to meet these obligations. Private drinking water suppliers in particular will often lack the capability to engage with Mori and comply with these obligations. IN CONFIDENCE Page of . This has been an ongoing area of ambiguity since the legislation was enacted. It is also not clear how the obligations to give effect to Te Mana o te Wai in water services legislation relate to the concept of Te Mana o te Wai in the National Policy Stateme nt for Freshwater Management and regional plans prepared under the RMA that relate to freshwater . . I am propos ing to repeal the requirements to give effect to Te Mana o te Wai in the Water Services Act and the Taumata Arowai the Water Services Regulator Act. . I am also propos ing to include a new operating principle in the Taumata Arowai the Water Services Regulator Act, which would require Taumata Arowai to take account of the National Policy Statement for Freshwater Management , and any regional plans prepared under the RMA that relate to freshwater , as part of the exercise of its functions, duties and powers. . These changes will provide much clearer direction to all parties about how they are expected to discharge their obligations in this area. Te Mana o te Wai is integrated in the National Policy Statement for Freshwater Management and regional plans prepared under the RMA that relate to freshwater . Taumata Arowai will continue to play the lead role in determining how the regulatory regime incorporates this concept. It also has the benefit of linking Taumata Arowais decision making to broader freshwater plann ing, of which Te Mana o te Wai is only one aspect. . This approach is consistent with the commitment the Government has made as part of its coalition agreements to rebalancing Te Mana o te Wai in the National Policy Statement for Freshwater Management. The new operating principle will require Taumata Arowai to take account of any changes to a rebalanced Te Mana o te Wai once this process is complete. Implementation . Proposals will be implemented by the Department of Internal Affairs , Taumata Arowai, and the Commerce Commission, as relevant. Financial implications Rates Rebate Scheme . The proposed amendment to the definition of rates in the Rates Rebate Act to include water charges, will include an additional approximately per annum being captured in the Rates Rebate Scheme. . The additional costs can be met from within the existing Rates Rebate Scheme, Benefit or Related Expenses appropriation for the immediate future, meaning no immediate changes to appropriations or the Crowns fiscal forecasts are required. . The Rates Rebate Scheme is a demand based scheme that is periodically adjusted to reflect macroeconomic factors, such as CPI movements and changes to the number of eligible rat e payers. Changes to the appropriation, including increases, are actioned through forecast adjustments , rather than Cabinet approval. . The new definition of rates will capture the additional in the calculation of adjustments over the longer term, contributing to an increas e in adjustments required . As the Scheme is demand driven and subject to multiple other macroeconomic influences , it is not certain whether this will occur within the forecast period. ()(b)(ii) ()(b)(ii) IN CONFIDENCE Page of . The Treasury ha s been consulted on this impact and is comfortable with the proposed amendment to the definition of rates in the Rates Rebate Act . Costs related to consumer protections . The proposed approach to consumer protection is designed so that additional costs are not incurred at the outset. The initial monitoring through information disclosure will be part of the Commerce Commissions proposed activities under the economic regulation regime that will apply to local government water service providers . . Where monitoring leads to significant escalation and follow up or if regulations are made to introduce further requirements relating to consumer protections , this w ould result in additional costs to the Commerce Commission. For example, there w ould be costs associated with the development and maintenance of a mandatory service quality code, and with work required to undertake compliance monitoring and enforcement activities. . If future costs are incurred, these are proposed to be recovered through levies. This would be consistent with the approach that has already been agreed for the new economic regulation regime in Local Water Done Well stage : water services regulatory system ECO MIN . Legislative implications . Legislation is required to give effect to the proposals in this paper and, if agreed, they will be included in the Local Government Water Services Bill, . I am seeking approval to issue drafting instructions to the Parliamentary Counsel Office to prepare this Bill. I am also seeking authority to approve matters that may arise during the course of drafting and that may be required to align with the decisions in this paper. I will report back to the Cabinet Legislation Committee on any substantive matters that have been considered and approved during the legislative drafting process, when approval to introduce the Bill is sought. . I will engage with the Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs when issuing drafting instructions in relation to the proposals relating to consumer protection and amendments to the Commerce Act . . I anticipate amendments may be required to a number of other pieces of legislation, including: . the Local Government Act ; . the Local Government (Rating) Act ; . the Taumata Arowai the Water Services Regulator Act ; . the Water Services Act ; . the Rates Rebate Act . The third party would be assessing if the child or young person understands and that the decision is based on their own perceptions of their gender. Why government intervention is required This RIS proposes that the selfidentification process replaces the existing process under the Births, Deaths, Marriages, and Relationships Registration Act (the BDMRR Act). The existing process is not inclusive and fails to support peoples autonomy over how their gender is recognised. It medicalises a deeply personal expression of selfidentity by requiring applicants to provide evidence of medical treatment. This requirement excludes those who cannot or choose not to undertake medical treatment. This evidence is then assessed by a Family Court judge who determines if the amendment can be made. The Family Court process is perceived to be costly, intimidating and difficult to navigate, making it inaccessible for many people. It also excludes those who identify outside of the binary options of male or female or whose gender changes over time. Government intervention is required as a legislative amendment is needed to resolve the above issues. The other option considered An alternative option to a selfidentification process or the existing process (status quo) is assessed in this RIS. This would require a person to provide a statutory declaration and medical evidence they have undergone treatment to physically conform with their gender. A selfidentification process is preferred ahead of this option and status quo. The impact of the preferred option a selfidentification process A selfidentification process will provide for a more accessible and inclusive process that enables birth certificates to reflect a persons gender. The change will: align better with human rights discourse and societys understanding of sex and gender, including by demedicalising the experience of being transgender or intersex; better enable transgender and intersex New Zealanders to access services with less risk of being outed or experiencing discrimination; support the validation of transgender and intersex people, contributing to a greater sense of social belonging and improving their wellbeing; provide greater accessibility to a birth certificate that reflects a persons gender due to lower costs and reduced administration involved in an application; and Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs INCONFIDENCE

()(g)(i) Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Page of Provide sex markers options that are inclusive of a range of gender identities Status quo . The Family Court process allows people to show the binary sex markers on their birth certificates: female or male. Select c ommittees recommendation . The select c ommittees recommendations sought to incorporate sex marker options outside of the binary. I t recommended that people could apply to change the sex marker to male, or female, or to two new options intersex , or X (unspecified). Departments advice agree that a sex marker option outside the binary should be provided but should be provided for outside the primary legislation . We su pport the inclusion of a nonbinary option to be available to show gender identities outside of the binary male and female as it helps to give effect to a self identification process. . A single umbrella term under which all nonbinary gender identities are captured fails to adequately recognise and provide for an inclusive selfidentification process. We advise that an appropriate mechanism be placed in the legislation to enable a more inclusive and flexible process where the spectrum of gender identities can be agreed and used by applicants. . We propose replacing the single umbrella X (unspecified) , proposed by select committee to represent all nonbinary gender identities, with a mechanism that enables publicly informed decisions about the number of sex markers and the terminology used to represent nonbinary genders. This mechanism will need to be able to be provide the necessary assurances around maintaining the integrity of the birth register, balanced with a need to ensure changes can be made through an open consultation process, relatively quickly. . We are considering two options for the mechanism to determine the number of and terminology used for the nonbinary options. These are: . setting them in regulations ; or . providing the RegistrarGeneral with the ability to set the number and terminology following a public consultation process. The RegistrarGeneral would also be given the power to review the settings at any time but at least every four years. . The main benefits to delegating this ability to the RegistrarGeneral over having this determined under a normal regulation making process would be that it would likely be quicker to complete and implement and likely slightly less costly.

. Col in van Noordt and Luca Tangi have developed a discussion paper on public value creation of AI within public administrations. The paper focusses on capability, both technical and also the role of leaders in aligning AI use with wider organisational objectives. They also observe that more digitally mature organisations are likely to understand and take advantage of AI opportunities. Iwi and Mori representatives wish to work actively with the Government on AI. . Our Briefing for the Incoming Minister for Digitising Government included context about our approach to engaging with Iwi and Mori on digital government matters, including our Mana rite Agreement with the Data Iwi Leaders Group (Data ILG). We understand Data ILG may also seek to brief you directly on their interests in digital. . Data ILG has expressed to us strong interest in working with the government both on the opportunities that AI presents to Mori, and also on the risks of AI for Mori. These could include risk of bias andor lack of protection of Mori data that Mori consider to be a taonga (treasure). We see significant opportunity in working with Data ILG on AI work that will benefit Mori and the Crown and we will continue to engage actively as we progress the AI work programme. We participate actively in international AI collectives . While we are cautious about comparing ourselves to other jurisdictions as political settings, legislative reach, social licence and AI capabilities differ, other nations seem to be facing similar issues in respect of AI benefits and risks. Some comparator nations, such as the United Kingdom, Australia and the European Union are developing regulatory frameworks for AI. Singapore has issued a National AI Strategy. Like New Zealand, Australia and Canada have released guidance supporting Public Service use of AI. Global collaboration on AI issues is increasing through initiatives like the UK AI Safety Summit and its Bletchley Declaration . The OECD has also AI principles and a classification framework for AI systems.
