Chair Cabinet Legislation Committee Local Government (Water Services Preliminary Arrangements) Bill: Approval for Introduction Proposal . This paper seeks approval to introduce the Local Government (Water Services Preliminary Arrangements) Bill which will give effect to stage two of the Local Water Done Well reform programme . This Bill holds a category priority on the Legislation Programme (must be passed within the year). . The Bill provides for the preliminary and foundational provisions relating to the new framework proposed in Local Water Done Well which will enable councils to self determine how they wish to transition to the new , long term water services delivery model. The enduring settings are proposed to be given effect in a further bill the Local Government ( Water Services ) Bill to be introduced in December . . I propose that the Bill is introduced on May , be referred to the Finance and Expenditure Committee and be enacted by early August . Policy . In February , we fulfilled our commitments to repeal the previous governments unpopular water services entities regime , restoring local government responsibilities for water services delivery, and halt the establishment of the mega entities. Cabinet also agreed to begin work on the new policy proposals for Local Water Done Well, to be implemented in two further Bills CAB MIN . Local Water Done Well provides a new approach to local government water services delivery, with a critical emphasis on financial sustainability a nd funding for growth. . In March , m y policy paper Local Water Done Well stage : Establishing the framework and transitional arrangements was approved by Cabinet. It contained the first set of proposals for the new framework . These proposals are preliminary in nature and set expectations on councils to present their intentions to transition from their current service delivery models to financially sustainable water service delivery models that meet water quality regulatory standards ECO MIN . . The Bill imposes requirements on councils in the near term, which will prepare them for water services delivery under the long term settings. Requirements include foundational information disclosure, firstly through the preparation and delivery of water services delivery plans , and then later through a more formal regime if the Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs and I determine that one or more councils are ready to provide enhanced information in prepar ation for the long term economic regulatory framework. . To enhance flexibility during the transitional period, streamlined consultation and decision making requirements are made available for councils who wish to establish or amend water services council controlled organisations under Local Government Act provisions . enkv Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government IN CONFIDENCE
Chair Cabinet Mori Crown Relations C ommitt ee New Plymouth District Council (Waitara Lands) Bill progress of local bill and inclusion of Crown interests Proposal . This paper updates the Committee on progress of the New Plymouth District Council (Waitara Lands) Bill. It: . informs the Committee about the local Bill; . seeks Cabinets approval to advising the Governor General of the inclusion of Crown interests in the local Bill, being the Crowns underlying title to reserves in Waitara; and . seeks Cabinets agreement to a time limited tax exemption of six months for the Waitara hap entity (as defined in the local Bill as the entity representing the Waitara hap). . The local Bill provides the opportunity to resolve the longstanding issues at Waitara and to make a positive contribution to the relationship between local government and Mori. Executive summary . The New Plymouth District Council (Waitara Lands) Bill (the local Bill) provides an opportunity for the Government to support the efforts of New Plymouth District Council (the District Council) to strengthen local government Mori relations. The local Bill seeks to resolve the longstanding issues at Waitara which result from the confiscation of Mori land in the nineteenth century, which is today owned by the District Council (the Waitara Endowment Land) and leased to residents and businesses with perpetual rights of renewal. Proceeds from the Waitara Endowment Land may only be used at present for a limited range of activities, and the aim of the local Bill is to unlock the funds for the benefit of Ng Manukorihi and Otaraua (the Waitara hap) and the wider Waitara community. . There are two critical issues without which the Waitara hap will not support the local Bill. This paper seeks your agreement to the steps necessary to resolve those issues. . First, the hap seek the inclusion of Crown underlying title to six District Council reserves which the D istrict Council proposes to transfer to the Waitara hap entity (upon payment of their value through a valuation mechanism in the Bill). The transfer of underlying title has been agreed by the Minister of Conservation. This paper seeks Cabinets agreement to advise the Governor General of the Crowns agreement to the inclusion of Crown interests in a local Bill. It is a procedural requirement of the Standing Orders that a message from the Governor General to the House confirm the inclusion of Crown interests in a local Bill before the Bill may be passed. Proactively released from the Department of Internal Affairs INCONFIDENCE Page of . Secondly, I propose that the Waitara hap entity be given a six month time limited tax exemption from the of commencement of the local Bill. This will provide time for the Waitara hap entity or its subsidiary to obtain a determination of its status as a charitable entity. . The Waitara hap have agreed to support the Bill. My officials are working with the Waitara hap and the District Council to finalise redrafting of the local Bill, including a preamble that tells the historical story of the Waitara hap, and a side agreement between the Waitara hap and the District Council that will support the implementation of the local Bill. . I consider that Government support for the local Bill will make a valuable contribution to improving local government Mori relations and confer wider benefits on the Mori Crown relationship. The local Bill represents an innovative resolution to longstanding issues by the District Council. . If this Bill were not to pass, the local Waitara community will miss the opportunity to benefit from million in funding which is unlocked by the Bill. Under the local Bill, the sums will be applied to housing development and associated growth and job creation, hap development and hap and community health and wellbeing initiatives, and the restoration of the Waitara River. Background . The local Bill broadens the purposes for which the District Council can apply re ntal income and proceeds of sale of Waitara Endowment Land. The local Bill was reported back to the House by the Mori Affairs Committee on August with significant amendments from the version as introduced. Following further negotiations between the District Council and the Waitara hap, significant changes are proposed to be made at committee of the whole House via a Supplementary Order Paper (SOP) in the name of Jonathan Young MP, the member in charge of the Bill. This local Bill will bring wider b enefits to both the Waitara community as a whole and the Mori Crown relationship more broadly. The local Bill relates to hectares of land confiscated from Te Atiawa in . Waitara, North Taranaki, is a place of historical importance to Mori and all New Zealanders. The first shots in the New Zealand Land Wars were fired on the Pekapeka block at Waitara in , due to escalating tensions regarding contested land purchases. . All of the land at Waitara was confiscated from Mori in under the New Zealand Settlements Act . Much of the land was vested in the local authorities in and this is today owned by successor local authorities. Perpetual leases (long leases with an automatic right of renewal) were created over approximately hectares o f the land (the Waitara Endowment Land) and these leases remain in place today, administered by the District Council. . In the census, . per cent of Waitara residents identified as Mori. Te Atiawa is the local iwi, and Waitara is home to Manukorihi and Otaraua hap. Proactively released from the Department of Internal Affairs INCONFIDENCE Page of Te Atiawa Treaty settlement negotiators elected not to purchase the land, leaving issues unresolved . In the early s, the District Council resolved to make the Waitara Endowment Land available for Te Atiawa for Treaty settlement purpos es. This was disputed by leaseholders who instigated legal action against the District Council. After a lengthy court dispute, the Court of Appeal confirmed the District Councils right to sell the land. . For a number of reasons, Te Atiawa Treaty settlement negotiators elected not to purchase the land. This created divisions within Te Atiawa and the Waitara hap tried to withdraw from the iwi and the Treaty settlement. Ultimately, the Treaty settlement was finalised with the Waitara hap included but the iss ue of Waitara lands unresolved. New leadership at the District Council has prioritised resolving ownership of the Waitara Endowment Land . The District Council, under new leadership, has worked hard over the past months to build a relationship with the Wa itara hap and wider iwi. The Mayor and Chief Executive of the District Council see the local Bill as a way to move forward, bring benefits to the Waitara hap and for the District Council and Waitara hap to work together to improve wellbeing for the Waitara community. . The District Council perceives the local Bill as a once in a generation opportunity to resolve ownership of the Waitara Endowment Land, clean up the Waitara River and to provide opportunities for the Waitara hap and community. They are publ icising their promotion of the local Bill in these terms among the local community. The local Bill seeks to resolve the longstanding issues at Waitara Progress . In , the District Council promoted the local Bill sponsored by Jonathan Young, MP for New P lymouth. The local Bill as introduced transferred some land to the local iwi trust, Te Kotahitanga o Te Atiawa, and enabled leaseholders on the Waitara Endowment Land to purchase the freehold title to the same land. . The local Bill was referred to the Mori Affairs Committee. At the public hearings of submissions on the local Bill it became clear that neither the iwi, Te Atiawa, nor the Waitara hap supported the local Bill. The Mori Affairs Committee recommended substantial changes, with the agreement of t he District Council, to enable more equitable outcomes for the local Waitara hap and wider iwi. The Mori Affairs Committee report on the Bill to the House on August foreshadowed further changes being necessary and noted that the Waitara hap were due to enter further discussions with both the District Council and Taranaki Regional Council (the Regional Council). The local Bill had its second reading on August . Proactively released from the Department of Internal Affairs INCONFIDENCE Page of Recent changes raise a procedural issue around the scope of the Bill which needs to be addressed . Further negotiations took place between the Waitara hap and both the District Council and the Regional Council. This led to the SOP now proposed which further amends the local Bill as reported back by the Mori Affairs Committee. It remains within the intention and spirit of the Mori Affairs Committee commentary on the local Bill as reported back to the House. . Some of the changes proposed by SOP are out of scope of the original Notice of Intention to promote the local Bill publicised by the District Council. Standing Order () provides that no am endment may be made to a local B ill that is outside the scope of the notices advertising the intention to introduce or promote the local B ill. Jonathan Young MP has written to the House Business C ommittee asking them to waive Standing Order () to enable these changes to be made through the SOP. Additionally, from November the District Council is publishing a revised Notice setting out the changes to the scope of the local Bill. The changes ar e critical to the Waitara haps support for the local Bill. Unanimous agreement of the House is needed to waive Standing Order () which may be indicated by the House Business Committee. . Jonathan Young MP and I have also written to the Mori Affairs Co mmittee to inform them of the further changes to the Bill since their commentary. I am satisfied that while these changes were not in the Mori Affairs Committees commentary, they are within the spirit of that report and will therefore be acceptable to the Mori Affairs Committee. The local Bill will not proceed to further House stages until the Mori Affairs Committee has endorsed the Bills progression. Provisions in the local Bill and the substantial Supplementary Order Paper . The proposed SOP substantia lly refines the local Bill. The SOP makes significant improvements to the way the local Bill seeks to provide an adequate resolution to the longstanding issues faced by the Waitara hap while also resolving the concerns of leaseholders in the Waitara Endow ment Land. It achieves an effective balance between the interests of the Waitara hap and leaseholders of the Waitara Endowment Land and it brings benefits to the wider community in Waitara and the Taranaki region. . The local Bill returns or enables the return of all District Council reserves (including some with Crown underlying title) in Waitara to the Waitara hap and some other District Council land. It also enables leaseholders of Waitara Endowment Land to purchase the freehold title to the same land. Proactively released from the Department of Internal Affairs INCONFIDENCE Page of . The proceeds of sale of freehold and income from leaseholds are divided equally between the District Council and the Regional Council as follows: . The District Councils proceeds are further divided equally between the Waitara Community Fund and the Hap Land Fund, overseen by an independent statutory Board. The Board makes determinations as to distributions from the Waitara Community Fund, for the benefit of the Waitara community. The local Bill establishes the Hap Land Fund Committee as a committee of t he Board. The Hap Land Fund Committee comprises members of the Waitara hap and determines the Boards spending of the Hap Land Fund which must be for the purpose of buying, developing and managing land in and adjacent to Waitara for the benefit of the W aitara hap; and . The Regional Councils proceeds fund the work of the Waitara River Committee, a council committee with equal membership between the Regional Council and iwi authorities of any iwi with mana whenua over the river catchment. The Waitara Rive r Committee is to distribute per cent of funds toward the environmental, cultural and spiritual health and wellbeing of the Waitara River and per cent toward any matter in Waitara or the lower catchment of the river within the Regional Councils responsibility. . The refinements to the Bill, agreed through extensive discussions between the District Council, the Waitara hap and Te Atiawa iwi trustees, and proposed to be implemented by the SOP include: . all of the land to be transferred in the local Bill will be transferred to the Waitara hap rather than the iwi trustees; . the inclusion in the local Bill of all of the Council owned reserves in Waitara, should the hap elect to initiate the transfer; . the potential for transfer of six reserves that have a pa rtial or whole Crown underlying title to the hap at the haps election and on terms that the Crown is reimbursed for the value of the underlying title; . a time limited tax exemption of six months for the Waitara hap entity; . should the District Council ever sell its interests in the leased land, it must offer these rights to the hap first. Valuation instructions for these interests have been agreed between the District Council and the hap; and . a preamble that tells the haps story of Waitara and its con nection to the whenua. . Both the inclusion of the Crown underlying titles and the tax exemption were critical in ensuring the hap remained in negotiations with the District Council. For example, one of these reserves, Pukekohe Domain, is an original p sit e and was also the location of the constabulary quartering during the New Zealand Land Wars. This site is culturally significant to both hap and they aspire to establish a cultural base at the site. . The District Council and the Waitara hap will conclude a binding side agreement to support the implementation of the local Bill. This will set out how the mechanisms in the local Bill will be applied in practice, including for example arrangements for governance of the reserves and an agreement that neither t he Waitara hap nor the District Council will seek a change to the reserve status of land without the others consent. The District Council has agreed to transfer title to reserve land in Waitara to the Waitara hap. Six of the reserves are wholly or partly derived from the Crown and the Crown retains underlying title. This means that, should the District Council seek to divest its interests in the land, title r everts to the Crown. . The inclusion of the Crown underlying title to six reserves in Waitara enables the hap to elect to purchase those reserves at any time in the next years. Cabinets agreement is sought to including the Crown underlying title to the se six reserves. . The transfer will be fiscally neutral to the Crown as the value of the Crown underlying title will be paid by the District Council or the Waitara hap. The underlying titles have been valued at . million. As the value is greater than in itially anticipated, one reserve will be purchased on enactment of the Bill. Agreement has been given by the Minister of Conservation for the local Bill to provide the perpetual right for the Waitara hap to purchase the remaining five reserves. If the transfer of the five remaining reserves is made after November , an market valuation will be required through a mechanism provided for in the Bill. . Under Standing Order , no local Bill may contain any provision that affects the rights and priv ileges of the Crown unless the Crown has given its consent. The consent of the Crown is given by a message from the Governor General in accordance with Standing Order . I seek Cabinets agreement to advise the Governor General that the Crown consents to the inclusion of Crown interests in this local Bill. In this case, the Crown interest is in the potential sale of the underlying Crown title to six reserves in Waitara to the Waitara hap. Tax exemption . The Minister of Revenue and I have agreed that transfers of land from the District Council to the Waitara hap entity under the arrangements in the local Bill should not be subject to income tax. The District Council as a local authority is exempt from income tax and the disposal of land by the District Council would therefore not be subject to income tax. Nevertheless, I recommend that a specific provision be included in the local Bill for the avoidance of doubt. . The Minister of Revenue and I have also agreed to propose to Cabinet a temporary tax exemption for transfers from the Hap Land Fund to the Waitara hap entity in the local Bill. The temporary tax exemption will be in place for six months from the of commencement of the Bill. The tax exemption is critical to obtaining the support of the hap t o the arrangements in the local Bill. It will provide a bridging mechanism, giving the Waitara hap entity or its subsidiary enough time to obtain charitable status. Following the expiry of the six month temporary exemption, the prevailing tax rules will apply on a go forward basis. . Cabinets agreement is sought to account for the temporary tax exemption through the between Budget contingency. The fiscal implications of the temporary tax exemption are likely to be small. The Hap Land Fund is expected to total no more than . million in the initial six month period. This would lead to maximum potential tax revenue of . million each year. Proactively released from the Department of Internal Affairs INCONFIDENCE Page o f . I do not consider that the temporary tax exemption risks setting a precedent. The circumstances in Waitara are uniq ue. In addition to the historical factors, the unique circumstances include that this is endowment land, so the funds provided under theBill are not obtained from rates and are not otherwise available for general use, andthat the interests of the leaseho lders are protected by the local Bill. My officials are not aware of any comparable circumstances and I consider the likelihood of similararrangements emerging is low. The proposed tax exemption is a pragmatic response tounique circumstances and does not provide a precedent for other local authorities. . The District Council expects that the arrangements in the local Bill will unlock fundingof million over the next twenty years as leaseholders purchase freehold title. The District and Regional Councils have agreed that all of this money should be used inWaitara to build the local economy and benefit the wellbeing of the Waitaracommunity. The arrangements in the local Bill would distribute this funding in the formof: . million to restore the health and wellbeing of the Waitara River; . million in a Waitara Community Fund for the general benefit of the Waitara community; and . million in a Hap Land Fund for the purchase, development or management of land at Waitara. Missed opport unity . The Waitara hap will not support the Bill if the underlying Crown title is not included in the transfer of the reserves, and the tax exemption issue is not resolved. If this Billwere not to pass, the local Waitara community will miss the opportunity to benefit from million. Under the local Bill, the sums will be applied to housing development and associated growth and job creation, hap development and hapand community health and wellbeing initiatives, and the restoration of the W aitara River. . Should the local Bill not pass, we will lose the opportunity to support local governmentas it finds innovative solutions to longstanding issues, bringing improvements to therelationship between local government and Mori. I recommend that the Crown undertakes all steps necessary to enable the local Bill to succeed. Next steps . Chair Cabinet Social Wellbeing Committ ee Proposed amendments to the Films, Videos, and Publications Classification (Urgent Interim Classification of Publications and Prevention of Online Harm) Amendment Bill Proposal . This paper seeks agreement to amend clause of the Films, Videos, and Publications Classification (Urgent Interim Classification of Publications and Prevention of Online Harm) Amendment Bill ( the Bill) . The proposed amendment w ould remove sections L O (the filtering provisions) from the Bill. Relation to government priorities . The proposals in this Bill are a direct response to the Christchurch terror attack s and address some gaps and limitations in our classification legislation . Executive summary . The proposals in the Bill w ere developed as a direct response to the Christchurch terror attacks and address specific inefficiencies and ambiguities in our classification legislation. On December , Cabinet agreed to the proposals set out for the Bill CAB MIN refers. . The Bill was introduced to Parliament in May and was referred to the Governance and Administration Committee (the Committee) at its First Reading on February . I inherited the Bill from the previous Minister of Internal Affairs and have previousl y indicated that I was open to refining the Bills filtering provisions depending on what came out of the Select Committee stage , given the strong views in this area . . Internet filtering can be a useful tool to prevent access to and mitigate harms from obje ctionable (illegal) content online. An example of this is the current Digital Child Exploitation System (DCEFS), which specifically filters child sexual abuse material. Child sexual abuse material is universally accepted as abhorrent and blocking this type of material has not been challenged. Further expansion of the categories of illegal material to be filtered needs detailed consideration to ensure the proper safeguards are there to prevent abuse of this power. . The current proposals leave this detail to b e determined in regulations to allow flexibility for new technologies. On balance a statutory filter provision needs more detail about the safeguards. To achieve that , the detailed work that was planned following enactment of the Bill would need to be brou ght forward. Progressing this work now would risk a further delay to the implementation of the other key regulatory and enforcement provisions of the Bill. This is consistent with the advice that I have received from my officials. Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs INCONFIDENCE Page of . Submitters also acknowled ged that more detail is needed before progressing the filtering provisions. T he submissions received on the Bill throughout the Select Committee stage have indicated that there is a lack of public mandate to progress with the current filtering provisions a t this time. Submissions highlighted the need to set out the specific scope of the filter in primary legislation and emphasised the need for further public consultation and community engagement . . These submissions are consistent with wider community feedback received during huis held on the report of the Royal Commission of Inquiry into the terrorist attack on Christchurch masjidain on March . Feedback from those huis emphasised the need for greater community engagement and co design of policie s on a wide range of areas relevant to the classification and censorship system such as hate speech and balancing reform in that area with the right to freedom of expression, as well as greater scrutiny of the standards of media and online reporting on m inority and faith communit y issues . . This paper therefore, seeks agreement to remove the current filtering provisions from the Bill and investigate a voluntary approach to filtering . Background . In the aftermath of the Christchurch terror attacks, internet service providers (ISPs) and online content hosts worked collaboratively with Government to prevent people from spreading and accessing online footage of the attacks. While these efforts were largely effective, the experience highlighted inefficiencies and ambiguities in our censorship system for responding to objectionable online content. This Bill was developed as a direct response to the Christchurch terror attacks by addressing these inefficiencies and ambiguities in the Films, Videos, and Publications Classification Act (the FVPC Act . . On December , Cabinet agreed to the following policy proposals in the Bill CAB MIN refers : . knowingly livestreaming objectionable content will become a criminal offence punishable by up to years in prison; . allowing the Chief Censor to make interim classification decisions; . allowing take down notices to be issued to require the removal of objectionable online content; . making online content hosts subj ect to a civil pecuniary penalty of up to ,, if they do not comply with an issued take down notice; . ensuring safe harbour provisions in the Harmful Digital Communications Act would not apply to objectionable online content; and . enabling the e stablishment of regulations that would allow the government to implement web filtering of objectionable content if required. . The Bill updates the FVPC Act to allow for urgent prevention and mitigation of harms caused by objectionable content online. The te rm objectionable refers to already illegal content as defined in the FVPC Act ; this includes content which describes, depicts or expresses, or otherwise deals with matters such as sex, horror, crime, cruelty or violence in such a manner that the availab ility of publication is likely to be injurious to the public good. It is an offence to make, possess, supply or distribute objectionable content. Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs INCONFIDENCE Page of . The Bill will improve the way we regulate objectionable content, including violent extremist and terrorist co ntent found online. Specifically, the Bill amends the Act to: . criminalise knowingly livestreaming objectionable content; . allow the Chief Censor to make interim classification assessments in relation to publications (both physical as well as online) likely to be found objectionable in urgent situations; . allow take down notices to be issued to require the removal of objectionable online content; . make online content hosts subject to a civil pecuniary penalty of up to ,, if they do not comply with an is sued take down notice; . ensure the safe harbour provisions in the Harmful Digital Communications Act would not apply to objectionable online content; and . enable the establishment of regulations that would allow the Government to implement filtering o f objectionable content online if required (the filtering provisions) . . I inherited the Bill from the previous Minister of Internal Affairs and was keen to progress it to Select Committee stage to hear views on the filtering provisions, as there were arguments for and against. . The Bill was introduced to Parliament in May and was referred to the Committee at its First Reading on February . On April I attended t he presentation of the initial briefing on the Bill and signalled to the Committee that I was particularly interested in submissions and discussions on the filtering provisions . . Since then, the filtering provisions have been the most submitted upon aspect of the Bill. The majority of the submissions that mentioned the filtering provisions were opposed to it. In contra st, the submissions that touched on other provisions of the Bill were mostly supportive and only recommended some minor technical changes. . The views expressed by submitters on the Bill align with community feedback from huis on the report of the Royal Commission of Inquiry into the terrorist attack on Christchurch masj idain on March , specifically that proposals relating to freedom of expression should be developed through co design and engagement with communities. Internet filtering can be a useful tool to prevent access and mitigate harms from objectionable co ntent online . In New Zealand, internet filtering already takes place without a legislative mandate or regulatory framework. This currently include s the voluntary DCEFS , which specifically filters child sexual abuse material . This filter is run by the Department of Internal Affairs ( DIA). While the DECFS is voluntary for ISPs, the majority of ISPs in New Zealand use the filter, which means that approximately per cent of New Zealand internet users are protected from child sexual abuse material. Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs INCONFIDENCE Page of . The p roposed internet filtering provisions in the Bill provide an enabling framework and set out obligations on Government when implementing any mechanism to prevent access to other kind s of objectionable content , outside of child sexual abuse material and imag ery. The filtering provisions would not establish a filter but would give Government explicit statutory authority to explore and implement such mechanisms through regulations in the future. The filtering provisions are in clause of the Bill under new sec tions L to O . . If established, the purpose of a filter would be to prevent access to content that is already illegal to possess or distribute. It is one of a range of tools that can be used to assist in mitigating the harms of objectionable content online. These harms can include revictimization for example, recurring distress and trauma to victims from viewing an incident again or having others see footage of their experiences and being unintentionally exposed to this type of footage . Some of the most objectionable content on the internet is pe ddled by sites that will never respond to New Zealands or any other jurisdictions request to remove such content . A filter c ould act as a last line of defence when other approaches to remove this content ha ve failed. Submissions indicate that there is a lack of public mandate to progress with the current filtering provisions at this time . On April , written submissions closed for the Bill and the Committee received a total of unique written submissi ons. The Committee received submissions that specifically referred to the filtering provisions in the Bill. Out of those, four submitters supported filtering and submitters were against filtering. A further submissions, while not referenc ing the f iltering provisions specifically, were opposed to the Bill in full due to concerns that the Bill w ould impose on New Zealanders freedom of expression , which is the predominant reason for opposing the filter . . Some submitters acknowledged that there may be benefits to filtering objectionable content . However, this support was qualified by the need to clarify the detail and scope of any proposed filter. The filter being set in regulations was not seen as the best approach as there would be a lack of Parliamen tary oversight into the development of the filter, and a risk of insufficient legal safeguards. As currently drafted, the legislation is not intended to be too prescriptive in order to provide sufficient flexibility so that developments in technology do not undermine the policy intent. . However, s ubmitters opposed to filtering noted that there is a need for more specific detail on the scope, design and operation of the filter in the Bill. Submissions from academics, the tech nology sector , ethnic commu nity groups and interest bodies prefer that the Government consult on these aspects of any potential filter before finalising proposals and progressing legislation to implement a filter. This was reflected specifically by those in vulnerable groups that th e filtering provisions are intended to protect. There were also concerns raised about the potential infringement o n freedom of expression and the effectiveness of a filter , as it can be easily circumvented. . Several submissions suggested that the filter pr ovisions be removed from the Bill and be progressed as a stand alone legislation so that there is appropriate Parliamentary decision making and oversight of this issue. There was some commentary that any work on filtering should be considered as part of a wider review of the media regulatory landscape. There have also been suggestions of a voluntary approach like the existing DCEFS. Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs INCONFIDENCE Page of . I did consider options to redraft so that the filter is not set in regulations but primary legislation. However, I decided aga inst this as it would not address the issues of a lack of detail about the propose d design and operation of the filter. It would also not address concerns about the potential infringement on freedom of expression and the effectiveness of a filter. . While there appears to be a lack of public mandate to progress the filter, there are also additional issues to consider. This includes ensuring that the creation of a filter is fit for purpose, which would require setting out the exact scope of the filter and br oader public consultation. There is also the risk of the Bill being further delayed to allow time to determine technical specifications of the filter, which would mean other key regulatory and enforcement proposals in the Bill that are needed now would be unable to be progressed. My preferred approach is to remove the current filtering provisions from the Bill and investigate a voluntary filter . As noted above in paragraphs to , filtering can be a useful tool to prevent access to and mitigate harms from objectionable content online noting that this is content that is already illegal . However , having heard from submitters throughout the select committee process, it appears that there is strong opposition for a statutory mandated filter for objectionable content online and more work is required in this area . Therefore, my preferred approach is to remove the filtering provisions from the Bill and investigate a voluntary approach to filtering. This approach would amend clause , Part A of the Bill by removing: . section L: Electronic system to prevent public access to objectionable online publications; . section M: Establishment of electronic system; . section N: Approval of electronic system for operation; and . section O: Review of decisions and actions relating to operation of electronic system. . To allow for Cabinet consideration of the above proposal s, I have written to and obtained permission from the Committee Chair to exten d the report back of the Departmental Report to June . The Department of Internal Affairs will continue to investigate a voluntary filter . There is some support for the concept of filtering objectionable content , particularly among Internet Service Providers (ISP). This is important as any filtering would work at the ISP level. I also think that there is a place for filtering as it can reduce harm for the most vulnerable, such as young people, from inadvertent access to objectionable content. However, I acknowledge that setting the filter in regulations is not the best approach. I have therefore directed my officials to investigate and provide me with advice on alternative options for progressing a voluntary approach to filtering for ISPs . A voluntary approach would align with the existing mechanism in place to filter child sexual abuse material and imagery . Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs INCONFIDENCE Page of . I do not recommend removing the provisions and progressing stand alone legislation to implement filtering objectionable content at this stage. Submitters who suggested this approach str essed that the legislation would need to set out specific details, such as the exact scope of the filter, technical capability details as well as governance and technical oversight arrangements. I anticipate these issues will be within scope of work to pro gress a voluntary filter. Stand alone legislation to provide statutory authority to a voluntary filter can be explored in due course if there is evidence of sufficient public mandate for this to occur or a voluntary approach is unsuccessful . . In relation t o submissions suggesting this issue be considered within the wider media review (the review) , I note that the purpose of the review is to dev elop and establish an overarching framework for regulating and moderating media and online content. Proposals devel oped within th at broader framework may have potential cascading implications on aspects of work to progress a voluntary filter. I have been advised by my officials that they will remain mindful of possible links between proposals developed as part of the r eview and filtering options, and where appropriate align these workstreams as necessary . Next steps . If Cabinet approval the removal of the filtering provisions , the Bill will be amended to remove sections L to O in clause , Part A. This will requi re a delay to the final report back of the Departmental Report to allow time for the amendments to be drafted. Financial implications . There are no financial implications. The population implications have previously been stated in the previous Cabinet paper CAB MIN refers, which acknowledges that to the extent that any groups are disproportionately impacted by exposure to violent extremist and terrorist content online, the proposals aim to reduce that harm. These groups include ethnic communities, women, and people with disabilities. Human Rights . The proposals in this paper have previously been addressed in the initial Cabinet paper CAB MIN refers which , acknowledged that r egulating obje ctionable content that involves violent extremist and terrorist online content raises issues of consistency with the right to freedom of expression, recognised in section of the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act (NZBORA). . The proposals in this paper do not change the current definition of objectionable under the FVPC Act. While freedom of expression is not an absolute right, limits should not be imposed on it unless justified. New Zealand law already limits freedom of expression in this area by imposi ng a range of legal restrictions on the publication of objectionable content (which cover acts of terrorism). These limitations are reasonably justified because of the potential harm this content may pose to New Zealanders, as well as the wider direct or i ndirect harms to our communitie s. The proposals in this paper do not negatively impact on freedom of expression. Consultation . Changes to financing arrangements for the Opt Out Scenario cannot be ruled out There are other ways that access to finance by New Zealand water providers can be improved. The government s Opt Out Scenario does not consider these other options. Currently, almost all three waters services are provided by local authorities. Local authorities borrowing limits, whether imposed by LGFA or due to ratings agency policies, are generally consider ed to impose limits on optimal investment planning in the water sector. In the Reform Scenario, the new statutory corporations will have separate balance sheets to lo cal authorities, and will be able to raise finance without being impacted by these borrowi ng limits. A number of other financing arrangements are already available for the water sector and could apply in the Opt Out Scenario. Other financing changes could be implemented with law and other institutional reform: Central government has recently i ntroduced the Infrastructure Financing Facility FFF which enables finance to be raised from the private sector, ringfenced from eligible local authorities balance sheets Long term concession contracts have been used in New Zealand (in Papakura, sig ned by Papakura Council prior to the creation of Auckland Council) under which a third party provides water services for a fixed term ( years in Pap akura) and collects water rates or tariffs directly from customers. Usually, the concession contract requi res the third party to invest in and maintain the water assets and network and meet certain performance metrics . The third party provider accesses pri vate capital markets to finance the capital investment needs (growth, renewals and maintenance) Revenue bo nds are a common way for municipal government entities in the United States to raise finance for infrastructure investment, often in the water sector . Investors in these bonds are repaid from income created by the projects the bonds fund. These are separat e from the general obligations debt raised by the municipal government .

City and Regional Deals February lighttouch proposal submissions
City and Regional Deals is the Governments initiative for establishing longterm agreements between central and local government. The programme unlocks funding and resource opportunities to support councils to make improvements in their region, for example to roads, infrastructure, and the supply of quality housing.
City and Regional Deals primarily involve partnerships between local councils and central government. There is significant opportunity for collaboration from the private sector and iwiMori organisations. Local government is responsible for identifying opportunities for involvement and engaging with private sector entities and Mori organisations.
City and Regional deals will be enduring and will provide the certainty needed to attract and retain the necessary investments to deliver change. Deals make use of existing resources rather than relying solely on new funding, with central and local governments aligning our budget cycles and investment strategies to ensure resources can be used effectively.

Climate Implications of Policy Assessment
Climate Implications of Policy Assessment . None Population Implications . Vulnerable consumers, those experiencing material hardship, including disabled people, are most likely to struggle to pay their water bills. About eight percent of the population are estimated to face material hardship, but the proportion of households with people facing material hardship is likely to be less than that. Households experiencing material hardship are more likely to be younger, single parent, on a benefit as their main source of income, renters, Mori, or Pacific peoples, and people with disabilities. The proposals in this paper are intended to reduce the burden of water bills on vulnerable consumers. Human Rights . There are no human rights or gender implications arising from the proposals in this paper. Consultation . The Ministry for the Environment; Ministry of Health; Taumata Arowai, Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment; the Commerce Commission, the Treasury; Ministry for Primary Industries; National Emergency Management Agency; Toit Te Whenua Land Information New Zealand; Ministry of Housing and Urban Development; Ministry of Education; Ministry of Transport; Te Puni Kkiri; Te Arawhiti; Te Waihanga; Te Kawa Mataaho; Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade; Ministry of Social Development; Office for Disability Issues; and Inland Revenue Department have been consulted on this paper. . The Department of Conservation, New Zealand Defence Force, the Ministry of Education, and Department of Corrections have operational responsibility for three waters services and have been consulted in this capacity. . The Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinets Policy Advisory Group has been informed. Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government IN CONFIDENCE Page of . The Central Local Government Joint Three Waters Steering Committee and Rural Supplies Technical Working Group were consulted on these proposals at a high level. The Rural Supplies Technical Working Group highlighted the importance of being able to charge for water supplied for agricultural use on a different basis to drinking water, where both are supplied by the same scheme. This is consistent with the proposals in this paper. Targeted engagement on growth charging has also occurred with high growth territ orial authorities and the Property Council. Communications . As this paper forms part of a comprehensive set of proposals to transform the delivery of three waters services, communications will be part of the wider communications strategy for these reforms. . In April , in relation to my paper Strengthening Representation, Governance and Accountability of the New Water Services Entities Cabinet agreed that the Department of Internal Affairs will continue to provide information about the case for change and explain Government policy to help better inform the public about the reforms CAB MIN . The Department will also encourage an d inform the public about the opportunity to make submissions during the select committee process for the Water Services Entities Bill and the Amendment Bill. . My Office will play a key role in the development and rollout of communications to ensure message s are clear and appropriately tailored for the intended audiences. . My Office and the Department will also work alongside the Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs and the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment to develop external communications about pricing and charging, and the links to economic regulation and consumer protection, and ensure that this is aligned and consistent. Proactive Release . I intend to release this paper (subject to any redactions) to coincide with further announcements on the reforms. I note that this may occur outside of the usual timeframes in Cabinet Office circular CO () . Recommendations . The Minister of Local Governm ent recommends that Cabinet: . note that, during and early , Cabinet made a series of decisions to transform the three waters service delivery system, and create four new water services entities, and that these decisions are to be given effect through an initial piece of legislation the Water Services Entities Bill; . note that the Water Services Entities Bill is part of a broader, comprehensive suite of proposed legislation, including two additional bills: . a Water Services Entities Amendment Bill, which will fully implement the reforms; and . a Water Regulation Bill, to provide for a new economic regulation and consumer protection framework for the three waters system; Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government IN CONFIDENCE Page of . note that this paper is seeking policy decisions on the matters to be included in the Water Services Entities Amendment Bill or the Water Regulation Bill, which are needed to fully develop and implement the new system, and operationalise the water services entities by providing them with all the necessary powers, functions and responsibilities; . agree to the following policy objectives for pricing of water services: . economic efficiency : prices reflect the underlying costs of services and support the financial sustainability of water services entities in the long run; . affordability : water is an essential service and people on reticulated networks should be able to access water services regardless of their financial circumstances; . price stability : the rates of change in prices are not too high and price changes are clearly signalled in advance and smoothed over time; . costsharing: a key driver of the reforms is to address affordability issues, particularly for customers in smaller communities. Entities could use geographic average pricing to smooth costs across communities, thereby ensuring more affordable services for all; . horizontal equity : consumers in similar positions pay similar prices; . intergenerational equity : every generation (which can be thought of as being as small as the annual cohort of ratepayers) should be paying its fair share for assets and not requiring future generations to pay substantially more or less than their fair share through either over or under investment. Historically, funding and w ater infrastructure investment decisions have tended to favour current over future generations; . giving effect to Te Mana o te Wai and respecting Treaty of Waitangi principles: pricing can support Te Mana o te Wai by encouraging efficient usage of water. Pricing can also engage Article of the Treaty, and support equitable water service access and quality of service provision; . consistency with other government goals : pricing issues should support, or at least not undermine, government goals in other domains. For example, growth charges can have an impact on housing goals. Water services pricing can influence levels of water use which affects climate change goals including resilience and adaptation;

Commercial In Co nfidence Table : Citizen jury Devon (England) Background Description Costs involved Relevance for NZ context Feasibility for different individuals and community types Risks Benefits Design choices The CJ was sponsored by the Water Quality Division of the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra), the government department with responsibility for fostering sustainable rural development in England and Wales. Objective : policy on effective livestock management around water ways Necessary preconditions : rules of procedure provided; background information on the issue at hand provided to jurors and witnesses. Process : jurors were recruited and witnesses to the jury process. Jury was chaired by member of CJ project team as had most experience in chairing policy development and partnership working process in the environmental context The rules of procedure were discussed among jurors, and witnesses provided statements on this. Event held two weeks before the main jury proceedings. Main jury proceedings were held across three days in two locations; a civic space i n the city and a scientific research institute in the countryside with a working livestock farm. Jurors had a walking tour of the farm and the microbiology lab to gain extra context around the issue. Jury verdict was built around the sequential explora tion of issues of acceptability, culpability, necessity and responsibility to deliver clear outcomes and recommendations. The jury proceedings were formal with witness processes treated similarly to a legal jury. After each exploratory theme ( o f them) jurors developed partial verdictsresponses in closed discussions The total cost to run the jury process was , pounds (in pounds). Very formal process, unclear how this would transfer to NZ without further exploration into the mechanisms used (detail not available in literature) Not clear beyond general community involvement. Easy for participants to start to go beyond the questions asked of them due to personal thoughts and topical social affairs. Scope of issue jury is debating must be well defined to mitigate this The need for advertising the jury, its proceedings, decisions and its support by local government poses the risk of influencing the jurys decision (must be balanced) Good way to bring together and frame differing perspec tives from science, policy and practice into one agreed lens Nature of jury itself enables different community members to come together on single issue academic, scientists, policy makers, interest groups, general. Greater understanding gained by each party of each other (including between other witnesses) A way of building confidence in the public image of policy makers Structured process helped people to see final jury decisions as credible In this instance the jury verdict ultimately consider ed as a formal submission to this consultation CJ cuts across disparate domains of responsibility and expertise for the governance of environmental risks. It challenges decision makers to think more broadly about the political, moral and economic framin gs of otherwise narrowly conceived science policy problems CJs used to bring together both scientific and non scientific forms of expertise Jury is balanced in terms of age, gender, ethnicity and area of residence (urban and rural) and also expertise o r experience surrounding the issues (none to plenty of knowledge) Acceptance and recognition that all jury members will bring their own opinion to the issue Advertise in local media to ask for jury participants. Especially in the local newspaper as thi s is very effective. Advertise in strategic locations for participants where missing demographics e.g universities for young people

It employed PB to allocate funds for climate and environmental projects. Fresno has a population of about half a million. Participatory budgeting was introduced into the climate action by the local government after a series of initial meetings and sustained pressure by com munity leaders. Objective : joint allocation of m for climate and environmental projects. Necessary preconditions : steering group of people appointed by councillors; Staff support provided by a foundation (CVCF) partner who had good state and local contacts, dedication to stay involved and staff capacity to support Process and structures : Project eligibility funding guidelines developed through continual feedback from community steering committee (CSC) meetings open meetings attended by hundred s. Specifics decided on from outset were voting eligibility, process and lines of authority. City and CVCF staff assess project submissions and cut ineligible ones. Eligible projects presented to community members and community steering committee (CSC). rd binding vote by community to accept a proposal. th CSC meeting given more in depth info on eligible projects and asked to rank. CVCF and city staff ranked and created four proposed packages then presented at further CSC meeting. Minority communi ty also developed a th package on their own accord so another CSC meeting held to present this. th package got overwhelming support. Innovative engagement methods : town hall meetings at minority run churches with Q A sessions Preengagement : public bu lletin announcements and mailed announcements to neighbourhood residents as well as town hall type church meetings early in the process (right after the decision on the involvement of the public in climate action was taken). Engagement with ethnic minorities through meetings in minority run churches (QA sessions) Ethnic minorities developing a separate eligibilit y package (which ultimately won the funding). Larger budgets improve participation ratesinterest and have greater ability to address redistrib utive goals Areas with traditionally stronger base of civil engagement and organisations more likely to have successful long term PB institutional change Needs to be a wider part of community engagement practices so not just token nor onetime fun ding allocation
Commercial In Co nfidence Table : Participatory budgeting Paris (FR) Background Description Costs involved Relevance for NZ context Feasibility for different individuals and community types Risks Benefits Design choices In Paris, participatory budgeting was introduced in by then newly elected mayor Anne Hidalgo against the backdrop of declining voters participation. Politically, Paris has been known for giving little space for citizens participation in government. The Paris PB is the largest in scale and scope in the world . The number of people voting is increasing every year at a significant r ate. In , , people voted, , in , and close to , in , which represents about of the Parisian population. The funds involved are considerable as well. I n , . million euros were allocated to projects . In , . milli on euros went to city wide projects and boroughs projects. In , . million euros went to city wide projects and boroughs projects. A total of million has been earmarked for PB for . Objectives : to rebuild public trust by in creasing the role citizens have in governance and political decision making . Necessary preconditions : clear rules of engagement and criteria for eligible projects; Structures : City Evaluation Committee (Mayor, elected officials, technical experts and randomly selected group of citizens ); borough level committees to evaluate borough level projects (similar composition). Process : There is an annual cycle repeated every year: January February: proposals are submitted by individual Parisians or groups (no limi tation on age or nationality). This is supported by a variety of meetings, and resources are provided to help develop projects. March April: initial evaluation of feasibility and cost and co construction and collective discussion between citizens, NGOs and neighbourhood councils with a view to improve them AprilMay: finalised project submissions and their technical evaluation by Citys experts June August: projects are assessed and approved by city and borough level ad hoc Evaluation Committees August September: selected projects are announced, and citizens are encouraged to organize public campaigns to draw voters September: two weeks for online and in person voting by Parisians (no limitations on age or nationality) December: Winning projects are announ ced and added to the budget for the next financial year to be passed by the City Council of Paris Project implementation begins immediately in the new FY. The website has a track progress feature for citizens to monitor this. Funding allocation informat ion only, no information found on cost to administrate. Regular repetitive programme could be replicated, however likely to involve high costs to communicate, advertise and administer. It would be worth investigating to get a better understanding of the system for voting on projects and any security measures taken to restrict voting from outside the area or multiple votes by one person. Scale is much larger than would be able to be supported by NZ LG, especially in education Participa tion is open to any resident of Paris, there are no limitations on age or nationality. This encourages participation of youth and migrants. Targeting youth and children by reserving a certain amount of budget ( million euros) for children to vote on proj ects for youth children and education. This may encourage family participation in general. Targeting underrepresented and marginalised populations by reserving a certain budget ( million euros) for projects in deprived areas. Engagement and participat ion of marginalised populations is low because many projects are seen as lifestyle ideas and are not treating actual social problems Projects do not tackle more complex social issues because only the investment budget is available for PB (i.e. no long term large costs can be incurred for the city). Only a small number of ideas are in areas of solidarity, security or cleanliness. Information overload of citizens due to the large number of ideas and amount of information they need to make an informed decision. This may discourage participation. Work overload of the team and systems running the PB due to the need of processing and managing of a large number of ideas Encouragement of horizontal cooperation between institutions and people Promotion of constructive dialogue between citizens and government and among citizens Bringing new perspectives and fresh ideas to city management and development Better prioritisation of budgetary allocations by the government following the citizens needs Government opening up to citizens and introducing more flexibility in its processes Citizens being educated about public budget processes Citizens more empowered both through their better knowledge of the government, public finance and project manage ment and through gaining agency over the development of their communities Tangible results of civic engagement in every neighbourhood Political buy in and commitment from the senior officials and politicians allows to leverage the necessary resources to deliver and grow the programme and raises its profile among the population and overall. Support from the civil society helps the promotion of the initiative and increases awareness and participation. Comprehensive promotional campaign through multip le channels (online and offline) improves awareness and engagement and ensure high participation. Transparency of the process ensure credibility and legitimacy of the process. Ongoing engagement with the citizens, especially after the voting, ensures t hat citizens see and understand the tangible results of the PB they were involved in. This motivates them for participation in the next round, confirms credibility of the process and inspires more participation. While the use of new technologies is impor tant, offline activities are indispensable to galvanise participation. Respect for deadlines and quick realisation of winning projects are critical to maintain legitimacy and accountability. Continuity (i.e. repetition of PB every year) has impacted awareness and familiarisation and ensured PBs becoming a popular practice.

Commercial In Confidence CASE STUDIES Introduction In consultation with the Department of Internal Affairs we first undertook one case study on a citizen jury example ( the Victorias Citizens Jury on Obesity) and one on participatory budgeting (Participatory budgeting in Reykjavik ). Following a discussion w ith the working group we added a study on engagement with a strong need to involve Mori or Pacific people ( Out of the Shadows Bringing Waips Heritage to Life ) and a further one evidencing models for investing in the underlying relationships between lo cal government and communities with examples of soft infrastructure (Neighbourhood Empowerment Network in San Francisco ). Victorias Citizens Jury on Obesity Background The Victorias Citizens Jury on Obesity was initiated by Victorian Health Promotion F oundation (VicHealth) a statutory authority in the Australian state of Victoria with a mandate to promote good health of all Victorians. VicHealth identified obesity as a significant health challenge impacting the Victorians (and Australians more general ly) and decided to design an innovative collaborative response to achieve a high impact and wide support. The organisation newDemocracy Foundation, which is a leading Australian research institute specializing in democratic innovation, developed and imple mented the process of citizens jury. One of the design objectives was to give a random sample of everyday citizens a journey of discovery about their food choices. The citizens jury was focused only on food and the way we eat. The specific question w as formulated for the jury: We have a problem with obesity. How can we make it easier to eat better The complete process took place from August till October and resulted in asks (recommendations) for government, industry and the communit y to work together to tackle the obesity crisis. Specific objectives of the citizens jury For this jury, two objectives were central: Build trust through public accountability and accessibility, and Build consensus and provide recommendations how poor ea ting behaviours could be addressed. In the case of San Francisco, the neighbourhood resilience organisations were established by local communities encouraged and supported by NEN. The financing needs to be secured on the permanent basis because otherwise this resilience model is les s sustainable and effective. Benefits The whole community approach is inclusive and significantly strengthens the relationships between the local government and the community and within the community (e.g. residents, NGOs, businesses, police etc), incre ases mutual trust and enhances the understanding within the community. Residents are better educated and acquire skills necessary in stress situations. Community as a whole is strengthened due to better connections and knowledge of community residents, res ources and networks. Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs
Commercial In Confidence Design choices The important design choices that made this engagement a success are: Explanation: A lot of effort was spent at the early engagement stage to explain people why a certain plan was made , or a certain policy measure was proposed. The Discovery Bus Tours primarily aimed to show the rich local history and the immense interest of the public i n this history, which could be used to attract more visitors and boost local economy. At the same time, the proposed measures were directed at preservation and study of local history. The use of engaging language (plain English) and accessible visual produ cts is important to bring the point across. Clear vision of what the Council wants to achieve helped to frame the discussion and engage with the Councils proposals. Focus on the people: The engagement campaign put people in the centre. Council staff went where people were, both to physical locations and online locations. For instance, the Council realised early on that Facebook is the main channel of communication with the residents and provided most content and communication over its Facebook account and not via other social media. In terms of physical locations, instead of inviting people to the Councils premises, the Councils staff went on a road tour and met people at schools, shops and other places. This approach significantly increased the outreach and draw in some residents who are usually less involved in Councils matters (e.g. youth). Iwi involvement was (and continues to be) critical for the project, adding the valuable perspective and credibility to the process. Equal partnership: treating the community as equal partners in the process increases the credibility of the process and enhances engagement. Feedback: reporting back to the community is a part of the engagement process. People need to know what happened to their submissions, what decis ions were taken and why. This may increase their willingness to participate in the future local government activities and increases trust. Ongoing process: public engagement is an ongoing process that did not end with the adoption of the Year Plan. The Future Waip website is being used to inform about the decisions taken and the actions of the Council. Available at: https:www.c ambridgenews.nzbus tripthrough history Neighbourhood Empowerment Network in San Francisco Background The Neighbourhood Empowerment Network (NEN) was launched by the Mayor of San Francisco, Ed Lee, in response to the difficulties experienced by communities in New Orleans through hurricane Katrina. The analysis of the response to (and preventive measures in anticipation of) hurricane Katrina by Harvard Kennedy School of Government showed the complete breakdown of the working relationships between the residents and the government. The analysis issued several recommendations focused on increasing capacities of local residents. These recommendations were implemented by San Francisco in the form of NEN. NEN has been operating since supporting a mi x of community needs (development strategies, public health and safety and emergency management). It employs community development approach and leverages such techniques as place based planning, human c entred design, asset based organising and servant lead ership to engage communities and ensure the transfer of ownership back to the n eighbourhoods of their resilience. NEN has created a range of tools, programs, and technical resources that can be considered soft infrastructure that is necessary to support grassroots resilience building efforts that are applicable in the City of San Francisco and beyond. Commercial In Confidence INTRODUCTION MartinJenkins has been contracted by the Department of Internal Affairs to provide research and analysis of participatory practices in local government, in the context of the recent amendment to the Local Government Act to restore the promotion of com munity wellbeing to the statutory purpose of local government. Local government across comparable jurisdictions has evolved over recent years. The top down systems that support an elected representative system are still strong . However , there is an increas ing shift to include more active, ongoing citizen participation in local decision making and budget setting. Many citizens are no longer content to simply vote every three or four years and leave local governance to elected members in between elections . The range and scope of participatory practices internationally is enormous, as can be seen in this participedia https:participedia.net . The advent of new technologies and expectations of anywhere, anytime data and communication have presented both opportunities and challenges for local government. While on one hand technology can enable better participation, in some cases it can also exclude people and increase the division between people who are able to pa rticipate easily and those are not. Good participatory practices are designed to enable engagement from divers e groups of people to ensure that they are properly representative of local demographics . Practices strongly centred around a new technology can be difficult for older citizens to participate in , and practices with significant time demands could exclude people with multiple jobs and high family demands . There is emerging understanding in some of the international examples we looked at, that unless t here is some form of remuneration attached to participation, it can exclude large sections of society that simply cannot afford to participat e at the expense of actual or potential loss of income. This report looks at some of the literature on participato ry practices , as well as describing our own knowledge and understanding of examples we have come across. Th is is necessarily selective, as it is beyond the scope of th is project to find and document every method and incident of citizen participation , and t he methods are still evolving. We have sought to find examples where there is credible analysis of the practice , and an indication of its efficiency and effectiveness. We have found that much of the available academi c literature is focused on the theories of participation rather than on practical examples, or is about consultation and engagement, not participation. As with many emerging practices , there is a tendency to adopt the title with a loose interpretation and we have sought to identify practices tha t are truly participatory .

Commercial In Confidence KEY FEATURES AND SUCCESS FACTORS This section sets out the common features and success factors in effective community p articipation practices. Community participation is through different forms of a deliberative mini public, defined by political scientist Robert Dahl as an assembly of citizens, demographically representative of the larger population, brought together to l earn and deliberate on a topic in order to inform public opinion and decision making. Features and rationale The exact mandate and model of a participatory practice can vary. Whilst all feature a body of citizens who come together to deliberate on a given issue , this can range from providing a set of recommendations or options , through to formulating a proposal to put to popular referendum , and ultimately to making a collective decision on an identified topic that the convening body has already agreed it will accept. Their common feature is that they go beyond community consultation to a practice whereby citizens directly contribut e to decision making. It is reported in overseas jurisdictions t hat mini publics significantly increase tr ust in the decision making of a council. In a local government context, t he rationale underpinning mini publics is that they enable councils to engage citizens meaningfully in decision making , and can be designed to represent the demographic or demographics whose voices a council wants to hear on the topic. Research has concluded that that a group of randomly selected citizens, when given the information, resources and time to deliberate on a given topic, can produce an informed public judgement . They can also signal real public opinion on a policy issue. Minipublics provide a broader model of governance, expanding from a representative democracy where deliberation and decision making rests with elected representa tives alone, to one where decision making is shared. Elected politicians may not necessarily reflect the communities they serve,

Commercial In Confidence NEW ZEALAND CONTEXT Local government in New Zealand differs from many other countries in several ways , and participatory processes need to be selected which are appropriate , or can be adapted to this context: it does not operate core social services such as housing and benefit administration (although there are exceptions where, for example, Wellington City Council operate city housing on behalf of central government) it does not have responsibility for core emer gency services such as fire, police and ambulance it does not have responsibility for education most of its funding is from property tax ( in many other countries it is funded by central government) the role of Mayor is consistent across New Zealand, is ele cted by popular vote and is a functional role (some countries vary from area to area, have a system of rotation for the Mayoral role or it is elected by the Councillors and the role is ceremonial only i.e., has no voting rights or involvement in administer ing by laws or regulations) Like other countries New Zealand is experiencing decline in local government voting participation, particularly from youth and diverse communities. This voter apathy, as it is often called, is thought to be caused by the impre ssion that there is little ability to affect outcomes. Participatory practices have emerged as a response to this, although we have been unable to find strong evidence that they have increased voter numbers yet. There is evidence that New Zealand local gov ernment has been experimenting with participatory practices, especially with planning and spending prioritisation. Examples of efforts to include citizens in participation can be seen in Auckland Council s codesign lab, Wellington City Council s trials using Loomio to develop its Alcohol Management strategy and Waip a District Council s approach to engagement for its Te r Wai initiative. The limitation on local government adopting more participatory practices, appears to be the associated costs and the a dditional time they involve, which needs to be resourced . Changes to the Local Government Act have focused on increasing consultation for long term plans but have not fully anticipated the trajectory of public participation. The legislation is now se en by some as a barrier to more fluid, consistent participatory practices due to the: focus on point intime engagement guidance toward consultation based on pre established council policies and positions requirement for document type consultation material expectations of councils to allow people to present to them (reinforcing the engagement settings that some councils have , expect ing people to come to them to present) We note that these were all appropriate at the time of legislation and that at the time, it did a good job of setting the expectation of much stronger engagement practice around long term plan development. The comments we make on this are simply to point out that there could be more flexible expectations Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs
Commercial In Confidence OVERVIEW OF POPULAR PARTICIPATORY PRACTICES Practice Description Relevance for NZ Risks Benefits Participatory budgeting This practice allows citizens to make decisions on how funding is used. This is mostly practiced in Europe with limited examples in New Zealand but can be applied to ring fenced funds in NZ. Takes longer and costs more. Harder for some communities to participate, especially groups that have less available time, poorer communication ability or lack tech skills. Improved levels of trust in local government, if done well. Better spend on th ings that matter to community. Improved connection between local government and community. Citizen juries Decisions made by a jury that is representative usually on a single , significant topicissue. May not be compatible with NZ top down structures as genuine juries have full delegated decision making (as in a court ). Would only be practical in larger cities. Takes longer and costs more. Harder for lower socio economic participants. Can produce poor decisions if training and familiarisatio n is insufficient. Difficult to get true representation without power to require it ( like court juries) Decisions are more likely to be acceptable or explainable across the full range of community groups. Improves connections between local government and all communities
