Commercial In Confidence Postengagement actions In May , hearings o n the submissions were held. The submitters could present additional information, elaborate their submissions and answer questions of the Councillors. After the hearings, the Council held deliberations on the submissions. At deliberations, all submissions were considered taking into account such factors as the number of submiss ions per issue, the opinions expressed, knowledge of the district etc. After that, a workshop was held to review the financial implications resulting from deliberations. The submitters received feedback on what happened to their submission. A summary report on decision s taken during the deliberations was released and distributed through the media, the Future Waip website and Council website and offices. In addition, a letter or email was sent to those submitters who provided input that was not included in the summary report. This individual feedback included the record of decision made on the submission. Risks Local heritage is a risky topic for engagement. On the one hand, it may be of little interest f or the residents and require a lot of promotion and education. On the other hand, it is a very sensitive and even controversial topic. For example, the Council was accused by different sides of telling their version of truth. In , the Councils pro posal for a museum and theatre complex failed and was strongly criticised. A lot of patience, understanding and cultural competence are key mitigation measures. Advice from local iwi and history experts was sought were appropriate. Investment in local heri tage is not considered the core Council business by some residents who strongly and very vocally opposed the campaign. The complex project with many fast moving elements is at risk of getting messy and fail. The mitigation measure was to have very clear distribution of tasks and responsibilities and a robust time plan The cost may run high both due to the amount of materials produced and events conducted and due to the bilingualism (i.e. learning the correct pronunciation of all Mori words, creating bili ngual materials and checking them all takes time and money). The engagement linked the local history to the future planning. Commercial In Confidence Stakeholders involved A number of stakeholders worked together to ensure the successful outcome of the jury process: VicHealth managed the supplier consortium, handled stakeholder relations, chaired the steering group, defined the jurys remit, provided an overview of obesity and food in Victoria, drafted the final insights report (jointly with newDemocracy Foundation). Multidisciplinary supplier consortium of suppliers to be key creation and delivery partners of the jury process, combining leading expertise in democratic research, large scale deliberative facilitation, user experience design and social technologies. newDemocracy Foundation developed and implemented the complete citizens jury process, starting with the selection of jurors and finishing with co producing the insights report. Steering group was created to include key public health organisations that would be potentially involved in implementing the jurys recommendations. The group included key decision makers in government, industry and the community , namely the Department of Premier and Cabinet of Victoria , the Australian Food and Grocery Council, Australian Beverages Council, Australian Medical Association Victoria, Foodbank Victoria, Coles (major superm arket chain), Melbourne city council , Obesity Policy Coalition, CHOICE (consumer advocacy group), CPAN Deakin University and Tennis Australia. Media partners with regional newspapers to boost awareness and legitimacy of the initiative (The Herald Sun . million readers in Victoria every week day and Sunday Herald Sun by .m every Sunday) Jury: jurors started online process, participated in the face toface event (largest scale citizens jury in Australia). Process Jurors were recruited using stratified random selection . First, , invitations were sent, both by regular mail and electronically, to candidates drawn from two student databases and the VoteCompass database (VoteCompass is an interactive, online voting advice application; citizen s interested in public policy events register there). These sources were chosen to ensure a varies sample and to reach the young people who are typically a low response group. In the second selection round, jurors were selected to provide a representat ive sample of Victorian residents. Over a period of six weeks, the jurors engaged in online deliberation in a facilitated forum. In this way, they reviewed and discussed written submissions evidence ( items) presented by stakeholders, experts, indiv iduals and organisations as well as the steering group on the topic of the jury. The submissions included the readers poll in the Herald Sun and a youth poll. All submissions were made public. Following the online deliberations, jurors met in person for face toface deliberations. This stage lasted two days and was facilitated by an independent engagement expert and facilitator . The main objective at this stage was to collectively produce a report with recommendations to present to the steering group. T he deliberation was held in small groups, groups in total. Commercial In Confidence Stakeholders involved The main stakeholder involved was the District Council. The Council staff planned and carried out the engagement campaign. Local iwi w as involved starting from the early engagement throughout the whole process. The Waip community as a whole can be considered as a stakeholder because the Council treated it as a partner in this process. Process of engagement The project carried out a broad community engagement programme through a variety of channels and with a great number of various elements, mixing traditional approaches with highly innovative ideas. The early engagement process started in April . Sharing memories and stories was the central element of the early engagement campaign. Th e idea was to capture stories and visions of different generations, told from different perspectives, and to create a shared memory and understanding of Waip . Council staff visited rest homes and interviewed older residents. They also went to schools and asked their students about their hopes and dreams linked to Waip and to memories captured. Simple cost effective photo booths were installed to capture memories of Waip . Council used all imagery (photos, interviews) on its social media channels, which en couraged more people to share their stories and photos. The Council also ran print ads in local newspapers focused on key aspects of Waip s history (in ) and on Mori history (early ). Discovery Bus Tours started in autumn . Discovery Bus Tou rs were free bus tours, run by the Council, to heritage sites and places of historical significance, including battle sites of Land Wars of s. The bus tours proved extremely popular and were all booked out within days after being announced. Initially, seven , hours bus tours were offered in , and people participated in them. The bus tours had a professional guide on board who encouraged passengers to share their stories and knowledge. A local iwi member welcomed passengers on sites and told th e Mori history linked to the sites and Land Wars. At the end of each tour, participants were encouraged to get involved in the community discussion around heritage and make a submission towards the Year Plan. The bus tours returned in and cov ered new areas of the Waip district. Funding from the Ministry for Culture and Heritage was obtained for the additional bus tours in . In , people participated in bus tours. An interactive online map was created (discoverwaipa.co.nz) to explore the Waip district and its heritage sites as well as to discover the history around them. In October , Waip District Council was the only Council to officially commemorate the Land Wars. Local hap, schools, community and Council representatives participated in the ceremony. After months of the broad pre engagement, more focused engagement with the draft Year Plan started. Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs

Objective : various health policy decisions Necessary preconditions : Establishment of rules of conduct between jurors; an external facilitator supporting the jurors; the precise formulation of the topic, charge or question provided by organisers; s teering committees or advisory groups (in cases) made up of policy makers, discipline experts, advocacy group representatives, clinical practitioners, patients, caregivers. Process : recruitment of jurors (most had participants and three had participants). Nearly two thirds of the juries took place over days, usually on a weekend. Commercial In Confidence Table : World Cafes Background Description Costs involved Relevance for NZ context Feasibility for different individuals and community types Risks Benefits Design choices The World Caf is a methodology for hosting conversations about relevant questions and themes. The ideal is that there are multiple conversations that build of f of each other to explore the issue deeply. Objectives : to explore, develop and rehabilitate own opinions through engagement with others in the community. Process : the time and place of the caf as well as the topic can be announced in local media and social media. The size of the group depends on the size of the place and time available (can be from to participants). At the start the host defines the purpos e of the caf to the participants and divides them into groups of people per table. The groups will be rotating between tables in conversational rounds of minutes. During each round, participants discuss progressively deepening questions re lated to the issue. The questions should be prepared by the hosts in advance and clearly stated to the participants at each table at the beginning of each round by a table host. Table hosts facilitates the discussion of the group and summarises the results to the next group coming to hisher table. This next group then starts off where the previous finished, learning from and building on them. At the end of the conversational rounds, groups summari se their key findings and present them to the entire group. At the end, the entire group of participants convenes to connect all of the ideas into just a few shared key points. The cost of a World Caf is only as much as the host s would like to spend , so can be kept to a minimum. Generally the costs include the materials neededdesired (table cloths, markers, paper, name tags ), food and drink. World Caf is a relatively simple idea and format that could easily work in a New Zealand context. While the Caf label could create a preconception about the type of person who would be comfortable in that setting, it is not necessary to use that label or indeed host it in a Caf. The format could be adapted to work in a number of different environments so it could be used in contexts that are more familiar to the specific population types being targeted. Representation of underrepresented populations need to be encouraged both through the selection process and during the conversation in the cafe Can be used for a range of different topics and inputs Can be encouraged as a community led engagement Is able to be carried out in many locations that suit the communities Set a clear context of what is discussed and why Envisage the desired outcomes and design questions and processes to ensure the caf arrives to these outcomes Invest in the design of questions: the central questions need to be clear and matter to the participants Create a hospitable place, with food and drinks Use facilitators to encourage contributions from everyone (e.g. Talking Object technique is recommended) Use interactive and playful methods (e.g. use different colours for different issues and opinions, allow participants to draw on the tablecloth etc) Active listening and connecting different perspectives

Commercial In Confidence Table : Neighbourhood decision making Quarter associations and quarter contracts Switzerland Background Description Costs involved Relevance for NZ context Feasibility for different individuals and community types Risks Benefits Design choices Switzerland has a range of informal participatory structures in addition to formal local government. Quarter association and quarter contracts are a widespread form in smaller towns and villages. Quarters are basically defined neighbourhoods. Quarter assoc iations are territorially defined non governmental organisations and an informal form of community governance. Quarter contracts rely on citizen participation in individual quarters to identify priority projects and quarter community centres that organise social and cultural activities. Quarter association Objectives : protection of interests of the quarter residents and engagement with the local government on behalf of resident on planning issues . They see themselves as a counterpoint to the local administr ation. Necessary preconditions : legal basis in the Civil Code that made quarter associations legal entities, subject to certain requirements (e.g. regular reporting). Structures : Head committee for association elected by members. Process : Quarter statutes are passed by the members to define purpose of association and their work. Associations run own physical meeting points in their areas and websites. Association made up of members can be admitted or resign at any time who can be natural or legal perso ns residing in the quarter . In some cases they collect small annual membership fee. Citizens come to local association with issues, may use as an official contact point through which to contact local government . Not liable to local government but can inte ract frequently based on local policy or a memorandum of understanding . Quarter associations may also procure fuel, fertilizer etc on behalf of their members as well as run community libraries and centres. Quarter contracts Objectives : engage locals in planning processes and promote projects to locals . Structures : specific bodies that work on defining development priorities for their areas. Process : a bit similar to PB process , but with more decision making powers delegated to residents . Municipal Council designates a budget each year for (typically small) projects in a given quarter . Interested residents submit a project proposal . Project group (made up of quarter residents) assess project against contract aims, analyses project, contacts partners, drafts a budget and an action plan . A piloting committee (made up of mayor and another councillor, and reps from other party members on council, tenants association, traders association, social workers, another association and a resident all from the quarter (area), chosen on annual basis by municipal decision) supports the project, implementation and evaluation occur. na Something similar could be adapted to be workable in New Zealand. It is similar to Business Improvement Districts model in use by Auckland and Wellington City Councils albeit with a more social focus. These forms are used specifically in the settlements with smaller populations (less than ,). Per town, there are typically several such organisations ( e.g. the town of Aarau has , population and quarter associations). Objectives : joint planning and implementation of initiatives Process : Tables are established on identified topics that the council seeks to advance. Experts can be added to the Table as an advisory body to the Table, drawn from NGO connections and supported by them. The role of the Table is to develop strategy, support strategic implementation through developing a work plan including community engagement strategies, and to monitor and evaluate. The extent of the involvement of people with lived experience can vary fro m providing advice to co design. The Table incorporates extensive community engagement to inform its work. No information found on costs This could be adopted for a specific purpose in New Zealand. Due to the administration and formality, it is more likel y to be of use for a nationally significant issue, or for a large council like Auckland. The tables tend to be made up of representatives from NGOs associated with the relevant sectors so is not typically a direct engagement. The table members then enga ge with he relevant communities. The effectiveness of the model is dependent on the skills of the facilitator. Without this: All the parties required for the shared outcomes may not be willing to participate The Table becomes a place for talking without a dvancing anything People involved in the Table are not solution focused. Conversation stations usually investigate personal, difficult, even uncomfortable issues (e.g. euthanasia). Whanganui Distric t Council implemented one in . Objective : to investigate difficult issues in an informal situation on a personal level; to investigate possibilities of public dialogue, explore social dynamics, and question who we are to each other as strangers and as members of our common society . Necessary preconditions : a large dice with discussion questions written on each side; a dialogue facilitator. Process : In a public, but fairly private space (e.g. street caf) a table(s) with a large dice is set up. The dice have discussions questions written on its sides. The questions can be interchangeably personal social political. Once two persons sit down at the table(s), the facilitator invites them to start a conversation. The facilitator is not present on site, bu t is in a car nearby, able to observe and hear the dialogue. The facilitator asks people to throw the dice and discuss the question selected in this manner. The facilitator announces the end of the conversation. Currently, permanent audio has been installed that can be activated by pushing a button. It prompts people to spin a wheel to start conversation. A version of this practice is: a person (e.g. elected local government member) is sitting at the station awaiting a second person to join. Commercial In Confidence Table : Tools for collating citizens ideas and ranking them or voting them up e.g., Ethelo Background Description Costs involved Relevance for NZ context Feasibility for different individuals and community types Risks Benefits Design choices Ethelo https:ethelo.com is an online engagement and decision making platform. Ethelo is comprised of two entities: Ethelo Decisions a technology company dedicated to helping organizations focus collective intelligence to make the best decisions more quickly and Ethelo Democr acy a non profit society dedicated to a more effective, citizen engaged democracy. Ethelo Decisions undertakes commercial projects to fund the development of the Ethelo technology, which is provided to Ethelo Democracy and its partners for the cost of hardware. The Ethelo algorithm was developed to enable fair outcomes in complex multi stakeholder negotiations. Objectives : to harness the power of collective wisdom for governance and group decisions. Process : Ethelo is a patented algorithm that uses an extension of morphological analysis. It is compatible with and a complement to processes such as conjoint analysis, the Monte Carlo Method and decision trees. It incorporates a novel approach to liquid democrac y using trust networks . The algorithm combine s various decision parameters (options, issues, criteria, constraints, influence, and fairness ) and build s a space of potential outcomes . These are evaluated and ranked according to aggregated analysis of the participants. It finds outcomes with high average support and low variance in satisfaction among participants .

Key groups involved : Department of Communities and Local Govt (DCLG) for research and guidance on emerging planning practices Planning Aid and Locality for advice and funding (National organisations which support local community organisations). NP steering group Community members Independent examiners Process : Neighbou rhood planning usually instigated by the Local Authority, the Parish, Town Councils or by individuals or existing community groups. Those wishing to submit a plan send their proposed neighbourhood area to get approved by the local planning authority. A ste ering group is often created of local stakeholders. Local partnerships are developed, community engagement and consultation occur, and an evidence base is built. The plan is developed through continuous consultation with the community. Local planning auth ority and an independent body review and modify the plan to ensure it meets all legal planning requirements. The plan is publicised. The plan is then put to a public referendum. The plan is adopted by a simple majority vote. Generally whole planning develo pment process takes between months. Innovative engagement methods : Many media forms were used, including digital and social . A neighbourhood plan website is usually developed including contact details with the overseeing committee so people can provi de their feedback. Other engagement techniques used are workshops, shop units street stalls, questionnaires, model making, school or college projects. Capacity building : Local authorities have a duty to support neighbourhood planning under the Localism Act (). Consultants often brought in when internal capacity was lacking for community members involved. Due to the novelty of the process, both consultants and local authorities were learning on the. National organisations (e.g. Planning Aid and Local ity) provide resources for capacity building , also for local authorities . Neighbourhoods draw on governmen t funded support to help develop their neighbourhood plans. Most used these funds to access planning consultancy support to supplement local authority support mainly at the plan writing stage The UK govt has set aside m between to support the development of neighbourhood plans or neighbourhood development orders. Eligible community organisations neighbourhoods can apply for grant funding of up to ,, as well as technical support. An additional , is available for certain groups (such as neighbourhood area with population of , plus, involves a designated business neighbourhood plan, includes design codes, housing a llocations or three or more Parishes are jointly writing a plan). General estimates to create a NDP can range from less than , to more than three times this depending on complexity and the area. Local planning authority is typically responsible for the costs of independently reviewing the plan and of holding the referendum
Commercial In Confidence The second stage is an assessment of the proposed ideas by the citys Construction Board (i.e. professi onal engineers, architects, builders etc.). They look into the feasibility of the projects and estimate their costs. The feasibility criteria are pre determined and include: fit in the budget, projects are on the city land, projects do not require extensiv e planning or consultation. The Construction Board discards ideas that are beyond the scope of the process and informs the participants about the reasons for rejection by email. The Construction Board also consults with Neighbourhood Councils on the feasib ility and costs. For example, in , the Construction Board assessed ideas and left over most popular ideas that also met criteria for the online vote. This stage takes three months and ends in June. The third stage is voting (in October). First, the voters need to be authenticated via the National Voters Registry (online). Voters also need to choose online, in which of the districts (neighbourhoods) they will vote. Each resident has one vote. To cast a vote, a re sident divides the available budget up between hisher favourite projects. As a resident vote, heshe will see how the overall budget is reduced, and the remaining projects that are over budget are greyed out. To prevent against bias in voting, e very time a voter clicks on the site , ideas are presented in a random order. The vote is electronic, secure and binding. Voter can go back and correct their votes several times; only the final vote counts. A dvanced security measures are utilized to protect user and website information (for instance, the technology provider does not have access to personal data). The software used for the vote is open source (Open Active Voting ). The tallying is done by the City Council, and winners are announced through a special cer emony. Results are also emailed to participants of the voting. The final decision on the implementation of projects is taken by the City Council, who committed to formally process the highest voted proposal on a monthly basis and implement them (in , of proposals were implemented). Each year around ideas are implemented by the City Council and Neighbourhood Councils . Execution of projects starts shortly after the voting is finalised; construction projects usually start the year following the voting (in summer). While most projects relate to construction and infrastructure (e.g. improvements to parks, playgrounds, roads) and are relatively small, there are examples of other projects. For instance, one of the early successes was an idea put for ward by a nine yearold girl requesting more school field trips. Larger scale projects included renovation of a small disused power station into a youth centre and an increased provision of shelters for homeless people. Posters and billboards were used all over the city. It has used professional marketing companies and a multi channel marketing campai gn to make people aware of the participatory budgeting process. This has included Google and Facebook ads, Twitter and advertisement on radio and TV. Comedians have been hired as the face of the process. In addition, an extensive outreach campaign took pla ce offline in places, like shopping malls, schools, retirement homes and other. Risks Ensuring broad participation and especially representation may be a challenge, despite wide campaigning and creative use of media. At the moment, relatively little is known about the demographics of the participants of the budgeting process. A small recent evaluation suggested that the participation is biased towards those who are university educated, those on higher incomes and people aged to . Citizen participants do not have ultimate decision making authority, which could lead to frustration, especially as not all proposals can be implemented by the City Council. Small budget available for allocation through the participatory budgeting may discourage participation as people feel that this budget will not create meaningful changes and that only small projects will be implemented. The large number of ideas places a strain on both city officials , in terms of their capacity to manage and assess them, and on the IT systems. Commercial In Confidence Timing Processes should be c arried out during the term of council and not near an election in order to reduce politicizing issues The time commitment required from citizens needs to be considered carefully. Requiring substantive amounts of time can be a barrier to participation, but enough time needs to be allowed so that people can access and understand enough information and deliberate it. In all instances, ti me frames need to be defined and explained. Deliberation s of a citizens jury take place over a short intensive time period This encourages participation , as it is a short term commitment for each individual . The recommended duration of citizens juries is four to five days but may be shorter depending on the issue at hand. Key considerations are to allow time for participants to engage and assess the evidence (including hearing witnesses , and studying written ev idence ), the oppo rtunity to receive expert advice and additional research if necessary , and sufficient time for deliberation and decision making. Part of a wider and longer term strategy of trust building Participatory processes are part of wider community engagement . They work best in places with a strong culture of community engagement , and when the process, the proceedings and the final decisions are publicly available. If the process is repeated regularly, people become more fami liar with it and participation increases, especially as the decisions taken in the process are implemented. Evaluation and feedback mechanisms are built in to the design of the process from the beginning, and the learnings incorporated into the design of future processes

The reintroduction of wellbeings into the Local Government Act, provide s new context for the relationship between Local Government elected members and officials and the public. In this report we explore some of the ways this has been approached internationally. These differences between local government in New Zealand and its international counterparts have an impact on the type and scale of participatory practices they can adopt. In considering examples, we need to be cognisant that often local government in other counties operate at a different scale, have higher overall budgets , more diversity of expertise and increased ability to address the needs of community in a holistic manner.

Stakeholders involved NEN has a whole community approach to stakeholder engagement and involves all types of organisations, networks and individuals located in a specific neig hbourhood. It is an alliance of residents, neighbourhoods (neighbourhood organisations), business associations and businesses, nonprofits and charitable foundations, faith based organisations, civic agencies, government and academic institutions. Examples of soft infrastructure NEN has developed nine programmes targeting different aspects of community resilience. Each of the programmes provides a framework for community action and a variety of resources, such as templates and guides that can be used by n eighbourhoods and smaller communities. NEN also provides technical support to communities in the form of workshops, seminars and other informational, educational and training events. In collaboration with the Institute for Civic and Community Engagement (I CCE) at San Francisco State University, the NEN created a NEN university that aims to improve local communities through resilience education. Students earn class credit for projects, such as community asset mapping and leadership training, that make commun ities more resilient and better places to live. In addition, there are two NEN Leadership Academies (one for youth) that equip participants with skills to advance resilience in their communities. NEN also facilitates the engagement between communities and its leaders (including local government). The engagement focuses on risks shocks that communities are likely to experience and how they can work together to develop and implement mitigating strategies. This pre engagement is an investment in the relatio nships between leadership and communities and helps to higher levels of trust and reciprocity with communities, which will increase cooperation during disasters and accelerate recovery from them. Empowered Communities Program (ECP) is an umbrella programme for resilience building. ECP harnesses the expertise and resources of all stakeholders to develop and implement overall resilience plans in each neighbourhood. Under ECP, NEN provides the communities with templates for resilience plans and guides them thr ough the process to develop their own plans. NEN takes an advisory and facilitator role in this process, while the community drives the development of all plans and makes decisions on leadership and operations. NEN supports the four working groups that wer e set up in each neighbourhood: ) children and their families; ) seniors and people living with disabilities; ) immigrant communities; and ) small business and non profit organizations. These groups meet monthly for discussions, while NEN provides tech nical expert advice, helps with advocacy and investment planning. The Steering Group of NEN oversees the implementation of the neighbourhood plans. The HUB Program is a part of ECP and supports communitys overall preparedness on a daily basis. NEN conduc ts workshops with local organisations to help them understand their role in the community, their community needs in case of disaster and realise the benefits of teamwork. Commercial In Confidence can make decisions that favour their own political interests and are subject to pressure and influence from interest and lobby groups. Even if this is not the case, trust in politicians is low and declining. Decisions made a by a cross section of society that the broader public can identify with may seem more acceptable or even more legitimate. The approach does require a deep theoretical shift in how the role of elected members is viewed. Research by Professor Lyn Carson of the University of Sydney Business School has further concluded that a well facilitated group of citizens can make better decisions than a group of experts as they are coming to the topic with an open mind. She also provided evidence that the approach builds trust in local government, for example where a mayor in one local authority that used deliberative dialogue increased their percentag e share of the vote at the next election, in contrast to the declining vote their party had for the position of mayor in all other parts of the state. Minipublics are a stronger mechanism tha n advisory models, such as panels. Such mechanisms can contrib ute to this broader governance, particularly when they are formal mechanisms with established channels to decision makers. However, they do not transfer decision making to the citizens. F ormal long standing mechanisms are also not accessible for all divers e communities as they may not be culturally appropriate and require members to have capacity to participate and to be comfortable engaging directly with authority. They also invest power in a small number of people, whereas m ini publics depoliticise issue s by involving interested individuals, not advocates , and different individuals over time . Attributes of effective formal participation models The context in which participatory processes operate is important. Our r esearch confirm s a range of engagement and participation mechanisms are required for diverse voices to be heard , and to build the credibility of each mechanism . One mechanism is rarely sufficient. Within this context, c ommon themes were that participatory models: are more effective when the council adopt s a broader view of governance , and actively supported mechanisms which engage its diverse populations meaningfully in its decision making. are more effective when they are endorsed by the elected members, from where they derive their status and authority, but primarily work with the council organisation to ensure a link between policy and implementation are more effective when participants are perceived as ordinary citizens, reflective of the community , rather than as lobby groups , and the selection process and outcomes are transparently communicated are more credible when they allow for the participation of many individuals over time , and of different individuals and different demographics who are selected according to the voices needed for each topic
Commercial In Confidence participants . Citizens are involved in making and agreeing these rules of engagement. For example, in joint planning: There is a clear understanding on the scope of the planning , the legal force of the final plan , how it will be implemented and by whom, and how this will be supervised There are clear rules for the planning process, including the timeframe and what should be achieved, roles and responsibilities, how the plan will be agreed , including who can vote Participatory processes are designed to be transparent to and share information with the wider community, which creates legitimacy and acceptance of the decisions . Once a participatory process is established, citizens agree on the process and decision making criteria . They are supported by external experts as required, and by local government staff who can provide technical expertise , an understand ing of how council operates, and a secretariat function where required . However, the council has delegated decision making to the citizens. For example , in participatory budgeting, participants decide on appropriate proposals and projects if council officials did this it would simply be grant giving . Participation, recruitment and selection Once the council has decided to establish a participatory process , the purpose and the way citizens can get involved are widely promoted using a variety of media, channels and methods which are both digital and non digital. This increases participation in collective processes such as participatory budgeting and increases the pool of people willing to serve on a citizens jury. It i s the first step in transparency and increases the legitimacy of the decision s taken at the end of the process . This is further enhanced when: Participation is extended to groups who cannot vote in elections , for example young people between and new migrants Strategies are designed and implemented to reach marginalised and under represented populations, and people not otherwise involved in civil society organisations. This can include special events for families and youth, multi lingual tools, and visits to community meeting places such as places of worship Participatory budgeting and joint planning do not normally require a selection process as usually anyone can participate. However, a selection process is required for citizens juries. To reduce bias and ensure a jury that is reflective of its community, participants are chosen from the positive responses by stratified random selection . Participants can be selected to match the demographic of the whole city or community , or on selected demographic s. Enablers and incentives Participatory processes should be designed and promoted so that : Potential participants feel it is worth the ir time and effort . The greatest incentive is that it will be a fulfilling experience that will make a positive difference , with tangible results . Fundamentally this is achieved by the council communicating that it will accept the outcome of the process. Other motivating factors can include scale, for example that the funds available for allocation in a Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs
Commercial In Confidence participatory budgeting process are reasonably large , or that participation is a development opportunity, with participants learning new skills such as project management . Barriers to participation are minimised . This can include providing stipends or an honorarium for citizens jurors. For participatory processes that require meetings, it can include food, childcare, transport , meeting locations that are easily accessib le (including remotely ), varied meeting times . interpreters and multi lingual documents, and a defined time commitment . Adequate s upport for participation The processes are wellresourced, with a commitment in advance to funding , and adequate time from council staff Council staff are trained well in advance to be able to run an effective promotion, recruitment and selection process es, and to provide technical support throughout the participatory process . Staff also play a role in helping participants to understand how local government works. Subject matter advice is also available from independent external experts where appropriate . For example with citizens juries, there should be a diverse range of experts and witnesses to support varied and balanced perspectives on the issue. Eviden ce considered must be made public to ensure transparency and increase the legitimacy and acceptance of the jury. Citizens juries have a facilitator with the expertise to run a deliberative dialogue process, including supporting all participants to contribute and to critically assess complex information. This ensures participants can contribute effectively even when they have no prior knowledge or experience of the topic. The facilitator helps the group to weigh up strengths and weakn esses of options and make some decisions. Independent oversight by a steering group is also advisable to prepare the jury proceedings . This also supports a process that facilitates quality decision making, i ncreas ing the legitimacy and recognition of the j ury. Council staff also act as a secretariat . This may range from note taking, to writing the outcomes document for a citizens jury on behalf of the citizens. This improve s the efficiency of the process and reduce s the burden on participants. For joint pl anning processes, the plan a can be written by a specially created committee of community or neighbourhood representatives. Scale and reach Participatory budgeting in particular works best in small scale environments, so that participants have a rich understanding of the community to inform their choices , and also experience its results. There should be transparent and regular communication and information provided to citizens during the exercise. This can be two way: t he use of on line too ls and open data can expand participation, with a wider group of citizens providing ideas and opinions to inform the deliberation of participants. Tools that have been used successfully include Twitter, Facebook, emails, web site, online forums, special o nline platforms and online ideation tools, and also face toface meetings, and physical stalls. Based on their knowledge, the jury could select witnesses they wanted to hear from. The additional evidence and the jury deliberation were made public. The decisions on what to include in the final jury report were made by supermajoritarian voting (). To ensure the minority views and dissenting voice are heard, the jurors could write minority reports that were also included in the final report. To facilitate consensus, the jurors were sometimes asked to vote on can you live with the recommendation instead of a simple yes or no to a recommendation. In total, the jury considered asks, but settled on to include in the final report. The online and offline work was organised in small groups that were regularly mixed to avoid factions. To help jurors analyse the large amount of information, the mix of synchronous (webinars) and asynchronous (example) learning approaches was used. The jurors had access to expert opinions throughout the entire process. The steering group witnessed the entire process, but jury was able to reques t periods where no observers were present. In addition, facilitators used email, news groups, chat rooms, blogs, wikis and podcasts to share info and facilitate inte ractions. The jury process was highly publicised and received media mentions in print, online and radio. Stakeholders involved The main stakeholders participating in the process are: Reykjavik C ity Council has formally accepted the platform as a collaborator and provided initial investment. It also operates the voting and provides a part of an investment budget to be allocated through the process. It implements the projects voted by the citizens. Internal Audit monitors the election and does a security audit of the system each year, before, during and after the vote. Neighbourhood Councils support the process by advising the Construction Board on the feasibility and cost. They also participate in the implementation of the projected selected. Citizens: different groups of people participate in the discussions of projects and voting. Basically, anyone can register on the platform to submit project ideas and discuss them (the authentication process is via a verified social media account or email password). Authentication for voting on projects is run by the National Voter Registry, so that only those eligible to vot e in Reykjavik can participate. Process Each year, the City Council allocated a certain amount of citys investment budget for the allocation through participatory budgeting. Initially, it was million Icelandic krona (approximately NZD million, about . of the city total budget) and in amounted million Icelandic krona (NZD . million, about . of the city total budget), divided between districts (neigh bourhoods) of Reykjavik. The participatory budgeting process can be roughly divided into three stages: generating ideas, assessment and voting. The first stage starts in March with a call for ideas for improvement projects and their refining and discussin g online. The idea can be submitted to the platform by any registered participant (as mentioned, authentication with a Facebook account or email password suffice). The pitch needs to contain a short description and an image of the location as well as shar e the exact location on a digital map. Registered participants can like and comment on other proposed ideas, add points for or against them. The city also runs face toface meetings to generate ideas. The meetings are run everywhere, from shopping malls t o retirement homes to schools. The staff uses tablets and feeds the put forward straight into the online process. We identified four attributes that are present within effective participation models : draw information and perspectives in from the community are credible with communities are well supported and facilitated are influential with elected members and departmen ts of the council Risks of participatory processes are: they are more expensive than traditional decision making processes, and the choice to spend rate payers money in this way can be open to criticism if the facilitator is not skilled enough to manage the process, this can result in poor decisions the breadth of th e topic is narrow, and the community does not set the agenda . The quality of the process is critical to ensure acceptance and legitimacy it is highly dependent on buy in from the governing body trust in the council would be detrimentally affected if the g overning body did not accept the recommendations of the group. Success factors Whilst many details vary across the settings and methodologies of the participatory processes we have reviewed , there are some common factors that contribute to the ir success . We have set these out below, including s pecific success factors for citizens juries , participatory budgeting and joint planning . Settings The community does not set the agenda. A topic is selected by the council and a question is carefully framed for the group to consider . However, a n important feature of the most effective participatory processes is that the council has at the outset agreed that it will accept the recommendations of the group . Participatory processes are further strengthened when they are actively promoted by elected members. The council take s responsibility for endorsing and communicating the outcomes of the process , which provide s decisions with authority . National and local policy provides clear guidance yet flexibility to participatory processes . Communities across New Zealand are safe, resilient and thriving Regulated activities minimise harm and maximise benefits to people and communities Three Waters Reform Building an efective, afordable, resilient and sustainable three waters system (drinking water, stormwater and wastewater) will provide lasting benefits for our communities our economy, and the environment. We are responsible for leading the reform of the three waters system, and for monitoring the performance of Taumata Arowai the new waters services regulator. The service delivery reforms involve a systemwide transformation of the way three waters services are regulated and provided to communities. A comprehensive, integrated package of reform proposals and a support package for local government have been proposed. A key system change is the active recognition and provision of te mana o wai statements that proposed water services entities will be required to embed into their operations from governance to delivery. We will support the Government in making its final decisions on the reform proposals and will implement the reforms that are agreed. We will support the Government to implement the reforms, and lead the significant work required to design and transition to the new system. This includes working with the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment to establish new economic regulation and consumer protection regimes necessary to ensure three waters services are delivered eficiently, efectively and afordably to consumers. The Department will also monitor Taumata Arowai to ensure water services are provided to standards necessary to achieve improved and more consistent public health and environmental outcomes for the benefit of all consumers and communities. Regulatory system stewardship We have developed a strategy to move our regulatory services from a focus on compliance, to a focus on regulatory system stewardship so that communities in New Zealand are safe, and the wellbeing of iwi is improved. The strategy positions our regulatory services to be at the forefront of regulatory excellence. We are concurrently implementing a new strategic direction for gambling that emphasises community wellbeing aligning to our outcomes and the Governments wellbeing agenda. We will continue to focus our gambling advice on the regulatory settings needed to manage harm from online gambling by New Zealanders, along with improved measures to minimise harm from Class Gambling (pokie machines). This work will ensure New Zealanders who choose to gamble are protected, especially those most vulnerable to gambling harm. Department of Internal Affairs NG TAKUNE RAUTAKI STRATEGIC INTENTIONS Modernising content regulation and providing greater protection against online harms We will be modernising the media content regulatory system and providing greater protection against online harms through the content regulation review. The review will be supported by the Ministry for Culture and Heritage and will lead to a modern, flexible and coherent regulatory framework to address all harmful impacts of media content, regardless of the way the content is delivered. We will complete the legislative process to amend the Films, Videos and Publications Classifications Act to ensure prevention and mitigation of harms caused by objectionable publications. The Department is also progressing recommendation of the Royal Commission of Inquiry into the terrorist attack on Christchurch masjidain to make further amendments to that Act in relation to racism. Embedding the Countering Violent Extremisms (CVE) Online team and reduction of online harmful content We will help facilitate the swif removal of online violent extremist content from platforms and continue to build strong working relationships with government agency partners, overseas law enforcement and technology platforms. In doing so, we will ensure New Zealanders know where and how to report online violent extremist content. This will require a community approach and trusted relationships with civil society. As our capability grows, we will explore further online prevention initiatives, in consultation with relevant government and nongovernment agencies. AntiMoney Laundering (AML) implement mutual evaluation recommendations We will support the statutory review of the AntiMoney Laundering Countering the Financing of Terrorism Act. The review will result in recommendations for regulatory and legislative change to strengthen the AML framework. We will also focus on implementing the Financial Action Taskforce Mutual Evaluations recommendations to strengthen the AMLCFT framework and our delivery of services to ensure the integrity of and public trust in New Zealands financial system. Privacy leadership and facial recognition The Department is responsible for providing privacy leadership in government though the role of the Government Chief Privacy Oficer (GCPO). We set standards and guidance, build capability within government agencies, and provide assurance to Ministers on privacy matters. Inappropriate use of facial recognition technology by government agencies poses a risk to New Zealanders. We will provide improved tools and guidance to better manage this risk for current users of this technology, while supporting continued innovation in how it is used in government. Department of Internal Affairs NG TAKUNE RAUTAKI STRATEGIC INTENTIONS Mori are supported to realise their aspirations Creating an indigenous approach to communityled development The Department is working with hap to codevelop a framework for hapled development. The Department has identified gaps in the way Mori access our existing funds and the Communityled Development Programme. There is a need and opportunity to scope a new tikanga Mori approach that better supports Mori to lead their own development. Hapled development is about supporting Mori to achieve their aspirations, on their own terms and in their own time. The Department is starting a hapled development journey from a place of mana motuhake selfdetermination, recognising the need to codevelop a strengths and Tiritibased approach. This is an opportunity for the Department to learn from existing programmes, such as the Communityled Development Programme, to better support hap in a te ao Mori way. Department of Internal Affairs NG TAKUNE RAUTAKI STRATEGIC INTENTIONS Communities are supported to develop and prosper Community resilience to natural hazards and climate change New Zealand communities are exposed to a wide range of natural hazards which are being exacerbated by the efects of climate change. The Community Resilience work programme is a partnership working with local government to help better manage these risks through investing in risk reduction measures and supporting councils to manage natural hazards and the efects of climate change. The programme will provide the Government with options for reforming the Land Information Memorandum (LIM) system by which local government discloses information on natural hazard risk to property buyers and sellers. We are also contributing a community resilience perspective to the Governments work programme on the reform of the Resource Management System and the development of the National Adaptation Plan. A community funding system that is inclusive and flexible The Department is undertaking a review of Crown community funding with the objective to support a community funding system that is more flexible, inclusive and honours Te Tiriti o Waitangi. Findings from an analysis into community funding identified the current system to be complex and adhoc with limited strategic direction. This has resulted in barriers for communities, ineficiencies in the system and inequitable funding outcomes. We will identify potential options for a funding system that represents the most efective investment in community development and has a longterm intergenerational impact for iwi, hap and communities, utilising goodpractice principles. This review will align with changes being considered in the distribution of Lottery funding to ensure consistency and allow for more efective outcomes across community funding. Charities Act Review We have resumed the work to modernise the Charities Act by addressing practical issues that impede the efective functioning of charities, while ensuring the necessary transparency for public trust and overall confidence in the sector. This work is expected to lead to legislative proposals in . Department of Internal Affairs NG TAKUNE RAUTAKI STRATEGIC INTENTIONS Racing industry recovery We will complete the implementation of the racing industry reforms, working alongside key industry stakeholders such as Racing New Zealand to support a sustainable racing industry. The Racing Integrity Board (RIB) and the TAB NZ Board have been established as per the Racing Industry Act . The newly appointed RIB will promote and ensure high standards of animal welfare, integrity and professionalism by those in the racing industry. Hon Sir Bruce Robertson was commissioned to review the greyhound industrys response to the recommendations in Hon Rodney Hansens report on animal welfare. Sir Bruce found that improvements in animal welfare and transparency should be made but the point has not been reached where immediate action by the Minister must be taken. We will support the Minister of Racing and Minister of Primary Industries with work required to follow up on the recommendations outlined in the review. This will include the RIB monitoring progress and reporting back to the Minister of Racing by the end of on the implementation of the recommendations. New Zealand Libraries Partnership programme Local libraries are safe spaces that support lifelong learning and ofer access to essential online services. The New Zealand Libraries Partnership programme supports libraries to play a role in supporting their communities and people seeking jobs as part of the COVID recovery. The programme is leveraging strategic partnerships to develop a foundation upon which the longterm sustainability of libraries can be achieved. Strengthening the library workforce is a key factor in achieving this outcome, and the programme is ofering professional development to ensure that libraries continue to be able to support the communities that depend on them. Supporting implementation of new requirements of the Aotearoa New Zealand Histories curriculum The introduction of the new compulsory history curriculum in presents an opportunity to connect young people with the histories and stories of Aotearoa New Zealand. We are working across the heritage system to determine how agencies can collectively support communities to tell their own local history to meet the new requirements. The role of the National Library and Archives New Zealand is to support teachers, students, hap, marae and local libraries to access their collections, resources and services to support locally led story telling. This includes the development of local resources for students working with public and school libraries and professional development and support. This approach will help to grow enquiring New Zealanders who are knowledgeable about the people, places and events that have shaped Aotearoa New Zealand. Conclusions . As indicated by the analysis table above, the preferred process option is option three: a selfidentification process that requires a statutory declaration process without evidence of medical treatment. When compared, this option meets all the criteria (except integrity) better or much better than the status quo and is better at meeting the criteria than option two. . A selfidentification process is worse than the status quo in respect of the integrity criterion because of the removal of any form of third party assurance that can act to mitigate fraudulent applications. However, unlike the other options, this option provides a process that is primarily based on selfidentification and is likely to better meet the needs of transgender and intersex people. . We consider the risk of the preferred process option being used for unlawful reasons is sufficiently mitigated by the requirement for a statutory declaration and additional requirements where a person applies more than once. . The selfidentification process is beneficial for children and young people. This option increases the accessibility and inclusivity of the process for children and young people and mitigates risk that and year olds may not be able to obtain guardian consent. It is flexible and recognises existing views that gender is not age restrictive and that older adolescents are more able to understand important decisions. Lastly this option supports the integrity of birth register information and the autonomy of children and young people through requirements that focus on ensuring the child or young person understands the decision and it is based on their selfidentified gender. Conference support The Ministry contributes part of the funding for a biennial international gambling conference held in New Zealand and an associated international think tank. The conference will take place twice in the period, in February and . The Ministry is budgeting for an , contribution towards the costs of each conference and think tank. Holding international conferences on gambling harm in New Zealand promotes the country as a world leader in preventing and minimising gambling harm. It also enables practitioners, researchers, industry representatives and government officials from around the world to meet and exchange ideas specific to gambling harm. . Intervention services The Ministry has increased the indicative budget for the period from the previous period to accommodate an increased focus on service development to address persistent gambling harm (see Table ). Section . describes additional funding for piloting new intervention services. Within th is budget, the Ministry intends to explore the potential for more innovative intervention services. In particular, it will seek to fund or develop services that are clientcentred and enhance the mana of consumers. The Ministry will base new approaches on successful regional or local models, where they exist, and will codesign them with stakeholders, and particularly with consumers. Indicative priority areas for to are to: explore innovative ways to treat the whole person through joinedup gambling, drug, alcohol and mental health services pilot and evaluate new service models to address gaps in current service provision . The pilots will focus on delivering both public health and intervention services across regions (particularly rural regions) and responsiveness to Mori lay the foundations to pilot and introduce residential care and peer support into the intervention service mix in the medium term develop the range of online selfhelp available deliver services that are responsive to the needs of different population groups; in particular, those groups where there is strong evidence of inequality and inequity in gambling harm. Consultation . The following agencies have been consulted on this paper and the draft Bill : Treasury, State Services Commission, Ministry of Health, Ministry of Justice, Land In formation New Zealand, Ministry for Business Innovation and Employment , Inland Revenue, Ministry for Primary Industries and Sport New Zealand. RITA has also been consulted on the draft Bill. Minor changes have been made to the Bill following consultation. ldrz ()(h) ()(h) Proactively released by the Minister for Racing IN CONFIDENCE Page of Binding on the Crown . The Racing Industry Bill will bind the Crown. Creating new agencies and amending law relating to existing agencies . The Bill disestablishes RITA and creates TAB NZ, with the objectives of facilitating and promoting racing and sports be tting , maximising its profits for the long term benefit of New Zealand racing and maximising returns to sports , while ensuring harm minimisation is prioritised . The Bill also creates the RIB, a single entity responsible for the investigative and adjudicative functions of racing, while maintain ing independence between these functions. The current integrity system, the Judicial Control Authority and the Racing Integrity Unit, will be disestablis hed at the point the RIB is established. . TAB NZ and the RIB will be established as statutory bodies, each with board s of up to seven members appointed by the Minister for Racing . Both agencies will be required to present their statement s of intent (SOIs) and business plan s to the Minister for Racing, for tabling in Parliament. . The Bill transfers racing responsibilities held by RITA , to the three racing code bodies (Thoroughbred Racing New Zealand, Harness Racing New Zealand and Greyhound Racing New Zealand) . The Bill amends the accountability requirements of the codes, requiring them to submit their SOIs and business plans to the Minister, for tabling in Parliament. Allocation of decision making powers . The draft legislation does not involve the allocation of decision making powers between the executive, the courts, and tribunals. The Bill creates powers to make regulations to specify further detail related to the operation of the RIB, including the judicial committees and appeals tribunals. Associated regulat ions . The clauses which relate to the establishment of the RIB (clauses to ) will come into force on a to be made by Order in Council . The following Order in Council powers are also included: . ending the statutory restriction on club property transactions without the club first obtaining code approval; and . enabling the transfer of club property to the code, with payments to the club and local community where warranted. . In addition, given the scale of the changes , the Bill creates powers to make regulations if required , in the following ways : . if a commissioner is appointed to resolve a significant disagreement between the codes , whose decision would be binding on those involved, levying the codes for the associated costs ; . specifying further detai l related to the operation of the RIB, including the judicial committees and appeals tribunals; . setting the level of funding for the RIB if a funding agreement cannot be reached; ldrz Proactively released by the Minister for Racing IN CONFIDENCE Page of . prescribing the independent body responsible for assessing and approving TAB NZs request to introduce new betting products; . setting the decision making framework and fee arrangements for the independent body responsible for assessing and approving TAB NZs request to introduce new betting products ; and . prescribing a process and criteria that codes must apply when negotiating with clubs about the use of surplus venues, having due regard to any community interests in the venue. Other instruments . The Bill does not include any provision empowering the making of other instruments deemed to be legislative instruments or disallowable instruments . Definition of Ministerdepartment . The Bill continues the definition of Department within the Racing Act . It includes the option for the Department to be the designated agency that will admin ister the levy relating to the appointment of a Commissioner in clause . Commencement of legislation . Except for clauses , , to , and clause in Schedule , the Bill will come into force on July . Clauses , and clause in Schedule , will come into force the day after Royal assent. Clauses to will come into force on a to be determined by Order in Council. It is anticipated this will take place within months of the Bill being enacted. A deferre d commencement i s required to prepare the current integrity system for the transition. Parliamentary stages . It is intended the Bill be introduced on or before December and referred to the Transport and Infrastructure select committee, for a select committee process of four months. Given the timeframes, approval is being sought for PCO to make any technical changes to the Bill prior to introduction. The Bill must be passed on, or before, June . Proactive release . Consultation and agency feedback We have consulted with the following agencies: Department of Corrections, StatsNZ, Crown Law, Ministry for Women, Ministry of Health, Oranga Tamariki Ministry for Children, Ministry of Education, Ministry of Social Development, Ministry of Youth Development, Ministry of Justice, Te Puni K kiri, Ministry for Pacific Peoples, Sport NZ, New Zealand Transport Agency, New Zealand Police, Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (Immigration), Inland Revenue, Public Service Commission, Office of See section of the BDMRR Act and clause I of the Bill, which state that a persons sex should be determined by the general law of New Zealand. ()(f)(iv) Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua Department of Internal Affairs INCONFIDENCE Page of Ethnic Communities, Human Rights Commission, Office of the Privacy Commissioner, and Treasury. The Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet has been informed. The above agencies are generally supportive of selfidentification, for example, the Office of the Privacy Commissioner stated: The Privacy Commissioner supports the proposal to introduce a self identification process to enable a persons gender to be recognised on their birth certificate. The Commissioner notes that the proposal would create consistency between birth certificates, and passports and driver licences which are more commonly used as identity documents and have a selfidentification process for recognising gender. The Commissioner considers the proposed self identification process to be privacy enhancing as a person is no longer required to provide sensitive medical information to change their registered sex. We have addressed many of these agencies previous concerns, including around the previously proposed onetime limit on changing sex markers and the requirements for children to access selfidentification. Some concerns remain around requirements for guardian consent as described in paragraphs and above. During consultation agencies raised new concerns about how people who were born overseas but now reside in New Zealand will access official documents that recognise their gender. For example, transgender asylum seekers or transgender M ori who were born overseas and whose birth cannot be registered in New Zealand. We recognise this is an issue but consider it outside of scope of the selfidentification proposals discussed in this paper it would not be appropriate to legislate a process to amend information for births registered overseas. We will consider if and how this matter could be resolved and provide you with further advice. As requested by your office, a summary of the agency feedback received during the development of the advice about selfidentification is included at Appendix B . Communications We have provided your office with a communications plan and frequently asked questions to support work on introducing a selfidentification process. We are ready to work with your office on an announcement following Cabinet of your intention to progress the Bill with selfidentification and refer the selfidentification SOP to Select Committee. We will provide yo u material to support this announceme nt along with the final Cabinet paper in early May . We consider that an announcement soon after Cabinet approval is important. Proactive communications clearly setting out the rationale for the changes and what they involve will preempt and potentially mitigate opposition to selfidentification. Providing information on the changes early will also be important so interested individuals and communities can prepare to engage with the changes at Select Committee. Contact Tracing is a public health method which identifies persons who may have come into contact with an infected person and subsequently collects further information about these contacts. By tracing contacts and isolating them, public health authorities aim to reduce further infections in the population. Contact tracing in New Zealand is performed by our public health authorities. Cost ofliving implications . The proposals in this paper will require unplanned spending for a number of councils in the financial year. Relative to total council spending , this will be small expenditure and have little effect on ratepayers for larger councils . It will have a more significant impact on small er councils. Cost Does the option minimise fiscal andor compliance costs Counci l s without Mori wards will incur costs at least every six years for public engagement on whether to establish Mori wards . The extent of the engagement will depend on individual council policies. Councils with Mori wards are not required to continue to consider whether to disestablish existing Mori wards. Any council that proposes establishing Mori wards is likely to incur the cost of conducting a poll , including costs relating to community engagement . If a council chooses to hold a poll with the triennial local elections they can reduce their costs, vs holding a standalone poll. Under this option councils would not be required to consider Mori representation at least every six years, which would reduce the cost of consultation on proposals. Coverage of key segments of the community Solution design and ease of use drives high adoption across our vulnerable and at risk people. Compliant usage across at risk segments as good as or better than the average adoption. Degree of expected compliant or noncompliant usage This can be hardwired into physical hardware but is discretionary by app users. Statistical sampling of segments of users and confirming the solution is activated and working. This can be instrumented into the solution design. Extrapolation of non compliant use must keep us above the critical mass of adoption.
CovidCard CovidCard is a dedicated hardware device which performs much the same function as an app, but can potentially achieve the necessary levels of compliant adoption across broader segments of society. CovidCard is designed to be worn on a lanyard around the neck, for both easy compliance monitoring in venues where it might be required, but also to enable optimal device function.
CovidCard Design The CovidCard is a Bluetooth Low Energy (Bluetooth LE) device approximately the size of a credit card. It is designed to be worn on a lanyard around the neck when you are in environments where people congregate. This includes public transport, workplaces, bars, restaurants, gyms, hospitals, large gatherings and events. Openly wearing a CovidCard contributes to easily assessing and enforcing compliant use, as required.
CovidCard does not store any personal information on the card itself, and no card data is automatically stored in the cloud or elsewhere. A cards own broadcast identifier is cryptographically , and rotated approximately every fifteen minutes to ensure anonymity of the cardholder. Only the aforementioned Crown Entity has the ability to decrypt IDs and associate them with a cardholder. Cards cannot track user location as they do not contain locationaware technology such as GPS. Only days of data is stored on the card and the battery for each card will only last for approximately months.
CovidCard detects and records close contacts using Bluetooth LE and stores this data securely on a persons card. No contact data is automatically stored in the cloud or elsewhere and only days of close contacts will be stored. Cards do not track user location as they do not contain GPS capability.
CovidCard exists within a system of policies, operational management and other tools and should be considered as such. A detailed assessment of existing contact tracing capabilities is not within the scope of this document. Consideration has been given to the wider strategic context into which the CovidCard might be deployed.
CovidCard has a nonrechargeable battery with a typical month battery life. Once the battery is depleted contact records are lost and become irretrievable as records are encrypted using a key held in volatile memory which is lost if power is lost. At that point, cards are recycled or disposed of.
CovidCard has no notion of location as it does not use GPS or have a network connection. Cards simply receive and record properlyformed transmissions from other nearby cards and use this information to help determine close or casual contacts. Records of other cards are retained on the card, not on any phones, computers or servers elsewhere, for a maximum of days.
CovidCard is designed as a temporary solution for COVID. The battery on the device will only last around months Deploying CovidCard in New Zealand in advance of relaxing border restrictions is likely the time when CovidCard is able to deliver the greatest value as this will be a time of elevated risk.
CovidCard makes contact tracing faster, more accurate, and more scalable if effectively integrated with existing contact tracing efforts. The main benefits of CovidCard are:
CovidCard must be deployed in advance of any second wave of COVID. Otherwise, by the time we distributed cards to everyone we would have already had our second Level lockdown and would have been moving down the Alert Levels again. While CovidCard could play a role with essential workers during a Level lockdown, lockdown alone can control the spread of the virus in the wider community. The time when CovidCard should be deployed will likely be characterised by complacency in the community regarding COVID.
CovidCard should be evaluated against its ability to meaningfully slow the spread of COVID. An ongoing Cochrane Review of digital contact tracing solutions identified multiple modelling studies that can inform the evaluation of the CovidCard (including Kucharski ; Ferreti ; Hinch ; Plank ; Grice ; Vaithianathan ). Three of these studies focus specifically on the New Zealand context (Plank ; Grice ; Vaithianathan ).
CovidCard would enable close contacts to be immediately notified and asked to selfisolate and could immediately provide contact details of close contacts to contact tracing teams. Four days, on average, can likely be saved between potential exposure and isolation, thus reducing tertiary infections. Downloading the cards of close contacts would also enable rapid isolation of secondorder contacts which we consider a necessary further step if elimination is the goal.

How the RUC Collector may use Personal Information provided by DIA The Personal Information received by the RUC Collector from DIA may be used to: a) ensure that an individual applying for or utilising public service s is not required to provide identity and Life Event records that DIA holds. b) assist in the location of individuals . c) enable the prevention, detection, investigation and prosecution of offences, and the conduct of civil proceedings including judicial review. . How the RUC Collector may use Personal Information provided by the Registrar General The Personal Information received by the RUC Collector from the Registrar General may be used to: a) ensure that an individual applying for or utilising public services is not required to provide identity and Life Event records that the Registrar General holds. b) update the records of an individual upon their death. c) update the records of an individual upon a name change. d) update the records of an individual upon their marriage or civil union. e) contact individuals who ma y wish to update the name on their account to a different name. f) provide additional protection to information provided by the Registrar General where the individual concerned has an active Non Disclosure Direction under the BDMRR Act. Customer Nominated Services AISA PUBLIC LY AVAILABLE of g) enable the prevention, detection, investigation and prosecution of offences, and the conduct of civil proceedings including judicial review. . Adverse Actions The RUC Collector can reasonably be expected to potentially take any of the following Adverse Action s based on the information received from another party : a) decline to provide requested public services. b) update the known names associated with a n individual . c) engage in the collection of debt to the Crown . d) investigate any matter that may constitute an offence under any legislation it administers and prosecute the offence or report any suspected offence to the New Zealand Police. e) engage in civil proceedings.
