Currently, the contact tracing process is entirely manual: patients are asked to recall their close contacts over the last few weeks, and these are followed up with phone calls from contact tracing teams based at each district health board (DHB). Aside from being labourintensive, the process relies on human recall, which may be unreliable particularly for interactions that occurred further into the past.
Currently, the intense physical distancing measures implemented at Alert Level are acting as a strong safety net for cases not detected at the border and the case and contact management system. If the intensity of physical distancing decreases (by deescalating to Alert Level or by a decrease in compliance), this lowering of protection will induce a critical reliance on effective case management (including detection) for stopping existing transmission and any new transmission associated with a leaky border.

New Zealand Certificat e of Identity A Travel Document (other than a New Zealand Passport or New Zealand Refugee Travel Document) issued by the Government of New Zealand to an individual not a New Zealand citizen for the purposes of facilitating their entry into or exit from any country. This document states the known identity but not the nationality of that individual . New Zealand Certificat e of Identity Information Information relating to the individuals New Zealand Certificate of Identity history, including any information relating to any applications by the individual for a New Zealand certificate of identity . New Zealand Citizenship An individual holds New Zealand citizenship if they have obtained New Zealand citizenship under the Citizenship Act or the Citizenship (Western Samoa) Act whether by birth, descent, grant, or othe rwise than by descent, and it has neither been renounced or deprived. Customer Nominated Services AISA PUBLIC LY AVAILABLE of Term Definition New Zealand Citizenship by Birth An individual is a New Zealand citizen by birth if: the individual was born in New Zealand on or after January and before January ; or the individual was born in New Zealand on or after January , and, at the time of the individual s birth, at least one of the individual s parents was: a New Zealand citizen; or entitled in terms of the Immigration Act to be in New Zealand indefinitely, or entitled to reside indefinitely in the Cook Islands, Niue, or Tokelau. New Zealand Citizenship by Descent The process for obtaining New Zealand citizenship when the individual is born overseas and at least one parent is a New Zealand Citizen by Birth or grant (except where the individual is entitled to New Zealand Citizenship Otherwise than by Descent). New Zealand Citizenship by Grant The process for obtaining New Zealand citizenship when the individual is born overseas, applies for citi zenship by grant, and satisfies the Minister that the individual meets the statutory requirements of the Citizenship Act or the Citizenship (Western Samoa) Act and attends a ceremony if required. New Zealand Citizenship Otherwise than by Descent An individual born outside New Zealand shall be deemed to be a New Zealand citizen otherwise than by descent if that individuals father or mother is then: a New Zealand citizen, or a New Zealand citizen by Descent, pursuant to the Citizenship Act ; a nd either: a head of mission or head of post within the meaning of the Foreign Affairs Act ; an employee in any part of the State services, or a member of the Armed Forces, on service overseas; a person working overseas for the public service of Niue, Tokelau, or the Cook Islands; an officer or employee of New Zealand Trade and Enterprise (as established by the New Zealand Trade and Enterprise Act ) on service overseas; an officer or employee of the New Zealand Tourism Board (as established by the N ew Zealand Tourism Board Act ) on service overseas. New Zealand Passport A Travel Document issued by the Government of New Zealand to a New Zealand citizen. New Zealand Passport Information Information relating to an individuals New Zealand Passport history , including any information relating to any applications by the individual (including any supporting documents provided by the individual) for a New Zealand Passport. New Zealand Refugee Travel Document A travel document (other than a New Zealand Passport, New Zealand Emergency Travel Document or a New Zealand Certificate of Identity) issued by the Government of New Zealand to a refugee to facilitate international travel. This briefing seeks your approval to upload the final version of the Cabinet Legislation Committee paper: Rates Rebate (Specified Amounts) Order (the paper) to CabNet. The paper is attached as Appendix A . Background . On March , you agreed to adjust two key settings of the Rates Rebate Scheme(the Scheme) for the financial year LG refers. These adjustmentsreflect CPI (Consumer Price Index) inflation of . percent for the year ended December by: a)raising the maximum rebate available from to ; and b)raising the income abatement threshold from , to ,. . You also agreed to proceed to the Cabinet Legislation Committee, to seek approval ofan Order in Council which adjusts the two key settings of the Scheme. The Order inCouncil has been drafted by the Parliamentary Counsel Office and is provided withinAppendix A of the paper. During consultation a change was proposed to the Cabinet Paper . Hon Grant Robertson, Minister of Finance, Hon Carmel Sepuloni, Minister for SocialDevelopment, and Hon Dr Ayesha Verrall, Minister for Seniors were consulted on theproposals. . During Ministerial consultation, Minister Sepuloni asked if the proposed increase in theScheme was sufficient given the anticipated high rate increases expected this year in most councils. She also made a specific suggestion to adjust the two key settings of the Scheme using the average wage (as with Superannuation) rather than CPI. . The Department of Internal Affairs (the Department) notes that while the Scheme provides a modest amount of financial assistance, other cost of living subsidies (suchas the Accommodation Supplement) and adjustments to income support remain moreeffective at insulating lowincome ratepayers from high rate rises . . The Department considers that if you were to proceed with Minister Sepulonis recommendation, you would need to review the Scheme at a more strategic level inthe context of other subsidies and supplements that are available to lowincom e households. This could not be completed in time for an adjustment to the Scheme totake effect on July . . Adjusting the Scheme by more than CPI would also likely exceed the currentappropriation for the financial year . . Talking points on the adjustment level are provided to assist you in the CabinetLegislation Committee meeting on June should questions arise ( Appendix B ). Next steps . Following your approval, the Department will upload the paper to CabNet by May. Your Office will complete the lodgement process. . The Cabinet Legislation Committee is scheduled to consider the paper on June . . Cabinet and the Executive Council are scheduled to consider the Order in Council on June . If Cabinet approves the papers recommendation to waive the day rule, the Order in Council will be in the New Zealand Gazette on June , with the Order in Council taking effect from July . . The Department will inform councils of the upcoming changes, and work with them to ensure the seamless adoption of the annual adjustments to the Scheme. . The Department will also write to Grey Power and Age Concern, as representatives ofthe largest rates rebate applicant group about the adjustments. . A draft press release on the adjustments to the Scheme is attached for yourconsideration in Appendix C . Recommendations . The Department of Internal Affairs recommends that you: a)note that a change w as proposed from your Cabinet colleagues on the Cabinet Legislation Committee paper: Rates Rebate (Specified Amounts) Order ; b)approve the Cabinet Legislation Committee paper: Rates Rebate (Specified Amounts) Order for uploading to CabNet YesNo by May ; and c)agree to the Department proactively releasing this brief ing on its website, within working days of the Rates Rebate (Specified Amounts) Order being in the New YesNo Zealand Gazette . DIA access the driver licence photograph under section () of the LTA , which authorises a person who is acting in the course of the persons official duties as an employee of the Department of Internal Affairs to access and use driver licence photograph s from Waka Kotahi to verify the identity of a particular individual. The access and use of the driver licence photographs are controlled through the API , which is programmed in accordance with the instructions of an employee of DIA acting in the course of their official duties. The API is configured to access and use the driver licence photographs for the verification of the identity of the person using the Identity Check service. DISCUSSION The results show that the card, even with a basic algorithm, is capable of performing recall greater than of contacts in most situations. The two office trials (which were different runthroughs of the same scripts with different cards) showed similar results. There is no significant difference between the means at a confidence (P .), demonstrating that the results were repeatable despite a small number of cards not being activated. As the required contact duration to be considered a close contact increases, false positive rates fall in more sparse environments (cafe) and increase in denser ones (construction, party).

Darrin Sykes Deputy Secretary Enterprise Services
Darrin Sykes MNZM JP CMInstD is Deputy Secretary Enterprise Services. This role spans strategy, implementation and performance for the branch, organisational capability and culture development, organisational infrastructure and system investment, and smart delivery of core organisational services. Core organisational services are delivered by the following teams: Workplace Services Group He Ringa Manaaki; Human Resources Pmanawa Tangata; Finance Kkiri Turu; Communications Te Manu Karere and Branch Development Support Te Waka Aukaha.
Darrin also comes from a strong sports and recreation background including being director and Chair for a Touch Rugby NZ for years. Darrins service and contribution to the sport of Touch Rugby in New Zealand was recognised in when he was awarded a Member of the New Zealand Order of Merit (MNZM). Darrin was also a Board Member of Sport WellingtonNuku Ora from to .
Darrin also has held several directorships on governing boards; Capital Coast District Coast Board Government appointee from , where he was Deputy Chair and then Chair of the Finance, Risk and Audit Committee; and Sport New Zealand Board Member Government appointee from . Darrin was an external reviewer for the Performance Improvement Framework selfreview of the Health Quality and Safety Commission (HQSC) and is again a reviewer assisting the Commission in . Darrin has been a member of the Institute of Directors of NZ since and has been a Chartered Member (CMInstD) of the Institute since .
Darrin is Ngti RangitihiNgti Awa and brings a strong set of public service skills and experiences to Te Tari Taiwhenua. Darrin joined Te Tari from the Office of Mori Crown Relations Te Arawhiti where he was the Deputy Chief Executive, Organisational Services. Darrin has worked in the MoriCrown Relations space for over years including his role as Acting Deputy Chief Executive People, Culture and Enabling Services, Oranga Tamariki; Chief Executive CFRT; Acting Deputy Secretary Support Services Te Puni Kkiri and as the Director Waitangi Tribunal. Darrin is a current Public Service Commission Corporate Development Board Member appointed back in .
Darrin is the Touch NZ National Director of Referees and is also a member of the Federation of International Touch Rugby Referee Commission where he has served continuously since . Darrin was awarded Life Membership of the Federation of International Touch in January .

Summary of qualitative feedback At the conclusion of the pilot, we distributed a brief, anonymous survey soliciting information about willingness to document personal contacts using various method s and general feedback on the pilot. The response rate for the exit survey among participants was less than anticipated (), and could be a reflection of the dist ribution method (daily diaries were administered via a link in an SMS, whereas the exit sur vey was fully anonymous and a link was sent out in a mass email to staff in the medical ward) Among respondents, including pilot participants and nonparticipants, stated that they currently do not keep a written record of people they are near in public places, and stated that they log their details into guest books of venues. The willingness to document personal close contacts using variou s methods is summarised in Table . Most respondents were not at all willing to keep their own personal diary on paper or on line. Similarly, were very willing to use a passive app on their smart phones, while one third were very willing to use an ac tive app. The method with the highest proportion of respondents who were very willing to use it was a co ntact card (i.e., Bluetooth card) at , which was also the method with the smallest proportion of respondents who were not at all willing to use (. ). None of the respondents who were not at all willing to use a contact card actually participated in t he pilot study. This is an analytical tool to help assess the potential for policies and programmes to increase wellbeing. In the Living Standards framework there are four capitals presented. To generate the most wellbeing each capital needs to be strong and they need to work well together. The Four Capitals (natural, human social, and financial and physical) are the assets that generate wellbeing now and into the future Looking after intergenerational wellbeing means maintaining, nourishing and growing the capitals The norms, rules and institutions that in uence the way in which people live and work together and experience a sense of belonging. Includes trust, reciprocity , the rule of law , cultural and community identity , traditions and customs, common values and interests.All aspects of the natural environment that support life and human activity . Includes land, soil, water , plants and animals, minerals and energy resources.Natural Capital Social Capital Financial and humanmade (produced) physical assets, usually closely associated with supporting material living conditions. Includes factories, equipment, houses, roads, buildings, hospitals, nancial securities .The capabilities and capacities of people to engage in work, study , recreation, and social activities. Includes skills, knowledge, physical and mental health.Human Capital Financial and Physical Capital
Department of Internal Affairs TE MAHI KIA PAI AKE A AOTEAROA M TE IWI O AOTEAROA MAKING NEW ZEALAND BETTER FOR NEW ZEALANDERS Tirohanga Whnui mai i te Pou Whakahaere Overview from the Chief Executive Kia tuia te rangi ki te whenua, te whenua ki te rangi M te mahi tahi e rangonahia ai te whanaungatanga M te whanaungatanga e t mai i te manaakitanga N te manaakitanga ka pup ake te kaitiakitanga Mna e rarau ake, ktahi ka puta te kotahitanga Tau, tau, tau ana e I am pleased to present the Te Tari Taiwhenua Department of Internal Affairs Strategic Intentions for . This document outlines our priority areas for the next four years, as we aim to serve and connect people, communities and government to build a safe, prosperous and respected nation. The Department of Internal Affairs has an incredibly varied remit with many responsibilities and functions for example, our worldleading online passports service, protecting the nations precious taonga, maintenance of the charities register, administration of births, deaths and marriages, censorship compliance and gambling regulation are just part of what we do. As we look to , we are focusing our efforts towards progressing four broad outcomes for the benefit and wellbeing of all people. People can easily access the services and information they need We provide important services to New Zealanders throughout their lives, and we are making our services easier to access and use. We are continually working to integrate services across multiple agencies, designed around the needs of our customers not us as a Department. Utilising our system leadership roles, the Government Chief Digital Officer and the Government Chief Privacy Officer, we drive digital transformation across the public sector, and make sure the digital world is a safe environment for New Zealanders to participate in. Iwi, hap and communities across New Zealand are safe, resilient and thriving Communities are the cornerstone of our society and their wellbeing is vital in making New Zealand a great place to live, work and play. We regulate, to keep New Zealanders and their communities safe from harm. This will include establishing a new water regulator and strengthening our work in minimising the distribution of objectionable material. Our Office of Ethnic Communities strives to ensure diversity is celebrated, respected and embraced in New Zealand. We will also continue to support communities to lead their development and achieve their aspirations, through initiatives such as the Communityled Development Programme. Peoples sense of belonging and collective memory builds an inclusive New Zealand Through Archives New Zealand and the National Library of New Zealand, we are the privileged guardians of our nations most precious taonga, including Te Tiriti o Waitangi. Protecting New Zealands heritage for now and for future generations continues to be a strong focus for us. We are investing in significant new storage infrastructure, more effective ways to manage electronic records and improvement of online access to our collections. As Crown partners to the Treaty of Waitangi, as well as guardians of the physical Treaty document, we will work to strengthen MoriCrown relationships by engaging effectively with Mori and contributing to Maihi Karauna, the Crowns strategy for Mori language revitalisation. Department of Internal Affairs STRATEGIC INTENTIONS New Zealand is a wellfunctioning democracy, across central and local government We strive to support effective partnerships between central and local government, addressing regional and Government objectives and to enable the system to work cohesively. We do this by taking a collaborative approach to community resilience, supporting the urban growth agenda, and local government financing and funding. We also support members of the Executive to ensure they can carry out their duties effectively. Our outcomes are aligned with the Governments priorities and will guide the direction of our work over the coming years. We have many areas in which we can focus our efforts, but will also need to adapt our ways of working to deliver our many diverse functions effectively for both New Zealanders and the wider public service. Within our Department, he tngata, our people are the heart of our organisation and we will continue to make sure our Department is a place where everyone feels safe, healthy and respected. Celebrating our people, supporting their development and fostering a culture rich in wellbeing, inclusion and diversity will continue to be a priority for us because we know our people are at their best when they can bring their whole selves to work. Our outcomes are aligned with the Governments priorities and will guide the direction of our work over the coming years. I look forward to seeing our progress in achieving our outcomes over the next four years, and I know our people will work with a spirit of service and a commitment to making New Zealand better for New Zealanders. Paul James Chief Executive October Department of Internal Affairs TE MAHI KIA PAI AKE A AOTEAROA M TE IWI O AOTEAROA MAKING NEW ZEALAND BETTER FOR NEW ZEALANDERS Te huatanga me te Hkai o ng Mahi Nature and Scope of Functions T Ttou Whainga Ko t te Tari Taiwhenua he whakarato me te hono i ng iwi, ng hapori me te kwanatanga ki te hanga motu haumaru, tnui, whai mana hoki.Our Purpose The Department of Internal Affairs serves and connects people, communities and government to build a safe, prosperous and respected nation. Our purpose remains consistent, even as the functions and services we perform evolve and develop to meet the changing needs and expectations of people and the Government. We aim to make New Zealand a better place to live and to enhance the lives of New Zealanders. We work with people, communities, and other parts of government both central and local, to build a safe, prosperous and respected nation. Our Ministerial Portfolios We are responsible to eight Ministers, administering seven Portfolios within the single Vote Internal Affairs. The Minister of Internal Affairs is the Vote Minister and the Responsible Minister overseeing the Governments ownership interests in the Department. Portfolios and Responsible Ministers are: Internal Affairs Hon. Tracey Martin Community and Voluntary Sector Hon. Poto Williams Ethnic Communities Hon. Jenny Salesa Government Digital Services Hon. Department of Internal Affairs STRATEGIC INTENTIONS Mtou Kawenga me Mtou Mahi Our roles and functions The Department operates under a single Vote of million (operating expenditure) to support activities under the seven Portfolios. We have a broad range of responsibilities and functions that span information and communication technologies (ICT) investment, information management, working with communities, ensuring effective regulatory frameworks are in place, supporting the Executive and local government and delivering a range of services to support and foster New Zealands cultural identity. Our system leadership roles include the Government Chief Digital Officer (GCDO) and the Government Chief Privacy Officer (GCPO) to lead the digital transformation of government across the State Sector. In this respect, we support our State sector colleagues to transform their services through better investment in ICT and to maintain the privacy of New Zealanders governmentheld information. We also play a system leadership role with respect to local government. We are responsible for linking central and local government more effectively to achieve improved outcomes for citizens and communities. The Department is responsible for the National Library of New Zealand and Archives New Zealand. These institutions play an important role in preserving New Zealands documentary heritage and ensuring a full and accurate public record is created and maintained. We are also responsible for the Office of Ethnic Communities, which supports the many diverse ethnic communities that make New Zealand their home and the benefits that diversity brings to New Zealand society. Our specific functions include: Managing and protecting the integrity of national identity information, including life events such as births, deaths, marriages, citizenship and issuing passports Regulating activities in several sectors including: gambling, censorship, government recordkeeping, charities, unsolicited electronic messages, antimoney laundering, private security personnel and private investigators Providing policy advice to government on local government, ethnic communities, community and voluntary sector, fire and emergency services, identity, information and communications technology, information management, digital safety, gambling and racing Building, preserving and making accessible New Zealands information, documentary heritage and public records Providing information, resources and advice to communities to support their aspirations Administering grant funding schemes and promoting trust and confidence in the charitable sector Supporting the effective operation of government and the Executive Coordinating and managing official guests of government visits to New Zealand Supporting public and government inquiries and reviews Department of Internal Affairs TE MAHI KIA PAI AKE A AOTEAROA M TE IWI O AOTEAROA MAKING NEW ZEALAND BETTER FOR NEW ZEALANDERS Administering a range of statutory functions for the Minister of Local Government, including for Lake Taup and offshore islands Leadership in the direction and operational approach for digital across the core public service. We administer pieces of legislation or regulation. We monitor the performance of two Crown entities (Fire and Emergency New Zealand and the Office of Film and Literature Classification) and manage the appointment process for members of a range of trusts, committees and boards. Digital identity is proof of who you are online. It is a digital representation of your identity information, and other attributes which may include biometrics, that you can use to prove who you are online, to access services digitally.
Digital identity service providers accredited under the Digital Identity Services Trust Framework have shown that their services meet certain requirements, including privacy and security.
Digital identity service providers can apply to be accredited under the Digital Identity Services Trust Framework.
Digital identity service providers can become accredited under the Framework. This means they have proven that they meet, and continue to meet, the standards for using, storing and sharing personal and organisational information.

Digital technologies designed for populationwide deployment are new to the playbook. There is, as yet, limited evidence of how these tools may help. This is the first global pandemic since the advent of the smartphone.
Digital technologies hold some promise for accelerating symptomatic people into testing and both broadening and accelerating the quarantining of close contacts. Do both exceptionally well and the virus can be contained. Apps have been rolled out in a number of countries already but despite reasonable numbers of people downloading tools ( in Singapore and Australia), compliant use lags and any contribution made to manual contact tracing efforts so far is insignificant.
Digital technologies hold some promise of helping to fight COVID. In practical terms, the big potential levers are in getting people tested faster, isolating infected people quickly, and quarantining close contacts.
Digital technologies must be assessed rigorously in order to estimate the possible impact of these tools. Impact does not come from the mere existence of tools they must be promoted, downloaded and used as intended at an absolute minimum. Any tool must work as intended and we must take a clear headed view of what our embedded assumptions are on the path to impact.

Each CovidCard is registered to an individual. Keeping data independent of other Government databases is considered a critical plank to establishing public trust and confidence in the scheme.

Each CovidCard is both advertising its presence and scanning for the presence of other CovidCards . Algorithms on the card assess the radio signal strength (the RSSI) and accelerometer outputs over the duration of the encounter to accurately identify close contact events.
Each CovidCard is both advertising its presence and scanning for the presence of other CovidCards. Algorithms on the card assess the radio signal strength (the RSSI) over the duration of the encounter to identify close contact events. The current clinical definition of a close contact is an encounter of fifteen minutes within two metres of the contact . Additionally, cards would record casual contacts who do not fit the definition of a close contact and a list of these could also be provided to contact tracers.

Effective risk and assurance systems and good practices are key components of effective governance. Good risk management practice helps to identify key risks to delivery and enables early intervention before risks impact on outcomes. Assurance supports governance bodies in their decisionmaking, provides evidence of how well business risks are being managed, whether opportunities are being taken, and how well the business is performing. Applying more consistent risk and assurance advice and support over priority andor higherrisk projects and programmes is helping to further embed good risk management practices as integral to the Departments mahi, and ensure we focus on the right things. The Departments Assurance Policy and Framework supports an integrated view of assurance.
Effic iency assumptions are implausible WICS modelling makes implausible as sumptions about the efficiency in the Reform Scenario. The government assumes that the Reform Scenario will deliver percent capital expenditure (capex) savings and percent operatin g expenditure (opex) savings. The capex saving is not grounded in any actual evidence, but rather on WICS observations. The implausibility of capex savings has also been addressed in previous analysis by Castalia for Local Government New Zealand and the Joint Steering Committee . Economies of scale in capex are not availabl e in New Zealand water services, except for minor potential cost savings in procurement . The opex saving is also derived from Ofwat and Scottish observations. However, for WDC the opex e fficiency is implausible because WDC already has comparable opex to Watercare . Furthermore, the government and LGNZ representatives have assured councils that no jobs will be lost in the water sector. Given the profile of WDCs opex ( mostly power , labour a nd outsourced services), it seems unlikely that significant further savings are possible. WDC is likely to improve water service delivery if it op ts out, yet WICS assumes no such improvements In any case, WDC is likely to improve its services ove r the next years, yet WICS modelling assumes that WDC will make no efficiency gains under the Opt Out scenario . As a result, the OptOut scenario , as modelled by WICS, likely overstates WDCs costs . WDC will be subjected to water quality regulation, a nd obtain guidance and expertise from Taumata Arowai. Corporatisation and improved performance of other water service providers will lead to changes at WDC that drive better performance as WDC seeks to match the benchmarks set. Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs CONFIDENTIAL Castalia Economic regulation is likel y to apply across the sector, not just to four amalgamated entities. The governments assumption that it cannot regulate all council owned water services is inconsistent with the Commerce Commissions regulation of electricity distribution businesses and i nconsisten t with the experience in multiple overseas jurisdictions where economic regulators are capable of regulat ing many entities. Economic regulation is also likely to enable benchmarking and comparisons. WDC should examine how it can provide a constru ctive coun terproposal to the government Water services are critical to wellbeing, so it is very important that options are considered that are locally appropriate. Water services should be safe, resilient, reliable, and customer responsive, at least cost. Some ref orm of the sector is necessary i n some parts of New Zealand. However, the analysis needs to done to determine where water services fall short of this objective, and for what reasons. Other than opting out, the Reform Scenario is the only option that has be en presented to WDC and other lo cal authorities. This report has shown that the Reform Scenario is founded on unsound evidence and faulty analysis. The promised benefits of reform are unlikely to materialise. There are risks to the Whangrei community fro m losing control of water servic es, and accountability of those tasked with governance to local customers. We recommend that WDC carry out a proper net benefit analysis, potentially with other local authorities that have a similar viewpoint. This is likel y to be many councils, since the WICS analysis has consistent faults that apply to all local authorities. Such an analysis should include the full range of options together with transparent data and sound and contestable analysis so these options can be pr operly evaluated. T here is plent y of analysis, evidence and now a rich data set in the RFI responses for WDC and like minded local authorities to be able to identify alternative and better reform options. WDC could prepare a constructive counterproposal th at achieves desirable objectives , while avoiding the risks and costs of the Reform Scenario .

Ethnic pay gaps are calculated as the difference between the average salary for an ethnic group and the average salary of those not in that ethnic group, expressed as a percentage of the average salary of those not in the ethnic group. Kaimahi who disclose an ethnicity are included in every ethnic pay gap calculation. Kaimahi who disclose more than one ethnicity are included in more than one ethnic pay gap calculation. Kaimahi who did not disclose their ethnicity are excluded from the calculation. A negative pay gap is where the average salary for that ethnic group is higher than the average salary of those not in that ethnic group.

New Zealands plan is to stay covidfree, which implicitly accepts an almost closed border until we see highly accurate rapid testing or a widely deployed vaccine in New Zealand. Meanwhile, all arrivals will continue to require a quarantine period.
Executive Summary This report outlines the findings from a feasibility trial of an early prototype of the Bluetooth enabled CovidCard in a single medical ward in Nelson Hospital. The Bluetooth card used in this field trial did n ot contain a close contact algorithm to filter RSSI values and does not fully reflect the final CovidCard product. The feasibility trial aimed to test, refine, and evaluate the data collection procedures, card firmware and software, and determine the accep tability of a Bluetooth card for contact tracin g in a real world setting. The six day trial started on the May and concluded on May . Forty two participants were recruited into the study who wore the devices for every working hour. The Bluetooth card registered a median of close contacts per da y compared to only three per day for the self report surveys. The recorded median duration of time spent with a close contact was mins for the self report surveys and mins for the Bluetooth card. The discre pancy between survey and card data reinforces existing critiques of self reported close contact data There was high concordance of reported close contacts reported between the Bluetooth card and ultra wide band devices suggesting close contacts are bein g accurately detected by the Bluetooth card, a lbeit with little precision. The large majority () of participants reported they would be very or somewhat willing to use a contact tracing card in the future However, the nature and extent of the feasibili ty trial prevents any substantive conclusions about the effectiveness of the Bluetooth card given the relatively weak ground truth (survey data and a limited number of UWB devices) and absence of a close contact algorithm installed on the card firmware . The feasibility trial did highlight a number of areas that require improvement before larger field trials are considered. There were substantial challenges with the card firmware and software that led to data loss and increased participant burden. The lack o f intensive surveillance methods prevented a detailed analysis of card performance in different environments (e.g. a robust ground truth). Recruitment and enrolment processes were developed and conducted ad hoc. Substantial improvements are required to se cure the uptake necessary to conduct a full scale field trial. Limited visibility and coordination between partners due to the time constrains resulted in an ad hoc approach to data management and analysis which has limited the extent of some analyses and increased researcher burden . Based on the o utcomes from the Phase One feasibility trial of the prototype Bluetooth card , we recommend: Major improvements to card firmware and software, including integration of a close contact algorithm. Conducting closed f ield trials to evaluate card sensitivity an d performance in different settings with robust ground truthing. Proactively Released by the Department of Internal Affairs

Executive summary . In June , Cabinet established the million Three Waters Infrastructure Investment and Service Delivery Reform Programme tagged operating contingency, a portion of which remains unallocated. In Budget , a Transforming Three Waters Service Delivery for New Zealanders: Transition and Implementation tagged operating contingency of million was established to provide for establishment and transition costs. . The original cost estimates supporting the Transforming Three Waters Service Delivery for New Zealanders: Transition and Implementation Budget initiative, although based on reasonable assumptions at the time, were made ahead of significant policy decisions that impacted on the overal l costs of delivering the three waters reform programme. . The October decision to proceed with reform CAB MIN means there is now more certainty regarding the three waters reform work programme through to July and beyond. Following further detailed planning, the Department of Internal Affairs now needs to increase its capacity and capability to deliver and implement the reform programme. This includes a significant policy and legislative programme, a large programme of entity establishment and transition activity, and ongoing engagement and public information activity. . Other notable cost pressures relate to key judgements about the best approach to transition, in particular the scope and level of support available to iwiMori and the local government sector to participate meaningfully in the transition process. This is an area where additional investment can help to derisk the transition process and ensure entities are set up with the best chance of success. . I have worked with the Minister of Finance and our officials to fully understand these cost pressures, determine which areas it is appropriate to fund, and develop an approach to funding the priority areas. . I consider the Three Waters Infrastructure Investment and Service Delive ry Reform Programme tagged contingency to be an appropriate avenue for funding the most critical and urgent cost pressures, an approach that has been supported by the Minister of Finance. . I am seeking agreement to reallocate . million of the unallocated portion of the Three Waters Infrastructure Investment and Service Delivery Reform Programme tagged operating contingency to address cost pressures and fund additional investment in the following areas: . policy advice, legislation, ministerial services, and the most urgent communications activities: . million; . supporting iwiMori to participate in the three waters service delivery system: . million; . supporting the local government sector to engage with the reforms and enable a smooth transition: S. million; . the Future for Local G overnment Review: . million. Existing COVID response measures may drive inequities or disproportionately affect atrisk populations. For example, the current appbased solutions such as the NZ COVID Tracer app are likely to exacerbate these inequities as atrisk populations have limited access to smartphones and may live in areas with low connectivity (Digital Inclusion Research Group). While the lockdown may have disproportionately benefited these populations from a COVID infection perspective, it has worsened existing economic and other health inequities (e.g. Rheumatic fever). The Government cannot pursue COVID response measures that may exacerbate health inequities caused by established systematic problems in the health system. For Mori, this would represent a failing to uphold the principles of Te Tiriti o Waitangi.

Extension of timeframes for remediation of earthquake prone buildings Hon Chris Penk, in his capacity as Minister for Building and Construction, is expected to ta ke a Cabinet paper titled Proposal to form Building (Earthquake prone building deadlines and other matters) Amendment Bill to the Cabinet Economic Policy Committee on March and Cabinet on April . The paper seeks agreement to bring forward a review of the building seismic risk framework. It also seeks agreement to a four year extension to the by which earthquake prone buildings must have completed their seismic remediation work. The extension a pplies to buildings with remediation dates ending from April onwards. The proposed extension is expected to come into force through legislative amendment late and to apply retrospective ly. This means some building owners may be in breach of their seismic strengthening obligations for several months. The paper proposes encouraging territorial authorities to take a considered approach to enforcement during this period, as buildings that have not completed the required remediation will be conside red compliant again within a few months , once the legislation comes into force. Most of the affected buildings are priority buildings which are considered highest risk under the framework. We are concerned that the proposed approach to the interim peri od creates risks for territorial authorities , compromising the integrity of the ir statutory enforcement role. They may be exposed to legal liability if an earthquake happens during that period the likelihood may be relatively low, but the consequences co uld be significant . The Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment have included a short paragraph highlighting these concerns . Contact: Frdrique Bertrand

Finally, the prioritisation algorithm used to rank reidentified card contact data has potential to impact false positive rates with further work. Additional features such as number of cards in range when a card event is seen (card density) and timeofday could be used to train the model. Unfortunately these features are not effective in our field testing both would be contrived in the field trials and are only meaningful when considered over a longer period of time with a greater number of cardholders. Other machine learning models were tested (see Appendix ), and there is potential for greater optimisation of their parameters to better prioritise close contacts over casual ones.
Finally, the rank correlation showed a positive correlation between the order of the ground truth contacts, when ordered by duration multiplied by intensity or RSSI, for all trials. This shows that even with a basic algorithm on the card, the card is able to rank contacts in a broadly similar order to ground truth rankings. However, given the limited processing power and security controls on the card, ranking of contacts would be more suitable to be performed after the card data is downloaded. Ranking contacts offcard will allow other features to be included which may increase accuracy, and for prioritisation algorithms to be modified as the needs of health services change.

Human rights, gender implications and disability perspective . There are no human rights, gender or disability implications associated with this paper. Legislative implications . The local Bill is required to implement the District Councils resolutions to provide the arrangements set out in this paper. . As this Bill is a local bill, it can only be read on a members day. Jonathan Young MP and I have asked the House Business Committee that it be read on December , and that the committee of the whole House and third reading stages be run together to enable the local Bill to be passed by the end of November as requested by the District Council. The panel considers that information and analysis summarised in the RIA meets the quality assurance criteria. Publicity . I do not propose any Government publicity given t his is a local Bill. I do not propose to publicly release this paper given that it relates to a loc al Bill and it would be inappropriate for a government announcement when the local Bill is appropriately publicised by the District Council. Commercial in Confidence In addition, while Cabinets recently agreed proposals to establish a new online casino gambling regulatory system are an overall positive move, they present indirect risks to TAB NZs longterm financial sustainability because the proposals potentially strengthen the market position of TAB NZs biggest competitors. The Minister for Racing intends to work with the Minister of Internal Affairs on areas of common interest between the portfolios on these matters. It is proposed that distributions to the racing industry should be protected by extending TAB NZs monopoly to all racing and sports betting offered online to New Zealanders. Specifically, it is proposed to: . make it illegal for any entity other than TAB NZ to offer betting on sports or racing events to a New Zealandbased customer; . repeal the Point of Consumption Charge (POCC) sections within the Racing Act, as it will no longer be collectable under a monopoly model; . establish the Department of Internal Affairs as an interim regulator, in anticipation of this function being transferred permanently to the online casino regulator when it is established in CABMIN. refers; . strengthen the governance and oversight provisions for TAB NZ; and . strengthen harm minimisation and consumer protection regulationmaking powers in the Racing Act. This proposal comes with some risks, including that the proposed interim enforcement regime may not be sufficient for TAB NZ to receive the related payments from Entain. It is also possible that there will be a reduction in Crown revenue from the loss of GST paid by some offshore operators. It is estimated the amount of GST collected in from offshore operators that related to income from sports and racing wagering was approximately . million. It is expected this will be offset by increased revenue through TAB NZ or other similar GST eligible spending, though it is not guaranteed. The Racing Industry Amendment Bill is on the Legislation Programme, with a Priority (to proceed to select committee by the end of ), which would implement this proposal. However, to protect the viability of TAB NZ and longterm financial sustainability of the racing industry, this should be progressed as soon as possible. Background The New Zealand racing codes are almost wholly reliant on TAB NZ for funding. The New Zealand racing industry was responsible for generating approximately . billion in valueadded contribution to the New Zealand economy in . It is responsible for sustaining , fulltime equivalent jobs across the country, including people employed in industries that support the racing industry. Following the Messara report, the declining racing industry was reformed via the Racing Act to ensure it could be selfsustaining CABMIN. refers. A major change was to establish TAB NZ as a statutory entity focused on wagering and responsibility for running the industry was devolved to the racing codes. The reforms also: . progressively repealed the totalisator duty on TAB NZ (redirecting funds to the racing industry); Commercial in Confidence qwkdm Commercial in Confidence The Minister of Internal Affairs is to report back to Cabinet in October with further details on these proposals. The Minister for Racing intends to work with the Minister of Internal Affairs on areas of common interest between the portfolios. These proposals however only cover online casino gambling (e.g. online casino table games and online pokies) and do not cover online sports and race wagering. For TAB NZ to enter into the online casino market would require amendment to the Racing Act. However, such a change will not be pursued as it is considered that TAB NZ should only operate in its traditional wagering space, and not gambling. While there will be no direct impact on the way TAB NZ operates under the online casino proposal, the changes are likely to strengthen the position of some of TAB NZs closest competitors in New Zealand. This is due to the proposal for licensed operators to be able to advertise as part of licensing conditions. Most of the global operators, who currently are not permitted to advertise to New Zealanders, offer onestopshops (casino, sports and lottery products) so it is possible that sports and racing products offered by licensed casino operators may benefit from increased brand recognition, even if permitted advertising is limited to solely casino products (and licenced operators are not permitted to cross pollinate and use casino products to promote sports and race wagering). It is proposed to protect distributions to the racing industry by extending TAB NZs monopoly to all racing and sports betting offered online to New Zealanders The popularity of online gambling continues. The status quo, including the Entain partnership, does not protect the racing industry adequately from this trend. Offshore operators can offer an attractive product to New Zealanders but make a minimal contribution to the New Zealand racing industry. Decreasing returns will create a risk to jobs and export markets within the racing industry. There is also a risk of future requests of government financial support if legislative and regulatory settings have provided for the erosion of this income stream. Agreement is sought to address the effects of offshore online betting now and in the future by extending TAB NZs monopoly to online settings. Specifically, it is proposed to: . make it illegal for any entity other than TAB NZ to offer betting on sports or racing events to a New Zealandbased customer; . repeal the POCC sections within the Racing Act as it will no longer be collectable under a monopoly model (in the POCC revenue collected was approximately . million); . create an interim regulatory regime; . strengthen TAB NZs governance and government oversight provisions; and . strengthen harm minimisation and consumer protection regulationmaking powers in the Racing Act. To address TAB NZs current and future customer leakage and to maximise the value from the Entain partnership, this monopoly should be implemented as soon as possible. Other options to increase returns to the racing industry have been considered, but they offer less certainty of outcome and lower returns in the short to mediumterm. For Barring its Class operations, TAB NZ only offers wagering products. These involve to real world people, animals or events and result in differing odds (e.g. favourite horses or teams paying lower odds than others with worse records) as opposed to pure gambling which are more games of chance (e.g. independent of form or a track record). In May , the racing industry received a government support package of .m, to help it weather the financial difficulties caused by COVID . Commercial in Confidence qwkdm Commercial in Confidence Governance and oversight improvements The Entain partnership (which introduces a for profit business into the equation alongside a returntoindustry model) marks a significant change in the New Zealand gambling landscape and requires the Act to still ensure TAB NZ has appropriate strong governance to enable it to deliver on its statutory objectives, functions and purposes. It is therefore proposed to update the skills required on the TAB NZ Board under s() of the Racing Act to also include: contract monitoring, legal and financial monitoring, to ensure it can better provide governance and oversight of Entain. It is also proposed to introduce new ministerial powers to require additional reporting and informationgathering from TAB NZ to better ensure that the Government has sufficient oversight. While some Ministerial reporting is currently undertaken on a voluntary basis by TAB NZ, there are no powers to compel this, nor specify the information to be reported or the level andor standard of reporting. The Department of Internal Affairs would monitor TAB NZs compliance with these reporting requirements as part of its role as interim regulator. Current harm minimisation regulationmaking powers are not fitforpurpose This proposal means TAB NZ would be the only domestic legal provider of online sports and racing betting. Given this restriction of choice of operators, it is important to ensure there are adequate harm minimisation protections for domestic TAB NZ consumers. About one in five people in New Zealand experience harm as a result of their own or someone elses gambling. Among other things this includes financial harm; relationship disruption; psychological distress; reduced involvement at work and criminal activity. The existing harm minimisation regulations in the Racing Act only apply to landbased TAB NZ venues. The Minister for Racing therefore proposes to expand the harm minimisation regulationmaking power to also cover TAB NZs online operations. The intent of a new regulation making power would be to ensure international best practice harm minimisation standards for online products can be included as part of the monopoly. It would also allow any online harm minimisation requirements imposed on TAB NZ to be aligned as required with those placed on online casino operators and to ensure there are no loopholes relating to minimising the harm from gambling between the regimes. Additional consumer protection regulationmaking powers As with harm minimisation, the restriction of choice for New Zealanders with the online monopoly means it is important that there are appropriate consumer protections for domestic TAB NZ consumers. In particular, New Zealanders should not be excluded from accessing TAB NZ services without an appropriate reason, such as having an identified gambling problem, as opposed to restrictions being placed on someone simply because they are too successful at wagering. It therefore proposes to create a new regulation making power to ensure TAB NZ cannot restrict otherwise lawful customers from accessing its online products without an appropriate reason. This would act as a backup reserve power if required. Power to Act on detailed decisions Within the agreed parameters outlined in this paper, there are still detailed decisions to be made (e.g. what aspects of the interim framework are more appropriately placed in Commercial in Confidence qwkdm Commercial in Confidence noted, these costs are to be recovered from TAB NZ. Given the need to progress quickly, Cabinets agreement is sought for the Minister for Racing, the Minister of Finance and Minister of Internal Affairs to be authorised to make changes to the Department of Internal Affairs appropriations to provide for this. Legislative Implications This proposal requires amendments to the Racing Act. There is already a Racing Industry Amendment Bill on the Legislation Programme, with a priority (to proceed to select committee by the end of ). However, given the urgency, this should proceed as soon as possible. This proposal would mean the POCC sections within the Racing Act need to be repealed as it will no longer be collectable under a monopoly model. There is a minor change to the POCC provisions included in the upcoming Statutes Amendment Bill, which therefore would need to be removed from that Bill. Regulatory Impact Analysis The Regulatory Impact Analysis (RIA) for these proposals was assessed by an Internal Department of Internal Affairs panel who concluded that the information and analysis summarised in the RIA partially meets the quality assurance criteria. The Panels comments are below. The panel considers that the RIA does a good job of setting out the limitations and constraints on the analysis. In particular, uncertainty about the quantifiable benefits is clearly identified. As such, the panel considers that the analysis provides a suitable basis to support decisionmakers consideration of the policy proposal. The RIS partially meets the quality assurance criteria because there has been no opportunity to consult on the policy proposal. Information obtained from earlier consultations and the departments understanding of the sector more generally are included in the RIA, which helps to mitigate the lack of consultation on this proposal. Population Implications Extending TAB NZs monopoly to online betting will have the most impact on rural communities, through the flow on effect of sustainable returns to the racing industry which largely sits within rural and suburban settings. The impact on gambling harm experienced by particular groups of the population will largely depend on the nature of TAB NZs harm minimisation practices. This will be considered as part of the detailed work on harm minimisation regulations. Gambling related harm is not experienced evenly across our communities, and Mori, Pacific, Asian and young people are at greater risk. Human Rights The proposals in this paper are not inconsistent with the rights set out in the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act and the Human Rights Act . Use of External Resources No external resources were employed in the development of the advice leading into and the drafting of this Cabinet paper. Commercial in Confidence qwkdm Commercial in Confidence Consultation This paper was consulted on with Parliamentary Counsel Office (PCO), MFAT, Ministry of Health (MoH), Treasury, Inland Revenue, Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE), and Sport NZ. The Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet was informed. MoH are supportive of the monopoly proposal subject to there being a strong harm minimisation framework in place backed by the harm minimisation regulations. Sport NZ supports extending TAB NZs online wagering monopoly to protect community interests and minimise gambling harm. Sport NZ wishes to emphasise TABs dual role in racing and sports betting and that sports betting is a rapidly growing segment of TAB NZs business which relies on continued cooperation from the sports sector. Sport NZ also notes the proposal presents risks to sport funding, including potential losses from POCC and likely declines in BIUC revenue, and that while increased TAB NZ distributions may offset these losses, this is not guaranteed. MBIE requested the following agency comment be added to this paper: MBIE (competition policy) does not support extending TAB NZs statutory monopoly to online sports and racing gambling services. Restraints on competition and consumer choice should be no more than is reasonably necessary to achieve the public interest objectives. Establishing a monopoly provider to promote the sustainability of the New Zealand racing industry appears to contravene this principle. Other options such as a licensing regime or narrowing the scope of the monopoly to the racing industry only (allowing New Zealanders to continue to bet on offshore sporting events with overseas providers) should be considered. If an online monopoly is created, we support stronger governance and reporting requirements for TAB NZ to ensure the public interest is achieved. The Department of Internal Affairs will ensure any communications to regulated parties and the wider public about the monopoly are clear about how these relate to the upcomin wider online gambling reforms. Foreword The Gambling Act sets out requirements for an integrated problem gambling strategy focused on public health. The Ministry of Health (the Ministry) is responsible for developing and refreshing this strategy every three years , as well as for implementing it. The Act specifies consultation requirements for developing the strategy and the levy rates. The Strategy to Prevent and Minimise Gambling Harm to (the strategy ) is the integrated problem gambling strategy required in the Act. This strategy sets out the Ministrys response to prevent and minimise gambling harm, after considering the: submissions on the consultation document and the Allen Clarke analysis of submissions Sapere Gambling Harm Reduction Needs Assessment (Rook et al ) (see Section .) reflections in the Progress on Gambling Harm Reduction to : Outcomes report (Ministry of Health, ) Gambling Commissions report to responsible Ministers and the independent report prepared for the Commission about the Ministrys revised strategy proposals document and associated problem gambling levy rates (Gambling Commission ) . The Ministry acknowledges that the submissions it received during its consultation presented multiple stories from a range of perspectives on gambling and minimising gambling harm. At times, these storylines came close together or even intersected, but the points of view were shaped by very different aims and objectives. The Ministry acknowledges that all these perspectives are real and valid, and the goals and outcomes of the strategy matter to all submitters. Nevertheless, differing perspectives result in different interpretations. The strategy sets out a new direction for change, to provide new and more relevant services to support the needs of people affected by gambling harm, expand the range of services and learn from people with lived experience. While gambling services were excluded from the scope of the Government Inquiry into Mental Health and Addiction Services due to the timeframes associated with the strategy refresh, the strategy proposals align strongly with the changes recommended in He Ara Oranga , the report of the Inquiry (Government Inquiry into Mental Health and Addiction ) . For example, they recognise the importance of placing people at the centre of a service, using service codesign and lived experience, having consumer networks, expanding the range and choice of services to be more holistic and culturally appropriate, and strengthening the mix of peer, cultural, support and clinical workforces, communities, tngata whaiora and whnau. From , following the establishment of provinces which took over many government functions, the Colonial Secretarys Office became the channel for communication between the central and provincial governments. Because many administrative duties were carried out at provincial level, a unified departmental structure was slow to develop. The Colonial Secretary coordinated concerns as diverse as charitable aid, mental hospitals, harbourmasters and cattle inspection.

Full Impact Statement Template Impact Statement : A Digital Identity Trust Framework Section : General information . Purpose This Regulatory Impact Assessment provides an analysis of options and advice regarding interventions aimed at introducing consistency and trust into the digital identity ecosystem in New Zealand. Th e analysis and advice ha ve been produced for the purpose of informing final policy decisions to be taken by Cabinet. The Department of Internal Affairs is solely respon sible for the analysis and advice set out in this Regulatory Impact Assessment, except as otherwise explicitly indicated . . Key Limitations or Constraints on Analysis
Full Impact Statement Template The ambiguity of terminology Digital identity is an ambiguo us term. As a result, the c ompari son of terms such as dig ital identity framework, digital identity ecosystem or digital identity services can be challenging because definitions are inconsistent and sometimes conflicting . As a result, this made it challenging to compare and analyse data sets and information. The estimation of costs and benefits While the benefits of the Trust Framework are highly likely to outweigh the costs, it can be challenging to measure the costs and benefits of digital identity and thus provide accurate figures for analysis . For example, d ifferent sectors benefit in different ways banks may save money by improving inefficient onboarding processes, while government agencies may end up spending more money to provide a better service to the public. Also, a large increase in demand for compliance testing may increase costs to government, but not the benefit. As a result, The Department cannot have high confidence in its assessment of costs and benefits. The lack of reliable figures to base analysis on While officials have captured substantial anecdotal evidence regarding digital identity service challenges, it is rare for that information to be accompanied by reliable figures . For example, Non Governmental Organisations have stated that obtaining Police checks multiple times for volunteers is time consuming and a significant frustration, but they are unable to quantify the full extent of the problem. As a result , the Department has had to base some of its analysis on assumptions and cannot have high confidence in some of its assessment. The u ncertainty regarding the details of compliance testing Assessment of information systems is required to establish what should be tested for compliance and how it will be tested . This will not take place until phase one of the Trust Framework ( ). As such, the analysis in this document could only be predicated on a basic concept of compliance testing and broad estimates of the costs involved. The gaps in our evidence regarding value Evidence demonstrated that business, government, and the public were all aware of the issues around digital identity services and wanted them resolved so that the value of information could be realised. This value, however, is different for each participant in the ecosystem . For example, a builder might value the ability to digitally share the ir qualifications because that reduces the time spent gaining access to a building site, while the construction company running the site values this process because it is less resource intensive than a process requiring physical documents . As a result, it was difficult to quantify and categorise value for all the participants of the ecosystem. It was also challenging to identify which participants might look to implement solutions based on the Trust Framework first.

Full Impact Statement Template Section : Problem definition and objectives . What is the current state within which action is proposed Digital identity is a critical enabler With more and more activities taking place online, the ability to digitally share information about oneself to access services and conduct transactions is increasingly becoming a critical enabler of daily life and a fo undation for the economy. For example, on any given day, a person might use digital identity services to: Open a bank account Pay bills Shop online Work from home Undertake education Access healthcare Access government services As a result, digital identity services have significance for individuals, businesses, organisations, government agencies, and society in general. The current state of d igital identity in New Zealand The digital identity ecosystem in New Zealand that is, the network of users, relying parties, information providers, and infrastructure providers that support the digital sharing of information for a variety of purposes has emerged in an ad hoc fashion and lacks consistently applied standards and pro cesses for sharing, storing and using personal and organisational information in a digital environment. As a result it is unstructured , and inefficient . Government plays a role, but it is not a comprehensive or overarching role. Instead government applies some rules and provides a RealMe verified identity , which is a government sponsored identity verification service among many private sector solutions. The private sector drives the marketplace, but businesses and organisations vary in how they implement identification, security and privacy, and in how they store, manage and use peoples information. All of this undermines consumer trust in digital identity services, impedes the flow of information, and prevents the realisation of the potential benefits on offer. Intervention will bring consistency and trust Almost certainly. A government intervention to imbue the digital identity ecosystem with consistency and trust would encourage the use of digital identity services, enable the flow of information, and position the digital identity ecosystem to reali se the significant social and economic benefits digital identity services can provide. The implementation of a Trust Framework would be the best option for a government intervention.
Full Impact Statement Template Without intervention the situation will not improve A private sector response that would address the aforementioned issues in a comprehensiv e fashion is highly unlikely to emerge and the private sector would continue to develop its own rules and standards without government direction . The challenges within the digital identity ecosystem would remain unchanged, but would be increasingly exacerbated by the ongoing digital transformation occurring in all spheres of life a trend recently accelerated by the Covid pandemic. Trust in digital identity services would remain low, information would remain siloed, and the flow of information impeded. Furthermore, without intervention the digital identity ecosystem in New Zealand w ould not be positioned to realise the significant opportunities trusted digital identity could offer, the economic benefits of which alone are estimate d at approximately NZD . billion per annum .
Full Impact Statement Template Some standards (e.g. t he Evidence of Identity standard) are just best practice guideline s, as opposed to mandated requirements. Some legislation prescribes outdated or onerous requirements (e.g. those organisations wanting to be verified relying parties under the Electronic Identity Verification Act are required to be listed in a schedule to the Act) . As a result, this collection of regulatory instruments is not fit for purpose in terms of imbuing the digital identity ecosystem with consistency , trust and scale . New g overnment regulation could provide the overarching structure to support the digital identity ecosystem . Government regulation would be prefe rable to private arrangements because it would bring consist ency to the ecosystem . Private arrangements tend to promote fragmentation and inconsistency since the y are usually implemented through bilateral or multilateral contracts between several parties. Furthermore, through consultation , private sector stakeholders have indicated a preference for the establishment of a government led compliance regime to consistently apply common rules across the digital identity ecosystem . Any move to advance regulation in the digital identity ecosystem will directly impac t: RealMe and its funding . RealMe is the governments foremost digital identity service . Uptake for the service has not been as high as originally anticipated and the market has changed significantly since it was introduced. While RealMe is based on a centralised model, globally and in New Zealand there has been an emergence of digital identity service providers who are developing decentralised operating approaches that allow the customercitizen to have greater control of their information . These new approaches seek to realise the economic benefits while minimising data transfer and enhancing security and privacy. It is anticipated that RealMe (or parts of it) will be brought into the Trust Framework, however, because the scope and nature of its involvement has yet to be determined, the expected impacts on its funding are currently unclear. The Electronic Identity Verification Act . It is highly likely t hat legislative amendments to the Act will be required to facilitate the practical use of the Trust Framework for agencies. Potentially, a wide r range of legislation. The Trust Framework Bill would not supersede other legislation, but minor amendments may be required to remove obstacles in other legislation and facilitate opportunities for the Trust Framework and digital solutions . This could include, for example, an amendment to allow the use of digital signatures instead of requiring a physical signature on a paper document . Amendments could be made to any Act dealing with the use of personal information and identity such as the Privacy Act , the Public Records Act , the Identity Information Co nfirmation A ct , Birth, Deaths, Marriages, and Relationships Registration Act , Passports Act , Citizenship Act , Land Transport Act , The Children, Young Persons, and Their Families Act Oranga Tamariki Act , Family Violence Act , and the Vulnerable Childrens Act . Full Impact Statement Template The establishment of an accreditation team to ensure entities are complying with the rules of the Trust Framework . The introduction of a new Bill to establish the powers of the Trust Framework , its governance board and accreditation team , as well as introduce amend ments to preexisting legislation to ensure align ment with the Trust Framework. This would be achieved in two phases. Phase one: the implementation of an interim Trust Framework to allow compliance testing of digital solutions ( ). Under the interim Trust Framework, officials will develop the Trust Framework rules (largely based on existing and developing standards and legislation) and work with a limited number of entities to test their systems against the rules. This will provide participating entities with an opportunity to align their systems with the Trust Framework and ensure they are well positioned to become formally accredited once the Trust Framework is established in legislation (see below) . It also provides government with the ability to assess existing and emerging digital identity solutions to ensure they are meeting best practice for identification management, privacy and security while the legislation is under development. This approach aligns well with international models such as Australias Trusted Digital Identity Framework. In this interim phase, a cross agency governance group will be established to approve the rules and the compliance testing process. Work will also be initiated t o develop a Bill to formally establish the Trust Framework and make amendments to pre existing legislation necessary to give effect to the Trust Framework. This Bill is likely to be introduced to the House of Representatives in . The anticipated cost o f this phase is . million .

Option Legislative amendments to status quo supported by publication of best practice standards : make amendments to relevant legislation such as the Electronic Identity Verification Act (the EIV Act) and mandat e Identification Management Standards for agencies, to enable a wider range of user consented information sharing and oversight by government. The Government Chief Digital Officer (GCDO) would publish the standards that make up the proposed Trust Framework as best practice guidance for public, private and non government sector entities. Option Trust Framework: government department based gov ernance and accreditation (preferred option) : Establish a Trust Framework, overseen by a governance board established within a government department. On this board, government representati ves would have voting rights on amendments to the Trust Framework, while non government independent advisors would support their decision making. The board would be supported by a n accreditation team, based in a pre existing government department. A Bill w ould be introduced to establish the powers of the Trust Framework and its governance board, and to make any consequential amendments required. This option would be implemented in two stages phase one: interim Trust Framework ( ), which will be an i nformal testing and transition phase, and phase two ( ) which will involve the formal implementation of the Trust Framework in legislation. This option aligns with Australia which has implemented a standards based Trust Framework with government led accreditation and governance. Option Trust Framework: accreditation scheme run at a distance from primary government : Similar to Option but with an independent governance b oard established outside of an existing government department. The board would also establish a new entity responsible for accrediting participants in the Trust Framework. This would result in less government control over the governance of the Trust Framework, but would allow for representation of non government interests on the board. There would be no interim phase under this option, and it would only become operational once the new entity is established and a new Trust Framework Bill was passed. Options and are not necessarily mutually exclusive. It would be possible to start off with Option and then move to Option in the future if the government determined there would be value in such a move. The development of these options was informed by extensiv e stakeholder engagement , involving surveys, focus groups and consultation with over organisations, including public agencies, Crown entities, digital service providers, financial institutions, and academic institutions. It was clear from this consultation that the development of a trusted ecosystem would be important for both the economy and society. Consultation also too k place with a wide range of international partners, all of whom are attempting to implement national level responses to digital identity issues.
