Full Impact Statement Template Section : Implementation and operation . How will the new arrangements work in practice The preferred option would be formally given effect through the implementation of new legislation , which will establish the powers of the Trust Framework and its governance board. It will take time to develop and pass legislation, yet there is an increasing imperative to implement some form of Trust Framework in the near future, especially as Covid is accelerating digitalis ation in all aspects of life. As a result, The Department is proposing a two phase solution : Phase one: the implementation of an interim Trust Framework ( ). In this phase there is no legislation in place and the Framework is not legally enforceabl e. Phase two: the formal establishment of the Trust Framework ( ). In this phase, the Trust Framework is established in legislation and becomes legally enforceable. This approach will allow the Department to meet the demand for a near term solution to bring trust and consistency into the digital identity ecosystem, while also providing the space to develop the Trust Framework legislation, standards and accreditation process. In phase one () a cross agency governance board will be appointed by the Department, wh ich will also establish a team to conduct compliance testing on digital identity solutions . The governance g roup w ill consist of representatives f or the Government Chief Digital Officer, the Government Chief Information Security Officer , the Government Chief Data Steward, the Office of the Privacy Commissioner and a government Te Ao Mori representative. The board would also have the ability to co opt non voting members, and to appoint an advisory body comprised of government and non government experts and stakeholders. O ptions for closer participation of non government partners in the governance of the Trust Framework could be considered during the legisl ative process . The team responsible for carrying out compliance testing would be established in the Department of Internal Affairs with the Government Chief Digital Officer . Organisations wishing to operate under the Trust Framework in phase one will do so in an informal manner in which they undertake compliance testing that will test their ability to adhere to best guidance recommendations, as there will be no legislation in place . Phase one will also present an opportunity to test operational policies and processes to ensure the Framework is appropriately positioned to bring more participants into the trusted ecosystem in the future in an efficient and effective manner . While the compliance testing will help to provide the government with assura nce in the near term, in the longer term legislation is preferred. Establishing the Trust Framework accreditation and governance bodies in legislation would give them legal enforceability thus engender ing greater trust and participation , while also supporting sustainability. Additionally, e stablishing a new mechanism for both government and non government agencies to provide digital identity services without new legislation could be viewed as running counter to the original intent of the Electronic I dentity Verification ( EIV) Act. Full Impact Statement Template While the Department considered whether an independent Crown Entity could carry out the accreditation and governance, the preference was for keeping these functions within a government agency. This was because the rules for accreditation to an identity recognition system should be made and administered by the government, given that responsibility for any breach of security by a government agency would be the responsibility of the government.

Full Impact Statement Template Section : Monitoring, evaluation and review . How will the impact of the new arrangements be monitored The Minister for Government Digital Services will retain overall responsibility for the Trust Framework. In phase one of the Trust Framework ( ), the Department will establish a cross agency governance group that could include appropriate representation from the private sector and iwi in a non voting capacity . Among other duties, that group will be responsible for monitoring the performance and effectiveness of all aspects of the Trust Framework and reporting back to the Minist er for Government Digital Services on a six monthly basis. In phase two ( ), once the Trust Framework has become officially established through legislation, a governance board will be formally appointed through the standard Appointments and Honours process and will assume the aforementioned monitoring and reporting duties. Reporting requirements will be formalised in the legislation as part of phase two of the Trust Framework ( ), including which organisation will have responsibility for this (note not necessarily the Department) . The type of data that could be reported could include the number of parties accredited to the Trust Framework , the number of compliance assessments undertaken, the number of disputes that have arisen and how many have been resolved, privacy or security related issues and their resolution , and the number of active participants in the Trust Framework. The Trust Framework legislation would also likely include a requirement that the governance board must review and report on any matter relating to the Trust Framework that is specified by the Minister in a written request.

Central to the case for water services reform is the need to achieve large efficiency gains in the operation of water services through increased organisational scale. These efficiency gains a re needed to keep water services affordable to consumers , as entities take on more debt to upgrade and better provide these services. If scale efficiencies cannot be realised, the geographic communities most at risk of cost increases will be those in rural and provincial areas , with relatively small and geographically dispersed populations. . GMP per EGM broken down by territorial authority (TA) has seen Porirua City, Auckland City and Horowhenua District remain in the top Tas for GMP per EGM. Hastings District returns and continues to feature frequently. A new addition to the top this quarter is QueenstownLakes District, which is not generally this high in comparison to the other TAs. It has however reduced the number of venues and EGMs compared to the previous quarter and it could be that the venue that is no longer operating was a lower GMP venue, but further analysis would have to be conducted to confirm this. Porirua City, Hastings District and QueenstownLakes District have seen an increase in GMP per EGM compared to the last quarter, but Auckland City and Horowhenua District have seen a decrease, likely owing to the overall lower GMP, both nominally and adjusted for inflation.
GOVERNMENT PAYROLL PROGRAMME: FINAL REPORT Proposal This paper provides a final report to Cabinet on the outcome of a two year All ofGovernment programme to improve Government payroll systems. This programme ended on September . Relation to government priorities This work programme relates to the Governments Workplace Relations and Safety priority. Executive Summary In Cabinet commissioned the Government Chief Digital Officer (GCDO) in the Department of Internal Affairs (DIA) to lead a two year All of Government programme to improve Government payroll systems and simplify payroll system procurement GOV Min. Time limited funding was provided for the programme, which aimed to improve governments access to quality payroll providers, and to ensure that public service agencies have effective and consistent payroll processes that comply with the Holidays Act . The Payroll Programme was supported by a cross agency Executive Advisory Board and undertaken in conjunction with the Te Kawa Mataaho Public Services Commission (PSC) and the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE). The PSC has oversight of employment relations, and MBIE administers the Holidays Act . In line with Cabinets original mandate, the Payroll Programme was closed on September . The Programmes objectives of overs eeing agency payroll projects, improving payroll practices, and coordinating payroll procurement were achieved. However, ongoing risks and issues in the government payroll system will need continued oversight and vigilance. Background On September , Cabinet GOV MIN endorsed the establishment of a two year work programme to improve government payroll systems and simplify payroll system procurement. Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs IN CONFIDENCE IN CONFIDENCE Time limited funding of . million was provided for the programme, which was led by the Government Chief Digital Officer (GCDO) and delivered in conjunction with PSC and MBIE. The purpose of the Cabinet directed Programme was to provide Ministers with assurance that: . expenditure on payroll systems was warranted by providing oversight of government payroll projects, including investment and project assurance; . payroll project risks are managed; . payroll systems are fit forpurpose and are provided at a reasonable cost by providing a coordinated approach to the market for government payroll systems; and . capability is established to support the payroll community of practitioners and share good practice and guidance with agencies. A Payroll Executive Advisory Board met frequently during the two years of the programme to provide the programme with governance oversight and strategic direction. The Board was chaired by the GCDO and included finance and human resource leaders from MBIE, PSC, The Treasury, New Zealand Police and Inland Revenue. W hen it established the programme, Cabinet requested six monthly updates on progress : . the November progress report was provided GOV MIN refers ; . the May progress report was considered by Ministers outside of a Cabinet process due to the impact of COVID ; . the November report back did not progress ; . the May progress report was provided DEV MIN refers. The Payroll Programme has now closed, and t his paper provides a final report to Cabinet on its outcomes. Outcomes from the Payroll Programme In line with Cabinets original mandate, the Payroll Programme was formally closed on September and the Payroll Executive Advisory Board disestablished. The funding approved by Cabinet has now been exhausted and all Payroll Programme resources have been stood d own.

Government Response to the Interim Report of the Justce Commitee on the Inquiry into the Local Electons and Liquor Licensing Trust Electons, and Recent Energy Trust Electons Introducton . The Government welcomes the Justce Commitees interim report on its Inquiry into the Local Electons and Liquor Licensing Trust Electons, and Recent Energy Trust Electons. . The Government has considered the recommendatons and responds to the interim report in accordance with Standing Order . Background . In December , the Justce Commitee initated an inquiry into the local electons and liquor licensing trust electons, and recent energy trust electons. . Shortly before the inquiry was initated, the Commitee presented its report on its inquiry into the general electon and local electons. This report made twenty recommendatons on local electons, which the Government responded to in May . . As part of the inquiry into the local electons, the Commitee invited comment on the recommendatons in its prev ous report, including the recommendaton that the Government consider giving responsibility for running all aspects of local electons to the Electoral Commission. Interim recommendatons . The interim report makes two recommendatons that reiterate two themes of the Commitee s previous report. We reiterate our previous recommendaton that the Government consider giving responsibility for running all aspects of local electons to the Electoral Commission. We reiterate our previous recommendatons that the Government align, as much as practcable, the rules for parliamentary and local authority electon candidates concerning donatons, advertsing, campaigning, pecuniary interests, and complaints. . Additonally, the interim report noted that the Commitee was not able to consider all the issues raised in the Inquiry. It recommended that the Justce Commitee of the rd Parliament considers and reports on these issues in detail. Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government icqnczt

Government response . The Government thanks the Justce Commitee for the work it put into the preparaton of the interim report. The Government will consider centralisaton of local electons as other priorites allow . In responding to the Commitees report on the Inquiry into the General Electon and Local Electons, the Government noted that centralising the delivery of local electons is a fundamental change that would need to be carefully worked through The Government noted that the Commitee was consultng with stakeholders and the wider public about this recommendaton and looked forward to the Commitees further advice. . The Government previously agreed to consider the recommendaton as other priorites allow, and restates that positon in this response. The Government will consider aligning the parliament and local electoral frameworks more closely in due course . The Government agrees that broadly aligning, where possible, the principles and procedures for parliamentary and local electons can make it easy to understand and partcipate in all electons, and uphold the integrity and efectveness of electons. . The Government has agreed in principle to a review of parliamentary electoral law. It would be best to sequence changes to local electon rules so that they refect any future changes to parliamentary electon rules. The Government agrees to consider opportunites for aligning the parliamentary and local electoral frameworks more closely in due course. Government transparency is upheld
Government transparency is upheld Statutory inquiries: Administration and support of public and government inquiries and Royal Commissions We will continue to provide advice on, and support for, the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in State Care and the Care of FaithBased Institutions. This includes running monitoring and assurance systems to ensure the Royal Commission delivers its redress and final reports on time and within budget. Through Archives New Zealand, we also provide digitised historical records to support the Royal Commissions work. Public Records Act Regulatory Uplif Public Ofice audit programme A robust and accessible public record increases government transparency. Archives New Zealand is the regulator of public recordkeeping and its monitoring framework is a key regulatory tool in ensuring that a full and accurate public record is created and maintained. We have refreshed the public recordkeeping audit programme, aiming to improve information management maturity in the public sector. Each audited public ofice is expected to provide an action plan based on prioritised recommendations. The Chief Archivist is a statutory role under the Public Records Act with the power to set standards and direct the actions of public agency chief executives for records and information management. The Chief Archivist is dutybound to act independently in relation to the disposal of public records. This statutorily independent role is needed to assure the integrity of the record of government. Transformation of records disposal authorisation and implementation across government Archives New Zealands Appraisal, Disposal and Implementation (ADI) redesign project will fundamentally redesign our regulatory system for supporting sustainable appraisal and disposal processes and their successful implementation by public ofices in a digital environment. Robust appraisal activities ensure that an organisation has considered all requirements for the retention or destruction of information. This increases business eficiency, controls information management costs, and reduces the risks of legal breaches. Digital investment and ICT assurance The Department plays a role in coordinating government investment in digital technologies. We will use a datadriven approach to coordinate investment, develop a digital roadmap, review investment policies and guidance, and consider how to better support the investment needs of smaller agencies. A current focus for many government agencies is new payroll systems. We are providing greater oversight of these investments, supporting government payroll practitioners, and establishing a panel of payroll systems and services. Organisations are increasingly using new ways of working, but at the same time cyber threats are increasing and keeping data safe is challenging. We will gather data and insights on the level of assurance within agencies, support agencies to raise their assurance capability, and provide advice to Ministers on digital risks across government and any interventions that are needed. Growth charging . note that growth charges currently play a significant role in funding investment in new three waters assets; . note that growth charges for infrastructure have several benefits including: . ensuring that new residential and commercial development is economically efficient . mitigating concerns of existing users around growth investment . reducing the financing burden for water service providers . avoiding windfall gains to landowners when decisions to expand networks are made; . agree to enable growth charging for water services entities for drinking water, wastewater and stormwater; . agree that growth charging be enabled through a statutory instrument called a water infrastructure contribution; . agree that water infrastructure contributions operate on a principles based model rather than the more prescriptive development contribution model; . agree that water services entities be required to issue and consult on a water infrastructure contributions policy that sets out the schedule of charges and the methodology used to set those charges (either separate from or included in the funding and pricing plan); . agree to provide for transitional arrangements that allow water services entities to apply existing growth charges, without the need to set a new methodology for up to three years; . agree that the tools under the Infrastructure Funding and Financing Ac t be used to provide infrastructure vested with water services entities; . agree that water services entities not have access to financial contributions under the Resource Management Act ; . agree that water infrastructure contributions be able to be charged at resource consent, building consent, service connection or due to an increase in demand; . agree that water infrastructure contributions be able to be charged at a single point in time or as annual or quarterly charges for a set period; . agree that the Crown be exempt from paying water infrastructure contributions, in the same way that it is currently exempt from paying development contributions;

Hardcopy distribution: Prime Minister Minister for Racing Leader of the House I N C O N F I D E N C E ldrz Proactively released by the Minister for Racing IN CONFIDENCE Page of Office of the Minister for Racing Chair Cabinet Business Committee Racing Industry Bill: Approval for introduction Proposal . This paper seeks approval for the introduction of the Racing Industry Bill (the Bill). The Bill provides the Governments final legislative response to the recommendations of the Review of the New Zealand Racing Industry (the Messara Report). Policy . On November Cabinet agreed policy proposals for the first stage of work to reform the New Zealand racing industry CAB MIN refers. A key element was establish ing the Ministerial Advisory Committee for Racing (MAC) to drive and inform government decisions on the Messara Report recommendations . The MAC provided an interim report to the Minister for Racing on February , and a final report on June . . On April Cabinet agreed to a stepped change, with two Bills proposed for DEVMIN , DEV MIN , CAB MIN . refer. The Racing Reform Act came into force on July . It put into place transitional arrangements , including reconstituting the New Zealand Racing Board (NZRB) as the Racing Industry Transiti on Agency (RITA) and measures to increase the financial sustainability of the industry. . In November Cabinet agreed to further policy proposals for inclusion in a second Racing Bill. A key proposal is the separation of the racing and betting functions. The revised governance structure will empower the racing codes to manage the industry and set its direction for the future . A separate entity (TAB NZ) will have a sole focus on providing betting on racing and sports. In addition, Cabinet agreed policy proposals to maximise the contribution of racing industry property to the revitalisation of the industry, and the introduction of an approval mechanism to enable consideration of new betting products, while ensur ing that harm minimisation is prioritised DEV MIN , DEV MIN , CAB MIN ., CAB MIN refer. . Legislation is required to implement Cabinets policy decisions. The Racing Industry Bill will empower the industry to revitalise itsel f and become more sustainable and profitable . It creates a statutory framework that incentivises the industry to make hard decisions and pivot towards a stronger commercial orientation. The Bill: . disestablishes RITA and transfers RITAs betting functions t o TAB NZ , a new entity created as the sole betting operator for racing and sports, with RITAs racing responsibilities transferring to the racing codes; . creates the Racing Integrity Board (RIB) , a single entity responsible for all integrity functions, incl uding investigative and adjudicative functions; Review of the New Zealand Racing Industry, John Messara, July . ldrz Proactively released by the Minister for Racing IN CONFIDENCE Page of . creates a statutory process that can be used if a club and its code cannot agree the utilisation of surplus venues through the industry led Future Venues Plan process ; . introduces an approval mechanism for new wagering products, while balancing the Governments responsibility to prevent and minimise harm from gambling; and . refreshes the purpose of the Act to provide a high level overview of the overall racing industry, recognition of the potential harm from gam bling products, and recognition that racing property should remain in the racing industry and be used for maximum industry benefit. . The property proposals within the Bill are significant and are likely to be contentious.

He Hinonga Karauna Crown entities The Department of Internal Afairs monitors three Crown entities and is responsible for managing the Governments relationship with them. Ofice of Film and Literature Classification The Ofice of Film and Literature Classification (OFLC) is an independent Crown entity under the Crown Entities Act . This means it performs its functions at arms length from the Government. The ofice has two primary functions: to classify publications such as films, books or computer files which may need to be restricted or banned to provide information about classification decisions and about the classification system as a whole. Fire and Emergency New Zealand Fire and Emergency New Zealand (FENZ) is a Crown agent under the Crown Entities Act . This means it is required to follow government policies. It is responsible for delivering both rural and urban fire and emergency services throughout New Zealand. FENZ is responsible for over , staf and volunteers and is therefore one of the largest organisations in the state sector. FENZs main functions are to: promote fire safety provide fire prevention, response and suppression services stabilise or render safe incidents that involve hazardous substances provide for the safety of persons and property endangered by incidents involving hazardous substances rescuing people trapped because of transport accidents and other incidents provide urban search and rescue services. INCONFIDEN CE Pages of Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs I N C O N F I D E N C E I N C O N F I D E N C EIn Confidence Office of the Minister of Internal Affairs Cabinet Business Committee Proposal This paper seeks agreement to amend the Gambling Act (the Act) to exempt licensed Class lotteries from the prohibition on selling their lottery tickets online or by phone . Relation to government priorities This proposal resolves a long standing trouble for approved charity and non commercial fund raising. In , a temporary exemption was given to Class lotteries Class lotteries are those with prizes that exceed , that are used to fundraise for charitable or non commercial purposes. In , Class licenses were granted to the likes of Coastguard New Zealand, the Heart Foundation, sports and surf lifesaving clubs, local hospices, the Cancer Society, Southland Charitable Hospital Trust, Rotary Clubs, and the Auckland Rescue Helicopter Trust. Section of the Act prohibits and makes it illegal to offer remote interactive gambling . This is gambling by a person at a distance through a communication device. There are four exceptions : gambling conducted by Lotto NZ and TAB NZ , sales promotion schemes , and gambling offered by offshore gambling operators . This limits Class operators to selling lottery tickets via post or in person and receiving payment by cash or cheque. However, New Zealanders are using cash less often to purchase goods and services , and cheques are no longer an option as they have been phased out by banks. There is also a security risk of sending cash or credit card details in the mail. In , as part of the COVID response, Class lotteries were exempted from the prohibition on remote interactive gambling . This mean t that tickets could be sold online and remotely. Due to the emergency nature of the COVID related legislation, all amendments had an expiry . For Class lotteries the exemption expires on October . Class gambling includes large scale lotteries, housie (otherwise known as bingo), instant games and other forms of gambling run by incorporated societies. This financial year, the regulator has approved Class licences, of which have been for large scale lotteries. Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs I N C O N F I D E N C E I N C O N F I D E N C E I am concerned about the prospect of Class operators having to return to nondigital sales or being in breach of the law if they do not. R emoving digital or remote sales will likely result in: a loss of customers, both existing and new, because purchasing lottery tickets will become too hard under the old rules ; less money for community purposes , due to the additional resource required to manually handle ticket purchases, the cost of printing and increased postage as NZ Post winds down its postal delivery service in favour of courier delivery ; increased safety risks for volunteers selling tickets doortodoor or on the streets ; and a negative impact on an important revenue stream at a time when faced with rising operational costs . Organisations such as the Heart Foundation and Coastguard rely on these lotteries to raise money for their work in the community. For the Coastguard, its lottery programme is its second largest fundraising stream. It runs lotteries per year which generate about .m per annum ( about of its annual income in FY). This was only possible because of the temporary exemption. The best option is to make the exemption permanent From a gambling harm perspective, Class lotteries present a relatively low risk. This is because this form of gambling is non continuous i.e. you cannot continue to play because there is a delay between purchasing a ticket and waiting for the result, and people cannot immediately reinvest any winnings. In the time that th e temporary amendments have been in place, examination of harm treatment data showed that people were not presenting for Class gambling harm . The Department of Internal Affairs (the Department) regulates Class lotteries and has been monitoring activit y since the temporary exemption came into effect. During this time, t here has been no noticeable increase in applications. The exemption has resulted in less work for the regulator, as they have not had to enforce the old rules or educate applicants that t hey cannot take online or remote sales. This frees the regulator up to concentrate on more harmful forms of gambling i.e. Class (pokies) and casino gambling. If the provision became permanent, t he regulator would continue to monitor activity in this area. Licence holders would still have to apply for a licence for each individual lottery they wish to conduct, and comply with the Lottery Game Rules , the rules by which lotteries and sweepstakes follow. If appropriate, the regulator can place conditions on a Class licence to address any concerns.

House Party The house party trial was a single event divided into two: a twohour long semiscripted scenario (party, n) and a onehour long unscripted scenario (party, n). The first scenario involved guests mingling normally, followed by a seated restaurantstyle dinner and pub quiz. Participants were assigned seating positions but were free to move around the house. The second scenario was unscripted and participants mingled freely. There was an hour between scenarios where cards were collected from the first scenario and new cards handed out for the second. Participants were randomly assigned a single card, worn on a lanyard and had IDs in the range . Some participants arrived late (e.g. Card IDs , ,) and others left early (e.g. Card IDs , , ,,) so were not present for the entire event, and their cards were only turned onoff when they arrivedleft respectively. Furthermore, because some participants left between the first and second scenarios, there were participants in the first scenario (party, n), and participants in the second (party, n).

How to have your say Written submissions on the proposals outlined in this discussion paper are due by pm, Wednesday, September . Please refer to the key questions throughout the discussion document to help guide your feedback on the proposed Trust Framework regulations. Your input will play an important role in ensuring the final regulations are effective in supporting the gr owth of trusted and secure digital identity services for New Zealanders. Please send your submission to Digital.Identitydia.govt.nz Use of Information The information provided in your submission will be used to inform the development of the regulations, including advice provided to the Minister. We may contact you directly if we need to clarify any matters raised in your submission . Release of Informati on It is usual practice for all submissions made to the Department to be on its website. We may also publish our submissions analysis, which will include a summary of submitters views and the names of individuals or organisations that have made submissions. Submissions may also be subject to a request made under the Official Information Act . The Privacy Act governs how the Department collects, holds, uses, and discloses personal information about submitters and the information they ha ve provided. Submitters have the right to access and correct personal information. Any personal information you supply to us in your submission will only be used for the purpose of assisting in the development of policy advice associated with the issues an d proposals canvassed in this discussion paper. Please clearly state in your submission or covering email or letter, if you do not wish to have your name, or any other personal information . In addition, if there is information in your submission you do not want released, please make this clear in your submission or associated covering letter or email and explain why. For example, some information may be confidential because it is commercially sensitive or personal. You may also ask for your detai ls to be withheld if your submission is requested under the Official Information Act . We will take your statement into account and will consult with submitters when responding to requests under the Official Information Act. Next Steps When the submiss ions period closes on September , we will analyse the submissions and use the findings to inform the development of final advice on the regulations for consideration by the TF Board and the Minister for the Digital Economy and Communications. We ant icipate the regulations will be developed and gazetted in . Proactively released by the Minister for Digitising Government

How we will work Delivering on its strategy requires RSG to develop and implement an operating model which supports system collaboration, and adopting common approaches across systems where this makes sense. Effective implementation of the strategy is heavily dependent on RSG having the right capabilities, at the right time, in the right place. This means RSG needs to consider if the current type and configuration of functions and capabilities is optimal. For example, does the existing organisational design free up system groups to focus on driving regulatory excellence through their compliance and enforcement, investigation, licensing, and information and education functions Does it provide the right combination of business support functions at the required level of expertise Does it ensure access to the necessary expertise to drive regulatory excellence Does it facilitate ease of embedding new regulatory functions RSG will consider these questions in terms of strategy alignment during the coming year.Business capabilities RSG has identified that one of the most critical elements of its strategy is the development of a crossRSG culture, unifying and strengthening the RSG identity. This is key to RSG becoming more than the sum of its parts , and a desirable place for people to work. The strategy also signals a shift in workforce capability requirements this is evident in the increased emphasis on the collection, analysis and dissemination of data and information; identifying new and better ways to achieve our outcomes; making more use of digital technologies; and being able to provide assurance that regulatory functions are safe and effective. Channels There is an opportunity for RSG to review the use of its current channels to assess how well they support the achievement of regulatory outcomes. While the extent to which each channel is used will differ by regulatory system, the rationale for the use of each is likely to be similar (providing information on the internet when it is easily communicated and often accessed, facetoface for more complex communication, social media andor social marketing for driving social change, etc.). Strategyrelated changes which will underpin the operating model include: Assurance plans will enable realtime, meaningful information about system performanceTimely and accurate data and insights gathered by RSG will support evidencedriven regulatory interventions and inform sound policy design Longstanding, active and trusting relationships will ensure hap, iwi and Mori have a say in how we work Stakeholders engaging with more than one RSG regulatory group will be able to navigate seamlessly between themRegulated parties, coregulators, partners and others who access or provide RSG with data and information will do this with ease Welldefined and consistent business processes will identify the tasks that are most important to RSG and system groups, and streamline these to improve efficiency and effectiveness RSG kaimahi will have core capabilities which support them to add value across RSG and DIA regulatory systemsThe RSG operating model will facilitate the embedding of new regulatory functions regardless of the nature of the system

Hpai Hapori Community Operations
Hpai Hapori Community Operations kaimahi are in the forefront of supporting communities to improve outcomes. The Funding for Change programme in the Waikato region is making an impact by supporting Waahi P (Marae) with mobile digital kiosks and a mtauranga (knowledge) succession repository. This approach preserves and shares the rich cultural heritage of Waahi P with younger generations. By providing access to prkau (traditional stories), waiata (songs or chants), interviews with kaumtua (elders), and the history of Waahi P, the project ensures that these valuable resources are accessible and engaging for current and future beneficiaries of Waahi P.

I I Gambling Harm to (attached) . The Strategy builds on five previous strategies and consists of a strategic framework and a t hreeyear Service Plan that sets out the activities the Ministry considers are required for the to period , to make further progress towards preventing and minimising gambling harm. The Ministrys budget ed spending for to is . million (Table refers) . This represents a million () increase compared with the average cost of the preceding three levy periods (which averag ed an appropriation of . million each) , but is less than one percent of the . billion forecast player expenditure over the same period . Table Ministry of Health Budget (GST exclusive), to Service (m) (m) (m) Total (m) Public health services . . . . Intervention services . . . . Research and evaluation . . . . New service and technology pilots . . . . Ministry operating costs . . . . Total (m) . . . . The investment in the Strategy is necessary because the gambling harm needs assessment required under the Act to inform the Strategy found that significant changes were necessary to make inroads into reducing gambling harm. For example, it found the number of people affected by gambling harm continues to increase in line with population growth, harm reduction impacts have plateaued over the past seven years, service use rates have declined and systemic inequities persist for the most affected at risk population groups. Key proposals for the Strategy and Service Plan The Strategy propose s to refocus and revitalise activities to better meet the needs of people affected by harmful gambling and achieve further gains in gambling harm reduction . This is in line with the needs assessment and the recommendations of He Ara Oranga (see below ). Key changes include : . expand ing the mix of services to more closely match those available for addictions generally (by a dding residential care and peer support ), facilitat ing codesign and use of consumer networks to de velop more targeted and appropriate service models; . strengthen ing enablers t o su pport the se services such as workforce development, training , addressing cultural and language barriers, and the use of technology ; and . using pilots, evaluation and action research to inform decision making . The additional million will be invested in piloting new service models and technology to manage and mitigate gambling harm , covering public health and intervention services co designed with stakeholders and consumers , and seek ing to build resilience by enhancing the mana of service users . The pilots will also address service gaps and areas of systemic, persistent gambling harm and would be evaluated and supported by action research. This investment will enable current levels of se rvice to be maintained while the Ministry tests new service models and identif ies those activities that more effective ly address gambling harm . Local Water Done Well Stage : Further Decisions Portfolio Local Government On July , following reference from the Cabinet Economic Policy Committee, Cabinet: Background noted that, as agreed by Cabinet in February CABMIN, the legislative strategy involved in implementing Local Water Done Well includes three pieces of legislation: . the Water Services Acts Repeal Act passed in February which repealed the previous governments legislation and restored ownership and responsibility for water services to local government; . the Local Government (Water Services Preliminary Arrangements) Bill introduced in May which will establish initial components of the new framework and transitional arrangements; . the Local Government Water Services Bill anticipated for introduction in December and enactment in mid which will provide enduring settings and frameworks; noted that policy decisions for the third Bill above are being sought through a suite of three papers, the first two of which have already been agreed: . Local Water Done Well Stage : Water Services Delivery System ECOMIN; . Local Water Done Well Stage : Water Services Regulatory System ECOMIN; . Local Water Done Well Stage : Further Decisions attached under ECOSUB; Further decisions relating to local government water services delivery arrangements authorised the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Local Government to make final decisions on the design features of the new water organisations I N C O N F I D E N C E sshjfdn ()(f)(iv) I N C O N F I D E N C E CABMIN. Supporting longterm contracting arrangements noted that, under sections and of the Local Government Act , local government organisations (councils and councilcontrolled organisations) can enter into contracts and joint arrangements relating to water services with bodies that are not local government organisations for a maximum of years; agreed to extend the permitted maximum length of contracts and joint arrangements for water services from to years; Improving how stormwater networks are managed agreed that the legislation will provide that territorial authorities are responsible for managing and maintaining stormwater networks in their city or district, including overland flow paths and urban watercourses that are both on private land and related to the operation of the stormwater network in urban areas; agreed that the legislation will include provisions that require territorial authorities to: . develop a stormwater network risk management plan to identify risks and hazards related to stormwater networks; . work with private landowners as required to protect and maintain the conveyance capacity of overland flow paths and urban watercourses; . develop (as required) stormwater rules that would provide direction to private landowners on their responsibilities for maintenance and protection of the conveyance capacity of overland flow paths and urban watercourses on their land; agreed that the legislation will provide for stormwater rules and rulemaking powers to support the management of overland flow paths and urban watercourses on private land, including that the rules (and rulemaking powers, as the case may be) will: . be made pursuant to stormwater network risk management plans; . set out landowner duties, including access to land, and notification requirements; . replace current bylaw making powers as they relate to urban stormwater networks; agreed that the legislation will include requirements relating to stormwater network risk management plans, including that these plans will: . identify any hazards that relate to a stormwater network, including (without limitation) emerging or potential hazards; . assess any risks that are associated with those hazards; . identify how those risks are to be managed, controlled, monitored, or eliminated; . be provided to Taumata Arowai for review and comment, prior to being finalised; agreed that the legislation will set out private landowners statutory rights and responsibilities in relation to overland flow paths or urban watercourses that are on their land, including provisions to the effect that: . where a landowner impairs or alters an overland flow path or watercourse, without resource consent or in breach of a stormwater rule, they would be responsible for either eliminating the impairment or meeting the costs of the territorial authority, if they do that on the landowners behalf; I N C O N F I D E N C E sshjfdn I N C O N F I D E N C E CABMIN. . a private landowner would not be responsible for an impairment or alteration of a stormwater network if that impairment or alteration was caused by the act or omission of another person; . a private landowner would be required to notify the relevant territorial authority before undertaking any work that might affect the stormwater network; agreed that the legislation will provide for an enabling framework for the development of service agreements, which can be used by territorial authorities, water organisations and other agencies to support the integrated management of the stormwater network; agreed that the legislation will reflect the complex relationship between stormwater networks and transport corridor stormwater infrastructure, and define transport stormwater infrastructure as including the infrastructure that is owned or operated by a transport corridor manager to collect or discharge stormwater relating to a transport function of the corridor; Charging and billing for water services, by water organisations agreed that the new legislation will include a suitably modified version of the current legislative framework for local government rating, to enable water organisations to identify which ratepayers should be charged for water services; agreed that the legislation will require councils to share relevant billing information with water organisations (to enable the identification of ratepayers), and allow councils to charge a reasonable fee for this service; agreed that the legislation can include any technical amendments that are needed to cater for situations where consumers may have to pay both water organisations and councils for water services at the same time, due to water organisations being formed partway through a rating year; agreed that the legislation will allow water organisations to charge a serviceability fee to properties that could be, but are not, connected to the water network; Rates Rebate Scheme and associated financial implications noted that: . except for ratepayers in Auckland, who pay water charges to Watercare, water costs are included as part of council rates under current arrangements; . under the current approach in the Rates Rebate Act , rebates are applied to the rates bill only and not water charges (which are not considered rates and so are not eligible for the rates rebate); . if water charges are split out from rates bills and charged by new water organisations rather than councils, some recipients of a rates rebate would receive a lower rebate, even though their total expenses (rates and water) may not have changed; agreed to amend the definition of rates in the Rates Rebate Act to include water charges, so that ratepayers will not receive different levels of rebate depending on whether they are billed for water charges as part of their rates bill, or separately through a water organisation; I N C O N F I D E N C E sshjfdn I N C O N F I D E N C E CABMIN. noted that the above amendment will result in a per annum increase in the cost of the Rates Rebate Scheme, because water charges paid to Watercare would now be considered rates and would be eligible for the rebate; noted that the additional costs can be met from within the existing Rates Rebate Scheme appropriation for the immediate future, meaning there is no current impact on the Crowns fiscal forecasts; noted that the Rates Rebate Scheme is a demandbased scheme that is periodically adjusted to reflect macroeconomic factors, and that the new definition of rates will capture the additional in the calculation of adjustments required over the longer term, contributing to an increase in adjustments made; noted that the Treasury has been consulted on the above impact and is comfortable with the proposed amendment to the definition of rates in the Rate Rebate Act ; agreed that the legislation will require water organisations to provide information to the relevant council(s) on the amount of water charges paid by a consumer during the year, in order to facilitate the administration of the Rates Rebate Scheme by the council(s); Charging for growth by water organisations noted that under Local Water Done Well, some councils will choose to shift their water services delivery into separate water organisations, and that those water organisations will need a specific mechanism to directly charge for new or additional demand on water infrastructure; agreed that water organisations will be enabled to use the development contributions regime in the Local Government Act , with the necessary modifications as an interim measure pending any future changes that may be made following work on development contributions settings as part of the Governments Going for Housing Growth policy; agreed that the legislation can enable a flexible approach in which: . water organisations are able to develop their own development contributions policy; . as an alternative to a separate water organisation development contributions policy, a water organisation and a council within its service area could agree to development contributions set by the water organisation being included in the councils policy; . a council within a water organisations service area can administer the organisations development contributions policy on its behalf; agreed that the legislation will include appropriate transitional arrangements, to ensure a smooth transition to charging for the growthrelated costs of water services infrastructure from a council to a water organisation; agreed that the Infrastructure Funding and Financing Act be amended so that the Infrastructure Funding and Financing model can be used for water services infrastructure that is to be vested with a water organisation; Tax exemptions for water organisations agreed to grant taxexempt status to water organisations; agreed that the legislation will provide that, if a water organisation is wound up, there will be a requirement that assets must be transferred to another water organisation or to a council on windup; Borrowing in foreign currency agreed that the legislation will explicitly allow water organisations to borrow in foreign currency, to ensure they have access to the borrowing that may be required to meet the significant costs associated with water infrastructure; agreed that the legislation will also allow water organisations to enter into incidental arrangements, which allow water organisations to reduce their exposure to currency volatility; Rateability of land and assets owned by water organisations agreed that the legislation will provide that land owned by water organisations should be rateable; agreed that the legislation will require assets that are owned by a water organisation, but located on or under land the organisation does not own, should be rateable; noted that changes are not being proposed to the bespoke arrangements for the rateability of Watercares land and assets that apply under the Local Government (Auckland Council) Act ; Civil Defence Emergency Management costsharing arrangements agreed that the current Civil Defence Emergency Management costsharing arrangements with the Crown will apply directly to water organisations, to ensure financial separation of water organisations and allow them to directly seek partial reimbursement from the Crown for emergency expenses; noted that further policy decisions will be required prior to the establishment of any financially independent water organisation (including Watercare) to ensure these arrangements apply appropriately to the water organisations and local authorities, with no material fiscal impacts for the Crown; authorised the Minister of Local Government, the Minister of Finance, and the Minister for Emergency Management and Recovery to make further policy decisions on the application of costsharing arrangements; Approach to consumer protection noted that: . information disclosure will be part of the new economic regulation regime for local government water services, as agreed by Cabinet in June ECOMIN; . information disclosure could be used to oversee aspects of the consumer experience, and enable the Commerce Commission to learn more about how existing consumer protection settings are working in practice, and identify potential shortcomings; I N C O N F I D E N C E sshjfdn I N C O N F I D E N C E CABMIN. agreed that the legislation should clearly enable the Commerce Commission to require public reporting from water service providers on consumer protection issues, and to publicly summarise and analyse the information disclosed; agreed that the legislation will also include the power for the Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs to make regulations relating to consumer protection measures, to provide flexibility to consider what may be needed in the future, particularly if information disclosure reveals that issues exist; agreed that regulations could be used to specify requirements relating to: . complaint processes, the provision of information, the recording of complaints, andor reporting; . providing access to an external consumer dispute resolution process; andor . other matters relating to consumer protections that the Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs considers necessary and appropriate; noted that service quality codes could be a useful consumer protection mechanism, but that the development of such codes should be sectorled in the first instance; agreed that the Commerce Commission will be able to issue guidelines to water service providers on matters relating to a service quality code; agreed that the legislation will enable the Commerce Commission to make a service quality code in relation to the provision of water services, where no sectordeveloped code exists or, in the opinion of the Commission, the purpose of Part of the Commerce Act could be better met by a mandatory code; agreed that, before making a mandatory service quality code, the Commerce Commission will be required to provide a report to the Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs containing the reasons for doing this; . compliance, enforcement, and investigation powers similar to those under Part of the Commerce Act will be applied to the economic regulation of water services, as agreed by Cabinet in June ECOMIN; agreed that the legislation will enable similar compliance and enforcement powers and mechanisms to be applied to consumer protection requirements, to ensure the Commerce Commission has access to adequate and appropriate tools, and provide consistency across regimes; Local Water Done Well Stage : Further Decisions Portfolio Local Government On July , the Cabinet Economic Policy Committee: Background noted that, as agreed by Cabinet in February CABMIN, the legislative strategy involved in implementing Local Water Done Well includes three pieces of legislation: . the Water Services Acts Repeal Act passed in February which repealed the previous governments legislation and restored ownership and responsibility for water services to local government; . the Local Government (Water Services Preliminary Arrangements) Bill introduced in May which will establish initial components of the new framework and transitional arrangements; . the Local Government Water Services Bill anticipated for introduction in December and enactment in mid which will provide enduring settings and frameworks; noted that policy decisions for the third Bill above are being sought through a suite of three papers, the first two of which have already been agreed: . Local Water Done Well Stage : Water Services Delivery System ECOMIN; . Local Water Done Well Stage : Water Services Regulatory System ECOMIN; . Local Water Done Well Stage : Further Decisions attached under ECOSUB; Further decisions relating to local government water services delivery arrangements authorised the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Local Government to make final decisions on the design features of the new water organisations ; I N C O N F I D E N C E emppemb ()(f)(iv) I N C O N F I D E N C E ECOMIN Supporting longterm contracting arrangements noted that, under sections and of the Local Government Act , local government organisations (councils and councilcontrolled organisations) can enter into contracts and joint arrangements relating to water services with bodies that are not local government organisations for a maximum of years; agreed to extend the permitted maximum length of contracts and joint arrangements for water services from to years; Improving how stormwater networks are managed agreed that the legislation will provide that territorial authorities are responsible for managing and maintaining stormwater networks in their city or district, including overland flow paths and urban watercourses that are both on private land and related to the operation of the stormwater network in urban areas; agreed that the legislation will include provisions that require territorial authorities to: . develop a stormwater network risk management plan to identify risks and hazards related to stormwater networks; . work with private landowners as required to protect and maintain the conveyance capacity of overland flow paths and urban watercourses; . develop (as required) stormwater rules that would provide direction to private landowners on their responsibilities for maintenance and protection of the conveyance capacity of overland flow paths and urban watercourses on their land; agreed that the legislation will provide for stormwater rules and rulemaking powers to support the management of overland flow paths and urban watercourses on private land, including that the rules (and rulemaking powers, as the case may be) will: . be made pursuant to stormwater network risk management plans; . set out landowner duties, including access to land, and notification requirements; . replace current bylaw making powers as they relate to urban stormwater networks; agreed that the legislation will include requirements relating to stormwater network risk management plans, including that these plans will: . identify any hazards that relate to a stormwater network, including (without limitation) emerging or potential hazards; . assess any risks that are associated with those hazards; . identify how those risks are to be managed, controlled, monitored, or eliminated; . be provided to Taumata Arowai for review and comment, prior to being finalised; agreed that the legislation will set out private landowners statutory rights and responsibilities in relation to overland flow paths or urban watercourses that are on their land, including provisions to the effect that: . where a landowner impairs or alters an overland flow path or watercourse, without resource consent or in breach of a stormwater rule, they would be responsible for either eliminating the impairment or meeting the costs of the territorial authority, if they do that on the landowners behalf; I N C O N F I D E N C E emppemb I N C O N F I D E N C E ECOMIN . a private landowner would not be responsible for an impairment or alteration of a stormwater network if that impairment or alteration was caused by the act or omission of another person; . a private landowner would be required to notify the relevant territorial authority before undertaking any work that might affect the stormwater network; agreed that the legislation will provide for an enabling framework for the development of service agreements, which can be used by territorial authorities, water organisations and other agencies to support the integrated management of the stormwater network; agreed that the legislation will reflect the complex relationship between stormwater networks and transport corridor stormwater infrastructure, and define transport stormwater infrastructure as including the infrastructure that is owned or operated by a transport corridor manager to collect or discharge stormwater relating to a transport function of the corridor; Charging and billing for water services, by water organisations agreed that the new legislation will include a suitably modified version of the current legislative framework for local government rating, to enable water organisations to identify which ratepayers should be charged for water services; agreed that the legislation will require councils to share relevant billing information with water organisations (to enable the identification of ratepayers), and allow councils to charge a reasonable fee for this service; agreed that the legislation can include any technical amendments that are needed to cater for situations where consumers may have to pay both water organisations and councils for water services at the same time, due to water organisations being formed partway through a rating year; agreed that the legislation will allow water organisations to charge a serviceability fee to properties that could be, but are not, connected to the water network; Rates Rebate Scheme and associated financial implications noted that: . except for ratepayers in Auckland, who pay water charges to Watercare, water costs are included as part of council rates under current arrangements; . under the current approach in the Rates Rebate Act , rebates are applied to the rates bill only and not water charges (which are not considered rates and so are not eligible for the rates rebate); . if water charges are split out from rates bills and charged by new water organisations rather than councils, some recipients of a rates rebate would receive a lower rebate, even though their total expenses (rates and water) may not have changed; agreed to amend the definition of rates in the Rates Rebate Act to include water charges, so that ratepayers will not receive different levels of rebate depending on whether they are billed for water charges as part of their rates bill, or separately through a water organisation; I N C O N F I D E N C E emppemb I N C O N F I D E N C E ECOMIN noted that the above amendment will result in a per annum increase in the cost of the Rates Rebate Scheme, because water charges paid to Watercare would now be considered rates and would be eligible for the rebate; noted that the additional costs can be met from within the existing Rates Rebate Scheme appropriation for the immediate future, meaning there is no current impact on the Crowns fiscal forecasts; noted that the Rates Rebate Scheme is a demandbased scheme that is periodically adjusted to reflect macroeconomic factors, and that the new definition of rates will capture the additional in the calculation of adjustments required over the longer term, contributing to an increase in adjustments made; noted that the Treasury has been consulted on the above impact and is comfortable with the proposed amendment to the definition of rates in the Rate Rebate Act ; agreed that the legislation will require water organisations to provide information to the relevant council(s) on the amount of water charges paid by a consumer during the year, in order to facilitate the administration of the Rates Rebate Scheme by the council(s); This is the third paper in a series of papers seek ing decisions on proposals to progress the third stage of the Local Water Done Well programme following on from the two papers that were considered in June . . This paper seeks the remaining policy decisions for the Local Government Water Services Bill, The proposals relate to t hree main areas : . additional proposals relating to local government water service s arrangements , to support and enable the approach set out in my paper, Local Water Done Well stage : water services delivery system ECOMIN affecting : .. powers relating to water infrastructure and services; .. how stormwater networks are managed; .. charging arrangements for new water organisations, including ensuring they can charge for growth; .. other matters relating to water organisations; . an approach to consumer protection, to complement the new economic regulation regime agreed for local government water services through the paper Local Water Done Well stage : water services regulatory system ECO MIN ; . changes to how Taumata Arowai operates , the water quality regulatory framework , and to address other drivers of cost and regulatory burden through the water system . This includes changing the requirements relating to Te Mana o te Wai in the Water Services Act and the Taumata Arowai the Water Services Regulator Act . Relation to government priorities . The Speech from the Throne, in December , stated that the Government w ould repeal the Three Waters legislation and restore council ownership and control, with stronger central government oversight, and strict rules for water quality and ongoing investment. . Moving towards sustainable long term investment in water services infrastructure through Local Water Done Well will play a critical role in supporting housing growth. ()(f)(iv) IN CONFIDENCE Page of Executive summary . Local Water Done Well sets out a clear direction for financially sustainable water services, underpinned by a robust regulatory system. It puts an emphasis on meeting regulatory standards, and the transparent and sustainable performance of these services but provides for local choice about the form of service delivery structures. . During June and July , I am seeking decisions on three papers, which together will give effect to the third stage of the Local Water Done Well programme: . Local Water Done Well stage : water services delivery system ECOMIN , June ; . Local Water Done Well stage : water services regulatory system ECOMIN , June ; . this paper Local Water Done Well stage : further decisions . . I expect to make announcements shortly, once decisions have been made on this final paper . This is likely to be around the same time as my second Bill , the Local Government (Water Services Preliminary Arrangements) Bill, is enacted (August ). . This paper seeks the remaining policy decisions needed for legislative drafting for my third Bill the Local Government Water Services Bill proposed for introduction in December and enactment in mid . The proposals cover three main areas . . Firstly, there are additional proposals relating to local government water service s arrangements . These support and enable the approach set out in my paper, Local Water Done Well stage : water services delivery system ECOMIN . Lifting the link to refer to the National Policy Statement for F reshwater Management has the benefit of linking Taumata Arowais decision making to broader freshwater planning, of which Te Mana o te Wai is only one aspect . Background . In February , we enacted the Water Services Acts Repeal Act . This fulfilled our commitments to repeal the previous governments unpopular water services legislation, restore local government responsibilities for water services, and put a halt to the establishment of the mega entities. . That was the first stage of the Local Water Done Well programme. As outlined in my February paper, Water Services Acts Repeal Bill: Approval for Introduction CAB MIN , the policy and legislative approach for implementing the new water services system will be progressed through two further Bills . . In March , I report ed back to the Cabinet Economic Policy Committee (ECO) with the first set of policy proposals for the replacement regime . The Local Government (Water Services Preliminary Arrangements) Bill was introduced in May , and is expected to be enacted in August . That Bill sets the early foundations for the new system, and support s and progress es some initial activities . IN CONFIDENCE Page of . Through the February paper, I was invited to report back to ECO with the second set of policy proposals for the replacement regime, to inform a Bill to be passed in the second quarter of . It was noted that Bill will include provisions relating to long term requirements for financial sustainability, provide for a complete economic regulation regime, make amendments to the water quality regulato rs empowering legislation, and make refinements to the water services delivery system settings. . This is the third paper of a suite of papers, i n June and July , that reports back and seeks decisions on these matters. The first two papers sought agreement to: . a new approach to local government water service s delivery arrangements; . the establishment of a new economic regulation regime for local government water service providers; . some initial changes to the Water Services Act, to help reduce the regulatory compliance burden on small drinking water suppliers. . If agreed, the proposals in these papers will inform the development of the Local Government Water Services Bill . Once in place, this package of legislation will implement this Governments Local Water Done Well policy , and bring about a new approach to water services delivery and regulation .
