I have been considering advice on a range of detailed and technical matters, and am now seeking decisions on the proposals that need to be given effect through legislation. These are discussed further below. . It is important to address many of these matters because water organisations will be separate from the councils that establish and own them. The legislation and standard approaches that currently apply to councils will not and, in some respects, should not automatically apply to water organisations . We need to equip water service providers with modern and fit forpurpose powers relating to water infrastructure and services Modernised powers to carry out work on land, control connections, and manage other issues . Current legislation relating to water services has often fallen behind similar legislation that applies to other utilities in New Zealand or other jurisdictions. It is generally old, often contains gaps, and is spread across multiple Acts. The application of this legislation can be challenging for some councils, particularly where they lack capability or ready access to legal advice. . I have identified several areas in which modernising the legislation relating to water service providers functions and powers would enable more effective delivery of water services. This would help to reduce costs, streamline processes, and support priori ties such as urban development. . I am proposing changes in the following areas: . Powers for water service providers to control connections to water services and infrastructure. These are powers that enable councils to approve connections by private individuals or businesses to water supply, wastewater andor stormwater infrastructure, and include the ability to set design or engineering requirements. These powers are a critical part of urban development. Modernisation should reduce compliance costs by providing greater certainty and consistency. Water organisations is the general term used to refer to all of the models of water service provider except where councils continue with direct in house delivery. The term water service provider includes all forms of water service provider and councils. IN CONFIDENCE Page of . Powers for water service providers to carry out work on land in relation to water services infrastructure . These are powers that are required by all kinds of utility providers (water, telecommunications, electricity, and gas) to ensure infrastructure can be constructed or maintained, particularly where it is on private property or underground. The proposed ch anges will simplify and streamline the use of these powers, while providing appropriate protections for all parties, and are important for both ongoing maintenance and new development. . A modernised approach t o the current bylaw regime relating to water services . Councils use bylaws to control water catchments (such as reservoirs), manage trade waste, and to set restrictions relating water supply or wastewater infrastructure use (for example, sprinkler use during droughts, or disposing of toxic substances in toil ets or drains). I am proposing the current system is replaced or supplemented with new, fitforpurpose statutory provisions , including requirements for management plans and enforc ement rules . This will enable more effective and consistent management, while still addressing local issues and needs. . I am seeking agreement to provide in the legislation for modernised powers relating to water services infrastructure, including powers for water service providers (councils and water organisations) to: . control connections to water services infrastructure ; . carry out work on land relating to water services infrastructure . . I am also seeking agreement to provide for a modernised approach to the bylaw system relating to water services. I expect t his would include statutory provisions covering the following areas. . Firstly, the legislation will need to enable water service providers to control drinking water catchments by specifying land within a controlled drinking water catchment area , which would be covered by a water catchment management plan. . These plans would set out arrangements for the control and protection of the area, including access , activities that might be undertaken , use of water , and restrictions or prohibitions regarding contamination of water in the area. Any rules with respect to land that is not owned or controlled by the water service provider would only be by agreement with the owner. . Secondly, water service providers will need to be enabled to manage trade waste . This is commercial and industrial liquid waste that is discharged into the wastewater system. I am proposing t his would be done through trade waste plans (developed with local consultation ), and supported by a system of permits, certification and registration. Domestic customers would also be subject to this regime if discharges were beyond a normal household level (for example, a home workshop working with toxic chem icals ). This is not intended to apply in relation to Crown land. Legislation relating to Crown land in general, and public conservation land, already contains mechanisms to enable access, providing the activities and access are consistent with the lands status and legislative purposes. IN CONFIDENCE Page of . Trade waste plans would set out conditions on the quality, quantity and timing of discharges , as well as testing. Local plans will allow flexibility in controlling the thresholds and conditions for discharges to meet local conditions for example, the capacity or vulnerability of local systems. Customers will be able to seek a review of a permitting decision, possibly through the court system. . Each of t he above approaches will need to be underpinned by an offence regime to enable appropriate and effective enforcement. The legislation will also need to enable water service providers to manage water supply and wastewater services with offence and infringement tools. . I anticipate t he legislation will include necessary offences and penalties (including infringements), with penalties modelled on similar offences in other legislation . The Department of Internal Affairs will work with the Ministry of Justice to develop the details needed for legislative drafting. . The legislation will also need to provide for detailed transitional arrangements , cover ing matters such as timeframes, suspension of current mandatory bylaw revie ws during the transition period, revocation of bylaws (if relevant) , and appropriate safeguards and requirements around the forming of new management regimes (which will function as secondary legislation). . I am seeking delegated authority to approve matters that may arise during the course of drafting and may be required to align with the decisions in this paper . This would include approving detailed matters relating to these proposals. Supporting long term contracting arrangements . Sections and of the LGA relate to contracts and joint arrangements for water services. Under these provisions, local government organisations (councils and CCOs ) can enter into contracts and joint local government arrangements with one another without restriction. However, there are limitations on the length of contracts and joint arrangements that involve third parties (such as the private sector) . . The maximum length of a contract or joint arrangement for water services involving bodies that are not local government organisations is years. . I am not considering changes to these sections of the LGA other than to ensure new water organisations are also considered to be local government organisations in future. However, I am interested in views on whether the maximum length of a contract or joint arrangement should be extended to years. This woul d reflect the long lifespan of water infrastructure, and the potential opportunities to enter into longer contracts. . I am seeking a decision on whether the maximum length of contracts and joint arrangements relating to water services should remain at years or be extended to years instead. For example, the Local Government Act , the Resource Management Act , the Water Services Act , Te Ture Whenua Mori Act (where relevant) and other utilities legislation . IN CONFIDENCE Page of . There are concerns about the capacity of local government organisations to effectively design and manage long term contracts. The prevalence of information gaps on New Zealands water network further complicates effective design and management of longer term contracts. . The current year limit is consistent with the common length of public private partnership contracts globally (about to years). It is also the maximum period for which resource consent s can be granted , for taking water and discharges . This effectively puts third party providers on the same footing for recovering capital costs as councils, which typically repay debt for a new water treatment plant over a term of between and years. . An argument can be made for extending the limit to years, as this may enable certain types of public private partnerships, such as build , design and operate cont racts, for high capital expenditure assets. The development costs of the asset could be recovered over a longer period or to match the economic life of the asset, which can lead to low costs per annum for providing this infrastructure. . Regardless of whether changes are made in this respect, I am exploring potential mechanisms for providing the local government sector with support to enter into successful long term contracting arrangements. Support mechanisms could include guidance materi al and targeted assistance for councils. We also need mechanisms to improve how s tormwater networks are managed and help reduce risks to people and property . Overland flow paths and urban watercourses are an urban areas natural drainage system providing critical overflow capacity for the stormwater network. While stormwater network infrastructure has been designed to collect and divert stormwater from urban development, in almost all c ases it will discharge that stormwater to the nearest overland flow path or urban watercourse. . Private ownership, uncertainty around legal responsibilities, limited regulatory tools , and information gaps are key challenges that affect the protection and maintenance of the conveyance capacity of overland flow paths and urban watercourses . These issues are exacerbated by urban intensification and climate change. . Together , these challenges mean that initiatives to protect and maintain the conveyance capacity of urban watercourses are difficult to implement and more likely to be reactive than proactive. This can expose people and property to significant flood risks. A lack of proactive interventions and maintenance was identified as a contributing factor to flooding impacts on properties in the Auckland floods in January . . Regional councils, territorial authorities, and transport corridor managers all have overlapping responsibilities for managing the impacts of stormwater in urban areas. Stormwater network infrastructure owned by other public agencies and private property o wners is often physically connected to council stormwater network s. Local context may also affect how those responsibilities are allocated. Improving the integrated management of stormwater and its impacts relies on effective coordination across those agen cies and networks. IN CONFIDENCE Page of . I have identified some mechanisms to support integration between key agencies and improv e the management of overland flow paths and urban watercourses . My proposals fall into the following related areas: . specify ing territorial authority and private landowner statutory roles and responsibilities ; . enabling new planning and regulatory tools through stormwater network risk management plans and stormwater rules to support riskbased management of overland flow paths and urban watercourses ; . enabling territorial authorit ies, regional council s, and transport corridor managers to put in place service agreements to support the integrated management of stormwater networks. Roles, responsibilities, and new planning and regulatory tools . I am proposing to include provisions in the legislation that state that territorial authorities are responsible for managing and maintaining the stormwater network in their city or district (service areas) including overland flow paths and urban watercourses that are both on private land and related to the operation of the stormwater network in urban areas . . As part of this approach, the legislation w ill require territorial authorities to: . develop a stormwater network risk management plan to identify significant risks and hazards that impact on the function of critical stormwater network assets ; . work with private landowners as required to protect and maintain the conveyance capacity of overland flow paths and urban watercourses ; . develop (as required) stormwater rules that would provide direction to private landowners on their responsibilities for maintenance and protection of the conveyance capacity of overland flow paths and urban watercourses on their land . . The legislation w ill provide for these stormwater rules and associated rule making powers to support the management of overland flow paths and urban watercourses on private land . The se would : . be made pursuant to stormwater network risk management plans ; . set out landowner duties including access to land, and notification requirements ; . replace current bylaw making powers as they relate to the urban stormwater network. . The legislation w ill also include requirements relating to stormwater network risk management plans. These plans would have an operational focus, and require stormwater network operators to : . adopt a risk based approach to identify any hazards that would impact on critical stormwater network assets , including (without limitation) emerging or potential hazards; IN CONFIDENCE Page of . assess any risks to the operation of the network, including any risks to people or property that are associated with those hazards; . identify how those risks are to be managed, controlled, monitored, or eliminated. . The intention is that the plans will improve flood risk information , to inform proactive management of hazards and risks to the operation of the stormwater network, and to people and property. They will also provide a framework for stormwater rules to support the management of overland flow paths and urban watercourses on private land . . Prior to being finalised, stormwater network risk management plans w ill be provided by the territorial authority to Taumata Arowai for review and comment. This w ill complement the approach to risk management plans that has been adopted for drinking water and wastewater in the Water Services Act . It would provide an opportunity for Taumata Arowai to issue guidance and align environmental standards for stormwater management to improve consistency. . I am also proposing the legislation w ill set out private landowners statutory rights and responsibilities in relation to overland flow paths or urban watercourses that are on their land. This would include provisions to the effect that: . where a landowner impairs or alters an overland flow path or watercourse, without resource consent or in breach of a stormwater rule they would be responsible for either eliminating the impairment or meeting the costs of the territorial authority, if they do that on the landowner s behalf; . a private landowner would not be responsible for an impairment or alteration of a stormwater network if that impairment or alteration was caused by the act or omission of another person; . a private landowner would be required to notify the relevant territorial authority before undertaking any work that might affect the stormwater network. Service agreements . Stormwater management has a range of interfaces and overlapping jurisdictions . This means different parties need to work together to manage their respective statutory roles and functions to support the integrated management of the stormwater network . . Service agreements can be a useful mechanism for managing the interactions between these parties. Many councils already use similar service level agreements to man age cross agency interactions. T hese agreements can set out the roles and responsibilities of each party, how they will work together and share information, and a dispute resolution process. . I am seeking agreement that the legislation provides for an enabling framework for the development of service agreements , which can be used by territorial authorities , water organisations and other agencies to support the integrated management of the stormwater network . IN CONFIDENCE Page of . The legislation will include the core features of these agreements, but their use would not be mandatory. This approach reflects the cooperative nature of the agreements, and the need to provide some flexibility for the parties to adopt arrangements that are appropriate to lo cal circumstances. Definitions . Finally, I consider the legislation should reflect the complex relationship between stormwater networks and transport corridor stormwater infrastructure. . Stormwater infrastructure in transport corridors has been developed to enable the transport functions of those corridors. To protect that transport function, particularly in relation to local roads , which (apart from Auckland) are owned and operated by territorial authorities, I am propos ing the legislation define s transport stormwater infrastructure, by recognising that the primary purpose of that infrastructure is for transport purposes. . The defin ition of transport stormwater infrastructure will include the infrastructure that is owned or operated by a transport corridor manager to collect or discharge stormwater relating to a transport function of the corridor . . The intention is that the definition recognise s and protect s the transport function and investment in this infrastructure. It w ill not include matter s related to the operation, maintenance or level of service related to transport stormwater infrastructure. While these are important issues for integrated management across those stormwater networks , I consider service agreements should be the primary mechanism to ensure territorial authorities and transport corridor manage rs work effectively together within their respective statutory responsibilities . We need to consider various matters relating to c harging for water services , including ensuring water organisations can charge for growth Charg ing and billing for water services . In my previous paper, it was agreed that the legislation will enable water organisations to assess, set and collect water services charges separate from their owner councils. I am now seeking agreement to further details to support and enable this approach. . Water charges are currently included as part of council rates (except for Watercare, which bills property owners directly). The Local Government (Rating) Act provides a framework for identifying who is liable to pay rates (that is, who is the ratepaye r), which broadly aligns with who owns the property. . The new legislation will need to include a suitably modified version of the current legislative framework, to enable water organisations to identify which ratepayers should be charged for water services. . I am not proposing any changes to the way usage charges are assessed for residential properties, or changes to the existing arrangements that apply for tenants and landlord s. Current arrangements would continue, whereby bills for water charges are raised directly with the property owner, but tenants are liable for any consumption related component of that bill. IN CONFIDENCE Page of . Water organisations will need to be able to contact their customers to communicate any new arrangements, and to bill them for water charges. I am proposing the legislation require s councils to share relevant billing information with water organisations (to enable the identification of ratepayers) , and councils are allowed to charge a reasonable fee for this service. . When a new water organisation is set up, there may be a period in which the obligation to provide water services has been transferred but the necessary billing systems are not yet in place. If this occurs, the council(s) and water organisation will be willing participants who have agreed to the of transfer. It is reasonable to expect they will cooperate to develop any pass through billing arrangements that may be needed. . I do not consider the legislation needs to include transitional provisions to deal with these kinds of billing arrangements. However, there may be situations where a water organisation is formed and begins charging for services part way through a rating ye ar. This may cause issues where rates are charged over the course of the full year, even if the component of the rates related to water charges is calculated based on the part of the year the council provides water services. This may mean that a consumer i s paying for water charges to both a council and a water organisation at the same time. . I am seeking agreement that the legislation can include any technical amendments that are needed to cater for these situations . Unconnected properties . There is a question about whether properties should attract water cha rges where there is no active connection to the water supply. Under current arrangements, the treatment of these properties differs from council to council. In most cases, though, unconnected prop erties that are serviceable by the network are charged water related rates. . I am proposing the legislation allows water organisations to charge a serviceability fee to properties that could be, but are not, connected to the water network. This fee is for the option to connect to the water network, recognis ing that the owners of these properties receive a benefit from the network through increased property values, and from any fire hydrants located nearby. Interaction with the Rates Rebate Scheme . The Rates Rebate Scheme provides support to low income owner occupiers. Just over , households currently receive a rates rebate, about percent of which receive New Zealand Superannuation. The level of subsidy available to a household depends on bo th their income and their rates bill. . Councils administer the Rates Rebate Scheme, and the rebates are funded by the Crown . The a ctual costs of the Scheme fluctuate based on demand , and the Department of Internal Affairs has a statutory obligation to reimburse councils for any rebates granted to eligible ratepayers. C osts for the year were . million and an appropriation of up to million per year is in place for and outyears. . Except for ratepayers in Auckland, who pay water charges to Watercare, water costs are included as part of rates under the current arrangements. The water charges that Watercare issues are not considered rates and so are not eligible for the rates rebate. IN CONFIDENCE Page of . When water charges are split out from rates bills, some recipients of a rates rebate would receive a lower rebate, even though their total expenses (rates and water) may not have changed. This is because under current legislation the rebate would be applie d to the rates bill only, and not the water charges. . I am seeking agreement to amend the definition of rates in the Rates Rebate Act to include water charges. This will mean ratepayers will not receive different levels of rebate depending on whether they are billed for water charges as part of their rates bill, or separately th rough a water organisation. . I am advised th is amendment will result in a per annum increase in the cost of the Rates Rebate Scheme. This reflects that the Crown would need to fund additional rates rebates for Auckland ratepayers, as water charges paid to Watercare would now be considered rates and would be eligible for the rebate . The additional costs can be met from within the existing appropriation for the immediate future, meaning no immediate changes to the Crowns fiscal forecasts are required . However, as the scheme is periodically adjusted for macroeconomic factors, such as CPI, the new definition of rates will impact adjustments required over the longer term. . The proposal will create an additional administrative burden on councils who currently administer the Rates Rebate Scheme as they would have to assess water charges as well as rates bills. To mitigate this, I am proposing that water organisations should be required to share information on the amount of water charges paid by consumer s during the rating year , with the administering council . This would enable a streamlined application and assessment process for eligible ratepayers and councils . Charging for growth by water organisations . Under Local Water Done Well, some councils will choose to shift their water services delivery into separate water organisations. As agreed in my previous paper, these water organisations will be given the power to set their water charges directly and indep endently. . Water organisations will need a specific mechanism to directly charge for new or additional demand on water infrastructure. This will help to achieve financial sustainability, through funding appropriately for growth and keeping water charges to existing r atepayers lower than otherwise. It would also support the Governments housing and urban development objectives. . Wider work is underway by officials from the Minist ry of Housing and Urban Development and the Department of Internal Affairs to improve infrastructure funding settings as part of the Governments Going for Housing Growth policy . . . Until any future policy and legislative changes are made in this respect, I am proposing as an interim measure that water organisations should be enabled to use the development contributions regime in the L GA , with the necessary modifications. . I am seeking agreement that the legislation can enable a flexible approach in which: . water organisations are able to develop their own development contributions policy; ()(b)(ii) ()(f)(iv) IN CONFIDENCE Page of . as an alternative to a separate water organisation development contributions policy, a water organisation and a council within its service area could agree to development contributions set by the water organisation being included in the council s policy; . a council within a water organisations service area can administer the organisations development contributions policy on its behalf . . There will need to be appropriate transitional arrangements , to ensure a smooth transition to charging for the growth related costs of water services infrastructure from a council to a water organisation . . I am also proposing that the Infrastructure Funding and Financing Act be amended so that the Infrastructure Funding and Financing model can be used for water services infrastructure that is to be vested with a water organisation . I note that amendments to this Act to enable it to be used by water organisations will be progressed as part of the Infrastructure Funding and Financing Act Amendment Bill, and not as part of the Local Government Water Services Bill. . I am not proposing that water organisations will be able to charge financial contributions under the Resource Management Act (RMA) . Financial contributions are an unsuitable funding tool for water organisations. It is more appropriate to allow water organisations to recover the costs attributable to growth by charging development contributions instead. Debt collection and powers of receivers relating to water organisations . In my previous paper, I noted that water organisations will need the ability to collect overdue amounts. It was agreed that the legislation will include provisions to the effect that those organisations should rely on commerc ial debt practices to address this. . I also noted that additional options were being explored, and I would provide further advice in this paper. . I am not recommending that water organisations have stronger powers to collect overdue amounts from customers. However, I consider it would be desirable for the legislation to include provisions that deal with situations in which a water organisation itself defaults on a debt. . The LGA and Receiverships Act contain longstanding provisions that allow a receiver to be appointed where a council defaults on a debt. Among other things, a receiver may collect rates to repay the debt. These provisions are a modification of standa rd receivership arrangements that include safeguards reflecting the special character of local authorities for example, a receiver may not act in a way that interferes with services that are essential to public health and safety. They are necessary to pr ovide lenders confidence that, if a local authority defaults on a debt, the lender can recoup the loan. IN CONFIDENCE Page of . The Local Government (Water Services Preliminary Arrangements) Bill contains similar provisions that apply directly to Watercare if it defaults on a debt. These are needed as financial separation of Watercare and Auckland Council will mean that receivers w ill no longer be able to rely on the powers granted to them under the LGA to collect Watercare debts from Auckland Council ratepayers. The receiver will be able to levy water services charges on consumers rather than collect rates, as rating is not possi ble for Watercare. . New water organisations that achieve financial separation from their parent councils will need similar provisions to ensure receivers can act appropriately in the event that a water organisation defaults on a debt. I am proposing the legislation includes provisions that would: . allow the receiver to assess and collect for a given financial year both the amounts owed by the water organisation for that year and the reasonable costs incurred in collecting that amount ; . prohibit the receiver from having any interest or security in water services infrastructure assets; . allow the receiver to collect the amount through water services charges assessed on consumers. Other matters relating to water organisations Enabling e xemptions to be sought from some of the minimum requirements that will apply to water organisations . In my June paper ECO MIN , it was agreed the legislation will include a set of minimum requirements that w ill apply to all water service providers including water organisations, and councils that continue with in house delivery. It was also agreed there will be additional requirements for water organisations , and further requirements for water organisations that involve consumer trusts . . I am aware t here may be situations in which a council s preferred water service delivery arrangements may not meet some of these requirements. For example, one council has already approached me about transferring their water services and assets to an existing, locally owned co operative in their region. The co operative owns and operates the regions electricity distribution network and a fibre o ptic communications network. . The council in question sees several benefits arising from their proposal, including preservation of community ownership and a reflection of the districts distinct community identity, as well as significant benefits from an economic regulation perspective as the lines company is already a regulated entity. This solution shows an innovative approach from a council that is considering alternative options to achieve financial sustainability and accelerate their ability to respond to economic regulation. Howev er, the solution itself does not meet all of the minimum criteria that have been agreed for future water organisations, such as activities of water organisations will be limited to the provision of water services, and directly related activities ECO MIN . IN CONFIDENCE Page of . As important part of Local Water Done Well is providing councils with the flexibility to identify and establish the deliver y arrangements that work for them . However, I also recognis e there are some minimum requirements and expectations that are non negotiable. This is particularly the case with regard to privatisation, which will not be permitted under any circumstances , as well as requirements for financial sustainability and meeting regulatory standards . . To achieve an appropriate balance between these factors , I am proposing the legislation includes a process that enables councils to seek an exemption from some of the minimum requirements that are due to apply to water organisations. This approach w ill allow for a case bycase consideration of each proposal, and maintain a clear set of requirements for water organisations in legislation. . Having a clear process will introduce flexibility into the water organisation requirements and give councils a broader scope to develop their future service delivery arrangements. The flexibility can be balanced by: . limiting the requirements that are eligible for an exemption; . ensuring the appropriate level of approval for exemptions; . the assessment criteria and process associated with considering exemptions. . I am proposing that the ability to seek and grant an exemption w ill apply to the following legislative requirements , only : . water organisations must be companies; . activities of water organisations will be limited to the provision of water services, and directly related activities; . ; . only councils or consumer trusts can be shareholders of a water organisation. . The legislation w ill place further limits on exemptions to ensure that no form of privatisation is permitted. This w ill let councils develop proposals , similar to the energy trust model seen in consumer owned power distribution companies. . Councils w ill be required to submit exemption applications to the Secretary for Local Government (the Chief Executive of the Department of Internal Affairs ). The Secretary will assess applications, and work with the Commerce Commission, Taumata Arowai and Inland Revenue to provide advice to the Minister of Local Government . . The assessment , advice and final recommendations will be based on whether the councils proposal for water services: . meets the legislative objectives of Local Water Done Well; . maintains the core requirements that are nonnegotiable bottom lines for all water organisations , including that the proposal and scope of the exemption do not involve any form of privatisation; . will provide water services that are financially sustainable; ()(g)(i) ()(g)(i) IN CONFIDENCE Page of . satisfies me th at the financial sustainability of water services would be put at greater risk if the exemption were not granted . . Exemption approvals w ill be granted through Order in Council, made on the recommendation of the Minister of Local Government . This w ill provide an appropriate level of Cabinet oversight of decisions that involve exempting councils from statutory requirements as well as public transparency about the outcome of those decisions. . The exemptions process w ill include the ability to as the case may be : . grant an exemption from a requirement through Order in Council; . modify a requirement if a full exemption is not needed; . impose additional conditions on water organisations; . decline the exemption application. . Councils that have an exemption application approved and then go on to rely on that exemption when forming a new water organisation will be required to provide information on this matter on their websites. Transitional tax issues . Currently water services are mostly supplied by councils, which are all primarily exempt from income tax under the Income Tax Act . It is expected that in future some councils will transfer water infrastructure assets, and responsibility to supply water services, to new water organisations. . If councils decide to transfer water services, they will need to consider existing legislation that applies with respect to tax obligations and employees . In the absence of any amendment to tax legislation, this may have tax implications for both the council and water organisation. . The general tax policy approach to facilitating restructuring in response to changes in Government policy is to provide specific transitional tax relief in legislation, with the broad policy objective of enabling reform to be carried out on a tax neutral b asis and to remove any tax consequences arising solely from the restructure. ()(b)(ii), ()(f)(iv) IN CONFIDENCE Page of . Consistent with this approach, I am proposing the legislation includes new provisions that treat the transferor and transferee as the same person for the purposes of the Income Tax Act and Goods and Services Tax Act . This would apply when council s transfer water services to a water organisation, or when water services are transferred from a single council water organisation to a multi council water organisation. This will allow those transfers to occur without triggering income tax or GST conseque nces and provide a tax neutral result. . This is a situation that has been dealt with a number of times in the past, such as the transfer of electricity services in , and the amalgamation of district health boards into Health New Zealand in . . A feature of these examples was that the transfers were mandatory and had to happen within a set period. There is no mandated transfer in the case of water services. I am therefore recommending making the new tax relief provisions available for a period of five years from enactment, as they are intended to be transitional provisions only. Tax status of water organisations . Councils are tax exempt, but are able to form CCOs that are subject to income tax. One of the reasons CCOs pay tax is because they may be operating in areas where they are competing with private enterprise s meaning they should be subject to the same conditions, including being subject to income tax, to allow their performance relative to private enterprise to be compared. . This will not be the case for water organisations, as water services are inherently a monopoly market with a sole provider. . Water organisations will either be owned by one or more councils, one or more consumer trusts, or potentially a combination of the two. I expect councils considering whether or not to transfer water services into a new water organisation will take tax status into account, as income from water services delivered in house by councils is not taxable. . I consider the new water organisations are similar to public purpose Crown controlled companies (e.g., Crown Infrastructure Partners, City Rail Link Limited). An income tax exemption is provided to these companies if the entity : . is solely owned by the Crown, or majority owned by the Crown with only local authorit ies or other tax exempt entities as its other shareholders; . is not engaged primarily in a commercial activity with a profit making objective. . These criteria are applied because the purpose of the exemption is to: . reduce compliance costs for the entity without reducing government revenue or creating economic distortions (meaning there should not be any private sector investors involved to benefit from the exemption ); . to exempt entities whose primary purposes are to assist in carrying out the Governments social objectives, rather than to make profits. General tax rules would continue to apply to any transactions after that timeframe, including existing rules contained in Schedule of the LGA . IN CONFIDENCE Page of . I am proposing to g rant tax exempt status to water organisations . I consider water organisations satisfy the criteria above. While it may be the case that the y will seek to make a profit from their day today operations, this will be for the purpose of funding capital expenditure on water infrastructure. . The prohibition on distributions to shareholders discussed below ensures that private individuals will not be able to receive a private pecuniary benefit or profit from the income tax exemption. . Additionally, if a water organisation is wound up, there will need to be a requirement that assets must be transferred to another water organisation or to a council on wind up. This ensures that a taxable consumer trust or private shareholder would not receive any of the water organisations assets (including any untaxed accumulated gains). . If a council applies for an exemption from a minimum requirement for water organisations (see previous section) , their tax status may be affected if they no longer meet the criteria discussed above. Ability to borrow in foreign currency . The LGA prohibits councils from borrowing in foreign currency, but is silent on whether CCOs are able to do so. In , a legislative amendment was made to allow Auckland Council, and thereby Watercare, to borrow in foreign currency due to its large bo rrowing programmes. . Many water organisations (which may include a form of CCO) will need to borrow significant amounts to meet infrastructure costs. As the total amount of borrowing required for water infrastructure is expected to exceed the amount of New Zealand based lendin g available ), I am proposing the legislation explicitly allows water organisations to borrow in foreign currency. . Water organisations would also be allowed to enter into incidental arrangements, such as derivatives and hedges, which allow water organisations to reduce their exposure to currency volatility. Rateability of land and assets owned by water organisations . I am proposing that land transferred to water organisations should be rateable. I propose the legislation requires land owned by water organisations, and assets that are owned by the organisation but located on or under land the organisation does not own, should be rateable. This aligns with the way that land and assets of other network providers, such as electricity and telecommunications, are rated. . Councils will have the option to remit those rates if they decide that the water organisation, which they will likely be shareholders in, should not have to pay them. ()(g)(i) IN CONFIDENCE Page of . Under the Local Government (Auckland Council) Act , Watercare has bespoke arrangements for rateability of its land and assets. Watercare is not required to pay rates on assets it owns, if those assets are on land that it does not own. Watercare is required to pay rates on land that it owns; however, the rates are subject to a special calculation. These rules relating to land and assets are concessionary towards Watercare and were agree d as part of the negotiations during the formation of the Auckland Co uncil in . I am not recommending changes to these rules for Watercare or extending them to other water organisations. Civil Defence Emergency Management cost sharing arrangements . I am proposing the current Civil Defence Emergency Management cost sharing arrangements with the Crown would apply directly to water organisations. This will ensure financial separation of water organisations and allow them to directly seek partial reimbur sement from the Crown for emergency expenses. . The Civil Defence Emergency Management Act (CDEM Act) enables the Crown, without further appropriation, to reimburse or pay a local authority for expenses it incurs because of an emergency, as long as the criteria in a Government policy in force befor e the emergency occurred are met. This provision of the CDEM Act will need to be amended to also refer directly to water organisations. . Objectives and principles for government financial support are in the National Civil Defence Emergency Management Plan Order (the National Plan), which is secondary legislation. The National Plan will also need to be amended to include water organisat ions. . The current financial arrangements (set by Cabinet) are in Section of the Guide to the National Plan. These arrangements include that, above a threshold, the Crown will partially reimburse local authorities at percent for certain essential infrastruc ture recovery repairs following an emergency (the cost sharing arrangements). . . For instance, the threshold that needs to be met before eligibility for reimbursement is based on a fixed percentage of the capital value of the area of the local authority. How the threshold is calculated will need to be reconsidered to ensure it is appropriate for both water organisations and local authorities after water infrastructure assets have been transferred, and remains fiscally neutral overall for the Crown. . I am seeking agreement that these further policy decisions are delegated to myself, the Minister of Finance, and the Minister for Emergency Management and Recovery.

I am seeking agreement to a set of pricing objectives building on previous considerations and outcomes noted by Cabinet . In the October paper, Further decisions on the three waters reforms CAB MIN , a range of pricing outcomes were set out, but not explicitly agreed by Cabinet. From those outcomes I have developed the following objectives to inform our decisions on pricing and charging. . My proposed objectives are: . Economic efficiency : price s reflect the underlying costs of services and support the financial sustainability of water services entities in the long run. . Affordability : water is an essential service and people on reticulated networks should have access to water services regardless of their financial circumstances. . Price stability : the rates of change in prices are not too high and price changes are clearly signalled in advance and smoothed over time. Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government IN CONFIDENCE Page of . Cost sharing : a key driver of the reforms is to address affordability issues, particularly for customers in smaller communities. Entities could use geographic average pricing to smooth costs across communities, thereby ensuring more affordable services for all. . Horizontal equity : consumers in similar positions pay similar prices. . Intergenerational equity : every generation (which can be thought of as being as small as the annual cohort of ratepayers) should be paying its fair share for assets and not requiring future generations to pay substantially more or less than their fair share through either over or under investment. Historically, funding and water infrastructure investment decisions have tended to favour current over future generations. . Giving effect to Te Mana o te Wai and respecting Treaty of Waitangi principles : pricing can support Te Mana o te Wai by encouraging efficient usage of water. Pricing c an also engage Article of the Treaty and support equitable water service access and quality of service provision. . Consistency with other government goals : pricing issues should support, or at least not undermine, government goals in other domains. For example, growth charges can have an impact on housing goals. Water services pricing can influence levels of water use which affects climate change goals including resilience and adaptation. The Government policy statement is an important tool for achieving this objective. . The October paper also referred to vertical equity, whereby consumers with a higher ability to pay (or more assets) pay progressively more than those with less ability to pay. On further consideration, I consider that a means tested system for generating water bills would be overly complex, expensive to operate and lead to further distortions in pricing. Under the status quo, rating valuations have been used as a proxy for ability to pay but can create inequities as the value of a pro perty is not always well correlated to the wealth or income of the owner. Using means testing or rating valuations would result in complex price structures that do not always relate well to the actual costs of service provision. . For these reasons I prefer affordability, rather than vertical equity, as an objective. I consider the needs of financially distressed consumers in Part B of this paper. Not all the above objectives will be reflected directly in legislation and different policy tools will be used to achieve different objectives.
I consider four councils with Mori wards should not have to hold a poll: Bay of Plenty Regional Council because their Mori constituencies are established under a local Act, not via the Local Electoral Act processes; Waikato Regional Council because their Mori constituencies were established under the previous process in the Act, and there was an opportunity for the public to demand a poll at that time; Wairoa District Council because the council conducted a binding poll at the local elections and the poll was in favour of establishing Mori wards (and is therefore out of scope of this proposal); and ptiki District Council because the Council conducted a (non binding) poll at the local elections, before resolving to establish Mori wards, and that poll was in favour of establishing Mori wards.

ICT incident response The Department plays a role in supporting allofgovernment responses to cybersecurity and privacy incidents, as well as the COVID pandemic. We will continue to lead responses to allofgovernment ICT supplier outages and incidents, provide advice and assurance to Ministers on digital aspects of responses, and assist agencies leading responses by communicating advice and providing support as needed. Local government works collectively to address national objectives At a system level Our Ue te Hntore Local Government Branch aims to achieve a collaborative systemswide, public service approach in which central and local government work together for the benefit of people, communities, business and the environment. Central to our system stewardship role are our Partnership Directors. They have strengthened connections with the sector by building direct relationships with local government chief executives and mayors. They also continue to navigate and make pathways for understanding with local government and iwi Mori. This positive change is critical for the implementation of the Government reform agenda of the Three Waters Reform, Climate Change, the Resource Management Act Reform and the Future for Local Government Review. Future for Local Government Review The Minister of Local Government has established an independent review into the Future for Local Government in response to major reforms under way that will impact the sector. The Review is intended to identify how our system of local democracy and governance needs to evolve to be fit for the future. The Review will run to April . As part of our role as stewards of the local government system, we need to ensure that the reforms afecting local government are integrated and support a coherent system framework, including in its current state and any transition to a future state. This role requires the provision of policy advice to Ministers on the key strategic issues facing the local government sector, building productive partnerships with local government to achieve the Governments policy objectives for the sector, and collaborating with other central government agencies to ensure their work on local government is consistent. Following the major milestones of the Review the Department will undertake work to consider whether and how to progress the Reviews recommendations. Governance and democracy reform The regulatory framework for local government elections needs reform to ensure there is an enduring system in place. The Department will progress a programme of reform that is informed by the Future for Local Government Review. We anticipate that the Future for Local Government Review may also identify other areas of the local authority governance framework where reform should be prioritised. The Department will also complete the work currently under way to make improvements to the process for establishing Mori wards and constituencies. IN CONFI ENCE . I also considered an opton o making any part o a block o Mori land that is unused nonr ateable. I have not proposed this opton, other than where the land has a Ng Whenua Rhui kawenata, as unused land in this case is likely to have a comparatvely low value compared to land that is in use. Making this land nonrateable may have litle impact on the rates assessed. Also there are many examples in back country propertes o arms with partally unused land. It would be difcult to just y an exempton or partally unused Mori land when no such exempton is available or general land. A statutory rates remission process for and under deve opment . I propose we introduce a statutory rates remission process or Mori land under deve lopment. Currently local authorites have considerable discreton over their rate remission policies or Mori land and may not include development remissions in their policies. . A statutory remission process will provide owners o Mori land a right to apply or a rat e remission when land is under development, without having to rely on the local authoritys policy. However, the decision about whether a remission is granted, or how long it is granted, and on what conditons it is granted, will remain with the local authority. This will allow local authorites to apply a natonally consistent approach to their decisions, without each council having to develop its own policy or land under development. . Providing rate remissions during development will allow scarce capital to be devoted to deve loping land, rather than paying rates. Once development is completed, the remission would cease and the land would be rateable in the same manner as any other land. In the long run this will be benefcial to local authorites as it strengthens both their ratng base and their community. . During the development process owners are incurring the costs o development. How ever, the benefts that come rom development, either by occupying the property or housing, or generatng income i the development is or commercial purposes, are unlikely to commence untl development is complete or well advanced. Managing cash fows through the development period is challenging or any land owner and will usually be more so or Mori landowners given the restrictons on mortgaging their propertes to obtain development fnance. . This would be in additon to, rather than in place o , the existng remission policies, whi ch potentally cover a wider range o maters than land development. However, in relaton to remissions or development, the statutory obligatons I propose would take precedence over the local authoritys current policies. . I propose that: . Objectve the objectve o the remission be to acilitate the occupaton, dev elopment and utlisaton o Mori land or the beneft o its owners. This re erences the purpose o the TTWM Act. . Treatng mu tp e Mori and b ocks as one for ratng purposes . I propose that multple blocks o Mori land that come rom the same parent block be tre ated as one or the purpose o calculatng their rates liability, i they are used as one business unit. I there is doubt about whether any partcular block involved in such a proposal comes rom the same parent land block, the local authority may apply to the Registrar o the Mori Land Court or a ruling. This would be implemented on the applicaton o the entty or person using the land. . This will result in the same rates liability or say blocks totalling hectares in area as o ne hectare block. The Far North District Council has taken this approach with some success, including one case where it supported the establishment o an Ahu Whenua trust covering blocks o Mori land. Treatng these blocks as one or ratng purposes reduced the rates rom , to , a year. . Secton o the Ratng Act specifes that two or more ratng units must be treated as onei they are: owned by the same person or persons; and used jointly as a single unit; and contguous or separated only by a road, railway, drain, water race, river, or stream (the contguous test). . Mori land ofen ails to meet this test because progressive ownership succession mea ns blocks rarely have exactly the same ownership. Titles rom the original parent block may also have been alienated, meaning it does not meet the contguous test. Treatng blocks used as one as one ratng unit or ratng purposes will assist in making their development economic, supportng our regional development goals. IN CONFI ENCE An abi ity to write of rates arrears . I propose that the Ratng Act be amended to enable local authorites to write of rates on: all land i it considers the rates are uncollectable; and Mori land only, where successors to interests in a block o land fnd themselves liable or rates debts o deceased owners. . The power would be an administratve power, provided to the chie executve o each loc al authority. To provide protecton rom abuse o the power, local authorites would be required to disclose the amount o rates writen of each year in the notes to fnancial statements in their annual report. . Rates arrears are a signifcant disincentve to Mori landowners engaging with and deve loping their land. The presence o large rates arrears on Mori land inhibits constructve relatonships between local authorites, iwi and Mori landowners. . Successors to interests in a block o Mori land that is in arrears efectvely inherit the arr ears. In the case o general land, i the owner passes away with debts in excess o their assets, the land would be sold and estate creditors sufer the shortall. In the case o Mori land, because o the constraints on its sale, rates arrears are shared among cur rent and uture owners. This presents an impediment to the next generaton o owners developing their whenua. . Local authorites have no statutory authority to write of rates. The LGA provides that elected members o a local authority can be held personally liable i the local authority has intentonally or negligently ailed to en orce the collecton o money it is law ully enttled to receive. The combined efect o these arrangements provides a power ul disincentve or local authorites to write of rates arrears. . The consequence is that local authorites tend to allow uncollected rates to acc umulate, with penaltes accruing, untl they are prevented by statute rom commencing collecton acton. Rates are not statute barred rom collecton untl six years afer the last payment or the various rates instalments or the year. By the tme a rate is statute barred, or every , originally assessed, with accumulated penaltes the outstanding debt will have grown to ,. Since Mori land is over represented in propertes in arrears, this tends to disproportonately infate the size o the r ates arrears actually incurred on Mori land. . Currently the only tool local authorites have to manage arrears are rates remissions. Rem ited rates are shown in the rates records as having been paid by the local authority. Local authorites can be reluctant to remit rates because that can be seen as condoning nonpayment. . While my main concern is with the efect o rates arrears on the development o Mori land, I can see no reason why this power should be constrained only to Mori land. There may be rare cases where collecton o rates on general land is impractcal. In those cases, writng of rates may be more help ul than allowing rates arrears to accumulate untl they are statute barred rom collecton. Sectons to , Local Government Act . IN CONFI ENCE Background Mori and . Mori land is governed by TTWM Act. The preamble to that Act includes the statement it is desirable to recognise that land is a taonga tuku iho o special signifcance to Maori people and, or that reason, to promote the retenton o that land in the hands o its owners, their whanau, and their hap, and to protect whi tapu: and to acilitate the occupaton, development, and utlisaton o that land or the beneft o its owners, their whanau, and their hap. . TTWM Act places a number o restrictons on the ability o owners to deal with Mori land. The land may not be sold without the approval o the Mori Land Court, which is required to prioritse ownership remaining with people with an ancestral relatonship with the land. This makes it impractcal to mortgage the land and precludes the land being sold on the general land market. . Mori land is approximately fve per cent (about . million hectares) o the New Zea land land area and is predominately concentrated in the mid to upper North Island. Mori land is commonly held by multple owners (some blocks have more than , owners). There are about . million interests in , Mori reehold land blocks. The average Mori land block is hectares with owners. Multple ownership creates additonal costs and challenges in achieving consensus or acton, including collectng unds to pay rates. . Mori reehold land tends to be more isolated, in smaller holdings and, less useable than general land: per cent o Mori reehold land is classifed as being o lower quality and only per cent o Mori reehold land is considered suitable or arable use. Up to per cent o land is considered landlocked, and about , ( per cent) o Mori land ttles are smaller than fve hectares, with approximately , ( per cent) being smaller than one hectare. Around a third o the total indigenous vegetaton on private land is on Mori land, with approximately per cent o Mori land having indigenous orest cover. . At the same tme there are many examples o Mori land having been developed into succe ss ul arming units or being used or commercial orestry. Notwithstanding, it has been identfed, through detailed whenua block by block analysis, that there is an opportunity to improve the per ormance o Mori land. This could result in estmated benefts o . billion (present value (PV) million) . billion (PV million) over years, increasing livelihoods and wellbeing derived rom this land. . While much Mori land is in rural setngs, there are signifcant areas o Mori land in some urban communites, especially Tauranga, Rotorua, and Taup and in many smaller communites. Some o this land has been subdivided into house sites while some remains in large blocks that could, i the owners wished and were able, be substantally developed. In those locatons vacant Mori land has the potental to prov ide homes or its owners. The Whenua Mori programme . IN CONFI ENCE Ofce o the Minister o Local Government Ofce o te Minita Whanaketanga Mori Chair Mo ri Crown Relatons: Te Arawhit Commitee Whnau evelopmentThrough Whenua: Ratng Maters Proposal . This paper seeks Cabinet policy approval to amend the Local Government (Ratng) Act (the Ratng Act) to beter enable Mori land owners to develop and use their land, including or housing, and to modernise provisions in the Ratng Act relatng to Mori reehold land (Mori land). Executvesummary . The proposals in this paper represent the next step in our programme o whnau deve lopment through whenua. We have previously agreed to invest . million over our years in a whenua Mori programme to assist owners o Mori land to develop that land. We have also agreed to proposals to amend Te Ture Whenua Mori Act (TTWM Act) to improve outcomes or Mori land owners. . This paper presents a package o ratng measures to: support the development o , and provision o housing on, Mori land; and to modernise ratng legislaton afectng Mori land. . Current ratng practces have long been recognised as an impediment to owners enga ging with and developing their land. In partcular, the accumulaton o rates arrears discourages owners rom ident ying with and putng orward proposals to use their land, or ear the local authority will frst require them to pay of rates arrears. My proposals to address this are to: provide local authorites with a power to writeof arrears; and make unused Mori land (including Mori land protected by a Ng Whenua Rahui kawenata) nonrateable. . Other key elements o my proposal are to: provide a statutory remission process to promote rates remissions or land under development; treat multple Mori land ratng units as one or the purpose o calculatng rates i they are used as one economic unit, which will reduce uni orm charges and lower the overall rates charged; and allow multple homes on a Mori land ratng unit to have separate rate accounts, which will enable the owners to access rates rebates i they meet the requirements or a rebate and simpli y the administraton o rates in those cases. . I also propose some modernisaton o the Ratng Act, including protectng Mori land made general by amendments to the Mori Afairs Amendment Act rom abandoned land or ratng sales. IN CONFI ENCE Other maters . note that the Whenua Mori (Ratng and Other Maters) Bill has a priority in the legislaton programme; and . invite the Minister o Local Government to issue drafing instructons to the Pa rliamentary Counsel Ofce to proceed with this Bill. Authorised or lodgement Hon Nanaia Mahuta Minister o Local Government Mini ta Whanaketanga Mori Page f fdorymq Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government IN CONFIDENCE Appendix A: Financial implications of proposals for local authorities Proposal Implications Writing off arrears. This proposal is an enabling proposal. Local authorities will not be required to writeoff rates, but may choose to do so. Therefore , the financial effects will depend upon t he decisions local authorities make. Important ly, The Department of Internal Affairs expects t hat the proposal will be used to write off rates earlier than would otherwise occur, so t hat the proposal will affect the time at which rates are written off, rather t han t he amount of rates written off. Therefore, there would be no loss of income to local authorities. There would also be a cash flow advantage to local authorities, in that an earlier writingoff of rates will result in an earlier recovery of GST input tax which the local authority has paid to the Inland revenue department when t he rates were originally invoiced. Making unused land and land subject to Nga Whenua Rahui kawenata nonrateable. This type of Maori land is the class of Maori land on which rates collection is the poorest. It includes, but is not limited to, landlocked and inaccessible Maori land. Owners are reluctant to pay rates on this land because t hey derive no economic benefits from the land and are likely to perceive themselves as not receiving benefit from council services. It is likely that local authorities do receive a small amount of income from t his land, so there would be a small financial cost to local authorities of making t his land nonrateable. There would also be an administrative cost to local authorities in identifying unused land and adjusting rating records to apply t he new law. In the cases where a Nga Whenua Rahui kawenata applied to part of a rating unit, the local authority would have to contract its valuation service provider to split the value of t he property between the rateable and nonrateable part of t he property. This would be a desktop exercise, so would have a low cost to process (likely less than per affected rating unit). A key objective of the proposed transition provisions for the Bill would be to provide local authorities with sufficient time to use existing staff resources to carry out this work. Rates remissions for land This is an enabling provision. Local authorities will not be required to under development remit rates when development occurs but may choose to do so. Therefore , the financial effects will depend upon the decisions local authorities make. There is a small risk that if a local authority remits rates, and a development does not proceed, the local authority will be unable to recover t he remitted rates. Treating multiple Maori land blocks as one for rating purposes The amount of uniform charges assessed for each rating unit varies from council to council, and can vary within different parts of a council district. Charges in the order of , per rating unit are common. While the impact on the rates for individual properties is significant, the likely impact of this proposal on local authority incomes is low, because it will take time for owners of Maori land to take advantage of t he opportun ity presented , and many properties are not suited to development. IN CONFI ENCE Supportng the deve opment of housing on Mori and . A key objectve o the Whenua Mori Programme is to promote the use o Mori land byi ts owners or housing. Ratng issues are requently identfed as one o the barriers to housing on Mori land. . I recommend allowing the practce o apportoning rates on a Mori land ratng unit betw een diferent homes and treatng those apportonments as a single ratng unit or the purposes o the rates rebate scheme. This will put owners o homes on Mori land on a level playing feld with other homeowners when it comes to accessing the rates rebate scheme. . Apportonment will make it easier or individual home owners to pay the rates or their home s and or local authorites to collect rates on homes on Mori land. I propose that once rates are apportoned, liability or rates on the home rests only with the home owner. . Strict applicaton o the law means that the owners have to make a collectve arr angement among themselves to collect rates rom the various home occupants on the property, pay it over to the local authority, and manage among themselves the issues that arise where some owners are unable or unwilling to contribute their share. There are many Mori land sites with multple homes on them. The extreme case ofcials have identfed is a site with homes on it. Sites with or more homes are not uncommon. Frequently owners o Mori land aspire not only to build individual homes but communites o homes on their land, where the size o the site permits it. . The current rules around the defniton o a ratng unit ocus on the individual ttle as ther atng unit. Where multple homes exist on one ttle, legally local authorites should keep them in one rate account. An excepton occurs where an occupaton order has been made under s o TTWM Act. Such an order provides the owner in whose avour the order is made exclusive use and occupaton o the whole or any part o that land as a site or a house. . I do not regard reliance on occupaton orders as a conclusive soluton to the admi nistratve problems in ratng multple homes on Mori land. Applicants have to incur costs in making such applicatons and may not be success ul. The Court may only make an order i it is satsfed that there is a sufcient degree o support or the applicaton among the owners. With multple owners who may be geographically spread ar and wide, obtaining the necessary owner support or an order may be logistcally impossible. . I note that currently there is no obligaton on the Mori Land Court to not y the rel evant territorial authority when an occupaton order is made or changed. I propose a minor amendment to TTWM Act to require the Court to not y the territorial authority o any new or changed occupaton orders so that the territorial authority can ulfl its obligatons under the Ratng Valuatons Act . Modernisingthe RatngAct . My ofcials research has shown that much o the current law relatng to Mori land ratng is litle changed rom the Mori Land Ratng Act . IN CONFI ENCE knowledge or consent. The Amendment Act was repealed in but afected land rem ained as general land. The retenton o Mori land in Mori ownership is o undamental importance, and this is refected in TTWM Act. Had this land not been converted to general land by the Amendment Act, it would have retained its status o Mori reehold land and there ore maintained its protecton rom abandoned land and ratng sales. The efects o the Amendment Act were raised as a signifcant issue in hui around the country during the Shand Inquiry. . A Cabinet paper estmated the amount o afected land to be , hectares. The pa per noted that incomplete records made it difcult to accurately measure the amount o afected land. . The Ratng Act provides local authorites two routes to collect rates on general land. Whe re land has been abandoned, it can apply to the District Court or approval to sell the land. It can also apply to the High Court or permission to conduct a ratng sale. It is there ore necessary to close of both sale avenues to efectvely protect this land rom urther sale. . I recently enquired o local authorites o abandoned land sales in train. I consider it is contrary to the Crowns Treaty obligatons to allow these sales to contnue. . Finally, both statutory provisions allow local authorites to lease land to recover rate arr ears rather than sell it. My ofcials have been unable to ident y any situaton where local authorites have leased rather than sold land to collect arrears. However, leasing land without owner agreement is also a orm o alienaton and could create urther complicatons about compensaton or improvements made by lessees i the owners were identfed and wished to reengage with their land. . I am sympathetc to local authorites wish to collect rates on this land, partcularly whe re an adjoining land owner is actually using the land and deriving economic beneft rom it. For Mori land, the person using the land is liable or the rates unless the land is vested in trustees. . There ore, I have proposed that or ratng purposes only, local authorites may treat land as Mori land or the purposes o collectng rates rom a person other than the owner. This will allow local authorites to charge an occupier or rates on this land. C arifying trustees ob igatons . The Ratng Act provides that, i trustees are liable to pay rates, the trustees are liable or rates only to the extent o the money derived rom the land. From tme to tme local authorites are advised by trustees that the money derived rom the land is insufcient to pay the rates. Currently they have no means o veri ying that claim. . I propose that we add a provision to the Ratng Act that where trustees state there is insufc i ent money derived rom the land to pay the rates, they must, i requested by the local authority, provide copies o any accounts provided to benefciaries to support that claim. Land is considered abandoned i rates have been unpaid or three years or more and: the ratepayer is unknown; cannot be ound afer due inquiry and has no known agent in New Zealand; is deceased and has no personal representatve; or has given notce to the local authority that he or she has abandoned the land. I propose that both the LGA and the Rating Act be amended to include the purpose statement of TTWM Act as the purpose of their specific provisions relating to Maori land rating. The purpose statement for the TTWM Act states it is desirable to recognise that land is a taonga tuku iho of special significance to Maori people and, for that reason, to promote the retention of that land in the hands of its owners, their whanau, and their hapu, and to protect wahi tapu: and to facilitate the occupation, development, and utilisation of that land for the benefit of its owners, their whanau, and their hapu. . Inclusion of purpose statements in statutes is an important way for Parliament to signal what legislation is intended to achieve. Section () of the Interpretation Act states The meaning of an enactment must be ascertained from its text and in the light of its purpose. Hence purpose statements can assist users and the Courts in determining the meaning of particular statutory provisions. . While the absence of purpose statements has not directly contributed to the current problems with the rating legislation , I consider inclusion of purpose statements will encourage users of the legislation to think about the application of the specific provisions relating to Maori land in a constructive manner. . I intend, subject to advice from Parliamentary Counsel, that this would be done by adding a further clause to the overall purpose of the Rating Act and to the purpose of local authority revenue and finance policies. IN CONFIDEN CE Proactively released by the Minister for the Community and Voluntary Sector Office of the Minister for the Community and Voluntary Sector Chair Cabinet Legislation Committee Charities Amendment Bill: Approval for Introduction Proposal I am seeking Cabinets agreement to introduce the Charities Amendment Bill. The Charities Amendment Bill is intended to be introduced in September and passed by June . Executive Summary This paper seeks Cabinets agreement to introduce the Charities Amendment Bill (the Bill). The Bill summarises a suite of proposed chang es to the Charities Act (the Act) to modernise the Act and ensure it supports charities to thrive, while ensuring sufficient public transparency. The Bill makes legislative amendments, and includes the provisions to: . Enable reduced financial reporting requirements for very small charities to mitigate compliance burden; . Clarify who an officer is and their role, and measures to improve governance; . Clarify and improve compliance and enforcement under the Act; . Increase the transparency and fairness of regulatory decision making by the Chief Executive of the Department of Internal Affairs and the Charities Registration Board ; and . Introduce a simpler appeals mechanism by e mpowering the Taxation Review Authority to hear appeals under the Act. Subject to Cabinets agreement, I intend to introduce the Bill in September . I expect that the Government will refer the Bill to be scrutinised by the Social Services and Community committee later this year. I expect that the Bill will be passed by June , subject to other Government priorities. Under the Charities Act, regulatory functions are split between two bodies, the independent Charities Registration Board and the Chief Executive of the Department of Internal Affairs . While the Board is responsible for all registration and deregistration decisions, it delegates most decisions to Charities Services (under delegat ion from the Chief Executive under the Act).
