IN CONFIDENCE Allocation of decision making powers The Bill will expand the TRA , an existing tribunal, to take on a new function to hear appeals under the Charities Act . This new function requires the allocation of several decision making powers including confirming, modifying, or reversing the decision of the original decision maker; exercising powers of the original decision maker; making orders ; regulating its procedures ; conducting hearings ; hearing evidence; awarding costs; and stating cases for the High Court. These powers are consistent with the current powers of the TRA . The Bill provides the Chief Executive of the Department of Internal Affairs with a power to exempt very small charities in tier from meeting the XRB standard for reporting. The power could only be used to exempt charities that are defined by financial thresholds in regulations. The financial thresholds will then be subject to my recommendation as the Minister for the Community and Voluntary Sector. Associated regulations Regulations associated with the TRA may be made to enable the procedures for appeals to an Authority under the Charities Act. These regulations will include notice of claim requirements, filing fees and directions hearing procedures. These regulations will be completed within months of enacting the Bill, to align with the commencement of the appeals provisi ons. The drafting task of developing these regulations will be small as the policy and drafting on the procedures for appeals has already been completed. Regulations may be created for reducing reporting requirements for very small charities. These regulations w ould include setting maximum financial thresholds that will determine whether a charity qualifies as a very small tier chari ty. These financial thresholds will relate to the total amount of assets, and the total annual operating expenditure, o f any given charitable entity. I currently consider that appropriate thresholds to determine what a very small charity would be total assets of less than , and total expenditure of less than ,. The timing for the development of th ese regulations is largely dependent on the outcome of the XRBs consultation. If regulations are made to reduce reporting requirements, these will require consultation with the sector. Other instruments The Bill does not include any other instruments. Definition of Ministerdepartment The Bill does not contain or alter a definition of Minister, Department or Chief Executive of a department. IN CONFIDENCE Proactively released by the Minister for the Community and Voluntary Sector Charities currently report to one of four tiers developed by the XRB. The four tiers are based on the charities annual expenses or operating expenditure of its previous two financi al years. Each tier has its own standard with more rigorous reporting required from larger charities, while smaller charities can use more simplified reporting. Even the current simplified reporting can be burdensome for the smallest charities , which are often volunteer run and time poor. To minimise the compliance burden while balancing the benefit of transparent reporting, Cabinet has agreed to provide the ability to exempt very small charities from reporting to the XRB standard. These charities would instead report basic financial information in their annual return CAB MIN . The XRB are aware of the compliance burden on small charities and are currently consulting on proposed changes to Tier and notforprofit reporting . The objective of this work aligns with Cabinets agreement to reduce the compliance burde n on small charities. However, findings from the XRB consultation will not be available until after the consultation period, which ends on September . I have therefore included the exemption power in the Bill, in the instance the outcome of the XRB consultation does not align with this policy change. My officials will continue to work with XRB on developments following their consultation. Financial implications Th is paper does not seek new funding . As part of Budget , the Government announced funding to expand the Taxation Review Authority to hear charities appeals and fund the associated legal costs expected with a more accessible appeals body. Budget funding was also secured to cover fees for the two new Charities Registration Board members, and one FTE to support the enhanced regulatory decision making processes. IN CONFIDENCE Proactively released by the Minister for the Community and Voluntary Sector Background The Bill will modernise the Charities Act The Charities Act (the Act) provides a registration, reporting and monitoring system for entities that carry out charitable purposes and therefore have a public benefit. Registering for charitable status brings several benefits, including eligibility for tax exemptions and funding opportunities. The Act is a key piece of legislation for the not forprofit sector. The charitable sector is diverse, ranging from large iwi organisations, churches and education providers to local providers of social services, toy libraries and sports clubs. Since the Act was introduced in , the sectors operating environment has changed; including the disestablishment of the Charities Commission in and changes to the financial reporting requirements for charitable entities in . Cabinet commissioned work to modernise the Act in to ensure it was fit for purpose and suited the needs of the charitable sector SWC MIN . The fundamentals of the Act were noted to be sound. In March , Cabinet agreed to a rescoping of the programme to focus primarily on making practical improvements to the Act SWC MIN . Policy There are several policy proposals given effect to in the Bill In February , Cabinet agreed to policy proposals (outlined in Table ) to amend the Act to support charities to thrive, while ensuring sufficient public transparency CAB MIN . The Bill gives effect to the legislative changes agreed to by Cabinet and is attached as Appendix A . Cabinet also authorised me to make minor and technical changes that align with the policy intent. IN CONFIDENCE.In line with coalition agreements, I propose councils that do not disestablish or rescind a decision to establish Mori wards will have to follow a binding poll process. . I consider that there are two key variables for possible polls on Mori wards: .. Timing: Whether the outcome of any polls should apply from the or local elections; and .. Prompt: Whether polls should be imposed on councils or occur only if communities effectively petition their councils . . I have considered four options to meet the coalition agreements that reflect different combinations of decisions on timing ( or local elections) and prompt (petition or no petition) : Option A: the outcome of polls take effect at the local elections after a mandatory poll in late ; Option B: the outcome of polls take effect at the local electionsfollowing a petitions process in late and polls in early ; Option A: the outcome of polls take effect at the local elections after a mandatory poll at the local elections ; and Option B: the outcome of polls take effect at the local elections following a petitions process in early and polls at the local elections . . T hese options and their risks are detailed below. . Option A is my preference. This option has l ower cost s for councils, as poll s held alongside the elections will be less expensive than standalone polls. This option also carries less implementation risk, as councils will have more time to implement the poll results and reconfigure their representation arrangements prior to them taking effect . However, this choice means the poll outcome will apply later, from the elections . . A list of the councils that will be affected by these proposals and four councilsthat I consider should not have to hold a poll is attached at Appendix C. Option A: the outcome of polls take effect at the local elections after a mandatory poll in late . This option would require councils to hold a poll in late if the y did not hold one when originally establishing Mori wards since . The result of this poll would be binding and determine if a council has a Mori ward (s) for the elections. These polls will take councils approximately three months to conduct. . Following mandatory polls in late , some councils will need to complete arepresentation review prior to election processes starting in April . This doesnot allow enough time for the standard representation review process . I propose Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government IN CONFIDENCE IN CONFIDENCE that, if the poll results mean a representation review is required, councils be allowed to complete a truncated representation review. This shortened representation review process will remove the Local Government Commissions appeal function. Councils will make the final decisions on their representation arrangements. . Remov ing the appeal function carries some risk that councils may fail to comply with legislative provisions, as well as risks of missed opportunities for enhancing effective representation of communities , or of incumbent councillors manipulating representation arrangements. To mitigate the non compliance aspect, I propose that the Commission be given a legislated role to provide technical guidance to councils going through this shortened representation review process. These councils will also be required to carry out a standard representation review in the next term of local government. . A no outcome in the polls will have different effects for the two categories of councils : .. Councils that established Mori wards without having held a poll would have a choice to either use their previous representation arrangements from before the establishment of Mori wards ( if viable to us e or population figures) or complete the truncated representation review process described above . .. Councils that resolved to establish Mori wards in the local government term would be able to keep their current representation arrangements or undertake the truncated representation review process. These councils will also have to complete a truncated representation review if the outcome of the poll is yes. Option B: the outcome of polls take effect at the local elections following a petitions process in late and polls in early . For the councils that have resolved to establish Mori wards since , without holding a poll, this option would allow electors to petition their council in late to hold a poll in early . The results of these polls would be reflected at the local elections. . Because of the timeframes of this option, councils would not have time to undertake a representation review and would instead only have time to make a resolution on their representation arrangements. This removes: .. the public submissions process; and .. the Local Government Commission appeals process. . Councils would have approximately six weeks to make their final decisions by early April , shortly before election processes begin. . This option has significant risk due to the tight timeframes for petitions, polls , and representation arrangement decisions , and there being no community consultation on representation arrangements. Impact analysis Regulatory impact statement s . The Department of Internal Affairs Regulatory Impact Analysis panel (the panel) has reviewed the completed RIA in accordance with the quality assurance criteria in the CabGuide and considers that the information and analysis in: The RIS Changing timelines to enable local elections to be delivered(Appendix A) meets the quality assurance criteria. The RIS Binding polls on the establishment of Mori wards (Appendix B) partially meets the quality assurance criteria. . The panel made the following statement about the information and analysis in theRIS Binding polls on the establishment of Mori wards : .. The RIA was developed within a very tight, ministerially set, timeframe to deal with the implementation of Government a coalition commitment to undo legislative changes made by the previous government. These factors ()(f)(iv) ()(h) ()(h) Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government IN CONFIDENCE IN CONFIDENCE limited the analysis and consultation that could be undertaken and the evidence available. They also required the policy problem and objectives that underlie the commitment to be backfilled . .. While these limitations are acknowledged in the RIA, their consequences could be stated more clearly and explicitly addressed. .. While the panel found the identification of policy objectives related to the stated policy problem, and the development and use of criteria based on those objectives to be useful, there was insufficient analysis of the relative value of Mori wards as a mechanism for meeting effective representation objectives. As a result, the panel did not feel the application of the criteria provided a compelling assessment of the policy commitment against the status quo. .. In relation to the transitional application of the poll provisions to existing Mori ward decisions, the panel did not believe the use of similar criteria was appropriate to assessing process and timing options to achieve the Governments objective. The panel did not find the Departments preference for the status quo to be useful in this context and felt more explicit exploration of the relative cost, timing, and process implications of the options considered (for instance, the impact on the integrity of representation reviews) would have enabled a more useful comparison of the relative merits of the other options. .. On this basis, the panel felt that the RIA failed to fully meet the complete and convincing criteria prescribed by Cabinet. The context within which the proposals were developed also precluded any meaningful consultation with affected parties. This is acknowledged in the RIA which does include some evidence of stakeholder views from previous consideration of the underlying issues. Climate implications of policy assessment . The Climate Implications of Policy Assessment (CIPA) team ha s been consulted and confirms that the CIPA requirements do not apply to these proposals as the threshold for significance is not met. More work needs to be done to determine if the proposals in this paper are consistent with the rights and freedoms affirmed in the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act and the Human Rights Act . Reinstating polls on the establishment of Mori wards may raise issues of discrimination on the basis of ethnicity. A final determination will be possible when the legislation is drafted. Use of external resources . No external resources were used during the development of these proposals . Consultation . The following agencies were consulted during the development of these proposals : the Ministry of Justice, the Electoral Commission, Statistics NZ, Land Information New Zealand, officials from the Local Government Commission, Parliamentary Counsel Office, Te Arawhiti , and Te Puni K kiri. The Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet (Policy Advisory Group) and the Treasury were informed. Only officials from the Local Government Commission were consulted on Options B and A in this paper. . The Ministry of Justice has raised concerns about the remov al under Option A and B of the role of the Local Government Commission in hearing appeals in the proposed truncated representation review process . . Statistics NZ ha s raised concerns about the ability under Option A and Option B for councils to roll back to pre Mori ward representation reviews because of population data accuracy issues and difficulties where statistical boundaries have changed in the meantime. Department of Internal Affairs officials are currently working with St ats NZ officials to see how this risk can be mitigated. . Due to the time constraints, consultation with the local government sector has been very limited so far. L ocal Government New Zealand ( LGNZ ), Taituar, election service providers, and NZ Post (and their business division Datam) have been consulted on the proposed changes to election timeframes and are supportive of these changes . . There has been no public consultation and no consultation with iwi and Mori. Legislative timeframes mean this will not be possible before the Bill is introduced. Statistics NZs implementation concerns also apply to this option. Option A: the outcome of polls take effect at the local elections after a mandatory poll at the local elections . For the councils that have resolved to establish Mori wards since , without holding a poll, this option would require councils to hold a poll at the local elections. . If the results of a poll require a representation review these would be undertaken under standard timeframes and processes in the term of local government. Option B: the outcome of polls take effect at the local elections following a petitions process in early and polls at the local elections . For the councils that have resolved to establish Mori wards since without holding a poll, this option would allow electors to petition their council tohold a poll at the local elections. A petition in early by at least per cent of electors would require a council to hold a binding poll alongside the local elections to determine if councils have Mori wards at the localelections. . If the results of a poll require a representation review these would be undertakenunder standard timeframes and processes in the term of local government. Special case: Tauranga City Council . The Tauranga City Council c ommission ers resolved last term to establish Mori wards for these elections without having held a poll . Because the Tauranga City Councils term begins in July , I propose that the Council be allowed to make a resolution to disestablish its Mori wards before the elections. If the council does not disestablish, it will be required to either hold a poll or accept petitions for a poll before the elections . Mori wards provide for dedicated, elected representation for New Zealanders on the Mori electoral roll . . Legally privileged An urgency application has been filed in the Waitangi Tribunal regarding these policies . As part of a broader claim relating to policies in the Coalition Governments Day Plan, it asserts that restoring binding polls on Mori wards breaches the Treaty and its principles. The Tribunal is currently considering whether the claim is suitable for an urgent hearing. Fixing postal voting timeframes Background . Under the Local Electoral Act there is a . day voting period for postal voting in local elections. Under the Local Electoral Regulations , all postal voting papers must be delivered in the first six days of the voting period. Responsibility for meeting this statutory requirement sits with local electoral officers. NZ Post provides almost all the postal services for local elections. . NZ Post has struggled to deliver voting papers within the six day window in recent elections. NZ Post has now informed the Department of Internal Affairs that it will take up to two weeks to complete nationwide delivery of voting papers for local elections for the and future local elections. This creates a risk that some voters will not have a reasonable opportunity to cast their vote. Proposal: Adjust statutory timeframes of local elections processes . I propose extending the voting period so that the delivery period for postal papers can increase from six to calendar days. The statutory for the close of voting will remain as the second Saturday in October every three years. . The extra time will come from shifting a number of statutory timeframes for local elections , including a slightly shortened nomination period and shifting the cut off for electors to be included on the printed roll earlier. . At the same time as extending the delivery period to enable people to receive their votes, I propose some other small adjustments to statutory dates to address some lingering issues in the local electoral timeframe. This will allow more time to print voting papers, and starting the mailout earlier in the week so any mistakes identified do not have to be fixed over a weekend. These timeframes would also apply to by elections and polls, where applicable. Further policy decisions may be required . The policy proposals above have been developed under time constraints in order to meet the goal of having these changes apply from the local elections. It is likely that I will need to seek a number of further policy decisions from Cabinet at the same time as seeking approval to introduce this Bill. INCONFIDENCE To mitigate the risks around spoofing, D aons technology includes D facial liveness detection . This is intended to ensure that the face presented is a genuine live and present individual. .. Key stage limitation To reduce the risk of a brute force attempt, limits are in place at each stage of the process . An individual in a session may only make a limited number of attempts to enter correct identity details matching those contained within an identity document , and may only make a limited number of attempts at the passive liveness challenge before they are subject to a hour lock out. The limited number of attempts within the process reduces malicious attempt s to spoof liveness and to learn from previous failed attempts. Any individual who fails to confirm their identity within these session limitations will have to try again later after the lockout period has elapsed , if allowed by the requesting organisation, or use another method such as presenting their physical identity documents in person at a requesting organisations offices. . The privacy statement and Terms of Use are displayed on the DIA interface. The privacy statement varies depending on the requesting organisation utilising the Identity Check service. The individual is also provided a link to the Terms of Use for the Identity Check service which include s an acknowledgement of the privacy statement. The individual is not able to proceed until they have agreed to the Identity Check Terms of Use. At any time whilst using the Identity Check service the individual can access the privacy statement via a link at the bottom of the screen. Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs
INCONFIDENCE .. Collection whilst using the service The individual is asked to provide details of their identity document . They select the document they would like to use then provide the following information as contained on the document: document number document version number (driver licence only) name of birth . Once it has been confirmed that the information provided is valid and the document meets the validity requirement and is not lost or stolen , the individual is asked to provide access to their devices camera to take a live photo when prompted. If they do not provide access, then they will not be able to proceed to use the Identity Check service. Prior to the passive liveness check commencing a sample of the ambient light is made . If the light conditions are not sufficient the individual is advised to move to another location. The next stage is a passive liveness check, the individual is provided instructions on how to complete the passive liveness check. When the individual is ready to begin they will push a button to start, and a live photo is collected . A still photograph (selfie) is extracted from one of the frames within the live photo along with a series of other comparison frames. The individual is not able to review the selfie. The selfie and comparison frames are processed by the liveness engine. The selfie is also compare d to the document image held by DIA or Waka Kotahi. If the individual fails the passive liveness check, they can reattempt the passive liveness check a further four times. Therefore, one session may result in multiple sets of comparison frames and selfies being captured. .. Collection of driver licence information from Waka Kotahi If the individual selects to use their New Zealand driver licence for their identification, then DIA will first confirm the provided driver licence information with Waka Kotahi using the Driver Licence Verification Service.

Metadata For each use of the Identity Check service a new session is created, metadata about the timing of events of each stage of the process are captured by the I dentity Check service . A transaction ID is also collected from the requesting organisation when the individual is transferred to the Identity Check service. This transaction ID is used to allow the requesting organisation and DIA to know theyre communicating about the same individual for the purposes of that Identity Check transaction. An Identity Check ID is also created by DIA which is also shared with the requesting organisation to enable identification of the relevant successful transaction . .. Use of the live photo The live photo will be used to select the appropriate frame for creation of the selfie and extraction of the comparison frames. The live photo will not be used by DIA for any purpose other than offering individuals the ability to confirm their identity to the requesting organisation . .. Use of the comparison frames A series of comparison frames are taken from the live photo automatically . These images are used to enable passive liveness detection. The comparison frames will not be used by DIA for any purpose other than offering individuals the ability to confirm their identity to the requesting organisation. .. Use of the selfie A still photograph (selfie) is taken from the live photo automatically. The selfie is used for passive liveness detection and is compared with the relevant photograph from the selected identity document. The selfie will not be used by DIA for any purpose other than offering individuals the ability to confirm their identity to the requesting organisation. .. INCONFIDENCE . Accuracy .. Ability to compare accurately The facial recognition algorithm is provided by Dao n and configured by DIA based on recommendations by Daons biometric experts. Information related to the accuracy of the algorithm as independently assessed by NIST through their FRVT program is available at https:pages.nist.govfrvthtmlfrvt.html . The configuration of the system is weighted towards providing a negative comparison result if there is any doubt to ensure robust evidence of identity. The NIST results indicate with a configured threshold to accept in million chance of a false accept, they see a false reject of in every attemp ts. As DIA allow multiples attempts , this would approach closer to in , chance of a false reject in three attempts. In real world operation m any factors affect the effectiveness of facial recognition systems. Lighting conditions, like variations in light and shadow, can distort facial features and make details less visible. The angle and pose of the face also matter, as non frontal or obstructe d views can be challenging. Changes in appearance due to age ing, weight fluctuations, and cosmetic alterations can complicate matching. Movement during image capture or in real time can blur facial images, reducing system effectiveness. Additionally, image quality, resolution, noise, and compression artifacts can hinder accurate extraction and analysis of facial features. Considering these factors is crucial for developing reliable facial recognition technologies. The Identity Check process and thresholds attempt to account for these factors through customer interaction and tuning. DIA has completed testing of the facial recognition algorithm with real users. While the sample size was limited the results reflected those of the NIST testing . .. Passive Liveness detection The passive liveness algorithm is provided by Daon and configured by DIA based on recommendations by Daons biometric experts. The effectiveness of the algorithm has independently been reviewed by iBeta. iBeta is nationally accredited as a test lab by the National Voluntary Lab Accreditation Program (NVLAP Testing Lab Code ) to the requirements of ISOIEC : (General requirements for the competence of testing and calibration laboratories). They are an expert in the field of biometrics. The iBeta results showed the systems performed accurately during their testing. DIA has completed testing of the liveness algorithm with real users. W hile the sample size was limited the results reflected those of the iBeta test. .. Human oversight There is currently no ongoing human oversight as part of the photograph comparison process. However, DIA are currently exploring the need to set up a project to review the previous comparisons completed over a period. This work is intended to input into the enhancement roadmap for the product, for example if people wearing glasses are unable to use the service successfully more often instruction may be provided to remove an individuals glasses before utilising the service. .. INCONFIDENCE . Executive Summary .. Introduction The Identity Check service is provided by DIA Service Delivery and Operation s to provide quick and convenient identity verification. Individuals are directed to the service from other organisations needing to confirm the individuals identity . Given that people are seeking services it is critical that barriers to access services are reduced. One such barrier for applicants is establishing their identity. The Identity Check service leverages technology to provide remote identity verification, without individuals being required to visit a requesting organisations premise s or to have a RealMe Account. The tool uses facial recognition technology and evidence of passive liveness (to prove that the captured live photo is a person and is not, for example , a deep fake ). At the start of the Identity Check process the individual is advised how the service works and what they will need to do. They are asked to provide consent to share the results with the requesting organisation for the purposes of verifying their identity. An individual using the Identity Check service is required to complete two initial steps : Provision of their identity document information Completion of a passive liveness check. The identity document details are compared to the information held in the relevant identity document database . Then the liveness check is completed using a series of comparison frames from the live photo captured. A still photograph (selfie) is also automatically extracted from the live photo , and the selfie captured is compared to the photograph held in the relevant identity document database. Currently , supported identity documents are New Zealand passports and New Zealand driver licences. When an individual is using a New Zealand passport as their identity document, the confirmation to the requesting organisation is authorised under the I ICA. When an individual uses a New Zealand driver licence as their identity document, the details are confirmed to DIA with the consent of the individual using Waka Kotahi NZ Transport Agencys Driver Licence Verification Service. When the identity document details (from either their passport or driver licence ) match the information provided and a successful passive liveness check and photographic comparison has been completed , then the following information is provided to the requesting organisation: the transaction number confirmation the individual passed the passive liveness check confirmation of a successful result from the identity document photograph comparison the full name the of birth if applicable, the selfie . .. Assuming all planned controls are implemented and functioning effectively , there are no zone one risks and t wo zone two risks . INCONFIDENCE . Project S ummary .. Problem Statement The Identity Check service is provided by DIA Service Delivery and Operation s to provide quick and convenient verification of an individuals identity . Individual s are directed to the service from other organisations needing to confirm the individuals identity . Given the individuals using the service are seeking services , it is critical that barriers to access services are reduced. One such barrier for individuals is establishing evidence of identity. If an individual wishes to obtain services from a requesting organisation , the individual may currently be required to visit the requesting organisation in person to confirm their identity through the provision of physical identity documents , prior to being able to obtain services . A key component of organisations being able to take services fully online is the requirement to be able to confirm an individuals identity online . The purpose of the Identity Check service is to increase the ability for individuals to complete all interactions online. Organisations utilising Identity Check are required as part of their contract with DIA to provide at least one other method for individuals to confirm their identity. Individuals must still be able to confirm their identity in person if the y desire. .. Identity Check Service The Identity Check service is provided by DIA Service Delivery and Operations . Individual s are directed to the service from requesting organisations . This release of the Identity Check service will enable verification that the individual using the device is the same person as the individual whose identity document details were provided . The individual s details, passive liveness confirmation and photograph comparison result are sent to the requesting organisation with consent from the individual . Certain requesting organisations will also be provided with the individuals selfie with their consent , where the requesting organisation has a business purpose for receipt, such as inclusion of the selfie on a physical card being issued. The Identity Check service currently allows verification of an individuals identity using either a New Zealand passport or New Zealand driver licence . The individual chooses which identity document they wish to use . If a New Zealand passport is used it must be current or less than two years expired , and not be reported lost or stolen. If a New Zealand driver licence is utilised it must be current and not reported lost or stolen. The service is underpinned by a passive liveness and facial recognition solution provided by Daon and hosted in a DIA tenancy at Datacom New Zealand. INCONFIDENCE . PIA Scope This PIA covers : confirming the identity of individuals using their New Zealand passport or New Zealand driver licence . provision of the individual s details, passive liveness confirmation , and photograph comparison result to the requesting organisation with the consent of the individual. provision of the individuals selfie to the requesting organisation with the consent of the individual . delivery of the Identity Check service direct to the requesting organisation. This PIA does not cover : consideration of how the requesting organisation will utilise the individual s details and selfie once confirmed by DIA. the processes used by the requesting organisation for confirming the identity of individual s who do not utilise or are unsuccessful in using the Identity Check service. . Applicable Legislation .. Privacy legislation The Identity Check service is primarily intended for use by individuals within New Zealand and the service will be provided by a New Zealand Government agency therefore the New Zealand Privacy Act will apply. Currently the terms of use prohibit use of Identity Check by individuals outside of New Zealand. Therefore, this limit s exposure to additional overseas privacy legislation. .. Identity Information Confirmation Act The IICA governs the use of confirmation services. The IICA defines a confirmation service as one which confirms identity information of an individual to : contribute to the prevention of a crime (particularly identity related crimes) and ensure that agencies can use and, if necessary, record confirmed identity related information. Identity information is defined in the IICA as including New Zealand passport related information but not New Zealand driver licence information. The IICA is not a complete code and information that is not covered by it can still be shared, but that sharing needs to be lawful in its own right. Where there is an inconsistency between the IICA and other relevant legislation, including the Privacy Ac t and the Passports Act , the IICA prevails (s of the IICA). This means where the IICA applies, it needs to be complied with where it deviates from the requirements of that other legislation . Because the purpose of the Identity Check s ervice is to confirm the identity of the individual for a requesting organisations purposes, it falls within the definition of a confirmation service when a New Zealand passport is used for verification purposes . Therefore, where the IICA applies (the sharing of passport details, other personal information and the result of the identity verification) the IICA needs to be complied with. Where other personal information is shared that sits outside the IICA (the driver licenc e confirmation ), sharing needs to be lawful in some other way, for example, by being authorised in accordance with the Privacy Act . Land Transport Act The Land Transport Act (LTA) sets out the responsibilities and general requirements for all individual s in the land transport system and associated agencies such as Waka Kotahi. The LTA includes a requirement that all drivers must be licensed. It also governs the issuance and management of driver licences and the licensing system. The LTA requires that d river licences have a photographic image of the holder (s()) . Whilst there are tight restrictions on the access to d river licence images (s), the LTA expressly provides for the use of d river licence images for the purpose of verification of a persons identity by DIA (s() ). Therefore, the LTA directly provides for a service, such as Identity Check , that permits DIA to use driver licence photo graph s to verify the identity of a particular individual when facilitating an identity verification service for other organisatio ns. INCONFIDENCE . Architecture .. High level process The Identity Check service involves an identity verification workflow which includes several key stages : the individual consents to the results being shared with the requesting organisation. the individual chooses the type of identity document they would like to use to confirm their identity. the individual enters their identity document details as contained on their identity document. the identity document details are either retrieved from the New Zealand passport database or queried with NZTA and confirmed to match those provided. a live photo is captured of the individual. a still photograph (selfie) and a series of comparison frames are taken from the live photo and used to complete a passive liveness challenge to provide assurance that the live photo is of a live and present individual . the selfie is compared to the photograph held in relat ion to the identity document provided . A back end record stores each attempted Identity Check verification and the outcomes of each stage. If multiple live photos are captured as part of the process , each series of selfies and comparison frames will be stored. The live photo is not stored. Where a successful verification is made the Identity Document Federated ID is stored . .. INCONFIDENCE Full Impact Statement Template Coversheet : Progressing Digital Identity : Establishing a Trust Framework Advising agencies Department of Internal Affairs Decision sought Approval to proceed with the preferred option Proposing Ministers Minister for Government Digital Services Minister of Internal Affairs Summary: Problem and Proposed Approach Problem Definition What problem or opportunity does this proposal seek to address Why is Government intervention required New Zealand lacks consistently applied standards and processes for sharing, storing and using personal and organisational information in a digital environment. As a result, systems and services have been developed in an unstructured and inconsis tent manner that creates inefficiencies, increases security and privacy risks and hinders interoperability. This is undermining consumer trust and confidence in digital identity services at a time when more and more transactions are taking place online, a nd the ability to share information digitally to assert ones information is becoming increasingly vital to daily life and a key foundation for the economy. A governance and compliance regime is required to ensure that those who are providing digital ident ity services consistently meet legislation and standards for using, storing and sharing personal and organisational information. This will imbue the ecosystem with consistency and trust, encourage uptake, enable the flow of information, improve user experi ence, reduce identity theft, and position the digital identity ecosystem to realise the significant social and economic benefits digital identity services can provide. Summary of Preferred Option or Conclusion (if no preferred option) How will the agencys preferred approach work to bring about the desired change Why is this the preferred option Why is it feasible Is the preferred approach likely to be reflected in the Cabinet paper The preferred government intervention, as outlined in the Cabinet paper, is the implementation of a regulatory framework to ensure minimum standards are consistently applied across the digital identity ecosystem . This intervention would include : The establishment of a Digital Identity Trust Framework (Trust Frame work) to set the rules (standards, legislation) for those participat ing in New Zealands digital identity ecosystem. The establishment of a governance board to exercise control over the Trust Framework and to update and maintain its rules as required . INCONFIDENCE Page of Responses to claims made by Castalia Claim Response Investment estimates WICS modelling is entirely based on a top down, New Zealand wide assumption that a massive nationwide investment programme is necessary for all council water services. This is despite WDC and all other local authorities submitting detailed bottom up information about planne d capital investment. (page ) This is incorrect. The WICS modelling takes information councils provided (through the Request for Information process) on asset values , lives and valuations and projects future renewals investment based on industry standard rates of economic depreciation, making adjustments for differences in input costs (e.g., relative wages and material costs) between New Zealand and the UK. It uses council supplied populati on growth projections to estimate the future capital costs of providing for growth. In assessing the likely costs of meeting water quality and environmental standards, WICS uses council population density, topography and other geographic variables to model the likely scale of investment required based on what water services providers that operate across the United Kingdom, and which share similar population and geographic characteristics, have made to achieve current levels of compliance with EU standards. The applicability of these standards to New Zealand was reviewed by Beca New Zealand who found that the investment projections from the WICS modelling may well underestimate the necessary investment costs given the pressures of managing and delivering impr ovement and asset renewals backlogs simultaneously, the higher seismic risk profile of New Zealand, and cost pressures associated with climate change and iwiMori aspirations that are not quantified in the WICS investment projections. WICS makes no adju stment for the overlapping nature of growth and replacement investment (page ) The replacement investment represents the cost of replacing the asset base with a modern equivalent of that asset whilst providing the same or higher level of service in the long run. Growth investment to meet new demand will increase the asset base, therefore, increasing (rather than reducing) the future replacement need. INCONFIDENCE Page of Office of the Minister of Internal Affairs Chair Cabinet Legislation Committ ee Films, Videos, and Publications Classification (Commercial Video on Demand) Amendment Bill: Approval for Introduction Proposal . This paper seeks Cabinet Legislation Committee approval for the introduction of the Films, Videos, and Publications Classification (Commercial Video on Demand) Amendment Bill (the Bill). Policy . The policy relating to the content of th e Bill was agreed by Cabinet on September CAB MIN . The Bill was given a priority of Category for the Legislation Programme, and Cabinet has indicated an intention to have it introduced into the House in CAB MIN refers . The Bill is attached as Appendix A . . The purpose of the Bill is to address a regulatory gap where Commercial Video on Demand (CVoD) content is not currently subject to mandatory classification requirements prior to being made available in New Zealand. . The Bill will enable CVoD content to be rated and labelled in the same way that films are already regulated under the Films, Videos, and Publications Classification Act (the Act) . Regulated CVoD providers will be required to label content by: . selfrating content using their own systems that have been approved by the Office of Film and Literature Classification (the Classification Office) ; . selfrating content using the Classification Offices online tool and resources; or . submitting content to the F ilm and Video Labelling Body (the Labelling Body) for rating and labelling, with certain content to be referred to the Classification Office for classification where appropriate . . Nothing in the Bill will prevent the Chief Censor from calling in CVoD cont ent for classification on an as necessary basis , in accordance with the powers afforded by section () of the Act. This is consistent with the treatment of all publications in New Zealand. . Cabinet also authorised me to take remaining policy decisions necessary to enable final drafting of the Bill. The final Bill provides that only CVoD providers who are specified in a Schedule to the Bill will be subject to the new requirements. This Schedule will be ame ndable by Order in Council upon the recommendation of the Minister of Internal Affairs. The principal consideration for whether a CVoD provider should be specified in the Schedule will be the potential for risk of harm, as established by assessment again st three criteria prescribed in the Bill. Regulatory impact analysis . A Quality Assurance Panel with representatives from the Department of Internal Affairs and the Treasury considers that the Supplementary Analysis Report meets the Quality Assurance crite ria. Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs INCONFIDENCE Page of . The Quality Assurance statement for the original Regulatory Impact Assessment (RIA) was that it did not meet the Quality Assurance criteria. In particular, the Quality Assurance Panel considered that there was limited analysis of the size of the probl em, and limited evidence that the problem needs addressing now instead of waiting for the intended wider review of the media content regulat ion regime . The Panel also considered that the RIA did not establish the criteria that will be used to determine which providers will be regulated, provided little information about the costs to providers, and whether the preferred option (Option ) would increase inconsistency of classification when considered across all household video content. . The Minister of Finance and I agreed that the Department of Internal Affairs would do supplementary analysis of the above issues, including the Supplementary Analysis Report attached to this Cabinet paper which addresses the definition of CVoD. . The Panel c onsiders that the Supplementary Analysis Report fully addresses the Panels concern that the original RIA did not establish the criteria which will be used to determine which providers will be regulated, and whether consideration will be given to exemptin g small or niche providers. The Panel also considers that the Supplementary Analysis Report goes some way to addressing the Panels concern that the regulatory proposals would increase, rather than decrease, inconsistency of classification when considere d across all household video content. . The RIA, with Supplementary Analysis Report , is attached as Appendix B . Further supplementary analysis will be part of other Departmental workstreams . Authorised for lodgement Hon Tracey Martin Minister of Internal Affairs Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Films, Videos, and Publications Classification (Commer cial V ideo onDemand) Amendment Bill Government Bill Explanatory note General policy statement The objective of this Bill is to reduce the potential for harm to consumers from view ing inappropriate content. The Bill will do this by requiring that commercial video ondemand ( CVoD ) content that is made available in New Zealand display appropri ate and consistent labelling, if the provider is specified in the Schedule to the Bill. This labelling will provide information about that contents rating and a description so that consumers can make an informed decision on whether to view it. Providers of commercial (subscription and transactional) video ondemand content are displaying inconsistent ratings and descriptive notes (or no ratings at all) for con tent available on their platforms. This is because of the gap in current legislation where ondemand online content in New Zealand is not subject to mandatory rating requirements, as films for cinematic or DVD release are. This Bill will ensure that consumers see more consistent ratings and descriptive notes across the main CV oD platforms in New Zealand. The Bill will amend the Films, Videos, and Publications Classification Act (the Act) to clearly address the identified regulatory gap. Key changes that the Bill will implement are set out below. Requirements for specified CVoD providers to label content before it is available in New Zealand Providers of CV oD content will be required to comply by following the current process for the labelling of a film. This involves provid ing content to the Film and Video Labelling Body (the labelling body) for rat ing and labelling. The labelling body will refer certain content to the Office of Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Film and Literature Classification (the Classification Office ) for classification, before issuing a label; or selfrating content that they make available using systems that have been approved by the Classification Office. This can be achieved either by using the Classification Offices rating tool or using their own system, with approval from the Classification Office. Once content is labelled under the Act, that label must be used by any other provider providing that content. These labelling decisions can be reconsidered by the Classifi cation Office where necessary. Establishment of criteria and process to identify and list regulated providers Providers that are required to comply under the new requirements will be listed in a schedule of the Act. The schedule can be amended by an Order in Council, with the final decision being made by the GovernorGeneral on the recommendation of the Minister of Internal Affairs. The Minister will need to consult the Chief Censor before making a recommendation to amend the schedule. The Ministers recommendation will be based on an assess ment of the potential risk of harm to consumers from CV oD content being made available without appropriate labels. The Bill sets the following criteria that the Minister must consider in determining the potential risk of harm: market presencethe share of the New Zealand market that a provider cur rently has or is expected to have; and nature of contentthe nature of content being offered by a provider, or inten ded to be offered by a provider, and the potential of that content to cause harm to consumers; and compliance with and commitment to another recognised classification frame work in New Zealandwhether a provider is using a classification framework that is recognised as being effective in ensuring that consistent and appropriate information is provided to consumers, and the extent and reliability of the pro viders commitment to that framework. functions of Classification Office The Bill will update the functions of the Classification Office to ensure that the new requirements for CV oD content are clearly within the scope of its operational work. The Classification Office will have the following new functions and powers: providing an online rating tool that specified CV oD providers may use to rate and label content they make available; and approving selfrating systems that are developed by specified CV oD providers to rate and label their content; and reviewing and monitoring the operation and outputs of both the online rating tool and any selfrating systems.Films, Videos, and Publications Classification (Commer cial V ideo onDemand) Amendment Bill Explanatory note Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Amendment to definition of film to clarify that it includes video ondemand content V ideo ondemand content falls within the existing definition of a publication, but does not clearly fall within the definition of a film (which is a subset of publications). The Bill replaces the definition of film in the Act to clarify that it includes video on demand content. (CV oD is a subset of video ondemand content that is made available to consumers on a subscription or transaction basis.) Clarifying that video ondemand content is a film means that the requirements in rela tion to classifying and rating films will apply to any video ondemand content that is not specifically exempted from those requirements (eg, video ondemand content that is not provided by a specified CV oD provider is exempted through an amendment to section ). The Classification Offices powers in respect of publications (eg, com plaints process, enforcement provisions, and offences and penalties) will also apply. Anticipated introduction of new fees for use of CVoD rating and labelling tools The new regime introduced by the Bill will also permit new fees to be set for the use and review of CV oD rating and labelling tools. Fees under the Act are set in the Films, Videos, and Publications Classification (Fees) Regulations . Work is underway to update the fees framework, including the level of the CV oD fees for specified CV oD providers. However, the following provisions come into force earlier, on July : the machinery clauses that set out the title, commencement, and principal Act details: the amendments to the interpretation provision set out in clause () that insert new defined terms relating to video ondemand: the new provisions that insert a schedule of transitional provisions (which pro vides for rating decisions made under the broadcasting codes to be treated as ratings made under new Part A): the provisions that insert new Schedule (which lists specified CV oD provid ers), and that enable that schedule to be amended by Order in Council. Clause states that the Bill amends the Films, Videos, and Publications Classification Act (the principal Act). Part New rating and labelling requirements for specified providers commercial video ondemand content Clause amends section (which defines terms used in the Act) to insert new defini tions of approved selfrating system, CV oD online rating tool, commercial video on demand content, selfrating tool, specified CV oD provider, and video ondemand con tent. It also amends the definition of film to provide that video ondemand content comes within the definition. This will have the effect that the existing requirements that apply in relation to classifying and rating films apply to video ondemand content (unless an exemption applies). The definition of specified CV oD provider refers to new Schedule (inserted by clause ). That schedule lists the companies to whom the new requirements will apply. The definition ensures that subsidiaries and affiliated companies of the listed companies are also specified CV oD providers if they provide commercial video on demand content in New Zealand. The companies listed in new Schedule are Alphabet Inc., a company registered and based in the United States of America (which is the parent company of Google LLC which provides the Google Play service): Amazon.com, Inc., a company registered and based in the United States of America (which provides Amazon Prime Video through an af filiate): Apple Inc., a company registered and based in the United States of America (which provides Apple TV and iTunes services); Lightbox New Zealand Limited, a company registered and based in New Zea land:Films, Videos, and Publications Classification (Commer cial V ideo onDemand) Amendment Bill Explanatory note Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Microsoft Corp, a company registered and based in the United States of Amer ica (which provides Microsoft Films and T elevision): Netflix, Inc., a company registered and based in the United States of America: Sky Network Television Limited, a company registered and based in New Zea land (which includes its division that provides NEON): Sony Interactive Entertainment Europe Limited, a company registered and based in the United Kingdom (which provides the PlayStation Store service): The Walt Disney Company, a company registered and based in the United States of America (which includes its business unit that provides Disney). Clause inserts new section A, which is about new Schedule AA (transitional, sav ings, and related provisions) inserted by clause . Clause amends section , which lists certain types of film that are exempt from labelling requirements. The amendment adds to that list any video ondemand content made available by a person who is not a specified CV oD provider. The effect of this amendment is that the requirements to rate and label video ondemand content will only apply to the providers listed in new Schedule . Section () currently provides that the Chief Censor may require films that would otherwise be exempt to be labelled. An amendment is also made to that subsection to clarify how it applies in the case of video ondemand content. If video ondemand content is made available, or proposed to be made available, in New Zealand by a person who is not listed in new Schedule , the Chief Censor may require the person to apply for the issue of a label in respect of that content. Clause inserts new Part A , which deals with rating and labelling commercial video ondemand content made available by specified providers. New section A provides that the requirements in the Act and regulations apply in respect of commercial video ondemand content that is made available in New Zea land by specified CV oD providers, even if those providers are not resident or incorp orated in New Zealand. New section B imposes a duty on specified CV oD providers to rate and label the commercial video ondemand content that they make available in New Zealand. It sets out the following methods that a CV oD provider may use to comply: rating and labelling the content using an approved selfrating system; or rating and labelling the content using the CV oD online rating tool provided by the Classification Of fice; or applying to the labelling body for the issue of a label. New section C applies if commercial video ondemand content has previously been rated. It requires specified CV oD providers and the labelling body to apply the same rating, classification, and description to the content. New section D requires a specified CV oD provider who is selfrating video on demand content that has not previously been rated toExplanatory noteFilms, Videos, and Publications Classification (Commer cial Video onDemand) Amendment Bill Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs label the content in accordance with the rating by the selfrating tool; or if the tool identifies the content as potentially being objectionable, refer the content to the Classification Of fice for classification. New section E provides for specified CV oD providers to apply to the Chief Censor for approval of a system to rate and label commercial video ondemand content. The Chief Censor may enter into an agreement with a specified CV oD provider that sets out the terms and conditions on which the provider is approved to use their own sys tem to rate and label the content they make available in New Zealand. New section F requires the Classification Office to annually review specified CV oD providers use of selfrating systems, and enables regulations to prescribe fees to be paid by the providers to meet the cost of those reviews. New section G provides that any person may complain to the Chief Censor about the rating that a specified CV oD provider has assigned to commercial video on demand content. The Chief Censor may refer a complaint to the provider, or classify the content, or refuse to take action if the Chief Censor considers the content has been correctly rated. Clause inserts a new provision that allows the list of persons who are specified CV oD providers in new Schedule to be amended by Order in Council, made on the recommendation of the Minister. Before making an Order in Council, the Minister must consult the Chief Censor. The main criterion for recommending an order amend ing new Schedule is whether the deletion or addition of a persons name will increase or reduce the risk of harm to viewers of commercial video ondemand con tent made available by the person. Clause inserts new Schedule AA (transitional, savings, and related provisions). See also new section A inserted by clause . Clause inserts new Schedule , which lists the commercial video ondemand pro viders to whom the new rating and labelling requirements will apply . Part Related amendments Clause amends section , which deals with labelling of films. The amendment clarifies that the section applies to video ondemand content that is made available to persons in New Zealand. Clause amends section , which deals with applications to the labelling body for the issue of a label. The amendment clarifies that the section does not apply to com mercial video ondemand content that a specified CV oD provider has already rated using a selfrating tool. Clause replaces section (), which deals with the issue of labels in cases where the Classification Office has examined a film. The amendment makes it possible for the Classification Office to direct a specified CV oD provider to issue a label.Films, Videos, and Publications Classification (Commer cial Video onDemand) Amendment Bill Explanatory note Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Clause amends section to add the following new functions of the Classification Office: to develop, provide, and maintain the CV oD online rating tool for use by speci fied CV oD providers: to approve selfrating systems developed by specified CV oD providers: to review the use of selfrating tools by specified CV oD providers. Clause amends section , which creates an offence for issuing labels that may cause a person to believe they were issued under this Act when they were not. The amendment ensures that specified CV oD providers using approved selfrating systems are excluded from the offence provision. Clause amends section , which defines the term distribute. The amendment is to an example and is designed to make it clear that the terms provide access and make available, when used in the Act, mean the same thing.Explanatory noteFilms, Videos, and This included allowing providers to self classify content using their own systems approved by OFLC or on line tools and resources provided by OFLC. Instructions were issued to the Parliamentary Counsel Office (PCO) to draft an amendment Bill with the aim of introduction in November . The Quality Assurance panel considered that the Regulatory Impact Assess ment (RI A), which accompanied the policy proposals at the Cabinet Social Wellbeing Committee (SWC) , did not meet the Quality Assurance criteri a. This Supplementary Analysis Report (SAR) has been undertaken to address the panels assessment that the RIA did not establish the criteria which will be used to determine which providers will be regulated, and whether consideration will be given to exempting small or niche providers. This was, effectively, uncertainty about the definition of CVoD. Following c onsideration of policy proposals by SWC, Cabinet authorised the Minister of Internal Affairs to undertake targeted consultation on the CVoD definition, and the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Internal Affairs agreed that a SAR addressing the CVoD d efinition would be provided to Cabinet prior to Cabinet considering the Bill in November . Because the supplementary analysis work on the CVoD definition does not present major changes to the original policy objectives or their expected regulatory impa ct, DIA has proceeded by updating the existing RIS rather than undertaking a new one. New material is incorporated in italics. The additional analysis included in th is RIA covers: Background information ( page ) Three objectives identified to assess the propo sed recommended approach on the CVoD definition criteria ( page ) Two options that were considered for clarifying the CVoD definition, and assessment against the three objectives ( page s ) Information about the targeted consultation that was conducted , and the four key themes that emerged from submissions ( page s ) Information about market research that was considered as part of our analysis ( page ) Analysis of submissions received ( page s ) Refined objectives for assessing our re commended approach ( page ) Our recommended approach to clarify the CVoD defin ition and providers ( page s ) Assessment of our recommended approach against the Option prop osal that we consulted on (page ) Assessment of recommended approach against the thre e refined objectives ( page s ) Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs RIA : CVoD definition analysis Impact Statement T emplate Analysis of how the recommended approach affects different types of providers ( pages ) An explanation on further analysis to be undertaken as part of a separate DIA workstre am (page ) Limitations to supplementary a nalysis: Time constraints due to Ministerial direction , and targeted consultation undertaken on only one option. The Minister of Internal Affairs has required CVoD content to be brought under the Classification Act regime this term. In order to meet this t imeframe, we conducted a condensed two week targeted consultation on the CVoD definition and invited written submissions from specific industry and regulatory stakeholders. The condensed consultation timeframe may have meant that some stakeh olders did not have enough time to make a submission, so did not provide feedback. However, three submitters we engaged with were given additional time (of up to week) to provide their feedback. We accommodated these requests where we were able to. Targe ted consultatio n was al so only undertaken on one proposed approach (Option ) . While it would have bee n preferable to consult on more than one option, we determined that the Option proposal clearly fell short of meeting our objectives when compared to Op tion . As such , we provided this advice to the Minister and received direction from the Minister to undertake targeted consultation on only one option. We are confident that our recommended approach has been developed and refined in consideration of feedback received f rom consultation on the proposed CVoD definition. Our concerns are summarised under the quality assurance criteria of complete and convincing, and consulted. Com plete and convincing There is limited analysis of the size of the problem, particularly the magnitude of the risk from misclassifying content and the degree to which other information offered by commercial video on demand providers (e.g. in the synopsis an d genre label that a consumer sees before viewing) mitigates the risk. There is also limited evidence that the problem needs addressing now, instead of waiting for the intended wider review. The RIA does not establish the criteria which will be used to det ermine which providers will be regulated, and whether consideration will be given to exempting small or niche providers. Other options could have been considered. For example, encouraging providers to join the voluntary system, with the chance that regulat ion might follow if that was unsuccessful. Information about impacts of options is light. Two examples are: Little information about the costs to providers, and the extent to which costs will be passed onto consumers whether through higher prices or redu ctions in content (lower profitability minority audien ce content might be at greater risk). Whether Option would increase, rather than decrease, inconsistency of classification when considered across all household video content a point raised in submis sions. The RIA identifies risks of non compliance with Option but is not convincing that these risks will not also manifest for Option . The RIA could have assessed what factors might lead providers to comply and had an implementation plan for gaining compliance. Consulted The RIA generally summarises and responds to the feedback from public consultation well. Consultation elicited many issues, and providers said they required more information before they could estimate the cost of options and the time r equired to implement them. Further, targeted, consulta tion would likely help, and ultimately result in sufficient analysis to inform Ministers decisions. Supplementary Analysis Report The Minister of Finance and the Minister of Internal Affairs agreed th at the Department of Internal Affairs would do supplementary analysis of the above is sues, including the Supplementary Analysis Report attached to this Cabinet paper which addresses the definition of CVoD. The Panel considers that the Supplementary Analysi s Report fully addresses the Panels concern that the original RIA did not establis h the criteria which will be used to determine which providers will be regulated, and whether consideration will be given to exempting small or niche providers. The Panel also considers that the SAR goes some way to addressing the Panels concern that the regulatory proposals would increase, rather than decrease, inconsistency of classification when considered across all household video content. Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs RIA : CVoD definition analysis Impact Statement T emplate Impact Statement: The F ilms, Videos, and Publications Classification Amendment Bill standardising classification for Commercial Video on Demand content Section : General information Purpose . This Regulatory Impact Statement (RIS) has been prepared by the Department of Interna l Affairs ( DIA). DIA is solely responsible for the analysis and advice set out in this RIS except as otherwise explicitly indicated. This analysis and advice has been produced for informing policy decisions to be taken by Cabinet. . This RIS provides analysi s of the proposed amendment to the Films, Videos and Publicatio ns Classification Act (the Classification Act). This amendment requires Commercial Video onDemand (CVoD) content, which is accessed online on demand after payment of a fee, to be classifi ed in accordance with the Classification Act. This proposal is being made following public consultation. Limitations to analysis: Scope, delivery pressures due to Ministerial priority, and lack of financial information to accurately assess financial implic ations for providers . The scope has been narrowed to only includ e visual media content that is accessed online on demand by a user who has paid a fee. Usercontent (e .g. YouTube free content) and Free Video on Demand ( FVoD, e.g. TVNZ on Demand ) services are out of scope for this proposal. Including other form s of visual media content within this proposed change, while desirable, is not preferred as doing so could add additional complexity and delays in bringing CVoD content within the classificatio n regime. Out of scope content would also be addressed as part of the upcoming broader reform of New Zealands media content regulation regime. . Addressing a regulatory gap that creates a risk of harm to children and young people, from watching inappropria te CVoD con tent , is a priority for the Minister of Internal Affairs . The Minister has required proposals to be enacted before the end of this term . DIA and MCH are currently undertaking scoping work on a broader reform which will mitigate any risks arising from this change . An extensive reform of the current regime w ill take at least to months to complete and is largely dependent on Government priorities. Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs RIA : CVoD definition analysis Impact Statement T emplate . Due to time constraints we have been unable to conduct an extensive analysis of the current rese arch regard ing content classification and harm reduction. We are confident that the research we have found indicates a real risk of harm to children and young people regarding insufficient information and warnings provided for visual media content. There i s a lack of financial information from the industry to accurately gauge financial or cost implications for CVoD providers from the proposed change . What is the context withi n which action is proposed . There is inconsistent and inadequate information being provided to New Zealand consumers of Video on Demand content. This makes it difficult for parents and caregivers as well as children and young people to make informed decisi ons about what content is appropriate to view. There is evidence to show that viewing inappropriate content can lead to the risk of harm. This creates a risk of har m to children and young people, as well as other vulnerable groups of society such as peopl e with mental health issues, eating disorders or people still traumatised by suicide. . The current system provides this information through classifications and consumer warnings provided by OFLC under the Classification Act. Classifications provided by OFLC have been tailored over the years to provide clear and concise information to New Zealanders which highlights topics that are of concern. OFLC also utilises its Youth Advisory Panel which helps them understand the topics that are of concern for younger vi ewers. This information can then be used by other organisations to provide advice and support to consumers who find the content distressing. . An example of this is the Mental Health Foundations advice for viewers of Reasons Why . The show depicted scene s of rape and suicide which had not been made clear by the warning labels provided by Netflix at the time of release. The Foundation now has advice on its website for parents and caregivers to discuss the themes in the show as well as for younger viewers w ho may wish to watch or have been affected by the show. There is a risk of harm to children from watching inappropriate content . New Zealanders are concerned about what children and teens are watching. An OFLC study showed per cent of New Zealand respond ents were moderately to highly concerned about children and teens exposure to content. Likewise, parents of participants in a UK study by OfCom were more worried about what their children watched on Netflix on personal devices, than on public broadcast t elevision. . Research has found that children viewing vi olent media content showed long term increase in aggressive thoughts, behaviour and angry feelings. The producers of the Netflix series Reasons Why were warned against the graphic portrayal of suic ide in the show. . The study by Ofcom has shown that children are increasingly more interested in content that they can view on their own devices. As this removes a degree of parental discretion it shows the need for up front classifications that can inform a child or young persons decision making. What regulatory system, or systems, are al ready in place Key features and objectives of current regulatory system . The current media content regulation regime comprises the Classification Act and the Broadcasting Act (the Broadcasting Act). The Classificat ion Act provides for the classification of films (e .g. cinema and DVD release) and was transferred to DIA in August from the Ministry of Justice. The Broadcasting Act is administered by MCH and provides for the establishment of the four broadcasting c odes : Pay Television , Free to Air Television, Radio and Election Programmes. Each code has its own set of classificat ions and audience advisories . . The objectives of the current regulatory system are to provide accurate and reliable information to New Zeala nd consumers of medi a content. This is achieved using standards and classifications with advisory notes for content across platforms with some tools tailored to particular platforms (e .g. the free toair television watershed). The intention was for a consi stent and well under stood media content regulation regime , which has been developed and en hanced over the last few decades. This system is trusted by New Zealanders as a means of understanding what is present in media content but is now failing to keep up with modern changes in technology because of its age. . The two Acts are based on viewing platforms that were available at the time they were designed more than years ago. This has resulted in areas of regulatory uncertainty around media content availabl e on new and emerging platforms (e .g. online and on demand). The current regime did not anticipate technological change, or the shifting ways New Zealanders now view, consume and interact with media content. This means that content that is broadcasted (Pay Television, Free to Air Television and Radio) is covered by the Broadcasting Act while Cinema and DVDs are covered by the Classification Act. . Both regulators under the ir Acts are required to conduct research into media content and the use of the regulatio ns. OFLC als o provide educational material for use in schools to enable better understanding of classifications and media use. This helps support use of the classifications and informs their application by regulators. Understandin g the classification system: New Zealanders Views, . Colmar Br unton.
