INCONFIDENCE Page of The current regulatory and operational environment for digital identity carries risks for users and government . On November , Cabinet considered the paper Developing Options for a New Approach to Digital Identity DEV MIN , CAB , and agreed that the government will continue working with citizens, agencies and the private sector to: develop options for a new approach to digital identity, including the long term role of government and the private sector in the provision of digital identity services; and identify regulatory gaps. . Cabinet invited the Minister for Gover nment Digital Services and the Minister of Internal Affairs to report back to Cabinet Economic Development Committee by October on the outcomes of this work. However, Cabinet also made provision to provide interim papers on significant issues. . We have identified three regulatory and operational gaps that obstruct innovation and the development and adoption of digital identity services: people have limited control over how their information is used and growing concerns that they are unnecessarily expose d to privacy and security risks; a lack of efficiency and coordination between organisations in the public and private sectors, making user consented information sharing more difficult and resulting in services that cannot work with each other in a truste d way; and a lack of governance and structure resulting in inconsistent laws and standards (including statutory limitations on what attributes and data sets can be shared) and their uneven application in both the public and private sectors. . Focus group res earch shows Mori have lower levels of trust than other groups over government holding and sharing information about them. Participants in the focus groups attributed this distrust to the misuse and abuse of Mori data, creating biased assumptions of Mori and a narrative not informed by Mori. There is a need to actively promote Mori involvement in digital identity and work through concerns Mori have. . Additionally, the inconsistent application of data privacy, identification and security standards can le ad to systematic issues and breaches. This poses risks to both customers and businesses, undermining trust and confidence in the digital identity ecosystem further and slowing adoption. . We recommend the immediate creation of a Trust Framework in order to address these gaps, and to ensure secure and trusted access to digital identity services in New Zealand. Comparable jurisdictions (countries such as Australia, Canada and the United Kingdom which do not have single identity registries) are choosing to deve lop trust frameworks to address regulatory gaps similar to ours. An analysis of international initiatives and approaches has informed the Trust Framework recommendations in this paper. . Officials have regularly engaged with a working group with members from a wide variety of relevant public and private sector stakeholders (as outlined in the Consultation section) to test , support and inform the analysis and evidence base for regulatory gaps and solutions. The working group are broadly supportive of the imple mentation of a Trust Framework.
INCONFIDENCE Page of Trustees should not be directors on the board of the water organisation . We propose that consumer trust s should be prohibited from appointing trustees as directors on the board of the water organisation. . This would provid e appropriate separat ion of governance and management roles for a water organisation. The prohibition will also prevent the conflicts of interest that would arise if a trustee also holds a water organisation board position. . We do not propose extending this prohibition to councillors and mayors given the separation that will exist between a water organisation and councils under the consumer trust model. The prohibition will apply to all owners, so in a mixed ownership model th e prohibition will apply to both councillors and trustees. A council should be unable to interfere in the business of a consumer trust . We propose that Bill should expressly provide that settlor councils cannot intervene in the affairs of a trust once it is settled. . Under trust law, it is possible for a settlor to design the trust deed in a way that gives them an oversight role. This would allow a council, as settlor of a trust, to define a role for itself in the trust deed, such as the power to appoint a nd remove trustees. We propose a legislative prohibition on the settlor council including any role for itself in the operation of the trust to ensure appropriate separation . Transfer restrictions should apply when a consumer t rust is being wound up . The provisions relating to the transfer of assets will apply on the wind up of a trust. Ordinary trust law will apply, subject to any legislative restrictions in Bill . . We consider that Bill should be clear that the restrictions on transferability of ownership interests will include a requirement that water services and assets must be transferred to another water organisation or to a council upon the wind up of a consumer trust. The Trusts Act also requires that the trust deed state how the trust p roperty is to be distributed upon wind up. Under both provisions, settlor councils will have to stipulate the distribution restriction. The Secretary for Local Government should approve a trust deed . We propose that Secretary must approve the trust deed be fore a consumer trust is settled to ensure that minimum legislative standards are met. . We also propose that any amendment to a trust deed must also be approved by the Secretary. Under the Trust s Act , the variation of a trust deed requires the unanimo us consent of beneficiaries or a court decision. Regulation making powers should be available if they prove necessary . We propose that Bill should include regulation making powers as a back stop power if any unexpected issues should arise. Consumer trust election rules should be made in the trust deed with backup regulation making powers . The trust deed will provide for trustee elections under our proposed approach . We propose that Bill should provide high level principles and some specific requirements Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs The Department of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua

INCONFIDENCE Page of Covid has highlighted the importance of digital identity for ensuring access to essential services . Physical distancing requirements have made it more difficult for people to access essential public and private sector s ervices (e.g. welfare payments, doctor visits), whilst placing strain on agency resources. As a result, digital capability is becoming a greater priority for public and private sector entities. Examples of how digital identity services can help the Covid recovery include: supporting a mobile and transitionary workforce by making it easier for workers (e.g. returning health care professionals) to prove their qualifications and eligibility to work; making it easier for people that rely on government servic es to prove their eligibility through secure sharing of personal information (e.g. name, of birth, Inland Revenue number, bank account, residency status); providing digital alternatives to requirements that identity documents be certified in person b y an approved practitioner (e.g. establishing a business relationship with a customer under the Anti Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act or for conveyancing property under the Land Transfer Act ); and facilitating the develo pment and maturation of open banking services. . There is an opportunity to combine innovation in the public and private sectors with the public sectors information and resources to provide trusted, integrated, people centred digital services. Covid has accelerated demand for and innovation in the private market for digital identity services. The absence of an agreed set of rules to assure the trustworthiness of digital identity services is a key barrier. A Trust Framework will establish a regulatory fram ework to provide this assurance. Establishment of the Trust Framework A trust framework is a regulatory framework that will set out rules for the delivery of digital identity services . The Trust Framework would consist of five component parts where it: defines the roles of participants involved in providing digital identity services, such as information providers (e.g. passports, utility companies ) and relying parties (services that rel y on the asserted information, such as liquor stores relying on a of birth), so that it is clear which entities should be accredited ; sets out rules that accredited participants must follow, with a focus on identification, privacy and security requir ements that are based on laws and standards that are either existing or in development ; establishes a body to accredit the participants that have demonstrated they can adhere to the rules of the Trust Framework ; makes the rules of the Trust Framework legally enforceable upon all accredited participants, who will be audited to ensure the rules are complied with ; and

INTRODUCTION The global COVID pandemic has highlighted an opportunity for improved practices for tracing close contacts of known or probable cases of the virus in New Zealand. Our proposed solution is a Bluetooth Low Energy card (CovidCard) that detects and logs other cards within a close (m) radius of itself. The efficacy of the cards for recording close contacts was tested using closed validation trials where the cards were worn by participants who then acted a role in a directed scene, or were closely monitored in a closed environment. This report summarises all of the trials, the methodology used to evaluate the CovidCard performance, and presents results of the cards ability to record close contacts.

Identity Check is a quick and secure online identity validation tool. Consent is provided, passport or driver licence details added, and a photo provided to confirm identity. No personal data are shared with third parties. Instead, government records are checked to ensure a match to the data provided. Results show a percent success rate.

Identity theft What is identity theft
Identity theft can damage your personal and financial reputation. This can have serious impact on your life, if you can no longer prove who you are and what is yours.
Identity theft is when someone uses your personal information to pretend to be you. This could be done to commit identity crimes such as taking out loans or accumulating speeding tickets, avoiding arrest or court orders by appearing to be a different person. It could also involve maliciously impersonating you, perhaps to make it appear that you believe or think something controversial.

The Inquiry heard and observed that, as elected leaders, mayors felt the pressure and weight of responsibility in the lead up to and during an emergency. There was, however, inconsistent understanding about their role and governance responsibilities once a state of emergency had been declared. We heard that controllers who did not have senior management experience were less aware of the governance roles of elected officials. We also heard that local and group controller responsibilities and accountability lines are ambiguous, convoluted, and not clearly understood. Mayors . Local authority mayors and chairs (or a delegated elected official) serve on the regional CDEM Group and are responsible for declaring a state of local emergency. During an emergency response they retain their usual governance responsibilities and accountability to communities. However, during an emergency there is variation in what the mayors governance function looks like in practice. This lack of shared understanding left some mayors feeling disempowered or superfluous. The governance role of mayors and chairs, as outlined in NEMA guidance, should be strengthened, and clarified in legislation. Presently the Chair and Mayors are the governance on the CDEM Joint Committee and are responsible for all decisions, yet once a State of Emergency has been declared we effectively become redundant All decisions are then made by the Group Controller or his offsider. So surely there must be a way to retain the governance, for checks and balances Mayor of Wairoa, Craig Little . Mayors need to be clear on the specifics of their local governance roles and how to best serve their communities during an emergency. This includes how they work with, and are supported by, the controller and other key roles, including the Public Information Management function. . Mayors are a known name and face in their communities and can provide a high level of trusted reassurance during an emergency. People look to their mayor or regional council chair for information and leadership. They need to be visible and provide good quality, timely, accurate communication to their communities and media, and respond proactively to mis or disinformation. . Some mayors leaned into this leadership role during the severe weather events. They offered strategic communications, leveraged community contact networks, their local communities and wider audiences on what was happening, gathered intelligence on local needs and situational development from their local communities, and shared information with the controller to inform tasking decisions. However, the approach of mayors was not consistent across regions, and they received differing levels of support from the Public Information Management function. Impact analysis Regulatory Impact Statement . A Regulatory Impact Assessment (RIA) was prepared to accompany the papers on refocusing the water services reforms focusing particularly on the proposals to change to a entity reform model. This RIA was reviewed for quality assurance purposes by a Department of Internal Affairs impact assessment panel, which provided the following statement. . The panel considers that the information and analysis summarised in the RIA partially meets the quality assurance criteria. . The RIA clearly explains the problem and need for action. The analysis around the benefits of the entity model compared to the status quo is compelling, with a substantial amount of supporting evidence. The analysis comparing the different new options could have been communicated more clearly at times. Including more detail around what potential shared services are being progressed in practice would also have been useful. . The RIA includes all of the necessary information or , where appropriate , makes links to previous RIA. There is a clear and concise description of the problem and the options , though much of the analysis is technical and could have been communicated in a more accessible way. There does not appear to have been direct consultation on the new options with all relevant stakeholders, but the RIA does clearly show how the new option is a direct response to stakeholder concerns , and has been informed by extensive consultation. Impact and options for implementation of Three Water transfer arrangements for Council Controlled Organisations that provide water related services
Impact of block tariffs on vulnerable consumers . Water services entities may consider the use of block tariffs or low usage charges to try and improve affordability of water. For example, under a block tariff, the first cubic metres of water is priced relatively low, but then the next cubic metres is charged at a higher price. . This type of pricing structure rewards all households with low consumption patterns with low prices, but this means that higher consumption households end up paying much more regardless of their ability to pay. . However, vulnerable households are sometimes large and possibly overcrowded. This means they sometimes consume more water, even if the amount per person is relatively low. A block tariff in a large household could lead to undesirable rationing behaviour and have a negative impact on people with specific medical conditions who require large quantities of water. Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government IN CONFIDENCE Page of . Decisions around the use of block tariffs or low usage charges will be made by each water services entity as part of its funding and pricing plan. However, due to the significant impact these pricing structures can have on vulnerable households, I recommen d creating a regulation making power that would enable the Government to limit or prohibit or limit the use of low usage or block tariffs for residential customers, if it were necessary. I propose that these regulation making powers only come into effect from July to avoid disruption in the initial stages of the reform.
Impact of volumetric pricing on vulnerable consumers . As part of setting pricing and charging plans, water services entities may consider using volumetric charges for a portion of the overall charge residential consumers pay. With volumetric (or variable) pricing, consumers pay based on the volume of water they use. Volumetric pricing is one means water services entities could use to give effect to Te Mana of te Wai as it incentivises more efficient use of water and water conservation. More than half of households already pay some form of volumetric charge. Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government IN CONFIDENCE Page of . The use of volumetric charges can have negative impacts on vulnerable consumers. Preliminary data (from Watercare) suggests that the biggest predictor of household water usage is the number of occupants in the household. Larger households also generally tend to have lower incomes. In addition when water costs are collected through volumetric charges, the cost is typically passed on to tenants who are much more likely to be in financial hardship. . A very high proportion of volumetric charges is not necessarily required in order to achieve efficiency gains, because there are substantial fixed costs in supplying drinking water. . As an example, Kpiti Coast District Council introduced a combination of water meters and recovering about percent of its drinking water costs from volumetric charges to achieve a reduction in water usage of about percent. Tauranga City Council achieved similar levels of water savings to Kpiti but has a tariff structure t hat recovers more than percent of its drinking water costs from volumetric charges. At the other extreme, Christchurch City Council introduced water meters but no volumetric charges and has seen relatively little improvement in water conservation. It is now planning to introduce a volumetric charge for households with high water usage patterns. . Decisions around the use of volumetric pricing will be made by each water services entity as part of their funding and pricing plan, taking into account the pricing principles and consultation with their community. It is possible some entities may set a high ratio of volumetric pricing but balance the impact of this on vulnerable consumers in other ways. . Given the significant impact volumetric pricing can have on low income households, I recommend there should be the ability to limit, through regulation, th e ratio between fixed and volumetric water revenues. This would enable the Government to put a cap on the total amount recovered through volumetric charges for residential customers if this were considered necessary in order to protect vulnerable consumers . . As a point of clarification, this regulation would not limit the volumetric charges on the bill for any individual consumer. There would be no cap on their volumetric charges. The restriction only refers to the proportion of total charges recovered by the water services entity, which is an average across all residential consumers.
Impact on sports funding . The impact on funding for sports should also be acknowledged. The loss of the Point of Consumption Charge (approximately .m per annum to sports organisations) will see a fall in revenue for National Sporting Organisations (NSOs). It is anticipated that the monopoly will, however, see an uplift for sports but this is not guaranteed. . In addition, the monopoly will also likely cause a decrease in the revenue received by NSOs and racing codes from BIUC charges for the use of their racing and sports information from offshore providers. If New Zealanders are unable to bet with offshore provider s, it can be expected the value of BIUC agreements with NSOs and racing codes will drop . We are unaware of what this decrease in value may be, however the degree of this decrease for any NSO will likely depend on the proportion of New Zealanders who bet with that offshore provider, as opposed to overseas bettors on any given sport or racing type. . Despite this impact , the racing codes (who collected . million the financial year from BIUC agreements via TAB NZ acting as an agent for them) support the monopoly proposal. However, the financial impact on NSOs is uncertain and likely to depend on the individual sports . Stakeholder ViewsPublic Consultation Public consultation . This specific option has never been consulted with the public and stakeholders. Ideally, consultation would be undertaken . However, due to the constraints and limitations listed earlier, there is no opportunity for this to occur. . However, the issue of regulation of online gambling and sports and racing betting has been actively discussed for some years and the previous Government announced in May in agreed in principle to TAB NZ having an online monopoly, subject to further work being undertaken. From this , we anticipate there are likely to be a range of views on the options. For example, offshore operators are likely to favour a regulated online gambling market they can legitimately enter and participate in , and oppose TAB NZ being given an online sports and racing betting monopoly, andor a raised POCC rate.

Implementation Two aspects of the strategy implementation are worth noting: the extensive use of pilots to test new service and design models, and a joint work programme with DIA to address areas of mutual interest related to gambling harm. Extensive use of pilots The Ministry intends to follow an open process to develop, pilot, evaluate and implement the proposals in the strategy. In response to significant interest from stakeholders, the Ministry will hold a series of workshops to determine the size, location and characteristics of the pilots, before inviting specific proposals through a procurement process. Requests for proposals would set out more detailed funding proposals. Historically, the Ministry has offered this form of funding through a competitive tender, such as those for the research innovation rounds held under previous strategies. However, the Ministry wish es to test the opportunity for greater collaboration on some pilots, to make more effective use of resources. Pilots may include both public health and intervention components, and the Ministry will evaluate all pilots to inform future service provision. Joint work programme with the Department of Internal Affairs The proposed strategy involves areas in which DIA and the Ministry have mutual responsibilities or interests: for example, areas in which the policy or regulatory settings are outside the direct control of the Ministry , or where the Ministry s work requires input from DIA, which administers the Act and the broader regulatory and policy framework. One example is work that looks at the potential to trial and evaluate an enhanced MVE database that supports facial recognition and other administration service improvement for excludees and affected others. The Ministry would work through the details of such a project with DIA and industry, and potentially other affected stakeholders, to ensure the design was robust and likely to be effective. To provide visibility for this type of work, the two departments are establishing a joint work programme covering the priority areas. They expect the programme to include the following topics: MVE and host responsibility use of technology research into areas of mutual interest such as effectiveness of class policies, prevalence of online gambling or socioeconometric drivers of gambling expenditure NCGM locations policy potential changes to the levy formula. Some elements of this work programme will be led by DIA (eg, changes to the levy formula, which is set in legislation) and others will be led by the Ministry. In collaboration with DIA, the Ministry aims to identify and use opportunities for diverse perspectives to clarify what gambling harm minimisation means for different parts of the health sector and to work with the health sector to implement the strategy through the future service plan. The proposed service plan provides more detail about the Ministry s response to the recommendations identified in the Sapere needs assessment. . Outcomes monitoring The Ministry has reviewed progress towards gambling harm reduction outcomes to assess what has been achieved over time in gambling harm minimisation. This review complemented the needs assessment discussed above and provides information about the nature of gambling harm in New Zealand and changes over time. Research shows that while the proportion of the population at risk of gambling harm, as measured by the PGSI is at the lowest levels seen for years, the level of harm in the overall population has remained relatively stable for the last five to seven years (at about ) (Abbott et al ; ThimasarnAnwar et al ). This plateau effect has also been observed overseas (Abbott ). Similarly, the number of people presenting for gambling support and treatment has not increased in line with population growth. Yet this figure represents only a small fraction of the estimated numbers affected by gambling harm. In fact, the overall number of at risk gamblers in the population has increased in line with population growth. Importantly, while inequalities between population groups by age, social deprivation, gender and ethnicity have reduced in absolute terms, in relative terms, disparities in exposure to gambling and experience of gamblingrelated harm persist and have been relatively static over the past five years. A refocusing and revitalisation of activities is warranted The outcomes review and the needs assessment together suggest that, while there has been some success in reducing gambling harm since the first strategy in , in the past few years, the number of people affected by gambling harm has been growing. We need to refocus and revitalise gambling harm responses in the service plans if we are to make further gains in reducing gambling harm and health inequalities and inequity in the experience of gambling harm by a range of population groups , particularly Mori and Pacific peoples . Economies of scale are n ot available in water services from amalgamations at the level WICS claims Castalia has previously advised DIA, LGNZ and the Joint Steering Commi ttee that the economies of scale claimed in WICS slidedecks from administrative amalgamations were Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs CONFIDENTIAL Castalia implau sible . In New Zealand, only minor economies of scale are achievable through institutional reform , and these will be mostly in management and proc urement (not infrastructure capex). FFF Castalia showed that economies of scale are unlikely to be availa ble in New Zealand on the basis of the evidence presented by WICS, Frontier Economics and in the economic literature relied on by the government . The findings in Castalias Economies of Scale report ha ve not been rebutted . WICS claims that the perc ent capex efficiency gain emerges when water entities achieve a population of , or more. It also claims that entities serving a minimum population of , increase capex efficiency as they approach the , population number. This claim has no b asis in the economic literature. In fact, the literature that looks at the specific question of whether economies of scale are available from administrative amalgamations find that there are none except in highly specific circumstances, not present in New Zealand . Economies of scale estimate is based on non credible evidence When preparing the Economies of Scale report, Casta lia reviewed the WICS slidedecks . Access to the underlying models and assumptions was refused . In the Economies of Sca le report , we were advised FFF that the economies of scale assumption was based on England, Wales and Scotland observations. However, we now know that the supporting evidence for the percent capex efficiency is a single Scottish observation from . FFF WICS economies o f scale claims are rejected by peer reviewers FarrierSwier FarrierSwier peer reviewed WICS approach and had access to the underlying models . It found that WICS analysis cannot be used to definitively conclude that amal gamation in and of itself will lead to material efficiency gains in New Zealand . FFF Its review did not assess whether the outputs from the WICS analysis are reasonable or free from error. FFF FarrierSwier also state significant care should b e taken when relying on the capital efficiency gaps estimated by WICS. This is particularly important , given the significant step up in investment forecast for the year period and the role that the capex efficiency assumption plays when estimating benef its from amalgamation and as sociated reform. Dan Corry Chief Executive, New Philanthropy Capital (former Senior Advisor to the UK Prime Minister, ) In the end, regulatory outcomes have to be something the public accept as fair. If you dont have that, whatever nice theories you have, the system collapses. A big question should always be how does the public view this Dan Corry Chief Executive, New Philanthropy Capital (former Senior Advisor to the UK Prime Minister, ) Strategic context RSG and other regulators are operating in an environment where change is the new normal and can occur rapidly and unexpectedly. COVID has prompted governments and businesses alike to reflect on how agile and adaptable they are, whether their digital platforms and services are fit for purpose, and how well they are operating in an increasingly global context. Challenges facing regulators include disruptive trends relating to the speed and scale at which technology innovations can effect change across whole sectors, the degree to which peoples views have become more polarised informed by social media and power imbalances caused when industry expertise exceeds that of the regulator. In New Zealand, health and economic outcomes are being viewed as interrelated and there is a growing concern about harms to communities and the disproportionate effects of these on some communities in particular. In this regard, there is an increasing and strongly felt desire for regulators to address inequitable outcomes for hap, iwi and Mori. There has been a significant maturing of regulatory practice and professionalism in recent years, resulting in a much greater understanding of the need for many regulators to have and maintain a social licence , to be able to anticipate and respond to industry changes (which affect their ability to regulate effectively) and to be able to show that they are making a measurable difference. For some this is easier than others. Concepts of regulatory stewardship what adopting a wholeofsystem, lifecycle view of regulation, and taking a proactive, collaborative approach, to the monitoring and care of the regulatory system(s) within which they have policy or operational responsibilities means for specific systems and regulators is increasingly well defined and understood. One size does not fit all. Related to this, many regulators are challenging the traditional siloed ways of working and are looking for partners or collaborators with whom they can identify new and more innovative interventions using different tools and approaches.

The report of the Working Group on Representation, Governance and Accountability recommends that: The Crown provides equitable resourcing to enable the full and effective participation of iwi and hap in the Three Waters regime (recommendation ). . This recommendation is provided in the context of several other recommendations that are intended to ensure the Treaty and its principles are given effect to when exercising powers and functions under the legislation, and that Te Mana o te Wai is recognised as an overarching objective guiding decision making, planning, governance, accountability and service delivery by the water services entities. . The additional funding of . million will enable: . base departmental capability to support policy development, establishing mana whenua governance arrangements, specialist Treaty advic e, implementation of Te Mana o te Wai, and iwiMori engagement; and . an increase in the direct funding to iwihap to provide assistance for the establishment of the Te Mana o Te Wai mechanism for the new water services entities.
Increased investment by the Crown to support local government through the transition period: . million . The Heads of Agreement between the Crown and Local Government New Zealand (LGNZ) anticipates a close partnership between local authorities and the National Transition Unit (NTU) through the transition process, with significant council involvement in transition planning and entity establishment processes. . The Heads of Agreement recognised there will be transaction costs associated with facilitating the transfe r of assets, liabilities, revenue, staff, contracts and information that will result in councils incurring direct and indirect costs, and that provision for such costs would be made within the million Transforming Three Waters Service Delivery for New Zealanders: Transition and Implementation tagged contingency. The Head of Agreement also anticipated the Crown providing funding support to enable LGNZ and Taituar to support the Crown and the local government sector through the transition period. . Decisi ons about the appropriate level of investment in these activities represents a judgement call, balancing the risks of being perceived to underfund councils, the level of council engagement required to be full and meaningful, and the risks to the entity establishment process and councils management of business asusual activity. . The Minister of Finance and I consider that providing reasonable funding to enable council st aff to participate actively in the entity establishment process is essential for delivering four fitforpurpose water services entities by July . Investment in this activity will be important for building local momentum behind the reform process, and for managing workforce risks through the transition period. . Funding of . million is sought to increase the direct support to councils to an equivalent of approximately FTEs (from FTEs), and modestly increase the wider engagement with the sector. Increasing the total number of clinically relevant close contacts identified The full extent to which contacts are missed by manual contact tracing efforts is not well understood. In New Zealand, the current manual contact tracing system has been able to track up to of selfreported known close contacts within days, with the target of reaching of selfreported known close contacts within days. Modeling efforts assume a high percentage of close contacts will be traced (also referred to as tracing fraction), ranging from (Ferretti ) to (Kucharski and Hinch ), while others (Vaithianathan ) illustrate the impact of a range of percentages of contacts traced (). Importantly, there is a difference between assumed tracing fractions (percentage of all close contacts, known or unknown, traced) and realized tracing fractions (percentage of selfreported known close contacts ultimately traced).

Inequalities and inequity in health Some people experience differences in health that are not only avoidable but also unfair and unjust. Equity recognises that people with different levels of advantage require different approaches and resources to get equitable health outcomes. We usually refer to differences in health experience occurring between population groups as health inequalities . A health inequity is an inequality that we can attribute to social, cultural and economic factors, rather than biomedical ones. Inequalities and inequity in health occur between groups because of a range of wellrecognised socioeconomic, cultural and biological factors. The most common factors are sex, age, social deprivation, ethnicity and education. Similarly, the components of the service plan for the next three years focus on each service area (public health, intervention services, and research and evaluation) to support the plan s key actions and priorities. Interim Government Response to Social Services and Community Committee report Petition of Jenn Hooper: Develop Changing Places facilities
Interim Government Response to the Report of the Social Services and Community Committee on Petition of Jenn Hooper Proposal . The paper seeks approval for the attached interim Government response to the Social Services and Community Committees report on Petition of Jenn Hooper. . It also seeks Cabinets agreement for the Department of Internal Affairs to consult with Local Government New Zealand and the Society of Local Government Managers on the recommendations of the Committee, before a final response is lodged with the Cabinet Office. Background . Petition of Jenn Hooper was referred to the Committee on April . The petition requested, That the House of Representatives encourage the Government to support the development of a nationwide network of Changing Places facilities. . Changing Places facilities are highspecification bathrooms designed and built to cater to the needs of people with significant physical impairments. Features include mechanical hoists and adultsized changing tables, and more space around items such as toilets and sinks, as well as wide doors. In partnership with Hamilton City Council and sponsors, in early Ms Hooper oversaw the construction of the first changing places facility in New Zealand at Hamilton Gardens. A second changing place bathroom has just been completed at Westfield Mall in Newmarket, Auckland. . On August the Committee heard from the Department of Internal Affairs (the Department), the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE), the Ministry of Health (MoH) and the Office for Disability Issues (ODI). . In their oral submission to the Committee, MoH recognised that initiatives such as Changing Places bathrooms provide clear benefits to the disability community. They supported the intent of the petition, but do not have any responsibility for regulation, funding or delivery of public toilets. ODI supported this comment. MBIE noted that they provide written guidelines for minimum performance building standards. The Department in its oral submission noted that local authorities in New Zealand provide public toilets under section of the Local Government Act . The Department administers the governance framework under which local authorities operate. On this basis, the Department considered that the local government sector itself, through Local Government New Zealand, would be best placed to oversee the development of a network of fully accessible bathrooms if agreed. Proactively released by the Minister for Local Government IN CONFIDENCE IN CONFIDENCE Page of Committee report and recommendations . The Committee presented its report to the House on June . The Committee made three recommendations, which support the substance of the Petition. The Committee recommended the Government: develop a nationwide network of bathroom facilities for those with extensive and complex disabilities that is based on the population density of towns and cities; make available capital funding to support smaller local councils to develop fully accessible bathroom facilities and purchase the required equipment; and require the Ministry of Health and all District Health Boards to review and make changes to policies that result in some outpatients or visitors with extensive and complex disabilities being changed on the floor of standard accessible toilets. The delay of the dissolution of Parliament means a response is due earlier than anticipated . Standing Order requires the Government response to be tabled within working days of the Committee report. . The House was due to be dissolved on August for the election, providing for a response back to the Committee days after Parliament resumed, in approximately early November. The extension of Parliament has meant the response will be instead due on August. The Government is focussed on the COVID response, and consequently, a substantive crossportfolio response cannot be achieved within the remaining timeframe. . To meet standing order requirements, I therefore recommend Cabinet agree to the interim response attached as Appendix A . . A substantive response responding to the three recommendations will be made in . Financial implications . There are no immediate financial implications from tabling the interim Government response. I will address any financial implications when I report back to you with the final response. Legislative implications . There are no legislative implications arising directly from the interim Government response. However, once further work on the Committees recommendations is undertaken, legislative change may be proposed. Again, I will report back to you on this in the final response. Population Implications . There are no immediate population implications arising from the interim Government response. I will address any implications when I report back to you with the final response. Proactively released by the Minister for Local Government IN CONFIDENCE IN CONFIDENCE Page of Human Rights . There are no immediate human rights implications arising from the interim Government response. I will address any implications when I report back to you with the final response. Disability perspective . Physical and mental wellbeing is one of the top five priorities for Budget . The Petition of Jenn Hooper fits within the wellbeing priorities. There are no immediate disability implications arising directly from the interim Government response. I will address the disability perspective more when I report back to you with the final response. Intervention In the year, over , people sought help from Ministryfunded services, for problems due to their own or someone else s gambling. Most of these people were in crisis. If brief interventions in nonclinical settings are included in this analysis, the total increases to more than , people. In the three years to , there was a slight decrease in the total numbers of reported interventions. The decline over the period is attributable to fewer new clients coming forward. The numbers of existing clients receiving interventions has been relatively static over the period. Going further back, the number of people seeking interventions has been relatively stable for five to seven years. Similarly, the proportion of people reporting some form of harmful gambling behaviour in the HLS surveys remained static, at approximately percent of the population, between and . Importantly, these static rates belie the fact that the actual number of people affected by harmful gambling is increasing in line with population growth, and intervention services growth is flat. Similarly, needs assessment and outcomes monitoring reports show that only percent of potential clients for gambling support services (that is, people whose reported harm results in a moderate to high PGSI score) actually access or present at these services. This low service use is also evident for other forms of addiction. Improving intervention and service use rates remains a challenge. It will require further work to address systemic or persistent barriers to access and inequities based on ethnicity or socioeconomic factors. Introduction This Government is committed to putting the wellbeing of current and future generations of New Zealanders at the centre of our work. Physical and mental wellbeing is one of the top five priorities for Budget . This work includes improving the terms on which individuals and groups take part in society. Background The Social Services and Community Committee (the Committee) met between May and June to consider the petition of Jenn Hooper. On August , the Committee heard from the Department of Internal Affairs, the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment, the Ministry of Health, and the Ministry of Social Development. On June the Committee released its report with three recommendations that support the substance of the Petition. The Committee recommended the Government: develop a nationwide network of bathroom facilities for those with extensive and complex disabilities that is based on the population density of towns and cities; make available capital funding to support smaller local councils to develop fully accessible bathroom facilities and purchase the required equipment; and require the Ministry of Health and all District Health Boards to review and make changes to policies that result in some outpatients or visitors with extensive and complex disabilities being changed on the floor of standard accessible toilets. Government Response The Government has examined the recommendations and notes this is an important issue requiring full consideration across government agencies with disability, Health and Local Government implications. The House was due to be dissolved on August for the election, providing for a response back to the Committee days after Parliament resumed, in approximately early November. The extension of Parliament has meant the response will be instead due on August. A substantive crossportfolio response cannot be achieved within the remaining timeframe. To this end we propose to produce a substantive response in early , but have requested that the Department of Internal Affairs begin consultation with Local Government New Zealand in the meantime. Introduction from Suzanne Doig, Deputy Chief Executive, Toi Hiranga l Regulation and Policy I would like to present to you the final decisions of our organisational change process. I appreciate the feedback you have provided during the consultation period and the thought that went into this. It helped refine our thinking and test our assumptions and rationale for what was proposed. I would also like to thank everyone for your professionalism and for the manaakitanga you have extended to each other over the past weeks. These decisions have not been made lightly and I would like to acknowledge all those who are affected by the final decisions that have been made. Why change is necessary Late last year, the Minister of Finance announced an ongoing Fiscal Sustainability Programme to embed a culture of responsible spending across government, requiring us to make permanent baseline reductions from the financial year. In Budget , the Government implemented a reduction of . in the Departments permanent baseline, after Ministers asked us to find more than the initial . savings requested of us. Te Tari identified initiatives to enable us to meet that target. The initiatives broadly covered reducing costs, reducing discretionary spending and finding more efficient ways to deliver our mahi. While the majority of initiatives did not affect our people, some did and resulted in this organisational change that impacts positions and kaimahi. Final decisions have been made This document outlines the final decisions for the Toi Hiranga l Regulation and Policy Branch organisational change, as well as the implementation plan for putting those changes in place. We carefully considered all the feedback received over the consultation period, and now the leadership team and I will be implementing the new structure as outlined in the consultation document with some adjustments. We received submissions of which were group submissions. The common theme of the feedback across all groups was for the retention of roles, as there are concerns that the reduction in staffing will mean that other people, teams or groups will need to pick up work. I acknowledge this, but I am clear that the reduction in capacity means that we will have to deprioritise some work and focus our mahi more narrowly where possible. We also received submissions proposing alternative changes such as reporting line changes, mergingconsolidation of teams, disestablishing vacant positions so we can retain filled positions that were proposed to be disestablished, and the need for new additional resourcing. We have made some changes as a result, but in most cases we were not able to accommodate Section Two: Branch Context and Background The Toi Hiranga l Regulation and Policy organisational change consultation process began on April . The financial environment we are currently in requires us to operate within reduced Crown funded baselines from July . Opportunities we identified to cut spending in non personnel related costs did not go far enough to meet the cost savings required for the Governments Fiscal Sustainability Programme and the additional emerging cost pressures we are experiencing as a Branch. We therefore had to propose some organisational structure changes to meet the spending reduction required. The following principles were used to form the consultation proposal: . Firstly, closing down vacant positions where possible, some of which have been deliberately held vacant in recent months in anticipation of baseline reductions. . Consolidating management structures and leadership positions where possible, while still ensuring the right level of technical and kaimahi oversight. . Ensuring the right level of capability is retained to deliver the core requirements of the mahi we are accountable for. You will be familiar by now with how the nature of our funding across the Branch varies; some areas are Crownfunded, while others are funded through thirdparty revenue managed through memorandum accounts, or other forms of cost recovery. We can only count reductions in Crownfunded expenditure towards the baseline reductions required of the Department. As many of you noted through the consultation process, the changes proposed for Toi Hiranga amount to more than the . initially sought by the government. That is because many parts of the Branch were already facing significant inflationary cost pressures (for example, the average salary at Te Tari Taiwhenua increased by over from to ; salary increases almost always need to be funded from existing baselines). While groups in the Branch have been absorbing these inflationary costs through savings such as reduced contractor use, reduced travel, and recruitment delays, we had reached the point where we could no longer afford all the roles in the current structure. This has been factored into the final decisions, but we have not drawn a distinction in this final decision document between unfunded roles and roles disestablished to meet baseline reduction requirements. As mentioned earlier, I know the concern remains that the reduced staffing capacity will have flow on effects for kaimahi both within the teams and across the Branch. I reiterate there will be no expectation for kaimahi to do the job of multiple people. The reduction in capacity will mean that work will need to be deprioritised.

Issue: Experiences of service inequity . The current pattern of water service provision reflects the pattern of local political choices over many decades, which have resulted in significant service inequities for Mori. In the most egregious examples, territorial authorities have laid water pipes past predominantly Mori communities on their way to servicing predominantly Pkeh communities without making any provisions to supply the Mori communities. . This type of discrimination engages Article III of the Treaty. The Treaty obligations of water services entities have been considered by Cabinet CAB MIN and are incorporated in the Water Services Entities Bill. Given these obligations, where the costs of providing services to currently under served communities are not dissimilar to servicing other communities on the network, the water services entities should be rectifying the situation. Ideally this should be done without any additional expense for the community that has experienced this discrimination. Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government IN CONFIDENCE Page of . This undoing of discrimination is important. The choice facing Government is whether to specifically provide for it in primary legislation (over and above the existing Treaty and Te Mana o te Wai requirements) or as a topic to be covered off in a Government policy statement. Ideally, this is not an enduring issue (as it should be rectified in the next decade or so). I propose dealing with this through the Government policy statemen t, given the general legislative Treaty obligations. I have also sought to ensure that all the other legislated policy decisions will allow and enable this redress. In addition, the entities will be required to conduct assessments of the three waters servi ces in their service areas, which I have proposed in my paper, Policy proposals for three waters service delivery legislative settings, through which they must consider equity of service provision including for iwiMori.
Issue: Growth charging . In the current system , growth charges play a significant role in funding growth infrastructure. The two most significant charges for water infrastructure are: . development contributions: a statutory charge under the Local Government Act available exclusively to territorial authorities, levied typically when a resource or building consent is issued; and . infrastructure growth charges: a contractual charge levied by Watercare for anyone connecting to its networks. . The Local Government Act provides detailed principles for the use of development contributions, at the heart of which is that they may only be used for genuine growth assets caused by the development(s) being charged. The Crown is exempt from paying development contributions, except for Kinga Ora. . While rates and volumetric charges form the large majority of revenue directed to the three waters, growth charges in their various forms still provide a significant source of revenue. In the current financial year, growth charges associated with three waters costs are expected to provide around million in revenue across the country, compared to total growth investment of around . billion. About half of that revenue is received by Watercare, broadly in line with Aucklands share of residential development. . Although the three waters reforms will likely change, and may over time reduce, the use of growth charges, the core benefits they provide in delivering infrastructure and housing outcomes will remain. The risks associated with removing them entirely are acute. Although uncertain, it could potentially slow the rate of growth investment and with it, housing development. Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government IN CONFIDENCE Page of . I recommend that water services entities are enabled in statute to use growth charges. . The primary strengths of a statuto ry growth charge are that it: . provides more consistency and certainty across New Zealand as to the approach taken to growth charges, particularly in the near term; . mitigates risk of excessive use of such charges in response to broader system users preference; . provides the Government the ability to design the regime, and allow it to evolve over time, in a way that is supportive of broader Government priorities (relating to residential and commercial development); . removes any possible ambiguity about the appropriateness of growth charges, and thus reduces the risk of challenge of their use; and . provides a mechanism to charge for stormwater growth and to charge prior to connection. . I recommend that the statutory charge is called a Water Infrastructure Contribution (WIC). A statutory approach provides for both clarity and assurance of approach in the near term, with the ability for the system to evolve as national level policy priorities change. . There are three broad options for design of a statutory growth charge: . a development contribution like approach: one modelled closely on development contributions with minor changes a relatively prescriptive regime; . a principles based approach: providing some basic boundaries and guiding principles but providing more flexibility in methodology for water services entities; or . an unconstrained approach: no specific boundaries or direction provided in legislation (similar to Watercares infrastructure growth charges but enabled by legislation). . I am proposing a principles based regime that would sit between the current development contributions m odel and Watercares infrastructure growth charges. I further propose that water services entities be required to issue and consult on a Water Infrastructure Contribution policy that sets out the schedule of charges and the methodology used to set them. I propose that the Crown be exempt from paying water infrastructure contributions, as it is exempt from development contributions under the status quo. . Given the time it may take the newly established water services entities to develop and apply a new policy, I propose that the legislation provide for transitional arrangements that allow to water services entities to set growth charges on the basis of any existing charges used to fund growth infrastructure (including development contributions, infrastructure growth charges and financial contributions) for up to the first three years of operation. Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government IN CONFIDENCE Page of . The principles based approach would be flexible enough to enable growth investment to be more adequately funded than though a more prescriptive regime. Without any constraints, the water services entities could charge excessively beyond what can reasonably be attributed to growth. This risk would be mitigated by a clear set of principles in legislation, the ability of the economic regulator to set guidance and rules if required, and direction through the Government policy statement if appropriate. . Under the Resource Management Act , financial contributions can be required as a condition of resource consents. I recommend that water services entities not be able to impose financial contributions under the Resource Management Act , and that councils no longer be able to impose financial contributions to fund assets vested with water services entities. . The Infrastructure Funding and Financing Act established a new funding and financing model to enable private capital to support the provision of new infrastructure for housing and urban development. I propose that the Infrastructure Funding and Financing Act be amended to enable its use to fund infrastructure to be vested with water services entities. Charging for water infrastructure contributions over time . Development contributions can only be charged at a single point in time. However, levies charged under the Infrastructure Financing and Funding Act can be charged over a period of time, rather than as a one off, and targeted ra tes can be used in a similar way. . I propose that water services entities be able to charge water infrastructure contributions as an annual or quarterly charge rather than a one off. For large growth charges, charging as an annual charge over several years, with the entity financing the upfront costs, may provide a better balance between water entity and development interests and reduce overall financing costs. Triggers for payment . Development contributions can be charged when a resource consent is granted, a building consent is granted, or a service connection is provided. In addition to these, I recommend also allowing water infrastructure contributions to be charged when water andor wastewater network demand increases absent any form of property development. This is enabled under infrastructure growth charges and primarily enables charges when commercial demand increases and would be a useful addition to accurately price increases in demand.
Issue: Should existing rating exemptions apply to water services . Currently local authorities recover the costs of providing water services through rates. . There are some types of land that do not have to pay rates. As listed in Schedule of the Local Government (Rating) Act , this includes land used for: . public gardens, reserves, public halls, land used for games and sports (except horse and greyhound r acing), museums, art galleries, swimming pools, by a local authority; . conservation land and reserves; . state run, notforprofit education; . religious purposes; . a crematorium or burial ground; . district health board land; . marae; . certain uses of Mori freehold land; . roads; . airport runways; . railways and stations; and . land used as part of a wharf. . While this land is non rateable, targeted rates can be charged on this land for water supply, sewage disposal, or refuse collection (but not stormwater). It is unclear to what extent territorial authorities actually charge targeted rates on non rateable land for drinking water and wastewater services. Officials judgement is that most territorial authorities would already be charging non rateable landowners for water services.
Issue: Should water services entity land be non rateable . The land that will be held by water services entities may currently be non rateable because it currently belongs to local authorities. The land could remain non rateable or it could become rateable when it is transferred to the water services entity. . The i ntention of the reforms is that water services are fully funded. In accordance with this general principle, water services entities should pay rates, rather than receive an implicit subsidy from local government. I recommend that land transferred to water services entities should be rateable. However, water services entities will not be required to pay rates on pipes through land they do not own (an interest in land) or on assets located on land they do not own.
Issue: Stormwater charging . Currently, local authorities predominantly charge ratepayers for stormwater services through general rates (either based on capital value or land value) or targeted rates (also often based on capital or land value). Sometimes the targeted rates are applied to specific geographic areas. Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government IN CONFIDENCE Page of . Stormwater has public good character istics and it is difficult to identify service users, therefore it needs to be priced and charged differently to drinking water and wastewater. Stormwater systems are non excludable: it is impossible to exclude people from using and benefiting from them. This makes it difficult to create user charges for stormwater systems. . A key choice in charging for stormwater is whether all properties in a service area should contribute to its costs (at differing levels) or if it should only be paid for by properties that receive drinking water or wastewater services from a water services entity. . Charging all properties in an entitys service area, albeit at different levels, acknowledges the public good nature of stormwater systems with everyone in an area benefiting from them, though the level of benefit will vary. This is my preferred option. . Only charging properties that already receive drinking water or wastewater services would be somewhat simpler from a water services entity billing perspective. However, in most territorial authorities, all properties contribute to the cost of stormwater systems, so this approach is likely to lead to increased bills for water services entity customers compared to the status quo. . I propose the following process for determining the stormwater charge within a water services entity service area: . the water services entity calculates the total cost of delivering stormwater services in its service area based on input methodologies set by the economic regulator; . the charge is apportioned to rateable properties based on: .. the capital value of the property (this is the same methodology as general rates); and .. whether or not the property is connected to a reticulated stormwater network. This criterion enables rural properties to pay less than urban properties, reflecting the lower burden that rural properties place on stormwater systems, and the generally lower level of benefit they receive from them. Alternatively, a system based on geographic zones could be used. . The exact formula for apportioning the ruralurban split or a more fine grained zonal pricing system would be set by the regional representative group , in consultation with the water services entity. . Charging based on rateable value will have significant distributional impacts across regions. Generally, property values are highest in urban areas and lowest in small towns. . Charging properties based on their rateable value would also require that territorial authorities share their rating information with water services entities on a rea sonable cost basis. However, the water services entity would not be expected to make any contribution towards the costs of establishing rateable values. We propose including provisions in legislation to enable this information sharing. Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government IN CONFIDENCE Page of . My officials have very poor information on current stormwater charges across this country, due to a lack of transparency and local authority data. I propose that this new system come into effect no later than July , but that it can be brought into effe ct sooner through regulation. I also propose a regulation making power so that the responsible Minister can put in place an appropriate transitional pricing approach and methodology in the first three years that water services entities are in existence.
Issue: recourse for nonpayment . While a very small sub group may be unable to afford their water bills, there will also be a very small sub group who are unwilling to pay their water bills. It is entirely appropriate that water services entities can recover non payment. Under the status quo, territorial authorities can obtain payment directly from a mortgagee or demand the sale of a property to recover unpaid rates. . I do not recommend that water services entities can obtain payment from the mortgagee or demand the sale of a property to recover unpaid water bills. These forms of recovery are relatively heavy handed and not appropriate for the recovery of water services debt alone. Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government IN CONFIDENCE Page of . I recommend that water services entities follow standard commercial processes for recovering unpaid bills from property owners, modelled on Watercares processes. The obligation to pay a bill will be set out either in statute or in customer agreements (dependent on legal advice and drafting approach). . An escalation regime for nonpayment for domestic customers is recommended as follows: . reminder letters followed by warning notices that outline consequences of further nonpayment, and offer of payment plans; . water restrictions and use of debt collection agencies for prolonged non payment; and . legal action to recove r debts due to the water services entity. . Interest and additional administrative, collection or legal costs may be charged by a water services entity for prolonged nonpayment. . Disconnection will not be an option for dealing with unpaid debt from residential households (but flow restrictions are available). . For commercial customers, the escalation pathway for non payment would be the same as for domestic customers but would include the ability to disconnect water services for non payment. However, this should only apply where there is no domestic element to a commercial supply, and it must not apply where there are shared meters or mixed use scenarios like apartment buildings. . The economic regulator will have a general power to issue guidance on anything relevant to its statutory duties. I would expect that the consumer protectioneconomic regulator would provide guidance to the water services entities on dealing with residential water customers who are in debt, and the service quality code is expected to include the conditions for the provision of water servic es to customers experiencing a form of hardship or other vulnerability, such as obligations of suppliers in dealing with nonpayment. . Debt collection primarily contributes to economic efficiency and equity outcomes. In particular for commercial customers, it is important that prices reflect the costs of that service. If the business is unable to pay the costs of water, then its business model is inefficient and needs reconsideration. . Debt collection also contributes to equity outcomes by ensuring that ther e is not excessive bad debt which would force other consumers (including vulnerable and low income consumers) to pay more for their services than they otherwise should have to. Implementation . My previous paper, Delivering the three waters reforms (July ), explained how the reforms will be implemented. Decisions on the proposed approach were made through that paper CAB MIN . Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government IN CONFIDENCE Page of . The proposals in this paper, my accompanying paper, Policy proposals for three waters service delivery legislative settings, and the Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs paper, Economic Regulation and Consumer Protection in the Three Waters Sector, form important parts of the comprehensive approach to implementing the three waters reform programme, which was originally considered in a suite of papers in . These proposals need to be progressed if the overall programme is to be delivered effectively and within the desired timeframe. Financial implications . The proposals made in this paper have one quantified financial implication for the Crown. The proposed legislative changes to the Rates Rebate Scheme will result in an additional . million of expenditure in that Scheme, with a corresponding impact on the operating balance and net core Crown debt. Legislative implications . Cabinet has already made several decisions that have been included in the Water Services Entities Bill. I am planning a second piece of legislation to support the three waters reform programme.
Issue: should undeveloped and unconnected properties be charged for water services . There is a question about whether properties should attract drinking water and wastewater charges situations where there is not an active connection. These situations are: . an undeveloped property that is in an area with reticulated services but that has never been connected to the network; . an unoccupied property that wishes to disconnect from services while unoccupied; and . an occupied property that chooses to disconnect for a substantial length of time and selfsupply. . I propose that all properties that are serviceable by water services entities networks should have to pay a contribution to those networks. They receive a benefit from the network in their increased property value, and from any fire hydrants near them. They should contribute to the network that creates that benefit. They could be charged at a lower rate in recognition of their non consumption, but they still ought to pay for the possibility that they can connect to the networks at any time. The water services entity also has no ability to refuse the connection (so long as there is a pre exist ing connection point such as a toby). If there is insufficient capacity in the network to connect a property, then it would not meet the definition of serviceable. . An exception to this serviceability charge should be made for non rateable land. Land that is per cent rateable should be liable to per cent of the charge. I also propose removing serviceability charges on Mori freehold land. . These exceptions would support the general policy of unrated land not being burdened with charges when they are not receiving any services.

Key issues You previously requested information on international approaches to regulating online content. Internationally, governments are seeking to modernise their media content regulatory regimes to mitigate the risk of harm posed by online media con tent. Recently, there has been a proliferation of international proposals for developing new comprehensive regulatory frameworks for online content , particularly across Europe. These proposals place greater accountability on online platforms for the user content they host. International regulatory frameworks for online content offer opportunities for l essons and alignment. However, regulating online content is complex and since most of these proposals have not been enacted yet, it is like ly that the effectiveness of different approaches and any unintended consequences will not be known for some time.

Legislated pricing principles would guide tariff setting decisions . I recommend setting out pricing principles in legislation. These are enduring principles that would inform price setting . The proposed principles have been drawn from a review of legislated principles in other jurisdictions, including the OECD, England, Scotland, and Ireland. . The suggested principles are: . Simplicity . Tariffs should be simple, transparent and easy to understand for consumers. . Non discrimination . No undue preference shown to or no undue discrimination against, any class of customers, so that purchasers of services with the same cost pay the same price (with the exception that a water services entity may charge lower (or no) growth charges to Mori communities, if this is to remedy an historic inequity in service provision). Customers in different places are not different classes of customer, if a decision has been made to geographically average their prices. . Full cost recovery . Tariffs should reflect full cost recovery in the long run: the price for each service reflects an appropriate contribution to the full underlying efficient cost of delivering that service so that over time the full efficient costs of providing that service across all users is recouped (except for growth charges which are not intended to fully recover costs). Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government IN CONFIDENCE Page of . Resource efficiency . Tariffs should promote resource efficiency: prices should generally be structured to signal to customers the costs associated with their water use decisions. Using water efficiently contributes to Te Mana o te Wai, by extracting less water from ecosystems, and reduces climate impacts. . While not requiring volumetric charging and metering, application of the resource efficiency principle will likely result in more focus on the relationship between price and consumption. I included this principle based on the advice of the Central Local Government Three Waters Steering Committee. They see resource efficiency as very important for promoting Te Mana o te Wai and better managing overall consumption of water, thereby avoiding or deferring the need for future investment. I regard this as an enabling principle. Each water services entity will make its own decision on whether to introduce meters and volumetric charges in areas where they are not already present, in consultation with communities. . I propose that the pricing principles come into effect at the same time as the information disclosure requirements are introduced through the new economic regulation regime (likely July ). This would avoid excessive change and disruption in the first few years of operation, as well as giving the economic regulator time to issue input methodologies, determinations and guidance. In the period prior to this, proposals are set out from paragraph to enable direct regulation of charges.

Levypaying gambling sectors Since , the levy has applied to four gambling sectors: noncasino gaming machine (NCGM) operators , casinos, the New Zealand Racing Board and the New Zealand Lotteries Commission. We recommend that these four sectors remain as the levy paying gambling sectors for the levy period commencing July . The Minister of Internal Affairs has also instructed the Department to review provisions governing online gambling and the class (NCGM) gambling regulatory framework . The Ministry is providing a harm m inimisation perspective into these reviews, which may result in changes to levy paying sectors . The Act anticipates s uch change ( section ()(a) refers). The levy rates and levy recovery Section of the Act prescribe s a relatively complex formula to calculate the share that each levypaying sector will pay towards the cost of the Strategy, and to calculate each sectors levy rate . This includes consideration of player expenditure (the money lost by players in each se ctor), presentations (the number of customer presentations for help to gambling harm services attributed to each sector) , the total cost of the Strategy to the Ministry and any over or under payment of the levy by each sector in the levy periods to . For the period to June , each gambling sector is forecast to have overpaid its share of the levy funding required when the levy was set. The levy formula treats any over recovered levy amount from a sector as a credit against that sectors levy liability in the next levy period. The overrecover ed amount is . million , made up of a forecast . million extra in levy payments to Inland Revenue and a million underspend of the current appropriation, by June . The underspent amount will be expense transferred into . Given the total cost of the Strategy for to is . million, this leaves the total amount to be raised in sector levy payments to maintain fiscal neutrality as . million. The proposed weighting s A key decision is required on the levy weighting s. The weighting s do not affect either the total levy amount require d or the Ministrys appropriation and the services it purchases. They only determine the portion of the total levy amount each levy paying sector will pay towards the total cost of the Strategy . This portion of the total levy amount is divided by that sectors forecast expenditure to derive the levy rate for that sector, which is then set in regulations. The levy formula uses weightings based on playe r expenditure and presentations, as described in paragraph , as prox ies for harm attributed to each levypaying gambling sector . Each weighting is expressed as a combination of percent expendit urepercent presentations. For example , means percent based on each sectors share of total expenditure and percent based on that sectors share of total presentations.
