Page of . establishing a dedicated Water Services Funding Agency , which could operate on a similar basis to the LGFA; and . direct l ending by the Crown (as the last resort) . . Several of the se options present challenges that would need to be overcome to provide confidence that the required funding can be raised: . LGFA option : Ther e would be transitional advantages (such as simpler debt settlement processes with councils) and potential longer term advantages in water services entities borrowing via a modified LGFA. However, there are significant barriers to progressing this option, because of the requirement for unanimous agreement by shareholding councils. The different risk profiles of councils and water services entities, and the weaker initial financial positions of some of the entities, also complicates this option. . A dedicated Water Services Funding Agency (WSFA) : This would operate on a similar basis to the LGFA , by pooling risk and achieving scale and market access benefits. This option could be enabled through legislation, but any decision to establish a WSFA would require further Cabinet consideration. The existence of a credible WSFA backstop option gives the Crown greater leverage when engaging with banks, institutional lenders and the LGFA for private market financing solutions. If required, this option would be preferable to the Crown providing direct lending to entities,

Page of Appendix D: Population impacts Who is more likely to experience gambling harm Mori are more likely to experience gambling harm, especially from pokies Mori make up of all high risk gamblers despite only making up . of the overall adult population. Some level of gambling harm was experienced by of Mori pokie players compared to of non Mori pokie players. Mori are also over five times more likely to be high risk gamblers than the general population, suggesting that Mori are more likely to experience gambling harm as a result of their own gambling, or someone elses. This is a result of numerous causes, including the number of gaming m achines and venues in areas of high deprivation areas where Mori are more likely to live, as well as reflecting the wider inequities faced by Mori. Pacific peoples also face disproportionate gambling harm Although Pacific peoples are less likely to part icipate in gambling ( in comparison to the national average of .), they experience higher rates of harmful gambling (. compared to the national average of .). Pacific peoples have the lowest median income (,) compared to other population groups and are more likely to live in higher deprivation areas and therefore have greater access to pokie machines. This proximity can lead to increased time and money spent gambling. Asian communities are also at greater risk Research also shows that some Asian communities disproportionately experience gambling harm. The proportion of Asians who gamble is relatively low when compared to Mori, Pacific people and EuropeanOther; however, those who do gamble are more likely to experience harm compared to E uropeanOther. The Health and Lifestyles Survey found that Asian people were more likely to be moderate riskproblem gamblers (.) compared with people of EuropeanOther ethnicity (.). For women , pokies can be a double edged sword Although being male has generally been considered a risk factor for gambling harm, recent studies have shown that when New Zealand women gamble, it is to a similar extent to men. Gambling on pokies in local communities appears to offer women especially respite, distraction, comfort and time out from family, while placing them at a heightened risk of experiencing problems and harm. For disabled people, the impacts are not known Little is known regarding the extent to which disabled people experience gambling related harm. This is an area that is not well covered in current research.

I propose to introduce additional direction making provisions into the Water Services Entities Act, to allow the responsible Minister to direct entities where collaboration or a whole of sector approach is required. These direction making powers would be subject to consultation with entitie s, and Cabinet decision making processes. The directions would need to be presented to the House of Representative s and would be disallowable instruments . . The direction making powers would be modelled on those available to responsible Ministers of Crown entities under the Crown Entities Act, and would be limited to the following purposes: . to improve (directly or i ndirectly) the provision of water services ; . to secure economies or efficiencies through the provision of shared services ; . to borrow through the WSFA (acting jointly with the Minister of Finance) ; . to develop expertise and capability ; . to ensure business co ntinuity; . to manage risks to the Governments financial position . . The direction could be given to one or more entities , or their subsidiaries. Before giving the direction, the Minister would be required, to the extent that the Minister considers necessary in the circumstances, to: . consult with those entities to which the direction is proposed to apply; and . consult with persons that the Minister considers are representative of the interests of persons likely to be substantially affected by the proposed direc tion. . The Minister would also be required, as soon as practicable after giving a direction, to: . notify the entities to which the direction will apply that the direction has been given and when it will come into force; and . present the direction to the House of Representatives. . I also seek agreement to the establishment of digital services solutions, platforms and technology as shared services that will transfer to water services entities to collectively own and govern once established.

Advice commissioned from Aon concludes that r isk sharing across entities (mutualisation of risk) is desirable to ensuring adequate and affordable risk management . Without a shared approach, entities with concentrated exposure to natural hazard risks may struggle to manage and insure these risks . . Voluntary collaborative arrangements when they decide it is their mutual interest to do so , such as in support of specific initiative and might be more important during the establishment period. This could include agreement for one entity to maintain infrastructure or network services that cross entity boundaries. . I note that the Water Services Entities Act already allows for such collaborative and intra service arrangements. Expectations on entities to collaborate for mutual benefit could be reinforced through the Government p olicy statements. This could, for example, be in the development of rules and their approaches to the regulation of trade waste , so as to ensure a consistent approach for industry and businesses across service areas. Page of Appendix : NZSIS Roles and Responsibilities . The DirectorGeneral of Security is responsible for stewardship of all NZSIS information assets, with the authority to delegate ownership to the Knowledge Manager. . The Knowledge Manager is responsible for: i. the management and flow of information, including DIA Information management; ii. ensuring the risk mitigations outlined in this Privacy Impact Assessment (PIA) report are implemented across NZSIS. . The NZSIS Chief Privacy Officer is responsible for: i. advising NZSIS Senior Leadership on the adequacy of NZSIS systems for storing, managing and protecting DIA Information; ii. monitoring compliance with the Privacy Act, in conjunction with the Compliance and Risk Manager; iii. promoting robust privacy practices across NZSIS; and iv. overseeing investigations into complaints lodged with the Privacy Commissioner regarding NZSIS access to or use of DIA Information. . The Manager Strategy and Accountability is responsible for: i. managing and responding to Official Information Act (OIA) requests and Privacy Act requests on behalf of NZSIS; and ii. managing privacy issues in conjunction with other relevant business units. . The Compliance and Risk Manager is responsible for: i. acting as the operational lead for access to and use of DIA Information by NZSIS teams; and ii. liaising with the DIA Service Delivery and Operations Risk and Assurance staff to conduct the annual joint audit of NZSIS access to DIA Information under the DAA. . An Authorised Officer is as defined in the DAA.

Page of . This Bill reflects the principles that underpin Local Water Done Well. It highlights the importance of decision making proximate to affected communities, long term strategic planning and high quality, responsive, resilient and sustainable water management throughout New Zealand. Key to the framework is bolstered central government oversight, which will ensure efficiency and accountability within the sector. We have encouraged collaboration where possible, while leaving decision making at a local level, as l ocal decision makers know their communities best. A new financially sustainable model for Watercare . This Bill will also implement Auckland Councils recommendation for a new financially sustainable model for Watercare. . Watercare and Auckland Council proposed in their draft long term plan to increase water charges by . percent from July with further significant increases projected in future years. This has been reported publicly as costing an average Auckland household an additional per year in water char ges (an increase from , to ,). . Earlier this year I agreed to undertake a process with Auckland Council to develop a policy solution that would enable Watercare to take on more debt, ideally without adversely impacting Auckland Councils borrowing capacity or credit rating. Auckland Council has developed a range of alternative service delivery models aligned with Local Water Done Well, supported by the Department of Internal Affairs and Crown Infrastructure Partners, and review ed by the Treasury. . In March , Cabinet delegated final policy decision s on the future of Watercare to the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Local Government, in consultation with coalition partners . .
Page of . While all public wastewater treatment plants have resource consents, approximately percent of plants are currently operating on expired consents and have been doing so for an average of four years and almost percent of these plants will come up for consent renewal in the next years. . Wastewater standards will directly address this infrastructure challenge by reducing regulatory burden; delivering much greater standardisation of treatment systems and related infrastructure; enabling cost efficiencies in the design, consenting, build and operation of wastewater systems; and providing councils with greater certainty of costs through standardisation and longer term consent durations. . Based on case study, cost savings of up to percent for consenting processes could be realised, depending on the type of plant and consents required. Moving from shorter term consents to mandatory year duration consents will mean that reconsenting costs are not incurred as frequently. Further cost efficiencies will be achieved through infrastructure design solutions that will introduce greater standardisation. . The Local Government (Water Services) Bill (the Bill) will introduce a new approach to wastewater standards, in terms of the standards themselves and how they are made. The Bill proposes that the wastewater standards are a single standard rather than a minimum (or maximum) that must be implemented by regional councils in resource consents and cannot be exceeded, apart from on an exceptions basis. . The Bill also proposes to align the process for making wastewater and stormwater environmental performance standards with the process for making drinking water standards. This will involve the standards being made through an Order in Council (as regulation s), on the recommendation of the Minister of Local Government. Stormwater standards will be made at a later . . The intention is to make the new standards as soon as possible after the enabling legislation is passed so that the many councils that have treatment plants requiring consent renewals can accrue certainty and cost effectiveness benefits from the new standa rds. . The introduction of wastewater environmental performance standards is the first stage of a new wastewater regulatory system. Once the wastewater standards are in place this will enable the second stage of wastewater regulatory reform the introduction of infrastructure design solutions. . Infrastructure design solutions are a new tool provided for in the Bill that will help to further reduce the costs of design and consenting of wastewater treatment plants in particular for the smaller scale plants that make up approximately percent of council owned wastewater treatment plants in New Zealand. . I have requested that the Authority work at pace to ensure the Order in Council relating to the standards is made as a priority by . The proposed standards will cover discharge of wastewater to land, discharge of wastewater to water, beneficial reuse of biosolids, and risk based monitoring and reporting requirements for wastewater network overflows. . To expedite this process, I am seeking delegated authority to issue drafting instructions to Parliamentary Counsel Office to prepare the draft Order in Council, after public consultation is completed. Page of Purpose . In August , Cabinet agreed that the National Engineering Design Standards (NEDS) should be a mandatory requirement for water services providers ECOMIN refers. This briefing sets out our proposed approach to implement the NEDS. Background Scope and purpose of the National Engineering Design Standards . The proposed National Engineering Design Standards (NEDS) provide technical standards for design and construction of drinking, wastewater and stormwater reticulation network infrastructure (water services network infrastructure). . The NEDS are intended to provide a consistent set of design standards to developers, contractors, water service providers (currently councils and CCOs) and regulatory engineers on how to design, construct and commission public three waters water services network infrastructure. . Currently, the technical standards for design and construction are set out in council engineering codes of practice (codes). These codes provide guidance to developers and contractors on the design and construction of water services network infrastructure. . The codes also provide guidance on products that will meet the standards and requirements. This approved products register (e.g. pipes and inlets) is a key feature of the codes, and functions in a similar way to approved products under the Building Code. The approved products register also supports developers and contractors to practically implement councils codes. . Developers and contractors must demonstrate that the water services network infrastructure they are proposing to vest in the council (e.g. the transfer of ownership and ongoing maintenance and renewal obligations of those assets,) or connect to the public three waters network, meets the technical standards in the relevant code. Councils also use the technical standards in the codes to guide the maintenance, renewal, upgrade or decommissioning of the new or existing public water services network infrastructure. . Currently, there are up to different engineering codes in use nationally. Although there is a degree of commonality between codes, the differences between regional, city, and district requirements for reticulation networks have created small, fragmented markets, and hindered the mobility of suppliers, potentially leading to higher costs than necessary. . The current arrangements also create challenges for councils. Where they can, councils do work with others or borrow standards but reviewing and updating councils engineering codes is an ongoing task that requires significant expertise and resource. This is significant challenge for smaller councils. In this context this includes three waters network as defined in the Water Services Act . This includes drinking water, wastewater and stormwater network infrastructure that is owned and operated by a water services provider, which could include Council, Water Services Organisation or a Government Department. Page of As part of its cyclone recovery efforts, Auckland Council intends to start making buyout offers t o the owners of Category propert ies under the Future of Severely Affected Land (FOSAL) programme before the end of . However, there are concerns that FOSAL purchases would trigger section of the LGA. The Department of Internal Affairs (DIA) considers that this is likely , due to estimates of the costs involved and the number of properties affec ted. DIA would also like to clarify that the existing exemption for the specified councils outside of Auckland continues to apply. Having to amend the LTP requires consultation using the special consultative procedure and an audit review of both the consultation document for the amendment and the final amendment itself. Satisfying these requirements would take a considerable amount of time, effectively delaying the work on FOSAL purchases. Proceeding without complying with these requirements would expose the effected local authorities to the risk of its decision being challenged in the Courts for not being consistent with section . DIA investigated different options to support the specified councils in providing certainty to impacted property owners as soon as possible. Of these options, the proposed Order will enable the effected councils to act sooner on its buyout decisions without exposing themselves to unnecessary legal risks. What would the proposed Order include The proposed Order would exempt the specified councils from section of the LGA until June . The purpose of this amendment is to enable the specified councils to make decisions on whether to make voluntary buyouts to property owners for properties that have been severely impacted by severe weather ev ents in , without having to go through the prescribed process for amending its LTP. The specified councils would not be exempted from all consultation requirements in the LGA. The specified council s would still be required to consult in a way that c omplies with the LGA. The proposed Order would not require a particular consultation procedure to be followed. It is for each Council to determine what form of consultation is appropriate in the circumstances.

Page of Executive summary . On April , Cabinet considered my paper Refocusing the water services reforms: strategy and urgent decisions CAB MIN . This was the first in a series of papers reporting back on options and proposals to refocus the reforms, to achieve our intentions to deliver more affordable water services and infrastructure. . Through that paper, I obtained agreement to a new strategic and legislative approach, and to key changes to the reform model including increasing the number of water services entities from four to , and amending the establishment timeframes. . At that time, I noted that a second paper would follow in May to provide further advice on some matters. In this paper, I am seeking to confirm the detailed proposals relating to: . the approach to the entity go live dates including confirming that the Auckland and Northl and Water Services Entity would go live on July ; and the timing for establishing the other entities and applying economic regulation ; . community priority statements which would be new instruments (distinct from Te Mana o te Wai statements) to provide communities with an avenue to communicate their interests in a body of water, and their priorities for how the environmental impacts of the entities activities on that body of water might be managed ; . a legislative process to support and guide locally led, voluntary mergers between entities to recognise that, in time, councils and communities in higher cost regions may wish to see the benefits of further amalgamation; . entity financing arrangements including provid ing in legislation for the establishment of a backstop financing mechanism, through the establishment of a dedicated Water Services Funding Agency ; . shared services arrangement s including providing in legislation for the responsible Minister to be able to di rect water services entities where collaboration or a whole of sector approach is required, and seeking agreement to the establishment of a digital shared service , which would be owned and governed by the entities . . As discussed in the April paper, leg islation is required to give effect to most of the decisions in that paper as well as the decisions in this follow up paper. In recognition that this legislation needs to be progressed quickly, I am seek ing approval to include a Water Services Entities Amendment Bill on the legislation programme, with a priority category two must be passed before the general election. . Drafting is already underway for this Bill. I am seeking agreement to issue the remaining instructions on the matters in this paper as soon as possible. . I am intending to submit a third paper in June on matters that do not need to be included in the proposed legislation but are still necessary to give effect to the new model . This will consider the implications of the change in approach on programme funding, implementation , and the reforms more broadly
Page of Planning for the next three inste ad of years will reduce the burden on these councils. By focusing on recovery, a three year plan would offer their communities more useful information and strategic direction than a year plan could. It will provide a basis for financial planning, and future council decisions. It would deliver accountability to communities. In addition, the consultation requirements related to Long Term Plans will be carried over to the proposed three year plan. This preserves the interests of stakeholders and ensures that council planning can capture the views of stakeholders. Councils would also be encouraged to plan for the longer term implications of decisions in the three year plan, where practicable. Background to the issues requiring an Order in Council Under the Local Government Act (LGA ), local authorities must always have a long term plan covering consecutive years. Councils prepare and adopt a long term plan every three years, in consultation with their communities. They are required to adopt a long term plan by June , to come into effect on July . Severe weather events early this year have resulted in high pressures on council resources from recovery efforts and uncertainty on the scale of infrastructure damage and recovery funding. These constraints are impeding these councils ability to meet their planning obligations under the LGA . Given these challenges, we consider that the proposed O rder achieves the purpose of the SWERL Act. Its purpose is to assist councils and communities to respond to, and recover from, the impacts of severe weather events. It also ensures that activities normally undertaken by councils and their communities, such as planning, continue to be undertaken. DIA investigated different options for long term planning to support these councils achieve uninterrupted recovery and functional plans. Of these options, the proposed Order will require the least council resources while still providing future direction and a basis for decision making in the me dium term, despite the uncertainties over infrastructure damage and recovery funding. It also retains community consultation on the councils intended direction for the next three years. What would the proposed three year plan include Under the draft Order, the three year plan will provide most of the same information as a long term plan, but for at least three instead of ten years. Councils will be allowed to forecast further if they wish. The three year plan will identify key challeng es for the coming years, describe the councils intentions to deal with these, and discuss how this will be funded. The plan will also discuss things that are expected to have a significant impact on councils during the next three years, including levels o f service to be delivered during the recovery. Councils will still need to prepare and adopt an annual plan for each financial year, with the three year plan acting as the annual plan for . The proposed Order does not include audit requirements for the three year plan, as this is impractical given the quality of the information available at this time and the content of the plan. Annual reports will continue to be audited.

The Scheme is not the only form of accommodation support The Rates Rebate Scheme is one of a suite of policy instruments designed to support households to meet their living costs. Other cost of living subsidies (such as the Accommodation Supplement) and adjustments to income support remain more effective at insulating low income ratepayers from rate rises than the Rate Rebate Scheme. Th ese mechanisms are also more effective at addressing equity concerns between renters and homeowners. In response to questions What are the financial implications on the appropriation In , the Scheme is estimated to co st million. This estimate is within the appropriation of million for the financial year. It is difficult to predict the impact that the increase in the cost of living will have on the uptake of the Scheme, so the Department will monitor th e appropriation through . In the last three years, the appropriation for the Scheme has increased by million. For this reason, the uptake will be closely monitored, and remedial action will be taken if necessary. Any increased uptake of the Sche me will be accounted for in the October or March baseline updates. How will people find out about the adjustments to the Scheme The adjustments to the key settings will be in the New Zealand Gazette . I will also issue a press release. The Depart ment will inform councils and key interest groups, such as Grey Power and Age Concern, of the adjustments to the Scheme. Details of the adjustments will also be shown on the Departments Rates Rebate webpage. Why not adjust the Scheme by using the average wage (as with Superannuation) rather than with increases to the Consumer Price Index (CPI) If I was to adjust the Scheme using the average wage, we would need to review the Scheme at a more strategic level . This would need to be a comprehensive re view in the context of other subsidies and supplements that are currently available to low income households. Such a review could not be completed in time for an adjustment to the Sche me to take effect on July . Adjusting the Scheme with average wag e growth would also likely exceed the current appropr iation for . Why does the adjustment need Cabinet approval every year In , Cabinet decided that the two key settings of the Scheme should be adjusted each year to reflect the increase in CPI for the previous calendar year. Background Why are national wastewater standards needed . Much of the wastewater infrastructure in New Zealand was built to years ago and is approaching the end of its useful life. Around percent of New Zealands wastewater treatment plants service populations of or less, meaning the costs are disproportionately spread across a smaller ratepayer base. . A report prepared by the New Zealand Infrastructure Commission Te Waihanga looked at the cost of consenting infrastructure projects in New Zealand. The report found the cost of consenting to be considerably higher in the waste and water sectors, which was largely driven by the amount of expert advice and intensive engagement required. The report also found that the most significant indirect costs we re those associated with delay. Funding is often set aside for infrastructure upgrades, yet unable to be used due to significant delays in the consenting stage. The cost of construction and availability of resource may change considerably in the meantime, resulting in higher costs. . New Zealand lacks a national approach to managing wastewater discharges and overflows, as well as to monitoring and reporting. The current system: results in expensive and inconsistent bespoke arrangements for wastewater discharge consents and consent conditions, with a lack of certainty for network operators when they plan and fund individual plants; adds expense and time to consent processes involving multiple rounds of engagement; and disincentivises councils from addressing wastewater overflows, due to inconsistent definitions and approaches that impact the management of the scale and frequency of overflows. . Approximately percent of wastewater treatment plants will require reconsenting in the next years, including approximately percent of plants already operating on expired consents. Implementing improvements to consenting processes now will ensure the benefits can be quickly realised by a large number of wastewater network operators, the majority of whom are councils. What benefits will the wastewater standards provide . Establishing national wastewater standards will set clear requirements that must be met by wastewater infrastructure. The standards will provide a framework which broadly takes into account the receiving environment (e.g. ocean, freshwater, high and low mixing environments, and land). . This enables some flexibility for councils to make decisions locally about where they should discharge wastewater (e.g. water or land), and then apply the relevant standard in their consent application. The standards will provide a clear consenting pathway for each wastewater network.

The NEDS would enable a national approach to standards and requirement for the design and construction of water services network infrastructure (e.g. similar sized manhole covers for drains across New Zealand). While the transition from the existing codes to the NEDS will be challenging, councils and the water sector have been calling for national standards for water for many years. . The National Transition Unit (NTU) under the previous three waters reform was progressing work on NEDS and had developed and consulted on four NEDS for drinking water networks, wastewater gravity networks, wastewater pumped systems, and stormwater networks. The four draft NEDS were circulated to the sector in September .While sector feedback was received and recorded, the draft NEDS were not and finalised. . We provided you with advice LG on the cost of finalising the four draft NEDS, so that they would be available as a voluntary standard, which was estimated to be around K K. While we believe this still reflects the costs to finalise the existing drafts, further work and costs will be incurred to provide for the additional requirements to implement the mandatory NEDS. Page of Background . Earlier this year, I was asked to report back to Cabinet with options to refocus the water services reforms, looking particularly at three priority areas: . the number of entities and their boundaries; . how Mori rights and interests are reflected in the new system; . the timing and sequencing of implementation. . On April , Cabinet considered the first of a series of paper s reporting back on these areas, Refocusing the water services reforms: strategy and urgent decisions CAB MIN . . In that paper, I explained that, while there continues to be a strong rationale for reform, it ha s become clear that the fourentity reform model presents challenges for community acceptability . There continue to be concerns across local communities that this model for water service delivery results in loss of local influen ce and voice. . To help address this issue, I obtained agreement to proceed with a new model, in which there will be water services entities instead of four. The new entities will be more closely based around existing regions, and every territorial autho rity owner will be represented on the regional representative group. This approach will better align the entities to communities of interest, thereby strengthening local representation and influence . . I also explained that moving to a model involving more entities would have a number of implications, and mean s we will forgo some of the economic benefits associated with the four entity model . However, there are ways to recoup some of the scale economies that might otherwise be lost due to smaller entities, such as through financing mechanisms and shared servicesfunctions across entities . . Further work has been undertaken to develop proposals on entity financing mechanisms and shared services arrangements. I am seeking decisions on these proposals through this paper. . I am also seeking to confirm the detailed proposals on the other matters that were signalled in my previous paper where these need to be given effect through legislation. The remaining areas will be included in a third paper, in June , cove ring implementation and financial implications. This briefing seeks your agreement to adjust the maximum rates rebate and income abatement threshold for the Rates Rebate Scheme (the Scheme) in line with the . percent increase in the Consumer Price Index (CPl). Background . The Scheme allows lowincome ratepayers to access a rebate on their council rates. . Applicants apply for a rebate directly to their council and, if successful, they either have their rebate applied to their rates account or are paid a cash refund if their rate:s have been paid in full. The Department of Internal Affairs (the Department) then reimburses the council. . Eligible applicants include: . residents who are ratepayers for the property to which the rebate is being claimed; and . residents who own a nonseparately rated unit in a retirement village, and who contribute to the outgoings of the retirement village; and . on Maori land, residents of individual houses on the same block (upon request). . The applicants income used in the assessment is that earned from the previous tax year. For example, a person applying for a rebate in the year from July to June is assessed on their income for the financial year ending March :. The definition of income also includes an applicants partners income. Adjustment history . In , Cabinet agreed that the maximum rebate and income abatement threshold should be adjusted annually, in line with movements in the CPI for the previous calendar year CAB Min () () refers. The maximum rebate available and the income abatement threshold have been adjusted in most years since . . In , you agreed to adjust the Schemes key settings by . percent, in line with CPI. The maximum rebate increased from to , and the maximum income abatement threshold increased from , to ,, as stated in section () of the Rates Rebate Act (the Act). Previously identified issues with the Rates Rebates Scheme . In December , we informed you that the Department has been preparing to provide advice to you to address identified issues with the Scheme. Given the complexity and overlapping mandate with other government departments, and the full work programme of the Branch, this has not been a priority. We expect to finalise our advice providing options through the Briefing to the Incoming Minister at the end of this year. Page of Considering Mori representation remains important. In the context of cyclone recovery, I consider that this is something that councils should be able to opt into if they consider they have the resources to undertake the process. The Supplementary Order Paper will delay the commencement of the mandatory Mori representation provisions Under my proposals in this paper, the mandatory requirement for local authorities to consider Mori representation would not come into force until the day after the local elections. The status quo would remain in the meantime in which councils can optionally consider Mori representation. In , the Government passed the Local Electoral (Mori Wards and Mori Constituencies) Amendment Act . The Act removed all mechanisms for binding polls to overturn councils decisions to introduce new Mori wards or Mori constituencies because they had become a barrier to improving Mori representation in local government. This makes it easier for councils to consider introducing Mori wards. There are still provisions in the Bill that need to come into effect this year The Bill also : makes changes to support Auckland Council to provid e for fair and effective representation of Aucklanders. The Bill aligns the membership restrictions of Auckland Council with all other territorial authorities in New Zealand. Currently, Auckland Council is limited to exactly councillors plus the mayor, while other territorial authorities can choose between five to councillors and the mayor. creates two new processes for unitary authorities to adjust local board area boundaries (one for minor changes and one for more significant changes). updates the processes for tied elections, including an automatic judicial recount before any coin toss, and enables all candidates to submit electronic nominations . These provisions will all need to come into effect this year, so the Bill should still be passed in th e current term of Parliament. Page of Section : Delivering an option How will the new arrangements be implemented . If Option is agreed, there would be changes to the primary legislation. The Department would be responsible for implementing this. The Minister has signalled his intention to seek to implement this monopoly as soon as possible to address TAB NZ s current and potential future loss of revenue and to maximise value from the Entain partnership . Prior to full regulation the Department will enforce the monopoly as an interim step . The Minister for Racing has directed that the monopoly be implemented quickly and ahead of the broader regulation of online gambling generally. However, this will require a two phased approach to enforcement regulation. . Until full enforcement and oversight of the online monopoly is able be transferred to the dedicated online regulator in , the Department would undertake an interim regulator role. This is intended to assure Entain that the monopoly is being regulated and therefore release the payment to TAB NZ as per the partnership agreement . . While the interim framework will be place with the passing of the legislation and any associated regulations; the degree to which any powers are utilised and the resources dedicated to this function during the interim period will be an operational matter for the Department, given this arrangement would likely only be required for months. . It is expected that the Department will take a pragmatic approach to establishing and implementing this interim role, while still ensuring adequate enforcement. This could involve the Department intervening with operators breaching the monopoly issuing initial warning when breaches are brought to its attention and rais ing issues with regulators in other jurisdictions. . We acknowledge that in the short term, until a fully empowered online gambling regulator is established under the Gambling Act enforcement in the sports and race betting space may be problematic. . As noted, w e anticipate the more reputable operators would want to avoid breaching New Zealand law, if for no other reason than to protect their ability to operate in other markets that are regulated (where the regulator in that jurisdiction would look closely at any breaches in other jurisdictions), and not jeopardise a possible future New Zealand online casino licence. We anticipate that group of offshore operators would leave the New Zealand market , including those who are most popular with New Zealanders but it will be challenging to enforce rules for other operators who may not be licensed anywhere, or only licensed in jurisdictions with minimal oversight.

Amendments to the Water Services Act . On April , Cabinet approved the policy proposals tabled by the Minister Responsible for RMA Reform in the paper First Resource Management Act Amendment Bill: Addressing a Small Number of Time Critical Changes CAB MIN .. Cabinet agreed for the amendment of the Resource Management Act (RMA) to exclude the hierarchy of obligations contained in the National Policy Statement for Freshwater Management (NPS FM) from resource consent applications and consenting decision making processes. That Bill is due to be enacted by the end of . . Te Mana o te Wai informs how the NPS FM is implemented. Te Mana o te Wai imposes a hierarchy of obligations that prioritise the health and wellbeing of water first over the health and needs of people and the ability of people and communities to provide for their social, economic and cultural well being. . I received advice on the implications of excluding the hierarchy of obligations in the NPSFM on Taumata Arowai the Water Services Regulator when setting wastewater standards and on councils when issuing consents for wastewater treatment plants. Under th e Water Services Act , Taumata Arowai must give effect to Te Mana o te Wai when undertaking any function, power or duty and may develop wastewater environmental performance standards. Taumata Arowai have begun developing wastewater standards consistent with the current provisions. These standards are expected to be operational from mid and will apply when new consents are issued. If the hierarchy of obligations is removed from consenting decisions but is in place when the standards are formulated, councils will still be bound by the likely higher standard. . I was authorised by Cabinet to determine if amendments to the Water Services Act are required to ensure consistency with the proposed changes to the RMA, specifically whether the Te Mana o te Wai hierarchy of obligations should be disapplied to the setting of the wastewater standards. Interim amendments to the Water Services Act are recommended to ensure that Taumata Arowai do not apply the hierarchy of obligations when developing wastewater standards. This will mean that councils will be able to issue consents consistent with the Governments new approach to the NPS FM. I expect to provide a longer term solution through the Local Government (Water Services) Bill which will address the regulatory settings for Taumata Arowai in more detail. . I have asked officials to instruct Parliamentary Counsel Office to draft minor and transitional amendments to the Water Services Act , to align the Governments approach to hierarchy of obligations relating to Te Mana o te Wai. This is consistent with the Cabinet decisions referred to above. enkv Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government IN CONFIDENCE
Page of . Councils will still need to get consents for their wastewater networkstreatment plants, but the process will be much simpler as regional councils will not need to create bespoke sets of consent conditions for each networkplant. Instead, all parties will know the requirements from the outset and once granted, all consents that the standards apply to will be for a year period. This standardisation and longer consent duration will eliminate some consenting costs as many plants are currently granted with s hort to medium term consent durations. It will also enable greater certainty of costs for councils in the management of their wastewater networks and in consenting processes. . Wastewater standards provide an opportunity to: give clear environmental performance expectations to communities for wastewater infrastructure; streamline consent processes; provide certainty to councils as network owners about the costs of infrastructure investments and upgrades; ta ke advantage of economies of scale in plant design, procurement and operator capability training; make compliance and enforcement more achievable and transparent; and enable performance benchmarking, to drive improved efficiencies and environmental outco mes over time. There will be further benefits once infrastructure design solutions are in place . The Bill provides for a new discretionary regulatory tool infrastructure design solutions which will support the use of modular infrastructure for waste water treatment plants. The solutions will set out the design and operating requirements for standardised modular wastewater treatment plants or components that are deemed to meet the wastewater standards. The infrastructure design solutions will be simila r to Acceptable Solutions, such as those relating to drinking water (under the Water Services Act ), and under the Building Act . . Infrastructure design solutions will result in faster consenting processes and potentially significant cost savings, and over time will enable network operators to standardise the design and procurement of infrastructure, and enable modular, off theshelf solutions to be installed. . The infrastructure design solutions are initially likely to focus on small treatment plants. They are not in the scope of consultation on proposed wastewater standards. They will be developed and publicly consulted on once enabled through legislation as part of the implementation of the standards. What cost efficiencies will be achieved . The proposed wastewater standards are expected to deliver significant costefficiencies that may include reduced consenting costs of up to percent based on case study. This includes reductions in costs associated with the consenting process including staff time, technical assessments, feasibility assessments, legal costs and consultation and engagement costs. . In some cases, there may also be reductions to capital upgrade costs and ongoing operating costs such as staff training and maintenance. The cost savings on an individual plant will depend on specific circumstances, such as the type or size of the plant, t reatment processes, and options for where the plant discharges. However, over time, further costs savings are expected as materials are standardised, and modular options are available that comply with wastewater standards. G ambling harm is widely believed to be underreported, in part due to the stigma that is felt around problem gambling, which has been identified as a barrier to people seeking help or accessing services and support . The Ministry of Healths proposed strategy for to includes new initiatives to address how stigma from gambling harm can be reduced. . I propose to do more to reduce pokies harm and do it quickly I consider the best way to tackle pokies h arm in the short term is to make regulatory changes under the Ac t. I propose to update these regulations to set stronger and clearer requirements to reduce gambling harm. We could do this quickly to reduce the level of harm being experienced. There are gaps in the current regulations, as some key aspects of harm minimisation were not covered when the R egulations were created in . A recent decision in the District Court Department of Internal Affairs v Suppressed NZDC has shown, as outlined below, the benefits from setting more prescriptive requirements for identifying gambling harm in venues. The defendant was charged with failing to take reasonable steps to ensure that the venues harm minimisation policy was used to identify a problem gambler. The reasonable steps included having systems to track multiple cash withdrawals and regular long play durations. The Judge held that as these steps were not included in the harm minimisation policy, they were not self evident requirements. The decision noted that these steps could be prescribed by regulations and that venue staff and gamblers would benefit from this . The current regulations cover a limited number of topics , with a low level of prescription. The current Regulations and legislative framework are summarised in Appendix A. Further cost efficiencies are expected once infrastructure design solutions are in place by enabling standardised wastewater treatment plants or components of treatment plants to be commissioned and delivered faster. . Additional information about potential cost efficiencies is provided in the discussion document, the interim Regulatory Impact Statement (attached as Appendix B )and attached factsheets: Wastewater and Stormwater Environmental Performance Standards, and Infrastructure Design Solutions (Appendix C ). What will the standards cover . I am proposing to set four sets of draft wastewater standards. The standards will cover discharge to water, discharge to land, beneficial re use of biosolids, and risk based monitoring and reporting requirements for wastewater network overflows. . The proposed standards will target cost effective ways to manage wastewater plants and networks while protecting public health and the environment. The initial tranche of standards focuses on the main contaminants from wastewater treatment plants. . The standards will also take particular account of small wastewater treatment plants (serving populations of less than ,). This is because approximately half of New Zealands treatment plants service populations of this size. These plants have characte ristics that are different to those that service larger towns and cities. . The wastewater standards proposals are only intended to apply to wastewater treatment arrangements that service communities (that is, treatment plants and significant reticulated networks). The standards may apply to all public networks (owned by a territo rial authority or its service delivery arm such as a council controlled organisation, a government department, or the New Zealand Defence Force). . The proposals are not intended to apply to privately owned networks, onsite systems that treat wastewater within the same property boundary, or small wastewater systems that service schools or camping grounds (such as those operated by the Department of Co nservation or the Ministry of Education). Treatment arrangements of this nature will be excluded as part of the drafting when the Order in Council for the wastewater standards are prepared. Nature of the standards . Under the current legislation, any standards are minimum standards, which means a regional council considering an application for a resource consent that relates to a wastewater network could not grant a consent with conditions that are less restrictive than the standards. They could impose conditions over and above the standard. . In July , Cabinet agreed to amend the Water Services Act and Resource Management Act (the RMA) to make changes to how wastewater standards will be implemented through resource consents CAB MIN . refers. The Minister of Local Governm ent was authorised to work with the Minister Responsible for RMA Reform (and other Ministers) to develop the appropriate policy approach and the necessary legislative changes. . These changes will be implemented through the Local Government (Water Services) Bill (the Bill). The Bill proposes wastewater standards are a single standard rather than a minimum (or maximum) that must be implemented by regional councils in resource consents and cannot be exceeded, apart from on an exceptions basis. Page of . We think there are significant benefits for a regulatory system (both for regulators and those who are regulated) from consolidating the national oversight, performance monitoring and standard setting for wastewater, and stormwater water services network infrastructure within one regulator the Authority. . For water service providers and the water services industry, a consistent regulatory approach for three waters networks will provide clarity and certainty on network standards and requirements. Those standards and requirements will need to be consistent with the Authoritys renewed mandate, to ensure that costs are proportionate. . Consolidating all the three waters standard setting in the Authority will build stronger and more effective relationships with water sector. Through its work on wastewater standards, the Authority is already building those relationships, and these can be leveraged to support the development and implementation of the NEDS. . However, we acknowledge that administering the NEDS will require the Authority to broaden its capacity and capability from predominately sciencebased regulation to include engineeringbased regulation. While these capabilities are already required to deliver infrastructure design solutions for wastewater treatment, the inclusion of this new function for the Authority will require an uplift in that standard setting capacity and capacity. . In considering whether the Authority should administer the NEDS, we evaluated whether this task would be better allocated to Crown Infrastructure Partners (CIP). While the content requirements of the NEDS fall within their capabilities and it has synergies with their wider infrastructure and procurement roles, they do not have the same level of focus or connection to three waters services that the Authority has. . We also note that as CIP transitions to become the future National Infrastructure Agency, they will go through a period of transition and establishment as they build their full set of functions, and there is a risk that progress on the NEDS could be reprioritised as wider priorities are reallocated across the infrastructure sector (e.g. the reprioritisation of the NES on infrastructure) and subsequently delayed. . However, while we are proposing that the Authority should have the legislative accountability for administering the NEDS, we think that it is important that the development of the NEDS is aligned with wider network infrastructure standards. To provide that assurance, we propose that CIP should provide a technical review of the NEDS ahead of wider consultation (discussed below). The development, content and review of the National Engineering Design Standards . As noted above, the focus of the NEDS is public water services network infrastructure. The content for the initial draft NEDS for drinking water, wastewater (gravity and pumped systems) and stormwater networks developed by the National Transition Unit drew on best practice approaches in councils existing engineering codes of practice. We are proposing that content of those initial draft NEDS should be used as a starting point for the matters that would need to be included in the future NEDS. Page of level of regulation in relation to Class gambling in terms of both topic s covered and the level of prescription, providing the opportunity for a much stronger harm reduction approach. New Zealand takes a public health approach to reducing harm from gambling. My officials assessed the Regulations against best practice approaches for harm minimisation and identified some key gaps. The current regulations do not adequately use some of the key levers for reducing pokies harm controls in the gam bling venue, restrict ions on machine features, and enforcement tools to drive compliance. For example, the current regulations: do not specify procedures for harm minimisation policies, such as how and when venue staff should check on players ; have few restrictions on the gaming features known to attract players and encourage continuous play; and have no associated infringement offences. The legislative framework provides an opportunity to create a stronger harm minimisation approach. The matters to be covered in the discuss ion document , outlined in the next section, are expected to be relatively uncontroversial, although stakeholders will likely have different views on the optimal approach. Overview of the Discussion Document I am seeking agreement to consult with stakeholders and the public on their views on ways to strengthen the requirements in the Regulations, through the discussion document , Reducing Pokies Harm , attached to this paper as Appendix B. Comparing the current regulations against best practice approaches to harm reduction has identified the areas where improvements are needed and will be most effective. This resulted in three focus areas summarised below. The venue : Government has not stipulated specific actions that venues must undertake. Staff who work at pubs and clubs lack the tools to identify problem gambling and intervene effectively. The mechanisms and criteria for intervening are either not prescribed or not clearly prescribed in organisations harm minimisation policies and practices . Training and record keeping requirements need addressing . The machines: The number , nature and impact of gaming machine features designed to keep people playing has increased significantly as technology has developed. There are considerable opportunities to reduce harm through restricting game features and jackpot branding . Enforcement : Few of the chargeable offences and infringement offences in the Act relate to breaches of harm minimisation requirements, and there are no enforcement options for breaches of the current regulations. A strong enforcement toolkit needs a spectrum of responses, including proportionate, lower level options for small to moderate breaches . Page of What engagement has informed the development of the standards so far . The Authority has engaged with engineering and environmental industry experts and key stakeholders to ensure the proposed standards represent a cost effective and proportionate approach to consenting. A technical review group, made up of territorial author ities and regional councils, industry experts, members of the Water Services Authority Board and Mori Adv isory Group, has also provided the Authority with external assurance. . This engagement will result in a set of standards that: reflect appropriate treatment limits for treatment plants set by councils; are applicable to all plants, including those serving , or fewer people; and support efficient and cost effective consent ing that balances risk and benefit while enabling effective environmental and public health protections. . The Authority has also engaged with a number of councils in their capacity as network operators, and with a number of regional councils as consenting authorities. This engagement has allowed the priorities and concerns of these councils to be incorporated in the proposed standards. . Feedback from smaller councils included concerns about affordability and ensuring that wastewater standards are tailored to the specific characteristics of their plants. Larger councils had a focus on planning for infrastructure resilience to support popul ation growth. Regional councils are cautiously optimistic about the proposals but wanted clear direction on how the proposed standards interact with existing national direction and regional plans this has been clarified in the Bill. . I am seeking Cabinets agreement to release a discussion document that will support public consultation on the proposed wastewater standards . Building on the constructive feedback already received, I intend to seek further input through a public consultation process. I am seeking Cabinets agreement to issue a discussion document that will support consultation. . The Authority will publish the interim Regulatory Impact Statement (RIS) to support engagement on the proposals and to provide additional detail for interested parties. The interim R IS will be and finalised further to the outcomes of consultation. . The outcome of public consultation will inform the refinement of wastewater standards to ensure they are meeting environmental performance outcomes, while improving consistency and certainty, and reducing costs for councils and ultimately consumers of wate r services. Page of . minimum technical standards for the design, construction and operational performance of three water network (reticulation) infrastructure; . information requirements (e.g. data standards) these could be included directly in the NEDS or could reference other national asset data standards to reduce disruption; and . requirements for vesting water services network infrastructure and for connections to the network. . The technical standards will be performance based and the NEDS will include commentary and guidance on how to implement the standards andor requirements. Variations . Although providing national consistency is a primary objective of the NEDS, there will be a need to enable some regional or local variations to the standards to reflect geographic, climatic and geological differences between regions that impact network performance. Potential examples of where a variation could be required include: . higher water volumes in areas subject to more extreme rainfall; . higher seismic design requirements in areas more susceptible to earthquakes; and . specific construction requirements where there may be specific soil types or geological conditions (e.g. potentially liquefiable soils). Approved products . A key feature of councils existing codes is the identification of approved products that are deemed to meet the standards and requirements in the codes. The inclusion of approved products mirrors the approach taken in the Building Code and provides a practical and costeffective pathway for developers and contractors to determine what types of water services network infrastructure will meet the codes requirements for vesting or connecting to the network. . While providing for certification of approved products centrally by the Authority would have benefits in the current New Zealand context, it would be both costly and time consuming to certify all the products that are currently in use. This could cause significant disruption for both water services providers, the wider development community and suppliers. . To address those issues, we propose that we adapt the existing approach that is used to identify that building products meet the requirements of the New Zealand Building Code. Under this model, the Authority can (subject to accreditation criteria) appoint product approval bodies. The product approval bodies would evaluate products against performance requirements of the NEDS and approve those products as suitable to be vested andor connected to the public three waters network. Clutha District Councils Lawrence supply Taumata Arowai has been reviewing Clutha District Councils Drinking Water Safety Plans, including the plan for the Lawrence drinking water supply. The Lawrence supply takes water from Phoenix Dam, which is treated using filtration, chlorination, and ultraviolet disinfection before being distributed to consumers. The review of the Lawrence supply included a site visit that identified several concerns. These include highly coloured water and signs of cattle activity in the dam, insufficient infrastructure to monitor the supply, key treatment processes not working effectively (with mu ltiple activated alarms), and signs of rodent activity (coupled with open water channels) inside the treatment plant. We met with the Clutha District Mayor and Chief Executive on March , and followed up with a letter on March . Clutha Distric t Council issued a boil water notice for the Lawrence supply on March . In our letter to the Clutha District Council on March , we asked Clutha to provide a plan of how they intend to manage the risks identified by March . We will prov ide further update s to you if there are ongoing concerns. Virus prevalence in Canterbury groundwaters project In November , Christchurch City Council applied for an exemption to the contact time rule in the drinking water rules. This rule requires wate r to be held in a tank after chlorine is added, to allow time for it to kill any viruses. The exemption was not granted because it was for a process that is for primary disinfection, and exemptions can only be granted for residual (secondary) disinfection. The cost to the council to comply with this rule is hundreds of thousands of dollars, but the level of virus risk in the Canterbury groundwaters is not well understood. Binding on the Crown . The Local Government (Water Services Preliminary Arrangements) Act binds the Crown . Creating new agencies or amending law relating to existing agencies . The Bill enables the appointment of a Crown monitor to administer an interim economic regulation regime for Watercare . . The expenses of the Crown monitor will be recoverable from Watercare, based on a framework set by the Minister of Local Government. The Crown monitor is required to report quarterly to the Minister of Local Government on the exercise or performance of its functions, powers and duties. The regime is transitional, and will cease when full economic regulation of water services is implemented as part of the next Bill.

Cost ofliving implications . The proposals in the discussion document are intended to lead to cost savings for councils who operate wastewater treatment plants, and for regional councils who are responsible for consenting, and ultimately for communities and ratepayers. Where the standards apply to Crown network operators, cost efficiencies are also likely to be achieved. . As well as reductions in consenting costs there may also be reductions to capital upgrade costs and ongoing operating costs such as staff training and maintenance. The costs savings on an individual plant will depend on specific circumstances, such as the type or size of the plant, treatment processes, and options for where the plant discharges. However, over time, further costs savings are expected as materials are standardised, and modular options are available that comply with wastewater standards. Financial implications . There are no Crown financial implications associated with this proposal. Legislative implications . The proposals in this Cabinet paper have no implications for primary legislation. The proposals in this paper relate to secondary legislation to put in place wastewater standards. . The Bill, which provides for the process for making the wastewater standards and their content, is expected to be enacted . Impact analysis Regulatory Impact Statement . Page of Authority would maintain a register of product approval bodies, and approved products. . While a product approval body could be an industry provider, we anticipate that (at least initially) they will primarily be water service providers. Water service providers are also best placed to monitor the ongoing performance of approved products. . We think it is likely that most, if not all, of the existing approved products will meet the NEDS requirement, given that the initial drafts have been drawn from best practice approaches in existing councils engineering codes of practice. This will reduce the potential disruption on suppliers and the sector of introducing the NEDS. . The national register of approved products (maintained by the Authority) will support water service providers to identify other suitable products that are used in other regions. We think that over time, the current regional differences in approved products will reduce as approved products are adopted nationally. . To ensure that new products can be identified and deployed quickly, provision should also be made in NEDS, to enable alternative solutions (like the approach in the building code), where the developers or contractors and water service providers can agree to adopt alternative processes or approaches that meet the NEDS performance standards. Review, consultation and adoption . We are proposing that Water Services Authority may review the NEDS at any time to respond to new approaches or issues but that a review should occur at least every five years. When reviewing the NEDS, the Authority should be required to consult with the public, industry bodies, the economic regulator and other relevant infrastructure agencies . The NEDS will need to be developed with appropriate technical and sector input, and reviewed regularly as new engineering methodology and products are developed. Our engagement with the water sector has highlighted the importance of ensuring that both the industry and waters services providers are well represented on any technical reference groups that may be established to support the development of the NEDS. . As we have noted above, through its work on wastewater standards, the Authority is already building relationships with the water sector. We think it is already well placed to establish the industry and water sector technical reference groups needed to support the development and implementation of the NEDS. . To ensure that there is appropriate oversight of the NEDS, we propose that their development should be subject to the same requirements as the drinking water standards and wastewater standards, which includes an Order in Council process (including the preparation of a regulatory impact assessment). Funding . We are proposing that the administration of the NEDS should be levy funded. I see these proposals to reduce harm from pokies gambling in pubs and clubs as potentially a first step in more systemic reforms of the Class gambling system. There are broader issues which are likely to be more difficult to address and more contentious than the proposals in this discussion document. These issues include the concentration of gambling venues in high deprivation communities, the equity of distribution of community funding sourced from gambling, and the incentives in the system for pokies societies and venues to prioritise harm minimisation and community benefit. In raising these issues, I am mindful of how important the community funding derived from pokies is to our communities and that other portfolios such as the Community and Voluntary Sector, Racing, Sport and Recreation and Local Government will have an interest in any changes to the broader system settings for gambling in New Zealand. Some of the issues outlined above could potentially be addressed through f urther changes to regulations, while others would require legislative amendment. A wider review of the Gambling Act is a medium term action in Kia Manawanui Aotearoa: Long term pathway to mental wellbeing. Also, a s i ndicated earlier , online gambling is now considered to be at least as harmful as landbased pokies gambling. The companion paper, Options for restricting the online gambling market, presents advice on options to restrict the online gambling market in New Zealand and minimise the harm caused, particularly from offshore operators . In addition, I am proposing the legislation is amended so that the chief executive of a water services entity would have to set out how the entity will respond to community priority statements. This would occur through an annual consumer engagement stocktake, which is an existing mechanism for the entity to report on consumer and community views. These annual stocktakes would include reporting on matters such as the number of community priority statements that have been submitted, key themes, and actions the entity will take or has taken in response to them. . It is important to note that there is no change to the legislative requirements to give effect to Te Mana o te Wai, or the ability of mana whenua to make Te Mana o te Wai statements under the Water Services Entities Act. The proposed new instrument is distinct from the Te Mana o te Wai statement. . Under the Act, Te Mana o te Wai statements for water services may be provided to a water services entity by ma na whenua whose rohe or takiw includes a water body in the service area , or whose interests in the service area are recognised in a Treaty settlement a ct. Under my new proposals, Mori communities or individuals who are not mana whenua would also be able to provide a community priority statement (for example , a community group who undertake planting or restoration work on a relevant water body ). . Under the Act, all persons performing or exercising duties, functions, or powers under the A ct must give effect to Te Mana o te Wai, to the extent Te Mana o te Wai applies to those duties, functions or powers. Entities must also respond to Te Mana o te Wai statements issued to them by mana whenua. . The requirement to give effect to Te Mana o te Wai is a requirement that has been in place in the resource management system since . Te Mana o te Wai statements are a structured way to enable water services entities to give effect to Te Mana o te Wai, as they make investment decisions in areas like wastewater services where mana whenua have long standing interests. Te Mana o te Wai statements also provide a strong link to enabl e the entities to be work well with their Treaty partners , and to support Treaty settlement obligations that exist at place ( such as Waikato river settlements). . Community priority statements will not have the same legal weighting as Te Mana o te Wai statements, but will be a valuable input that I expect regional representative groups, entity boards and chief executives to consider. . The other difference is that an entity has to include information on actions it plans to take, or has taken, in response to a Te Mana o te Wai statement in its planning and reporting documents (for example, statement of intent or asset management plan). Responses to community priority statements would be included in the annual consumer engagement stocktake. As these statements are provided to regional representative groups, they may take the themes raised into account when setting the strategic direction of the entity . Page of Allocation of decision making powers . The Bill does not involve the allocation of decision making powers between the Executive, the courts and tribunals. . The Bill enables the High Court to make orders as part of the foundation information disclosure regime administered by the Commerce Commission, together with civil pecuniary penalties and a criminal offence. . The Bill also enables the High Court to make orders as part of interim economic regulation administered by the Crown monitor, together with civil pecuniary penalties where Watercare does not apply with the charter made by the Crown monitor. Secondary legislation instruments . Regulations are not required to bring the Bill into operation. . The Bill contains provisions : . that enable the Secretary for Local Government to make rules in relation to further detailed content and other requirements relating to water services delivery plans ; . allowing Orders in Council to confirm the territorial authorities that will be subject to the additional information disclosure requirement, which will enable the Commerce Commission to request and use the information for their core role as the future econ omic regulator; . that empower the Commerce Commission to specify additional information that is required, by a determination, from territorial authorities that Orders in Council apply to ; . that enable the Crown monitor to make a charter that imposes obligations on Watercare as part of interim economic regulation. . These instruments are considered secondary legislation and will be subject to consultation and publication requirements. Definition of Ministerdepartment . In accordance with drafting convention by Parliamentary Counsel Office, the Bill includes definitions of a department and Minister consistent with the definitions in the Legislation Act . . A definition of government department is also provided in the Bill as any other public service agenc y that the Secretary for Local Government may consult with when considering the acceptance of a water services delivery plan. Commencement of legislation . The Bill will commence on the day after it receives Royal assent , with the exception of the provisions relating to financial independence of Watercare from Auckland Council . These come into force on a set by Order in Council on recommendation of the Minister of Local Government , with a backstop of July . Parliamentary stages . Page of The panel considers that the information and analysis summarised in the interim RIS partially meets the quality assurance criteria. The interim RIS accompanies a public consultation document on proposed national wastewater environmental performance standards (wastewater standards). The consultation document seeks views on standards covering specific areas (discharge of wastewater to la nd and water, reuse of biosolids, and monitoring and reporting requirements for wastewater network overflows). The interim RIS sets out analysis that narrows the scope of the wastewater standards to these areas. The interim RIS sets out assumptions and limitations on analysis. This includes having wastewater standards in place as soon as practicable after enactment of the Local Government (Water Services) Bill. This has impacted the assessment of the scope of the standards that can be implemented in the time available. The interim RIS also notes challenges with quantifying the savings from introducing wastewater standards. While efforts have been made to quantify savings, these are based on assumptions and will depend on the details of the wastewater standards. analysis of potential savings that is based on the details of the proposed standards will be important for final policy decisions. The interim RIS partially meets the convincing criteria. It would have been improved with further information on what aspects of the current process for consenting wastewater treatment plants are working effectively and how these have been considered in developing the proposed standards. This information would be useful for final policy decisions. The interim RIS indicates a good level of early consultation on the details of the standards, which will be supported by the planned consultation process. However, the panel considers the interim RIS is only partially consulted because narrowing the scope of the standards to specific areas has not been widely consulted. The interim RIS is clear and complete given the stage in the policy process. . A final Regulatory Impact Statement will be developed and will accompany my proposal to the Cabinet Legislation Committee for approval of the draft Order in Council enacting the standards. Population Implications Pokies gambling is a source of ongoing inequity between Mori and nonMori , and it has disproportionate impacts on a number of population groups. See Appendix D for more detailed information on the population implications of pokies gambling . As discussed earlier, there is also a strong correlation between community deprivation and higher numbers of gaming machines and the amount spent on them. This means gambling harm from pokie machines is experienced by those who are least resilient to impacts such as emotional and psychological distress, damage to relationships, child neglect, debt, family poverty, study and employment issues. The least resilient are less likely to be able to access services, and more likely to have other related health concerns such as those related to alcohol and smoking. There is also a strong correlation between gambling on pokies and family violence, and a link to fraud and other related crimes. Women and children are particularly vulnerable to the strain caused by gambling harm. Little is known regarding the extent to which disabled people experience gambling related harm.
