Page of . It is my intention that the two instruments are distinct and complementary. It is important that the mana of Te Mana o te Wai statements is protected and upheld in the legislative framework for these reforms, and the way in which the future entities and regulators conduct their business. Community priority statements have been designed to be distinct from Te Mana o te Wai statements , and are a separate mechanism. The distinction between the two mechanisms recognises the special taonga of water for mana whenua. Confirming details for a locally led, voluntary merger process . As indicated in my previous paper, I consider it would be desirable to provide for a legislative process that allows water services entit ies to merge. This recognises that, in time, councils and communities in higher cost regions may wish to see the benefits of further amalgamation, in terms of greater investment, increased efficiencies and service standards , and lower charges. . I expect this to be a locally led process , with merger proposals formally initiated by regional representative groups . They could involve two or more existing entities merging to form a new entity. Mergers would proceed if agreed by per cent of the regional representative group s (the threshold for their other decisions under the Act) . As described below, these decisions would be informed by the details contained in a merger proposal, and community consultation. . The legislation would need to include a few procedural requirements relating to the merger process, to ensure there is clarity to the entities, their customers and staff, council owners, mana whenua, and financial institutions about what is involved. . I am proposing there would be several steps in this process , involving the following components: . Step : Internal investigation s by a n entity of the merits of a merger . This would include informal discussions with the other entity (or entities) about this proposal, and reaching an agreement on whether to proceed to the next step. These initial investigations could be prompted by various s ources including suggestions by an entity board, its owners, andor consumers. It could also be suggested by one of the statutory assistance and intervention bodies under the Water Services Entities Act (Crown Observer, Crown Review Team, or Crown Manage r) or through the system wide review processes in that Act. . Step : Formal initiation of a merger proposal. This would be done by agreement by the regional representative group. It would involve formal identification of the other entity (or entities) that would be party to the merger and an obligation on that entity to consider the proposal. It would also include notifying the responsible Minister and monitor (under the Water Services Entities Act) of the proposal; public notification; and notifying any other entities with which there are service agreements in place. Page of . Step : Development of a merger p roposal . The entities involved would work together to prepare a merger proposal . This would include all of the critical details around the proposed future new entity such as the case for merging, associated costs, benefits, and risks, and the current picture within each entity . The draft merger proposal would be shared with the responsible Minister , monitor, and regulators for feedback. This would enable them to consider the potential benefits and risks of the proposed merger, and any system wide implications. This would also include consideration by the Commerce Commission in accordance with the business acquisition provisions in Parts and of the Commerce Act , as appropriate . . Step : Voting by the relevant regional representative groups . Merg ers would proceed if agreed by per cent of each regional representative group. These decision s would be informed by the details in the merger proposal , as well the consultation and engagement with communities that members of these groups , or the entities themselves, have undertaken. Requirements relating to community consultation and decision making in the Local Government Act would likely apply to voting decisions by individual council members on the groups representing the views of each territorial authority owner . . Step : Impl ementation of the merger. If there is a decision to proceed with the merge r, a detailed implementation plan and proposed new entity constitution would be prepared . The implementation plan would include the change management strategy for the new merged entity, transition steps (outlining transfer of staff, financial reconciliatio n, accountability documents and constitution development), a strategy to ensure continuity of services, risk mitigation, and governance arrangements . . Step : Order in Council . Th e names and service areas of each water services entity are specified in Schedule of the Water Services Entities Act. There would need to be an Order in Council process for amending this Act to reflect the creation of a new entity through the merger process. A new entity constitution would also need to be made through regulations. . I am also proposing that the legislation provides for the Crown inter vention bodies (Crown Observer, Crown Review Team, or Crown Manager) to play a stronger role in the entity merger process . This would occur in limited situations, where an entity is under significant financial stress, experiencing irreparable governance difficulties, or not able to deliver minimum levels of service to consumers , and a merger is identified as a potential solution by a Crown intervention body . I understand from the Minister of Finance and the Treasury that this is an important risk management strategy, which seeks to improve services to consumers where an entity is unable to deliver services t o a minimum standard, and seeks to reduce the Crown fiscal risks.

Part B Game features . Part B considers how gambling harm can be reduced at its source, by reducing harm associated with the gaming machine experience. . The proposals selected for Part B of the discussion document may help improve at risk users ability to control their gambling, reduce spending and time spent gambling. . The proposals are based on (a) information to address the fallacy of having any control in the game, and (b) removing some of the key reinforcing features that keep people gambling. Option s Description and discussion . Pokies machines could be required to display more information (such as: return to player; volatility of games; harm minimisation messages). RTP (return to player) ratio of games The r atio refers to the level of loss a player should expect on average when playing a particular game. Most games in NZ are set at the higher end of the to requirements (e.g. near , or . lost for a single game bet of ). Providing information on this aspect of the game is not likely to assist players when choosing between different games or machines. However, being informed (and reminded) of the level of loss they should expect when they gamble on a machine could assist with better decision making, for those that struggle to control thei r gambling. Volatility of games The likelihood of winning as well as the likely size of wins. A highly volatile game gives a low chance of winning, but wins are likely to be large. A low volatility game gives a high chance of winning, but wins are likely to be low. Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Regulatory Impact Statement Being informed about volatility of games may help at risk players make decisions, especially those who are chasing losses, and assessing the likelihood of regaining those losses. Harm minimisation messaging Currently gaming machines are required to periodically provide information about how much money has been gambled and how much has been lost. This provides potentially useful information to the person using the machine, but also a break. Stronger messaging suggesting a break (or even offering to stop the game for a period) could be used. Messaging could also be made more prominent. . Display losses as losses Stop partial losses being presented as wins . Th at is, a user might gamble . on a single game and have a return of . but this will usually be presented as a . win, even though the user has lost . Providing information about the amount that was lost, instead of presenting the amount of the users own money they didnt lose on a gamble as a win, could help at risk users understand and better assess their chances of winning or losing. . Prevent the ability to make multi row bets Multiple lines operate together to disguise losses as wins. Preventing multi row bets could reduce harm by not disguising losses and might make EGMs less attractive and reduce the speed at which money is spent . . Reduce maximum stake of . The current maximum stake of . is relatively low compared to s ome other jurisdictions but c onsideration could be given to reducing the maximum stake for instance , ., or . This would likely reduce the level of harmful gambling but could impact on people who currently gamble without harm, making gaming machines gambling less attractive for that group. . Prevent or limit the number of free spins Research shows that gamblers prefer to play EGMs with free spi ns. Free spins have been associated with loss of control over time and money spent gambling. Free spins have also been explicitly linked to the notion of getting value for money which was attractive both to social and problem gamblers. Preventing or limiting free spins may reduce the attractiveness of the EGM to problem gamblers, as well as others. . Maximum number of games in an hour Pokies machines have a maximum number of games that could be pl ayed in an hour . This could lead players to take a break from playing. . More information and restrictions on jackpots Pokie machines could be required to provide information about how much of any stake is being used for jackpots . Maximum jackpot size could be reduced. Signage showing jackpot levels could be prohibited. . Some of our initial thinking on the Part B proposals, below, has been provided in the discussion document for validation or feedback : These options could lead to reductions in timemoney spent gambling andor breaks in play, so gamblers get out of the gambling zone. Some changes could take longer to implement depending on the complexity (e.g. whether both current and new machines must comply with the new regulations, or just new machines). Any software changes would need to consider and be consistent with international gaming machine standards. Cost is dependent on specific changes. Changes to machine features will incur software costs which will vary depending on the option and rollout requirements. Pokie machines are becoming increasingly addictive due to technological developments and game features will become ever more sophisticated. Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Regulatory Impact Statement Changes to game features will have an impact on reducing gambling harm, but the size of the impact is uncertain. Some people engage with technical information such as odds volatility more than others.

Paying for water services . I recommend that residential property owners continue to be liable for water services payments, including for both fixed costs (costs of connection and maintaining the service) and consumption related charges. Currently, property owners pay rates, which include a component for three waters services. In Auckland, Watercare charges property owners for its drinking and wastewater services. . In situations where residential properties are occupied by tenants, Section of the Residential Tenancies Act provi des for the landlord to be responsible for all outgoings that are incurred whether the property is occupied, such as general rates. The same section also provides that the tenant is responsible for all outgoings that are exclusively attributable to the ten ants occupation of the premises, including charges for water provided to the premises based on consumption. . I am not recommending changes to the Residential Tenancies Act . I consider it appropriate that landlords should pay the fixed costs of water s ervices. These are a cost of property ownership that, in turn, may be reflected in the level of rent charged. Landlords should be able to pass on any variable cost directly to tenants. . I recommend that the property owner should be liable to the water services entity for the entire water bill, including consumption charges. This reflects the status quo in places that currently have volumetric water charging. My reasons for this approach are that: . requiring charges to be split between landlords and tenants would result in complex billing arrangements, and increased administrative costs that would be passed on to all consumers; Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government IN CONFIDENCE Page of . water is an essential service and water servic es entities will not be allowed to disconnect service for non payment. In general, property owners are good at paying their rates, with only one to two percent of rates bills unpaid. Tenants will have varying abilities to pay, and invoicing them directly f or consumption charges would result in higher collection and bad debt costs for the entities; . other things being equal, property owning landlords should realise an equivalent reduction in their rates bill when water bills are split out from rates (though t his is dependent on decisions by territorial authorities); . landlords can pass waters services costs through to tenants via rents. . For commercial properties, there are a variety of arrangements depending on lease terms. I propose replicating the relevant provisions of the Local Government (Rating) Act (with suitable modification), which outline when lessees are liable for rates instead of the property owner. Trade waste charges are billed to the business generating the waste rather than the property owners. . I also propose replicating the relevant provisions of the Local Government (Rating) Act (with suitable modification), which outline who is responsible for paying rates for Mori freehold land.

Peoples sense of belonging and collective memory builds an inclusive New Zealand Collective memory is enhanced by New Zealands documentary heritage Thuhu: Preserving the Nations Memory programme Thuhu: Preserving the Nations Memory includes the development of a new building in Wellington for Archives New Zealand. This will preserve and make accessible the record of government in fitforpurpose, modern and resilient facilities that will ensure the best standards of care. The new Archives building will physically connect to the National Library via an airbridge, creating a national recorded and documentary heritage campus. We are also planning for a new regional shared storage facility in TaitokoLevin for National Library, Archives NZ and Ng Taonga Sound Vision (subject to funding decisions) to provide additional storage capacity for the holdings and collections of these institutions. The recorded and documentary heritage campus creates the opportunity for the three heritage institutions to colocate, partner and collaborate. This will benefit our diverse audiences and provide improved public services through access to the collections in one location. Utaina AudioVisual preservation programme Utaina is the collaborative programme between Archives New Zealand, the National Library and Ng Taonga Sound Vision to preserve the audiovisual (AV) heritage content of significance to the nation. Magnetic media used to capture defining moments in our nations history and experiences of New Zealanders through the decades is ageing and the equipment required to play it back is now rare or obsolete. Utaina will transfer AV taonga from media such as open reel tape, VHS video tapes and compact cassettes into digital formats that both support longterm preservation and ofer greater opportunities for access by New Zealanders. Department of Internal Affairs NG TAKUNE RAUTAKI STRATEGIC INTENTIONS A culture of reading enhances literacy and knowledge Developing literate citizens Research shows that reading can transform peoples lives. Three national reading initiatives are underway at the National Library to grow a nation of readers. The Communities of Readers initiative Ptoi Rito was made possible with support from the Te Puna Foundation. Ptoi Rito is working with four to six communities where there are significant inequities in access to books, libraries and reading role models. Communityled, the goal is to weave a whriki of support to inspire a love of reading among tamariki and rangatahi. The newly established Te Awhi Rito New Zealand Reading Ambassador is a national role model advocating the importance of reading in the lives of young New Zealanders. Te Puna Foundation and other partners provided substantial support to make this role possible. The National Library also leads the He P Rito initiative, a crosssectoral national conversation on the value and impact of reading. A series of opportunities is being explored with the intention to build understanding and a shared national agenda. Services to Schools uplif All New Zealand children and young people should have equal opportunities to resources and knowledge that support their learning. The National Librarys Services to Schools is undertaking a significant programme of work to improve equitable access to library services and learning resources for school communities and young people with greatest need. To achieve more equitable access, the National Library is improving the reach and impact of services to school communities and developing new ways of supporting schools and kura in areas of high priority and need. This includes an increase in resources and services to support Mori learners and ensuring that services are responsive to curriculum changes and literacy priorities. Pilots The Ministry proposes to fund a range of new pilot service models that address inequity related public health and intervention services. Examples include cultural modelsservices, language support, online services, public health messaging and access for isolated communities. Pilot costs are based on current full time equivalent (FTE) personnel costs at about , per year. The Ministry plans between three and five pilots of various sizes each year in the second and thi rd years, but a smaller number in the first year (), to allow for phasing. The Ministry does not currently know the exact size or number of these pilots; therefore, a more precise costing is not practical. The Ministry will meet the pilot evaluation costs from the research evaluation allocation. Technology The Ministry proposes to allocate a fund to support technologyrelated innovation. There is a strong consensus from both industry and service providers that the strategy should provide for greater use of technolog y to mitigate and manage gambling harm. The Ministry could use this fund to build on an established activity such as potentially funding a database with facial recognition capabilities, or trialling venue management modules or to develop online support tools or pilot tools to monitor and manage or limit player exposure to gambling harm. The Ministry will evaluate all trials. Peer support Peer support is a model that has been proven overseas and in New Zealand for other forms of addiction ( peer in this context means a person who has had a similar kind of relevant experience to other people that has had a significant impact on their lives) . The formal evidence for peer support in mental health and addiction is growing, and shows high satisfaction from consumers of services. Outcomes from peer services are as good as if not better than conventional services, yet there currently are no funded peer support positions within gambling harm services. The Ministry proposes to encourage training for and trial the introduction of peer services during this levy period. Costs are based on providing support for workforce developmenttraining in each year, plus funding additional peer support positions in years two and three . The Ministry has taken into account a range of factors, including current FTE costs and average peer support workers salaries and training costs. There are a few ways in which the Ministry could support this aim; however, its preference is for a limited number of workforce development scholarships. The Ministry has not yet determined the workforce development component costs for this, as more investigation into potential demand and timing is necessary. A significant policy and legislative programme is required to address important details necessary to enable water services entities to be operational by July . Progressing the reform programme requires a dedicated team of policy specialists and legislation experts, as well as access to specialist finance, accounting and legal expertise. . Demand is also expected to remain high for ministerial services and other related activities throughout the transition period, to support the high volume of ministerial correspondence, parliamentary questions, Official Information Act requests, media enquiries, and the administration of the various non departmental support packages. . In addition, there is significant demand to support the provision of public information about the reform proposals. Both Local Government New Zealand and the Working Group on Representation, Governance and Accountability have asked the Government to give fresh consideration to its ongoing communications and engagement with the public to build understanding of both the direct impact and the broader context of the Three Water s reforms. . The estimated cost pressure associated with policy, ministerial services and communications is estimated to be . million over the fiscal forecast period. The Minister of Finance supports funding . million of this cost pressure from the Three Waters Infrastructure Investment and Service Delivery Reform Programme tagged contingency, to support the programme until and the delivery of a public information campaign.

Preferred weighting There is no correct weighting option ; each is a subjective judgment about how to best apportion payments to each sector. There was broad support for the weighting option from the NCGM sector, two service providers, one local government and some gambling industry stakeholders. Gambling operators preferred weightings that limited their own levy liabilities. Casinos, the New Zealand Racing Board , the New Zealand Lotteries Commission and one local government stakeholder indicated support for the weighting. The Ministry notes there is now a stronger evidence based case to increase the weighting on expenditure . A broad range of submissions on the draft Strategy called for a greater weighting on expenditure, arguing it is a more current indicator of exposure to harm than presentations, which tend to be more subjective and reflect harm that has manifested as a crisis. Ministry officials consider that any weighting from to would meet the statutory weighting provisions, but note there is strong support for increasing the weight ing on expenditure to percent (the option). This support came from the NCGM sector , service providers and most other stakeholders. Casinos, the Racing Board and the Lotteries Commission all supported the status quo option, which also limits their levy liability compared to the option. The Gambling Commission also supports the option an d could see no justification for either or options . We have considered this advice and the information and analysis in the Cost Recovery Impact Statement attached to this paper. The Strategy includes public health, intervention, research and evaluation components, but ultimately it is intended to prevent and minimise gambling harm. There is now stronger evidence that a high weighting on presentations does not provide a fair allocation based on harm . Presentations tend to account for much , but not all , of the acute harm such as high risk problem gambling , but do not reflect any of the low to moderate harm that represents about half of all gambling harm . Player expenditure is more likely to attribute to a sector their share of this low to moderate harm and the nonintervention service components of the Strategy. While lowering the weighting on presentations might discourage diligent host responsibility , there are regulatory provisions in the Act that minimise th is risk. In any case, this risk is not a satisfactory reason for any sector not to pay a reasonable share of the budget. In our view, the and options both push the NCGM sectors share of the budget too far above that sectors share of expenditure while at the same time pushing the New Zealand Lotteries Commissions share of the budget too far below its share of presentations. We consider the weighting represents a suitable balance to enable the Strategy s costs to be spread fairly across all levypaying sectors. We recommend that the Committee agree s to a weighting for the problem gambling levy, for the period to . Table shows the resulting levy rates and amounts. Price shocks and rate of increase of prices . Cabinet has previously expressed the desire to manage price shocks for consumers and communities CAB MIN . Price shocks can create affordability issues, particularly when consumers are not expecting a price increase. . Changes to household water bills will occur in two ways: . Changes to pricing structures : the wide variety in tariff structures across the territorial authorities means that changes to simplify and harmonise tariff structures will result in changes in bills for individual consumers. There will be both increases and decreases to individual household bills from almost a ny changes in tariff structure, even if the overall level of revenue collected remains the same; and . Changes to price levels : changes to the actual level of prices, driven by the need to make up for historic under investment. . In the longer term, the proposed approach to economic regulation will help to mitigate the risk of price shocks through the ability of the economic regulator to use revenue smoothing. However, this smoothing occurs at the aggregate level and does not rule out relative price changes between different groups of consumers necessary to achieve horizontal equity and other objectives. . It is likely some of the pricing principles proposed above (full cost recovery and non discrimination) support price stability, once they are fully implemented. Full cost recovery also reduces the risk that prices include a monopoly profit, as monopoly profits are not part of the underlying cost structure and any surpluses are required to be reinvested. . There is a risk that, in the absence of any other constraints, some prices could increase significantly in the short term, especially where there has been significant historic under pricing andor large cross subsidies. s ()(h) s ()(h) s ()(h) Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government IN CONFIDENCE Page of . Officials are still in the process of collecting detailed information on current costs and prices for three waters services. The quality of this information is variable, in part because of the large variation in prices across territorial authorities, and because the revenue raised from water charges does not necessarily match the expenditure on water services. . The process of discovering current costs and charges is a major undertaking and will significantly increase transparency of existing charges, including existing inequities. Revealing the existing costs and associated charges for water services is likely to create a shock for some ratepayers, particularly if those costs have been funded through general rates. . While some price increases are likely to be both necessary and desirable to address historic underinvestment, there are three different but related regulatory powers (tools) that could be used to reduce price increases and changes in bills in the first few years: . A power to freeze existing tariff structures . This would be very effective at limiting changes in bills at the individual property level, if combined with a limit on price changes. But it would also have the effect of delaying the achievement of almost all other pricing objectives, other than price stability; . A power to regulate the rate of change in individual prices would limit price changes and generally keep the average bill stable. However, it would not be effective at reducing changes in the bills of all properties, unless combined with some sort of control of the tariff structure. It would also be ineffective for any new prices that may arise from a new tariff structure; and . A power to regulate the overall level of revenue from a particular service or customer group would enable changes in tariff structure while limiting the increase in average bills. There would still be winners and losers from the changes in tariff structures. . I recommend that the legislation include a regulation making power to freeze tariff structures, limit price increases, and regulate the overall level of revenue for particular services or classes consumer. This power would be limited to the regulation of household prices. This regulation making power would expire on the commencem ent of the first economic regulatory period, likely July . The economic regulator would need to be consulted on the making of these regulations. . Cabinet previously noted the work on collecting detailed pricing information from local authorities and i nvited me to report back on the outcomes of that work in June CAB MIN . My officials currently only have data on a small group of territorial authorities. I propose delaying this report back until November when they will have data on all territorial authorities. This report back will also include proposals on the most appropriate way to use, or not use, these regulation making powers to manage price shocks before the commencement of economic regulation. . . s ()(f)(iv) s ()(f)(iv) Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government IN CONFIDENCE Page of .

This paper sets out the proposed approach to pricing and charging of water services by water services entities. It seeks decisions to enable the drafting of further legislation to implement these decisions. Pricing principles . agree to include the following pricing principles in legislation: . simplicity: tariffs should be simple, transparent and easy to understand for consumers; . nondiscrimination: No undue preference is shown to or no undue discrimination against, any class of customers, so that purchasers of services with the same cost pay the same price (with the exception that a water services entity may charge lower, or no, water infrastructure contributions to Mori communities, if this is to remedy an historic inequity in service provision); and . full cost recovery: the price for each service reflects the full underlying cost of delivering that service (except for water infrastructure contributi ons); . tariffs should promote resource efficiency; . note that customers in different places are not different classes of customer, if a decision has been made to geographically average their prices; . note that more than half of households already pay some form of volumetric charge for their water; . note that all decisions about the use of volumetric charging will be made by water services entities, in consultation with their regional representatives group, consumers and communities; . agree to provide in legislation for two regulation making powers to protect vulnerable consumers, in areas where volumetric charging is used: . a regulation making power to limit the ratio between fixed and volumetric water revenues; and . a regulation making power to regulate or prohibit water services entities from using pricing structures, such as block tariffs or low user charges, that vary the unit price of a volumetric charge based on the level of consumption, for residential customers; This briefing provides you with advice on mixed use rural water schemes, and opportunities to further reduce regulatory compliance costs for these schemes. Mixed use rural water schemes . There are around mixed use rural water supply schemes across New Zealand. The schemes provide rural communities with both drinking water, and water for commercial farming purposes . The schemes are essential to rural econom ies and the health and wellbeing of rural communities . . Many of the schemes were established in the s and s with central government funding from the then Ministry of Works, sweat equity and sometimes financial contributions from local farmers, and agreements with local authorities to operate and maintain the schemes (often with ratepayer funding support) . Many of the schemes were initially established as stock water schemes, and over time they have expanded to provide drinking water to households, townships, and community facilities (such as halls, schools and churches) . . Typical characteristics of mixed use rural schemes, such as those in the Clutha District , include : . their supply of treated water at an agreed quantity for both human drinking and farming purposes, often based on restricted volume (trickle feed) to point s of storage on consumer properties ; . their supply of relatively large volumes water for farming purposes and small volumes for human drinking ; . the involvement of farmers in their governance and operation , often through scheme management committees, who work in close collaboration with council staff in their ongoing operation and maintenance ; . unclear legal ownership, though in districts such as Clutha the schemes are accounted for on the councils balance sheet , operated by council staff and managed through the councils long term planning process ; . their costs are generally paid for through a mix of variable water charges (based on agreed daily volumes of water) and rates ; and . their regulation by Taumata Arowai on the same basis as other council drinking wate r schemes . The mixed use schemes face financial challenges and need investment to modernise ageing infrastructure . The mixed use schemes face issues similar to those faced more generally by small rural district councils, including : . the need for capital investment to : .. replace and modernise aging infrastructure, much of which was built in the s or earlier ;

This briefing provides information about the role of Taumata Arowai in stormwater and wastewater regulation, as well as the options that were considered to arrive at the current settings. . A second briefing which considers the costs and benefits of Taumata Arowai retaining stormwater and wastewater functions as well as options for the reallocation of functions will be provided, should you wish, following this briefing. Background . The potential impact of poorly managed wastewater and stormwater on public health and the environment is significant . Urban water is the poorest quality in the country. Community views have changed since much of the infrastructure was built and consented , and sewage overflows on urban beaches are no longer acceptable. Poorly managed stormwater can exacerbate impacts of flooding or extreme weather events, as well as pollute local rivers or coastal environments . . Infrastructure is aging and in many parts of New Zealand has outlived its useful life. A large proportion of the network requires upgrades and greater investment in maintenance . Resource consenting arrangements and the corresponding monitoring or enforcement by regional councils are not transparent or consistent. Very little information is made available about whether wastewater infrastructure complies with consents, and much of our stormwater infrastructure is unconsented. At present, around percent of wastewater treatment plants are operating on expired consents. We also know wastewater infrastructur e is facing a wave of reconsenting, with percent of consents needing renewal by . . The system for managing and regulating stormwater and wastewater networks spans multiple agencies who have related and overlapping roles and responsibilities . A diagram of regulatory responsibilities can be found in Appendix A. Taumata Arowai was given a role in this system in an effort to address transparency issues through public reporting, and consistency of regulation through the setting of national baseline standards and performance measures . Taumata Arowai is not the primary actor in stormwater and wastewater management . It is worth noting that while Taumata Arowai has gained functions related to stormwater and wastewater, its functions are limited. Primary regulatory responsibility remains with regional councils and is managed mostly through consenting processes . . The functions held by Taumata Arowai are closely related to, and overlap with, the resource management and planning systems. The regulatory responsibility for stormwater and wastewater remains primarily with local government . The Ministry for the Environment (MfE) continues to play a role in the environmental management aspects of wastewater and stormwater networks through providing national direction and standards . Taumata Arowai has a limited role in the stormwater and wastewater regulatory system . The stormwater and wastewater functions Taumata Arowai holds are: . Setting national baseline standards and performan ce measures; . Holding and updating a register of networks and network operators; IN CONFIDENCE Pageof The Department of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua . Reporting on the performance of networks and network operators in a way that allows comparisons between networks; . Coordination between other parts of the system and providing support and guidance to network operators. . Taumata Arowai has yet to establish its stormwater and wastewater functions. A timeline for the standup of these functions is attached in Appendix . Setting baseline standards . As mentioned above, Taumata Arowai is responsible for developing and consulting on wastewater and stormwater environmental standards. Standards set by Taumata Arowai are related to, but different from, those set by MfE as they are intended to supplement existing environmental standards, through setting standards on the performance of networks, not just on network outputs (e.g. standards around leakage rates, rather than around end of pipe discharge). The standards that Taumata Arowai produce are more able to be responsive to system needs than those produced in National Environmental Standards NES), being easier to update, and being directly related to the performance information produced by operators. Setting performance measures . Taumata Arowai is also responsible for developing and publishing performance measures and targets for stormwater and wastewater networks. These measures will allow uniform data collection and reporting and can help to develop nationally consistent minimum standards. . Example measures include compliance against resource consents, as well as general asset management information . The measures will be phased in across multiple years, and the information received from network operators will be summarised in an annual report for the public. Over time, the information Taumata Arowai collects through mandatory reporting will provide comparisons, trends and examples of good practice. . Performance measures will allow operators and regulators to ascertain compliance with standards in a way that: . should improve operators understanding of performance; . increase certainty around monitoring for both operators and regulators; and . increase transparency, aiding in consumers understanding of performance. . Currently there are no nationally consistent performance measures for stormwater and wastewater operators, making national oversight impossible , as well as preventing any comparative understanding of performance or effectiveness of regulatory tools. . These functions increase the public accountability of network operators to their consumers and ratepayers and increase the accountability of regional councils giving additional incentive to monitor compliance. This comparative reporting also helps build public and sector understanding of best practise and allows for future benchmarking. System coordination . Taumata Arowai also has a system coordination role. National oversight and increased transparency around network performance means that Taumata Arowai will have the ability to support and provide guidance to operators, as well as identify system issues, capability gaps, and providing insight into the efficacy of settings for other actors in the IN CONFIDENCE Page of The Department of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua system. The role of Taumata Arowai as a water regulator means it has existing relationships with MfE, regional councils, and territorial authorities, giving it the ability to share information and feedback on the efficacy of existing system settings to inform policies developed by other actors and Ministers. . Additionally, Taumata Arowai has indicated its intention to monitor regional councils regulatory performance to get a better understanding of how regional councils are ensuring compliance and over time. Taumata Arowai has no infringement powers for stormwater and wastewater network noncompliance . Taumata Arowais functions with regards to stormwater and wastewater network non compliance are limited to reporting requirements, which support transparenc y and public trust, as well as supporting regional councils to better regulate network owners and suppliers. Specifically, its regulatory responsibilities are: . maintaining public registers of wastewater and stormwater network operators; . annual reporting on operators general performance and environmental performance to enable comparison between network operators; . producing the Annual Network Performance Report; . identifying and monitoring matters that affect the safety of drinking water, and the environmental performance of wastewater and stormwater networks; . providing oversight of, and information to central and local government in relation to the development of and compliance with, operations, standards, regulations, and other statutory requirements for wastewater and stormwater. Taumata Arowai has some general system support functions . Similarly to drinking water systems, the water reforms previously recognised a general lack of capability in New Zealand when it comes to wastewater and stormwater management expertise . In view of this, Taumata Arowai has general functions intended to support the functioning of the system as a whole. Functions specific to wastewater and stormwater include: . developing advice and guidance to enhance sector capability; . facilitating, promoting, or supporting research, education, and training, to support the environmental performance, management, and regulation of wastewater and stormwater networks , including: .. organising campaigns and promotional activities to raise awareness; .. supporting and contribute to useful research to inform decision making; .. working with education providers and sector to ensure fitforpurpose training is available to build sector capability. . identifying, preparing or promoting national guidelines and best practices that relate to wastewater and stormwater networks and network operators. Other agencies also have standard setting functions . A diagram outlining roles and responsibilities is attached in Appendix A. MfE is responsible for establishing National Direction under the RMA, in the form of National IN CONFIDENCE Page of The Department of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua Environmental Standards (NES) and National Policy Statements (NPS), or regulations. National Direction sets out how specific resources should be managed to protect the environment, strengthen the economy, and enable social and cultural wellbeing, where there are benefits of having a nationally consistent approach. The National Policy Statement for Freshwater Management (NPSFM) potentially has the greatest implications for wastewater and water quality aspects for stormwater management. . The NPSFM does not set specific standards for affected parties to meet, but rather provides an overarching approach to regulation and environmental management . Standards set by other parties should be in line with and informed by the NPSFM, including standards developed by Taumata Arowai and Regional councils in their relative roles. It is worth noting that work is being done which looks at the settings and impacts of the NPSFM, with the possibility that aspects of it will change. MfE is the agency leading this work. . Regional councils are responsible for establishing and implement ing objectives, policies and rules for natural resource management under the RMA, including for wastewater and stormwater discharges. They process resource consent applications to ensure regional requirements are met and adverse effects are avoided, remedied or mitigated. Regional councils must implement National Direction, and they are currently amending their freshwater plans to give effect to the NPSFM. After standards under the Water Services Act are made, regional councils must ensure any consents granted are not contrary to those standards. . The economic regulator is also likely to have some functions related to standard and performance measures. In its role to ascertain the financial sustainability of supplier asset management plan performanc e measures which support an understanding of levels of service that will need to be developed. Work is ongoing on the scope of the economic regulator and what its functions pertaining to stormwater and wastewater infrastructure will look like. We expect that information gathered by Taumata Arowai about network performance will be useful to the economic regulator when developing operational policies. Other options that were considered at the time of allocating stormwater and wastewater functions . To address the system issues identified earlier in this paper, Taumata Arowai was given new functions created to address the regulatory gap resulting in inconsistent and sometimes ineffective regulation of stormwater and wastewater networks . . The functions given to Taumata Arowai are directly related to increasing transparency around network performance and gaining national oversight of the function of the wider system. Several options were considered for where responsibilities should sit . Three agencies were considered as options for where the new functions would be best placed. These were: . Taumata Arowai; . Ministry for the Environment ; and . the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). IN CONFIDENCE Pageof The Department of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua . It is important to note that at the time these considerations were taking place, work had not started on the role of the economic regulator. . Taumata Arowai was found to be the preferred option as the stormwater and wastewater functions fit most closely with the other functions of Taumata ArowaiJ including its role in increasing sector capability and public trust. . The wastewater and stormwater functions allocated to Taumata Arowai have strong synergies with the drinking water functions they hold, and will utilise many of the same systems, approaches and scientific and technical expertise. Colocating these functions was deemed to enable skills and knowledge to be pooled, shared and developed further, helping create a centre of expertise for the broader system. This approach also addresses the problem of limited capability within the sector by centralising the pool of expertise. . Locating stormwater and wastewater functions within Taumata Arowai was also found to provide an opportunity to develop a wellintegrated, consistent approach to three waters regulation, and a more capable regulator. . An independent report also found it is more costeffective, as fewer staff are needed to deliver the functions in a single regulator, compared with locating them in MfE or the EPA. The synergies between these functions provide the opportunity to leverage the skills and expertise that already sit within the drinking water regulator. MfE was considered as an option . While MfE have related functions , the additional functions did not fit in well with MfEs mostly policybased functions and would have required MfE to set up new functions and develop new capability. . MfE has historically focused on the quality of freshwater at a catchment level, across all discharge types, rather than on wastewater and stormwater infrastructure. This has meant it has not had the expertise or given priority to work on three waters infrastructure which is an area that requires dedicated oversight, given the sheer size of the sector (both in dollar value and complexity spread across all councils), and impact it has on both ratepayers and their urban water quality. . Subsequently, MfE has developed a greater focus on implementation and has progressed policy work on compliance and monitoring in the resource management system. However, as it pertains to the regulation of wastewater and stormwater network s, MfE continues to respond to issues as they arise, and there no framework for regular review of regional council performance . The EPA was considered as an option . The EPA was not considered to be a good fit primarily because its core responsibil ities do not easily align with the stormwater and wastewater functions. Placing the stormwater and wastewater functions alongside the EPAs current roles and responsibilities would mean that the functions would primarily be used in the context of environmental protection rather than to support a coherent catchment level water system. It would also potentially lose some of the public health focus from the system. . The placement of the functions in the EPA would require adding in new capabilities into the agency and was the second most expensive option considered in the independent report (MfE being the most expensive option). IN CONFIDENCE Page of The Department of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua Taumata Arowai are currently in the process of developing standards . Taumata Arowai is currently working to stand up its wastewater and stormwater functions starting with updating public registers, developing standards, and introducing performance measures which were consulted on in late ). A timeline of the development and set up of the wastewater and stormwater functions are attached in Appendix B. The role of the economic regulator . The economic regulator was not considered through the options analysis as the scope of the economic regulator was not settled when the above considerations were made. . Work is ongoing as to the scope of the economic regulator, led by the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment. It is possible that there may be some overlap between the wastewater and stormwater functions Taumata Arowai currently holds and the functions of the economic regulator. This is contingent on the decision being made to include stormwater and wastewater functions in the scope of the economic regulator. . The suitability of the placement of the stormwater and wastewater functions currently held by Taumata Arowai within the economic regulator will be considered in the next briefing. There is an opportunity to reexamine allocation of environmental regulation functions for stormwater and wastewater . As Taumata Arowai are yet to establish their stormwater and wastewater functions, it is too early to assess whether the expected value and benefits of placing these functions with Taumata Arowai has been realised, or if they are better placed elsewhere . . However, there is merit in having centralised oversight within the environmental system that provides coordination, a degree of consistency and considers the environmental impacts of three waters infrastructure. For these reasons, we believe it is worth retaining Taumata Arowais performance measures, system oversight and coordination functions related to stormwater and wastewater. It is particularly important that there is a centralised place for these oversight and performance measurement functions , given the current variation in how regional councils operate and execute their regulatory responsibil ities. . There may be opportunity to look at whether standards setting functions could be consolidated or streamlined across Taumata Arowai and MfE, as part of the policy development for your next Bill, the Local Government Water Services Bill (Bill ). Next steps . If directed, officials will work with other agencies to develop alternative options for the placement of some or all of Taumata Arowais wastewater and stormwater functions. Consultation . We have worked with both Taumata Arowai and MfE in the development of this briefing, in the presentation of their suite of functions and considerations that led to their respective allocation of regulatory functions . The Department is making some changes to modernise RealMe with the login service recently being re platformed to a Microsoft cloud based solution. The shift away from the custom built RealMe login service will reduce operating costs and the need for ongoing investments to upgrade expiring components. It is expected that Microsoft will continue investing in the product to suppor t future improvements to user experience and security. However, RealMe login is only one component of RealMe services, and much wider changes will be needed to realise the value of digital identity and drive system change. . RealMe services are currently funded at approximately million per annum (including operating and capital expenditure) until June and However , additional investment is needed to develop modernised digital identity services that realise the potential benefits . Comparable jurisdictions such as Australia are investing significantly in digital identity. The current approach of multiple time limited funding requests for RealMe services will also need to change as it has undermined certainty about long term service provision , which in turn, impacted the ability of agencies and organisations to develop their services using RealMe. . However, government needs to do more than investing in digital identity services to realise the bene fits. People need to be able to access information or attributes about themselves and reuse them to obtain more services digitally. . Government has a key role in this as it holds a wide range of identity related information and attributes about people. There are multiple examples of attributes where there could be significant benefits for people, the economy and government if investment and other changes are made (including legislation in some cases) to make these available. These include attributes related to: . driver licencing information, which people commonly use to verify their identity, particularly where they do not have a passport ; . immigration to help prove the identity and eligibility of non New Zealand citizens within New Zealand ; . health to support access to services and to enable health professionals to prove their qualifications and skills (including health records such as vaccinations, and registrations such as the Health Provider Inde x held by the Ministry of Health) ; . education to support access to learning or access to services dependent on the outcome of learning already completed (such as the Record of Achievement administered by the New Zealand Qualifications Authority and other re cords associated to the National Student Number held by the Ministry of Education) ; . eligibility to make it easier to access services (such as peoples concession entitlements held by the Ministry of Social Development) ; and . business and employment, so people can represent themselves professionally or represent their organisation when undertaking activities such as compliance (including occupational licences and authorisation to represent an organisation held by the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Emplo yment). . Such information will need to be of utility for both users and receiving organisations, to encourage their participation in the digital identity system. Government will also need to change how it receives information as it is a significant user of identity services to determine who people are and their eligibility to access services (in this capacity, government is a relying party).

Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs CONFIDENTIAL Castalia Introduction The New Zealand government is proposing to reform the drinking, waste and storm water (three waters) sector. It proposes to amalgamate the three wa ters services of the local authorities into four regional public corporations . The government is proposing to amalgamate WDC s water services into a new statutory corporation called Entity A together with the water services of Far North District Counc il, Kaipara District Council and Watercare Services Limited , owned by Auckland Council (the Refo rm Scenario). The government has presented the only alternative to the Reform Scenario as being a situation where WDC remain s as a standalone water service prov ider under council control (the OptOut Scenario ). This report analyses the evidence underpinning both the Reform Scenario and the OptOut Scenario as follows : The Reform Scenario is analysed , and its underlying assumptions tested to determine whether th e stated level of household bills is robust (section ) . Specifically the analysis reviews : The estimates of the required level of assets for the Reform Scenario (section .) The estimated efficiencies apparently available in the Re form Scenario (section .) Other aspects of the methodology that raise questions (section .) . The OptOut Scenario is analysed and its underlying assumptions tested to determine whether the stated level of household bills is robust (section ) Finally, the risks and costs to the WDC community with the Reform Scenario are examined (section ). Government s Reform Scenario produces implausible household bill estimates The Reform Proposal predicts household bills for . The WICS analysis rests on two key assumptions : First, th at the capital stock invested in New Zealand water services needs to increase by a very large amount . Second, that the Reform Scenario will del iver large efficiency gains compared to the Opt Out Scenario . In our view , WIC S assumed scale of required increa se in capital stock , and of the achievable efficiency gains under the reforms, are both implausible. . Required investment estimate is overstated The governments case for reform rests on a claim that New Zealand water services require a significant capital investment over the next years. The government relies on WICS advice and analysis to set the level of investment for the Reform Scenario from to . WICS modelling is entirely based on a top down , New Zealand wide assum ption that a massive natio nwide investment programme is necessary for all council water services . This is Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs CONFIDENTIAL Castalia despite WDC and all other local authorities submitt ing detailed bottom up information about planned capital investment . Capital investment is needed in some parts of New Zeala nd now and in the next years to meet the dema nds of growth and due to historical deferred and underinvestment . There have been high profile asset failures. However, it is not clear that the investment is needed in all places, at the scale WICS claim. WICS are selective in estimating the nationwide re quired investment amount. WICS also use inappropriate Scottish comparators to support its claim that New Zealand needs to invest at equivalent levels. WICS estimate of required investment is significantly higher than the levels of investment that asset owner WDC has estimated will be required. WICS used projected investment requirements across three investment types that include replacement or renewal investment, enhancement investment, and growth investment projections. These projections are based on assumptions relating to asset lives, replace ment costs, inflation, population density, and projected connections growth. .. WICS approach to estimating required investment is unsound In order to estimate the requir ed investment, WICS uses English and Scottish comparators. WICS allocated New Zealand wide investment requirements for councils based on statistical relationship s and observed experiences in England and Scotland. The total investment required is made up of two key components that include enhancement and growth and asset replacement and ref urbishment . WICS model led the required investment using three approaches . WICS then cross check ed the modelled investment against information gathered from councils RFI re sponses . Efficient use of f inanc e can lower costs of service Efficient financing is an important co nsideration in investment planning for water utilities. The term of loans should ideally match the useful life of the asset the loans are financing. If the loan is repaid over a shorter period of time, then water bills after the loan is repaid will be lowe r than they otherwise would be. WICS assumes that amalgamated entities have greater access to financing and can make more efficient use of finance to lower the cost of service. Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs CONFIDENTIAL Castalia Executive summary The government is proposing to reform the drinking, waste and storm water (three waters) sector . The reform will involve amalgamating the water services of the local authorities into four new r egional statutory corporations , with centr alised management and a new governance structure . The structure will have indirect Board appointment rights for local authorities to be shared with mana whenua representatives. The government proposes to amalgamat e Whangrei District Council (WDC) into a new statutory corporation called Entity A together with the water services of Far North District Council, Kaipara District Council and Watercare Services Limited (owned by Auckland Council ) (the Reform Scenario). The government has given WDC two choices, join the Reform Scenario or Opt Out. WDC, along with other local authorities, has been asked by the government to consider the evidence and whether the governments proposal to reform the water sector will delive r benefits to its residents. The government also committed to providing Whangrei with million in funding under the better off package, a n additional million for stranded overhead costs under the no worse off package, and further comp ensation for any loss in WDCs debt headroom. These amounts are to be partfunded from the balance sheet of the new entity. The WICS analysis and mo delling underpins the case for reform. The government has relied on WICS for the claims that significant capital investment is needed in the New Zealand water sector, and th at amalgamation in to four separate entities with accompanying institutional changes is the only way to achieve the cost efficiencies to make the reform affordable .
