Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs Overview Your manifesto document Local Water Done Well sets out a clear direction for financially sustainable water services, underpinned by a strong regulatory regime. The regulatory environment for water services delivery include swater quality and environmental regulation, economic regulation and consumer protection . This slide pack provides an overview of the existing regulatory environment, opportunities to strengthen the regulatory regime, and an approach to stand up interim economic regulation over the next months. The contents of this pack are: Overview: recap of features of Local Water Done Well that support the stand up of the future regulatory environment Section : Economic regulation and Part of the Commerce Act Section : Proposed interim arrangements for economic regulation IN CONFIDENCE ()(f)(iv) Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs Regulatory Context IN CONFIDENCE Water services delivery by councils has a number of issues, including: In many places, investment in water services has not been prioritised and has been diverted to other priorities ; Many ratepayers not being informed on how much of their rates are being spent on water services; and It is often difficult for ratepayers and communities to make informed submissions on council proposals for water infrastructure and funding, or to hold their councils to account for poor decisions . Water services regulation already has water quality standards and some environmental standards ,but no economic regulation. There are currently few requirements on councils for the management of infrastructure, and none for infrastructure investment. There are requirements for councils to prepare an infrastructure strategy as part of their long term plans, as provided for in the Local Government Act . Existing requirements under the Act have not resulted in adequate investment in, or the substantial management of, water services infrastructure by councils. This is because while these plans are review ed by auditors, they are not reviewed by regulators and they cannot require investment. Evidence from overseas jurisdictions and other utility sectors in New Zealand indicates that economic regulation is indispensable for a well functioning water services delivery system. It plays a crucial role in safeguarding and improving the long term interests of consumers, and providing incentives and regulatory oversight to improve performance. We can provide you with an overview of economic regulation regimes in other jurisdictions. Multiple agencies will be involved in achieving comprehensive regulation of water services. Their work needs to be well connected to ensure a cohesive and effective approach to regulation. Department of Internal Affairs interim monitor and agency to provide support to councils in the development and assessment of their Water Services Delivery Plans; Taumata Arowai the water quality regulator; Commerce Commission long term economic regulator; and Regional Councils in regulation of environmental impacts . Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs Features ofLocal Water Done Well IN CONFIDENCE Effective regulation of water services is critical to improved delivery. Local Water Done Well provides for this by putting a greater focus on investment levels, revenue sufficiency, and sustainable performance of water services, and introducing more transparency and direction to councils. Many of the features of your manifesto policy will set in place the foundations for a strengthened regulatory regime The requirement for councils to prepare plans for how they will transition water services delivery to new models that meet requirements for investment and financial sustainability, is an important step to setting up a future economic regulation reg ime and continuing to build on drinking water and environmental regulation (quality regulation). The development of investment rules and criteria for assessing financial sustainability of the plans will be particularly important. Other features of Local Water Done Well also support the stand up of the future regulatory regime: The Minister of Local Government signing off councils plans once satisfied they meet requirements. The Government will not mandate any specific model for water services onto councils. A regulatory backstop to ensure councils deliver a viable plan that can deliver on outcomes for water quality, infrastructure investment and financial sustainability. Repeal of the Water Services Economic Efficiency and Consumer Protection Act and instead regulation of water services delivery under Part of the Commerce Act . The Water Infrastructure Regulator will set quality standards for water infrastructure. Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs Section : Economic Regulation and Part of the Commerce Act Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs A comprehensive approach to economic regulation is critical to the successful delivery of water services, as outlined in Loca l Water Done Well. Economic regulation aims for efficient market and supplier operations, along with consumer protection, particularly in industries with limited competition or when businesses wield substantial market power, such as in the water industry. It also supports the achievement of various health, economic, and social goals and ensures the delivery of services at a quality and resilience level that aligns with consumer and broader community expectations. Without economic regulation the monopoly nature of water services delivery would be detrimental to consumers, as the providers would have the ability to charge higher prices than in a competitive market. In the context of water services delivery, the key questions in the economic regulation space: How does the water supplier optimise operations for efficiency, resilience and sustainability What measures are in place to ensure fair pricing How does the supplier guarantee compliance with service quality and other standards Economic r egulatory tools include: Requiring public disclosure of certain information to understand the performance of those delivering water services; Benchmarking, monitoring, analysing and reporting publicly on performance; Regulating the revenues and quality of service, including the ability to require ringfencing of revenue for specific services ; Setting minimum standards for service quality that must be met; Reviewingapproving asset management plans and funding pricing plans; Setting and enforcing a service quality code to improve the quality of water services; and Enforcing and monitoring consumer complaints processes and monitoring the consumer dispute resolution service. Regulation for water services regulation would be added into Part of the Commerce Act and would be implemented from within the Commerce Commission (and the Water Services Economic Efficiency and Consumer Protection Act repealed ). The Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE) is the lead agency for policy advice on economic regulation, and will be briefing the Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs next week on this topic. Our initial view is that ifPart of the Commerce Act is used, it should be amended to make water services a regulated sector. There are some features of water services that may require more bespoke requirements, and further advice can be provided on these .Economic regulation of water services IN CONFIDENCE Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs Overview Part of the Commerce Act provides for the Commerce Commission to regulate the price and quality of goods and services for the benefit of consumers in markets where there is little or no competition. The Act sets out the particular goods and services that are subject to regulation and the legislative rules governing that regulation. Current industries regulated under Part include electricity lines services, gas pipeline services and certain airports serv ices. The telecommunications and dairy sectors are governed by their own respective legislation. Who decides which sectors are regulated under Part Parliament decided that electricity lines services, gas pipeline services and certain airports should be regulated under Part . Regulation under Part may also be imposed by the Governor General on the recommendation of the Minister of Commerce following a Part inquiry by the Commission. However, while a this is technically feasible route to regulation, this process is not considered suitable for water services. A Part inquiry would consume significant resources to collect and analyse evidence, take considerable time, and the outcome of the process would be uncertain (e.g., at the end of the process the Commission may recommend not to proceed with regulation). In making a recommendation to proceed with regulation, the Commission needs to consider the benefit to consumers through lower prices or improved quality would be greater than the costs of regulation, which include the cost of setting up and administering a new regulatory regime (which consumers would ultimately pay for through charges). The size and structure of the industry in question will have a material bearing on this assessment of costs and benefits, wit h the costs of regulating many smaller suppliers operating with a variety of corporate and non corporate structures potentially posing challenges to a regulator. In the current circumstances, the most effective and efficient mechanism for ensuring regulation would be for Parliament to pass legislation to place the regulation of water services under Part of the Commerce Act.Part of the Commerce Act IN CONFIDENCE Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs IN CONFIDENCE ()(f)(iv) Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs Differences between Part and the WSEECP Act IN CONFIDENCE The economic regulation parts of the WSEECP Act (as distinct from the consumer protection parts) have much in common with Part . The purpose statement and statutory objectives within the WSEECP Act are based on those in Part , with modifications made to reflect that water entities were to be publicly owned and prohibited from paying dividends. If Council owned water organisations were structured as companies with shareholdings and had the potential to pay dividends now or in future, then they would look a lot like existing companies regulated under Part . Many electricity distribution businesses have council ownership, for example. The general regulatory approach provided for in the WSEECP Act is similar to that in Part of the Commerce Act, including provision for information disclosure, quality only regulation and price quality regulation. The Act also provides envisages similar role and process for developing and applying input methodologies. However, the WSEECP Act included a broader range of regulatory tools than what is available under Part and generic competition and consumer law, reflecting the unique characteristics of the water sector. For example, the WSEECP Act included tools such as performance requirements that are broader than the Part approach of setting quality standards. The WSEECP also provided for the Commission to ring fence a portion of an entitys allowable return that would then be held in reserve in case of any unexpected investment requirements, thereby ensuring entities have the minimum required level of cash to finance their operations. Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs Part was designed to be flexible and adaptable to the regulation of a wide range of entities and is expected to be suitable for regulating water services. However, the effectiveness and efficiency of regulation will be very dependent on the structure of the industry. Other things being equal, regulation of a fragmented sector with many small suppliers and diverse corporate and non corporate forms is likely to be less effective and more costly than regulation of water services organisations organised into more conventional corporate structures operating at a scale suitable for the industry. Further, there are some unique features of water services that may better suit a bespoke approach to regulation not easily provided for under Part of the Commerce Act. There is a track record for industry specific regulation in New Zealand, including for example in the telecommunications industry. Sector specific regulation in the form of Part of the Telecommunications Act was brought in to remedy specific issues with customer service, fault service levels, and billing in the retail telecommunications sector. The benefits of sector specific economic regulation and consumer protection regulation could include: allowing the legislation to be designed in a way that reflects the unique characteristics of the entities compared with other monopoly businesses regulated under Part and generic consumer law, particularly that water services will be council owned and potentially delivered through a wide range of non standard corporate and non corporate forms certain regulatory approaches used under Part may not be effective or practical when applied to the council water services providers, given they will operate differently and face different incentives to other regulated businesses bespoke regulation may better reflect the need for significant improvements in efficiency. For example, Part does not allow for comparative benchmarking, which could be a useful tool in driving efficiency improvements in the industry. standalone regulation would enable a broader approach to setting performance requirements than the Part approach of setting quality standards a standalone regime could be used to place restrictions on distributions of surplus, or to ring fence funds, until such time that certain quality or service standards had been achieved it could provide for the specific consumer consultation requirements, which could then inform the setting of performance requirements, quality standards and minimum service levels. These benefits are nuanced and the relative merits of general or specific regulation are unlikely to be clear cut.Whether to use Part or sector specific regulation IN CONFIDENC E Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs Section : Proposed interim arrangements Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs Local Water Done Well outlines a requirement for councils to submit a Water Services Delivery Plan (plan) for how they will transition their water services that meets water quality and infrastructure investment rules. These plans, and the analysis that will underpin the plans, will be an important step to setting up a future economic regulation regime and continuing to build on drinking water and environmental regulation. The development of investment rules and criteria for assessing financial sustainability of the plans will be particularly important. There is an opportunity to use this process to support improvements in the information base, and to pave the way toward economic regulation. Content of the plans We recommend that the first plan has two component parts, with the relevant weighting to the sections dependent on whether councils are considering amending their existing delivery model or pursuing a new model, and how quickly they wish to stand up a new model: . Councils initial plans for: Intended delivery model: oE.g. direct ownership and management of services, council controlled organisation (CCO), joint CCO with other councils; existing approach or new. oTimeframe and establishment plan implementation plan and timetable to transition to the new model ( eg to stand up CCOs, or amendments to existing processes) and market capacity and local workforce assessment to deliver proposed model. Infrastructure investment pathway full accounting of the state of current assets (where known) and where they are in their lifecycle. Funding pathways: oFinancial sustainability plan proposed approach to pricing and charging consumers, and approach to finance and debt. What prices they will change their consumers How will these charges be kept separate from the rest of the rates that consumers pay oAsset management programme proposed investment path, including maintenance, replacement and renewal, building for growth and building to improve quality for consumers. . Baseline performance information: Key financials and other required information (to be developed alongside the Commerce Commission). Performance against current regulatory requirements ( eg Water Quality Plan how they will meet water quality requirements as per those issued by Taumata Arowai ). Performance against sustainable financing performance. Water Services Delivery Plans IN CONFIDENCE Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs Getting to a system of full economic regulation will take time to develop and implement. There are a number of key components that need to be stood up, for example the development, consultation and implementation of input methodologies. This typically takes several years, regardless of other future legislation that the Government may choose to implement. We recommend that interim economic arrangements are put in place to support improvements in the quality of information on assets, costs, and enhancing the transparency and accountability of water services. As the steward of local government, DIA is well positioned to help facilitate and organise an interim economic regulation regime, alongside MBIE and the Commerce Commission. DIA could build on existing monitoring frameworks and work alongside councils as they develop their Water Services Plans, to begin to build the information base that will support key indicators for future economic regulation (with the Commerce Commission). Crown Infrastructure Partners will also have a key role in the interim and future arrangements. As an interim step, Crown Infrastructure Parters could monitor the execution and delivery of capital plans. A staged transition to economic regulation A staged transition to economic regulation could commence with lighter touch requirements in the first months (e.g. a focus on the level of adherence to infrastructure investment rulesthe evidence that needs to be demonstrated for water services delivery plans), that are increased over time to achieve consistent information disclosure. There are several benefits to taking a staged transition to economic regulation. The staged approach allows: Time to build the information base, while using the information as it is developed to understand current performance and areas of risk. Considered development of the new policy settings and for local authorities to respond to these and implement changes. An opportunity to incrementally build requirements for councils. Given the phasing, this also may support higher enforcement of requirements at each step a scale of enhanced monitoring of some councils could be included on the basis of their earlier reporting. May provide more space for the economic regulator to define the relevant regulations without path dependency on the measures that have already been set. A greater opportunity to work with local authorities through the transition.Commencing economic regulation IN CONFIDENCE Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs Information disclosure is a key step to commencing economic regulation IN CONFIDENCE Information disclosure from councils is critical to development and implementation of economic regulation. In particular, information disclosure is needed early to inform the development of methodologies to establish price quality regulation (or similar). We recommend starting with information disclosure as a regulatory tool while councils develop their water services delivery plans. There are several options you can explore for improving transparency and quality of information during this interim period, including: Specifying information that must be included in water services delivery plans; An option to repeat the Request for Information process that DIA led previously in where councils were asked to provide information on their assets (potentially co developed with regulators and expert advisory group); Potentially introducing new planning andor reporting requirements for water services under the Local Government Act ; and Placing statutory obligations on council officers to sign off on the quality of information. To address gaps in information to inform economic regulation, we propose that DIA work alongside the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment and the Commerce Commission to establish what information can be collected through council water service delivery plans. If you agree, the following steps will form the approach to transition: We will advise you on a process to set the expectations and requirements for Water Services Delivery Plans (working with Taumata Arowai , MBIE and the Commerce Commission). As part of this process, we will work with MBIE and the Commerce Commission to specify information disclosure requirements for councils. The first Water Services Delivery Plans will be used to set expectations and to capture base line performance and financial information to inform establishment of economic regulation plus setting early expectations for performance .

This briefing provides advice on the water service delivery plans (the Plans) that councils will need to submit on their preferred water services delivery model . . Background . Local Water Done Well (LWDW) requires councils to submit Plans within months of repeal of the Water Services Entities Act for how they will transition their water services to a new model , that meets quality standards and is financially sustainable . A range of specific parameters for the Plans including the need to meet infrastructure investment rules, and direct ministerial approval were outlined. . We provided initial advice to you on the water services regulatory context on December . This advice is attached at Appendix A for your convenience. This advice noted that: . Historically councils have faced a number of challenges with water services, including incomplete information about the true cost of delivering water services, the state of water infrastructure, competing priorities, and providing transparency to communities on the investment in water assets relative to need ; . Effective regulation of water services is critical to improved delivery; . Water services regulation already has water quality standards and some environmental standards but no economic regulation ; and . Multiple agencies will be involved in achieving comprehensive regulation of water services. . Alongside overviews of water quality, economic and interim regulation, the previous advice also set out our understanding of what the Plans need to achieve: . Set expectations for the transition of water services by councils to meet quality and financial sustainability requirements; . Provide oversight of council planning to meet safe drinking water standards, ensure sufficient investment in maintenance and replacement of assets, considering future access and growth, and that they are pricing and borrowing sufficiently to fund their investment path; and . To inform the use of any regulatory backstop powers to ensure councils deliver a viable plan that can deliver on outcomes for water quality, infrastructure investment and financial sustainability . . This advice also noted that: . The Plans could require information on both councils initial plans for delivery (including intended delivery model, and infrastructure and funding pathways) and baseline performance information (including financial information, and performance against current regulatory requirements and other measures). . Information gathered through the Plans will contribute to the design of economic regulation and other policy settings ; and Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs The Department of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua INCONFIDENCE Page of . An indica tive process for developing requirements for the Plans and guidance for councils, and subsequent submission and assessment timeframes. . At present, there is no legislative framework to require provision of the Plans . Based on previous experience with respect to long term plans, we expect councils will prefer a clear legislative framework setting out any requirements for the Plans, and as such we recommend that a requirement for councils to complete the Plans is set out in the replacement legislation. . Your recent Cabinet paper CAB MIN outlined the proposed approach to progress a new water services legislative regime, in two phases. This advice signalled that the framework necessary to set out the Plans would need to be included in a first replacement Bill , in order to set clear requirements quickly for councils. Broad factors relevant to the plans . Councils will be starting in different places with respect to their future water service delivery model. We expect some councils will broadly retain their existing arrangements with some amendments to meet new requirements (for example financial ring fencing and sustainability ). These c ouncils may be able to leverage existing planning material , with some modifications, from their longterm plans. . However, c ouncils seeking to progress a more substantial change to their service delivery organising structures will require more lead in time and focus on their establishment efforts . Councils opting to use financially independent council controlled organisations (CCOs) , when available, w ould need to undertake additional implementation planning for the transfer of services , revenue and assets to the new organisation. This will be more complex for multi council organisations that will also need to negotiate and agree across councils on key parameters of the CCO (for example share allocations, funding and pricing approaches ) to inform establishment. . The development of the Plans will be a new activity for all councils . While c ouncils will need to adjust and plan for meeting any requirements over time, compliance in the immediate term may pose a problem . Larger councils may be able to pivot resources to absorb this work, but some smaller councils may face significant capacity constraints. Councils will likely need to undertake public consultation on their Plans, reducing the time available to them to develop materials. . LWDW describes greater transparency and strengthened planning and reporting for water services. These Plans would represent a n initial step towards achieving this, but the longer term planning and reporting framework for water will need to be integrated with broader local government planning and reporting. A range of intersections will need to be worked through, including : . Reporting and oversight material required by the Commerce Commission to enable economic regulation (including transitional arrangements) , regulation of financial ringfencing, and any information required to inform the use of regulatory backstop powers ; . The existing local authority planning and accountability regime , includ ing how to incorporate accountability to central government within a system that is predicated on accountability to communities ; . What a fit for purpose planning and reporting framework would look like for a range of water services delivery models ; and Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs The Department of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua INCONFIDENCE Page of . This approach poses no immediate issues and the Department will work to enable this, though we note some careful consideration of this will need to be considered when developing the regulatory backstop powers that may be informed, in part, by the Plans. . It should be noted that, besides the availability of new financially independent CCO vehicles, or other novel organisational arrangements, there is no legislative barrier to councils transitioning their water services to more sustainable models in the near term (for example, using existing CCO provisions in the Local Government Act). We expect some councils may wish to set up new organisations for water before all replacement legislation is passed, or before they complete their Plans. Where this happens, councils will be looking for clarity from the outset on the process for developing and approving Plans. Options for how the Plans should be delivered . In developing the approach to the Plans, there is a need to strike a balance between : . driving progress , with a fast transition of models, infrastructure investment lifting in the near term, and financial sustainability achieved sooner ; and . ensuring a supported transition for councils , that is responsive to their individual situations, provides a path to full compliance over time , and which does not set unreasonable expectations and planning burden on them in a short period of time . Require councils to deliver all content in a single plan, as articulated in LWDW . Councils could be required to meet all the requirements outlined in LWDW in a single plan within the original month deadline . This option would most closely align with LWDW . This would al low a more straightforward a ssessment of whether a councils Plan represents a more financially sustainable and viable model, as all supporting analysis regarding infrastructure investment pipeline, price paths and plans to meet regulatory standards would be compiled. . However, councils may experience significant issues in complying with the request within the time available, and this may be faster than all councils are able to achieve. This approach would also pose issues for the policy development process (for example, developing appropriate infrastructure investment rules for councils to respond to) , and the legislative timeframes to give effect to these . A two stage approach would allow the requirements to be built up over time . Alternatively, a twostep approach to the parameters and requirements of the Plans could be considered. In this model: . The first step would set out the foundational settings for the Plans, including that councils would be required to provide them and indicative content. These requirements would apply to a draft Plan that councils would need to submit for review . The Department recommends that a two stage approach be taken to the Plans. Th is option would enable more flexibility for councils who wish to move quickly to new service delivery models , while also reliev ing some pressure on councils to deliver complete plans several months after completing their long term plan . The submission of a draft Plan within months would continue to set expectations for the transition, and provide oversight of council planning for yourself and agencies through the process. . Some councils may seek to move quickly, and prefer to meet all requirements in a single plan . As noted, it may require time for the full regulatory regime , and the rules councils will need to meet, to be issued. The Department will work to provide as much confidence as is possible in what will be required of councils early, to help enable this flexibility . There is further optionality within a two stage approach . Within what has been proposed in Appendix B, there are opportunities to require some elements earlier (or later) as preferred. For example, setting and reporting against performance measures could be brought forward for inclusion in t he draft Plans . Conversely, some elements could only be required for the final Plans, for example funding and pric e path information. . There may also be value in not committing to the form of the second st age at this time. As noted previously, t he Plans are one part of the regulatory and oversight framework for water services that is currently being developed . In retaining flexibility, and not committing to the remaining specific requirements outlined in LWDW, there may be opportunities for reconsidering and potentially streamlining planning and reporting requirements and reducing the compliance burden on councils. This paper provides advice on: . the potential tax impacts of Cabinets decision to not prohibit water organisations from making distributions; and . the interactions between exemptions from minimum requirements and the tax status of water organisations. . Ministers decisions on these matters will inform the drafting instructions for the Local Government (Water Services) Bill (Bill ). Background . In June and July this year , Cabinet approved a series of papers which set out the policy detail of Local Water Done Well, including: . restor ing council ownership and control of water services; . establish ing clear outcomes based rules and minimum requirements for water services; . strengthen ing the regulatory regime through new economic and improved water quality regulation; and . provid ing a framework for new water organisation s designed specifically for water services. . In the third and final paper, Cabinet agreed (CAB MIN .) that water organisations should be granted tax exempt status. This proposed income tax exemption was recommended on the assumption that water organisations would not be able to provide distributions to shareholders, which had been proposed in the paper. . Cabinet also agreed that councils could apply for an exemption from some of the minimum requirements applying to water organisations. The Cabinet paper noted that granting such an exemption could affect the water organisations tax status. . Due to the outstanding tax issues , Cabinet authorised the Minister of Finance, Minister of Local Government, and Minister of Revenue to make further decisions during the course of legislative drafting in relation to how any tax implications associated with water organisations, distributions made by water organisa tions, and the exemption process for water organisations may be addressed. . Cabinet invited the Minister of Local Government to report back to the Cabinet Legislation Committee on any substantive decisions made under the delegated authority when approval to introduce the bill is sought . Why tax status is important . New Zealands tax settings reflect the principle that tax should apply to a wide definition of income (broad base) so that less tax needs to be collected (low rate) from each source. Tax exemptions put pressure on tax rates as they inherently reduce the total amount of potential income that is available to be taxed. Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs The Department of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua INCONFIDENCE Page of . The income tax exemption proposed for water organisations was justified on the basis that: . private sector investors would not be able to benefit from the tax exemption , due to the prohibition on distributions and restrictions on shareholders ; and . these organisations will have a primary public policy purpose of undertaking water related activities in a monopoly market , rather than a profit making activity in competition with the private sector. . As water organisations will be able to make distributions to shareholders, and taking into account the potential outcomes arising from exemptions from minimum requirements, we have modified our positions for consistency. . In developing a response to these issues , consideration has been given to both the impact this may have on the tax base and the precedent it may set in relation to other entities in similar circumstances. Tax status of water organisation s that meet all minimum requirements . As previously advised LG , allowing water organisations to make distributions means the tax status of the shareholders should be considered when determining the tax status of the water organisation. . Under the minimum requirements, shareholders of water organisations can either be councils or consumer trusts. Councils are broadly exempt from income tax; the income they derive, primarily through rates, is used for the benefit of their communities. . However, a consumer trust would be a taxable entity and would face no such restrictions on how it used the income it receives . A consumer trust can achieve income taxexempt status by applying for and maintaining charitable status. As previously advised LG , we believe consumer trusts created to hold shares in water organisations will easily fall within the other purposes beneficial to the community category of charitable organisations. This would both grant the water organisation a tax exemption and ensure that it only provides public, and not private, benefits. . Nevertheless, there may be good reasons that a consumer trust would not want to apply for charitable status. One reason could be if the council establishing the water organisation wanted the shareholding consumer trust to distribute income back to consumers in the same fashion that an energy trust does. Energy trusts are not able to gain charitable status, in part because of the intent to provide private benefits back to consumers , normally through a discount on lines charges . . It is important that the shareholders of a tax exempt entity are also tax exempt if there are no restrictions on distributions . Tax exemptions are primarily provided for specific public purposes. This briefing provides advice on a single standard approach to wastewater environmental performance standards (wastewater standards), where, once made by Taumata Arowai, the requirements in the standard would be implemented through resource consents. Stricter or higher requirements would only be included in a resource consent by a consent authority (regional councils) in exceptional cases. Since your last briefing outlining a minimum and maximum range approach LG refers officials have continued to develop the policy approach in relation to setting a single national standard. . This briefing outlines: . the approach taken in other jurisdictions and how wastewater standards operate; . how a similar approach might be implemented in New Zealand (including the implications for legislation, and whether changes might be required); . whether other changes could be made to incentivise use of modular design treatment plants as part of standardsetting; . how the approach would be explored and implemented through Taumata Arowais work programme; and . initiatives that could be pursued in the broader resource management system to achieve further regulatory efficiencies for wastewater treatment plants. Background . Taumata Arowai is currently developing wastewater standards covering core areas in resource consents for wastewater treatment plants. You have requested advice on your preference for a single standard rather than a minimum and maximum range approach , and information on how that could be achieved. The wastewater standards will apply to all receiving environments but will be particularly applicable for discharges to water. A single standard is consistent with international best practice and is the preferred approach . In previous advice we explored what a minimum and maximum range approach to wastewater standards might look like LG refers. . Either a minimum maximum range approach to standards or a single standard approach are possible in legislative and operational terms: A single standard approach would include tiers of standards based on characteristics such as population serviced by a plant or mixing level of a water body it discharges to. INCONFIDENCE Page of Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs . while both would require further work as part of Taumata Arowais work programme, in terms of the technical work it is much more complex to set a minimum maximum range; . both will require legislative change to the RMA, and probably the WSA, to be confident the approach can and would be implemented across the regulatory system. . On balance our advice is that a single standard is the better approach for the reasons outlined below. . A single standard approach is consistent with international best practice Taumata Arowais technical experts could not identify any other jurisdiction where a maximum standard approach was adopted. They advised that in other jurisdictions where a standard is set, plants are generally consented to a national standard. That is, it is not a minimum standard, it is the standard. . In this sense a discharge standard operates like the drinking water standards which set treatment requirements that suppliers are expected to meet. Requirements for higher levels of treatment are generally only set in exceptional cases, for example, where a wastewater plant discharges to a pristine or particularly sensitive water body. . In system terms, a single standard is a better fit with the existing RMA regime. While it will deliver standardisation in approach to resource consenting, together with the flow on standardisation of infrastructure and procurement, there will still be potential for consent authorities (regional councils) to set conditions in consents that are stricter than the standard. However, this ability will be limited through legislative change so stricter or higher requirements would only possible on an exceptions basis defined in legislation. . Taken overall, a single standard approach will allow for standardisation of treatment systems and related infrastructure, material cost efficiencies in the design, build and operation of wastewater systems and greater certainty for councils in terms of infrastructure and budget planning. The single standard approach will also allow for greater certainty, consistency, and cost control across the wastewater treatment plant consenting system. As with a minimum and maximum range approach, these outcomes are aligned with the objectives of Local Water Done Well. . The problematic areas for a minimum maximum range approach are related to the maximum standard which regional councils would not be able to go beyond when setting a resource consent. Taking expert advice, we have not been able to identify another jurisdictions that takes this approach. In system terms it is likely to present challenges for regional councils and network operators depending on how the maximum standard is configured for the following reasons: . there will be cases where a maximum standard will be inflexible to (or be perceived to be) inflexible to the water quality of a water body. Under the RMA, water quality, together with community expectations about what it should be, is the primary driver for consent limits rather than standardisation of Taumata Arowai sought advice from technical experts with experience in overseas jurisdictions such as the United Kingdom and the European Union where wastewate r standards have been in place for over years. INCONFIDENCE Page of ll Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairsinfrastructure. In a subset of cases, higher treatment than the maximum standard maybe required to deliver the right outcomes for the water body; . there is a risk a maximum standard will have unintended consequences, and will not provide flexibility where a wastewater operator voluntarily treats wastewater to a higher standard than in the resource consent (for example, to provide for reuse of wastewater), and inadvertently breaches their resource consent because wastewater is too good to discharge to water. . For iwiMaori there may be a perception that a maximum standard would cut across the health of the water body and their role as kaitiaki, by hardwiring in a maximum level of treatment that could lead to greater pollution than their aspirations. There may also be greater implications for those Treaty settlements which have catchment related requirements (such as the WaikatoWaipa or Whanganui settlements). . In order to progress a single wastewater standard approach, legislative change will be required to ensure consenting authorities implement a single standard approach in resource consents. You may also wish to consider including provisions in the WSA allowing Taumata Arowai to specify infrastructure and operating requirements that, if implemented by a wastewater operator, will meet the treatment requirements in the standard. Broader changes to the resource management framework might also be possible to streamline consenting pathways. These matters are dealt with in the remainder of this briefing. Realising the benefits of a single standard approach Regulatory efficiencies could be achieved where wastewater treatment plant design and consenting processes were aligned to a new wastewater standard . There is a significant opportunity for economies of scale and cost savings across the system if an endto end modular designconsentbuild approach was adopted for lowerrisk wastewater treatment plants for small communities (i.e. less than , people), aligned to comply with a new wastewater standard. These are likely to be smallerscale plants in provincial or rural areas with less complex treatment processes and will not generally include those with industrial discharges. . An example is where an oxidation pond may be currently used to treat wastewater. This is common throughout New Zealand, but treatment outcomes are highly variable and, as a consequence, these arrangements often breach resource consents. Reconsenting of oxidation ponds could occur with integration of a modular plant to lift treatment outcomes. This approach to upgrading plants is being implemented by some territorial authorities. Wastewater standards would incentivise the approach across New Zealand. . Of the wastewater treatment plants that will require reconsenting in the next decade, service populations of , people or less. These plants make up around percent of the total number of councilowned wastewater plants in New Zealand. . While there will be local differences, industry estimates of the costs of the design, consent and construction of those plants are up to million for plants servicing less than , people. It is estimated that, in some cases, up to half of those costs relate to design and consenting issues. In contrast, a modular offtheshelf wastewater treatment plant that was designed to meet the standard could be constructed and be operational for around million. Modular, standardi sed approaches to the provision of wastewater treatment are common internationally , but barriers to their adoption in New Zealand include: . no consistent approache s to consenting wastewater treatment plants; . councils operating in silos and rely on local consultants leading to bespoke design; and . lack of capabilityconfidence to procurement of standardised solutions internationally . . With the bow wave of wastewater treatment plants needing to be reconsented (and upgraded in the next years, the development of a pipeline of plants that could be commissioned and the use of modular design could drive these costs down further (LG refers. . Wastewater standards under the WSA are linked in legislation to resource consenting under the RMA. Section (D) of the RMA specifies that a consent authority, when considering an application for a resource consent that relates to a wastewater network (as defined in the WSA): must not grant the consent contrary to a wastewater environmental performan ce standard made under section of that Act; and must include, as a condition of granting the consent, requirements that are no less restrictive than is necessary to give effect to the wastewater environmental performance standard. INCONFIDENCE Page of Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs. Taumata Arowai was given powers to make wastewater standards under the WSA. Once the wastewater standards are in place, resource consents must not be granted contrary to, or less restrictive than, a standard. However, a consent authority may currently impose conditions that require higher treatment requirements. . Despite the recent legislative changes to both the RMA and the WSA to remove the Te Mana o te Wai hierarchy of obligations from resource consenting processes and the development of wastewater standards, there are still provisions that allow a proposed wastewater standard to be exceeded in consenting decisions. For example, where regional council policy requirements go beyond national policy requirements (e.g. by directing all wastewater discharges to land, as is proposed in the Northland Regional Council freshwater plans), and where regional plans and policy statements and some iwi management plans have embedded Te Mana o te Wai in their planning documents and the hierarchy remains operational. . To be able to implement the changes outlined proposed in this briefing relating to a single standard, legislative changes to the WSA and RMA legislation will be needed to: . provide more directive provisions that ensure regional councils cannot set additional or higher requirements than the standard (allowing for some specific exceptions); . allow Taumata Arowai to be able to set infrastructure and operating requirements that, if implemented by a wastewater operator, will meet the treatment requirements in the standard this could be used to specify design solutions such as integration of modular plants with existing oxidation ponds; and . allow an easier consenting path or preconsented option for lowerrisk smallscale modular wastewater treatment plants that met the standard. . These changes are critical to support councils in addressing challenges in the reconsenting the bow wave of wastewater treatment plants. Around percent of wastewater treatment plants will require reconsenting in the next years, with the most challenging issues where plants discharge to freshwater or low mixing environments like estuaries or bays close to the coast. . This does not mean lower environmental requirements for discharges to fresh water or coastal water. It means that a consistent approach to consenting the discharge of wastewater from treatment plants will be provided, which reduces the regulatory burden by targeting key weaknesses in the existing resource management regime. . Further work will be needed to develop and agree the appropriate policy approach and nature of the legislative changes. In your July Cabinet paper you are seeking the following legislative changes: . delegated authority to work with and agree the appropriate approach with the Minister Responsible for RMA Reform to progress these changes; . once changes to WSA and RMA have been agreed, delegated authority for you to authorise issuing of drafting instructions to include these changes in the Local Government Water Services Bill. . Taumata Arowai has started work on developing the wastewater standards . Taumata Arowais work programme is already focused on a single standard approach of this nature, by identifying the approach taken in other jurisdictions, and considering how they might need to be adapted to the New Zealand context. . To ensure the outcomes in this briefing are achieved, further work could be commissioned to identify: . what, in practice, are the situations in other jurisdictions where wastewater plants have needed to be consented above a national standard on an exceptions basis this evidence would be used to develop changes to the RMA to ensure regional councils cannot set additional or higher requirements than the standard except on an exceptions basis that would be specified in legislation; and . infrastructure design and operating requirements that, if implemented by a wastewater operator, would meet the treatment requirements in the standard for example, modular or package plants. The Local Government Water Services Bill (Bill ) will set out a range of new water organisations for councils to choose as their preferred delivery arrangements for water services. The Bill will include options to establish standalone water organisations, by themselves or with other councils, and either as council controlled organisations (CCOs ), council controlled trading organisations (CCTOs) or consumer trusts. . The purpose of this briefing is to give you advice and seek your decisions on options for a range of possible provisions in Bill with respect to infrastructure powers and local authority regulatory powers , and to ensure these may be used effectively by standalone water organisations . . Offences and infringements . . Role of bylaws . Currently local authorities have the ability to regulate the activities of their water services consumers and third parties through broad bylaw making powers under the Local Government Act (LGA) , with offences and enforcement powers set out directly in the Act. There are also some relevant provisions in the Local Government Act and the Health Act . . As part of the Local Water Done Well model, the enabling legislative framework for water organisations will need to allow for them to exercise some of these regulatory powers. . Bylaws are one of the few tools available to local authorities to manage relationships with their water services consumers. They cover a wide range of matters, including: . consumer responsibilities; . infrastructure design standards; . prohibition of certain discharges; . demand management (water restrictions); . charges; and . establishing local authorities rights to access water systems and read meters. . Bylaws can also regulate actions of third parties in relation to activities that may affect water services . For example, they can make it illegal to discharge certain substances into stormwater drains, control who can access drinking water catchment areas, and regulate work on or around networks.

The next steps section at the end of this briefing outlines the likely work involved. Key messages . Under the Water Services Act (the Act), all drinking water suppliers (except domestic selfsuppliers) are covered by the regulatory system, and required to provide safe drinking water. This was considered the most effective and straightforward way of protecting public health, and responding to the concerns raised in the Inquiry into Havelock North Drinking Water. The new regulatory regime has been designed to tailor regulatory settings to the size, risk profile, and complexity of supplies. . We understand you may be interested in reconsidering this approach, to reduce the potential regulatory burden that may be incurred by smaller suppliers. This is something that has been advocated by some stakeholders, and by members of the National Party and ACT Party. . You could consider excluding some smaller suppliers from being regulated, based on the number of people they serve. We have outlined two possible options: a threshold of people (option ); and a threshold of people, but only for lowerrisk supplies (option ). . Our initial view is that option could be a pragmatic way to make the regulatory system less burdensome with a level of risk that could be tolerable providing Taumata Arowai is able to provide support to unregulated suppliers (that want it). We would like to do further work to develop and test this option. We do not recommend option , as this would carry much greater risk and be more difficult to implement. . We have also outlined a further option (option ), which we suggest is progressed in parallel with option . This involves minimising the requirements that apply to other smaller suppliers, and giving these suppliers a longer timeframe to be compliant with the Act (beyond the current deadline). . To provide a basis for considering which if any of these options you might like to progress further, we have provided an overview of what being regulated is likely to mean in practice for smaller suppliers. This helps to indicate how much of a burden they might face if no changes are made. . Taumata Arowai is required to regulate in a way that is proportionate to the scale, complexity and risk profile of drinking water supplies. This means many smaller suppliers will be subject to minimal obligations, and will receive advice and support both to comply, and if emergencies arise. You will need to seek Cabinet decisions on policy proposals that involve changes to the Water Services Act. The Department would provide further advice on this in the context of Bill of your Local Water Done Well programme. Regulatory approach under the Water Services Act , and why it was introduced . Under the Water Services Act : . all drinking water suppliers except domestic selfsuppliers are covered by the regulatory system; and . all drinking water suppliers are required to provide safe drinking water. . This approach was taken in response to significant concerns raised through the Inquiry into Havelock North Drinking Water, and other work, about the previous drinking water regulatory regime in the Health Act. There were concerns that regime was failing to provide assurances that water supplies were safe and reliable. . The new regulatory approach sought to address two core issues with the previous arrangements: some suppliers were not being regulated effectively , and others were not regulated at all. . Advice in estimated that around , people were receiving drinking water from suppliers that were not regulated under the Health Act. The regulation of networked supplies was fragmented and weak, and many suppliers were effectively unregulated. . Under the Water Services Act, all suppliers were brought into the regulatory system. The Cabinet paper that sought the relevant policy decisions noted that: . the proposed approach would address many of the serious shortcomings with the current system, and provide New Zealanders and international visitors with the confidence that our drinking water supplies are safe and reliable. However, it involves a judgement call about how far to extend the regulatory perimeter, and the pros and cons of different options. We have approached the design of the reform proposals from the perspective that everyone should receive safe drinking water, but recognise that this will impose costs in the regulatory system that will be passed on to consumers. This included network supplies to fewer than people. It also included several kinds of specified self supply, many of which were institutions and facilities serving a lot of people (such as schools, campgrounds, universities, airports, and defence properties) . Strengthen ing the regulation of drinking water, wastewater and stormwater, Minister of Local Government , Minister of Health, and Minster for the Environmen t (July ). IN CONFIDENCE Pageof Proactively released by the Department of Internal AffairsThe Department of Internal Affairs Taumata Arowai . This approach was considered the most effective and straightforward way of protecting public health and addressing widespread compliance issues in suppliers of all size and type. Historically, there have been longstanding problems with non compliance as the size of the supply decreases. . It reflects that most consumers cannot assess the quality or safety of the water they drink, and have little or no choice about who supplies their water services. They have to put their trust in those responsible for supplying and regulating those services. . The Act requires suppliers to provide safe drinking water. It reflects that an essential principle of drinking water safety is that suppliers must own the safety of the water. . In practice, this means all suppliers need to identify and manage risks to their supplies, ensuring they can deliver safe drinking water on a consistent basis. . Domestic selfsuppliers are excluded from the Act because they are responsible for the supplies to their own properties, and therefore have the ability and incentive to manage risks to those supplies themselves. What does being regulated mean for smaller suppliers What do the smaller suppliers look Ike . Approximately percent of people in New Zealand receive drinking water from suppliers that are not local or central government. This includes: . Private suppliers that provide drinking water to a larger, often fluctuating, number of people, such as vacation hotspots, supplies used by water carriers, campgrounds, and rural schools. . Private suppliers that provide drinking water to more than one household or dwelling. . Domestic selfsuppliers, who are not regulated under the Act. . Many smaller supplies are located in remote communities, with poor infrastructure (including reliable electricity supplies necessary to run pumping, treatment and monitoring equipment) , limited access and greater distances to health services, and disproportionate exposure to severe weather events and their impacts. . Some smaller supplies, such as marae, campgrounds and community halls, have fluctuating populations and provide civil defence support in emergencies . This occurred in the aftermath of Cyclone Gabrielle in . Others could be characterised as shared domestic supplies providing household water; for example, where a farm supplies neighbouring properties, or a drinking water source is shared between adjacent holiday homes. This marked an important change from the previous legislative requirement to take all practicable steps to comply. That approach was highly problematic, as suppliers were deemed compliant If they started implementing a water safety plan. In effect this meant they could be technically compliant with the law, even though the water being supplied was not demonstrably safe. IN CONFIDENCE Pageof Proactively released by the Department of Internal AffairsThe Departme nt of Internal Affairs Taumata Arowai How are smaller suppliers regulated, and what ore they required to do . Smaller suppliers (who were not previously registered) have until November to register with Taumata Arowai through a free online selfservice portal. They then have a further three years to become compliant with the full requirements in the Act and relevant secondary legislation (including the Drinking Water Quality Assurance Rules and Drinking Water Standards). . During the transition period to November smaller suppliers are: . subject to a basic obligation to provide safe drinking water that complies with Drinking Water Standards; and . required to comply with any direction or compliance order issued by Taumata Arowai. . The Act does not distinguish drinking water suppliers by size, although it requires regulatory mechanisms to be proportionate to the scale, complexity, and risk profile of each supply. Instead, the stratification of supplies into different groups by size (or other characteristics) occurs through secondary legislation made by Taumata Arowai, particularly the Drinking Water Quality Assurance Rules. . These Rules group smaller supplies into two categories : . Very small community supplies that provide drinking water to up to consumers. (Approximately private supplies of this size have registered with Taumata Arowai, to .) . Small networked supplies that provide drinking water to to consumers. (Approximately private supplies of this size have registered.) . There are also medium networked supplies that provide drinking water to to consumers, and large networked supplies covering more than consumers. These are primarily council owned and operated supplies. . The population thresholds in the Rules were chosen to align with previous Ministry of Health thresholds that suppliers were familiar with under the Health Act. Under that regime, suppliers to or fewer people had minimal regulatory requirements outside of registering with the Ministry of Health. Very few supplies in this category did register as drinking water suppliers. How much of a compliance burden might there be for smaller suppliers, and how is Taumata Arowai mitigating this . Taumata Arowai regulates in a way that is proportionate to the scale, complexity, and risk profile of drinking water supplies. Regulatory resources are limited, and targeted to larger suppliers displaying risk. Typically, these supplies are more complex. At the smalltomedium end, Taumata Arowai will tailor any regulatory engagement to suit the needs of the supplier and community, alongside any indications of heightened public health risk. . Currently under the Drinking Water Quality Assurance Rules, the only obligations on drinking water supplies providing water to up to people are to: . test twice a year for E. coli, using an accredited laboratory to perform the testing analysis; and IN CONFIDENCE Page So Proactively released by the Department of Internal AffairsThe Department of Internal Affairs Taumata Arowai . make the results available to the owners and occupiers of all properties connected to the supply. . If the testing detects E. coli or other determinands that exceed maximum acceptable values, the Act requires a supplier to take certain actions, including: notifying Taumata Arowai, taking action to rectify the situation, and taking all practicable steps to advise affected consumers of the situation and what they should do to protect their health. . Once small suppliers register with Taumata Arowai, they must prepare a drinking water safety plan, which records the risks and hazards that impact a supplys drinking water and how they will be managed. Taumata Arowai has guidance and templates to make it easy to make a plan and manage the risks associated with supplying drinking water. . Acceptable solutions allow some suppliers to use offtheshelf, endpoint treatment systems (rather than centralised treatment that tends to be more expensive, labour intensive and require a higher level of maintenance) . . For a single household, an endpoint treatment system that meets acceptable solution requirements is estimated to cost ,. For a larger supply, such as a sports club or marae, this increases to an estimated ,. The costs are influenced by a range of factors, such as existing water supply configurations, location, and availability of tradespeople. . Suppliers that adopt an acceptable solution do not have to prepare a separate drinking water safety plan assessing the hazards and risks affecting their supplies. . There are currently three acceptable solutions, which relate to: . drinking water suppliers that abstract water from springs and bores; . mixeduse rural supplies (where at least of the water supplied is intended to be used for agricultural or horticultural purposes); or . supplies that rely on roof water. . Taumata Arowai will take an engagement led and educational approach to support smaller supplies coming into the regime. This will mean working with communities to understand their risks and needs, and to help them to build their capability. It will build off work already done through groups such as the Rural Supplies Technical Working Group, and the Marae and Papakainga Technical Advisory Group. . This approach will enable Taumata Arowai to further understand what the level of risk in these small supplies is, and therefore the most appropriate regulatory settings and interventions. There have been over notifications from laboratories where unregistered supplies have exceeded the maximum acceptab le levels of contaminants in drinking water since Taumata Arowai became the water services regulator in November . The acceptable solutions have been developed in collaboration with sector reference groups with experience of various supply types across New Zealand, including the rural sector. IN CONFIDENCE Pageof Proactively released by the Department of Internal AffairsThe Department of Internal Affairs Taumata Arowai Options for reducing the regulatory burden on smaller drinking water suppliers Relevant policy considerations . Following consideration of advice on smaller suppliers in December LG, you indicated an interest in reconsidering the regulatory approach to water suppliers in the Water Services Act. You asked for further advice on amending the thresholds for regulation. . We understand your main interest is in reducing the potential regulatory burden that could apply to smaller suppliers. The main option for achieving this could be to exclude some suppliers (in addition to domestic selfsuppliers) from the application of the Water Services Act based on the number of people they supply (population threshold). . Two variations of this option are outlined below. Both options are likely to require changes to the Act. Our initial view is that: . Option could be a pragmatic way to make the regulatory system less burdensome, with an overall level of risk that could be tolerable providing Taumata Arowai was still able to provide support to unregulated suppliers. We would like to do further work to develop and test this option. . We do not recommend proceeding with option , as this would carry much greater risk and be more difficult to implement . . We note that it is sometimes suggested that thresholds could relate to the number of connected properties or endpoint users being supplied. For example, members of the National Party and the ACT Party have previously suggested excluding supplies to endpoint users from the BillAct. (This is not terminology that has been used in legislation. The Department has interpreted it as referring to connected properties, rather than people.) . Taumata Arowai does not recommend using the number of connections as a basis for setting thresholds. This does not reflect the considerable variations in the number of people who use a connection (which could range from a person in a sole household to hundreds of people in a community facility). It would be difficult to implement and does not align with any legislative approaches that have been used previously. . We have also included a third option, which involves changing the regulatory approach andor timeframes that will apply to smaller suppliers (not amending thresholds, as such). This may be more straightforward to implement and require less legislative change and be a potentially useful addition to any attempts to make the regulatory system less burdensome. We suggest this work on this option is progressed in parallel with option . . Subject to your direction on these initial options, further work would be undertaken. We have outlined this in the next steps section. It would consider factors like how to design and implement the option(s), costs, benefits and risks, the detailed legislative amendments required, and implications for Taumata Arowai. . It would also involve engagement and testing with policy agencies with an interest in this matter, particularly the Ministry of Health, and others in the health sector. The IN CONFIDENCE Page of Proactively released by the Department of Internal AffairsThe Department of Internal Aff.irs Taumata Arowai Ministry is responsible for policy relating to public health and interests in drinking water. . A key factor when considering any potential changes to the current legislative settings would be the appropriate balance between public healthsafety and regulatory requirements. There would be a tradeoff between protecting public health something that is prioritised under the current settings and reducing the compliance costsburden on small suppliers. . Placing less emphasis on regulating smaller suppliers may mean there is a greater public health risk associated with these supplies, and raise further equity issues in small, rural communities (without council supplies). It also means Taumata Arowai, and local authorities, have limited ability to identify these supplies, and offer support when required in emergency situations and in providing tailored advice. . Continuing to require small supplies to register and undertake limited testing (paired with bespoke support and capacity building) would help to build a picture of where these supplies are located, the risks they face, and any localised source water issues. . This information would support Taumata Arowai and local authorities to ensure communities have reliable access to safe drinking water if existing suppliers face significant problems (as required in the Local Government Act ). Not collecting this data is more likely to adversely affect remote communities and those facing climate resilience challenges. . That said, removing certain small suppliers from the requirement to register and undertake limited testing does not mean Taumata Arowai could not continue to provide education and tools to support suppliers to keep their water safe. There are also provisions in the Act that seek to ensure domestic selfsuppliers are warned of potential water contamination issues, which could be applied to other nonregulated suppliers. . Taking a different approach to small supplies would provide opportunities for Taumata Arowai to place greater emphasis and focus on the larger andor higher risk suppliers. Option : very small suppliers to people and below are not regulated, and Taumata Arowal develops education material to be used on a voluntary basis . Under this option, all very small supplies to people and below would be excluded from duties and requirements in the Water Services Act. This threshold would align with how very small community supplies are defined in the Drinking Water Quality Assurance Rules. . The public health risks associated with this change could be mitigated by Taumata Arowai providing online guidance and education material to support these supplies in providing safe drinking water. Adherence to this material would be voluntary and they would not be regulated. . This would be similar to the approach that is currently taken to domestic selfsuppliers. It would recognise that very small suppliers have been subject to minimal regulation to . . Taumata Arowai recommends this option should focus on exempting supplies characterised as shared domestic supplies for example, those supplying neighbou ring IN CONFIDENCE PogeBo Proactively released by the Department of Internal AffairsThe Department of Internal Affairs Taumata Arowai properties. This would mean arrangements where a farm or holiday home supplies drinking water to a small number of neighbouring properties would not be regulated. . Taumata Arowai would continue to regulate small public supplies (for instance, some rural schools) and those supplying water for commercial style use, such as campgrounds and aged care facilities. . Because private supplies of this size have not been regulated, very little is known about them either in terms of how many supplies there are, their customer and risk profile, or how difficult it may or may not be for them to comply with the new regulatory environment. This makes it difficult to estimate how much impact this option would have in practice, if implement ed (potentially making it difficult to prepare a regulatory impact assessment that contains this data). . If there was an interest in knowing more about these supplies without them being regulated as such they could still be required to register with Taumata Arowai, but exempt from further requirements under the Act or secondary legislation. This would mean Taumata Arowai can collect basic information about these supplies, to inform emergency preparedness and assist local authorities to carry out assessments under the Local Government Act. Option : some small suppliers are not regulated If they are lowerrisk suppliers, serving under people NOT RECOMMENDED . Under this option, the threshold for exclusion could be extended to suppliers to a higher number of people for example, a threshold of people. . We have included this option to indicate alternative considerations, but do not suggest it is taken further. It would be a higher risk approach than option , and is likely to raise far more challenges. However, if you were interested in th is option, we have outlined some of the factors and limitations that would need to be worked through. . We would suggest it is limited to privately owned and operated schemes for domestic dwellings, where the number of people being supplied is relatively low and stable. As above, Taumata Arowai would recommend publicly operated and commercial suppliers continue to be regulated. . We do not consider this exclusion should be extended to smaller council or other public supplies, or to supplies that are serving higher risk communities or where the numbers of people drinking the water is highly variable. . There are risks with small supplies of this nature, particularly around excluding supplies that provide drinking water to vulnerable communities for example, rural schools, residential care facilities and community drinking water stations. Small supplies with fluctuating population s are also at higher risk. Campsites, marae, community halls and planned events fall into this category. . We note that this kind of approach would be a departure from the recommendations of the Inquiry into Havelock North Drinking Water, and take settings back to the situation that existed prior to the changes to the Health Act. Note that even if these supplies were not excluded from the application of the Water Services Act, they would still have the ability to seek an exemption from Taumata Arowai as per the provisions in section of the Act. There could be significant implications, unintended consequences, and potential gaps, which would need to be explored further. For example, we would need to consider what would happen to these suppliers in emergency situations ifTaumata Arowai did not have a rolemandate to provide support, and neither the Ministry of Health nor local authorities are resourced or required to do this. .
