Setting a limit of people would be similar to the neighbourhood drinking water supply under the Health Act. We understand the performance of suppliers of this size was not reported on by the Ministry of Health under that previous regime. Option : make it easier and less burdensome for smaller suppliers to comply, by extending the timeframes and reducing the regulatory requirements . This option could be an alternative to changing the thresholds, or it could be delivered in conjunction with either of the above options. As noted earlier, we suggest it is developed alongside option , as it would help to make the overall regulatory system less burdensome on smaller suppliers not captured by any other exclusions). . This option would not involve changes to who is regulated all drinking water suppliers (other than domestic selfsuppliers) would continue to be covered by the Act. However, we would consider how to further reduce or minimise the requirements that apply to smaller suppliers in the legislation andor in how Taumata Arowai applies its regulatory approach. . This would align with the current situation, in which Taumata Arowai is enabled and required to take a proportionate, riskbased approach. Taumata Arowai could be given greater flexibility and discretion when it comes to regulating smaller (lower risk) suppliers. . With this option, there would continue to be a strong emphasis on the importance of public health and drinking water safety for all suppliers, but there would be greater recognition that only a relatively light touch is likely to be warranted for very small supplies. It may be more straightforward to design and deliver than legislative changes to the thresholds affecting the sizes and types of supply being regulated. . One particular area that could be modified and where the burden on small suppliers could be reduced relates to drinking water safety plans. There are opportunit ies to amend the Act to make the requirements about what is included in these plans less prescriptive. Taumata Arowai could be given discretion to determine which supplies require a plan, and what they need to cover. . Amendments to the legislation could also be proposed to provide smaller suppliers with a longer timeframe in which to register with Taumata Arowai and to comply with the other requirements. This would give Taumata Arowai more time to provide guidance to smaller suppliers, and give those suppliers more time to understand the new regime and what it means for them. Fit and Proper Person Requirements Applicants will be required to grant permission for the TF Authority to validate information provided by the applicant to support a fit and proper person assessment of the applicant and any officer s responsible for the governance and management of the TF provider. This will include permission for the Authority to request a Police vetting check. The applicant would also need to provide information that demonstrate s the TF provider has appropriate policies and procedures in place to ensure employees entrusted with the delivery of accredited services meet fit and proper person requirements prescribed by the Authority. Assessment criteria The Act enables the TF Authority to accredit a provider if it is satisfied that they meet the requirements in sections to of the Act, any criteria for the assessment of applications, and any other requirements set by regulations. The New Zealan d Police may release any information they hold if relevant to the purpose of the vetting request. This may include : Conviction History Report . Infringementdemerit reports . Active charges and warrants to arrest . Charges that did not result in a conviction including those that were acquitted, discharged without conviction, diverted, or withdrawn . Any interaction had with New Zealand Police considered relevant to the role being vetted, including investigations that did not result in prosecution . Information regarding family harm where the applicant was the victim, offender or witness to an incident or offence, primarily in cases where the role being vetted for takes place in the applicants home environment where exposure to physical or verbal viole nce could place vulnerable persons at emotional or physical risk . Information subject to name suppression where that information is necessary to the purpose of the vet. Proactively released by the Minister for Digitising Government We propose that that the regulations provide for the TF Authority t o use the following criteria to assess applications for accreditation . There is sufficient evidence to satisfy the Authority that the applicant : is a company that is incorporated in New Zealand, an incorporated society registered in New Zealand, or a New Z ealand Crown entity or government department; will deliver one or more of the digital identity services specified in regulations established under the Act; has the capability to meet the service standards specified in the rules to an appropriate level of a ssurance; has demonstrated it will provide an internal complaints and disputes resolution process that meets regulatory requirements; and officers responsible for the governance and management of the TF provider are fit and proper persons that can be entru sted with the delivery of digital identity services; has policies and processes in place to ensure its employees entrusted with the delivery of accredited services meet fit and proper person standards prescribed by the Authority; has demonstrated that it i s financially sustainable; and has provided all the information specified in s ection and addressed to the TF Authoritys satisfaction any issues of concern arising from any past practises as an identity services provider that have be en the subject of an investigation by the Privacy Commission or the Authority, or resulted in a decision to previously decline, suspend or cancel an accreditation. Duration Accreditation will be for a two year period The Act provides that the accreditation of a TF provider or service expires at the end of the relevant period set by regulations (section () ). We propose that the regulations specify that a service accreditation ends two years ( months) after the it is granted by the TF Authority . We have considered options ranging from annual through to five yearly and indefinite accreditation. In proposing a two year accreditation period, we have sought to balance the need to provide the TF Authority, users and relying parties with appropriate assurance that TF providers are meeting accreditation service standards against the compliance costs associated with renewal requirements. We consider a two year accreditation period is appropriate given we are introdu cing a new regulatory system and there are likely to be changes in service standards given the rapidly evolving nature of the industry. We anticipate the rules will be in response to technology advances and commercial practice changes. Providers wi ll, need to demonstrate they are able to meet changes in service standards. Proactively released by the Minister for Digitising Government We note that the Act allows for regulations to establish different expiry periods for different types of TF provider, different types of service and different levels of service. Du ring the Trust Frameworks establishment phase, we consider that a standard two year period should apply to everyone. We anticipate that this is a matter the TF Authority may wish to review based on its experience administering the regulatory system two to three years after commencement. Renewal TF providers will be able to renew their service accreditations The Act includes provisions covering the accreditation renewal process (s ection ). In effect when TF providers apply for renewal, they will need to demonstrate that they continue to meet the accreditation requirements and standards specified in the Act, rules and regulations, unless different requirements for renewal applications are established in regulations. We propose that the TF Board consider i ntroducing regulations that refine the renewal application requirements when developing the next tranche of regulations. The aim will be to establish a renewal application process that provides the TF Authority with assurance that TF providers can continue to meet accreditation requirements, in particular any changes that have been introduced since an applicants original accreditation, while minimising renewal application compliance costs. Accreditation mark Users and relying parties will be able to identi fy an accredited service through an accreditation mark If approved, a TF provider will be able to deliver the accredited service or services under the Trust Framework and display an accreditation mark that would apply to each accredited service. The accred itation mark that would be applied to each specific accredited service is an important distinguishing factor, as some organisations with accredited services could also provide non accredited services, which do not display the accreditation mark. Display of the accreditation mark will help users in making decisions about who they want to share their personal information with. If they chose to use a TF providers accredited service, they will know that the: service meets the technical standards set out in the rules that apply to that service; service is delivered to a prescribed service level (as specified in the rules and regulations and discussed further in the next section of this paper); and TF provider has undergone an assessment for security and privacy and will give the user control over the identity information they choose to share. To reduce the risk of a user or relying party misunderstanding whether a TF provider is delivering an accredited service, we propose that the regulations specify that the TF Authority will only allow accreditation marks to be displayed against specific services, rather than being displayed as a generic accreditation by the organisation. Service Levels Overview As part of the accreditation process, the regulations will enable providers systems and processes to be assessed by the TF Authority to determine what level of service they can provide when delivering information, binding, andor authentication services. Each of the ser vices will have four service levels. The service level indicates the capability that a TF provider can deliver their associated service to. Service levels will indicate to prospective users and relying parties what level of assurance a given service may a chieve. Levels of assurance are specific to attributes (or pieces of information about a person), not the service or organisation. Therefore, the service level will indicate to other people the capability of an accredited service and the expected level of assurance that service can provide. Proposed regulations The regulations will provide for the service levels that will apply to the delivery of information, binding, and authentication services. The requirements and standards TF providers will need to mee t to achieve a given service level will be set out in the rules. The rules will require compliance with the New Zealand Identification Management Standards (NZIMS ), which will be incorporated by reference. The levels of assurance set out in the NZIMS will form part of the requirements prescribed for each service level. Further details on the service levels contained in the New Zealand Identification Management Stan dards are available via this link: https:www.digital.govt.nzstandards andguidanceidentification mana gementidentification management standardsapplying thestandards Benefits In practice, service levels will help relying parties understand the outcome of assessment processes without having to know what the process was . They will give relying parties and other digital service providers an understanding of how robust the TF providers processes are. Establishing the service level through the accreditation process will also allow TF providers who rely on other providers f or information, binding , or authentication services to understand what level of assurance that provider can deliver. This increases the level of trust that relying parties and other TF providers have in the Trust Framework. Complaints and dispute resolution Overview Part of the Act establishes processes for dealing with complaints and disputes. It enables any person to complain to the TF Authority if they believe a TF provider has breached the TF rules, regulations, terms of use of accreditation marks, or provisions of the Act. The Act ( section ) also provides for regulations that set out requirements for TF providers to provide and operate their own internal complaints and disputes resolution processes. These processes can be used as a first port of call by complainants to address and resolve issues directly with the TF provider. Any complaints not resolved using this internal system can then be referred to the TF Authority for consideration. This approach is consistent with the principles established in the Act that gui de the TF Authoritys approach to complaints management , which are that : processes for complaints should be fair, accessible and have particular regard to tikanga Mori; complaints should be resolved in a timely and efficient manner; and complaints should be resolved at a level appropriate to the seriousness and nature of the complaint. Proposed regulations TF Provider internal complaints process We propose that the regulations require that every TF provider must: receive and consider complaints about any service provided by it, including complaints that the provider has failed to comply with the TF rules, regulations, terms of use of accreditation marks, or other requirements arising from provisions in the Act; establish and maintain p olicies and procedures for dealing with such complaints fairly, promptly and without undue formality; publicise its complaints policies and procedures to users, prospective users, relying parties and other stakeholders with an interest in its services; and ensure that complainants are aware that in the event they are dissatisfied with the outcome of the internal complaints process they may lodge a formal complaint with the TF Authority. The ability of an applicant to comply with these requirements will be a ssessed when they apply for accreditation. Potential future regulations for a dispute resolution scheme The Act also allows for the development of regulations to establish requirements and criteria that would enable the TF Authority to recommend a dispute resolution scheme for the Ministers approval. Any scheme would need to complement and operate alongside the TF Authoritys complaints process which can lead to the TF Authority applying a range of remedies where it finds a TF Provider has breached legisla tive requirements. It identifies: the general policy intent of the Bill and other background policy material ; some of the key quality assurance products and processes used to develop and test the content of the Bill; the presence of certain significant powers or features in the Bill that m ight be of particular Parliamentary or public interest and warrant an explanation . This disclosure statement was prepared by the Department of Internal Affairs . The Department of Internal Affairs certif ies that, to the best of its knowledge and understanding , the information provided is complete and accurate at the of finalisation below. Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Part One: General Policy Statement The objective of this Bill is to reduce t he potential for harm to consumers from viewing inappropriate content . The Bill will do this by requiring that commercial video on demand (CVoD ) content that is made available in New Zealand display s appropriate and consistent labelling , if the provider of that content is specified in the Schedule to the Bill . This labelling will provide information about that contents rating and description so that consumers can make an informed decision on whether to view it. Providers of commercial (subscription and transactional) video on demand content are displaying inconsistent ratings and descriptive note s (or no ratings at all) for content available on their platforms. This is because of the gap in current legislation where on demand online content in New Zealand is not subject to mandatory rating requirements, as films for cinematic or DVD release ar e. This Bill will ensure that consumers see more consistent ratings a nd descriptive notes across the main CVoD platforms in New Zealand. The Bill will amend the Films, Videos, and Publications Classification Act (the Act) to clearly address the identified regulatory gap . Key changes the Bill will implement are : Requ irements for specified CVoD providers to label content before it is available in New Zealand Providers of CVoD content will be required to comply by following the current process for the labelling of film. This involves providing content to the Film and Video Labelling Body (the labelling body) for rating and labelling. The labelling body will refer certain content to the Office of Film and Literature Classification (the Classification Office) for classifi cation , before issuing a label ; or selfrating content that they supply using systems which have been approved by the Classification Office. This can be achieved either by using the Classification Offices rating tool or using their own system, with approval from the Classification Office. Once content is labelled under the Act, that label will be included in a public regi ster and must be used by any other provider providing that content. These labelling decisions can be reconsidered by the Classification Office where necessary. Establishment of criteria and process to identify and list regulated providers Providers that are required to comply under the new requirements will be listed in a schedule of the Act. The schedule can be amended by an Order in Council , with the final decision being made by the Governor General on the recommendation of the Minister of Internal Affairs. The Minister will need to consult the Chief Censor before making a recommendation to amend the schedule . The Minister will also need to consider the potential risk of harm to consu mers from CVoD content being made available without appropriate labels before making a recommendation to amend the Schedule . The Bill sets the following criteria that the Minister must consider in determining the potential risk of harm : Market presence: the share of the New Zealand market that a provider currently has or is expected to have ; and Compliance with and commitment to another classification framework established in New Zealand: whether a provider is using a classification framework that provides consistent and appropriate information to consumers, as well as the extent and reliability of its commitment to that framework; and Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Nature of content: the nature of content being offered by a provider, and the potential of this content to cause harm to consumers. functions of Classification Office The Bill will update the functions of the Classification Office to ens ure th at the new requirements for CVoD content are clearly withi n the scope of its operational work. The Classification Office will have the following new functions and powers: providing an online rating tool that specified CVoD providers may use to rate and label content they provide ; and approving any SelfRating Systems which are developed by specified CVoD providers to rate and label their content; and reviewing and monitoring the operation and outputs of both the online rating tool and the any selfrating systems. Amendment to definition of Film t o clarify that it includes video ondemand content Video on demand content falls within the existing definition of a publication, but it does not clearly fall within the definition of a film (which is a subset of publications). The Bill replaces the defini tion of film in the Act to clarify that it includes video on demand content (CVoD is a subset of video on demand content this is provided to consumers on a subscription or transaction basis ). Clarifying that video on demand content is a film means that the requirements in relation to classifying and rating films will apply to any video on demand content that is not specifically exempted from those requirements. The Classification Offices powers in respect of publications (e.g. complaints pro cess, enforcement provisions and offences and penalties ) will also apply. Anticipated introduction of new fees for use of CVoD rating and labelling tools The new regime introduced by the Bill will also permit new fees to be set for the use and review of CVoD rating and labelling tools . Fees under the Act are set in the Films, Videos, and Publications Classification (Fees) Regulations . Work is underway to update the fees framework , including the level of the CVoD fees for specified CVoD providers. In December you requested from officials, information on international policy initiatives to comprehensively regulate online content. There is growing international concern over the risk of harm posed by online media content . Similar to NZ, other jurisdictions are also grappling with outdated media content regulatory systems that do not have the flexibility to respond to new forms of media and the risk of harm they pose. Previously, the dominant view has been that user content should be largely left unregulated to protect freedom of expression . This view holds that freedom of expression needs to be given paramount protection to reap the benefits of the internets user participation framework. These benefits include increasing public access to information, allowing public political discussion to occur at national and global levels, and giving greater political voice to marginalised group. . Recent highprofile cases of serious harm arising from content hosted on online social networks have propelled growing international debate over the responsibilities of online platforms and governments to regulate harmful online content. These high profile cases include the streaming of the March Christchurch Terror Attack, allegations of foreign election interference, COVID misinformation, the storming of the United States Capitol and violations of data privacy . There is also growing recognition that characteristics of the online environment amplify the volume, speed, and reach of harmful media content, which increases the risk of online media content causing harm to individuals, society and democratic institutions compared to traditional media . These characteristics or the online environment include: People are less inhibited when communicating online leading them to be more likely to create and share harmful media content. This is because social and cultural constraints on speech do not operate online to the extent they do offline. Contributing to this disinhibition effect is the relative anonymity of online content creators and sharers. In addition, the decoupling of content creators and content distributors weakens accountability, contributing to the disinhibition effect; Social bots and fake profiles are being used amplify the spread of harmful content; and Social interests and commercial incentives are in conflict the business incentives of online platforms are, in some cases, misaligned with protecting users and the broader public from harm. The business models of online platforms are structured around maximising audience engagement for advertising revenue. For this reason, recommendation systems usually prioritise pages which are visited most often and have the greatest time spent on them. Content that elicits an emotional response, such as outrage, disgust and anger

Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Page of Purpose . This briefing seeks your agreement on a first tranche of policy related to introducing a selfidentification process for recognising gender on birth certificates through the Births, Deaths, Marriages and Relationships Registration Bill (the Bill). Executiv e summary . It is important that transgender and intersex people are able to have their gender recognised on their birth certificates. Birth certificates are often used as a form of identity verification. If the sex recorded does not align with their gender, they risk being outed as transgender or intersex. These experiences have a detrimental effect on the mental health and wellbeing of transgender and intersex people . . The Family Court process for changing sex on a birth certificate is difficult to access for many people due to cost or the intrusiveness of the medical requirement. We recommend making the change more accessible by introducing a selfidentification process . This paper sets out the policy decisions required to introduce a self identific ation process. . Selfidentification would remove the requirement for a Family Court declaration and for evidence of medical treatment and would enable people to apply directly to the RegistrarGeneral with a statutory declaration form. . We think the selfi dentification process should be available for children and young people . Further work is required, however, to determine how we do that and ensure any change is in the best interest of the child or young person. We seek an inprinciple decision on this and will provide further advice in April . . There are risks, which will require mitigation measures, to progressing these policies in the Bill. These include: . a lack of consultation with Mori, Pacific peoples, and other ethnic communities; . organised opposition to a self identification process; and . not addressing broader questions about sex and gender. . Agencies that we have consulted are supportive of introducing a selfidentification process. However, they have had significant feedback on some of the specific policies we are considering. Background . You have indicated you would like to replace the Family Court process to change the sex on a birth certificate with a selfidentification process. Selfidentification was introduced to the Births, Deaths, Marriages and Relationships Registration Bill (the Bill) in at the recommendation of the select committee.

This briefing provides initial advice on timing, next steps and risks for progressing the Births, Deaths, Marriages, and Relationships Registration Bill (the Bill). It also seeks your agreement to amend the Bill through a Supplementary Order Paper (SOP). Executive summary . You have directed us to develop an approach to progress the Bill in the Legislative Programme. However, t he Bill as reported back from Select Committee would benefit from updating. Without amendments, the Bill may be difficult to implement in time and not work as effectively as intended. . We are aware that the selfidentification provisions inserted by Select Committee could be better aligned to human rights discourse, so they are appropriate for people of all genders. Issues with certain operational and access provisions in the Bill have also been identified since the Bill was deferred in . . It is possible to address the above issues and amend the Bill through an SOP. With an SOP, the Bill could still be enacted at the end of or in early . If you agree, we will commence work on the SOP and provide you with advice on policy proposals by August . . All options for progressing the question of selfidentification carry some level of risk, particularly stakeholder risks . The main risk for progressing the Bill is that groups opposed to selfidentification will criticise the lack of wider public consultation. To mitigate this risk, we will develop communications material to explain the rationale for this approach. . Progressing the Bill also means that there will not be the time to fully understand te ao Mori perspectives and incorporate them in the Bill. While targeted consultation could be undertaken on any amendments made through an SOP, broad engagement with M ori stakeholders may not be possible. To ensure the Crown is fulfilling its obligations under Te Tiriti o Waitangi you may wish to consider a larger piece of work that looks to understand and incorporate M ori perspectives in identity legislation generally, not just the specific issue of selfidentification . . You agreed to seek Cabinet approval to progress the Bill at the same time as Cabinet considers the Government response to the Working Group for Reducing Barriers to Changing Registered Sex . We are drafting a Cabinet paper and expect it will be ready for Cabinet Committee consideration in March . To help us draft this material, we would like to meet with you to discuss progressing the Bill in more detail. You are interested in progressing the Bill . On January , we discussed your priorities for the policy work programme . You directed us to develop a legislative bid to progress the Bill in the legislative programme, with a request for priority three to be enacted this year if possible. There are issues with the Bills self identification provisions . You have indicated your preferred option is to progress the Bill with the self identification provisions inserted by Select Committee in . The selfidentification provisions update the process for changing the sex recorded on a birth certificate to an administrative process based on selfidentification. This will benefit transgender and Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua Department of Internal Affairs INCONFIDENCE Page of intersex New Zealanders and make it easier for them to obtain a birth certificate that aligns with their gender identity. However, issues with the selfidentification provisions have been identified since the Bill was deferred in . First, the terminology used for sexgender markers may not meet all peoples needs . The sexgender marker options in the selfidentification provisions include female, male, intersex or X unspecified . Intersex is not an appropriate term to include as most intersex people identify as men or women. The marker reinforces the idea that information recorded should be based on biology as opposed to a persons gender identity. This could be considered out of step with human rights discourse and not respectful of intersex peoples right to self determination. . The marker options are also not inclusive of people who identify as nonbinary. While Select Committee included the option of X unspecified to recognise non binary gender identities, this is unlikely to be non binary peoples preferred term. . Since the Bill was deferred, Statistics New Zealand have reviewed the statistical standards for sex and gender, with standards expected to be finalised in March . Further work could be done so the current marker options for birth certificates align with Statistics New Zealands findings . Second, c ontinuing to use a sex field on birth certificates can be confusing . A persons chose n marker would appear under the sex field on birth certificates. This conflates sex and gender identity and could reinforce that the information under this field should be based on biology. For clarity , further consideration could be given to the terminology used for this category. Third, recording sex and gender on birth certificates may not be best practice . Recording sex or gender on birth certificates could be considered out of step with international human rights discourse, which recommends that official identity documents exclude the registration of this information. However, this discourse also recommends that where official identity documents include sex or gender, this information is based on an accessible selfidentification process. We will consider how to resolve the above issues . We will give further consideration on how to resolve the above issues with the self identification provisions. As part of this we will develop options for the scope of any work to address these issues, considering what could reasonably be completed so the Bill can be enacted in late or early . . We are aware of general views for and against selfi dentification, which have been well canvassed in the process to . However, we recognise any work to address the above issues would benefit from a better understanding of specific population groups views, such as M ori, Pasifika, and intersex people. We will consider how to incorporate a targeted consultation process into any work on the selfidentification provisions. We will provide you with further advice on the scope of work on the self identification provisions and approaches to targeted consultation by May . Not fully addressing the issues with the Bill raised by Crown Law . Another reason cited for deferring the Bill was issues raised by Crown Law in early . The Crown Law advice did not express significant concern about the selfidentification provisions. Its main query was whether there could be more guidance on how sex and gender is determined by the law generally. We agree that providing clearer guidance for determining sex or gender may be warranted but this work is broader tha n the Internal Affairs Portfolio and the B irths, Deaths, Marriages, and Relationships Act. To mitigate this, we can develop messaging explaining this work is beyond the scope of the Bill and the Departments role. . Another issue raised by Crown Law is about the consequences of selfidentification for the placement or transgender people in prison. Corrections Regulatio ns state that if a prisoner supplies a copy of their birth certificate they must be placed in a prison that accords with the sex on this document. This overrides all other considerations, including a history of sexual offending. The concern was that men, particularly those who have committed sexual offences, would take advantage of the selfidentification process to change their recorded sex and be placed in a female prison. . We previously worked with Corrections to resolve this issue, including looking at amending or removing the Corrections Regulation that refers to birth certificates as the deciding factor in placement of a person in prison . We will resume our work with Corrections on this issue.

Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Regulatory Impact Statement Appendix: Class Venue requirements of the Gambling Act and the Gambling (Harm Prevention and Minimisation) Regulations The Gambling Act and the Gambling (Harm Prevention and Minimisation) Regulations require: . The venue has a policy for identifying problem gamblers. The venue manager, or person acting on their behalf, must take all reasonable steps to ensure that the policy is used to identify actual or potential problem gamblers ( Section ). Failure to do so may result in a fine of up to ,. . There is always a staff member who has received problem gambling awareness training at the venue whenever gambling is available. A trained staff member must be able to approach a player and provide appropriate information about problem gambling ( Reg ). . A notice is displayed in the gambling area advising customers that you have such a policy and that a copy of the policy will be made available on request ( Section ). Failure to supply a copy of this policy when requested may result in the venue manager being fined up to ,. . Once a problem gambler has been identified, or there are reasonable grounds to believe that the person is a problem gambler, staff must approach that person and offer information or advice about problem gambling ( Section ). That information or advice must include a description of the self exclusion procedure ( Section () ). . After offering the advice and information an exclusion order may be issued by the venue manager (or person acting on their behalf). This prohibits the person from entering the gambling area for a period of up to two years ( Section () ). . An exclusion order must be issued promptly if a person has identified themselves as being a problem gambler and has requested that the venue prohibit them from entering the gambling area ( Section ). A venue manager (or person acting on their behalf) that fails to issue a self exclusion order when requested commits an offence and is liable for a fine of up to ,. . Staff must take all reasonable steps (including issuing an exclusion order) to provide continued assistance on an on going basis to a person they believe is a problem gambler after the initial approach if the persons ongoing behaviour means there are still reasonable grounds to believe the person is a problem gambler ( Section A ). . Excluded persons must not be permitted to enter the gambling area and must be removed if they do so (Section ). A venue manager (or person acting on their behalf) who allows an excluded person to enter the gambling area or fails to remove an excluded person may commit an offence and is liable for a fine of up to , ( Section ). . The venue manager must keep a record of exclusion orders ( Section A ), including: The persons name and of birth (if provided); and Whether the person self excluded, or received a venue initiated exclusion; and The which the exclusion order was issued and the of expiry; and Any conditions imposed on the persons re entry into the venue. . No one aged or under can gamble at the venue ( Section ). Offences may result in a fine of up to ,. . Providing credit for gambling is prohibited ( Section ). . No ATMs are permitted in the gambling area of a venue ( Reg ). . Class operator s must ensure that: maximum amount single play stake (for stand alone or linked machine) does not exceed .; maximum prize single play prize does not exceed , and; maximum single play jackpot prize a linked gaming machine does not exceed , ( Reg ). . Gaming machines must display certain messages at the election of the player, specifically: game information (odds, average winnings, player spend rates), player information (duration, amount spent, net winslosses). Machine must also display correct time ( Reg ). . Gaming machines must include feature that interrupts play every minutes and provides player information (duration, amount spent, net winslosses). Machine must include a feature that automatically pays out any winnings and credits to the player, if they do not wish to continue ( Reg ). . No advertising relating to a gaming machine jackpot s can be either outside the venue, or inside the venue in a way that is visible or audible to persons outside the venue ( Reg and ). . The following must be available to players ( Reg ): Pamphlets containing information about the odds of winning on gaming machines and the characteristics of problem gambling, including the recognised signs of harmful gambling and how to seek advice; and Signage that is clearly visible that encourage players to gamble only at levels they can afford and contains advice about how to seek assistance for problem gambling. Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Regulatory Impact Statement Section : Deciding upon an option to address the policy problem What criteria will be used to compare options to the Counterfactual . We developed a set of criteria to select proposals for inclusion in the discussion document. The interim criteria are: that some evidence (international or local) exists of their ability to reduce harm ; or they represent a best practice (international or local) response to reducing gambling harm ; or they are recommended by the regulator, or harm minimisation providers ; and they are not evidently impractical o r unfeasible; and we have an ability to make the requirement via regulation. . All proposals in the discussion document meet the above interim criteria . However, in the discussion document, the initial thinking for each of the three sets of proposals have been annotated with our initial perceptions of: the overall effectiveness in decreasing harmful gambling; the feasibility and practicality of the proposals ; an indication of the financial costs; and any initial assumptions and uncertainties with the proposals. . The final RIS criteria (for the next stage of decision making for reporting back to Cabinet with developed options for policy approval) will likely include: effectiveness whether the intervention is likely to be effective at reducing harm ; efficiency resourcing implications ; feasibility including: a. ease and ability to change ; b. fiscal cost to the regulator and the sector viability of using operational settings, rather than regulations social acceptability (i.e. to the general p ublic). What scope will options be considered within . In defining the scope as options to reduce harm in pokies venues using regulatory powers : the problem definition has been restricted to pokies harm in pubs and clubs ; and the available options have been restricted to existing regulation making powers , limited to: harm prevention and minimisation (section ); gaming machines (section ); admission to, and exclusion from, gambling venues (section ); exclusion of problem gamblers (section ); and infringement offences for the breach of any regulations (section ). . Within the scope, and to meet the specific objectives of the work, proposals can be considered within the three focus areas summarised below : the venue society and venue manager requirements ; the machines game features and jackpot branding; and enforcement tools offences and infringement fees for breaches of the current regulations.

This appendix outlines recent international proposed and enacted comprehensive regulatory frameworks for online content, which impose greater accountability on platforms for the content they host. These selected proposed and enacted frameworks are the German Network Enforcement Act, UK Online Safety Bill, The EU Digital Services Act, and the Irish Online Safety and Media Regulation Bill. Overseas proposed and enacted regulatory policies of online content vary in scope and design . There exists a vast breadth of design consideration for creating a regulatory framework for online content. The selected proposed and enacted frameworks for online content in this appendix vary in scope and design. For example, regulatory frameworks can be outcomefocused (i.e. requirements are to remove specified content), or procedural focused (i.e. requirements are to have processes in place to reduce harm andor illegal content (e.g. having a point of contact to regulators, enforcing their own terms of services, having a robust complaints system and transparency reporting on content moderation )). . As the largest provider of postal voting services, NZ Post has advised that it will take up to two weeks to deliver all voting papers for the local elections. . These proposals would for m a local electoral omnibus bill scheduled to complete all House stages this year. Restoring polls on Mori wards Background . Under the Local Electoral Act , Mori wards are an opt in provision for councils that allows them to decide whether specific members will be elected only by people on the Mori electoral roll . , The effect is similar to the Mori parliamentary seats, i.e., those on the Mori electoral roll vote for candidates for Mori wards, and those on the general electoral roll vote for candidates in general wards. . Before February , councils were required to hold a binding poll on whether to establish Mori wards if a petition of at least per cent of the people on a council s electoral roll requested it. Polls could also be initiated by councils. The result of the poll was binding on a council for two local government terms . . Between and , polls were held. One poll (Wairoa District Council) resulted in Mori wards being established. Two other councils also had Mori wards prior to the legislati ve changes (one of these council s established Mori wards via a local Act before the Local Electoral Act provisions were in place). . In , the previous Government removed the mechanism for binding polls on the establishment of Mori wards (initiated by either the council itself or by a petition of electors).

Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government IN CONFIDENCE Page of . The revenue split between household and non household connections varies across territorial authorities. On average, househol ds contribute percent of revenue (excluding development contributions). However, some territorial authorities appear to collect almost all their revenue from households, while others appear to collect very little of their revenue from households. The data suggests (despite differences between regional economies) that there are large cross subsidies between these two groups, but the direction of the subsidy is not consistent. . It is particularly important that businesses that use larger quantities of water face cost based pricing. This incentivises businesses to use water efficiently. I am concerned that some territorial authorities may have offered large commercial water users sweetheart deals with low prices for water services, as hidden incentives to locate in their districts. There is only anecdotal evidence on the scale of this issue, mostly from the establishment of Watercare. . To address such problems, I propose including provision for all drinking water supply, and trade waste and wastewater removal contracts (and the like) that are transferred to the water services entities will have their pricing provisions expire after five years. This should be sufficient time for businesses to adapt to a different (and possibly higher) water services price and will enable the water services entities to implement nondiscriminatory pricing. However, this period may be considered too short by businesses that have made significant capital investments recently, such as new water bottling plants. . This proposal would not affect contractors providing services to the water services entities. It is only where the water services entity supplies water, trade waste or wastewater services to a com mercial entity under a contract. . The decision to override pre existing contracts is likely to attract some scrutiny. It is generally considered to be less than ideal practice for the Crown to change pre existing contracts through legislation. On the other hand, it is important that all users pay their fair share of the cost of providing water services.

Advising agencies : Department of Internal Affairs Proposing minister : Minister of Local Government finalised : March Problem definition The policy problem is how to ensur e that local communities have appropriate input into decisions about their local government representation arrangements , while maintaining a balance of Mori representation and participation in local government decision making. Elected members currently have the ability to make decisions about Mori representation on local authorities (councils) , on behalf of their communities. Under previous legislation, this decision was subject to being overturned by a majority vote of electors. The Governments policy is that the community should be able to make the final decision on whether Mori wards and constituencies (Mori wards) are established or not, rather than the decision sitting with elected representatives . Forty six councils resolved to establish Mori wards since March , without the decision being subject to the requirement to hold a binding poll. Between and only two councils established Mori wards using the previous process under the Local Electoral Act (the Act) . Fourteen councils attempted to establish Mori wards, some more than once. Sixteen polls were held, and only one of these was in favour (narrowly) of establishing Mori wards. One council established Mori wards without a poll being demanded by electors. Government policy is that poll provisions should afford communities a choice in the establishment of a Mori ward. Executive summary In , the requirement that council decisions to establish Mori wards be subject to opportunities for binding polls was removed through an amendment to the Act. Prior to these amendments, a council resolution to establish a M ori ward was subject to a binding poll initiated by a petition signed by at least of council electors. Under both the previous and current methods for establishment, the decision to create or not create a Mori ward is binding on the council for two electoral terms ( six years). The previous Government made this policy decision with a view that there was an imbalance between community input on representation arrangements and Mori representation in local government. The policy rationale for these changes was that council decisions to create general wards were not similarly subject to challe nge through a binding Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government

Anthea Oliver Manager Operational Policy Hon Kieran McAnulty Minister of Local Government ti I ) INCONFIDENCE Yes Page of Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government Document A: Talking points for the Cabinet Legislation Committee meeting on May Key Messages This paper seeks agreement to adjust key settings of the Rates Rebate Scheme and seeks approval for an Order in Council to amend the Rates Rebate Act (the Act). In Cabinet agreed that regular adjustments to the Act must be made to account for inflation. The Rates Rebate Scheme is one of a suite of policy instruments designed to support househol ds to meet their living costs. Keeping the key settings at current levels will have negative effects on the value of the rebate to its recipients . Proposal I recommend that Cabinet agrees to adjust the key settings of the Rates Rebate Act The Rates Rebate Scheme (the Scheme) assists thousands of lowincome ratepayers to meet their living costs. Keeping the key settings at current levels will have negative effects on the value of the rebate to its recipients: o If the maximum rebate and income threshold remain static, inflation will diminish the value of the rebate to recipients . o If adjustments are not made every year, fewer people will meet the income threshold to qualify for the rebate. This will further diminish the intended impact of the Scheme for lowincome households. o After a period of nonadjustment , the cost of restoring the key settings to a desirable level could be considerable. Proceeding with the adjustments will also lower the risk of negative public reactions , particularly from senior citizen interest groups such as Age Concern and Grey Power. Senior citizens are the largest group of beneficiaries of the Scheme. Background and Context The Scheme assists lowincome ratepayers In , Cabinet agreed that regular adjustments to the Rates Rebate Act must be made to account for inflation. Ratepayers apply to their council for the rebate. Councils then process the applications and are reimbursed by the Department of Internal Affairs (the Department) . The proposed adjustments reflect the . per cent upward movement in the All Groups Index of the Consumer Price Index in the calendar year. The maximum rebate available will increase from to . This paper seeks agreement to release a discussion document for public consultation on New Zealands first national wastewater environmental performance standards (wastewater standards) on February . It includes proposals relating to: . discharge of wastewater to land; . discharge of wastewater to water; . the beneficial reuse of biosolids to land; and . monitoring and reporting requirements for wastewater network overflows . Relation to government priorities . This paper supports the Governments priority of rebuilding the economy anddelivering better public services. . Local Water Done Well sets clear direction for developing an enduring and sustainableframework for local council ownership and control of water services, with strict rules for water quality and ongoing investment in water infrastructure. . The approach in this paper is consistent with the objectives of Local Water Done Well.The proposed standards will reduce the regulatory burden on councils and other stakeholders and improve certainty and consistency in the regulatory system. They will also help to ensure wastewater infrastructure is cost effective, while still ensuring effective environmental and public health protections. Executive summary . I am seeking agreement to release a public discussion document on New Zealands firstnational wastewater standards. The discussion document is attached as Appendix A . . The Water Services Authority Taumata Arowai (the Authority) is developing these standards under the Water Services Act (the Water Services Act). . Upgrading public wastewater treatment plants is one of the greatest infrastructurechallenges facing New Zealand. Much of the wastewater infrastructure in New Zealand was built to years ago. It is approaching the end of its useful life and will need to be upgraded. Many networks have limited capacity to accommodate anticipated population growth. Treatment plants with capacity issues also have challenges dealing with the impacts of climate change, which is resulting in more frequent wastewater overflow s. Procedural mitigations DIA Information may only be provided by NZSIS to other New Zealand government departments or overseas intelligence partners in accordance with the Intelligence and Security Act (ISA), NZSIS policies and SOPs and the DAA requirements. NZSIS Managers are responsible for ensuring that any information released to external agencies (both foreign and domestic) meets NZSIS information sharing requirements. Any unauthorised andor inappropriate sharing of information derived from DIA under the direct access agreement with an external agency would be treated as a security breach and prompt an investigation, in which DIA would be consulted. Security breach investigations may lead to disciplinary action.

Progress is being made to support trustworthy Public Service AI use . Steps have been taken in respect of AI system stewardship in Aotearoa New Zealand. In July , the Public Services Commissioner assigned leadership responsibility for Public Service uptake of AI to the Government Chief Digital Officer (GCDO). As part of this role the GCDO has been asked to provide system leadership, set standards, steward agency uptake and work with providers on protections relating to AI services to government. . Whilst there is a clear AI lead for Public Service AI adoption, several other agencies also hold policy responsibilities for AI . These include MBIE (economy focus), MFAT (international trade focus), DPMCs National Cyber Policy Office (cyber policy focus), and StatsNZ (data ethics focus). We have established an interagency working group of these agencies to support collaboration . In late July , Public Sector System Leaders guidance to support government agencies seeking to use Generative AI tools to do so responsibly and in secure, transparent and privacy protecting ways. The guidance continues to be one of the most accessed resources on digital.govt.nz, attracting over , hits in its first six weeks of publication. . The GCDO is also working with a small group of agencies to pilot new, costly and highly impactful AI assistants being built into public service tools. The pilot will run until mid and its purpose is to build our collective understanding of the tools features, opportunities and risks, producing case studies, use cases and learnings to support agencies to make more informed decisions about using these types of AI tools.

Purpose The Department of Internal Affairs
Purpose of Document Decision sought: Release of a public discussion document seek ing views on how to strengthen harm minimisation regulations for Class gambling venues . (in effect, an in principle decision to consult on strengthen ing the regulations, without knowing exactly how) . Advising agencies : Department of Internal Affairs Proposing Minister s: Minister of Internal Affairs finalised : December Problem Definition Class gambling (known as pokies, refers to electronic gaming machines in pubs, clubs and TABs) has a higher risk of harm than other forms of gambling. The current regulations around harm minimisation have not been substantively reviewed since their inception in and are limited in terms of todays known best practice harm minimisation measures which means that people could be experiencing preventable harm . The risk of h arm may not be appropriately or optimally mitigated by operators and their venues. While machine numbers are declining, they remain the most common type of gambling harm for clients accessing intervention services. Executive Summary The level of harm associated with playing pokies is increasing and will continue to do so without Government intervention. This g ambling harm has a negative effect on i ndividuals and their whnau, friends and the wider community. This harm is also disproportionately affecting Mori, Pacific peoples and other population groups. The Gambling (Harm Prevention and Minimisation) Regulations are limited in scope and prescription and have not changed significantly since they were established in . The requirements in the Regulations do not correspond with the level of risk and the harm being caused . Advocates in the harm prevention and minimisation sector, as well as local authorities, have been asking for stronger measures for some time. A recent District Court decision has also identified that more prescriptive requirements might result in more effective enforcement. The regulation making powers in the Gambling Act are substantial, but the content of the current Regulations is limited. There is a significant opportunity to create a stronger harm minimisation approach by strengthening the current harm minimisation requirements . This could create a tangible reduction in level and impact of pokies harm on individuals and their communities. The discussion document sets out key information on: the pokies sector ; the current harm minimisation requirements and issues ; and the gambling harm being experienced due to pokies . The document presents some high level options for the public to comment on and asks a number of questions about the issues, the potential impact (including on different population groups) , and whether the proposals will be effective. It also seeks suggesti ons for any other solutions. This will inform the development of a formal set of regulatory proposals. An engagement plan is being designed to explicitly encourage input from the general public as well as the disproportionately affected population groups . The objectives of this project are expected to be relatively uncontroversial, as we expect that most parties would agree that reducing harm from pokies is a good objective. It is expected that key stakeholder s, including pokie operators , venues, and gambling harm treatment services , will have different views on the optimal approach. Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Regulatory Impact Statement Limitations and Constraints on Analysis The Minister asked that the scope of the discussion document be restricted to options to reduce harm associated with Class gambling venues and machines (gaming venues pokies), using the regulation making powers that already exist in the Gambling Act ( the Act) . Primary legislative change and regulation addressing any wider system issues (operating environment and inequity around community funding) are out of scope. In defining the scope as options to reduce harm in pokies venues using regulatory powers , the: problem definition has been restricted to pokies harm in pubs , clubs and TABs , and options have been restricted to what is achiev able using existing regulation making powers . One of the key constraints is the limited information available on the efficacy and cost of the various proposals. The decision to progress with a high level discussion document should support us to receive a wide range of information and feedback to inform the development of a formal set of regulatory proposals. Data and information is specifically needed on the: impact of many of the harm minimisation measures in the discussion document ; and the level and type of operational implications for organisations directly impacted. The key assumptions and uncertainties underpinning the impact analysis are that: regulatory c hange will only be progressed where it is the most effective response, but at this early stage there is some uncertainly about which harm minimisation measures are best provided for in operational rules rather than regulations, we are seeking input on the practicality and acceptability of measures, as the private nature of the activity and links to comorbidities means that the data and evidence is inevitably limited , and we are taking an open approach, by setting out a relatively wide range of potential measures for information and feedback rather than offering pre evaluated measures for comment . We do not think these limitations and constraints will impact on Ministers confidence in the approach taken in the draft discussion document and their decision to release it. QUESTION : Are there any other comments, or suggestions relevant to this consultation you would like to make Review of options for funding the classification framework Consultation documentAppendix A: Glossary Commercial classifications: Items submitted for classification under Section of the Classification Act. Broad ly speaking, these are mainstream commercial products distributed by commercial distributors or screened at film festivals. Crown classifications: Items submitted by government agencies under Sections and of the Classification Act for classification. These are typically not mainstream commercial products; many are privately owned such as images on computers. Commercial Video onDemand (CVoD): Visual media content that is accessed online ondemand by a user who has paid a fee, or as a reward. This includes Subscription Video onDemand and Transactional Video onDe mand. Subscription Video onDemand (SVoD): Visual media content that is accessed online ondemand by a user who is paying an ongoing fee for access. Wellknown examples of SVoD providers are Netflix and Lightbox. Transactional Video onDemand (TVoD): Visual media content that is accessed online ondemand by a user who pays a oneoff fee for access. Wellknown examples of TVoD providers include iTunes and Google Play. Quality assurance Reviewing agency: Department of Internal Affairs Panel assessment and comment : The panel considers that the information and analysis summarised in the RIA partially meets the quality assurance criteria. The RIA was developed within a very tight, ministerially set, timeframe to deal with the implementation of Government a coalition commitment to undo legislative changes made by the previous government. These factors limited the analysis and consultation that could be undertaken and the evidence available. They also required the policy problem and objectives that underlie the commitment to be backfilled. While these limitations are acknowledged in the RIA, their consequences could be stated more clearly and explicitly addressed. While the panel found the identification of policy objectives related to the stated policy problem, and the development and use of criteria based on those objectives to be useful, there was insufficient analysis of the relative value of Mori wards as a mechanism for meeting effective representation objectives. As a result, the panel did not feel the application of the criteria provided a compelling assessment of the policy commitment against the status quo. In relation to the transitional application of the poll provisions to existing Mori ward decisions, the panel did not believe the use of similar criteria was appropriate to assessing process and timing options to achieve the Governments objective. The panel did not find the Departments preference for the status quo to be useful in this context and felt more explicit exploration of the relative cost, timing, and process implications of the options considered (for instance, the impact on the integrity of representation reviews) would have enabled a more useful comparison of the relative merits of the other options. On this basis, the panel felt that the RIA failed to fully meet the complete and convincing criteria prescribed by Cabinet. The Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government

Business processes Having easily accessible and uptodocumented business processes and operating procedures is a requirement across RSG. I propose that the Committee authorise the submission of the Rates Rebate (Specified Amounts) Order (the Order) ( Appendix A ) to the Executive Council. Policy . The Order prescribes an amendment to section () of the Rates Rebate Act (the Act) to increase the maximum rebate an d the income abatement threshold of the Rates Rebate Sche me (the Scheme) from July . . The Order increases : .. the maximum annual rebate from to ; and .. the incom e abatement threshold from , to , per annum. . These changes reflect the . per cent movement of the Consumer Price Index (CP I) All Groups Index for the calendar year. Background The Scheme assists low income ratepayers to meet the cost of rates . The Scheme was introduced by the Act. The amount of rebate provided to a househ old is determined by a formula based on total household income, level of rates, and the number of household dependents. . To be eligible for a rebate, the applicant must be usually resident at, and the ratepayer for, the property for which the rebate is bein g claimed. . Eligibility for a rebate is based on income for the previous tax year. Applicatio ns to the Scheme for the rating year will be based on income earned in the year up to March . . The Scheme is administered by territorial authorities and the Department of Internal Affairs (the Department). Territorial authorities accept and process applications to the Scheme and provide the rebate to recipients. The Department reimburses territorial authorities for the cost of rebates.

Recursive contact tracing is practiced elsewhere. In midAp il, the Chinese city of Harbin, for example, chose a strategy to quarantine and test both close contacts and the close contacts of close contacts . Recursive contact tracing would enhance a strategy of elimination or suppression. Recursive contact tracing, enabled by CovidCard , effectively makes it possible to implement a highly targeted quarantine.
Recursive contact tracing, isolating secondorder contacts We consider the rapid identification of secondorder contacts to potentially be the most impactful feature of CovidCard . In addition to isolating firstorder close contacts of the index case, the secondorder contacts could also be notified to selfisolate. Although secondorder contacts may have been infected, the majority would not have yet become infectious effectively cutting the chain of transmission. We consider the timely isolation of secondorder contacts not possible without CovidCard .

Reducing Pokies Harm
Reducing Pokies Harm: Approval to consult Proposal This paper seek s agreement to consult the public on ways to reduce harm from Class pokie machines in venues throughout New Zealand by strengthening the regulatory requirements under the Gambling Act (the Act). Relation to government priorities Gambling can be a highly addictive activity. It can lead to debt, financial hardship, family violence, relationship strain and difficulties sustaining employment, among other harms. Some groups are disproportionately at risk of experiencing harm, including Mori, Pacific women and rangatahi. Stronger regulation would support the wellbeing of New Zealanders and their families by reducing the harm caused by pokies . Executive Summary New Zealand currently faces two urgent issues in the gambling environment : the growing level of online gambling with unregulated offshore operators; and harm caused by land based pokies in the domestic market. This paper is seeking approval to move swiftly on the lat ter by amending regulations made under existing legislation. Research shows that Class pokies are the most harmful form of land based gambling in our country. New Zealanders los e almost a billion dollars a year on pokies ; the majority of this comes from venues in high deprivation areas where people can least affor d it, but where many pokies venues are located. Pokie machines are designed to captivate and retain their audience , leading to continuous and addictive gambling . One in five pokie players are considered at risk gamblers. While percent of New Zealanders play pokies , pokies account for over percent of people seeking gambling harm treatment . The current Gambling (Harm Prevention and Minimisation) Regulations (the Regulations) do not cover all the elements necessary for a strong harm reduction approach (see Appendix A for the current regulations ). For example, they are not explicit about how venue staff must monitor and intervene in harmful gambling . A recent District Court decision has identified that more prescriptive requirements, which can be set in regulations, would

Regulatory Impact Statement . The Department of Internal Affairs Regulatory Impact Analysis (RIA) panel (the panel) has reviewed Chapter Water Services Entities Implementation Arrangements RIA (RIA) in accordance with the quality assurance criteria set out in the CabGuide. The panel provided the following comments. . The panel considers that the information and analysis summarised in the RIA meets the quality assurance criteria. s ()(f)(iv) s ()(f)(iv) Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government IN CONFIDENCE Page of . This RIA is an additional chapter to the substantial RIA prepared in May to support policy decisions on the reform of three waters service delivery arrangements and should be read in that context. This additional impact analysis is a complex RIA which addresses a number of disparate decisions needed to implement those decisions already made to reform water service delivery. Overall, the RIA does a good job of addressing the range of discrete issues, which are generally well explained. Mostly, constraints on the analysis are clearly set out. There remains a significant amount of work to be done through the transition to achieve smooth implementation of the reforms and to better understand the impact of changes on service delivery, including where detailed current information is not always readily available. In particular, this appl ies to the uncertain impacts of potential changes to pricing on households, including those that could experience difficulty paying their water bills.

Regulatory Impact Statement . Better purchasing decisions by the public that take into account natural hazard risks may also reduce future liability for government. Government has spent over . billion on natural hazards over the last decade. The total expected cost of all natural hazards is estimated to increase from . billion in to . billion in , or a compounding annual growth rate of .. The LIM is a key source of information for purchasers including natural hazard information . For many people, buying a property is the most significant investment decision in their lives. The LIM is one of the key information documents that prospective buyers and their advisors review when considering whether to purchase a property. Buyers commonly purchase their own LIM, but real estate agents may also provide a LIM to purchasers on behalf of vendors, particularly where a property is intended to be sold at auction. . The LIM is the main source of property information for purchasers and is currently a key tool for communicating natural hazard information to buyers, so they can make informed decisions. While there is no legal requirement to obtain a LIM, this is a common condition included in the standard Agreement for Sale and Purchase. . LIMs are recognised as a valuable information tool for communicating natural hazards information to owners and potential property purchasers, which can be as hazard data and information is received. The purpose of providing this information is to inform the market of special features or characteristics of the land that may affect value, suitability or saleability. This is a key consumer protection document for purchasers of real estate in New Zealand. . However, LIMs do not perform the same functions as a natural hazard risk assessment. Natural hazard risk involves not only understanding the hazard but also a range of other components including exposure and vulnerability. LIMs do not warrant that land is good or safe, or provide advice, but simply provide information based on which a purchaser can decide whether to buy a property. LIMs also only provide natural hazard information known to the council at the time. There are other sources of natural hazard information for purchasers and the public . LIMs are only one tool for communicating natural hazard information to the public. Other sources of councilheld natural hazard information include planning instruments (e.g. district plans), regional council land information requests, local authority websites, property files, and project information memoranda and natural hazard notices (Building Act ).
Regulatory Impact Statement an accessible selfidentification process with no eligibility criteria such as medical treatment and that a multiplicity of gender marker options are available. . In New Zealand the Human Rights Commission recommended that the process for people to update the nominated sex on a birth record is based on a rightsbased model of selfdetermination. It also recommended that people can nominate a nonbinary gender. An accessible process that works for transgender and intersex New Zealanders is important . Birth certificates are not intended to provide conclusive evidence of someones identity. However, they are often used by people to prove they are a citizen with the right to work and study in New Zealand and are listed as an acceptable form of identification in government guidance. There are many processes where birth certificates can be requested, including setting up a bank account or enrolling a child in school. While other documents can be used in many of the same processes (such as a passport or driver licence), birth certificates are often more practical as they are low cost and do not expire. Everyone born in New Zealand can access their birth certificate, including children who have limited options for documentation that enable them to prove their identity. . Any situation where a birth certificate is requested can be distressing for transgender and intersex people if the sex recorded does not align with their gender. It can place an extra administrative burden on transgender and intersex people to prove who they are. It creates a risk of people being outed as transgender or intersex or referred to as the wrong gender, leading to feelings of stress and anxiety or experiences of discrimination, such as being denied access to services or benefits, and verbal harassment. These experiences impact the wellbeing of transgender and intersex people, which contributes to higher rates of psychological distress, harmful substance use, and suicidal ideation and behaviour. . Being able to have their gender recognised on a birth certificate is likely to have symbolic importance to transgender and intersex New Zealanders. It shows that the government recognises who they are, supporting their sense of belonging and wider social cohesion. There are highly interested stakeholders with diverging views on amending sex on birth certificates Support for a selfidentification process . In support of changing to a selfidentification process are the transgender and intersex New Zealanders who are affected by this issue and the organisations who support Yogyakarta Principle recommends that if sex and gender information is registered, this is based on an accessible selfidentification process with no eligibility criteria such as medical treatment. See the Human Rights Commissions PRISM Report. For example, the antimoney laundering and countering financing of terrorism identity verification code of practice. Counting Ourselves recorded respondents experiences from not having an identity document that matched their appearance. The most common negative consequences were being denied services and being verbally harassed. Counting Ourselves found that per cent of participants had experienced high or very high psychological distress and per cent of participants had seriously thought about committing suicide in the last months.
