Regulatory boundaries and the effectiveness of established regulatory tools are being challenged by innovations in technology and business models, by the pace of change and scale of connectivity that these often involve, and by peoples changing views about their societies and the world around them. Examples such as cyber threats, artificial intelligence, climate change and extreme societal injustices present new types of challenge. Foresight review of the future of regulatory systems: Regulating in a disruptive world, Lloyds Register Foundation, March The goal of this strategy is to ensure Regulatory Services is at the forefront of regulatory excellence, so that hap, iwi and communities across New Zealand are safe, resilient and thriving, and the wellbeing of hap, iwi and Mori is improved. This strategy replaces the Regulatory Services Group (RSG) strategy and extends the systems approach that RSG has implemented since . It also establishes a strong regulatory stewardship approach to RSGs three current regulatory systems: Digital Safety, AntiMoney Laundering (AML) and Gambling. RSG was established in to bring together gambling, censorship compliance, antispam and AML regulatory regimes. Since then, the AML Groups remit and size has grown dramatically. More recently the Digital Safety Group, which brings together the censorship compliance and antispam functions, has also grown significantly following the introduction of an additional focus on countering violent extremism. This growth has demonstrated a recognition and confidence that RSG is able to effectively absorb, support and grow diverse regulatory functions. We developed this strategy in a rapidly evolving and digital context, where the hallmarks of effective regulation are: A clear focus on outcomes System leadership and influence based on strong relationships An agile, adaptable and capable workforce The sophisticated use of technology to target, deliver and evaluate regulatory impact. The strategy establishes RSGs regulatory stewardship approach by setting expectations regarding system leadership and delivering on system outcomes. It leverages the effectiveness of RSGs current regulatory systems by building a shared view of regulatory excellence and maximising the diverse capabilities of our systems. It supports the focus on the safety, resilience and wellbeing of hap, iwi, he tangata and communities in Aotearoa by strengthening RSGs regulatory foundations, capability and systems to ensure that RSG can readily home additional regulatory systems in the future. The strategy is a living document we have developed with input from other regulators, our staff, and internal and external stakeholders. Regulatory stewardship is a systembased approach to the design and maintenance of regulatory systems. It treats each regulatory system as an asset, designed with longterm sustainability in mind, and like many assets, requiring regular assessment and maintenance to ensure that it remains fit for purpose. Taking a stewardship approach helps to mitigate the risk of regulatory failure. The approach also provides insight into how systems can be strengthened and made to work better.

Released under the Official Information Act Section Six: Change protocol Introduction This protocol sets out the approach to managing the implementation of the structural changes arising from the OCE Organisational Change . This Protocol is consistent with all individual employment agreements and the Collective Agreement between the Public Service Association and the Department of Internal Affairs. Principles The process is designed to: ensure a fair and transparent process ; maximise the placement of employees into available positions ; ensure minimum disruption to business as usual ; observe the provisions contained in the relevant employment agreements and organisational policy ; and minimise uncertainty for employees . Who does this protocol apply to The protocol applies to all permanent employees of the d epartment including: permanent f ulltime and part time employees employees currently on all forms of leave including leave without pay and parental leave . For employees currently seconded to other positions the process will apply to their permanent substantive position. Fixed term (temporary) or casua l employees are not covered by this p rotocol even though their position may be affected by the restructure. In this case the relevant provision of their employment agreement will apply. Overview Employees are affected if their current position is being disestablished or changed significantly . If there is no significant change to the ir position, and there are the same number, or fewer, employees than positions in the new structure, employees will be reconfirmed. Released under the Official Information Act Employees who are not reconfirmed will be considered for reassignment. This involves considering whether affected employees skills can be matched to alternative positions that require similar skills in the new structure. Affected employees who are not reassigned will be consulted individually about other options. If no other options are identified, notice will be given , and redundancy provisions apply. Affected employees Employees who have been identified as being affected by organisational change will be consulted over the implementation process, and the employees will have a preferential right of appointment to vacancies within the branch . Before final decisions are announced, all potentially affected employees will be notified individually. Employees will be informed if they: have been reconfirmed in a position and are no longer affected, or are affected and will be considered for reassignment. Reconfirmation process There are no new positions proposed therefore reconfirmation will not be possible. Reassignment and expressions of interest As this proposal does not have any positions for reassignment there are no reassignment processes available in accordance with the change protocols. Appointment to another job permanent employees Employees with preferential status (who have not been reconfirmed or reassigned) may apply for a job in the Department that is not a suitable alternative job. The employee will be given preference to the extent that if the employee meets the selection crit eria for the job and is of equal or greater merit than any other applicants, the employee will be appointed. The appointment will be on the terms and conditions that apply for the job. Where the terms and conditions of the new job are of lesser value than the employees previous job, confirmation of appointment and any compensatory arrangements will be subject to agreement on a case bycase basis. Released under the Official Information Act Notice If the Department determines that no other option can be agreed, the affected employee will be provided notice in line with their employment agreement. Where a longer notice period is preferred for operational transition reasons, this may be agreed between the Department and the affected employee. During the notice period, the Department and the employee may consider any opportunities for other options that may arise. If an affected employee is appointed to another position within the Department during the notice period, the notice is withdrawn in writing. The employees employment is not ceased . Redundancy Where an affected employee has not been appointed to another position within the Department during the notice period and no other option is available , redundancy compensation will be paid at the end of the notice period in accordance with the affected employees employment agreement. Redundancy compensation is not payable where an employee is appointed to or offered another position in the State Services as provided for in section of the Public Service Act.
Released under the Official Information Act Appendix A: Approach to Working through Expressions of Interest and Alternative Opportunities for Affected Kaimahi In the first instance, a ffected kaimahi will be invited to participate in an Expression of Interest (EOI) process focussed on assisting kaimahi to look for an alternative job. Affected kaimahi will have access to support to apply for positions and prepare for interview s see Support Applying for Jobs further below. Kaimahi can also speak with their manager and Human Resources to get help and support during this period . Vacan t Positions within Te Tari There may be vacancies within the employees current Branch or the wider Department which affected kaimahi can apply for via a recruitment and selection process. Vacant positions that are under active recruitment can be found through Rehutai . To support affected kaimahi to find other jobs within Te Tari, we have made some changes to our recruitment approach during this period of organisational change . The key changes are: All vacancies will be advertised internally only for a period of ten working days. If a position is not filled, it will be readvertised internally only for a further ten days on a rolling basis (unless it is identified as time critical or specialised) . After being advertised internally only , positions identified as time critical or specialised may be advertised externally as well as internally kaimahi can still apply for positions that are advertised externally. Affected kaimahi who meet the selection criteria will be given preference for interview and appointment. Affected employees will have preferential right of appointment over non affected employees and external candidates in the event that their suitability for the position is assessed as being the same. Released under the Official Information Act Section Two : Branch Context and Background In the past, OCE informally received a small amount of administration support from the former Organisational Strategy and Performance ( OSP) Branch. This support was provided from members of their administration team and acted as an overflow to support the EA. They covered general administrative tasks including: the arrangement of domestic travel, catering, and venues, printing, CE expenses pr ocess, and some personal assistant support for the previous Director OCE (the current Director didnt use them). During the change process to establish the Te Urungi Branch it became apparent that the OSP administration team did not have the capacity to provide ongoing support to OCE so alternative arrangements for administration work needed to be considered. To provide some more consistent support for OCE and to remove the burden on the Te Urungi Branch, a hours per week Team Administrator position was established in August and recruited in September . In August , seeking more work hours, the T eam Administrator went on secondment to the Procurement team in the He Pou Aronui Branch. Current context for change The current position description of the EA covers the majority of the administration work of OCE. Since August , in conjunction with a change of kaimahi in the EA role, it was determined that it wasnt necessary to backfill the position , as the full workload was being managed by the EA. With the workload being managed within the EA role , it was decided to include the disestablishment of the Team Administrator role as part of the Baseline Reduction Programme , as it is considered that the EA role has the capacity to cover the workload . Branch approach to change OCE, like the rest of Te Tari Taiwhenua, is required to contribute to the cost savings target. Some of our contribution will come from discretionary operational funding that had traditionally been spent on small one off projects for the Chief Executive. However, OCE also needs to consider how we operate and what resourci ng is needed to support the Chief Executive , and this was the basis for change proposal . Future Direction With e very branch of Te Tari required to review their operating model to ensure they are as efficient as possible and able to absorb future cost pressures , it is especially important for the corporate functions to show they are fit for purpose and taking costs out of their operating model. Released under the Official Information Act Consultation document: Toi Hiranga l Regulation and Policy Organisational Change Page of Section Three: Branch Context and Environment The financial environment that we are in requires us, as a Branch, to operate within reduced Crownfunded baselines from July . We have identified opportunities where spending can be reduced in areas such as air travel, conferences and offsite venues, some training, the use of contractors and consultants, and recruiting through agencies. After this, however, we still have to propose some organisational structure changes to meet the spending reduction required. We need to make changes because of both the Governments Fiscal Sustainability Programme, and additional emerging cost pressures such as salary rises and meeting our share of rising corporate costs beyond our control, such as rent and insurance. The following principles were used to form this proposal for change: . Firstly, closing down vacant positions where possible, some of which have been deliberately held vacant in recent months in anticipation of baseline reductions. . Consolidating management structures and leadership positions where possible, while still ensuring the right level of technical and kaimahi oversight. . Ensuring the right level of capability is retained to deliver the core requirements of the mahi we are accountable for. As you go through this document, you will see that some areas within Toi Hiranga l Regulation and Policy may have more changes proposed than other areas of the Branch. Some of the factors that contribute to this are the number and type of vacancies in a group, workload, and the ability to scale down, deprioritise or reprioritise mahi. In the case of the Regulatory Services group, the proposals also take into account feedback received from workshops with kaimahi last year on the needs for the group, prior to the Fiscal Sustainability Programme being announced. Additionally, as I have raised in some previous communications with you leading up to this period, the nature of our funding across the Branch varies. Some areas are Crownfunded, while others are funded through thirdparty revenue managed through memorandum accounts, or other forms of cost recovery. The focus on the Crownfunded functions to proposed cost savings can make the impact on these areas look disproportionate and may appear inequitable. We can, however, only count reductions in Crownfunded expenditure towards the baseline reductions required of the Department. This means we cannot trade off any savings made in thirdparty funded functions against savings in Crownfunded functions. I have, however, asked those with thirdparty funded functions to look at whether there are any changes needed to improve our effectiveness and efficiency within existing revenue levels, as efficiency and effectiveness are clearly stated priorities for this Government regardless of how functions are funded. The proposed changes for the group are: The disestablishment of the Principal Advisor, Lead Operational Advisor and Principal Advisor CVE positions is proposed. Regulatory Services The proposed changes in the Regulatory Services group are larger, as we would be remiss to not take the opportunity to incorporate the valuable feedback received from kaimahi last year in workshops to review the Regulatory Services operating model. With the requirement to find both baseline savings and look for efficiencies more generally, the proposed changes take into consideration the refocussing on core delivery in regulatory stewardship activities and scaling back in areas where we have been able to operate beyond this for many years. The proposal takes into consideration the capability, structure and kaimahi oversight required for those delivering our regulatory stewardship activities and leveraging the benefit of being part of a group which has responsibility for more than one regulatory system, especially for the AML team. As a result, this change proposal sets out a proposed change to the operating model, to shift the group from a selfcontained singular systembased model (i.e. a selfcontained gambling system and a selfcontained AML system) to a multidisciplinary operating model, recognising the need for a broad suite of professional inputs to deliver system outcomes. Appendix B provides more information on this. The changes proposed for the group are set out below. a. Direct reports to the General Manager The proposed change in the operating model for the group requires the right oversight for each of the functions and disciplines to deliver our regulatory stewardship activities for the sectors we regulate. It is proposed to disestablish the positions of National Manager, Engagement, National Manager, Intelligence, Insights and Risk, and National Manager, Strategy and Capability and propose the establishment of new Heads of the function that deliver activities that are not core compliance and enforcement activities. It is proposed to establish a Strategy, Intelligence and Risk team led by a Head of Strategy, Intelligence and Risk. This function will be responsible for the maintenance of our regulatory strategy, turning our strategy into actionable business plans and utilising insights from intelligence and risk to help us focus our regulatory stewardship efforts. The alignment of the strategy function with the intelligence and risk functions will better allow us to create strategy and to implement it in a way that better recognises our environmental context and to respond to emerging trends and risks. It is proposed to establish an Implementation team led by a Head of Implementation. This function will establish the strategic direction and approach for the Regulatory Systems group to delivering interventions that encourage proactive compliance by regulated parties, and ensuring implementation of regulatory changes are delivered endtoend for both Released under the Official Information Act Consultation document: Toi Hiranga l Regulation and Policy Organisational Change Page of regulated parties and our kaimahi. It is proposed that this function will have oversight of the engagement, operational policy and education activities with delivery of these activities strictly project planned, managed and delivered. It is proposed to establish an Investigations and Prosecutions team lead by a Head of Investigation and Prosecutions. This function will be responsible for setting the strategic direction for all our investigations and prosecution activities, to ensure our efforts are aimed in areas that will enhance and improve proactive regulatory compliance and practice across the sectors we regulate and prevent harm in communities. Other changes proposed for the group are: The Principal Advisor, Regulatory Strategy is proposed to be disestablished, as the responsibility for the creation and implementation of group strategy will sit with the proposed new Head of Strategy, Intelligence and Risk. It is proposed to disestablish the Director, Regulatory System (AML) and establish a new Director, AMLCFT position. Further information is provided below on the proposed change. A minor change is proposed to the Director, Regulatory System (Gambling) job title to Director, Gambling and job description to reflect the proposed change to the multidisciplinary functional operating model.

AML directorate As mentioned earlier in this document, the baseline savings required in the Regulatory Services group are from Crownfunded areas. This has led us to make some difficult choices about the number and span of leadership roles proposed for the AML function compared to the Gambling function, which is larger in size and feesfunded. The proposed changes for the AML directorate and the proposed centralisation of functions such as Operational Policy, Investigations, Intelligence and Engagement, Information and Education, will support the AML function to retain key functions with the required level of professional oversight to deliver on regulatory stewardship for their sector. The following changes are proposed for the AML directorate. i) Director, AML, Deputy Director Operations, AML, and Principal Advisor, AML positions It is proposed to disestablish the Director, AML and Deputy Director Operations, AML positions. The proposed establishment of a centralised operational policy, intelligence, insights, engagement and investigation function, means that the AMLCFT directorates focus will be on the delivery of the core regulatory compliance and enforcement actions and lifting regulatory capability. Given the proposed size and scope of the AMLCFT function, and because it is a Crownfunded function subject to a reduction in baseline funding, having both a Director and Deputy Director is no longer affordable. It is also proposed to disestablish the position of Principal Advisor, AML, with the responsibilities of this position, such as stakeholder relationship management with cross agency and international partners, sitting with the new proposed Director, AMLCFT positions. Sector insights would sit with the new proposed Head of Strategy, Intelligence and Risk and Head of Implementation. ii) New Director, AMLCFT A new Director, AMLCFT position is proposed as a result of the proposed disestablishment of the Director, AML and Deputy Director Operations, AML and Principal Advisor, AML to reflect that the proposal creates centralised strategy, intelligence, investigations, operational policy and engagement functions. The directorates focus will be on the delivery of the core regulatory compliance and enforcement actions and lifting AMLCFT regulatory capability, and to work in collaboration with the proposed centralised functions to regulate the sector. The new proposed Director, AMLCFT, will be responsible for the AMLCFT regulatory stewardship function, setting the direction for the function and Released under the Official Information Act Consultation document: Toi Hiranga l Regulation and Policy Organisational Change Page of ensuring it is aligned to the Regulatory Systems strategic outcomes. To do so, they will work in collaboration with the newly proposed centralised functions. This proposed change and ongoing budgetary restraints may also need us to consider scaling back some of our international engagement in the AMLCFT space, to a level that we can sustain in light of our domestic responsibilities. The new Director, AMLCFT role is proposed to have as its direct reports the Operations Managers, the newly proposed Lead Regulators and the Practice Lead. iii) Manager Operations (Auckland) It is proposed to combine the two teams and reduce the number of Manager Operations in Auckland from two to one. These positions will lead complex regulatory stewardship activities through compliance monitoring, coaching, investigating and auditing regulated parties. They will support Managers and Practice Leaders in implementing best practice regulatory stewardship. This proposal is made as a result of a key piece of feedback from the workshops with kaimahi in , that we need more experienced regulators in the AMLCFT space. v) Practice Leader It proposed to reduce the number of Practice Leaders from two to one and for the position to refocus on a more traditional practice lead role of lifting regulatory practice and technical capability across the AML team, through training, education and practice support. Feedback was received during the workshops for increased training for regulators to lift capability. The role of training and supporting Managers to lift regulatory capability sits with the Practice Lead position. The combination of two Lead Regulators and one Practice Leader should create the right balance of uplifting capability through onthejob and training course learning. vi) Regulators and Senior Regulators It is proposed that the number of Senior Regulator and Regulator positions in Auckland and Wellington be reduced. In Auckland, it is proposed that the number of Senior Regulators reduce from six to four, and Regulators from six to five. In Wellington, it is proposed that the number of Senior Regulators reduce from three to two and Regulators from five to three. Released under the Official Information Act Consultation document: Toi Hiranga l Regulation and Policy Organisational Change Page of Introduction Introduction from Chief Executive Paul James Kia ora koutou, On December , the Minister of Finance formally announced an ongoing Fiscal Sustainability Programme to embed a culture of responsible spending across government. The first step in this programme is an Initial Baseline Exercise for government agencies designed to find around . billion a year in savings to deliver the Governments policy commitments and fund critical cost pressures. The changes proposed in this document and all changes being made across the Department have not been made lightly. However, they are needed to enable us to meet the Governments Fiscal Sustainability Programme and ensure we deliver what is required of us. This is likely to be the first stage of the Governments Programme. We can expect greater focus on restraint, reprioritisation, valueformoney, alignment to priorities and efficiencies for some time, possibly years. Manaakitanga and kotahitanga are key to how we work with each other and navigate this process to deliver outcomes for the people we serve. I encourage you to participate fully in the process and make sure your views and feedback are heard.
Released under the Official Information Act Consultation document: Toi Hiranga l Regulation and Policy Organisational Change Page of Introduction from Suzanne Doig, Deputy Chief Executive, Toi Hiranga l Regulation and Policy Like all branches in Te Tari Taiwhenua, to deliver to the Governments requirements and to ensure our future financial sustainability, Toi Hiranga l Regulation and Policy, needs to make a permanent reduction in its expenditure from July . As a Branch, we have two main sources of funding: funding granted to us each year by Parliament (called Crown funding) and revenue we earn from fees and charges, in areas like gambling and the Lake Taup harbourmaster (often called thirdparty funding or in the case of Toi Hiranga l Regulation and Policy, memorandum account funding). Our funding covers operating expenses (also known as OPEX), such as rent on the buildings we occupy, salaries, ICT costs and grants to organisations. It also includes capital expenses (CAPEX), which are assets we buy or develop, such as laptops and vehicles. The permanent baseline reduction of . announced by the Government only relates to Crownfunded activities. Our thirdparty funded functions are, however, still within scope of the Governments overall expectation that the public sector pursues efficiencies and improves its effectiveness in delivery of all its activities. The Department has identified initiatives to enable us to meet the . baseline reductions. The initiatives broadly cover: Cost reductions, such as reviewing building leases and freight costs. Efficiency savings, such as reviewing how we manage some of our services and store information. Reviewing what we insource and outsource. Introducing investtosave measures, where we invest money now to ensure ongoing savings in the future. Looking at how some services are funded. Reducing our discretionary spending on travel, contractors, consultants and events. Reducing some of our training programmes. Reducing or closing down some of our services and scaling back programmes. Closing vacancies that have been open for a long time. The Toi Hiranga l Regulation and Policy leadership team has identified that we cannot meet our savings requirements only by cutting back on expenses and holding vacancies. We need to reassess how we deliver our functions in line with our new funding levels, and this will require some organisational change that impacts positions and kaimahi. We are working with the PSA and following the Management of Change clause as per the Collective Agreement. Released under the Official Information Act Consultation document: Toi Hiranga l Regulation and Policy Organisational Change Page of This consultation document seeks your feedback about changes proposed in the Toi Hiranga l Regulation and Policy Branch. I recognise that change affects people. As a good employer the Department aims, as much as possible, to provide new opportunities and to assist staff through the change process. Consultation will be open and genuine, but total consensus need not be achieved before decisions are made. We also need to work within the parameters that have been set for us. I encourage you to provide feedback on the proposal and the change protocol described in this document over the next weeks. I also want to draw your attention to the support available during this process. These details are laid out in section of this document.

Removal and Disposal Policy The storage cost for these overseas books cost s the New Zealand taxpayer more than million a year in ongoing storage and building operation costs. However, storage is not the only reason for removing unused items from the librarys collections . It is good collection ma nagement practice to ensure that collections developed for their short term utility remain fit for purpose. Decisions around disposal of OPC items from our General Collection to , such as donating to other libraries, have been guided by our Principles for retention or deselection of the Overseas Collections held by the National Library of New Zealand PDF KB . We are now developing a new policy for removing and disposing of collection items. This will sit alongside other important policies that guide our activities, such as the Collections Policy and collection plans mentioned above. This new policy w ork will specifically inform how we make decisions about items to be removed (or deaccessioned) from collections in the future and how we dispose of these deaccessioned items. This will include decisions on whether we donate, export, or securely destroy th em, or use any other method developed as part of the policy process. Disposal of deaccessioned items from the OPC will be part of the implementation of this policy. As you have noted, I have requested that a Removal and Disposal Advisory Group be set up to advise our team during the development of this policy. Advisory Group members will bring their own expertise and the views of their organisations to the discussions . Requiring a Statutory Declaration Select c ommittees recommendation . The select committee recommended requiring a statutory declaration from people applying to change the sex on their birth certificate. They recommended the following prescriptions for the statutory declaration, requiring the applicant to state that they: . want the sex marker on their birth certificate to match their identified gender; . intend to continue to identify as a person of this gender; and . understand the consequences of the application. Departments advice agree with the select c ommittees recommendations . Requiring a statutory declaration with prescribed information would provide some assurance that the applicant understands the implications of changing sex on a birth certificate. It also provides some assurance that applicants are completing this process with the intent of living in their preferred gender, and reduces the likelihood of frivolous or fraudulent applications. Falsifying a statutory declaration is a criminal offence and can lead to imprisonment for up to three years. . A statutory declaration balances the interests of transgender and intersex people and the need to protect the integrity of registered birth records. It is important to maintain the accuracy of the birth register as its information is a source for documents like passports or driver licences.

Residential care Overseas experience indicates that residential care i s a beneficial form of treatment for a small number of people with severe addiction behaviours, and therefore would be an option for the limited number of people in New Zealand experiencing high levels of gambling harm. The Ministry currently funds some gambling harm support to people in alcohol and other drug residential treatment; however, demand does exist for residential treatment that provides gambling support first and foremost. The Ministry will work with providers to develop and pilot a clinically robust model of care, based on intensive treatment for people experiencing severe gambling harm, but likely allowing for support for coexisting issues in addition. It will then adopt a package ofcare approach to funding, similar to the way in which it funds alcohol and drug treatment residential care. The Ministry proposes to fund a small number of packages each year in the last year of the levy, with each package supporting about five people per year, depending on complexity of need. The Ministry expects to phase in this support with an established treatment provider, and has yet to decide whether to purchase on a capacity or demand basis, via a fee for service as required. . Ministry of Health operating costs Ministry operating costs (departmental expenditure) comprise contract management, policy and service development work, management of the research and evaluation programme, and management of the Client Information Collection (CLIC) database. The budget for these components has remained at around , a year for many years now. The KPMG Value for Money Review concluded that the Ministry s operating costs were reasonable. In the past, the Ministry devised the budget for its operating costs on the assumption that more funding would be required in the final year of each threeyear period, when the strategy for the next threeyear period was being developed. In fact, much of this work occurs in the second half of the second year of each threeyear period. For , the Ministry has phased the budget accordingly. Review of the Mtt Island Environmental Management Plan Under the Local Government Act the Minister of Local Government is the territorial authority for any part of New Zealand within regional council boundaries that is not already part of a local authoritys district. This includes islands, predominantly in the Bay of Plenty. Only two islands are populated Mtt ( residents) and Thua (one resident ). As the territorial authority, you are responsible for various duties and powers across a range of functions including resource management planning. The Department supports your role as territorial authority for the Offshore Islands by facilitating district planning and consenting functions. Both Mtt and Tahua have operative distr ict plans as required under current resource management legislation, and which need to be reviewed ten years after they are first made operative. The Mtt Island Environmental Management Plan was first made operative in May , requiring a review to be initiated prior to May . The Department has been contacted by Te Patuwai Tribal, a prominent hap and landowner on Mtt, requesting to engage the plan review process.

Local Government (Water Services Preliminary Arrangements) Bill: Approval for Introduction Portfolio Local Government On May , following reference from the Cabinet Legislation Committee, Cabinet: noted that the Local Government (Water Services Preliminary Arrangements) Bill (the Bill) holds a category priority on the Legislation Programme (must be passed by the end of ); noted that the Bill is the second bill as part of Local Water Done Well, and contains the preliminary arrangements for councils to transition into financially sustainable water services delivery models, together with arrangements for a financially sustainable Watercare; noted that the Bill will: . require councils to prepare a water services delivery plan within months of the Water Services Act coming into force; . contain bespoke Ministerial assistance and intervention powers if councils find it difficult or fail to deliver a water services delivery plan; . require councils to provide other specified information in relation to delivering water services; . contain streamlined consultation and decisionmaking requirements for the establishment or amendment of water services councilcontrolled organisations; . provide legislative provisions for a financially sustainable Watercare, together with interim economic regulation administered by a Crown monitor; noted that in March , the Cabinet Economic Policy Committee authorised the Minister of Finance and Minister of Local Government to make policy decisions on a financially sustainable model for Watercare ECOMIN; agreed that a Crown monitor will be appointed to Watercare from the day of Royal assent; S E N S I T I V E enkv ()(ba)(i) Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government S E N S I T I V E CABMIN. noted that the Minister of Local Government will report back to the Cabinet Appointments and Honours Committee in July on the appointment of a Crown monitor; noted that in April , Cabinet agreed to exclude the hierarchy of obligations contained in the National Policy Statement for Freshwater Management from resource consent application and decisionmaking processes CABMIN.; noted that at that time Cabinet also authorised the Minister Responsible for RMA Reform and the Minister of Local Government to determine if amendments to the Water Services Act were required to ensure the hierarchy of obligations would not apply to the development of wastewater standards; noted that the above Ministers have determined that minor amendments should be made to the Water Services Act to remove the hierarchy of obligations so that there is consistent application during standardssetting and resource consenting; agreed that an outofscope Amendment Paper to the Bill be released, to amend the Water Services Act to give effect to the decisions above; noted that, as the Amendment Paper is out of scope of the Bill, an instruction to the select committee will be required to have it considered, which can be debated along with the instruction for a shortened reportback ; authorised the Minister of Local Government to make minor and technical changes to the Bill up to its introduction; approved the Local Government (Water Services Preliminary Arrangements) Bill PCO . for introduction, subject to the final approval of the Government caucuses and sufficient support in the House of Representatives; agreed that the Bill be introduced by May ; agreed that the Government propose that the Bill be: . referred to the Finance and Expenditure Committee; . enacted by August ; noted that further policy decisions will be made in June and July , comprising the long term settings of Local Water Done Well, to be set out in a third bill intended to be introduced in December ; noted that the Minister of Local Government and the Minister for RMA Reform intend to write to local authorities and iwi to advise them of the decisions referred to in paragraph above. Second, councils will have months from the enactment of the Transitional Provisions Bill to prepare Water Services Delivery Plans to show how you plan to deliver financially sustainable water services. Water Services Delivery Plans will also include information about current water services. The purpose of the Plans is for councils individually or jointly to publicly demonstrate their intention and commitment to deliver water services in ways that are financially sustainable, meet regulatory quality standards for water network infrastructu re and water quality, and unlock housing growth. Through the development of these Plans, councils will provide an assessment of their water infrastructure, how much they need to invest, and how they plan to finance and deliver it through their preferred service delivery model. Ringfencing of water services and revenue from other council activities is a key feature of the Plans. Importantly, the Plans will be a way for you to provide transparency to your communities about the costs and financing of water services and empower you to make decisions about managing and delivering high quality water services that reflect your local nee ds and circumstances. The Plans will also support you to have conversations with other councils about joint plans for water services delivery. ()(g)(i) Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua Department of Internal Affairs INCONFIDENCE Page of The Government expects those discussions will, in many cases, progress to proposals for new council controlled or council owned water organisations to provide water services, the amalgamation of water services with those of other councils, or other shared services arrangements. My expectation is that those discussions and decisions are already happening at a local level, and should include mana whenua. As youll be aware, I have also asked my officials to support these early discussions that you may be having about your possible future service delivery arrangements. There are couple of key things I wanted to emphasise today about the Plans: o Plans can be developed by individual councils, or jointly where groups of councils are planning to jointly establish a water organisation o Plans are one off, transitional documents. They have no regulatory function LTPs continue to be councils primary planning and accountability document. o Plans must include drinking water, wastewater and stormwater but councils have flexibility about transferring stormwater in proposed new service delivery arrangements. o It will be up to councils to determine how best to engage with their communities as part of the Plan development process. o Plans must demonstrate how water services and their funding will be ringfenced from other council activities. The Department will be providing information and guidance to councils to support the development of Plans. The third area that Cabinet has agreed are steps towards a future economic regulation regime as part of Local Water Done Well. Economic regulation is a key feature of Local Water Done Well and is intended to ensure consumers pay efficient, cost reflective prices for water services, that those services are delivered to an acceptable quality and that water services providers are investing sufficiently in their infrastructure. Development of an economic regulation system for water services will be led by the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment,

Section : Implementing the preferred option How will it be implemented . The BDMRR Act will be amended to give effect to the selfidentification process. The Bill that reenacts the Act is awaiting second reading. Provisions that would introduce a selfidentification process are already in the Bill as reported back by Select Committee. It is intended that these selfidentification provisions will be amended through a supplementary order paper, which will be referred to Select Committee for further consideration. At Select Committee, the public will be able to comment on the self dentification process. It is intended that the Bill, with the selfidentification provisions, will be passed in early . . The Department is working with Te Puni Kkiri, the Ministry for Pacific Peoples, and the Office for Ethnic Communities to encourage participation in the select committee process by young people, Mori, Pacific peoples and ethnic communities. An engagement plan is being developed to support this work. This will include providing written information about the Bill to Iwi authorities, community organisations and media networks that have reach in these communities. . The Department will undertake work to update our systems, processes and application forms to implement the new selfidentification process. It is possible that this will take up to months, so delayed commencement of the provisions may be required. We are considering if transitional arrangements are required for any people who may have begun the Family Court process at the time of commencement. . The Department will undertake consultation and regulation development to determine: the number and terminology of nonbinary sex markers; the third parties who can provide the letter of support for applications for children and young people; and the extra requirements for where a person applies more than once. . The Department will work with the Department of Corrections on necessary amendments to the Corrections Regulations . The Department will also work with the Ministry of Justice and organisations that support transgender and intersex people Official recognition of transgender and intersex peoples gender will have positive impacts on their wellbeing and therefore will benefit wider society. Total monetised benefits Unknown Nonmonetised benefits Mediumhigh Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Regulatory Impact Statement to notify affected people and the courts of the change. We will work across government to update relevant websites. . Improvements to the process may trigger an increase in applications. The Department is aware of this and will prepare for this as part of implementation. . The Department is considering how to include a range of nonbinary and culturally specific markers into its applications and IT systems. We will also need to build in flexibility to allow the systems to adapt with evolving gender terminology. Monitoring, Evaluation, and Review . To ensure the objectives of changing to a selfidentification process are being met, the process will be reviewed five years from commencement of the Bill. As part of this the Minister must consult the Human Rights Commissioner, the transgender and intersex communities and any other persons and organisations considered appropriate. . Ahead of this formal review, the Department will survey applicants in the first few years after implementation to understand if the new process is meeting their needs. It is open to other stakeholders to contact the Department directly to raise any concerns they have with the new process. Depending on this feedback and these surveys the formal review could be brought forward. Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs SelfIdentification Changes Act Bill SOP Status Quo in Act: Family Court process Current Bill: Selfidentification as proposed by Select Committee SOP: Preferred selfidentification clauses Application Process (Adult) Application to amend registered sex is made to the Family Court. Medical evidence is required. The Family Court judge decides if the application is successful . Application to amend registered sex is made to the RegistrarGeneral. A statutory declaration is required. The applicant decides what sex appears on their birth certificate in line with what best reflects their gender. Medical Evidence Evidence of medical treatment is required in the application. What constitutes medical evidence is decided by the judge. This can range from hormone therapy to gender affirming surgery. Medical evidence requirement removed and replaced with statutory declaration process. Statutory Declaration NAThe applicant is required to state that they: want the sex marker on their birth certificate to match their identified gender; intend to continue to identify as a person of this gender; and understand the consequences of the application. Citizenship Eligibility Overseasborn citizens and permanent residents are included in the definition of eligible person. The definition of eligible person should exclude anyone whose birth is registered overseas. Statutory Review NAA statutory review of selfidentification provisions is to be undertaken five years after they are enacted. Available Sex Markers Binary sex markers only: Male Female An indeterminate marker is available for intersex people born with a variation of sex characteristics. Nonbinary sex markers available: Male Female Intersex X (unspecified)Different sex markers available: Male Female Nonbinary marker options to be set in regulations Multiple Amendments to Sex Marker No set limit. However, a de facto limitation exists via: requiring satisfactory evidence that the applicant will maintain their nominated sex. only two sex marker options are available.Only one amendment to registered sex unless the Registered General is satisfied that there are special circumstances. Applicants reverting back to their sex assigned at birth may do so without meeting the special circumstances criteria. More than one amendment to registered sex is allowed. Applicants who make more than one amendment may need to meet additional requirements, to be set in regulations. Applicants reverting back to their sex assigned at birth are exempt from meeting these additional requirements. Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs SelfIdentification Changes Process for Under s Status Quo in Act: Family Court process Current Bill: Selfidentification as proposed by Select Committee SOP: Selfidentification Age Categories All children and young people aged under apply via the same process. Children and young people aged under form one age category. and yearolds form a second age category. and yearolds who are or have been in a marriage, civil union, or de facto relationship can apply as adults. and yearolds Application ProcessThe guardian of an eligible child applies to the Family Court. Eligible or yearolds make a statutory declaration. Document Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua Department of Internal Affairs INCONFIDENCE Page of Purpose This briefing seeks your agreement to a second tranche of policy proposals on introducing a selfidentification process for recognising gender on birth certificates through the Births, Deaths, Marriages, and Relationships Registration Bill (the Bill) . This briefing also provides you with the draft Cabinet paper, Introducing a self identification process to recognise gender on birth certificates (Appendix A ), for you r feedback and ministerial consultation. Executive summary You have agreed to seek Cabinet agreement to introduce a selfidentification process to enable people to have their gender recognised on birth certificates. This briefing provides you with the associated draft Cabinet paper for your feedback and ministerial consultation. You have agreed to a first tranche of policy proposals (IA refers). This briefing seeks your agreement to a second tranche of policy proposals. These include: . setting in regulations a range of markers to recognise nonbinary genders; . allowing people to amend their registered sex more than once, but with additional requirements for subsequent applications; . establishing different age categories with different requirements for applications for children and young people; . that most applications for children and young people need to be accompanied by a letter of support from a third party; and . guardian consent requirements for children and young people. Subject to your agreement on the above proposals and feedback on the draft Cabinet paper, we propose the Cabinet paper is considered by the Cabinet Social Wellbeing Committee on May . Background You have agreed to introduce a selfidentification process to enable transgender and intersex people to amend their sex on their birth certificate. Provisions that would enable a selfidentification process were added to the Bill at the recommendation of Select Committee in . Cabinet approval of selfidentification was not obtained at this time and is now required to progress the Bill with a selfidentification process. We are proposing several changes to the selfidentification provisions as reported back by Select Committee. These changes will be made via a Supplementary Order Paper (SOP). You have agreed to seek Cabinet agreement in May to introduce a self identification process and the policy decisions needed to draft the SOP. The term transgender is used in this paper to refer to all people whose gender differs from their assigned sex at birth this includes people who identify outside of the malefemale binary who may use a range of terms to describe their gender including non binary. Intersex is an umbrella term for people born with a variation of sex characteristics (such as sexual anatomy, reproductive organs, hormonal andor chromosome patterns). Intersex people are born with sex characteristics that are more diverse than narrow medical definitions of male or female bodies. Like anyone else, an intersex person may grow to identify with a different gender. To enable this the birth register must be . We are not proposing any changes to how sex is registered at birth. Gender is not known at birth, so the information collected will continue to be based on sex. Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua Department of Internal Affairs INCONFIDENCE Page of You recently agreed to a first tranche of policy proposals on introducing self identification (IA refers), including: . requiring applicants to compete a statutory declaration; . removing the intersex marker option from the Bill; . excluding anyone whose birth cannot be registered in New Zealand from the definition of eligible person; and . requiring a statutory review of the selfidentification provisions five years after enactment. This briefing seeks your agreement to a second tranche of policy proposals that cover: . the number and terminology for a range of sex marker options; . the number of times a person can amend registered sex; and . the process for amending registered sex for children and young people. The first and second tranche of policy approvals are reflected in the draft Cabinet paper. Further policy approvals required to introduce a selfidentification process . This section outlines the remaining policy approvals required to introduce self identification. Provide sex marker options that are inclusive of nonbinary genders Status Quo The Family Court process allows people to show the binary sex markers on their birth certificate: female or male. Select Committees recommendation The Select Committee sought to add the option X (unspecified) to be inclusive of people who identify other than the binary (female and male) . Departments advice setting in regulations a range of markers to recognise nonbinary genders We proposed replacing the umbrella term X (unspecified) as it fails to adequately represent all nonbinary genders . We instead recommended a mechanism to enable a more inclusive and flexible process where a range of genders can be agreed and used by applicants. You agreed in principle to making one or more sex markers available for nonbinary gende rs and that these will be set in regulations or operational policy (IA refers). We recommend allowing a range of nonbinary sex markers that are set in regulations. Consultation can be completed when developing regulations to determine the number of and terminology used for these markers. Consultation can be used to gauge transgender and intersex perspectives and the perspectives of specific population groups, such as young people and Mori, Pacific and ethnic communities. This could include exploring culturally inclusive markers such as takatpui (Mori), faafafine (Samoan), or fakaleit (Tongan). Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua Department of Internal Affairs INCONFIDENCE Page of Setting the nonbinary markers in regulations will futureproof the legislation. Gender theory and terminology evolves rapidly, and regulations can be more easily reviewed and than primary legislation to ensure they meet the needs of transgender and intersex people. While setting the markers in operational policy would have been easier to review and update than regulations we do not recommend this option. It would require enabling the RegistrarGeneral to set the markers following a public consultation process. This would be a new type of decisionmaking power for the Regist rarGeneral , whereas the Executive routinely makes these types of decisions. There is a high level of public interest in this issue, which means that markers would be better determined by publicly elected members of the Executive. Setting the markers in regulation will also be more transparent, as the process and available markers will be clearly established in secondary legislation. Setting the markers in operational policy would also be costlier in the short to medium term. To assist the Regist rarGeneral, a new process and capability would need to be built that replicates the Departments existing policy development capability. Development of nonbinary markers would be better incorporated into the usual government regulatory process. The number of times a person can amend registered sex Status Quo Under the Family Court process, it would be rare but not impossible for a person to amend their registered sex more than once . While there is no limit on the number of times a person can apply, the requirements lend themselves to the amendment being permanent (eg the court must be satisfied a person intends to maintain their nominated sex). Select Committees recommendation The Select Committee recommended that under a selfidentification process only one change be allowed unless the Regist rarGeneral is satisfied that there are special circumstances. The exception to this rule is that if a person wants to revert to their sex at birth, they may do so at any time. Departments advice allow for people to amend their registered sex more than once, but with additional requirements for subsequent applications . We recommend that people can amend their registered sex more than once. Gender can be fluid and how a person identifies may change over time. Allowing only one amendment would be out of step with a true selfi dentification model. If a persons gender changes and they cannot amend their registered sex to reflect this, they no longer have control of how their gender is officially recognised. . We understand th at Select Committee recommended allowing only one amendment except in special circumstances to mitigate the risk of identity fraud. Where a person amends their registered sex their previous name and sex are not displayed on their birth certificate. This means a person cannot be easily linked to their previous identity, Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua Department of Internal Affairs INCONFIDENCE Page of Select Committees recommendation Select Committees recommended process is different depending on the age of the child or young person: . or year olds can apply on their own behalf with written consent from their guardian; and . years and under applications must be made on behalf of the child or young person by their guardian. The process only differs in who makes the application. Both age groups require guardian consent and a recommendation from a health professional. Departments advice different age categories to reflect older adolescents higher level of cognitive development We agree with the age categories recommended by Select Committee. These categories reflect that and year olds are generally more able to provide consent and can live independently from a guardian . This is consistent with other legislation in New Zealand (eg at years old a young person can consent to general medical procedures). It also aligns with other jurisdictions that ease selfidentification policies once a person turns (eg in Norway any person years of age and over can amend their recorded gender, no guardian consent is required). We recommend that the age categories have different requirements to reflect the different levels of cognitive development: . or year olds can apply on their own behalf with either : .. written consent from their guardian; or .. a letter of support by a third party. . years and under applications must be: .. made on behalf of the child or young person by their guardian; and .. be accompanied by a letter of support from a third party. Requiring third party assurance Status Quo The Family Court process requires the guardian making the application for a child or young person to provide evidence the child has undergone or will undergo medical treatment to enable them to assume their nominated sex. The purpose of the medical evidence is to assess a child or young persons physical confirmation or ability to physically conform with their preferred sex. This requirement medicalises a deeply personal expression of selfidentity and is out of step with a self identification process. Select Committees recommendation Select Committee recommended that applications for all children and young people be accompanied by a recommendation from a health professional. The recommendation from the health professional is to provide assurance that the child or young person Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua Department of Internal Affairs INCONFIDENCE Page of understands the consequences of the application and that the change is in their best interests. It would not be about current or planned medical treatment. The health professionals able to provide a recommendation would be medical practitioners, health practitioners registered with the P sychologists Board or the Nursing Council of New Zealand, councillors represented by certain bodies and registered social workers. Departments advice most applications need to be accompanied by a letter of support from a third party We recommend that applications be accompanied by a letter of support from a third party, with the classes of persons that can act as third parties to be prescribed in regulations. After consulting with other agencies, w e recommend that the role of the third party is different to that recommended by Select Committee with a stronger focus on informed consent. The third party would be assessing that the child or young person understands the change and that the decision is based on their own perceptions of their gender. This focus on consent is more aligned with a selfidentification process as it acts to protect the child or young person from undue influence (eg from guardians) and supports their autonomy over their gender. Given there is no need for gender affirming care under selfidentification, people outside of the health sector may be able to assess if a child or young person understands the change. In addition, restricting the third party to certain professions could mean the letter of support is difficult to access and out of step with the aim of reducing barriers to changing registered sex. We recommend the classes of people who can provide the letter of support are prescribed in regulations. This will provide time for further analysis on what classes of people will be suitable to act as a third party . In developing the regulations targeted consultation should be completed with potential professional groups or classes of people. These could include health professionals and people outside of the health sector, such as councillors or people who may know the child or young person well. The views of children and young people should also be sought on this matter. Parent or guardian consent Status Quo Under the Family Court process all applications for children and young people aged years and under need to be made by their guardians. There is no clear process in the BDMRR Act where there are disputes between guardians or where guardians refuse to apply on behalf of their child. Select Committees recommendation Select Committee recommendations require guardian consent for all age groups . However, Select Committee clarified that the Family Court can assist with disputes between guardians or where guardians refuse to apply on behalf of their or year old. In these situations, an application may be made to the Family Court to settle the dispute under the Care of Children Act . Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua Department of Internal Affairs INCONFIDENCE Page of Guardian is defined as all the guardians of a person (eg both parents jointly) unless: . one guardian is unavailable; . one guardian has applied to the Family Court, and the court has consented to the child or young persons sex marker being amended; or . if all guardians are unavailable the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki is the guardian. Departments advice guardian consent is not always necessary for and year olds As above, we recommend that guardians apply on behalf of children and young people aged years and under . To reflect their maturity, we recommend that guardian consent is not necessary for young people aged and , if they instead supply a letter of support from a third party. Enabling and year olds to apply with only a letter of support, partly mitigates concerns raised by other agencies about guardians not being accepting of their childs gender identity and refusing consent. It also mitigates concerns about young people who feel uncomfortable talking to their guardians about their gender, or who are estranged from their guardians. There may be a concern that the above risks are not being mitigated for children and young people years and under. We consider that guardian consent is still important for this age group. Not requiring guardian consent for this age group would be inconsistent with the process to change names under the Births, Deaths, Marriages and Relationships Registration Act (BDMRR Act) and other legislation (eg at years a young person needs parental consent to leave school early under the Education and Training Act ). It could also be considered out of ste p with a guardians responsibilities under the Care of Children Act for their childs development and for helping their child determine important decisions. The Ministry of Social Development noted that requiring guardian consent could allow guardians to exercise their responsibility in ways that negatively impact a child or young persons wellbeing. The Counting Ourselves survey found that participants who had an unsupportive family were more likely to have attempted suicide in the last months. We understand this is a concern, but not requiring guardian consent would be a significant change. Guardians will often be integral to supporting a child or young person to amend their birth certificate. At this stage, we recommend that the guardian consent requirement for those years and under is maintained. You agreed to a statutory review of the self identification provisions five years after enactment (IA refers). As part of this, any negative consequences of requiring guardian consent can be reviewed. Departments advice keep Select Committees definition of guardian We recommended keeping Select Committees definition of guardian that means all guardians jointly except in special circumstances. Guardians acting jointly is consistent with obligations under the Care of Children Act . As part of the statutory review The Youth survey found that only a third of transgender and gender diverse participants had told their parents or caregivers they were transgender or gender diverse. The Counting Ourselves survey found that per cent of respondents had been kicked out of home because they were transgender Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua Department of Internal Affairs INCONFIDENCE Page of five years after enactment (IA refers) consideration can be given to any negative consequences of requiring guardians to act jointly. Departments advice keep the Family Court mechanism to resolve disputes We recommend keeping Select Committees provision that clarifies that the Registrar General can uphold Family Court decisions on disputes between guardians or where guardians refuse consent for and year olds amending registered sex. There is likely to be a reduced need for this provision as and year olds can apply with only a letter of support from a third party. However, there may still be scenarios where this is useful (eg where the young person has trouble accessing a third party and their guardians refuse consent). Regulation making powers are needed to give effect to the above proposals Regulation making powers are needed to give full effect to the selfidentification proposals outlined above. We recommend a regulation making power that will enable regulations that prescribe: . the sex marker options other than the binary; . the additional requirements where a person amends their registered sex more than once; . the third parties who can provide a letter of support for applications for children and young people; and . any other matters required to give effect to a selfidentification process, which align with the overall intent of the proposals in this paper. Selfidentification has implications for Department of Corrections regulations We previously advised that there is only one instance where changing registered sex will have implications on other legislation. This is a Department of Corrections (Corrections ) regulation that requires that where a person supplies their birth certificate they must be placed in a prison that aligns with the sex recorded. This is out of step with the BDMRR Act and the Bill, which infer that birth certificate s should not be concl usive evidence of a persons sex .
Section F( ) of the Bill adds to this power by providing that Regulations under section may prescribe fees that must be paid by providers to meet the costs of the Chief C ensors annual review. This addition is necessary to enable the Chief Censor to recover the costs of monitoring and enforcing compliance with the provisions of this Bill.

Serverside Algorithm Performance The main evaluation process only performs the bareminimum of serverside processing: reidentifying the encrypted IDs to the card serial number, and filtering contacts to only those that meet the current definition of a close contact (i.e. within two metres for at least fifteen minutes). As discussed above, there is potential to further increase the accuracy of the overall system by ranking the list of contacts provided by the card. Across all trials and ground truth contacts the card achieves recall and false positive rate, and although many of our false positive contacts meet the definition of a casual contact, it would be preferable to be able to prioritise close contacts over casual ones.

Sharing information digitally remains challenging Information could remain siloed because businesses and organisations do not choose to participate in the Trust Framework The flow of information is impeded, and the potential benefits of digital identity are not realised Business and organisations are enthusiastic for government intervention to address the issue of silos Public sector and private sector service providers assume this risk. Officials are working closely with businesses and organisations to ensure their needs and requirements are met by the Trust Framework and encourage their participation. This is considered a moderate risk. Business and organisations have expressed enthusi asm for government led intervention but the full costs, policies and processes of participating in a Framework have yet to be determined Service delivery does little to improve customer experience People may not actually use the digital identity services that are more secure and private, simply because others are more convenient. Uptake remains low People prioritise service delivery Public sector and private sector service providers assume this risk. Service delivery remains the responsibility of service providers and not the Trust Framework, though bring ing consistency and trust into the digital identity ecosystem will enable service providers to improve their delivery. Unclear Costs become excessive for government andor private sector The actu al costs of compliance testing turns out to be significantly higher than the initial indicative costs. This would affect Government in phase one ( ) as government is covering the cost of this testing. In phase two ( ) the entity seeking accredi tation, whether public or private, will likely assume this cost. The Trust Framework requires more resources than anticipated to set up andor maintain, increasing overall costs for government. Budgets are undermined Costs discourage participation in the Trust Framework Reasonable costs will encourage participation Government assumes the risk with regard to the cost of testing. In order to mitigate this risk, government will cover the cost of compliance testing during phase one of the Trust Framework ( ) and work with partners to test and developed compliance processes in such a manner that compliance testing costs remain reasonable and appropriate going forward. The entity undergoing compliance testing assumes the cost of upgrading their systems. In the case of p ublic sector entities, government can mitigate this through budget planning, however, private sector entities remain responsible for their own budgets. The mitigation measures will ensure this is a low probability risk.

SmartStart is a multiawardwinning online platform making it easy for new and expectant parents to access services and information about the birth of their child. Parents can easily register their babys birth, find support and services in their area, update their benefit and Working for Families information and more online, any time, on any device.
SmartStart was developed in collaboration with the Department of Internal Affairs, Ministry of Health, Ministry of Social Development, Inland Revenue, Plunket and the New Zealand College of Midwives.

Some trials (particularly construction and party) had a high proportion of false positives compared to the others, however: Cardholders with only a few groundtruth contacts would have a high false positive rate if even one false positive was found. This could have been mitigated by weighting results on the number of ground truth contacts for each cardholder. The basic oncard algorithm prioritises high recall since missed contacts cannot be later recovered, but there is an opportunity for filtering out or deprioritising potential false positives after downloading and reidentifying contacts, using factors such as: Time of day Density of contacts at the time a contact was recorded Overall duration of contact The ground truth, especially for the unscripted trials, were largely entered by one person per trial. Although distances (intensity ) were typically consistent when spotchecked, the approach to rating of contact events (intensity ) differed by scorer. Proactively Released by the Department of Internal Affairs With greater consistency in scoring methodology the card contact algorithm could be tuned differently and decrease the likelihood of false positives in practice. Other yettobe tested algorithms for filtering events into a contact list on the card could potentially yield lower false positive rates.

Stability Does the option support stability of representation arrangements for individuals and communities Decis ions on Mori wards are required to remain in place for a minimum of six years to allow time for the changes to bed in before the decision can be reversed. This option is disruptive to council governance arrangements. Some councils may have Mori wards established at the local elections overturned after just one term. Truncated representation review processes, lack of an appeal right, and the possible roll back of representation arrangements may be very disruptive (e.g. , potential to remove councillor positions or general wards that were recently established) .
