Stakeholder Views Public consultation . The public and stakeholders were not consulted on the options. However, the issue of regulation of online gambling and sports and racing wagering has been actively discussed for some years and the previous Government announced in May in agreed in principle to TAB NZ having an online monopoly, subject to further work being undertaken. . We anticipate from conversations with stakeholders , there are likely to be a range of views on the options. For example, offshore operators are likely in favour of a regulated qwkdm Regulatory Impact Assessment online gambling market they can legitimately enter and participate in. They would likely express disappointment TAB NZ is given an online sports and racing betting monopoly. Previous consultation also indicated they would not be in favour of a raised POCC rate. . TAB NZ and the racing codes are highly supportive of TAB NZ having an online monopoly. While not having been directly consulted on the overall package in Option , some other elements of the package have been signalled with them and we believe they will be generally supportive of the optionpackage. TAB NZ has also expressed its desire to have the POCC rate raised. . Sport NZ supports extending TAB NZs online wagering monopoly to protect community interests and minimise gambling harm. However, while the racing codes support the monopoly, the views of individual NSOs are not known. The financial impact on specific NSOs is uncertain and likely to depend on the individual sports. Option One Counterfactual . Option would keep New Zealands gambling market model the same as it is now. Although TAB NZ would be the only authorised operator of betting products in New Zealand, there would be no legal barriers for offshore online operators to offer their sports and race betting products to New Zealanders, or for New Zealanders to play on offshore sites , provided they do not advertise here . . As noted, under the counterfactual option, t he Governments online casino regulation regime would be put in place coming into force at this stage in . While there will not be a direct impact on the way TAB NZ operates under the online casino proposal, the changes are likely to strengthen the position of some of TAB NZs closest competitors in New Zealand who are able to advertise as part of licensing conditions . . Given these factors, we consider under the counterfactual , it is highly likely offshore competition will further erode the revenue of TAB NZ although the rate and severity of this decline are unknown. . The other risks of the counterfactual are: there continues to a large grey market a grey market means that offshore operators are neither regulated nor operating illegally. Spending on offshore online gambling (i.e. the grey market) is expected to continue to increase over time. The advertising ban is only partially effective, and it will remain almost impossible to enforce for e.g. through advertising at overseas sports events broadcast in New Zealand ; TAB NZs long term revenue sustainability remains at risk in turn, this risks the racing industrys long term viability, and could impact jobs, especially in rural communities; and in the short term the additional payments provided for in the Entain partnership agreement for an online monopoly of million and ;
Stakeholder Public consultation . Targeted consultation was conducted in April to operationalise the POCC. Consultation highlighted the need for a reasonable rate of POCC that would not unfairly inflate offshore betting providers tax burdens compared to domestic providers. Consultation on a rate (the current rate) highlighted support for a lower rate amongst offshore operators, whereas TAB NZ TAB NZ reiterated its view that the current rate is too low in a letter to the former Minister for Racing in October . Additional assumption specific to this option . Some operators will continue to pay an increased POCC If the POCC is increased, some operators will continue to pay and returns to the racing industry will increase. However, depending on the rate of increase , some operators may decide to stop paying but continue to operate in the market offering better odds than TAB NZ, or leave the market entirely. Both outcomes would impact returns to the racing industry.

Statutes Ame ndment Bill (for information only) The Statute Amendment Bill (Bill) is the legislative mechanism for technical, short and non controversial amendments to existing legislation. The Bills are used to correct drafting errors and omissions, as well as to mak e minor technical changes to legislation and do not introduce policy change. Amendments may only progress with the unanimous support of the House of Representatives. Accordingly, all parliamentary parties are consulted on proposed amendments prior to their inclusion in such a Bill. In , the Bill did not receive unanimous support in the House and did not proceed. Recently, the Ministry of Justice, as the administering agency, has supported its Minister to undertake parliamentary consultation. The Bill no w has the unanimous support required to proceed. Impact on Local Government legislation In April , the then Minister of Local Government agreed minor and technical amendments could be made under the Statutes Amendment Bill to the: Local Government Act ; Local Government Rating Act ; and Water Services Act . The amendments are to: section D of the Local Government Rating Act and Schedule of the Local Government Act to move section D to Schedule of the Local Government Act to bring all annual report requirements for local authorities into one place; sectio n ()(a) of the Water Services Act to remove the word the before drinking water supply to make the section consistent with section ()(c) and ()(e); section () of the Water Services Act to update example in section () by removing the word the before drinking water supply to make it consistent with the other examples provided; ()(a) Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs

Statutory review of the selfidentification provisions Select committee recommendation . The select committee recommended a statutory review of the selfidentification provisions five years after enactment. This would require developing a report to present to Parliament. This would not include reviewing the basic change to a self identification process. Departments advice agree with the select c ommittees recommendation . The complexity of the policy and the sensitivity of this issue will make it important that the legislative settings are evaluated after enactment. A review would provide a transparent assessment of whether the policies supporting a selfidentification process are functioning well in practice.

Success of CovidCard relies on detecting a high proportion of the highrisk encounters that occur within a population. Highrisk encounters typically take place inside, at places such as bars, restaurants, at church services, at large events, or on planes or public transport. It is envisaged that CovidCard would need to be required to be worn in such settings to be effective.

Without an upgraded approach, we are left to choose between an indefinitely closed border or a shift to a strategy of suppression should the virus inevitably arrive again. The challenges within the digital identity ecosystem would remain unchanged, but would be increasingly exacerbated by the ongoing digital transformation occurring in all spheres of life a trend recently accelerated by the Covid pandemic. Trust in di gital identity services would remain low, information would remain siloed, and the flow of information impeded. Furthermore, without intervention the digital identity ecosystem in New Zealand would not be positioned to realise the significant opportunities trusted digital identity could offer. This option could be established in the near term. Phase one of the Trust Framework ( ), in which a small number of participants are informally linked to the Trust Framework, will allow for the testing of policiesprocesses and the mitigation of risks before the Trust Framework is established in legislation, giving it legal enforceability and enabling more participants into the trusted ecosystem. This phasing approach would al so allow for the Trust Framework to be scaled and transformed in the future, if required. This could be established at a reasonable cost. Estimated costs to government approximately million per annum. As a result of these factors, option is the Departments preferred option. This would achieve the objective of a consistent and trusted digital identity ecosystem . It would not be established in a timely manner. It would take years to set up this regime, ensuring that the challenges in the digital identity ecosystem remain unaddressed for some time. The costs associated with this option would be higher than any of the other options. Estimated at million per annum. Undertaking such a comprehensive approach from the outset might lead to a situation where the costs of the regime outweigh the benefits. Support HPA and DIA to embed work with class gambling operators to identify potentially harmful gambling behaviour and take effective action to prevent and minimise harm . Develop and refine guidelinestrain thetrainers training to promote host responsibility in other gamb ling environments (including online environments) so operators can identify potentially harmful gambling behaviour and take effective action to prevent and minimise gambling harm and create safer gambling environments . Underlying principles: closer to homek a aro mai kit e kinga Good health begins at home and in communities, so it makes sense to promote the development and implementation of regulatory and policy settings that create safer gambling environments, particularly for people and communities at greater risk of moderate to high levels of gambling harm. This involves enabling systemic changes to innovate and deliver more effective services that will minimise and prevent gambling harm, to keep people and communities well and to reduce the level of gambling harm people experience. Objective : Services raise awareness about the range and signs of gambling harms that affect individuals, familieswhnau and communities Families and whnau of problem gamblers can be badly affected by gambling harm. The Ministry therefore places great importance on improving health literacy, to drive behavioural change by helping families and whnau to recognise and address issues associated with gambling harm and to apply appropriate selfhelp or helpseeking behaviours. The Ministry will continue to work with HPA and other relevant organisations to target atrisk and vulnerable communities to increase awareness, reduce gambling harm and encourage associated positive behaviours. These are typically communities with a high social deprivation score, who are at increased risk because of increased access to NCGMs and vulnerable because they lack access to resources that would help improve their resiliency. The Ministry of Health will use evaluation activities, the consumer network and resultsbased accountability reporting to ensure that all organisations are working in the right way, with the right people. The Ministry expects the services it funds to have a robust health equity, cultural competency and health literacy focus, as well as input from consumer networks once established. It also expects service providers to build relationships with other relevant organisations and communities in the areas in which they operate. This is one way of sharing relevant information and increasing the overall awareness of gambling harm and indicators of potentially harmful gambling. Services need to better address the cultural and language differences of their target audiences. The Ministry expects that the proposed codesign approach and use of consumer networks will give consumers from vulnerable communities a stronger voice in the design and evaluation of services. Some consumers of water services will be households with inadequate income and resources to support their basic needs, including water services. Households experiencing material hardship will likely include occupants that are younger, single parents, on be nefits as their main source of income, Mori and Pacific peoples, people with disabilities, larger households, and renters. . Currently, there appears to be a very large range in average annual water charges across councils sampled by the Department of Inter nal Affairs, from a low of about to a high of about ,. The average is about , across the sample. Aucklands average is ,. In future, this range is expected to narrow as entities implement more standardised approaches to pricing, including possible geographic averaging across districts. At the low end of the range, prices almost certainly are below the long run cost of service provision and do not cover economic depreciation. . The c ombined cost of water bills and rates bills should not materially change when water services entities are initially set up, other things being equal. Over time, they should be more affordable than if the same level of services were to continue to be provid ed by councils. Rates bills should reduce to offset water being separately billed, unless territorial authorities decide to increase their revenues for other reasons.

THE STRUCTURE OF THE DEPARTMENT
TRIALS Over a twoweek period in May during alert level of COVID restrictions in New Zealand , eight validation trials were performed. These trials aimed to cover a wide range of natural situations, prioritising scenarios the technical team felt covered the most challenging environments for recalling close contacts that also had high potential for spreading an infectious disease. Scenarios were also prioritised if they were in the public interest (such as large gatheringsparties which were subject to additional restrictions during New Zealands alert levels), or covered a wide range of situations (e.g. queuing, oneonone meetings, casual contact, etc.). Seven of the trials covered five scenarios: office, cafe, construction site, taxi, and a house party. One scenario was repeated twice (office), and one scenario was broken into two trials for ease of evaluation (house party). There was one additional trial proximity that was also performed but was evaluated separately as it was designed to test specific aspects of the cards performance. The proximity trial methodology and results are included in Appendix .

Helpline and webbased services Helpline and webbased services provide: information access to intervention services for people unable to access face toface services referral to other gambling harm service providers information on selfhelp, peer topeer support options and assessment guides. Currently the Ministry funds two forms of telephonebased support, as follows. The Gambling Helpline provides a free service, and is a first contact point for people in crisis as a result of harmful gambling. It also provides a backup for other services that are not available , and ensures coverage in rural areas, where there are no face toface services. This is critical to the Ministry s service delivery model. The Asian Gambling Helpline is a limited service for the Asian community, provided by the PGF, and is funded out of psychosocial interventions and support services. Submissions from health groups and service providers, particularly those serving Pacific and Asian communities, called for more languageappropriate support. Suggestions included translating key information into common languages online, and extending the hours and range of interpreter languages available. The Ministry will explore ways to extend the reach of these frontline services with Asian and Pacific providers and the consumer network. It will also explore ways to increase the general helpline referral rate: currently only . percent of calls are referred to a treatment provider. Psychosocial interventions and support Psychosocial intervention and support services include a range of interventions delivered to individuals or groups in a variety of settings (including prisons). People affected by a family or whnau member s gambling can access the same range of services that is available to the gamblers themselves. The four core intervention areas are: brief intervention, full intervention, facilitation and followup services. Table : Structured p articipation in decision making using decision making tools e.g., CONSUL Madrid Decide (ES) Background Description Costs involved Relevance for NZ context Feasibility for different individuals and community types Risks Benefits Design choices Madrid Decide was started in as a counter to the growing political mistrust caused by the austerity measures in Spain. It has since become a platform CONSUL http:consulproject.orgen developed by the municipality in Madrid, for pub lic participation. It is now used in countries. Decide Madrid received the public service prize from the United Nations in . Objectives : for citizens to comment on proposed ordinances and make suggestions for changes to those ordinances ; to increase the transparency of the government and e participation. Process : The software was developed and funded by Madrids City Council. The website based on the software has five sections: debates, proposals, voting, processes (collaborative legislation) , and pa rticipatory budgeting. The intensity of participation in decision making depends on the level of verification. All citizens of Madrid (age ) are allowed to participate on the site. Registered users who provide only a username, email address, and passwo rd can participate in discussions, create proposals, and create expenditure projects. Users who provide the previous information and verify their residence and provide a mobile phone number can participate in discussions, create proposals, create expenditu re projects, vote for proposals, and vote for expenditure projects in the support phase. Users who provide the previous information and also fully verifies their account in person at a Citizen Assistance Office or via mail, can also vote for proposals in the final decision phase . Platform users participate in the drafting and modification of regulations and give their opinions on those regulations. The opinions will be considered by the City Council. The comments are considered by th e different government sectors for the final drafting of the ordinances. Platform users can join the discussion of any of the draft ordinances or policies. The public interaction is done through different users commenting online on the ordinance and on oth er users comments. Users can upvote or downvote another users comment. All discussions and votes are available for the public to see when anyone visits the website. Proposals which gain support from one per cent of the census population are then put to a binding public vote. In addition, several face toface deliberative spaces (i.e. local forums, physical voting booths) were set up to support the platform and to cater to the different needs of stakeholders involved . The tool could support a participator y budgeting process in New Zealand it is currently used in many local governments around the world. Special engagement campaign for youth and women (under represented voters) was conducted. Citizens give their input on local policies and regulations affecting their lives . Many different citizens have commented on many different ordinances and made suggestions for improvements (the site has , registered users of Madrid population ). Table : Objective priorities for action Objective : Services raise awareness about the range and signs of gambling harms that affect individuals, familieswhnau and communities Priorities for action Short to medium term priorities Long term priorities Target p romotional activities to reduce gambling harm and increase awareness of the range and signs of gambling harms at high risk communities. Work to increase access to services among people experiencing gambling harm and their families and whnau, including in rural areas. Develop tools and protocols to support the primary health care sector and other community services to include screening, brief assessment and brief and early intervention for gambling harm as part of general health screening and day today delivery . Underlying principles: peoplepoweredm te iwi hei kawe The health system plays an important role in providing people with the information they need to fully understand issues around health and wellness, including how to be healthy, access health services and manage their own health (health literacy). To improve health literacy, services need to work in partnership with service users, supporting and encouraging them to be health smart and to mitigate language and cultural barriers to accessing information. In this partnership between providers and users, different groups of people will need different forms of support, depending on factors such as: age; ethnicity; different worldviews, expectations and religious beliefs; location; and existing conditions or disabilities. Gambling harm can be associated with mental illness, other addictions and substance abuse, family violence and a range of other social issues. Enhancing awareness of the signs of harmful gambling, and opportunities for screening, among services that address these other health and social issues will help enhance the accessibility of services to prevent and minimise gambling harm. Objective : People access effective treatment and support services at the right time and place Provision of highquality, effective and accessible services to prevent and minimise gambling harm requires staff who are appropriately qualified and services that are culturally relevant to the communities they serve. Access to intervention services should be available in all areas where there is access to gambling venues. Continuing to provide dedicated Mori, Pacific and Asian services is crucial to help reduce gamblingharmrelated inequity and inequality. The Ministry will increase the emphasis on including consumer perspectives in service design and delivery (informed by research and evaluation). It will also explore culturespecific delivery models (where costeffective) with consumer networks and service providers. Talking Points Water Services Legislation Repeal Bill for Cabinet meeting Overview As part of the Governments day commitment, the Water Services Entities Act and Water Services Economic Efficiency and Consumer Protection Act will be repealed CAB MIN refers . It is my intent for Cabinet to consider the Repeal Bill in the week of February , Cabinet endorsement on February and the introduction to the House on February .
Talking points Repeal Bill The Repeal B ill will repeal the: o Water Services Entities Act (including the Water Services Entities Amendment Act and the Water Services Legislation Act ). o Water Services Economic Efficiency and Consumer Protection Act , which is administered by the Ministry for Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE). The Minister for Commerce and Consumer Protection has agreed to th e inclusion of the Water Services Economic Efficiency and Consumer Protection Act in this Repeal Bill . The Repeal Bill will: o end the entity model that was part of the water services Acts and reinstate previous legislation relating to water services that was in place, including legislation that was amended by the Water Services Entities Amendment Act and Water Services Le gislation Act ; o disestablish the Northland and Auckland Water Services Entity , its establishment board, and the chief executive of that entity. Employment arrangements with this entity will be terminated, and the employee will be entitled to any redundancy arrangements they may have in their contract; o will transfer any residual assets, liabilities, and information of that entity to the Department of Internal Affairs; o remove the statutory obligation to make an Order in Council setting the dates for establishment of water services entities. The Repeal Bill proposes that this provision commences on the of introduction of th e Repeal Bill. The Bill will retain technical amendments that improve the regulation of water services by Taumata Arowai, including the Taumata Arowai the Water Services Regulator Act , the Water Services Act , and related Acts. The Bill will repeal out of Local Acts.

Taumata Arowai Taumata Arowai is a new Crown entity, established on March , through the Taumata Arowai Water Services Regulator Act . It will not become fully operational until the Water Services Bill has been passed (expected in the second half of ). Taumata Arowais objectives relate to: protecting and promoting drinking water safety and related public health outcomes efectively administering the drinking water regulatory system building and maintaining capability among drinking water suppliers and across the wider industry giving efect to Te Mana o te Wai, to the extent that Te Mana o te Wai applies to the functions and duties of Taumata Arowai providing oversight of environmental performance of wastewater and stormwater networks promoting public understanding of the environmental performance of wastewater and stormwater networks.

Tax treatment of service delivery vehicles
Taxi The taxi trial (taxi, n) was a short ( minute) scripted trial to check that passengers in a small vehicle would be seen as close contacts by the card. There was no expectation of consecutive sets of passengers being recorded by each other since pickups may be many kilometres apart; however, we would expect all passengers to show on the drivers card. There were two passengers alternated seating positions: one in front and one in back; both in back; as well as frontback seating positions for a single passenger. The three participants (n) wore a single card around their neck, IDs (driver), and (passengers).

Te Tari Taiwhenua Department of Internal Affairs Appendix A: Timeline for the Overseas Collections (OPC) The Overseas Collections (OPC) form part of the National Librarys General Collection, which is a current use collection. The OPC contains mostly English language books purchased for general interest reading, with an emphasis on the arts and the humanities and general information for a public library readership. Some books that were no longer needed by public libraries were accepted into the OPC prior to . Plans to exit Wai re re House, a regional repository, triggered a review of the OPC to reduce the volume of the collections in line with the Librarys Collections Policy. Minister of Internal Affairs, Tracey Martin, approved the removal, over time, of all publications from the OPC, excluding those in subject areas identified as collecting priorities in the Overseas Collecting Plan. National Librarian Bill Macnaught announced the start of a project to rehome books from the OPC. The first lists of books for review are on the Librarys website. Internet Archive offers to take all books remaining after the review for digitisation to provide free access from their global digital library and to preserve the physical copies. Mr Macnaught begins discussions with the Chief Executive of Copyright Licensing New Zealand (CLNZ) about a possible agreement with Internet Archive and suitable mitigations to allay copyright concerns of rights holders. Book Guardians Aotearoa formed in response to the OPC project. Around , books donated to Lions and Rotary for a special oneoff fund raiser. Rachel Esson appointed Te Pouhuaki National Librarian in December. The National Library applies for a licence from ManatO Taonga Ministry for Culture and Heritage to export parts of the OPC to Internet Archive that may be subject to the Protected Objects Act . This licence is granted but has not used due to decisions taken subsequently. By April about percent of the OPC titles had been reviewed with input from Library stakeholders, with , books transferred to libraries in the New Zealand library network. Some books were transferred to the Alexander Turnbull Librarys research collections. A smaller, more focused collection of overseas publications was retained in the National Librarys General Collections (approximately percent of the OPC). In July the library announced its agreement with Internet Archive for all books left at the end of the OPC review to be donated for digitisation and preservation. Te Tari Taiwhenua Department of Internal Affairs Purpose . This briefing updates you on the background and development of a removal and disposal policy for the National Library. It describes how we intend to engage with stakeholders and the connections the policy has to the Overseas Collections (OPC). Background The need for a removal and disposal policy . Under the National Library Act , the National Librarian must obtain the approval of the Minister of Internal Affairs to remove any documents from the collections (s()). The Act also introduced the legislative requirement that the Alexander Turnbull Library collections are kept in perpetuity (s(a)). . The National Library has three broad collections the general collections, the research collections, and the schools collection. The schools collection is already covered by a disposal policy introduced in . However, the general collections, maintained to support current research needs, and the research collections, maintained to support longterm research needs and required to be kept in perpetuity, are not covered by a removal and disposal policy. . This policy is intended to provide the National Library with clear parameters for when items can be recommended for removal from its research and general collections by the Minister of Internal Affairs, and how they will be disposed of. It also covers process principles the National Library needs to follow when considering removal and disposal to support clarity and transparency around decisionmaking and to provide assurance for stakeholders. . There are a range of circumstances where items are considered for removal from the National Librarys general and research collections. For example, if they have been identified as violating an individuals privacy, or where they are part of a collection that is best housed elsewhere in New Zealand. In addition, it is good collection management practice to ensure items in collections developed for their shortterm utility and never intended for permanent retention are disposed of once that purpose no longer exists. Our approach to feedback and engagement: Ensuring good expert and stakeholder input . A Removal and Disposal Advisory Group has been set up to advise our team during the development of this operational policy. Advisory Group members bring both their own expertise and the views of their organisations to the discussions. . The Advisory Group comprises representatives from the Library and Information Association New Zealand Aotearoa (LIANZA); Te Ropu Whakahau (the leading national body that represents Maori engaged in libraries, culture, knowledge, information, communication, and systems technology); the New Zealand Historical Association (NZHA); the Professional Historians Association of New ZealandAotearoa (PHANZA); Auckland Museum; and the Council of NZ University Libraries (CONZUL). The Advisory Group is currently providing advice and input into the draft policy. . The Advisory Group has meet twice, providing input as the policy was being drafted and providing feedback on the first draft. They have also had opportunity to advise the Library on key stakeholders to engage with during the policys development. The Department has a broad range of responsibilities and functions that span Information and Communications Technology (ICT) investment, information management, working with communities, ensuring efective regulatory frameworks are in place, supporting the executive and local government, and delivering a range of services to support and foster social cohesion, inclusion and a sense of belonging. The Department is the home of the Government Chief Digital Oficer (GCDO) and the Government Chief Privacy Oficer (GCPO) and leads the digital transformation of government across the state sector. In this respect, we support our state sector colleagues to meet the needs of New Zealanders and the Government through better investment in ICT and to maintain the privacy and security of New Zealanders information. The Department is the home of the National Library of New Zealand and Archives New Zealand, which act as the memory of society and the memory of government respectively. These institutions play an important role in preserving New Zealands documentary heritage and ensuring a full and accurate public record is created and maintained. The AISA reduces multiple requests for the same information by different government agencies and removes the need to provide physical copies of information. It also improves the quality and consistency of information that agencies hold about an individual and makes it easier to detect issues such as identity fraud.

The Death Approved Information sharing Agreement (AISA) facilitates access to information about deaths. The AISA assists with the provision of public services by facilitating access to accurate death information for organisations. It also provides for updating records about individuals associated with the deceased individual so that their records are also accurate. Organisations may take subsequent actions based on the update of records relating to the deceased individual or associated persons, such as the granting of benefits or entitlements, if that is the agreed purpose for receiving the information.

The Department is working on an AllofGovernment (AoG) Roadmap to modernise government digital services across New Zealand. This includes a digital investment plan to support its implementation.The goal is to improve how New Zealanders experience digital government services, and to deliver greater efficiencies and productivity. By using reusable digital components, interoperable data, strong digital security foundations, and essential capabilities (such as digital skills and new funding models), customer experiences and efficiency will improve. The Department of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua Appendix A: How the Rates Rebate Scheme works . Four factors affect the overall cost of the Rates Rebate Scheme (the Scheme) to the Crown. These are: the Schemes key settings (the maximum rebate available and the income abatement threshold); the level of rates charged by councils; the uptake of the Scheme; and the incomes of residential ratepayers. Of these, only the Schemes key settings are within the Governments control. . Applicants apply for a rebate directly to their council and, if successful, either havetheir rebate applied to their rates account or are paid a cash refund if their rates havebeen paid in full. The Department of Internal Affairs then reimburses the council. . Eligible applicants include: residents who are ratepayers for the property to which the rebate is beingclaimed; and residents who own a nonseparately rated unit in a retirement village, and who contribute to the outgoings of the retirement village. . Based on the rates proposed to take effect f rom July , the level of rebate an eligible applicant receives is determined by the following: the applicant must pay the first of the rates on the property; the potential rebate is twothirds of the remaining rates, up to the maximumamount; from July , if the applicant and the applicants partner, andor joint home owner living at the property, have income in excess of , gross per annum, the rebate is reduced by for every of income above that amount (the abatement threshold); for every dependant, the abatement threshold increases by ; and from July , the rebate will be capped at a maximum of . . The applicants income used in the assessment is that earned from the previous tax year. For example, a person applying for a rebate in the year from July June is assessed on their income for the financial year ending March . . The Department of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua Appendix B: Talking points for the Cabinet Legislation Committee meeting on June I have agreed to adjust key settings of the Rates Rebate Scheme and seek approval for an Order in Council to amend the Rates Rebate Act . The Scheme assists lowincome ratepayers Ratepayers apply to their council for the rebate. Councils then process the applications and are reimbursed by the Department of Internal Affairs. In Cabinet agreed that regular adjustments to the Rates Rebate Act must be made to account for inflation. The proposed adjustments reflect the . per cent upward movement in the All Groups Index of the Consumer Price Index in the calendar year. The maximum rebate available will increase from to . The income abatement threshold will increase from , to ,. The proposed adjustments will take effect from July . The Scheme is not the only form of accommodation support The Rates Rebate Scheme is one of a suite of policy instruments designed to support households to meet their living costs. Other cost of living subsidies (such as the Accommodation Supplement) and adjustments to income support remain more effective at insulating lowincome ratepayers from rate rises than the Rate Rebate Scheme. These mechanisms are also more effective at addressing equity concerns between renters and homeowners. I recommend that Cabinet agrees to adjust the key settings of the Rates Rebate Act As I have noted, the Rates Rebate Scheme assists thousands of lowincome ratepayers to meet their living costs. Keeping the key settings at current levels will have negative effects on the value of the rebate to its recipients: o If the maximum rebate and income threshold remain static, inflation will diminish the value of the rebate to recipients. o If adjustments are not made every year, fewer people will meet the income threshold to qualify for the rebate. This will further diminish the intended impact of the Scheme for lowincome households. o After a period of nonadjustment, the cost of restoring the key settings to a desirable level could be considerable. Proceeding with the adjustments will also lower the risk of negative public reactions, particularly from senior citizen interest groups such as Age Concern and Grey Power. Changes to the Rating of Whenua Mori . The Local Government (Rating of Whenua Mori) Amendment Bill (the Bill) is currently progressing through Parliament. If enacted, one of the provisions of the Bill allowslocal authorities to establish separate rating accounts for individual homeowners, in circumstances where there are multiple houses on a single block of Mori land. If the houses are chosen to be rated individually, the occupant of the house becomes responsible for the rates on the house. This allows these ratepayers to apply for the Scheme, which they previously did not have access to. . There is no comprehensive dataset on the amount of housing on Mori land. This means the Department cannot be certain about the number of additional claims on the rates rebate scheme. However, the Department considers that the number ofclaims resulting from the Bill is unlikely to have a material impact on the appropriation. The Department of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua RESPONDING TO QUESTIONS What are the financial implications on the appropriation In , the Scheme is estimated to cost . million. This estimate is above the appropriation of . million for the financial year . It is difficult to predict the impact that the COVID lockdown and recovery period will have on the uptake of the Scheme, so the Department of Internal Affairs will monitor the appropriation through . This estimate includes those now eligible through the Rating of Whenua Mori legislative change . The Department of Internal Affairs appropriation for the Scheme has historically been underspent but is nearing its limit. The uptake will be closely monitored, and remedial action will be taken if necessary. Any increased uptake of the Scheme will be accounted for in the October or March baseline updates. How will people find out about the adjustments to the Scheme The adjustments to the key settings will be in the New Zealand Gazette. I intend to issue a media release. The Department of Internal Affairs will inform councils and key interest groups, such as Grey Power and Age Concern, of the adjustments to the Scheme. Details of the adjustments will also be shown on the Departments Rates Rebate webpage. Why not adjust the Scheme by using the average wage (as with Superannuation) rather than CPI If I were to adjust the Scheme using the average wage we would need to review the Scheme at a more strategic level. This would need to be a comprehensive review in the context of other subsidies and supplements that are currently available to lowincome households. This could not be completed in time for an adjustment to the Scheme to take effect on July . Adjusting the Scheme with average wage growth would also likely exceed the current appropriation in . What impacts will the Future for Local Government review have on the Scheme The review is wideranging in scope and could consider rates affordability, as well as specific mechanisms for supporting lowincome households . Whilst this is ongoing, maintenance of the Scheme as is proposed in this paper is still prudent . What impacts will the three waters reform have on the Scheme At this stage, no changes are required to the Scheme due to the reform programme. I will receive further advice next year in advance of any financing proposals that could impact the Scheme. INCONFIDENCE Page of Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government

Germany passed the Network Enforcement Act (NetzDG) in June , which makes commercial social networks with at least two million users, liable for hate speech that violates German law. The NetzDG Act followed rampant online hate speech during the European migrant crisis, which was linked to hate crimes in the physical world. The German Government initially sought to encourage social media companies t o voluntarily apply German hate speech laws on their platforms. However, the German Government ultimately determined that the voluntary efforts of social media companies were inadequate, and sanctions were needed to enforce platforms compliance with German hate speech laws. . Online platforms in scope must set up userfriendly complaint mechanisms to report illegal hate speech. Online platforms face significant fines if they do not remove manifestly illegal content within twentyfour hours of notice and other illegal content with a week of notice. . NetzDG has drawn criticism for its potential to stifle free speech, including from the former United Nations Special Rapporteur on the Promotion and Protection of the Right to Freedom of Opinion and Expression. The main criticism is that it bestows significant control on private companies over decisions affecting free speech as companies must make determinations over what is illegal content without law enforcement. This has led to concern that NetzDG will lead to excessive removal of

Background When individuals apply for public services from New Zealand government agencies, they are frequently asked to provide evidence of their identity or other aspects of their entitlement to the public services. The relevant evidence may be supplied in the form of physical documentation (e.g. a birth certificate), but in a number of cases agencies have set up authorised arrangements to permit specific information to be shared agency to agency. These arrangements are largely information matching agreements, and the limitations of th ese instrument s have led to an environment with many agreements that are narrow, expensive to administer and difficult to adjust in response to changing needs . DIA is leading the development of a small number of AISAs which are intended to replace the existing authorised arrangements and allow new purposes to better meet the needs of individuals and Partner agencies. This AISA covers the sharing of Personal Information with Partner s for the purposes of providing Customer Nominated Services. Customer Nominated Services are public services provided by the parties that individuals wish to utilise. The parties do not require the individuals information until the individual has initiated access to the public service. Studylink is an example of a Customer Nominated Service because eligible individuals are able to apply for a student loan, but uptake of the public service is not compulsory. The individual does not always need to consent to all the information sharing as some sharing is mandated or permitted by legisl ation , and will therefore occur by virtue of a n individual s decision to utilise a particular public service. Customer Nominated Services AISA PUBLIC LY AVAILABLE of . Objectives and p urpose s of this Agreement .. Objectives The objectives of this Agreement are to: a) gain customer service efficiencies and reduce the compliance load for individuals associated with provision of Personal Information through facilitating increased collaboration between parties ; b) verify aspects of an individuals identity or entitlement of a n individual applying for or receiving public services ; c) enable updating of records when an individuals circumstances change ; d) enable the prevention, detection, investigation and prosecution of offences, and the conduct of civil proceedings including judicial review; and e) apply Privacy by Design princi ples to the development and operation of the information sharing . .. Purpose s The purpose s of this information shar ing are to: a) notify an individual of public services they may be eligible to access ; b) verify an individuals identity; c) ensur e that an individual is not required to provide to a party identity or Life Event records that DIA or the Registrar General already holds , when applying for or utilising public services ; d) ensure eligibility and entitlement requirements are met when an individual is applying for or receiving public services; e) enable cleansing and updating of records upon the change in circumstances of an individual ; f) enable parties to provide additional protection to the Personal Information shared by the Registrar General where the individual has an active NonDisclosure Direction ; and g) enable the prevention, detection, investigation and prosecution of offences, and the conduct of civil proceedings , including judicial review . . Exemptions to information privacy principles For the purposes of this Agreement , Information Privacy Principles (IPPs) , and which are set out in Section of the Privacy Act are exempted (by the Order in Council) as follows: IPP : Source of Personal Information It is not a breach of information privacy principle for a party to collect Personal Information from , or within, a party in accordance with this Agreement and for one or more of the purposes specified in Clause .. IPP : Limits on the Use of Personal Information It is not a breach of information privacy principle for Personal Information collected by , or within, a party to be utilised in accordance with this Agreement and for one or more of the purposes specified in Clauses . Customer Nominated Services AISA PUBLIC LY AVAILABLE of IPP : Li mits on Disclosure of Personal Information It is not a breach of information privacy principle for a party to disclose Personal Information to a party , or within, a party in accordance with this Agreement and for one or more of the purposes specified in Clause .. It is also not a breach of information privacy principle for a party to disclose Personal Information to a party as part of making a request for Personal Information . . The public s ervices f acilitate d The public services that this Agreement is intended to facilitate are the: (a) accurate and efficient assessment of eligibility for and entitlement to receive public services that an individual appl ies for or decide s to utilise ; (b) accurate and efficient delivery of public services that an individual appl ies for or decide s to utilise ; and (c) the prevention, detection, investigation and prosecution of offences, and the conduct of civil proceedings including judicial review. . Information that is not about an identifiable individual will not be shared under this Agreement . Personal Information may only be shared under this Agreement where DIA the Registrar General is either the providing or receiving party. Current council consultation and decisionmaking requirements prevent councils from responding quickly to changing circumstances. Current legislation is out of and what should be simple processes are instead taking up councils time and reducing operating efficiency. Council reporting is not consistent across groups of activities and not done in a way that drives public accountability and easy assessmen t of council performance. Councils struggle to make local regulations and enforce them effectively with tools such as infringement fees. Councils are failing to generate efficiency gains that can be achieved through shared services. Council expenditure using rates revenue has caused excessive increases to costs on ratepayers. Councils struggle to recover costs effectively to ease rates burdens and are not providing sufficient information for cases where costs recovery would not be viable. Insurance risk financing is impacting ratepayers. Council borrowing limits are constrain ing on highgrowth councils. This instead encourages funding through rates revenue increases. There is a disconnect between elected members and council staff regarding access to information requirements and the ability for members to effectively represent their constituents. Elected members and local communities may have participation and engagemen t with council processes impacted by the conduct of council business inside business hours. Refocus the purpose of local government to guide council decision making, distinguish between the roles of central governme nt, local governmen t and the private sector, and help manage community expectations of core council services. Implemen t options to enable councils to adapt quickly to changing circumstances, and to save time and money while balancing democratic principles. Update local governmen t processes and modernise the law. Establish effective performance reporting and drive council accountability for communities. Provide councils with appropriate, modern tools for making and enforcing local regulations effectively. Consideration of greater delegation for councils to set infringement fees. Improve local government financial sustainability and consider options for balancing efficiency gains with local authorities over service levels and costs. Limit council expenditure on nicetohaves and consider options to protect ratepayers from excessive rates increases Remove legal constraints on cost recovery for councils (where fees have been set in statute) and require counci ls to demonstrate how they are recovering costs for certain activities, thereby supporting councils to ease the rates burden. Improve risk management practices (including approaches to insurance) and support a collective approach to insurance to minimise its impact on rates. Increase borrowing limits for highgrowth councils and improve the range of council funding tools beyond rates, thereby improving council activity funding and helping highgrowth councils to invest appropria tely. Review access to information for elected members , codes of conduct, conflicts of interest. Consider options to balance freedom of expression with the orderly conduct of council business and allowing councillors to effectively represent local communities. Ensure chief executives are aware of other commitments that elected members have on their time when considering council business and scheduling meetings. A return to this reflects the objective of refocusing councils to deliver the basics well and costeffectively. Some language changes are proposed to modernise the legislation and to connect with other Governmen t priorities. Amendmen ts to the Local Government Act , whether to the purpose statement or reinstated core services, would not change the responsibilities of local authorities under other legislation. Purpose statement I propose amending section (b) of the Local Governmen t Act so the new purpose of local government is, to meet the current and future needs of communi ties for goodquality local infrastructure, public services, and performance of regulatory functions in a way that is most costeffective for households and businesses , therefore supporting local economic growth and developme nt. The underlined explicit reference to the role of local authorities in stimulating their local economies is a new addition to the purpose statement that is consistent with expectations of councils in the Regional Deals and Going for Housing Growth programmes. The Ministers preferred option is that the poll provisions prior to the changes should be restored, and electors should have the option to petition councils to hold a binding poll on future Mori ward decisions by councils . Limitations affecting the analysis of transitional arrangements for holding binding polls on Mori wards established since The Minister of Local Government has decided to consider the following four options relating to councils that have established a Mori ward without a poll since the legislative amendments, and have not chosen to rescind their decision or disestablish their Mori wards : All councils that established or resolved to establish Mori wards since without a poll must e ither: hold a poll in early , with the results of the poll to apply from the elections (with variation in how resulting representation reviews are undertaken) ; hold a poll in early if a valid petition is received from electors in late with the results of any polls taking effect at the local elections (with variation in how resulting representation decisions are undertaken) ; hold a poll at the local elections, with the results of the poll to apply from the local elections; or hold a poll at the local elections , if a valid petition is received from electors in early . The results of the poll will apply from the elections. Options outside of the four outlined above have not been considered . The Ministers preferred option is for affected councils to hold a binding poll in late with the results of the poll to apply from the local elections. The Ministry will continue to support intervention practitioners to: register as health practitioners permitted to practise within a relevant scope of practice under the Health Practitioners Competence Assurance Act , or register with or be endorsed by DAPAANZ as having demonstrated the relevant specific competencies, or be equivalently registered with another relevant health professional body and hold at least six months postqualification experience as an addiction practitioner. A key focus is to align the gambling harm intervention workforce with the wider addiction workforce. Research shows that alcohol and other drug problems are often an issue for those experiencing harm from gambling. Adopting workforce standards with comparable standards across the broader addiction workforce will provide greater career mobility and pathways and help build a more resilient and sustainable workforce. As noted in the discussion of public health, Mori, Pacific and Asian stakeholders and service provider submissions noted the need for more effective workforce training, includin g training in cultural competence and the importance of understanding the different worldviews of potential clients. The Ministry will also explore appropriate level of training for kaiwhina and peer support workers (but not at DAPAANZ level). . Research and evaluation There is a consensus among stakeholders that we need more actionoriented research and evaluations and less of more of the same research. Section of the Act specifies that the strategy must include independent scientific research associated with gambling, including (for example) longitudinal research on the social and economic impacts of gambling, particularly the impacts on different cultural groups. It must also include evaluation. As well as addressing these requirements, the research and evaluation proposals below were informed by a review of the Ministrys information needs for research to inform policy and operational decisionmaking, learn from past research commissioning experience and align the research delivery with the general government policy direction for governmentfunded research services and consultation with the gambling sector. Adverse Actions Section Q of the Privacy Act requires parties to provide written notice to individuals before any Adverse Action is taken against them on the basis of Personal Information shared under an information sharing agreement, and give those individuals working days to dispute the information received. Parties will dispense with the notice requirements under sectio n Q if they have reasonable grounds to suspect a n offence has been committed, is being committed or will be committed and that the Personal Information is relevant to the prevention, detection, investigation or the prosecution of the offence , where advan ce notification to a suspect would be likely to prejudice the investigation or prosecution of an alleged offender or offence . Details of expected Adverse Action s as a result of information being shared under this Agreement are specified in the relevant Schedules. . Overview of operational processes The first time information is shared with each par ty relating to an individual , DIA the Registrar Gene ral will automatically allocate the individual a unique Partner Specific Customer Identifier (PSCID) in relation to the requesting party . The PSCID will be used going forwards by the parties when conversing about the identified individual with that party. The operational processes associated with this Agreement will vary depending on the transfer mechanism utilised. Possible transfer options , depending on the circumstance, are likely to include: API based transfer ; Direct system access ; Email ; Paper based transfer ; and Bulk transfer . As a first step of information sharing under this Agreement , a one off bulk exchange of information collected prior may occur to allow the receiving party to do a one off update of their records for one or more of the purposes specified in Clauses . The operational procedures detail the operational processes for providing and receiving information for each party. . Safeguards to protect privacy .. Staff The following safeguards exist to protect the privacy of individuals and ensure that any interference with their privacy is minimised: a) All parties to this Agreement , including their staff , will abide by the Public Sector Standards of Integrity and Conduct. b) The staff of all parties to this Agreement performing the services set out in this Agreement will hold all necessary statutory powers and delegations required for the provision of those services , and will comply with relevant operational policy and procedures. .. The Rates Rebate Scheme provides support to lowincome owner occupiers . The current Rates Rebate Scheme provides support to lo income owner occupiers. Just over , households cur rently receive a rates rebate, about percent of which are recipients of New Zealand Superannuation. The level of subsidy available to a household depends on both their income and their rates bill. When water charges are split out from rates bills, some recipients of a rates rebate would receive a lower rebate, even though their total expenses (rates and water) may not have changed. . The Department of Internal Affairs estimates that about a third of the current recipients of rates rebates (, households) could be affected by the splitting off of water bills. They would be the higher income recipients of rates rebates (those with a househo ld income greater than about , per annum). The Departments analysis suggests that eligible households with a single person on superannuation would be unaffected, but that eligible households with couples on superannuation will fall into the affected group. . I propose to deal with this by amending the Rates Rebate Act to include water bills as part of the definition of rates. This would have the advantage of leaving current beneficiaries of the Scheme no worse off than they would have been without the three waters reforms. It would however create an additional administrative burden on the territorial authorities, who currently administer the Scheme, as they would have to assess water charges as well as rates bills. Amending the Rates Rebate Act will have a very small fiscal impact for the Crown, as Auckland Council currently tops up rebates as if Watercare bills were a rate. After the reforms, the Crown would need to meet the additional cost of topping up the rebates for Aucklanders, at a cost of around , per year. This amount is less than the underspend in the current appropriation, but the Treasury has advised that this is a discretionary policy decision and so the costs will need to be met from the between Budget contingency. . I am also proposing to enable the water services entities to share billing information directly with territorial authorities, where the recipient of the bill has applied for a rates rebate. This would enable a streamlined application process for beneficiaries of the scheme

RSG aspires to be a place where: The publics confidence in DIA as a trustworthy government agency grows even stronger, as DIA will be associated with successful regulatory outcomes Government can home any regulatory system with confidence that it will stay on a pathway to growing effectiveness, capability and reliability DIAs kaimahi will flourish in the regulatory craft and go on to grow the capabilities of DIA and other regulatory agencies Whats not changing Some things in the strategy are not new. The core objectives of the strategic journey embarked upon in remain relevant: System leadership lifting the focus up and out Engaging, leading and influencing the wider ecosystems that our system groups are part of Establishing relationships and partnerships; taking opportunities to collaborate or leveraging connectionsThe how The strategy will enable this by: Ensuring each system is empowered and supported to be effective Organisational design that maximises the benefit of centralised functions, and distributes others to enable innovation and agility Establishing communities of practice and practice leadership Turning data, evidence and information into insights using robust ICT platforms Getting things done Embedding robust governance mechanisms; improving project management and business change Improving systems and processes; effective decisionmaking; performance evaluation The RSG strategy builds on these and describes whats important to get right in the next few years to be better system regulators. The Trust Framework Authority
The Trust Framework Authority administers the accreditation process for providers of digital identity services.
The Trust Framework Authority is a separate body function within the Department of Internal Affairs.
The Trust Framework Authority is the regulator for accredited digital identity services, ensuring accredited providers continue to meet the requirements for accreditation, responding to complaints, investigating noncompliance, and making sure New Zealands digital identity environment is working as it should.
The Trust Framework Authority is the regulator of accredited digital identity services in Aotearoa. It is a separate statutory function within the Department of Internal Affairs.
The Trust Framework Authority is the regulator of accredited digital identity services.

The Trust Framework Rules are split into several categories. To become accredited, digital identity service providers must meet the relevant rules for the service(s) they offer. This can be more than one category of rules depending on what that service is.
The Trust Framework Rules set out the operational requirements for how accredited services are provided, in order to have a safe and trusted digital identity environment. They define how people and organisations must work together to consent to share or validate a users information.

The Trust Framework does not enable Te Ao Mori approaches to identity Mori do not participate equitably in the digital identity ecosystem. Mori perspectives and approach es to identity are not enabled by the digital identity ecosystem. The digital identity ecosystem is not developed and maintained in partnership with Mori. Mori are not supported in leadership and decision making roles to ensure Mori perspectives about data are embedded in the trusted digital identity ecosystem . Undermines the governments commitments to digital inclusion Discourages Mori participation in digital identity and limits the potential benefits of digital identity for Mori communities It is necessary to encourage Mori participation and better understand the opportunities for M ori in implementing the Trust Framework. Government assumes the risk. To mitigate this the principles of the Trust Framework, which will be enshrined in the Trust Framework Bill , will include inclusion and Enabling Te Ao Mori approaches to identity . Additionally, there will also be a Te Ao Mori government representative on the governance board of the Trust Framework, with the ability to coopt nonvoting members and appoint an Advisory Board . The mitigation measures will ensure this is a low probability risk.
The Trust Framework promotes growth in digital identity services, which has the unintended consequence of exacerbating the digital divide and creates barriers for disadvantaged groups (e.g. the elderly, refugees). Discourage s participation Undermines th e governments commitments to digital inclusion The potential benefits of the Trust Framework remain unrealised for everyone in society
The Trust Framework promotes growth in digital identity services, which has the unintended consequence of exacerbating the digital divide and creates barriers for disadvantaged groups Discourage s participation Undermines th e governments commitments to digital inclusion The potential benefits of the Trust Framework remain People from all communities deserve the opportunity to participate in the digital identity ecosystem Both government and private sector assume this risk. The government will mitigate this risk by ensuring the principle of inclusion (below) will be enshrined in the Trust Framework Bill as one of the guiding principles for the Trust Framework and trusted digital identity e cosystem. Inclusive Everyone has the right to participate in the digital identity ecosystem. This risk will remain a realistic po ssibility . The Framework will not raise any regulatory barriers to inclusion but while it will set the standards that private sector entities will adhere to, it will be up to private sector entities to develop, invest in and offer digital identity services . The Trust Framework will enable users and relying parties to reduce the time and cost associated with a multitude of online and face toface transactions that require verification of identity and other personal information. Examples include opening new bank accounts; accessi ng and providing health services; completing property transactions; accessing N ew Zealand superannuation or other government services; completing an employee recruitment and appointment process; or verifying proof of age to enable access to age restricted products and services such as alcohol or ent ry to adult establishments such as , for example, a night club . The introduction of the Trust Framework aims to bring a stronger sense of security and increase trust and confidence in the use of d igital identity services within New Zealand. In summary, t he anticipated benefits of the Trust Framework include: enabling user controlled access to, and sharing of, personal information ; minimising identity theft and privacy breaches ; improving informatio n sharing efficiency ; reducing unnecessary sharing of information ; and improving access to online and face toface services that require the provision of identity and other personal information .

The Working Group comprised members, including representatives of the transgender and intersex community as well as medical and legal experts with experience in transgender issues. Kate Scarlet, a lawyer with substantial expertise in the process for changing registered sex, chaired the Working Group. Other members were Jack Byrne, Mani Mitchell, Jeannie Oliphant, Fleur Fitzsimons and Ahi WiHongi. In October Georgina Beyer resigned as a member of the Working Group for personal reasons.
The Working Group delivered their report in early . The Government response to the recommendations is now available and can be found below. Previously, a redacted version of the Working Groups report was publicly available. See below for the full version of the Working Groups report and recommendations.
The Working Group held its first meeting on November and will report back in February .
The Working Group identified practical improvements within the current system and within legislation. Though it did not consider changes to the law, the Working Group was clear that the Births, Deaths, Marriages and Relationships Act () should change to best serve the people who wish to change the sex recorded on their birth certificate.
The Working Group was established to engage people with lived experience of the current process to change registered sex on a birth certificate. Working Group members are representatives of the transgender and intersex community, and people with professional expertise relevant to the current process.
The Working Group was formed by the previous Minister of Internal Affairs Hon Tracey Martin to improve the Family Court process for changing registered sex on a birth certificate. In , the Working Group provided the Minister of Internal Affairs with a report and recommendations on practical improvements to the Family Court process to change sex information on birth certificates.
The Working Groups report and the Government response are now available ( April )
The Working Groups recommendations are wellplaced to make it easier for people to change the sex on their birth certificate. In some cases, the solutions recommended by the Working Group presented funding or regulatory challenges. In these cases, agencies have suggested alternative ways of addressing the core issue. Some recommendations cannot be implemented right now for capacity, equity or resourcing reasons.

The business units within the Department that work in relevant areas and are expected to use the information sharing provisions are Births, Deaths and Marriages (BDM) and the Digital Child Exploitation Team (DCET). The cafe trial had lower recall rates than all the other trials, on investigation there were three cardholders that were the main contributors to these poor results. One cardholder (wearing card IDs and ) was seated alone at a table with their back to a table of three other cardholders. This cardholder was within two metres of the table at all times, met the intensity threshold being used for ground truth (intensity), but presented low transmission risk and the card had poor RSSI values which were filtered out with the basic card algorithm. This effect could have been reduced if only one card had been used per participant and instead involved a greater number of participants in the same scenario. With multiple cards there are more people occupying a space that can otherwise only physically be occupied by one. An additional participant at the same table in this scenario would have had a lower intensity score with respect to the table next to them. Also, if a higher intensity rating had been used for analysis (intensity ) the backturned participant would not have been counted as a contact. Unfortunately, the contact event scores (intensity ) were not accurate because actual contact events were often fleeting and were not consistently rated.

About the Film and Video Labelling Body The FVLB is an incorporated society and a registered charity comprised of industry representatives. FVLB fees: http:www.fvlb.org.nznzpagesforms.html.Part I New Zealands classification system New Zealands classification system exists to support people to make informed choices about the media content they view and to minimise the availability of harmful material. New Zealands current classification system is set out in the two pieces of legislation below: The Classification Act regulates how games, films and other publications are classified. The Classification Act seeks to prevent harm to the public by restricting the availability of harmful material based on the extent, manner and degree of sex, horror, crime, cruelty and violence in a manner consistent with the right to freedom of expression. The application of the Classification Act that is most familiar to the public are the rating labels such as G, PG, M, R, R for DVDs, video games, and theatre releases. These ratings and classifications are issued under the Classification Act by the Film and Video Labelling Body (FVLB) and OFLC. The Broadcasting Act, requires classification of freetoair and pay television and creates a system of broadcasting standards. There are areas specified in the Broadcasting Act from which standards have been developed and people can complain to a broadcaster if they think these standards have been breached. The Broadcasting Act is familiar to the public through the G, PG and AO labels for freetoair and G, PG, M and for pay television. The options in this consultation only affect the Classification Act and the Regulations issued under the Classification Act. About the Office of Film and Literature Classification OFLC is responsible for regulating the classification framework set out in the Classification Act. Under the Classification Act OFLC: manages restricted content (classified as R, R, R, R or objectionable) and produces classifications to inform consumer choices; Review of options for funding the classification framework Consultation documentAbout the Review The Government is reviewing options for funding the classification system in two stages. This consultation is Stage of the Review. Stage of the Review is developing and implementing a new charging regime. A mixed funding model of annual Government funding and usercharges currently financially supports OFLC and the classification framework provided for by the Classification Act. This model was established in . Since then, there have been significant changes in the media content environment. The funding model is being revisited to assess if there is a more effective way of funding classification activities than the status quo. Funding levels for the classification framework are also being considered as part of the Review. Funding levels also need to be set for OFLCs new CVoD activities. Objectives The Reviews objective is to identify and implement a funding model that financially supports OFLC to enable New Zealanders to make informed viewing choices and minimise the availability of harmful media content. Scope The Reviews focus is on OFLCs charges for the classification of media content for commercial purposes and its new activities related to CVoD content. Also in scope are urgent, special, reduced fees and waivers for charitable organisations and individuals. The Review is not seeking to recover the costs of items submitted by government agencies for classification.Important terms used in this document Throughout this document, we draw a distinction between the two main categories of classification: Commercial classifications and Crown classifications. Commercial classifications items submitted for classification under Section of the Classification Act. Broadly speaking, these are mainstream commercial products distributed by commercial distributors or screened at film festivals. Crown classifications items submitted by government agencies under Sections and of the Classification Act for classification. These are typically not mainstream commercial products; many are privately owned such as images on computers. The current levels of people presenting for services are substantively lower than expected, representing only percent of the number estimated to be affected by moderate to severe gambling harm. Early intervention It is apparent that a number of New Zealanders who would benefit from gambling harm intervention are not seeking help . Likely causes for this (identified in submissions to this consultation from health and service providers) are the high level of stigma associated with gambling harm and societal attitudes towards gambling, as well as cultural, language and other barriers. While it is necessary to address the needs of those who have already developed a serious gambling problem and who need specialist help, it is clear that earlier preventionfocused interventions could help individuals and their families , whnau and communities to avoid developing harmful gambling behaviours and associated higher risks of harm. This approach aligns closely with public health programmes in the mental health and addictions areas of alcohol, tobacco and drug use, and family , whnau and partner violence prevention. The data from any single trial was too small to effectively train a model, so summarised data from all card contacts was collected together into a single file containing all card contacts. The summarised data was one line per card contact containing: total contact duration, maximum RSSI, mean RSSI, maximum and mean duration of nonreidentified events (i.e. at most minutes as per card ID rotation), maximum and mean intensityduration, a count of the number of card advertisements seen, and a boolean value indicating whether the contact was a close contact as identified from our ground truth. A Random Forest model (using base estimators) was evaluated using tentimes tenfold crossvalidation. During crossvalidation the dataset was randomly split into ten equallysized subsets (folds), and the model trained using nine folds and tested using the remaining heldout fold. This was repeated for every fold. The whole process was then repeated ten times ( folds evaluated) so that results were not adversely affected by a particular random selection of folds.

The dynamics of adoption and compliant usage are critically important to understand. A population level deployment of a symptom checker increases in usefulness proportionately with usage and can quickly reach a sample size that is useful. Conversely, a contact tracing app depends on extremely high levels of adoption because everyone needs the app for it to work it is subject to a network effect and modest levels of adoption render it useless.
