The economic regulator would have a role in implementing legislated pricing principles and regulations . The economic regulator would be able to issue guidance, input methodologies, andor determinations to the water services entities on how to implement the pr icing principles and any regulations. The choice of instrument(s) would be at the economic regulators discretion. The regulator could also cover off issues such as appropriate transitional measures, if the water services entity is not immediately able to fully implement the principle or regulations. Determinations and guidance could also deal with relatively rare situations where there may be tensions or trade offs between the principles. . I am also proposing to give the economic regulator the ability to is sue guidance, input methodologies, andor determinations on other pricing matters not covered by principles or regulations, so long as this is consistent with the overall statutory scheme and contributes to the purpose of economic regulation. This would gi ve the economic regulator a flexible suite of tools for effectively regulating water services entities. . As outlined above, the economic regulator would also have the power to alter tariffs if it determined that a water services entity was not implementing the pricing principles or regulations appropriately. Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government IN CONFIDENCE Page of Geographic averaging of prices can contribute to affordability at a community level . In the October Cabinet paper, a possible pricing outcome of cost sharing was set out, with the example of geographic averaging of prices. A key driver of the reforms is to address affordability issues, particularly for customers in smaller communities. The overall reform process will improve affordability by reducing costs through the efficiency gains that will be realised from service aggregation, improved financing, and improved incentives from independent governance and economic regulation. Entities can also use geographically averaged pricing to smooth and share costs across communities, thereby contributing to more affordable services for all. . Geographic averaging can occur at a few different levels: . Within a network: this is generally used by electricity distribution companies for their local networks. . Within a territorial authority district: some territorial authorities will already have implemented geographical averaging at this le vel for ease of administration and to promote greater pricing transparency. Averaging within a district may require averaging across different networks and between urban and rural communities. . Within the service area of a water services entity: this has th e advantage of improving affordability for smaller communities. Through consultation, some territorial authorities have come out strongly against this level of geographic averaging because it represents a transfer between territorial authorities with diffe rent historic approaches to three waters infrastructure investments. Rural territorial authorities generally support it and the sector is generally expecting this level of geographic averaging. . Geographic averaging would not occur at a national level as th is would require financial transfers between water services entities. . The legislation would enable water services entities, in consultation with their regional representative groups, to make decisions about geographic averaging (consistent with any Government policy statement). The economic regulator would not be able to override geographic averaging but would be able to provide guidance on its implementation. . There would be some exceptions to geographic averaging, including: . where communities have sought a higher level of service than is provided elsewhere in the water services area, or where communities receive a lower level of service than what is generally provided in the water services area; . new growth areas (where there i s a levy in place under the Infrastructure Funding and Financing Act , discussed with growth charging from paragraph below); . Water infrastructure contributions (growth charges, discussed from paragraph below); and Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government IN CONFIDENCE Page of . failing drinking water supplies (water services entities will have a duty to ensure communities have access to drinking water if existing suppliers are facing significant problems). To avoid this being gamed by private suppliers, they should not automati cally receive geographically averaged prices if the water services entity steps in and provides a drinking water supply on either a temporary or permanent basis. . I also propose that the Government policy statement may be used, if considered necessary, to provide for geographic averaging of prices. This could only require geographic averaging for residential customers and only for drinking and wastewater services. T he exceptions set out above would also apply. The proposed pricing formula for stormwater charging (set out from paragraph below) already enables geographic averaging. It is unlikely to be practical to begin any form of p rice harmonisation before . For this reason, the Government policy statement will not be able to provide any direction on geographic price averaging before . . Achieving geographic averaging would first require harmonising tariff structures, as far as possible, and then harmonising the actual price levels within those structures. There will need to be a long lead in time to achieve geographic averaging without causing significant price increases in some locations. The Government policy statement would have the flexibility to set out the overall requirement for geographic averaging, as well as detail on the transition to that goal. This would enable price changes to be smoothed over time and meet the legislated pricing principles. Part D: Transition and removal of cross subsidies . Under provisions already contained in the Water Services Entities Bill, the entities will present a funding and pricing plan to the entitys regional representative group at least once in every three year period. The plan must cover the entitys intended a pproach to pricing its services and charging consumers. The water services entity also must engage with consumers and communities on the proposals in the plan. . Several inputs will inform the funding and pricing plan. These include: . the regional representative groups statement of strategic and performance expectations; . the entitys asset management plan, and their capital structure and borrowing costs; . any constraints from economic regulation; . legislative pricing principles and regulations (set o ut further from paragraph below); . requirements and guidance from the economic regulator on price setting (set out further from paragraph below); . any directions from the Government policy statement. Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government IN CONFIDENCE Page of Water services entities are likely to have a variety of charges set out in a tariff list . I propose that all water services entity charges will be set out annually with the publication of a detailed tariff list. The tariff list would be based on the funding and pricing plan. The tarif f list is likely to cover the following services: . Water supply charges: these could vary with the type of service (for example, ondemand urban water supply vs. rural trickle feed), the type of water (drinking water or not), and the capacity of the connection. They may also be a mixture of fixed and volumetric charges. The use of volumetricvariable charges will not be mandated. . Wastewater charges: these could also be a mixture of fixed and volumetric (or assessedproxy) charges, that are likely to vary with the capacity of the connection. The use of volumetric charges will not be mandated. . Trade waste charges: more detailed information on trade waste is set out in the companion paper Policy proposals f or three waters service delivery legislative settings. . Stormwater charges: the approach to stormwater charges is set out in more detail from paragraph below. . Growth charges: the approach to growth charges is set out in more detail from paragraph below. . Connection charges and other miscellaneous charges. . Some charges and prices may be set by reference to hourly rates. Other charges may be sufficiently unusual or customised that they are not on the tariff list. . The economic regulator would have the power to direct the water services entity to directly alter the funding and pricing plan or the tariff list (without any consultation requirements) if the economic regulator determined that the plan or tariff lis t was inconsistent with the pricing principles and regulations, or any other constraints set by the regulator. The economic regulator could take this action on its own initiative or based on a complaint.

The proximity trial (proximity) was a distancesignalstrength test to capture the signal strength of the cards at different distances with different placements of the cards. The floor of an empty office was marked with lines at onemetre intervals. Participants wore five cards: on a lanyard around their neck, on a clip at their hip, on a clip on their chest pocket, on a band around their arm, and inside a walletbag that was held at roughly waist height. Each participant stood at either end of the course, walked to the opposite end and back passing each other in the middle. The participants then stood at their ends for two minutes, before one taking a step towards the other, waiting two minutes, then the other stepping forward. Over the twenty minutes they progressed towards each other in two minuteone metre intervals before meeting in the middle (where they stood together for two minutes).

Proactively Released by the Department of Internal Affairs FURTHER WORK A valuable next step for production testing is to run a larger field trial in a more open environment. A larger open trial would provide a more realistic context for evaluation of false positive rates: in many of the closed trials participants were close contacts, or in close proximity (i.e. casual contacts) with almost every other participant so false positives detected by the card were actually realworld near misses. The main challenge with running a large open trial is the accurate collection of ground truth (such that the closed or scripted trials allow), which exponentially increases in time to collect as the number of participants increases. This could be mitigated by asking participants to complete ground truth for their own interactions, although this may also introduce error into the ground truth data.

The regulations will be developed in two phases. The first set of regulations (covered in this discussion paper ) outline the necessary legal and procedural requirements to initially stand up the regulatory system. They will cover: Accreditation Services: Definition of the types of services that will be subject to accreditation under the Act . Accreditation Process : Accreditation requirements, application assessment criteria, and accreditation duration. Service Levels: Establishment of d ifferent service levels that providers can meet when delivering accredited services. Complaints and Disputes Resolution: The internal complaints and dispute resolution process requirements TF providers need to meet. Recordkeeping : The information to be ret ained by TF providers and the period they are required to retain that information. Reporting : The reporting requirements that will apply to TF providers. We anticipate a second set of regulations will be developed and recommended to the Minister for the Digital Economy and Communications by the TF Board in to address any necessary cost recovery arrangements and other operational matters required to fra me the TF Authoritys administration of the scheme. Th ese regulations may include: Cost Recovery: The establishment of fees for the partial recovery of the TF Authoritys ongoing costs for administering the Trust Framework, including consideration of accre ditation applications or renewals . It is anticipated that the TF Authoritys initial establishment and first two years of operating costs will be met from Crown funding without a contribution from fees . Disputes Resolution Scheme: The establishment of any requirements and criteria that the TF Authority must meet should it want to recommend a disputes resolution scheme , together with any proposed fees to recover costs associated with the provision of complaints and dispute resolution services . The establishme nt of a fees regime will be considered in conjunction with the development of the TF Authoritys complaints and disputes resolution operating model, which will consider the role, if any, of an external dispute resolution service provider. Third Party Asse ssors : Arrangements for the certification of third party assessors to carry out functions relating to the accreditation of providers, including appointment criteria, recordkeeping, and reporting requirements. Other Operational Matters: Any other operationa l matters that the TF Board considers should be established in regulation s to provide greater certainty to both the Authority and regulated parties on compliance requirements and ensure the costeffective management of the regulatory system by the TF Author ity. The regulations, for example, will cover any changes to accreditation renewal requirements and compliance order forms. Proactively released by the Minister for Digitising Government

The security controls limit the effectiveness of any potential oncard algorithm for ranking contacts because the card will only see a contact for at most fifteen minutes before it appears as a new, entirely different, contact ID. Therefore, the best place to rank contacts is once the card data has been downloaded and reidentified back to card serial numbers as serverside processing: once reidentified, contact data can be aggregated to overall contact duration, and assessed for other factors such as timeofday, and number of concurrent contacts. Ranking postdownload also allows for the opportunity to present card data to a human for more nuanced ranking, and for reprioritising automatically if contact definitions or contact tracing requirements change.

The CovidCard could address health and economic inequities. First, the CovidCard does not require any level of technical expertise so it is user friendly for people unfamiliar with technology or smartphones. Second, the CovidCard is not reliant on existing communications infrastructure such as mobile networks or internet connectivity. Third, it is envisioned the CovidCard will come at no cost to individuals, removing the direct financial barrier. Fourth, the CovidCard could enable targeted lockdown (with recursive contact tracing) so there will be a limited economic impact on most people. Fifth, the development, testing and implementation of CovidCard is being conducted in partnership with Mori to ensure the solution is responsive to Mori, is compliant with principles of Mori data sovereignty and uploads Te Tiriti o Waitangi principles. .. Trust, security and privacy The concerns voiced during our consultations were mostly focused on privacy, security and the use of data. We consider it critical to adoption that any solution is designed to ensure limited data is collected, use of data is limited, and that once COVID is no longer a threat, data is deleted.
The CovidCard has the potential to reduce this lagtime from notification of a positive test to the isolation of the firstorder close contacts (tracing delay). Upon notification of a positive test, all firstorder close contacts would be automatically notified of their exposure and instructed to selfisolate while awaiting contact from contact tracers. Though the Ministry of Health target is of known selfreported close contacts to be traced within days, approximately of close contacts are currently traced within days.
The CovidCard system includes both oncard and serverside algorithms. The oncard firmware algorithms must achieve high levels of recall to minimise false negatives and provide additional contextual information to support serverside processing. These algorithms need to also operate within the memory and battery lifetime constraints of the card. Once shipped, card firmware is unable to be .

There are cost pressures associated with implementing the three waters reform programme . In June , Cabinet established the million Three Waters Infrastructure Investment and Service Delivery Reform Programme tagged operating contingency, a portion of which remains unallocated. In Budget , a Transforming Three Waters Service Delive ry for New Zealanders: Transition and Implementation tagged operating contingency of million was established to provide for establishment and transition costs. . Decisions to allocate funding for three waters reform establishment and transition costs were made early in the policy process, prior to the full suite of proposals being developed and their financial implications being understood. This has given rise to several cost pressures. . The October decision to proceed with reform means there is now more certainty regarding the three waters reform work programme through to July and beyond. Following further detailed planning, the Department of Internal Affairs now needs to increase its capacity and capability to deliver and implement the refo rm programme. This includes a significant policy and legislative programme, a large programme of entity establishment and transition activity, ministerial services, and ongoing engagement, communications and public information activity. . Other notable cost pressures relate to key judgements about the best approach to transition, in particular the scope and level of support available to iwiMori and the local government sector to participate meaningfully in the transition process. This is an area where additional investment can help to derisk the transition process and ensure entities are set up with the best chance of success. .

There are significant differences between Scotland and New Zealand geographies Scotland is not a relevant compar ator for New Zealand water services because of fundamental differences betwee n the two countries geography. In water services, geography is impor tant for the cost and quality o f service. Denser urban areas tend to have lower average costs of service . Water services with more dispersed customers have to distribute drinking water, and pump wastewater over longer distances with more pipes, dispersed t reatment infrastructure and higher costs. Aside from some high level discussion of available water sources, and similar populat ions, WICS has not investigated why Scotlands geography is a good predictor of New Zealands water investment needs. The total land area and the geographical distribution of the population s are very different. WICS incorrectly assumes that lower population density in New Zealand implies lower levels of urbani sation . Table . illustrates how New Zealands population is more urbani sed than Scotland s, but despite thi s, New Zealand still has a lower population density. A larger majority of New Zealands population live in urban areas and the urban population is more likely to grow in New Zealand as compared t o Scotland.

There was also a general preference for a government led intervention to bring consistency and trust to the digital identity ecosystem. People fou nd the prospect of having greater control of their personal informati on to be appealing . Focus group participants preferred the government to take the lead on this issue because government was generall y viewed as a reliable actor motivated by public good rather than commercial gain. Industry demonstrated enthusiasm to work with government to develop a digital identity trust framework to set the rules of engagement for the digital identity ecosystem. Public agencies were keen to work together on approaches that could leverage each others insights and capabilities for efficient and consistent consented information sharing to address specific issues they each faced in delivering services to the public . Though t here were some concerns about the prospect of a government intervention . Users of digital identity services expressed concern about the potential for government to implement an intervention which might provide greater access to personal information for surveillance purposes. Mori representatives raised concerns about the establishment of a system that might see g overnment holding more information abou t them, largely due to historic m isuse and abuse of Mori data . Some individuals expressed a strong preference for tighter rules specifically for the private sector, based on an assumption that the private sector would be driven by a desire to monetise data, while public sector agencies would be focused on the delivery of public services. Gerrard Carter Committee Secretary Present: Officials present from: Rt Hon Winston Peters Hon Chris Hipkins (Chair) Hon Andrew Little Hon David Parker Hon Stuart Nash Hon Iain LeesGalloway Hon Jenny Salesa Hon Damien OConnor Hon Tracy Martin Hon Eugenie SageOffice of the Prime Minister Officials Committee for LEG I N C O N F I D E N C E aheeqbzw Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs INCONFIDENCE Office of the Minister of Internal Affairs Chair Cabinet Legislation Committee Films, Videos, and Publications (Urgent Interim Classification of Publications and Prevention of Online Harm) Amendment Bill: Approval for Introduction Proposal . This paper seeks approval for the introduction of the Films, Videos, and Publications (Urgent Interim Classification of Publications and Prevention of Online Harm) Amendment Bill (the Bill). . This paper also seeks policy approval to extend the current liability exemptions for staff and employees of online content hosts and internet service providers (ISPs). Under this proposal they would be exempted from liability when executing their duties, or acting on the instruction of the Government, to remove objectionable content from their respective platforms. Policy . Cabinet agreed to the policy proposals contained in the Bill on December CABMIN refers. The Bill was given a priority of Category (must be passed this year) for the Legislation Programme and Cabinet has indicated an intention to have it introduced into the House by March SWCMIN refers. . Under the Films, Videos, and Publications Classification Act (the Act), it is an offence to make, possess, supply or distribute an objectionable publication (including digital content). Such an offence is based on whether the availability of a given publication or digital content is likely to be injurious to the public good. . The Bill will improve the way we regulate objectionable content, including violent extremist and terrorist content found online. Specifically, the Bill amends the Act to: . criminalise knowingly livestreaming objectionable content; . allow the Chief Censor to make interim classification assessments in relation to publications (both physical as well as online) likely to be found objectionable in urgent situations; . allow takedown notices to be issued to require the removal of objectionable online content; . make online content hosts subject to a civil pecuniary penalty of up to ,, if they do not comply with an issued takedown notice; . ensure safe harbour provisions in the Harmful Digital Communications Act would not apply to objectionable online content; and . enable the establishment of regulations that would allow the Government to implement webfiltering of objectionable content if required. . Under the Bill, the definition of online content hosts has been aligned to that contained in the Harmful Digital Communications Act . The definition covers persons who have control over electronic retrieval systems, such as a website or an online application, but excludes ISPs. Page of aheeqbzw Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs INCONFIDENCE Policy approval for extension of liability exemptions to ISPs and online content hosts . As per Cabinets direction, CABMIN refers, officials undertook targeted engagement on an exposure draft of the Bill with key industry groups including telecommunication companies, ISPs, technology companies and representatives as well as Government agencies. . As a result of this consultation, I seek policy approval to one further proposed change, to extend the current liability exemptions for staff and employees of online content hosts and ISPs. Under this proposal these people would be exempted from liability when executing their duties, or acting on the instruction of the Government, to remove objectionable content from their respective platforms. This ensures a consistent approach to liability exemptions under the Act. . Several industry stakeholders raised concerns about the Act making them criminally liable when identifying, moderating and removing objectionable content, either in the execution of their duties or acting on Government instructions. Possessing, distributing and supplying objectionable material is a criminal offence under the Act. While the Act provides a defence to service providers when handling objectionable material, it only applies in restricted situations. The current defence would not apply where service providers may be required to search for variations of the content and forward links onto other service providers and online content hosts for the purpose of speedily removing objectionable content across different platforms (as was required in the wake of the March terror attacks). Industry stakeholders suggested making it clear that in such situations, staff and employees of ISPs and online content hosts are exempt from liability. . This exemption currently applies to Government and Office of Film and Literature Classification (OFLC) officials tasked with removing objectionable content. The extension of this exemption as proposed, would ensure a consistent approach by exempting service providers and online contents when removing all objectionable content, and not just those subject to an interim classification assessment. Regulatory impact analysis . A Regulatory Impact Assessment (RIA) was prepared to support Cabinets decision to proceed with these proposals in December CABMIN refers. . The Quality Assurance panel (the Panel) that evaluated the RIA concluded that it partially met Treasurys Quality Assurance criteria. . The Panel concluded that the RIA is complete and includes all necessary information. Consultation with stakeholders was focussed primarily on the regulatory proposals, due to the time and scope constraints on the analysis. Discussions from consultation resulted in refining the proposals and a commitment to release an exposure draft of the Bill. Climate implications of policy assessment . The Ministry for the Environment CIPA team have been consulted on this Cabinet paper and confirm the CIPA requirement does not apply. Page of aheeqbzw Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs INCONFIDENCE Compliance . The Bill complies with: . the principles of the Treaty of Waitangi; . the rights and freedoms contained in the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act and the Human Rights Act ; . disclosure statement requirements (a copy of that statement is attached to this paper); . the principles and guidelines set out in the Privacy Act ; . the relevant international standards and guidelines; and . the Legislation Guidelines ( edition), which are maintained by the Legislation Design and Advisory Committee. Consultation Officials from the Department of Internal Affairs led engagement on the policy proposals contained in this Bill . The Department of Internal Affairs led targeted consultation on these policy proposals with key industry, community, and civil society stakeholders from October to November . This engagement process involved seven workshops across the country, including specific workshops with youth. Attendees at the main workshops included representatives from major online content hosts, ISPs, community groups, and civil society organisations. In total, approximately people attended the workshops. Stakeholders were also invited to submit written feedback, of which were received. There was no formal consultation with iwi or hap on proposals in the Bill before policy decisions were made. Following engagement on policy proposals, an exposure draft of the Bill was circulated to key stakeholders . Further to the direction of Cabinet CABMIN refers, an exposure draft of the Bill served as a basis for a targeted consultation on the legislative amendments with key industry groups including telecommunication companies, internet service providers, technology companies, a civil society group, and Government agencies. Stakeholders provided written feedback on the exposure draft and several stakeholders met with officials to discuss the exposure draft. . Stakeholder feedback focused on terminology used in the Bill, the clarification of operational provisions, and comment on the establishment and operation of the filtering system. Stakeholders also commented on the quantum of penalty for failing to comply with a takedown notice as being potentially too low. . The filtering provisions of the Bill attracted a significant proportion of feedback. Stakeholders commented that it was important to ensure sufficient legislative safeguards existed to prevent improper use of the filter system. These safeguards will also ensure that the system was used in a transparent and accountable manner and is subject to appropriate oversight. Issues relating to the filter remain likely to be of interest to industry, communities and civil society groups throughout the legislative process. Page of aheeqbzw Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs INCONFIDENCE . Following stakeholder feedback, the Bill has been strengthened to more explicitly provide for appropriate checks and balances relating to the filter. Changes include lifting several provisions from regulations into the primary legislation, for example, clarifying that the filter only applied to objectionable material and identifying the full range of stakeholders that must be consulted on the design of the filter. . Stakeholder feedback also resulted in the clarification of terminology and operational sections in the Bill. Several minor changes were made to address potential inconsistencies between operational provisions. . Some agencies also queried whether the current proposed penalty level of a maximum of , for noncompliance with a takedown notice is sufficient. The penalty would apply to each takedown notice issued. . I consider that the proposed penalty level to be appropriate as it is commensurate with current penalty levels in the Act. However, officials will consider submissions on this subject and provide advice to me during the select committee process. If there is a strong case for adjusting these penalty levels, I will return to Cabinet for policy approval to adjust penalty levels and look to amend the Bill during its passage through the House. . The Bill was also referred to the Legislation Design and Advisory Committee (LDAC). LDAC made several recommendations relating to the Bill, including: . ensuring the policy objective is clearly defined and discernible; . ensuring the legislation is consistent with fundamental rights and freedoms, and any limits are appropriate and no more than reasonable limits that can be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society; and . ensuring an appropriate division between what matters are included in primary legislation and what matters are included in secondary legislation. . LDACs feedback was considered when revising the Bill. . The Government coalition and confidence and supply partners have been consulted on the Bill. . The following agencies were also consulted on this Cabinet paper: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet, Ministry of Justice, Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade, Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment, Ministry for Culture and Heritage, New Zealand Police, New Zealand Customs, OFLC, the Treasury, Office of Ethnic Communities, Te Puni Kkiri, Ministry for Women, Office for Disability Issues, Ministry for Pacific Peoples, and Ministry of Social Development. Binding on the Crown . The Act is binding on the Crown. Creating new agencies or amending law relating to existing agencies . The Bill will not create any new agencies. . The Bill will amend the law relating to OFLC and will enable it to issue interim classification decisions on publications that are likely to be objectionable. . The Bill will not remove any existing powers held by OFLC or the Chief Censor. Page of aheeqbzw Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs INCONFIDENCE Allocation of decisionmaking powers . The Bill does not involve the allocation of decisionmaking powers between the Executive, the Courts and Tribunals. Associated regulations . The Bill contains new regulationmaking powers to implement and support the establishment of an electronic system to identify and prevent access to objectionable online publications. Definition of MinisterDepartment . The Bill does not create a new definition of Minister or Department. Commencement of legislation . The Bill will commence by April . Parliamentary stages . The House Business Committee has determined its work programme for the next few weeks leading up to Budget Day. The Leader of the House has undertaken to proceed only with COVID related legislation, the annual review debate (which has to be completed preBudget) and ministerial statements as appropriate. . Consistent with this determination, I intend to introduce the Bill once Parliament resumes normal business. . I will propose that the Bill be referred to the Governance and Administration Select Committee for a consideration period of six months from this referral. Proactive Release . I propose to issue a press release once the Bill has been introduced into the House. . This paper, alongside relevant briefings and Cabinet papers will be proactively released and on the Department of Internal Affairs website. Page of aheeqbzw Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs INCONFIDENCE Recommendations . The Minister of Internal Affairs recommends that the Cabinet Legislation Committee: . note that the Films, Videos, and Publications (Urgent Interim Classification of Publications and Prevention of Online Harm) Amendment Bill holds a category priority on the Legislation Programme ; . note that the Bill will improve New Zealand regulation of objectionable online content; . agree the Films, Videos, and Publications (Urgent Interim Classification of Publications and Prevention of Online Harm) Amendment Bill includes a liability exemption for staff and employees of Internet Service Providers and online content hosts, who in the execution of their duties, or acting on the instruction of the Government, are tasked with removing objectionable content; . approve the Films, Videos, and Publications (Urgent Interim Classification of Publications and Prevention of Online Harm) Amendment Bill for introduction, subject to the final approval of the Government caucus and sufficient support in the House of Representatives; . agree that the Bill be introduced once Parliament resumes normal business; . note that I intend to issue a press release once the Bill has been introduced into the House; . note that I intend to propose that the Bill be: . referred to the Governance and Administration Select Committee for consideration; and . reported back six months from the of referral to the Governance and Administration Select Committee ; and . agree that the Minister of Internal Affairs may authorise the Parliamentary Counsel Office to make any minor changes to the Bill following consideration by the Cabinet Legislation Committee. This paper focuses on legislative provisions for pricing and charging . This paper covers proposals for the statutory framework and provisions necessary for water services entities to set prices and charge for their services. This includes provision for: . Specific requirements that are so important and enduring that they need to be enshrined in primary legislation, such as the legal mandate to charge consumers for water services, and the principles to inform the development of funding and pricing plans of water services entities. Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government IN CONFIDENCE Page of . Direction on matters of nationa l importance in pricing, including direction on geographic averaging and the treatment of costs associated with addressing historic inequities in service provision to Mori, that will be developed and given effect to through a Government policy statement. . Matters that will be dealt with by the economic regulator, including guidance, input methodologies and determinations to water services entities on how to apply pricing principles, and directions to alter funding and pricing plans to achieve consistency with pricing principles. . Matters that are best left to the boards of entities, having engaged and consulted with their communities and the regional representative group. Part B: Charging for water services and protections for vulnerable consumers . Our reform of three waters service delivery will result in better and more affordable water services than if their operation were to remain with councils. That said, there will continue to be households that will struggle to meet the costs of water services together with their other needs. The transition to more standardised prices and removal of historic subsidies and inequities will also result in gains and losses for different groups. . For this reason, I begin my discussion of pricing and charging by considering who should be charged for water services and what needs to be done to protect vulnerable consumers. In Part D, I discuss specific matters related to transition, and the provisions necessary to smooth pricing and reduce price shocks for all consumers.

The Local G overnment Electoral Legislation Bill proposes new obligations on councils to review Mori representation The Bill improves the processes by which individuals and communities are represented through, and can participate in, local government elec tions. The Bill amends the Local Electoral Act , the Local Government Act , and the Local Government (Auckland Council) Act . The key policy areas for the Bill are: . establishing a fit forpurpose process for councils to review their representation arrangements , including Mori representation; . improving governance flexibility at Auckland Council; . updating the process for tied elections; and . enabling all candidates to s ubmit electronic nominations. Reviews of representation arrangements must occur at least every six years. In each term of local government, approximately half of all local authorities must review their representation arrangements . The Bill changes the rep resentation review process to require councils to consider Mori representation as a mandatory component of those reviews unless they have already established Mori wards. This prioritisation can be performed manually, but sorting through potentially large contact lists will potentially lose time savings gained by using the CovidCard system. Fortunately, it is possible to rank contacts using machine learning by training a model using data provided from the cards and our ground truth contact information. When presented with new previously unseen contact data the model is able to produce a probability that the new data belongs to a real close contact. A list of contacts from a given card can be ordered by the probabilities to produce a ranked list, ideally with close contacts near the top of the list and casual contacts closer to the bottom.

Concordance between Bluetooth cards and self report daily diaries In this pilot, we aimed to establish whether the Bluetooth cards would capture close contacts, but we did not aim to evaluate effectiveness beyond its ability to capture any close c ontacts. In Figure we qualitatively compare the median number of close contacts between self report diaries and the Bluetooth . The median number of close co ntacts recorded per day o ver the study period was for the Bluetooth card s compared to only or the self report surveys. On the weekend, days and , the number of participants decreased with minimal staffing. Accordingly, the number of possible close contacts also decreased. This is reflected in the Bluetooth card data, as the median number of close contacts on the weekend was nearly half the median number reported on weekdays, days and . The differences in the median close contacts per participant between self report daily diaries and Bluetooth card data should be interpreted with caution: ) not all participants completed diaries each day, tho ugh Bluetooth cards were r ecording contacts each day; ) the duration of the contact for each interaction captured by Bluetooth cards was assumed to be one minute, but it could have been much less; ) diaries were reported by participants about all close c ontacts, regardless of whether those close contacts were definitively participants in the pilot. While known non participant close contacts were removed from the analysis, if the close contact was unknown, then their data was retained; and ) there were n o filtering close contact algorithm installed on the Bluetooth card, meaning that the cards may have at times applied a much wider definition of a close contact than the daily surveys (e.g., greater than m away). This work commenced with a smallscale field trial conducted May th in Nelson Hospital using a Prototype version of the CovidCard . This was followed by a series of closed and controlled scenario tests conducted May th in the Waikato region. These tests used Prototype cards which could be , enabling iterative card embedded software (firmware) development. These closed tests simulated common interactions across a range of scenarios including an office environment, a caferestaurant, a construction site, taxiUber trips and a house partysocial function. The tests have provided a strong realworld dataset to support the evaluation of the CovidCards contact identification performance relative to a robust observed reality (ground truth), derived through a combination of video capture and detailed trial observer records.

Ensuring that services and functions continue to enhance wellbeing over time requires anticipating how the environment we operate in may change, and positions ourselves to best meet the opportunities and challenges that arise. Building digital public services is at the forefront of our thinking so Government is as joinedup, and people centric as it can be. The Department of Internal Affairs has made great progress in making its services easier to use and more accessible and in supporting other government agencies in realising their digital ambitions. Meeting the challenges of regulation in the digital world and addressing barriers to digital inclusion will be a focus of attention in coming years. Ensuring that Government acts as a cohesive system is important and the Department will play an important role in system leadership for both central and local government. More effectively linking central and local government to address national objectives in areas such as community resilience and infrastructure is an important part of the Departments work. The Departments many and varied services will continue to provide value, including support for the Executive, registration of life events, community advice and development, public recordkeeping, library services, preserving and making accessible our documentary heritage, administration of grants, and enforcement and compliance across several regulatory regimes, including digital safety, gambling, financial transactions and charities. I believe that we are well placed to make good progress towards further developing services and activities to maximise their benefit to people, communities and the Government. I look forward to continuing to work closely with the Department as it delivers its roles and functions for the people and Government of New Zealand. Statement of Responsibility I am satisfied that the information on strategic intentions prepared by the Department of Internal Affairs is consistent with the policies and performance expectations of the Government. Hon. Tracey Martin Minister of Internal Affairs October

Three scenarios were scripted (office, cafe, taxi), others (construction site, house party) were natural situations that were only observed. All scenarios were recorded by at least one video camera, and some were recorded by two independently placed cameras (office, cafe, construction). The scripted trials were also monitored (with handwritten notes) by one or more observers during the trial. CovidCard data was downloaded from the cards within hours of each trial (typically less than one hour afterwards), and ground truth completed within five days of each trial completion.

Timetable for establishing the other entities and applying economic regulation . I have also been consider ing the approach to determining and communicating the go live timetable and process for the other new entities . . One option would be to include a timetable of go live dates in the Amendment B ill. However, this would be an inflexible approach, which would require a change to primary legislation if any of the dates needed to be amended during the establishment period. . My preference is to retain some flexibility around the dates , and to use an Order in Council process instead of primary legislation. The go live timeframes would reflect when each entity and its council owners are ready for this to occur based on them demonstrating this readiness in a number of critical areas . All of the entities would have to go live by July , at the latest, which is the backstop agreed by Cabinet in the April paper. . I am proposin g to develop and communicate the process that would enable an entity to go live, including which factors would need to be demonstrated for this to occur. Given all of the work that will be required to get each entity and council ready, and the impact on staff involved in the transfer, there would need to be a minimum notice period between agreeing the go live and the day on which the entity will begin operating . This will give everyone involved sufficient time to prepare , and time for staff to be transferred . . I note that some councils have already indicated they would like their entity to g o live on July , as was originally anticipated. T here are practical constraints that may make it difficult to establish a large number of entities at once, though, and not all of the councils within an entity service area may be prepared for th is. I am, however, seeking to accommodate some of these request s so New Zealanders can enjoy the benefits of reform quickly, across a number of regions. Title: The Films, Videos, and Publications Classifications Amendment Bill Standardising classification for Commercial Video on Demand content with Supplementary A nalysis ( November ) Authoring agency : Department of Internal Affairs Location : https:www.dia.govt.nzResource material Regulatory Impact Statements Index Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs ... If so, did the RIA Team in the Treasury provide an independent opinion on the quality of any of these regulatory impact statement s YES For the RIA dated August , the Quality Assurance panel provided the following statement: The panel considers that the RIA does not meet the Quality Assurance criteria. The panel considers that the RIA is clearly written, and is transparent about the constraints on the analysis, and about many of the gaps in the analysis. Overall, the panel co nsiders that there is sufficient analysis for Ministers to make an informed decision not to pursue Option but does not provide sufficient analysis to inform the decision about whether Option (the preferred option) or Option is the best way of achievi ng the Governments objectives. Our concerns are summarised under the quality assurance criteria of complete and convincing, and consulted. Complete and convincing There is limited analysis of the size of the problem, particularly the magnitude of the risk from misclassifying content and the degree to which other information offered by commercial video on demand providers (e.g. in the synopsis and genre label that a consumer sees before viewing) mitigates the risk. There is also limited evidence that the problem needs addressing now, instead of waiting for the intended wider review. The RIA does not establish the criteria which will be used to determine which providers will be regulated, and whether consideration will be given to exempting small or niche pro viders. Other options could have been considered. For example, encouraging providers to join the voluntary system, with the chance that regulation might follow if that was unsuccessful. Information about impacts of options is light. Two examples are: o Little information about the costs to providers, and the extent to which costs will be passed onto consumers whether through higher prices or reductions in content (lower profitability minority audience content might be at greater risk). o Whether Option woul d increase, rather than decrease, inconsistency of classification when considered across all household video content a point raised in submissions. The RIA identifies risks of non compliance with Option but is not convincing that these risks will not a lso manifest for Option . The RIA could have assessed what factors might lead providers to comply and had an implementation plan for gaining compliance. Consulted The RIA generally summarises and responds to the feedback from public consultation well. Consultation elicited many issues, and providers said they required more information before they could estimate the cost of options and the time required to implement them. Further, targeted, consultation would likely help, and ultimately result in sufficient analysis to inform Ministers decisions.

()(a) Section Six: Change protocol Introduction This protocol sets out the approach to managing the implementation of the structural changes arising from the Toi Hiranga l Regulation and Policy Organisational Change. This Protocol is consistent with all individual employment agreements and the Collective Agreement (including the Section . Management of Change provisions) between the Public Service Association and the Department of Internal Affairs, which are available to view on . Principles The process is designed to: ensure a fair and transparent process; maximise the placement of employees into available positions; ensure minimum disruption to business as usual; observe the provisions contained in the relevant employment agreements and organisational policy; and minimise uncertainty for employees. Who does this protocol apply to The protocol applies to all permanent employees of the department including: permanent fulltime and parttime employees employees currently on all forms of leave including leave without pay and parental leave. For employees currently seconded to other positions the process will apply to their permanent substantive position. Fixed term (temporary) or casual employees are not covered by this protocol even though their position may be affected by the restructure. In this case the relevant provision of their employment agreement will apply. Overview Employees are affected if their current position is being disestablished or changed significantly. If there is no significant change to their position, and there are the same number, or fewer, employees than positions in the new structure, employees will be reconfirmed. Employees who are not reconfirmed will be considered for reassignment. This involves considering whether affected employees skills can be matched to alternative positions that require similar skills in the new structure. Affected employees who are not reassigned will be consulted individually about other options. If no other options are identified, notice will be given, and redundancy provisions apply. Affected employees Employees who have been identified as being affected by organisational change will be consulted over the implementation process, and the employees will have a preferential right of appointment to vacancies within the Branch. Before final decisions are announced, all potentially affected employees will be notified individually. Employees will be informed if they: have been reconfirmed in a position and are no longer affected, or are affected and will be considered for reassignment. Reconfirmation process Prior to announcement of the final decisions, an assessment will be made to determine if employees meet the criteria for reconfirmation. This assessment will be made by the General Manager or Director (Tier leader) for the group, with support from Human Resources and approved by the Deputy Chief Executive, Toi Hiranga l Regulation and Policy. Reconfirmation is where an employees existing job is compared to jobs in the new structure to determine whether they are the same or nearly the same. The criteria for reconfirmation are: the new job description is the same or nearly the same as the job the affected employee currently does the salary band is the same the terms and conditions, including career prospects are no less favourable the location is the same or in the same vicinity.

Treaty settlements and engagement with iwiMori I have instructed officials at the Department of Internal Affairs to engage with iwi to discuss the proposed amendments to the: o Waikato Tainui Raupatu Claims (Waikato River) Settlement Act ; o Te Arawa River Iwi Waikato River Act ; and o Te Awa Tupua (Whanganui Claims Settlement) Act . The engagement follows advice the Department received from Te Arawhiti and Te Puni Kkiri during the department consultation. It is necessary to engage with iwi as the amendments will change Treaty Settlement Acts. Transitional arrangements for local authorities The Repeal B ill contain s provisions to amend the Local Government Act s, specifically the Local Government Act to reinstate local authority ownership and responsibility for the delivery of water services, including the maintenance and upgrade of water assets. The transitional provisions will allow local authorities to include water services in their long term plans and proposed charge s for water services to be collected through rates . This planning provision is currently prohibited beyond July for most local authorities and prohibited for councils in Northland and Auckland Council beyond July . By including transitional provisions, including a provision for a local authority to seek an Order in Council to defer setting their long term plans until , t he Repeal Bill provide s local authorities with much needed legislative certainty for their long term plans, by providing an extension to the legislated adoption of June . The Repeal Bill also includes a clause to enable local authorities to delay the statutory review of bylaws that relate to water services. It has been necessary to include this transition clause as local authorities with water services bylaws excluded them from work programmes following the changes introduced by the water services legislation. I am informed that with the imminent return of water services to local authorities, the current obligations set out in the Local Government Act , without transitional arrangements will place undue pressure on local authorities. The Repeal Bill will require all water services bylaws to be reviewed by June . I gave offic ials at t he Department of Internal Affairs permission to undertak e limited engage ment with the sector experts to ensure the long term plan provisions will help local authorities meet their statutory duties . As a result of feedback from Taituar , drafting instructions have been issued to enable local authorities to continue with to implement policies where development contributions are linked to long term plans.

Trust Framework for Digital Identity
Trust Framework legislation
Trust Framework parameters Use of the Trust Framework is opt in; personal information will not be held in a centralised database Public consultation during Parliaments consideration of the Digital Identify Services Trust Framework Bill in late highlighted some concern that the Trust Framework may be seeking to establish a mandatory and centralised identity regime. Proactively released by the Minister for Digitising Government The proposed system will be decentralised with no new powers for the Government to collect or share peoples information without their consent. One of the key obj ectives of the Trust Framework is to support and enable users to choose what information about themselves is being shared with third parties. Also, it will not be compulsory for people to use Trust Framework accredited digital identity services, or even t o use any digital identity services at all. To ensure access, people will still be able to apply for government services in person using paper based systems, providing physical credentials to show who they are. Operation of the Trust Framework will involve user controlled data sharing The current lack of regulation in the provision of New Zealands digital identity services means individual services are often provided directly to an individual with varying levels of security depending on the strength of the service providers systems and processes. Access to, and sharing of, information is primarily controlled by the service, rather than the user. However, under the Trust Framework individuals will be able to access, claim, and share their own information th rough accredited digital identity services (identified by accreditation marks). This will occur as part of a standardised process to ensure personal identity data is handled securely and according to the users requests, as outlined in Figure on page . Government services The Trust Framework will apply to Crown entities and government departments as well as iwi, private sector , and other non government organisations that seek accreditation The Act and its associated rules and regulations will apply to C rown entities and government departments that choose to opt in and deliver services under the Trust Framework , alongside iwi, private sector , and other non government organisations . As Figure below shows , in addition to being relying parties, some Crown entities and government departments may also seek accreditation to provide accredited services. For some, this may be limited to being an accredited information provider. For others, it could include choosing to provid e other accredited services as infrastructure providers. Crown entities and government departments that wish to provide accredited services will need to meet the requirements specified in the Act, associated rules and regulations. For example, the identity verification service RealM e will continue to be provided by the Department of Internal Affairs . To be offered as an accredited service, however, the Department will need to meet the accreditation requirements. International Alignment In , the Government committed to a programm e led by the Department to develop options for a new approach to digital identity. That programme investigated how the Government could set up the right rules and environment to take advantage of new technologies, offering a modern approach to meet the evo lving needs and expectations of New Zealanders in the digital identity landscape. Proactively released by the Minister for Digitising Government Throughout and , the Department undertook extensive research and engaged with key stakeholders, including equivalent agencies internationally. New Zealand is not the only country in the process of implementing legislation to modernise its digital identity system. The Trust Framework will align with similar trust frameworks being developed in Australia, Canada and the United Kingdom, and will be a key foundation in the Governments commitment to achieving mutual recognition of digital identity services with Australia under the Single Economic Market agenda. Enabling Regulations The regulations will complement the technical and operational service related requirements established in the Trust Framework rules that apply to TF providers and their delivery of accredited services. It is our intention that the regulations will provide a flexible way for Trust Framework processes to evolve over time as the digital identity sy stem matures and technology develops . The development of the rules and regulations will be informed by eight principles to ensure they are people centred; privacy enabling; security enhancing; enabling of Te Ao Mori approaches to identity; sustainable; interoperable; and open and transparent. Further Information Appendix A provides a glossary of key terms used in this paper. Appendix B contains links to further information on the Trust Framework. Trusted citizenship and identity documents contribute to a sense of belonging
Trusted citizenship and identity documents contribute to sense of belonging Digital identity The Department is working with the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment, Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet, and Statistics NZ to develop a strategy to enable Aotearoa New Zealand to flourish and prosper in the digital world. This strategy is built around three themes: mahi ake (growth), mahi tahi (inclusion), and mahi tika (trust). Central to this is the work we are doing to progress the development of an approach to digital identity whereby people can have more control of their data, which is accessed with their consent. A regulatory regime that will accredit digital identity services against standardsbased rules for security, privacy, identification management and interoperability will improve individual, private sector and government trust and confidence in the digital identity system. We will also support a new approach to guide government investments in digital identity technologies. Modernising the Births, Deaths, Marriages and Relationships Registration Act Birth certificates are ofen the most accessible form of identity document for many New Zealanders. The Department is working on legislative and regulatory changes to introduce a selfidentification process for amending the sex shown on birth certificates. The Bill is currently making its way through the parliamentary process. The intent of the proposed changes is to significantly help transgender and intersex New Zealanders who need an identity document that reflects their gender in order to easily access information and services they need. T mtou kkiri i te panonitanga hei whakatukuki i mtou whinga How we will drive change to deliver our goals Oranga hap, iwi, and Mori is improved through an enduring, equitable and positive MoriCrown partnership. Mori, iwi and hapu aspirations, interests and rights are understood and respected Supporting iwi, hap and communities to lead their own development and manage their taonga as kaitiaki We strive to provide whnau, hap and iwi with easy access to collections, taonga and mtauranga held by National Library and Archives New Zealand. We also intend to understand and respond to their aspirations for caring for their own mtauranga. This may include enabling taonga to stay in communities to allow iwi and Mori to carry out their roles as kaitiaki. Whnau, hap and iwi have a desire to develop their own capability to ensure the future conservation and preservation of their taonga and mtauranga, in a way that is led and driven by them. We are working to establish internship opportunities that go beyond research to ofer skills growth and development experiences. We are also working to reduce barriers to access so that whnau, hap and iwi can actively work with their taonga and mtauranga. This includes developing a Moriled academic ofering on conservation and preservation of taonga. Iwi and hap can access whakapapa information The Department will work with iwi to understand their needs and expectations for collecting, storing and sharing iwi afiliation information, and are actively considering options that would provide the ability for Mori to selfassert whakapapa when registering a birth. If the Department were able to collect whakapapa data as part of birth registration, people could formally assert their iwi and hap afiliations, and iwi and Mori authorities could have access to that selfassertion data for their own purposes. This will support the Department in contributing to an improved MoriCrown relationship by contributing to the recognition of data sovereignty and considering better ways to support iwi afiliation. T Ttou Mhiohio me Matihiko Improving our systems to enable seamless, simple and fit for purpose services The Department continues to invest in delivering digitally enabled services that meet the expectations and needs of New Zealanders, at the same time as maintaining and modernising our existing digital assets. We are addressing these challenges through cloud computing and as a service solutions that improve our agility, consolidating the overall number of applications we have and applying iterative delivery and customercentred design approaches. The next four years will focus on shifing to native cloud digital platforms to provide the digital foundations for our future services. Key investments in service delivery areas will be leveraging customer relationship management, data and analytics, and system integration capability. These will be supported by continuing investment in cloudbased collaboration and corporate systems to enable internal productivity and flexibility. We will also continue the momentum of the Te Hpai O programme, which was initiated in . Te Hpai O will secure better tools to provide joined up, transparent, fitforpurpose services and enable our people to deliver great outcomes for Aotearoa. This includes continuing the implementation of our new finance system, Rehutai, which will extend the strategic finance functionality to support human resource and recruitment management, and also replace the Departments payroll system. Te Ara Vaka strategy implementation The successful implementation of the Te Ara Vaka strategy across the Department will ensure the inclusion of Pasifika perspectives by design and the creation of safe spaces to talanoa about Aotearoas Pasifika history. It will strengthen our workforce, with greater Pasifika representation in senior leadership roles (tiers ), with equal pay across the sector, and the recognition of cultural capability as a specialised skillset. The continued investment in the Te Ara Vaka strategy will make it easier for our Pasifika customers to use our services and support the Department to build stronger communities enabling them to be resilient, thriving and selfsuficient. Investment and asset performance Our assets support our ability to delivery successfully against our strategic intentions. The LongTerm Investment Plan has set out our commitment and direction for investment and asset management. It defines the principles that underpin our investment and asset management practices. This has informed the fouryear capital plan, which is a rolling plan of our capital intentions that is twice a year. The Department plans to review and renew the LongTerm Investment Plan within the next months. The fouryear capital plan is focused on keeping existing systems and infrastructure working well. The Department has little capacity for further transformative investment at the present time and will have to prioritise carefully to make best use of existing resources. Opportunities, and the risks that come with them, can ofen require tradeofs, while continuing to maintain core services to New Zealanders. To maximse our coverage and impact we need the right information, technology and systems to enable our people to work in an integrated and flexible way. Technology plays an important role in connecting our people, enabling us to operate as one connected organisation across our work locations. We also strive to have better outcomes for New Zealanders who use our services by making it easier for people to access and use them. T Ttou Rp improving our workplace environments Te Tari Taiwhenua owns buildings across Aotearoa in Auckland, Taup, Whanganui, Wellington, Christchurch and Dunedin. These include Archival and Library facilities, a Harbourmaster site and two properties that are used as ministerial residences. T Ttou Rp environmental sustainability at DIA We are supporting the directive of the Carbon Neutral Government Programme to achieve carbon neutrality by with the establishment of an inhouse sustainability programme. With the help of an external specialist we will capture, analyse and report our emissions data, establishing a baseline reading. We will then set our emissions reduction targets for the next four years and develop a plan to achieve these targets. The programme will identify ways to reduce our consumption of energy and fuel across all areas of the organisation. We will communicate these findings and engage with groups across the Department to implement a strategy to reduce carbon emissions. The programme is being supported by energy eficient upgrades to our owned buildings as part of the Forward Works Programme. This includes initiatives such as replacing fluorescent bulbs with LED lighting, and upgrading HVAC and lif systems to lowerenergy usage models. To reduce CO emissions from our vehicle fleet we are developing a transition plan for the move to electric vehicles, including installing charging infrastructure at relevant sites, as well as looking at optimising our fleet size. U N C L A S S I F I E D Authorisaton . The Privacy Act provides for the establishment of AISAs. Subpart of Part enables personal informaton to be shared between or within agencies via AISAs where it facilitates the provision of public services. Secton of the Privacy Act also authorises exemptons from, or modifcatons to, any of the informaton privacy principles (except principles and , which relate respectvely to the right to have access to, and correct, personal informaton). . Secton of the Privacy Act allows for the creaton of classes of partes to anAISA , allowing the Death AISA to extend beyond the core public service. Any organisaton wishing to join a class of partes will need to apply to DIA. Applicatonprocesses will ensure the organisatons that join a class understand their obligatons and have the capacity to meet the security and privacy protecton requirements of the AISA. . Operatonal documentaton to support the implementaton of the AISA will beprepar ed for each party in consultaton with the Ofce of the Privacy Commissioner. . The proposed Order in Council would approve the Death AISA and ensure thatperso na l informaton collected by the partes can be lawfully shared to facilitate access to death informaton, for the purposes described in the AISA. It would authorisespecifed exemptons from informaton privacy principles (source of personal informaton), (use of personal informaton) and (disclosure of personal informaton). Timing and day rule . The Order in Council will comply with the day rule and will come into force on April . Compliance . The Order in Council complies with: the rights and freedoms contained in the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act and t he Human Rights Act ; the principles and guidelines set out in the Privacy Act ; and the Legislaton Design Advisory Commitees Guidelines. Therefore, a death record for a transgender person who has not amended their birth record may not align with their gender at death, and therefore may not align with the gender by which they are known to organisatons. U N C L A S S I F I E D INCONFIDENCE Page of Office of the Minister of Internal Affairs Chair , Cabinet Legislation Committee Fire and Emergency New Zealand (Fire Safety, Evacuation Procedures, and Evacuation Schemes) Amendment Regulations Proposal . This paper seeks authorisation to submit the Fire and Emergency New Zealand (Fire Safety, Evacuation Procedures, and Evacuation Schemes) Amendment Regulations (the Amendment Regulations ) (Appendix A ) to the Executive Council . Executive Summary . Stand ards New Zealand has the New Zealand Standard for Automatic Fire Sprinkler Systems, NZS : (the sprinkler standard), which provides the rules for design ing, install ing, and maint aining automatic sprinkler systems. . The sprinkler standard does not include a requirement for hand operated fire fighting equipment to be installed, which is an important part of fire safety equipment, when automatic sprinklers are present in a building . . The proposed regulations will: . add the sprinkler standard, to the Fire and Emergency New Zealand (Fire Safety, Evacuation Procedures, and Evacuation Schemes) Regulations (Fire Safety Regulations) ; and . require hand operated fire fighting equipment that is compliant with the New Zealand Standard for Hand Operated Fire fighting Equipment, NZS :, to be installed in buildings where the automatic sprinkler system complies with the sprinkler standard. . The proposed changes ensure the minimum levels of fire safety currently required by the Fire Safety Regulations are maintained and apply to new or altered buildings . . The vast majority of buildings are unaffected by these changes. Building code requirements and existing evacuation schemes are also unaffected. Fire Safety Regulations need to be . The Fire Safety Regulations prescribe the minimum requirements for an automatic sprinkler system installed in a relevant building. The Fire Safety Regulations require an automatic sprinkler system to comply with one of the listed New Zealand Standards for Automatic Sprinkler Systems, when it is installed. An automatic sprinkler system is a fire suppression or fire control device that activate s when the air reaches a certain temperature. The definition of relevant building captures buildings that present comparatively greater risk to occupants in the event of fire, than buildings used for other purposes pzrrb :Document Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs INCONFIDENCE Page of The Fire Safety Regulations should include a reference to the sprinkler standard . On May , Standards New Zealand the sprinkler standard , which provides an integrated set of rules for the design, installation, and maintenance of automatic sprinkler systems, so these systems protect against the loss of life andminimise property damage from fire. The sprinkler standard is no t currently listed in the Fire Safety Regulations. . Adding a reference in the Fire Safety Regulations to the sprinkler standard will ensure that buildings with automatic sprinkler systems installed to the specifications inthe sprinkler standard are included in the Fire and Emergency New Zealand (Fire and Emergency) regulatory regime. The sprinkler standard does not require hand operated fire fighting equipment to be installed ; the Fire Safety Regulations shoul d require this . Hand operated fire fighting e quipment , such as fire extinguishers, fire hoses and fire blankets , supplement the components of sprinkler systems that are a fixed part of the building and fill the performance gaps where sprinklers may fall short. . The spr inkler standard removed requirements for hand operated fire fighting equipment to be installed . This means b uildings constructed or upgraded to the sprinkler standard may not have the same level of fire protection as buildings constructed to an ear lier version of this Standard. . Standards New Zealand acknowledge that hand operated firefighting equipment is an important feature in buildings but decided that it was out of place in the automatic sprinkler standard . Instead, the New Zealand Standard for Hand Operated Fire Fighting Equipment, NZS :, should be cited for this type of equipment. Consequently, the sprinkler standard does not require hand operated fire fighting equipment to be installed. . Where an automatic sprinkler system complies with the sprinkler standard, there should be a requirement for hand operated fire fighting equipment to be installed . This will maintain the current minimum fire safety requirements in all relevant buildings with automatic sprinkler systems (old and new ). Further information on when the fire safety regime requires building owners to install an automatic sprinkler system and hand operated fire fighting equipment is provided in Appendix B . Building Code requirements and existing evacuation schemes are not affected by these changes . These changes will not affect obligations and exemptions relating to automatic sprinkler systems and hand operated fire fighting equipment under the Building Code. Existing relevant buildings that already have an approved evacuation scheme will notbe affected by these change s. Fire Safety Regulations should include the sprinkler standard and require hand operated fire fighting equipment be installed . I recommend that regulation of the Fire Safety Regulations is amended to : . refer to the sprinkler standard. This will ensure that automatic sprinkler systems installed to this Standard are included in the Fire and Emergency regulatory regime. pzrrb Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs INCONFIDENCE Page of . include a requirement that where the automatic sprinkler system complies with the sprinkler standard, hand operated fire fighting equipment must be installed . The changes will come into force on August . If Cabinet agrees, the Amendment Regulations ( Appendix A ) will be submitted to the Executive Council on June . . The amendments to the Fire and Emergency New Zealand (Fire Safety, Evacuation Procedures, and Evacuation Schemes) Regulations will be publicly notified in the Gazette on June . Timing and day rule . No waiver of the day rule is sought. The Amendment Regulations will come into force on August . Compliance . Regulations Review Committee . There are no grounds for the Regulations Review Committee to draw the regulations to the attention of the House of Representatives under Standing Order . Certification by Parliamentary Counsel . The draft regulations are certified by the Parliamentary Counsel Office as being in order for submission to Cabinet, in reliance on Crown Law advice .
