Rachel Hayward Sec retary of the Cabinet jxzyp UNCLASSIFIED Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs UNCLASSIFIED Unclassified Office of the M inister of Internal Affairs Cabinet Establishing the Cyclone Gabrielle Appeal Trust Proposal This paper provides Cabinet with information about the Cyclone Gabrielle Appeal Trust (t he Trust), seeks funding for administration of the Trust, and seeks authorisation for relevant Ministers to have power to act on future decisions about the Trust. Relation to government priorities This relates to the Governments priorities from the Prime Ministers Statement of providing strong and responsible leadership as we rebuild from Cyclone Gabrielle. The Government intends to announce the establishment of a charitable trust. Cyclone Gabrielle, along with other recent extreme weather events at the start of , has ca used significant damage to many communities. Millions of dollars have already been donated to a wide range of organisations working on the immediate response to Cyclone Gabrielle recovery. The Government can complement existing donation appeals by establishing a charit able trust called the Cyclone Gabrielle Appeal Trust. The Trust will manage the Cyclone Gabrielle Appeal Fund and make decisions on how donations to the Fund will be distributed. One of the benefits of the Trust is that it will be able to proactively seek out and manage overseas, philanthropic, and corporate donations, which can often come with strings attached (for example the donation must go to a certain project or outcome) that more locallyoriented fundraisers may struggle to accommodate. There is also an opportunity to orient the Fund towards mediumterm recovery needs, to complement the sterling work of the Red Cross, mayoral relief funds and large corporate partners such as Stuff and NZME along with many more local fundraisers in raising money to deal with the immediate response phase. Establishing the Trust will help with ensuring that donation money goes to the areas hardest hit by Cyclone Gabrielle. Money collected by mayoral relief funds and regional community trusts will likely only be able to used in that region, and more populated, wealthier regions will be in a better position to raise money. If the Government appoints trustees and advisors tasked with taking a broader and needsbased view of recovery, it can ensure that donation money is more equitably matched to need. This briefing seeks your agreement to minor and technical policy changes to be included in the Births, Deaths, Marriages and Relationships Registration Bill (the Bill) . These changes would support the introduction of a self identification process. . The briefing also seeks authorisation for officials to provide confirmation of changes to the Parliamentary Counsel Office (PCO) for them to include in their drafting of the self identification supplementary order paper (SOP) . Executive Summary . Cabinet has ap proved your decision to introduce a self identification process to enable people to have their gender recognised on birth certificates CABMIN . Cabinet also approved associated policy decisions to update the self identification provisions briefi ngs IA and IA refer . We have provided drafting instructions to PCO for the self identification SOP. . Cabinet authorised you to make further minor and technical policy changes in line with their policy approvals. This briefing recommends the following changes: . a month delay on the commencement of the self identification provisions to provide time for technical updates and the development of regulations, with an option to change the commencement via an Order inCouncil; . retain the r ecords of all the amendments made to registered sex, but restrict access to protect sensitive information ; . redraft clause I to ensure it clearly conveys that birth certificates are not conclusive evidence of a persons sex; and . redraft clause ()(a) to clarify that where a person amends their registered sex and name, their previous name is not listed on their birth certificate. . Subject to your agreement on the above proposals , we seek your authorisation to confirm these decisions with PCO to incorporate in the self identification SOP. Cabinet has agreed to introduce a self identification process . You are introducing a self identification process to enable transgender and intersex people to amend the sex recorded on their birth certificate. Select Commit tee recommended changes to the Bill in that would enable a self identification process. However, Cabinet did not approve these changes because of the limited time available during Select Committee . . Provisions that would enable a self identification process were added to the Bill at the recommendation of Select Committee in , but were not approved by Cabinet at the time . The term transgender is used in this paper to refer to all people whose gender differs from their assigned sex at birth this includes people who identify outside of the malefemale binary who may use a range of terms to describe their gender including non binary. Intersex is an umbrella term for people born with a variation of sex characteristics (such as sexual anatomy, reproductive organs, hormonal andor chromosome patterns). Intersex people are born with sex characteristics that are more dive rse than narrow medical definitions of male or female bodies. Like anyone else, an intersex person may grow to identify with a different gender. Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua Department of Internal Affairs INCONFIDENCE Page of . You have agreed to policy changes to update the provisions recommended by Select Committee IA and IA refer . These included decisions on: . removing the intersex marker option from the Bill; . prescribing the number and terminology for a range of sex marker options in regulations; . enabling people to amend registe red sex multiple times; and . the process for amending registered sex for children and young people. . On May CABMIN , Cabinet approved your decision to introduce a selfidentification process and your policy decisions to update the provision s recommended by Select Committee. . The policy decisions will be used to revise the self identification provisions that were recommended by Select Committee in . The revised provisions will be included in a SOP that will be referred to Select Committee for consideration. Initial drafting instructions for the revised provisions have been provided to PCO. Further decisions are required for minor and technical aspects of the self identification provisions . We recommend the following minor and technical policy changes to the self identification provisions : . introduce a month delay on the commencement of the self identification provisions; . retain the records of all amendments made to registered sex, but restrict access to records of previous amendments ; . clarify clause I to ensure birth certificates are not considered conclusive evidence of a persons sex; and . clarify that , where a person has amended their registered sex and changed their name , their previous name is not listed on their reissued birth certificate. Recommendation : Commenc ing the self identification provisions mon ths after enactment , but allow an Order inCouncil to change the . A Bill is enacted (becomes an Act) when it has passed through all the Parliamentary stages and has received Royal assent (given by the Governor General) . The term commencement refers to the provisions in the Act take effect . Commencement dates can be set for an entire Act, or for specific sections . . The Bill is currently drafted to commence the day after it receives Royal assent. This is often the default decision if there are no specific reasons for delaying commencement. . We recommend commencing the selfidentification provisions months after the Bill receives Royal assent , but also provide that the commencement can be change d by Order inCouncil. Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua Department of Internal Affairs INCONFIDENCE Page of Rationale for delaying co mmencement of the self identification provisions We are confident the technical updates could be implemented within months . Delayed commencement would provide the necessary time to update our IT systems. We need to update the IT system that records birt h registration details, and all the downstream systems we operate that receive, verify or share birth registration information. The proposed timeframe allows for careful scoping to capture all the necessary changes across our systems , and ensures the vendor that we engage with to maintain our systems can resource the work to make the changes. We estimate that these updates would take up to months to complete. but we are less certain about timeframes for implementing regulations, so w e recommend including the option of seeking an Order inCouncil . A delay will also enable us to develop necessary regulations for the self identification provisions. This includes taking time to consult on key issues, including: . which sex markers other than the binary will be available; . who would be authorised to provide a letter supporting applications for children and young people ; and . additional requirements where a person applies to amend their registered sex more than once. . Given the complexity and sensitivity of this work, there is a risk that developing the regulations may not be complete d within months of enacting the Bill. Including the option of changing the commencement by an Order inCouncil would allow more time if its needed . Transgender and intersex communities might be disappointed in the delay, but the extra time is needed and gives them more opportunity to contribute to the regulations . Some transgender and intersex advocates might be disappointed by the delay, especially given the delays in progressing the Bill. However, this delay is necessary to introduce a self identification process. We can provide messaging about the reasons for the delays , including your commitment to consult on the necessary regulations with these communities. Recommendation : Retain records of previous amendment s to registered sex . When a person amend s their registered sex, the Births, Deaths, Marriages, and Relationships Registration Act (the BDMRR Act) restricts access to search for that persons previously registered sex on their birth record. The Bill carries these restrictions forward (with some alterations) in clauses , and . . The restrictions are intended to protect peoples privacy, preventing them from b eing outed as transgender or intersex. The limited conditions where information can be shared includ e measures to protect against the misuse of birth certificates to create multiple identities . Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua Department of Internal Affairs INCONFIDENCE Page of . Clause F of the Bill provides a different policy for when people amend their registered sex back to what was recorded at birth. Instead of restricting access, this provision requires the Registrar General to delete the record of the initial amendment to the registered sex. In effect, the persons birth record wo uld look like it had not been amended since birth. . We disagree with th e approach in clause F . We recommend keeping the record s of all amendments to registered sex on the birth re cord , but restrict ing access in line with clauses , and . Rational e for retaining the records of previous amendment s . Deleting records of any amendment to registered sex could make it more difficult to detect when people are using birth certificates to create multiple identities. Someone could have a birth certificate derived from a record that has been deleted . Government agencies , including law enforcement agencies, would not be able to see whether people had used the birth records to create alternate identities . . We do not think this would create a privacy concern. Information about previous amendments to registered sex would be restricted. . In general, the registers should accurately reflect changes over time, with privacy risks addressed by managing access to the records. This is the approach to adoption records, an d records of people who are under witness protection both of which have very significant privacy interests . Recommendation : Clarifying that a birth certificate is not conclusive evidence of a persons sex . Section of the BDMRR Act provides that a per sons sex should be determined by reference to the general law of New Zealand. The Select Committee recommended retain ing this provision in clause I of the Bill. . We interpret this provision to mean that birth certificates should not be considered conc lusive evidence of a persons sex. We recommend re drafting clause I to clarify this meaning . We would remov e the reference to the general law of New Zealand , and instead indicat e that: . birth certificates should not be the determining factor in decisions about a persons sex ; and . consideration should be given to other legislation and the common law. . Should you agree , we will work with PCO to develop how this provision is worded. Rationale for redrafting clause I . Crown Law previously advised that it is unclear what determining sex by the general law of New Zealand entails . Crown Law also noted that the drafting of clause I makes it unclear whether the policy intent is to maintain the distinction between sex recorded on a birth certificate and sex for other purposes . (i.e. whether it is intended that information on birth certificates should be conclusive evidence of a persons sex ). Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua Department of Internal Affairs INCONFIDENCE Page of . As discussed with you previously, we recommend maintaining the existing position that birth certificates should not provide conclusive evidence of a persons sex . This was set out in the Cabinet paper, Introducing a self identification process to recognise gender on birth certificates . The proposed redraft would clarify this position. . We are working with Corrections on a n amendment to th e relevant regulation s before the selfidentification process commences . Clarifying the provision could help mitigate some stakeholder concerns with a self identification process . Redrafting the provision will make the legislation more accessible and help people understand that birth certificates should not be the basis for determining a persons sex. The legislation would provide clarity for organisation s about not rely ing on birth certificates to determin e a persons access to women only places or services . This provides assurance that t here is little risk of information on birth certificates allow ing men to access women only places or services . . Some stakeholders may think we should go a step further and adopt Crown Laws advice that statutory guidance about how sex is de termined could be beneficial (for example, what factors should be considered to determine a persons sex). As previously advised, developing statutory guidance for how sex should be determined generally would be broader in scope than the BDMRR Act and the Internal Affairs portfolio. It would require a cross agency initiative as processes for determining sex are in place across numerous institutions. Recommendation : Clarifying that, where a person has amende d their registered sex and their name, their previous name will not appear on the birth certificate . Under regulations , where a person changes their name, the previous name would be printed on their birth certificate. Section ()(a) of the BDMRR Act and claus e () of the Bill provide an exception to this rule : where a person has amended their registered sex, their previous name is not included on the birth certificate. This helps to avoid outing a person as transgender or intersex . . However, t he way the rele vant provision is drafted in the Bill requires clarification. The Human Rights Commission advised that the provision is not entirely clear and risked misinterpretation they recommended drafting a more explicit provision . See paragraph of the Cabinet paper. See paragraph of IA Next steps for progressing the Births, Deaths, Marriages, and Relationships Registration Bill . E.g, if a person whose name was Gary amended their registered sex from male to female, and changed their name to Audrey, the fact they used to be called Gary would be omitted. If i t was not omitted, then there is a greater chance that people might think that the person is transgender. I seek Cabinets agreement to introduce a self identification process to enable a persons gender to be recognised on their birth certificate . I intend to introduce th e selfidentification process through the Births, Deaths, Marriages and Relationships Registration Bill. Executive summary . Since people have been able to amend their sex on their birth certificate. The process requires provid ing evidence of medical treatment to a Family Court judge who determines if an amendment to the birth register, and subsequently a birth certificate, can be made. . This process was considered progressive years ago but is now in need of improvement. It is not inclusive and fails to support peoples autonomy over how their gender is recognised . The Family Court process medicalises a deeply personal expression of self identity and is perceived as inaccessible for many people. . There is an opportunity to replace the Family Court process through the Births, Deaths, Marriages and Relationships Regis tration Bill (the Bill) . The Select Committee that consider ed the Bill proposed a new process where people would complete a statutory declaration to have their gender recognised on their birth certificate a self identification process. . Changing to a se lfidentification process will give transgender and intersex New Zealanders greater control over how their gender is officially recognised . It will enable transgender and intersex New Zealanders to use their birth certificate to access services (such as setting up a bank account or enrolling a child in school) with less risk of being outed or experiencing discrimination. It will help contribute to transgender and intersex peoples wellbeing and sense of belonging . . This paper seeks agreement to introduce a self identification process . It also proposes changes to the Bill to ensure selfidentification will reflect the needs of transgender and intersex communities as much as possible. This includes, for example, making self identification available to child ren and young people as well as adults. . These changes will be reflected in a supplementary order paper (SOP). I intend to refer this SOP to Select Committee to provide an opportunity for the public to engage on the selfidentification process . The ter m transgender is used in this paper to refer to all people whose gender differs from their assigned sex at birth this includes people who identify outside of the malefemale binary who may use a range of terms to describe their gender including non binary. Intersex is an umbrella term for people born with a variation of sex characteristics (such as sexual anatomy, reproductive organs, hormonal andor chromosome patterns). Intersex people are born with sex characteristics that are more diverse than narrow medical definitions of male or female bodies. Like anyone else, an intersex person may grow to identify with a different gender. Document Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs INCONFIDENCE Page of . I am not pro posing any changes to how sex is registered at birth. Gender is not known at birth and the information collected will continue to be based on sex. My proposals relate to amending how gender is recognised on birth certificates only. I am not proposing chang es to how other agencies and organisations determine a persons sex or gender , if that is necessary . I intend to maintain the policy position that birth certificates do not provide conclusive evidence of a persons sex or gender . Background Sex and gender are different . Gender is distinct from sex . Gender refers to a persons social and personal identity as a male, female, or another gender . Sex refers to a persons physiological features that characterise people as male , female or intersex . A persons gender is not always the same as their sex . . Society is changing to recognise the difference between sex and gender and that a persons gender may not be the same as their sex. In line with this shift, there is an increasing expectation that the Government should enable people to declare their gender on their official docum entation . Amending registered sex is a way fo r people to have their gender officially recognised . A persons s ex is re gistered at birth. Since people have been able to amend their registered sex, which is printed on their birth certificate , under the Births, Deaths, Marriages and Relationships Registration Act ( BDMRR Act ). . Under the current process, applicants need to provide evidence of medical treatment , which is then assessed by a Family Court judge who determines if the amendment can be made. While this process is about amending sex information, its existence recognises that a persons gender can be different to their sex. It is a mechanism for people to have th eir gender recognised. My proposal to introduce a self identification process for amending registered sex will make much needed improvements to this process. . I am aware that using a sex marker to represent gender conflates sex and gender . This is a compr omise I support to ensure there are no further delays to implementing a self identification process. Creating a separate gender marker on birth certificates has wider cost and timing implications for data collection and IT systems changes across government . In addition, the presentation of both sex and gender on birth certificates raises issues associated with outing a person as transgender or intersex. Improvements to the process to amend registered sex have previously been considered . The Bill was introduc ed in to re enact the BDMRR Act to modernise its drafting, and enable people to search online for birth, death and marriage records. The Select Committee considering the Bill recommended new provisions to replace the process for amending registered se x in . They proposed a process where people completed a statutory declaration to have their gender recognised on their birth certificate a self identification process. . The Bill was then deferred in February and is awaiting its second reading. In announcing their decision to defer the Bill, the previous Minister of Internal Affairs cited concern that the public had not been consulted on the self identification provision s. Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs INCONFIDENCE Page of Introducing a self identification process through the Bill . I intend to re sume progress on the Bill and to enact it this year if possible with a self identification process to recognise gender on birth certificates . Cabinet did not approve the introduction of a self identification process following Select Committee in . I wa nt to carry forward the Select Committees recommendation and am now seeking Cabinet agreement to the self identification provisions. . I would also like to make changes to the self identification provisions as they are drafted, to ensure they reflect the ne eds of the transgender and intersex communities. These changes will be reflected in a SOP. I intend to refer this SOP to Select Committee at the Bills second reading to provide an opportunity for the public to share their views on the self identification provisions. . I am not proposing any changes to how sex is registered at birth. Gender is not known at birth and the information collected will continue to be based on sex. . My proposals relate to amending how gender is recognised on birth certificates only . I am not proposing changes to how other agencies and organisations determine a persons sex or gender. Under the BDMRR Act, birth certificates are not intended to provide conclusive evidence of someones sex or gender. I intend to maintain this policy position. There is a strong case for introducing a self identification process The Family Court process to amend registered sex in the BDMRR Act needs reform . The Family Court proce ss to amend registered sex is not inclusive and fails to support peoples au tonomy over how their gender is recognised . It medicalises a deeply personal expression of self identity and is inaccessible . The process medicalises a deeply personal expression of self identity and is out of step with gender being about how a person perceives themselves. The process requires applicants to provide evidence they have undertaken medical treatment to physically conform with the sex they want recorded . The medical evidence is assessed by a Family Court judge who decides wheth er the application should be supported. . The medical evidence requirement excludes those who cannot or choose not to undertake medical treatment. For children and young people , the requirement could be seen to encourage medical treatment at a young age. This process was considered progressive in but is now seen as outdated and inconsistent with global developments. . The Family Court process is perceived to be costly , intimidating and difficult to navigate , making it inaccessible for many people . Countin g Ourselves , a survey of transgender and non binary people in New Zealand, found that per cent of respondents did not have the correct gender marker on their birth certificate. This is also reflected by the low number of applications to the Family Court to amend registered sex .

These changes refect the . per cent movement of the Consumer Price Index (CPI) All Groups Index for the calendar year. Background The Scheme assists lowincome ratepayers to meet the cost of rates . The Scheme was introduced by the Act. The amount of rebate provided to a household is det ermined by a formula based on total household income, level of rates, and the number of household dependents. . To be eligible for a rebate, the applicant must be usually resident at, and the ratepayer for, the property for which the rebate is being claimed. . Eligibility for a rebate is based on income for the previous tax year. Applicatons to the Sche m e for the ratng year will be based on income earned in the year up to March . . The Scheme is administered by territorial authorites and the Department of Internal Afair s (the Department). Territorial authorites accept and process applicatons to the Scheme and provide the rebate to recipients. The Department reimburses territorial authorites for the cost of rebates. Policy Cabinet previously endorsed regulatory changes to support harm minimisation in Class venues In March , Cabinet agreed to release the discussion document Reducing Pokies Harm, which focused on ways to strengthen the requirements in harm minimisation regulations for Class gambling (pokies in pubs, clubs and TAB venues ) SWC MIN refers. In June , this Government announced the new Strategy to Prevent and Minimise Gambling Harm for . It includes an action to identify improvement to the regulatory framework that could reduce gambling related harm. In September , following consultation on the discussion document, the Minister of Internal Affairs proposed a package of regulatory changes to enhance harm minimisation in Class venues, and to modernise infringemen t notice regulations related to payment of infringement offences. At that time, the Social Wellbeing Committee SWC MIN refers: . agreed to a package of regulatory amendments to improve harm minimisation in Class venues; and . agreed to introduce in fringement offences for failure to comply with the new requirements and existing provisions in the harm minimisation regulations. Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs and the Minister for Racing I N C O N F I D E N C E I N C O N F I D E N C E I am proposing one amendment to Cabinets previous decisions I propose that the regulation determining who must receive problem gambling awareness training be adjusted from earlier decisions to specify venue staff involved in supervising gambling. This will address sector concerns regarding the workability of this requirement. The need for change arises from targeted consultation on the regulations The Department of Internal Affairs (the Depa rtment) undertook targeted consultation on an exposure draft of these regulations with the Class gambling sector and gambling harm treatment providers in December and January . This process focused on the interpretation and implementation of the regulations and has identified necessary changes. All other changes are minor and technical, and I have approved these. In summary, these changes: . adjust the regulation regarding visibility of Electronic Gaming Machines from outside the venue, to accoun t for matters such as using fire exits; and . make minor changes to the requirements to support clearer interpretation and consistent regulatory enforcement. Timing and day rule Subject to Cabinets approval, I recommend that the proposed regulations be submitted to the Executive Council on May and in the New Zealand Gazette on May . I am proposing that: . Part of the Gambling (Harm Prevention and Minimisation) Amendment Regulations ; the Gambling (Infringement Offences) Regula tions ; and the Gambling (Infringement Notices) Amendment Regulations come into force on June , days after publication in the Gazette; . Part of the Gambling (Harm Prevention and Minimisation) Amendment Regulations come into force on September ; and . Part of the Gambling (Harm Prevention and Minimisation) Amendment Regulations and, Gambling (Infringement Offences) Amendment Regulations come into force on December . The proposed timing will allow the Clas s gambling sector appropriate time to implement changes before regulatory changes and associated infringements come into force. Some regulations will require more lead in time than others, due to requirements such as structural changes to venues. Phasing of the lead in time provides venues time to implement and ensures enforcement w ill not prematurely penalise liable persons.

U N C L A S S I F I E D Ofce of the Minister of Internal Afairs Chair Ca binet Legislaton Commitee Privacy (Informaton Sharing Agreement Facilitatng Access to Informaton about Deaths) Order Proposal . I seek approval to submit the Privacy (Informaton Sharing Agreement Facilitatng Acce ss to Informaton about Deaths) Order to the Executve Council. If approved the Order will give efect to the Death Approved Informaton Sharing Agreement (AISA)atached at Appendix A. Policy Finalising the proposed Death AISA . On November Cabinet agreed to policy proposals contained in a draf Death AISA CABMIN. This AISA has now been fnalised and will be given efect by the Privacy (Informaton Sharing Agreement Facilitatng Access to Informaton aboutDeaths) Order (Order in Council). . The law under which death informaton is collected, the Births, Deaths, Marriages andRela to nships Registraton Act (BDMRRA), requires formal agreements to allow the sharing of death informaton with organisatons, and only provides very limitedaccess to death informaton . It does, however, provide for other access arrangements to be made through an AISA. Where informaton sharing is not in place, the onus fallson the bereaved whnaufamily to provide documentaton to prove that someone has died. This can cause distress and inconvenience when whnaufamilies contnue to receive unwanted communicatons from organisatons that are not aware that the person has died. . The Death AISA will facilitate the sharing of death informaton with governmentagenc ies that are partes to the AISA and with a broader range of organisatons to improve outcomes for the whnaufamilies of New Zealanders who have died. It willalso improve the integrity of the customer informaton held by a range of organisatons and provide beter protecton against fraud by preventng the use of the details or assets of a person who has died. . The Department of Internal Afairs (DIA) has worked with the following agencies todevel op the Death AISA: Civil Aviaton Authority of New Zealand Department of Internal Afairs (DIA) Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet (DPMC) Fire and Emergency New Zealand Ministry for Ethnic Communites When the BDMRRA comes into force formal arrangements to allow the sharing of death informaton will stll be required Page of ikudgtnr Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs

U N C L A S S I F I E D Proactively released by the Minister for the Community and Voluntary Sector Page of Oral item Cabinet Social Wellbeing Committee: Modernising the Charities Act The Charities Act provides a registration, reporting and monitoring system to support public trust and confidence in charities .More than , charities are registered under the Charities Act (the Act). Charities spend around billion annually on charitable purposes and manage billion in assets. Some charities are widely known, such as Plunket Society or the Salvation Army. Many more are small charities that make a huge difference in communities, from maintaining marae to running toy libraries. I intend to resume policy work to modernise the Charities Act .Modernising the Act is about enabling the charities sector to thrive and to continue their valuable contribution to community wellbeing and social cohesion. .I intend to start by making practical improvements. To do so requires careful balan cing of principles like transparency with the compliance burden that small charities face from extensive annual reporting. I will take a balanced approach to looking at the business activities charities are involved in, while being mindful that the sustain ability of some charities is directly related to running successful businesses. A staged approach to deliver change and to pass an amendment bill this term .I will build on and progress the work that my colleagues launched last term. In , wide ranging and passionate views came through on the Act, through community meetings and submissions on a discussion document. .In restarting this work, I will shortly announce stage one. Stage one will lead to an amendment bill this term for a number of key areas publicly consulted on last term. .Stage one looks at: charities obligations; the regulators powers and decision making; the accessibility of appeals on decisions; and charities accumulation of funds and business activities. Progressing the re maining matters consulted on last term, such as advocacy by charities, is important. I will investigate a process for stage two next year. Targeted engagement before taking the first set of policy proposals to Cabinet .Policy development and testing wit h key stakeholders will focus first on small charities reporting requirements, and charities accumulation of funds and business activities. I will ensure that Ministers with portfolio interests in this work are kept informed of progress. Appendi x B: Privacy Commissioners s report on the Death Approved Informaton Sharing Agreement Page of ikudgtnr Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Deaths AISA Death Information Sharing Agreement For the purpose of facilitating access to information about deaths. UNCLASSIFIED of ikudgtnr : Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Deaths AISA Information Sharin.g Agreement This Agreement is established under subpart of Part of the Privacy Act to enable the Parties to share information about deaths. This Agreement assists with the provision of public services by facilitating access to accurate Death Information and Overseas Death Information for Organisations. It also provides for updating records about individuals associated with the deceased individual so that their records are also accurate. Parties to this Agreement may take subsequent actions based on the update of records relating to the deceased individual or associated persons, such as the granting of benefits or entitlements. This Agreement will ensure that personal information records held in Organisations databases or lists in electronic formats are from information held by the RegistrarGeneral when the individual in question has died. This will have a number of benefits including: Organisations having ready access to an authoritative source of registered death information in New Zealand from the Death Register. Other information currently available to Agencies may not be sufficient to clearly identify the correct individual, so having this new information avoids the risk of services and communications to a living individual being incorrectly discontinued; Organisations not having to approach the survivors of the deceased individual to require them to provide information andor a death certificate and thus placing an additional burden on people already dealing with complex issues following the death; Avoiding the risk that incorrect or false information may be provided to an Organisat ion; Organisations being aware of the death, so that whanau of the deceased individual do not receive official correspondence, subscription reminders, or invoices for charges which may cause significant upset or distress to the deceaseds family; and Organisations being able to take actions once they are aware that the individual has died, such as beginning the process to pay out an entitlement to the estate of the deceased individual, dealing with insurance, paying or changing social welfare or other benefits to survivors or changing accounts for survivors. This Agreement replaces the following agreements, which will be revoked once this Agreement is fully operational including the existence of operational procedures to share the required information: Agreement to provide birth and death information (Mortality Review Committees); AIA Services NZ Limited Information Supply Agreement; Cigna Insurance Limited Information Sharing Agreement; Domain Name Commission Information Supply Agreement; Forsyth Barr limited Information Supply Agreement; Government Superannuation Fund Information Matching Agreement; Maori Trustee Te Tumu Paeroa Information Sharing Agreement; Massey University Information Sharing Agreement; MyTrove Information.Sharing Agreement; National Provident Fund Information Matching Agreement; New Zealand Marketing Association Limited Information Sharing Agreement; University of Auckland Information Sharing Agreement; UNCLASSIFIED o ikudgtnr : Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Deaths AISA University of Waikato Information Sharing Agreement; Westpac New Zealand Limited Information Supply Agreement. UNCLASSIFIED of ikudgtnr : Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Deaths AISA . Background When people die in New Zealand, the law requires that the death is registered by the Registrar General of Births, Deaths, and Marriages. Many services cease or commence on the death of an individua l. The sharing of the information about deaths by the RegistrarGeneral helps to minimise encumbering whanau with unnecessary administrative processes at a difficult time. Both government and nongovernment Organisations need to have stringent processes in place to ensure that the correct person is noted as being deceased in their databases. If someone is mistaken ly identified as being dead, it can be very difficult for that person to convince other Organisations that they are, in fact, alive. DIA is leading the development of a small number of AISAs which are intended to replace the existing authorised information sharing arrangements and to allow new purposes to better meet the needs of individuals and Organisat ions. This AISA covers the sharing of information about deaths with New Zealand Agencies. The AISA is expected to better meet the needs of public sector agencies and Classes of Agencies and will allow more Organisations to receive information about deaths. . Objectives and purpose of this Agreement .. Objectives The objectives ofthis Agreement are to: a) enable updating of records when an individual dies; b) enable Organisat ions to gain customer service efficiencies and reduce the compliance load for individuals associated with the provision of information about deaths by facilitating increased collaboration; c) assist in the prevention of deaths; d) enable the prevention, detection, investigation and prosecution of offences, and the conduct of civil proceedings including judicial review; and e) apply Privacy by Design principles to the development and operation of the information sharing. .. Purposes The purposes of this information sharing are to: a) identify an individual and issue a Partner Specific Customer Identifier ifone does not exist; b) verify the details of the death of an individual; c) ensure that a person associated with an individual is not required upon the individua ls death to provide to a Party or Client death records that the RegistrarGeneral already holds; d) update the records of an individual or person associated with the individual upon the individuals death; e) cease providing a Personal Entitlement or Other Thing to an individual upon the individuals death. UNCLASSIFIED o ikudgtnr : Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Deaths AISA f) cease providing a Product or service to an individual or person associated with the individual upon the individual s death; g) to alter a Product or service being provided to a person associated with an individual upon the individual s death; h) offer or provide a Product, service, and Personal Entitlement or Other Thing to a person associated with an individual upon the individuals deth; i confirm or reaffirm whakapapa relationships; j conduct Mortality Reviews; k) cease enforcement action against a deceased individual or persons associated with the individual; and I enable the prevention , detection , investigation, and prosecution of offences, and the conduct of civil proceedings including judicial review. . Exemptions to information privacy principles For the purposes of t his Agreeme nt Information Privacy Principles (IPP , and which are set out in subpart of Part of t he Privacy Act are exempted (by the Order in Council as fol lows: a IPP : Source of Personal Information It is not a breach of Information Privacy Principle if a Party collects personal information from a Party in accordance with this Agreement and for one or more of the purposes specified in Clause .. b) IPP : Limits on the Use of Personal Information It is not a breach of Information Privacy Principle if a Party uses personal information collected by a Party in accordance with this Agreement and for one or more of the purposes specified in Clauses to . c) IPP : Limits on Disclosure of Personal Information It is not a breach of Information Privacy Principle if a Party discloses personal information to a Party in accordance with this Agreement and for one of more purposes specified in Clause .. . The public services facilitated The public services that this Agreement is intended to facilitate are: a the accurate and efficient assessment of eligibility for and entitlement to receive public services; b) the accurate and efficient delivery of public services by the RegistrarGeneral and the other public sector agencies that are Parties; c the provision by the Registrar General of accurate Death Information and Overseas Death Information to Parties that are New Zealand Private Sector Agencies for their use in accordance with Clauses to . d Mortality Reviews and advice on how to reduce preventable deaths; and e) prevention, detection, investigation, and prosecution of offences, and the conduct of civil proceedings including judicial review. Intermediaries may receive the raw personal information under this Agreement to enable Clients to use it for one or more of the purposes specified in the relevant schedule. Adverse Actions Process Section of the Privacy Act requires Parties to provide written notice to individuals before any adverse action is taken against them on the basis of personal information shared under an information sharing agreement and to give t hose individuals working days as defined in the Privacy Act to dispute the correctness ofthe information received. Parties may dispense with the notice requirements under section in the following circumstances: a) the Party has reasonable grounds to suspect an offence has been committed , is being committed or will be committed, and that the personal information is relevant to the prevention, detection, investigation or the prosecution ofthe offence, and advance notification to a suspect would be likely to prejudice the investigation or prosecution ofthe offence. b) the Adverse Actions consists only of removing the name of a deceased individual from a mailing list or a list used for marketing purposes . c) other legislation requires the Party to take immediate Adverse Action. Ifnotice has been dispensed under paragraph (c), notice of the Adverse Action must be provided as soon as practically possible, giving the individual an opportunity to dispute the correctness of the personal information relied on. . Possible transfer options, depending on the circumstance, are likely to include: a) API based transfer b) Direct system access c) Email d) Paper based transfer e) Bulk transfer. Safeguards to protect privacy ..Staff The following safeguards exist to protect the privacy of individuals and ensure that any interference with their privacy is minimised : a) All Parties to this Agreement, including their staff, will abide by the Standards of Integrity and Conduct set by the Public Service Commissioner . b) The staff of all Parties to this Agreement performing the services set out in this Agreement will hold all necessary statutory powers andor delegations required for the provision of those services, and will comply with relevant operational policy and procedures. .. Information Handling The following safeguards exist to protect the privacy of individuals and ensure that any interference with their privacy is minimised: a) No Party, excluding those who are Intermediaries, will provide the raw personal information obtained under this Agreement to other Organisations or any other third party including other Parties to this Agreement except as required by law or in order to comply with a court order. For the avoidance of doubt, this does not prevent a Party that has their information based on information received under this Agreement from disclosing their own information or a Party disclosing the information to their agents. UNCLASSIFIED of ikudgtnr : Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Deaths AISA b) Intermediaries may only provide the raw personal information obtained under this Agreement to Clients for one or more of the purposes specified in Clause except as required by law or in order to comply with a court order. The Intermediary must have a legal basis, other than this Agreement to be able to onshare the raw personal information to Clients. c) The raw personal informat ion obtained under this Agreement must not be made publicly available, including where a fee is paid, by any Party. d) Information received by any Party underthis Agreement, other than the Registrar Genera I, can only be used within the current legislative responsibiljt ies under the establishing legislation or the relevant government policies applying to that Party. e) Processes and procedures exist within each Party to ensure that information sent under this Agreement is transferred separately from information transferred under other agreements. f) Processes and procedures exist within each Party to ensure that the personal information received under this Agreement is only used for the purposes specified in this Agreement and remains protected. g) Processes and procedures exist within each Party to ensure that the personal information is not held longer than required. h) Each Party will handle Adverse Actions they may take in accordance with Clause ofthis Agreement. i) The PSCID will not be used as a unique identifier by any Party other than DIA and the RegistrarGeneral. j) No Party is obliged to provide any of the requested information to be shared under this Agreement. k) Awritten agreement governing the safeguards for the informat ion must exist betweeA each respective Intermediary and their Client, before the Intermediary shares information they received under this Agreement with the Client. I) Written agreements between Intermediaries and Clients, and any subsequent amendments, must be consulted on with the Registrar General and the Office of the Privacy Commission er prior to signing. m) Charities, Registered New Zealand Companies, Partnerships, Registered Limited Partnershiips, Friendly Societies, Credit Unions, Incorporated Societies and Intermediaries may only offer andorcommence Products and services where the deceased individual had a prior relationship with the Party. n) Where a Party discloses information under this Agreement to that Partys agent appropriate safeguards must be in place for the information provided. o) DIA will consult with the Office of the Privacy Commissioner regarding proposed operating procedures and any subsequen t changes. .. Accuracy The following safeguards exist to protect the privacy of individuals and ensure that any interference with their privacy is minimised: a) Parties will use reasonable endeavours to ensure that the information provided to other Parties is the most up to information available at the time it is provided. b) Appropria te mechanisms and standard procedures will be implemented by each Party to verify that personal information shared underthis Agreement is ofan adequate standard and quality. UNCLASSIFIED of ikudgtnr : Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Deaths AISA c) Where it is known that information has previously been shared under this Agreement by the RegistrarGeneral then updates as a result of a request for correction (including, where applicable and reasonable , any statement requested by the individual to be attached to tlhe information) must be communicated to the previous receiving Party and subsequently any Clients, as far as reasonably practicable. This does not apply to information supplied for the purposes of issuing a PSCID. .. Privacy Act Requests The following safeguards exist to protect the privacy of individuals and ensure that any interference with their privacy is minimised: a) Each Party will be responsible for responding to requests for personal information held bf that Party as appropriate in the circumstances . .. Privacy Breach The following safeguards exist to protect the privacy of individuals and ensure that any interference with their privacy is minimised: a) Where any Party has reasonable cause to believe that an actual or suspected breach of an IPP in respect of information provided under this Agreement , not covered by this Agreement, has occurred, an inspection andor internal investigation process will be applied utilising the identifying Partys standard processes. b) Where a Party identifies that a breach of any IPP in respect of information provided under this Agreement, not covered by this Agreemen t has occurred, the identifying Party will notify DIAs Privacy Officer as soon as possible. c) Where DIA or the RegistrarGeneral identifies that a breach of any IPP has occurred, in relation to information shared with them under this Agreement by another Party, and not exempted by this Agreement, DIA will notify the relevant Partys Privacy Officer as soon ai, possible. d) All relevant Parties shall ensure that reasonable assistance is provided to any investigation into an actual or suspected Privacy Breach in respect of information provided under this Agreement. e) Where a Party becomes of aware of actions amounting to a Notifiable Privacy Breach in relation to information they hold that was shared under this Agreement, in accordance with the Privacy Act , the Privacy Commissioner, and individuals will be notified by the Party. f) Any Party may suspend sharing under this Agreeme nt to allow time for a Privacy Breach tl be remedied . ..Audit The following safeguards exist to protect the privacy of individuals and ensure that any interference with their privacy is minimised: a) To ensure safeguards are operating as intended and are sufficient to protect the privacy of individuals, each Party will conduct regular internal first line assurance and internal audits of the operation of this Agreement. UNCLASSIFIED o ikudgtnr : Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Deaths AISA ..Security The following safeguards exist to protect the privacy of individuals and ensure that any interference with their privacy is minimised: a) All information provided under this Agreement will be appropriately secured when at rest and in transit in accordance with the New Zealand Information Security Manual (NZISM). b) Where a Security Breach is suspected or there is concern that a breach may occur, the identifying Partys internal investigation processes will be applied. c) Where a Party identifies that a Security Breach has occurred in relation to information provided under this Agreement, the identifying Party will notify DIAs Chief Security Officer as soon as possible. d) Where DIA or the RegistrarGeneral identifies that a Security Breach has occurred, in relation to personal information shared with them under this Agreement by another Party, DIA will notify the relevant Partys Security Officer as soon as possible. e) Reporting of near misses security investigations in relation to information provided under this Agreement will be provided by all Parties to DIAs Chief Security Officer on the agreed schedule. f) All relevant Parties shall ensure that reasonable assistance is provided to any investigat ion into an actual or suspected Security Breach in relation to information shared under this Agreement. g) Any Party may suspend sharing under this Agreement to allow time for a Security Breach to be remedied. . Reasonable assistance provided All Parties to this Agreement will provide each other with any reasonable assistance that is necessary in the circumstances to allow an individual to make a complaint about an interference with privacy and the Privacy Commissioner to investigate the complaint. If a New Zealand Private Sector Agency is unable to be held accountable for complaints about interference with privacy in relation to this Agreement, then DIA will be responsible for dealing with these complaints. . Management of classes At any time, DIA may agree to a New Zealand Agency becoming a member of a Class of Agencies specified in this Agreement and therefore becoming a Party to this Agreement. DIA must obtain the RegistrarGenerals consent prior to approval of the inclusion of a New Zealand Agency within a class. DIA does not need to obtain any other consent from any other Party prior to approval of the inclusion or removal of a New Zealand Agency within a class. Upon becoming a Party to this Agreement DIA will include the New Zealand Agencys name in the appropriate schedule and circulate the schedule to all Parties. Prior to including a New Zealand Agency into the Intermediary class DIA must give consideration to: a) the nature of the Intermediarys undertaking or activity and whether the Intermed iary has a genuine need and lawful purpose to use the personal information in carrying out that undertaking or activity; b) the Intermediarys policies and practices in relation to UNCLASSIFIED of ikudgtnr : Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Deaths AISA the security ofpersonal information; and the privacy of individuals; and c) any other matterthat DIA considers to be relevant. If a New Zealand Agency contained within a Class of Agencies wishes to no longer be Party to this Agreement, then they must advise DIA in writing. Upon receipt of this notification, DIA will remove the New Zealand Agencys name from the relevant schedule and they will cease to be a Party to this Agreement. The schedule will be circulated to all Parties and the removed NewZealand Agency. . Fees costs Fees associated with this Agreement, if any, as agreed will be notified by the RegistrarGene ral, or their delegated representative, in writing to the other Parties. . Dispute resolution Should any dispute arise relating to the interpretation or application of this Agreement, the respective Parties will meet in good faith to resolve the dispute or difference as quickly as possible. Ifthe Parties are unable to resolve the dispute within days, the matter will be referred to the Chief Executive of DIAs nominated representative for resolution. The Parties shall continue to comply with their obligations under this Agreement despite the existence of any dispute. . Review of this Agreement A joint review of this Agreement must be undertaken whenever any Party not included within a Class of Agencies believes that such a review is necessary. DIA shall conduct a review annually or at intervals specified by the Privacy Commissioner as specified in section ofthe Privacy Act . The report will be included in DIAs annual report. The Parties shall cooperate with each other in any review and will take all reasonable actions to make the required resources available. . Should Parties not included within a Class of Agencies be unable to agree on the amendments to this Agreement the matter will be dealt with in accordance with clause above. DIA will advise Parties included within a Class of Agencies a minimum of days prior to an amendment to this Agreement. In the event that the notified Party does not agree on the amendments then they must seek to be removed as a Party to this Agreement. Dog Control (Schedule ) Order Portfolio Local Government On June , the Cabinet Legislation Committee: noted that the Dog Control (Schedule ) Order will give effect to the decision to: . authorise K Medication Detection New Zealand through its medical alert function to certify disability assist dogs under the Dog Control Act ; . remove Top Dog Companion Trust as an approved organisation; . reinstate Assistance Dogs New Zealand and Perfect Partners Assistance Dogs Trust to Schedule of the Dog Control Act ; noted that a waiver of the day rule is sought: . so that the Order can come into force as soon as possible; . on the grounds that the Order will have little or no effect on the public and will result only in benefits; agreed to a waiver of the day rule so that the regulations can come into force on June ; authorised the submission to the Executive Council of the Dog Control (Schedule ) Order PCO .. Vivien Meek Committee Secretary Hardcopy distribution: (see over) U N C L A S S I F I E D hzagf Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government U N C L A S S I F I E D LEGMIN Present: Officials present from: Rt Hon Winston Peters Hon Chris Hipkins (Chair) Hon David Parker Hon Nanaia Mahuta Hon Stuart Nash Hon Jenny Salesa Hon Tracey Martin Hon Eugenie Sage Hon Ruth Dyson (Senior Government Whip)Office of the Prime Minister Officials Committee for LEG Hardcopy distribution: Minister of Local Government U N C L A S S I F I E D hzagf Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government UNCLASSIFIED P age of Office of the Minister of Local Government C hair Cabinet Legislation Comm ittee Dog Control (Schedule ) Order Proposal . I propose that the committee authorise the submission of the Dog Control (Schedule ) Order (the Order) to the Executive Council. This Order will add K Medical Detection New Zealand (KMD) to the list of approved organisations which have the a uthority to certi fy disability assist dogs under the Dog Control Act (the Act). This Order will also remove Top Dog Companion Trust from the list of approved organisations which have the authority to certify disability assist dogs , and correct a previous administrative error in which Assistance Dogs New Zealand , and Perfect Partners Assistance Dogs Trust were not transferred to Schedule of the Act. Policy . The Order prescribes regulations under section D of the Dog Control Act . This will enable K MD to become one of seven organisation s authorised to certify disability assist dogs. Background K Medical Detection New Zealand . On July , the Department of Internal Affairs (the Department) received and acknowledged an application from KMD seeking authorisation to certify disability assist dogs. . KMD is a registered charitable trust that is developing as an organisation . It intends to provide two distinct dog related support services: . Medical alert: This involves placing dogs with clients who live with a disabilityor illness that require a dog to assist them with their day today activities or alert them if an episode of their disorder has occurred, such as an epileptic fit; and . Medical detection: This involves assisting health and other agencies with the early detection of cancers, medical conditions, and contagious viruses, such as the norovirus. It does not involve pairing dogs with individual clients. . KMDs medical alert fun ction fits within the definition of a disability assist dog under the Act. Although medical detection dogs can be beneficial, detecting illnesses ordiseases is not assisting an individual with their disability in day today activities. I therefore do not consider KMDs medical detect service to fall within the definition of a disability assist dog. . For this reason, I have only approved the ability for KMD to certify disability assist dogs under the organisations medical alert function . Once approved, KMD will begin to provide its medical alert function to the public. Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government UNCLASSIFIED Page of The assessment process . Officials at the Department assessed KMD on three criterions : . Is there a need for the organisations disability assist dog service . Does the organisation have appropriate training practices and resources, and support for clients . Does the organisation have a legal, management, and governance structure that will ensure it can perform its role . The Departments officials have determined that KMD meet s all three criterions. Top Dog Companion Trust . My officials at the Department also advised me that there is an opportunity to remove Top Dog Companion Trust from the list of approved organisation s which have the authority to certify disability assist dogs under the Act . Top Dog Companion Trust is no long er practis ing and providing the service for which it was originally approved. Assistance Dogs New Zealand and Perfect Partners Assistance Dogs Trust . My officials have advised that due to an administrative e rror, Assistance Dogs New Zealand and Perfect Partners Assistance Dogs Trust were not transferred to Sched ule of the Act on the passing of the Local Government Regulatory Systems Amendment Bill . I propose to re add them to the Act as the organisatio ns are active and providing the service for which they were initially approved . Consultation with the Minister for Disability Issues .
