UNCLASSIFIED Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs INCONFIDENCE Page of Office of the Minister of Internal Affairs Chair Cabinet Social Wellbeing C ommitt ee Proposed amendments to the Films, Videos, and Publications Classification (Urgent Interim Classification of Publications and Prevention of Online Harm) Amendment Bill Proposal . This paper seeks agreement to amend clause of the Films, Videos, and Publications Classification (Urgent Interim Classification of Publications and Prevention of Online Harm) Amendment Bill (the Bill). The proposed amendment would remove sections L O (the filtering provisions) from the Bill. Relation to government priorities . The proposals in this Bill are a direct response to the Christchurch terror attacks and address some gaps and limitations in our classification legislation. Executive summary . The proposals in the Bill were developed as a direct response to the Christchurch terror attacks and address specific inefficiencies and ambiguities in our classification legislation. On December , Cabinet agreed to t he proposals set out for the Bill CAB MIN refers. . The Bill was introduced to Parliament in May and was referred to the Governance and Administration Committee (the Committee) at its First Reading on February . I inherited the Bill fro m the previous Minister of Internal Affairs and have previously indicated that I was open to refining the Bills filtering provisions depending on what came out of the Select Committee stage, given the strong views in this area. . Internet filtering can be a useful tool to prevent access to and mitigate harms from objectionable (illegal) content online. An example of this is the current Digital Child Exploitation System (DCEFS), which specifically filters child sexual abuse material. Child sexual abuse materi al is universally accepted as abhorrent and blocking this type of material has not been challenged. Further expansion of the categories of illegal material to be filtered needs detailed consideration to ensure the proper safeguards are there to prevent abu se of this power. . The current proposals leave this detail to be determined in regulations to allow flexibility for new technologies. On balance a statutory filter provision needs more detail about the safeguards. To achieve that, the detailed work that was planned following enactment of the Bill would need to be brought forward. Progressing this work now would risk a further delay to the implementation of the other key regulatory and enforcement provisions of the Bill. This is consistent with the advice tha t I have received from my officials. kzzqft Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs INCONFIDENCE Page of . Submitters also acknowledged that more detail is needed before progressing the filtering provisions. The submissions received on the Bill throughout the Select Committee stage have indicated that there is a lack of public mandate to progress with the curre nt filtering provisions at this time. Submissions highlighted the need to set out the specific scope of the filter in primary legislation and emphasised the need for further public consultation and community engagement. . These submissions are consistent wi th wider community feedback received during huis held on the report of the Royal Commission of Inquiry into the terrorist attack on Christchurch masjidain on March . Feedback from those huis emphasised the need for greater community engagement and c odesign of policies on a wide range of areas relevant to the classification and censorship system such as hate speech and balancing reform in that area with the right to freedom of expression, as well as greater scrutiny of the standards of media and on line reporting on minority and faith community issues. . This paper therefore, seeks agreement to remove the current filtering provisions from the Bill and investigate a voluntary approach to filtering. Background . In the aftermath of the Christchurch terror attacks, internet service providers (ISPs) and online content hosts worked collaboratively with Government to prevent people from spreading and accessing online footage of the attacks. While these efforts were largely effective, the experience highlighted inefficiencies and ambiguities in our censorship system for responding to objectionable online content. This Bill was developed as a direct response to the Christchurch terror attacks by addressing these inefficiencies and ambiguities in the Films, Videos , and Publications Classification Act (the FVPC Act. . On December , Cabinet agreed to the following policy proposals in the Bill CAB MIN refers: . knowingly livestreaming objectionable content will become a criminal offence punishable by up to years in prison; . allowing the Chief Censor to make interim classification decisions; . allowing take down notices to be issued to require the removal of objectionable online content; . making online content hosts subject to a civil pecuniary penalty of up to ,, if they do not comply with an issued take down notice; . ensuring safe harbour provisions in the Harmful Digital Communications Act would not apply to objectionable online content; and . enabling the establishment of regulations that would allow the government to implement web filtering of objectionable content if required. . The Bill updates the FVPC Act to allow for urgent prevention and mitigation of harms caused by objectionable content online. The term objectionable refers to alre ady illegal content as defined in the FVPC Act; this includes content which describes, depicts or expresses, or otherwise deals with matters such as sex, horror, crime, cruelty or violence in such a manner that the availability of publication is likely to be injurious to the public good. It is an offence to make, possess, supply or distribute objectionable content. kzzqft Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs INCONFIDENCE Page of . The Bill will improve the way we regulate objectionable content, including violent extremist and terrorist content found online. Specifically, the Bill amends the Act to: . criminalise knowingly livestreaming objectionable content; . allow the Chief Censor to make interim classification assessments in relation to publications (both physical as well as online) likely to be found objectionable in urge nt situations; . allow take down notices to be issued to require the removal of objectionable online content; . make online content hosts subject to a civil pecuniary penalty of up to ,, if they do not comply with an issued take down notice; . ensure the safe harbour provisions in the Harmful Digital Communications Act would not apply to objectionable online content; and . enable the establishment of regulations that would allow the Government to implement filtering of objectionable content online if required (the filtering provisions). . I inherited the Bill from the previous Minister of Internal Affairs and was keen to progress it to Select Committee stage to hear views on the filtering provisions, as there were arguments for and against. . The Bill wa s introduced to Parliament in May and was referred to the Committee at its First Reading on February . On April I attended the presentation of the initial briefing on the Bill and signalled to the Committee that I was particularly intere sted in submissions and discussions on the filtering provisions. . Since then, the filtering provisions have been the most submitted upon aspect of the Bill. The majority of the submissions that mentioned the filtering provisions were opposed to it. In contr ast, the submissions that touched on other provisions of the Bill were mostly supportive and only recommended some minor technical changes. . The views expressed by submitters on the Bill align with community feedback from huis on the report of the Royal Com mission of Inquiry into the terrorist attack on Christchurch masjidain on March , specifically that proposals relating to freedom of expression should be developed through co design and engagement with communities. Internet filtering can be a usefu l tool to prevent access and mitigate harms from objectionable content online . In New Zealand, internet filtering already takes place without a legislative mandate or regulatory framework. This currently includes the voluntary DCEFS, which specifically filters child sexual abuse material. This filter is run by the Department of Internal Affairs (DIA). While the DECFS is voluntary for ISPs, the majority of ISPs in New Zealand use the filter, which means that approximately per cent of New Zealand internet users are protected from child sexual abuse material. kzzqft Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs INCONFIDENCE Page of . The proposed internet filtering provisions in the Bill provide an enabling framework and set out obligations on Government when implementing any mechanism to prevent access to other kinds of objectionab le content, outside of child sexual abuse material and imagery. The filtering provisions would not establish a filter but would give Government explicit statutory authority to explore and implement such mechanisms through regulations in the future. The fil tering provisions are in clause of the Bill under new sections L to O. . If established, the purpose of a filter would be to prevent access to content that is already illegal to possess or distribute. It is one of a range of tools that can be used to assist in mitigating the harms of objectionable content online. These harms can include revictimization for example, recurring distress and trauma to victims from viewing an incident again or having others see footage of their experiences and bei ng unintentionally exposed to this type of footage. Some of the most objectionable content on the internet is peddled by sites that will never respond to New Zealands or any other jurisdictions request to remove such content. A filter could act as a last line of defence when other approaches to remove this content have failed. Submissions indicate that there is a lack of public mandate to progress with the current filtering provisions at this time . On April , written submissions closed for the Bill a nd the Committee received a total of unique written submissions. The Committee received submissions that specifically referred to the filtering provisions in the Bill. Out of those, four submitters supported filtering and submitters were against filtering. A further submissions, while not referencing the filtering provisions specifically, were opposed to the Bill in full due to concerns that the Bill would impose on New Zealanders freedom of expression, which is the predominant reason for oppo sing the filter. . Some submitters acknowledged that there may be benefits to filtering objectionable content. However, this support was qualified by the need to clarify the detail and scope of any proposed filter. The filter being set in regulations was not seen as the best approach as there would be a lack of Parliamentary oversight into the development of the filter, and a risk of insufficient legal safeguards. As currently drafted, the legislation is not intended to be too prescriptive in order to provide sufficient flexibility so that developments in technology do not undermine the policy intent. . However, submitters opposed to filtering noted that there is a need for more specific detail on the scope, design and operation of the filter in the Bill. Submi ssions from academics, the technology sector, ethnic community groups and interest bodies prefer that the Government consult on these aspects of any potential filter before finalising proposals and progressing legislation to implement a filter. This was re flected specifically by those in vulnerable groups that the filtering provisions are intended to protect. There were also concerns raised about the potential infringement on freedom of expression and the effectiveness of a filter, as it can be easily circu mvented. . Several submissions suggested that the filter provisions be removed from the Bill and be progressed as a stand alone legislation so that there is appropriate Parliamentary decision making and oversight of this issue. There was some commentary tha t any work on filtering should be considered as part of a wider review of the media regulatory landscape. There have also been suggestions of a voluntary approach like the existing DCEFS. kzzqft Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs INCONFIDENCE Page of . I did consider options to redraft so that the filter is not set in r egulations but primary legislation. However, I decided against this as it would not address the issues of a lack of detail about the proposed design and operation of the filter. It would also not address concerns about the potential infringement on freedom of expression and the effectiveness of a filter. . While there appears to be a lack of public mandate to progress the filter, there are also additional issues to consider. This includes ensuring that the creation of a filter is fit for purpose, which would require setting out the exact scope of the filter and broader public consultation. There is also the risk of the Bill being further delayed to allow time to determine technical specifications of the filter, which would mean other key regulatory and enforce ment proposals in the Bill that are needed now would be unable to be progressed. My preferred approach is to remove the current filtering provisions from the Bill and investigate a voluntary filter . As noted above in paragraphs to , filtering can be a useful tool to prevent access to and mitigate harms from objectionable content online noting that this is content that is already illegal. However, having heard from submitters throughout the select committee process, it appears that there is strong oppo sition for a statutory mandated filter for objectionable content online and more work is required in this area. Therefore, my preferred approach is to remove the filtering provisions from the Bill and investigate a voluntary approach to filtering. This app roach would amend clause , Part A of the Bill by removing: . section L: Electronic system to prevent public access to objectionable online publications; . section M: Establishment of electronic system; . section N: Approval of electronic system for op eration; and . section O: Review of decisions and actions relating to operation of electronic system. . To allow for Cabinet consideration of the above proposals, I have written to and obtained permission from the Committee Chair to extend the report back d ate of the Departmental Report to June . The Department of Internal Affairs will continue to investigate a voluntary filter . There is some support for the concept of filtering objectionable content, particularly among Internet Service Providers (ISP) . This is important as any filtering would work at the ISP level. I also think that there is a place for filtering as it can reduce harm for the most vulnerable, such as young people, from inadvertent access to objectionable content. However, I acknowledge that setting the filter in regulations is not the best approach. I have therefore directed my officials to investigate and provide me with advice on alternative options for progressing a voluntary approach to filtering for ISPs. A voluntary approach would align with the existing mechanism in place to filter child sexual abuse material and imagery. kzzqft Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs INCONFIDENCE Page of . I do not recommend removing the provisions and progressing stand alone legislation to implement filtering objectionable content at this stage. Submitters who su ggested this approach stressed that the legislation would need to set out specific details, such as the exact scope of the filter, technical capability details as well as governance and technical oversight arrangements. I anticipate these issues will be wi thin scope of work to progress a voluntary filter. Stand alone legislation to provide statutory authority to a voluntary filter can be explored in due course if there is evidence of sufficient public mandate for this to occur or a voluntary approach is uns uccessful. . In relation to submissions suggesting this issue be considered within the wider media review (the review), I note that the purpose of the review is to develop and establish an overarching framework for regulating and moderating media and online content. Proposals developed within that broader framework may have potential cascading implications on aspects of work to progress a voluntary filter. I have been advised by my officials that they will remain mindful of possible links between proposals developed as part of the review and filtering options, and where appropriate align these workstreams as necessary. Next steps . If Cabinet approval the removal of the filtering provisions, the Bill will be amended to remove sections L to O in clause , Part A. This will require a delay to the final report back of the Departmental Report to allow time for the amendments to be drafted. Financial implications . There are no financial implications. Legislative implications . Subject to Cabinet approval t he Bill will be amended to remove sections L to O in clause , Part A. This will require a delay to the final report back of the Departmental Report to allow time for the amendments to be drafted. Impact analysis Regulatory Impact Statement . The population implication s have previously been stated in the previous Cabinet paper CAB MIN refers, which acknowledges that to the extent that any groups are disproportionately impacted by exposure to violent extremist and terrorist content online, the proposals aim to reduce that harm. These groups include ethnic communities, women, and people with disabilities. Human Rights . The proposals in this paper have previously been addressed in the initial Cabinet paper CAB MIN refers which, acknowledged that regulatin g objectionable content that involves violent extremist and terrorist online content raises issues of consistency with the right to freedom of expression, recognised in section of the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act (NZBORA). . The proposals in this paper do not change the current definition of objectionable under the FVPC Act. While freedom of expression is not an absolute right, limits should not be imposed on it unless justified. New Zealand law already limits freedom of expression in this area by imposing a range of legal restrictions on the publication of objectionable content (which cover acts of terrorism). These limitations are reasonably justified because of the potential harm this content may pose to New Zealanders, as well as the wider direc t or indirect harms to our communities. The proposals in this paper do not negatively impact on freedom of expression. Consultation . In summary, previous papers highlighted that, in many parts of the country, communities cannot be confident that their drinking water is safe, or that good environment al outcomes are being achieved from wastewater and stormwater systems. They also raised concerns about the regulation, sustainability, capacity and capability of a system with a large number of localised providers, many of which are funded by relatively s mall populations. . The papers noted that hard data on the extent of the problem is variable and, in some cases, limited, which is in itself evidence of a wider systemic issue. However, overall, the following problems affect all of the three waters: . Weakne sses across the regulatory system . Both drinking water and environmental regulation exhibit, in differing degrees, inadequate stewardship, leadership, and compliance, monitoring and enforcement practices. . Funding and financing challenges . Three waters p roviders face a range of affordability issues and financial pressures. Many councils are struggling to fund plant and pipe infrastructure to the level required to meet standards and community aspirations, keep pace with population growth, and build resilie nce against natural events. Affordability challenges are particularly acute for smaller communities, rural and provincial councils, non council drinking water suppliers, and marae. These communities are finding it difficult to afford quality infrastructur e and services, especially within current structures and funding arrangements. . Capability and capacity challenges . Good capability is the key to meeting regulatory requirements, designing, procuring, delivering and managing three waters services, and unde rtaking complex public health and environmental risk assessments. However, it is often difficult for service providers to develop the capabilities required, and to access and retain people with specialist skills. These challenges tend to be greater for s maller rural and provincial councils, and non council drinking water suppliers (such as small private and community schemes, and marae). . The Government Inquiry into Havelock North Drinking Water ( Havelock North Inquiry ) provided considerable evidence for reform. The Inquiry concluded that the problems in Havelock North are not confined to that area, and there is a widespread systemic failure of water suppliers to meet the high standards required to ensure the safe supply of drinking water to the public. If action is not taken, there are risks of similar incidents occurring elsewhere, with potentially serious consequences. . The events that led to the Havelock North contamination event in , along with the findings of the subsequent Inquiry, have demonstr ated that the existing system does not adequately safeguard against the risk of catastrophic contamination incidents, or drive improved compliance with the drinking water standards. The Department of Internal Affairs commissioned two reports to explore capability and capacity issues facing local government three waters providers Castalia Ltd: Three waters asset management maturity in New Zealand (October ); and MartinJenkins: Three Waters Review interface between asset management and council governance (December ). UNCLASSIFIED This proposal supports access to justice, while best recognising the public and private benefit s of an appeal . A moderate fee might discourage vexatious appeals which could use up valuable tribunal time and resources . A moderate fee might also encourag e alternative avenues to resolve an issue ( for example, charities can object to an intended decision . If dissatisfied with the outcome of the objections process, they can appeal the final decision to the Authority ). To ensure the fee does not become a barrier to accessing the Authority , I am also proposing a fee waiver , which is a comm on tool to mitigate the risk that those with limited resources cannot access appeals and consider the specific public benefit of an appeal on a case bycase basis . Criteria for waiving a filing fee are discussed at paragraph .. Three other options do not recognise public and private benefit or support access to justice as well as the proposal I considered three other options that could meet the core objective to support access to justice including no fee, a low fee without a waiver, and a higher fee ( ) with a waiver. However , these options either do not appropriately acknowledge public and private benefit or do not support access to justice for all charities as well as the preferred proposal . Charging no fee or a low fee (without a waiver) assumes that the public benefit provided by appeals outweighs any private benefit to the appellant. The impact of this option is that the taxpayer would cover more of the Authority s operating costs than the proposed option . A higher fee (with a waiver) would require appellants to contribute more towards the cost of running the Authority . Most charities are small , so affording this fee may be more difficult than the other options . Therefore, relying heavily on the waiver process might still not support ac cess to justice for all charities . Proposals for procedural matters I am proposing several regulations to ensure that the Authority: . can process an appeal seamlessly from its commencement to conclusion; and . aligns with the wider tribunal system , while accounting for the charities context when appropriate ( for example, timeframes) . UNCLASSIFIED . The CVoD Amendment Bill will enable CVoD providers to self rate their content rather than referring material to OFLC or the Film and Video Labelling Body (FVLB). The classification rating of CVoD content before screening will minimise the risk of harm to children and young people. . It will also support informed viewing choices by all New Zealanders by ensuring the content has the appropriate classificationrating and advisory notes consistent with the New Zealand classification regime. T he CVoD Amendment Bill is expected to be passed into law by mid. The Department has commenced a Review into funding options for the classification system . The purpose of the Review is to return OFLC to a financially viable position, so that OFLC can continue to support New Zealanders to make informed viewing choices and minimise the availability of harmful material. . The scope of the Review includes considering the appropriate level of cost recovery (full, partial or no cost recovery) from the sector , and whether there is a more effective mechanism (fees andor a levy) to fund the classification framework than the status quo of government funding and user charges. . Public consultation is part of Stage of the Review. Stage is d evelopment and implementation of a new funding regime for OFLCs existing and CVoD activities . Issues with the current funding arrangements . There are three main issues with the existing funding arrangement s. Fees for current classification activities are not aligned with costs . The fees prescribed in the Regulations have not been reviewed since and are no longer aligned with costs in curred by OFLC. Inflation has also eroded the value of the fees. Over time, the income foregone from the fee levels not being regularly adjusted is significant. Expenditure associated with OFLCs classification activities has regularly exceeded income and this is projected to continue. Income from existing user charges has been declining . The size of the DVD market has decreased as media content is increasingly made available online through o nDemand and streaming services. OFLCs r evenue from user charges arising from the classification of DVDs is in decline. From to , revenue from user charges from classifying commercial publications , such as DVDs and films for release in theatres , has reduced by percent , from . million to . million. A funding regime for OFLCs new CVOD related activities is needed . OFLC will perform new activi ties related to regulating CVoD content and supporting providers to self rate their material. The new activities involve maintenance and enhancements of self rating tools and resources, auditing a nd reviewing provider s selfrating outputs, engagement with providers , and information to the public. A funding regime for these activities is needed. OFLCs classifies restricted material and the FVLB rates unrestricted material. Page of

Prior to COVID , territorial authorities were planning on spending up to . billion in capital over the next five years on water infrastructure. However, COVID is likely to cause significant decreases in revenue in territorial authorities over the short term. Revenues could decline by between per cent and per cent o ver the next financial year, and local authorities are facing increased cost pressures. As a result, borrowing will be constrained due to lower debt limits that flow from lower revenues, and opportunities to raise revenue through rates, fees and charges w ill be extremely limited. . Previous behaviour indicates that i nvestment in water infrastructure is an area where councils have constrained spending in response to financial pressures. Investment in water infrastructure is long term, and has a less visible impact on communities than other forms of council expenditure. . The Three Waters Review has highlighted that New Zealands water infrastructure already carries a burden of underinvestment. This is likely to worsen in response to COVID , and could have serious consequences for the condition of water infrastructure . We estimate that, in the absence of support from the Crown, territorial authorities will face pressure to reduce planned capital investment in three waters infrastructure by approximately . billion over the next three years. . A lack of investment in, and deterioration of, water infrastructure will perpetuate some of the systemic problems identified above. This could also jeopardise the effectiveness of the three waters regulatory reforms if councils are unable to afford to carry out the upgrades necessary to comply with drinking water regulatory requirements, for example. Options identification and analysis . Three Waters Ministe rs have been considering the potential for service delivery reforms for some time , and there have been prior Cabinet decisions on this topic . The latest paper proposes certain core components of the new service delivery model , thereby setting the basic di rection for further policy development work and discussions with local government. . The proposed approach involves: . the creation of multi regional, asset owning water providers, which would be statutory entities; . protecting public ownership within new serv ice delivery models and legislation , and developing ownership arrangements that involve local government. . The rationale for these proposals, and other alternatives that have been considered, is discussed below. This is based on advice that has been developed throughout the Three Waters Review. . Approaches to service delivery reform . Previous Cabinet papers identified three potential approaches to service delivery reform: . voluntary, sector led reforms to service delivery ar rangements; . establishment of a three waters fund to support voluntary service delivery improvements; and . creation (in legislation ) of an aggregated system of dedicated, publicly owned drinking water and wastewater providers. . In January , Cabinet Business Committee noted that the case for change to the current structural arrangements for the delivery of three waters services continues to build , and that changes to how New Zealand delivers three waters services are required . . At that time, it was agreed that central government would continue to support local government to make voluntary changes to service delivery arrangements , but set a oneyear deadline for the sector to demonstrate progress. Work would also be undertaken in parallel to explore t he other options identified above. . Since those decisions were made, the COVID response and recovery work has led to a reconsideration of this process . The preferred approach is to move ahead with service delivery reform through the creation of multi regional, asset owning water entities coupled with Crown investment in water infrastructure . This is considered to be the most effective mechanism for achiev ing the dual goals and multiple objectives referred to earlier in this document. . Alternatives to the proposed approach were identified. For example, alternatives to the economic stimulus could include: . asking councils to fund further investments on their balance sheets, by utilising further borrowing ; . support ing council debt through issuing some form of government bond ; . using alternative funding or financing arrangements to support further investment in three waters assets, such as Special Purpose Vehicles (SPVs) . UNCLASSIFIED . We also considered whether economic stimulus could accompany voluntary service delivery reform, or could be unconditional. . These options were assessed in terms of their feasibility and effectiveness in meeting the dual goals and objectives. Considerations included the likelihood the goalsobjectives will be met, the nature and extent of the effectimpact, timeliness, and certainty of outcome. . None of the alternative approaches were considered to be as effective as the proposed approach. In summary: . Asking councils to fund further investments on their balance sheets, by utilising further bor rowing , is unlikely to be effective and would not bridge the expected investment gaps . The decrease in revenues will severely constrain councils ability to take on more debt , and mean most councils will need to curtail almost all of their borrowing progr ammes. We estimated that, in aggregate, councils will only be able to borrow an additional million per annum without breaching debt torevenue limits. This is insufficient to bridge the expected billion investment gap. . Support ing council debt thro ugh issuing some form of government bond is only an attractive option if the differential is large and councils have a greater ability to take on debt than current circumstances allow. Overall, the likelihood of this occurring is low, and unlikely to be s ufficiently attractive to the sector nor sufficient to prevent deterioration of the infrastructure. . There are several challenges with using SPVs, particularly from an immediate response perspective, and they would not incentivise structural reform. SPVs are not well suited to brown field development or renewal of assets, which is what the bulk of this programme of work is looking to support in the short to medium term. SPVs also typically rely heavily on private or overseas equity investment to fund up front capital costs. Due to the economic shock relating to COVID , it is likely that ready access to private equity and capital will be limited, and the Crown will need to step in to help fill this gap in the short term. Even in instances where private e quity is available, borrowing costs are likely to escalate substantially for firms to access this form of capital. . Evidence to suggests that the political and economic barriers to voluntary reforms are high. Proceeding with a voluntary approach to s ervice delivery reform , or unconditional investment, would not guarantee th at reform will occur or be achieved in a way that meets the objectives . This would not represent a sound investment approach or good use of public money. Number of entities . The p referred approach involves the creation of a small number of multi regional water service providers , which would be asset owning . . It is anticipated that t his would realise a number of economic and other benefits associated with large scale providers, addr ess the many of the systemic issues and infrastructure deficits facing the three waters system, and help to deliver the reform objectives. Benefits include: Department of Internal Affa irs Supplementary information Page of rnfoawab Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government
UNCLASSIFIED . increased financial capacity and capability, with stronger, more flexible and resilient balance she ets, greater access to capital, and a more reliable investment pipeline; . opportunities to take a strategic and coordinated approach, to consider infrastructure needs at a larger scale and in the context of wider catchment outcomes; . building technical capab ilities, with access to a larger, more specialist workforce, and the ability to innovate and make use of new technology; . enabling financial efficiencies and lower operating costs, by consolidating administration and overhead costs, and improving organisati onal capabilities; . enabling more consistent water charges, with the ability to harmonise tariffs across much larger areas. . Many of these benefits are only realised (fully or partially) if the new entities are asset owning. Shared services models that do not involve asset ownership have a number of shortcomings, including the inability to access scale or scope efficiencies, and split accountabilities. . Wellington Water is a current example of a shared service council control led organisation that manages and operates drinking water and wastewater assets and services for its council owners. However, each of the councils continue to own water assets and raise revenue (on advice from Wellington Water) for the operation, maintenan ce and, where necessary, the upgrade of those assets. Wellington Water has no ability to make trade offs between operating and capital expenditure, nor can it cross subsidise between owners or ratepayers in different districts. . How many multi regional wat er providers would be created, and their boundaries, is a matter for discussion between Ministers and local government. However, it is proposed that f inal decisions on these matters would be based on the following factors: . scale benefits including at least one very large urban centre within each entity, to ensure the full benefits of scale are achieved through a larger network and population base; . communities of interest; . relationships with other jurisdictional boundarie s, including catchments. . UNCLASSIFIED . However, we consider that this option has a number of disadvantages and drawbacks, and would not be effective in achieving the benefits sought from multi regional models . For example: . Current provisions in the Local Government Act are not fit for this purpose, and present barriers to reform. It is likely to take as long to redesign and amend the existing legislative provisio ns, as it would to create bespoke provisions in new legislation (including some form of economic regulation). . They may not be sufficiently separate from local government to borrow at similar rates as other utilities , for example . Public ownership . Throughout the Three Waters Review, there has been a clear and explicit bottom line about public ownership. . On November , Cabinet agreed that the outcome of three waters reforms would include that existing three waters assets and services must remain in public ownership, and the system will incorporate safeguards to protect public ownership of this essential infrastructure, both now and in the future CAB MIN refers. . This decision is supported by the noting recommendatio n in January referenced earlier in this document, and recent discussions with Three Waters Ministers. . The Department strongly agrees with this position, and has not identified or assessed alternative options. There are significant disadvantages and r isks associated with privatisation , and no clear benefits . There would be extensive public and local government opposition to privatisation. . Evidence from overseas indicates that most of the similar jurisdictions that have successfully reformed their wa ter service delivery arrangements have created publicly owned entities. For example , Scottish Water is owned by the Scottish Government, while Tas mania Water (TasWater) is owned by local authorities and the Tasmanian Government. . There would be various w ays of structuring a public ownership model. The proposed approach involves local government collective ownership of the new service delivery entities, through local authority shareholders. This is the preferred approach, given local government currently owns the water assets that would be transferred to the new entities. This would enable local authorities to continue to have a strategic oversight role in relation water services, and maintain a link with other council responsibilities and local communiti es. . The basis for shareholding will need careful consideration and financial analysis. It could be possible to apportion shares on the basis of the condition of the assets that are transferred, to reward previous investment and good asset maintenance. There could also be potential to provide for some form of annual return to shareholderscouncils. Background The Charities Amendment Act (Amendment Act) introduced changes to the Charities Act (Charities Act), including improvements to the appeals process . From July , t he Taxation Review Authoritys jurisdiction will expand to hear charities appeals to provide charities with a more accessible appeals avenue prior to the High Court. Charities will be able to appeal decisions related to their registration under the Charities Act to the Authority . The Amendment Act provid es for the key details, like the specific decisions that can be appealed and who can appeal. The Amendment Act also includes provisions for regulations to provide for the Authoritys procedures and to give full effect to the Amendment Act . Cabinet noted in February that regulations may be required SWC MIN . Without regulations, filing an appeal will be free of charge. Processes that are not provided for in the Amendment Act will follow the District Court Rules . Having an accessible appeals process is important for charities. Registration brings significant benefits to a charity such as an income tax exemption. Decisions affecting a charitys registration status (such as potential deregistration) could significant ly impact on a charitys ability to raise funds for their intended purpose. Decisions about individuals ( for example, potential serious wrongdoing by an officer of a charity) do not affect a charitys registration status but can still cause disruption and could impact a charitys ability to fundraise . Consultation with stakeholders between November and January provided valuable and varied perspectives that informed final proposals . Submitters main concern was that the appeals process be as accessible as possible. Setting regulations can reflect the importance of access to justice while acknowledging other considerations such as the public and private benefit s that appeals generate (discussed below). Regulations will also ensure seamless end toend processes of the Authority and alignment with the wider tribunal system . Proposal for a filing fee I am proposing a single filing fee of with provision of a fee waive r For filing an appeal with the Authority under the Charities Act , I am proposing a single filing fee of with provision of a fee waiver . Establishing this moderate fee is consistent with access to justice as the fee amount reflects the public benefit by the Authority (for example, clarifying unclear law and the nature of peoples rights and duties) and any private benefit to the appellant ( for example, from obtaining a decision that specifically determines the appellants issue) . All fee amounts are inclusive of GST. UNCLASSIFIED Proactively released by the Minister for the Community and Voluntary Sector

UNCLASSIFIED Context . Over the past two and a half years, the Minister of Local Government has been leading a cross government review of the system for regulating and managing drinking water, wastewater and stormwat er (the Three Waters Review). A group of Three Waters Ministers has met regularly to discuss and provide input into this work. A large group of agencies, led and coordinated by the Department of Internal Affairs, have provided advice to these Ministers. . Cabinet has considered, and made a series of decisions on, a series of papers relating to the Three Waters Review: . Review of three waters infrastructure: key findings and next steps (April ). . Future state of the three waters system: regulation and service delivery (November ). . A Plan for Three Waters Reform (July ). . Strengthening the regulation of drinking water, wastewater and stormwater (July ) supported by a Regulatory Impact A ssessme nt. . Institutional arrangements for a drinking water regulator (September ) supported by a Regulatory Impact A ssessment and business case . . Three waters service delivery and funding arrangements: approach to reform (January ). . The current paper , Investing in water infrastructure to accelerate reform and support economic recovery post COVID (May ) , builds on and is informed by previous decisions made by Cabinet, as well as d iscussions with Three Waters Ministers about service delivery reform and infrastructure investment , and stakeholder engagement . The key decisions that are relevant to the current paper are outlined in this document . There has been no indication that these decisions need to be reconsidered. Problem definition . The problem definition is well established in previous Cabinet papers , regulatory impact analyses, and briefing material . Several of the Cabinet papers explored the problems and challenges facing the three waters system in considerable detail. The Regulatory Impact A ssessment , Strengthening the regulation of drinking water, wastewater and stormwater (July ) , also included an o verview of the key problems . . Some of these problems are already being addressed through significant legislative changes to the drinking wate r regulatory framework, and the creation of a new Water Services Regulator Taumata Arowai. The proposed programme of reforms to the service delivery system is intended to address many of the other problems, as well as supporting the long term effectiven ess and efficiency of Taumata Arowai and the new drinking water regulatory framework. Three Waters Ministers include the Ministers offor: Local Government; Health; Environment; Infrastructure; Rural Communities; Conservation; Climate Change; Commerce and Consumer Affairs; and Urban Development . Films, Videos, and Publications Classification (Commercial Video on Demand) Amendment Bill: Approval for Introduction Portfolio Internal Affairs Purpose This paper seeks approval for the introduction of the Films, Videos, and Publications Classification (Commercial Video onDemand) Amendment Bill (the Bill). Previous ConsiderationOn September , Cabinet agreed to amend the Films, Videos, and Publications Classification Act (the Act) to incorporate Commercial Video onDemand (CVoD) into New Zealands media classification regime. CABMIN Summary The purpose of the Bill is to address a regulatory gap where CVoD content is not currently subject to mandatory classification requirements prior to being made available in New Zealand. The Bill will enable CVoD content to be rated and labelled in the same way that films are already regulated under the Act. Regulated CVoD providers will be required to label content by: selfrating content using their own systems that have been approved by the Office of Film and Literature Classification (the Classification Office); selfrating content using the Classification Offices online tool and resources; or submitting content to the Film and Video Labelling Body (the Labelling Body) for rating and labelling, with certain content to be referred to the Classification Office for classification where appropriate. Regulatory Impact AnalysisA Quality Assurance Panel with representatives from the Department of Internal Affairs and the Treasury considers that the Supplementary Analysis Report (attached as appendix B) meets the Quality Assurance criteria. Compliance A Departmental Disclosure Statement is attached. UNCLASSIFIED Office of the Minister for the Community and Voluntary Sector Cabinet Social Outcomes Committee Policy proposals for regulations to enable appeals to the Taxation and Charities Review Authority Proposal I am seeking Cabinet agreement to policy proposals for regulations for appeals under the Charities Act . Relation to government priorities This is a matter that requires Cabinet approval now to ensure necessary regulations are in pl ace for when the Taxation and Charities Review Authority start s hearing charities appeals on July . Executive Summary This paper seeks Cabinet agreement to policy proposals to provide for new regulations under the Charities Act to support the Taxation and Charities Review Authority (the Authority) to hear charities appeals. From July , charities will be able to appeal decisions related to their registration under the Charities Act to an expanded Taxation Review Authority (renam ed as the Taxation and Charities Review Authority ). Setting limited matters in regulations will support the core objective of access to justice while recognising other considerations such as the public and private benefit s by appeals , and alignment of the Authority with the wider tribunal system. The proposals include: . a single fee of to file an appeal including provision to waive the fee in specific circumstances (this proposal supports access to justice while recognising the public and private benefit s from appealing decisions ); and . procedural matters to ensure the Authoritys processes run seamlessly end toend and align with the wider tribunal system. Targeted consultation between November and January confirmed that submitters main concern was that the appeals process is as accessible as possible . Some submitters noted that a small filing fee would be reasonable for appellants to contribute to the cost burden of running the tribunal , while t axpayers larger contribut ion recognises the public benefit in an appeals process . Entities and individuals (for example, officers of a charity) can appeal decisions by the Charities Registration Board and some decisions by the Chief Executive of the Department of Internal Affairs as set out in section A of the Charities Amendment Act . UNCLASSIFIED Proactively released by the Minister for the Community and Voluntary Sector
UNCLASSIFIED Office of the Minister for the Community and Voluntary Sector Chair, Cabinet Legislation Committee Charities (Taxation and Charities Review Authorities Appeals Process) Regulations Proposal I seek authorisation for submission to the Executive Council of the Charities (Taxation and Charities Review Authorities Appeals Process) Regulations . Policy Cabinet previously agreed to policy proposals for regulations to support the hearing of charities appeals New p rovisions relating to charities appeals in the Charities Act (the Act) come into force on July . The Act provides for regulations to be made for the procedure for appeals under the Act , including setting a fee to file an appeal , and the circumstances in which any fee may be r efunded, remitted or waived, in whole or in part. In April , Cabinet agreed to policy proposals and issue d drafting instructions Cab MIN refers. Cabinet agreed to a single fee of (inclusive of GST) to file an appeal with the provision of a fee waiver, and several procedural matters to ensure processes run seamlessly end toend and the Taxation and Charities Review Authority (the Authority) is aligned with the wider tribunal system. These procedural matters are: . A def inition for Registrar; . The criteria for granting a filing fee waiver (financial hardship and public interest); and . Powers for the Authority to: .. postpone a fee payment, recover a postponed fee and refund a fee; .. adjourn a case management conference, dete rmine preliminary issues in the absence of a party and dismiss an appeal if it is the appellant that misses the case management conference; and .. reinstate an appeal after an appellant fails to attend a case management conference due to exceptional circumsta nces or another good reason for not attending. UNCLASSIFIED Page of In Confidence Office of the Minister for the Digital Economy and Communications Chair, Cabinet Economic Development Committee Ta rgeted engagement on developing Digital Identity Services Trust Framework Regulations Proposal . I seek Cabinets approval for the Department of Internal Affairs (the Department) to release the document, Digital Identity Services Trust Framework Regulations : A discussion paper (attached as Appendix A), for targeted engagement with key stakeholders . Relation to government priorities . The proposed regulations canvassed in the discussion paper would set out legal and process requirements to enable the Digital Identity Services TrustFramework (the Trust Framework) to be established. Establishing the TrustFramework will be an enabler of digital transformation across the public sector and the economy and is a foundation in the Governments development of a Digital Strategy for Aotearoa. Executive summary . The Digital Identity Services Trust Framework Act (the Act) received Royal assent on April and will come into force on July . The Trust Framework will regulate the provision of accredited digital identity services, so that users can securely share digital information about themselves to accessonline services. . Under the Trust Framework individuals will be able to access, claim and sharetheir own information through accredited digital identity services. This will occuras part of a standardised process to ensure personal identity data is beinghandled securely and according to the users requests. It will give users morecontrol over their own data, including what they choose to share aboutthemselves and who they share it with. . I propose that the Department lead a targeted engagement process on the regulations . This will in clude engagement with the Data Iwi Leaders Group and Te Mana Raraunga (the Mori Data Sovereignty Network ), the Pacific Data Sovereignty Network, key financial institutions , data infrastructure providers , industry peak bodies , citizen and consumer rights groups and government agencies . . Officials will seek targeted stakeholders views on the establish ment of regulations covering: the types of digital identity services that may be accredited, accreditation requirements, accreditation service levels, T rust Framework provider (TF provider ) service levels, and TF provider record keeping and reporting requirements. Proactively released by the Minister for Digitising Government UNCLASSIFIED Page of . To enable these regulations to be developed and come into force by the Acts commencement of July , the Department needs to progress the consultation process before the forthcoming general election. I seek agreement for the Department to release the attached discussion paper for targeted engagement on the initial set of regulations over a four week period commencing August and ending September . . I consider the risk of targeted engagement over this period is low because of the cross party consensus on the need for the Trust Framework, the constructive relationship with stakeholders on this work, the technical and procedural nature of the proposed regulations which are grounded in good practi ce, and because the framework is opt in. . In the event the regulations do not come into force by July , the TF Authority will be unable to accredit TF providers and their services or effectively regulate their activities. This means the delivery of the anticipated benefits associated with introducing the Trust Framework will be delayed. Background The Act will commence on July , unless brought into force earlier by Order in Council . The purposes of the Digital Identity Services Trust Framework Act are: . To establish a legal framework for the provision of secure and trusted digital identity services for individuals and organisations; and . To establish governance and accreditation functions that are transparent and incorporate te ao Mori approaches to identity. . The Trust Framework enabled by the Act will establish a set of technical and security requirements which will protect the privacy and security of an individuals information when it is shared within the trusted environment. The requirements will apply to those organisations that choose to opt in to the Trust Framework to deliver accredited services. . The anticipated benefits of the framework include: . Enabling user controlled access to, and sharing of, personal information; . Minimising identity theft and privacy breaches ; . Improving information sharing efficiency ; . Reducing unnecessary sharing of information; and . Improving access to online and face to face services that require the provision of identity and other personal information. . Under the Trust Framework individuals will be able to access, claim, and share their own information through accredited digital identity services (identified byaccreditation marks). This will occur as part of a standardised process to ensurepersonal identity data is being handled securely and according to the usersrequests, as outlined in the diagram in Appendix B. Proactively released by the Minister for Digitising Government UNCLASSIFIED Page of Secondary legislation in the form of rules and regulations will enable the establishment of the Trust Framework . Regular and timely updates of trust framework regulatory requirements will benecessary to keep pace with changes in a rapidly evolving technology centred sector. Consequently, the Act enables many of the regulatory requirements to besecondary legislation as either r ules or r egulations . . The rules will establish the technical service requirements that T F providers will need to meet when designing and delivering accredited services. The rules have already been the subject of early consultation with key stakeholders and willundergo a further final round of consultation in the first quarter of . The rules cover: identification management, privacy and confidentiality, security and risk,information and data management and information sharing and facilitatingarrangements. . The regulations will complement the rules by establishing broader legal andadministrative process requirements that either need to be met by regulatedparties or clarify how the TF Board and TF Authority will manage aspects of the regulatory system. The Privacy Act continues to apply to the collection, use and retention of all personal information under the Trust Framework. . While the M ori Advisory Group appointments have been made, the TF Board appointments have not yet been completed and the TF Authority is not yetestablished. The Department will engage with both the Mori Advisory Group and the TF Board once established through the regulation development process . . The regulations will be developed in two phases. The first set of regulations which are addressed in the attached discussion paper cover the necessary legal and procedural requirements to initially stand up the regulatory system , including: . The types of digital identity services that may be accredited; . TF provider accreditation process, including accreditation requirements, application assessment criteria and accreditation periods ; . TF service levels that providers can meet when delivering accredited services; . TF provider internal complaints process requirements ; . TF provider record keeping requirements; and . TF provider reporting requirements . . It is anticipated that the development of second set of regulations will be recommended to the Minister for the Digital Economy and Communications by the TF Board in to: . Enable the introduction of fees to recover TF Authority costs associated with administering the accreditation process and the wider Trust Framework ; Proactively released by the Minister for Digitising Government UNCLASSIFIED Page of . Establish requirements and criteria that would enable the TF Authority to recommend enhancements to the dispute resolution scheme provided under the Act ; . Enable arrangements for the appointment and oversight of third party assessors that the TF Authority may choose to certify to carry out accreditati on functions on its behalf; and . Address other operational matters required to frame the TF Authoritys administration of the scheme. Proposed regulations Accredited services . The discussion paper proposes that the regulations specify that the following services can be delivered by TF providers as accredited services under the Act: . Digital Identity Information Service: provides an assessment of the accuracy of personal or organisational information; . Digital Identity Binding Service: ensures the connection of personal or organisational information to an individual or organisation; . Digital Identity Authentication Service: ensures the connection of a user to an authenticator and secures the sharing of personal or organisational information between Trust Framework participants by ensuring the authenticator(s) are held and controlled by an authorised holder ; . Digital Identity Credential Service: combines bound information and an authenticator to establish and maintain a reusable credential ; and . Digital Identity Facilitation Service (s): assists users to share credentials with Relying Parties. Accreditation requirements . Under the Act the TF Authority undertakes the accreditation of potential TF providers. The TF Authority will be appointed by the Chief Executive of the Department of Internal Affairs and be accountable to the responsible Minister . The discussion paper sets out the requirements that applicants for accreditation will need to meet, along with the assessment criteria the TF Authority will apply to applications . . The applicant will need to be a company incorporated in New Zealand, an Incorporated Society registered in New Zealand, a New Zealand C rown entity or a government department that intends to deliver one or more digital identity services. The organisation will need to demonstrate it is financially sustainable and can: . meet the service standards specified in the r ules; . provide an internal complaints process ; . meet fit and proper person requirements; and Proactively released by the Minister for Digitising Government UNCLASSIFIED Page of . address to the TF Authoritys satisfaction any issues of concern arising from any past practises as an identity services provider that have be en the subject of an investigation by the Privacy Commission or the TF Authority, or resulted in a decision to previously decline, suspend or cancel an accreditation. Length of accreditation period . The discussion paper proposes that the regulations establish an accreditation period of two years . A twoyear accreditation period is considered appropriate given we are introducing a new regulatory system and there are likely to bechanges to the service standards providers need to meet in response to therapidly evolving nature of the industry. Accreditation Mark . The proposed regulations will enable TF providers to display an accreditation mark against each of their accredited services. This will help users and providersknow that a providers service meets the standards for that service as set out inthe rules. Service Levels . The proposed regulations will also include provision for establishing service levels that TF providers meet when delivering information services, binding services andor authentication services. Service levels will not apply to credential and facilitation services as the r ules will establish a single standard for them which a provider must meet for accreditation purposes. . This feature of the regulatory system is intended to help relying parties and otherdigital service provider s understand how r obust a TF provider s processes are, facilitate cooperation between providers by reducing the time required to assess the other partys processes, and increase trust in the regulatory framework. Complaints process . The proposed regulations will set out requirements for each TF provider to operate their own complaints processes. Any complaints not resolved directly with the TF provider can be referred to the Authorit y to address as provided for in the Act . The requirement for TF providers to initially address complaints is good practi ce and will help encourage the resolution of complaints at the source wherever possible. It should also reduce the TF Authoritys workload . . Any complaints received by the TF Authority will be subject to a preliminary triaging process that enables it to identify comp laints about matters that already fall within the jurisdiction of the Ombudsman, the Privacy Commissioner; theInspector General of Intelligence and Security or another officeholder for onward referral to them . This will enable the Authority to focus on complai nts where there may be a breach of the requirements established by the Act or the associated rules and regulations. . The discussion document seeks feedback on the complaints process, particularly the internal complaints requirements TF providers would need to meet, andwhether this is a suitable mechanism to addressing complaints in the first instance. Proactively released by the Minister for Digitising Government UNCLASSIFIED Page of Record keeping requirements . The discussion paper sets out proposals for regulations on record keeping that will require TF providers to collect and retain information about their activities, store it in a secure database, and provide the TF Authority with access to those records at all reasonable times upon request. The regulations will require the T F provider s to retain information necessary to provide assurance that they have delivered accredited services aligned with the requirements specified in the rules and regulations. Reporting . The discussion paper proposes that the regulations establish annual reporting requirements for TF providers to help enable the TF Authority to monitor and assess their performance and that of the regulatory system. It proposes that the annual reporting requirements will cover organisational governance and management arrangements, information on service transactions, compliance and delivery, complaints and disputes resolution, f raud events, and each provider s financial performance. . In addition , it proposes that the regulations require providers to report separately and as soon as practical any actual or suspected fraud events and other events that adversely affect confidentiality, the integrity or availability of the digital identity service and have caused or present a risk of serious harm. This will helpensure the TF Authority is aware of significant events and is able to intervene or assist where necessary. Cost recovery . The discussion paper confirms that the TF Authoritys initial establishment and the first two years of operating costs will be met from Crown funding without acontribution from fees. Consequently , early entrants will not need to pay an initial accreditation fee. Later entrants and TF providers seeking to renew accreditations will incur a fee if cost recovery regulations are introduced. Fees are proposed to be introduced after two years once more information is availableabout the potential number of providers in the market. Timing of engagement on the discussion paper . To enable these regulations to be developed and come into force by the Actscommencement of July , the targeted stakeholder engagementprocess should take place before the forthcoming general election. Once engagement is completed, further Cabinet policy decisions to inform drafting instructions and Cabinet approval of the regulations are still required. . I have considered the risks associated with undertaking the engagement process prior to the forthcoming General Election and consider them to be low as: . There is broad cross party and stakeholder support for the establishment of the Trust Framework , which was demonstrated during the passage of the Bill; Proactively released by the Minister for Digitising Government UNCLASSIFIED Page of . The key non government stakeholders we are proposing to consult have already been engaged in the development of the associated rules and have a real interest in considering the associated regulatory requirements ; . The regulatory system is an optin arrangement which means parties are not obliged to meet TF regulatory requirements unless they choose to do so; and . The regulatory proposals are administrative in nature and reflect good practi ce in other regulatory systems . . In the event the consultation process does not take place prior to the election,officials advise that it would be unlikely that regulations will be ready before the Acts commencement of July . Therefore, the TF Authority would be unable to accredit TF providers and their services and effectively regulate theiractivities and the delivery of the anticipated benefits associated with introducing the Trust Framework will be delayed. Officials advise me that they are working through mitigations in the event of this occurring. Proposed targeted engagement . Relationship to the draft C ustomer and Product Data Bill (Consumer data right) . The Trust Framework and enabling rules and regulations will complement the draft C ustomer and Product Data Bill (Commerce and Consumer Affairs portfolio) which has been the subject of recent public consultation. . The proposed Bill intends to give consumers the ability to access and share data that is held about them with trusted third parties in a safe and secure manner.The Bill will also mean businesses have to make information about their productsavailable in a manner that will enable easy product comparison and switching.The Trust Framework will support this outcome by enabling people to securelyaccess and share their verified identity and related personal information digitally. . Officials from the Minist ry of Business, Innovation and Employment and the Department will continue to work together to ensure the alignment of bothregulatory systems . This will include assessing opportunities to reduce implementation and compliance costs potentially through the accreditation process along with other areas . Treaty of WaitangiTiriti o Waitangi Implications . The Act includes provisions to recognise and respect the Crowns responsibilityto give effect to the principles of te Tiriti o Waitangi. The legis lation recognises Mori interests in the protection and use of digital identity and provides for te aoMori approaches to be incorporated into the Trust Framework governance and decision making. Ways of embedding te ao Mori and te Tiriti o Waitangiperspectives and requirements in the regulations will be addressed during the targeted engagement process with the TF Board, the M ori Advisory Group, Data Iwi Leaders Group and Te Mana Raraunga. Cost of Living Implications . The introduction of the regulations proposed in the attached discussion paper will not have a direct or immediate impact on the cost of living. In the mediumterm the establishment and operation of the Trust Framework is expected to improve security leading to increased confidence in the use of the digital identi ty services system . This is expected to le ad to: . a reduction in costs incurred due to a reduction in fraud ulent activity ; . time and cost savings realised by users through the increased use of online services that enable them to access services remotely ; and . savings to R elying Parties through an anticipated reduction in transaction costs. Financial Implications . There are no immediate financial implications associated with initiating theengagement process on the development of the regulations. Population Implications . Research has identified several groups are at higher risk of not being digitally included in New Zealand including seniors, disabled people, people living in rural communities, and families with children living in low socioeconomic communities . Mori are also less likely to be digitally included than the wider population. . Several factors imp act on digital inclusion rates including motivation, access, skills, and trust. The development of the Trust Framework will help address the trust factor directly by enhancing security and enabling users to have greater control over the way their data is accessed and shared through accredited digitalidentity services . The framework is aligned with the Governments Digital Inclu sion Blueprint that aims to remove barriers to access for at risk groups in the population and ensure everyone can access and use online information, products and services. Population Implications While the appeals process is important for access to justice, appealing decisions is not a day today issue affecting charities. Most appellants will likely be registe red charities and charities seeking registration . In some cases, appellants may be individuals ( for example, an officer of a charity) . Having an accessible appeals tribunal before the High Court will particularly benefit smaller, less well resourced charities. Most of New Zealands charities are small and volunteer run. Around one third have an annual income under ,. Among those smaller charities are kaupapa Mori charities and charities run by, and dedicated to, population groups (including Pacific peoples, youth, disabled people, kaumtuaolder New Zealanders , ethnic communities and women). Some population groups, or sections of them, depend on charities for services that either state sector services or fami ly and whnau may not provide . UNCLASSIFIED which replicates a charitable trust established after Christchurch Earthquake Following the devastating Christchurch Earthquake, the Government quickly esta blished a charitable trust to complement existing donation appeals. The Christchurch Earthquake Appeal Trust (CEAT) raised approximately million in donations. Most of the funding was collected in the first year of the appeal, . CEAT funded a range of projects. Some of the bigger grants given out were mill ion to the rebuild and restoration of Isaac Theatre Royal and . million for water attractions at the new Christchurch City Council Recreation and Sports Centre in the eastern suburbs. CEAT currently has around , left to distribute. CEAT expects to make a final allocation in June this year, at which stage, with no funds left to distribute, the trustees will wind up the trust. Establishment phase includes bank account, website, trust deed, trustees and regis tration as a charity The Trust is currently being established. The name has been confirmed, officials are working on a t rust deed and charitable status (which enables donors to claim a tax rebate), and working with Westpac and Clemenger BBDO on establishing a bank account, website, multiple channels for donations, and other details of how the donation appeal process will work. The pertinent clauses of the draft Trust Deed are set out in Appendix A and closely follow the language of relevant legislation such as the Charities Act . It is important that the charitable trust also be registered as a charity under the Charit ies Act (a separate process) as it is this status which allows donors to claim a tax rebate on their donations. All relevant agencies are working to expedite the required registrations in time for launch. I am proposing three trustees, which replicates CEAT. One would be the Chief Execut i ve of the Department of Internal Affairs (who will be the original trustee for purposes of establishment), with two others one of whom will be Mori. I am recommending that decisionmaking authority on the appointment of the truste es, alongside other decisions about the administration of the trust, be given to the Minister of Finance, Minister of Internal Affairs and Minister for the Community and Voluntary Sector. It is proposed that these Ministers will also have authority to act on establishing a larger Advisory Board with local knowledge and expertise of the affected regions, which replicates the CEAT model. I propose that the Department provide secretariat support to the Trust and, in conjunct ion with Treasury as necessary, receive and hold donations on behalf of the Trust. Lotto will hold a fundraising lottery on March Under sec tion of the Gambling Act , the Minister of Internal Affairs may, from time to time, instruct the New Zealand Lotteries Commission to promote a lottery for any community purpose that the Minister thinks fit. On February I instructed the New Zealand Lotteries Commission to promote a special purpose UNCLASSIFIED ihpodtn Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs UNCLASSIFIED lottery for the purpose of Cyclone Gabrielle relief efforts. This special purpose lottery will be held on March . The proceeds will provide recovery funds for communities and community organisations that have been impacted by Cyclone Gabrielle. Neither I nor the Government have the authority to direct the Lotteries Grants Board on how to dis tribute the funds raised by the special draw. I do however expect that there would be a further conversation with the full Board (of which I am the presiding member) to explore whether it would consider contributing the proceeds of the special draw to the Fund, to be distributed through the Trust. Financial Implications The CEAT ensured that all donations would go towards earthquake recovery through the Gove rnment funding the cost to trustees, advisory board, and the Department of Internal Affairs secretariat. I propose the same for the Cyclone Gabrielle Appeal Trust. The secretariat for the Trust cannot be met out of baselines or with existing staff, as cost pre ssures already exist across the department. There are substantial roles for the secretariat including: . implementation (needs assessment, project research and development, imple mentation); . support for trustees and Advisory Board; . reporting, evaluation, audit and governance; . external relationships management. In the time available officials have determined that the secretariat, trustees, and advisory group will have costs of approximately . million annually. The trust and secretariat need to be operational as soon as possible, to best respond to the impact of adverse weather events. As such it is not possible to wait for the next annual Budget round to seek funding for the secretariat. The funding sought in this paper is for up to seven FTEs, board member fees and an advisory committee for up to four years. Distribution of CEAT funding is expected to conclude in , years after the fund was established, demonstrating that secretariat resource is likely to needed for several years. In addition to a Manager, Administrator and Principal Advisor, the remaining four FTE a re Advisors who could be based in the affected regions, to bring local expertise, or in Wellington. Considering regional placement of these roles will help address workforce pressures in engaging suitable resources. Costs for the administration costs of the Christchurch Earthquake Appeal for the first four financi al years was . million. For several reasons, it is considered that the costs will be substantially higher. This includes inflation since and that the advisory board will likely need to be large to reflect the wide range of regions and UNCLASSIFIED ihpodtn Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs UNCLASSIFIED communities impacted by Cyclone Gabrielle. Additionally, there are other funds being distributed across several regions, which the secretariat will have to consider. Under section of the ISA, NZSIS is authorised to, amongst other things, provide advice and assistance to any public authority (whether in New Zealand or overseas), any person or class of persons (whether in New Zealand or overseas) authorised by the Minister. This protective security services, advice, and assistance includes for the purposes of providing advice and assistance around personnel, information, and physical security, as well as advice around national security risks.
Under section of the ISA, NZSIS is authorised to provide advice and assistance to anyone responding to an imminent threat to the life or safety of any person in New Zealand, or any New Zealand citizen or permanent resident overseas, any person in any area that New Zealand has search and rescue responsibilities for, or any person outside the territorial jurisdiction of any country.

Should NZSIS obtain any information under the DAA for the purposes of a security clearance assessment then the limitations on further use of that information under section of the ISA will apply.
