convergence products usually allow a gambler the ability to play continuously, and therefore present higher risks of forming harmful gambling behaviours. Gambling provided through the four gambling sectors levied pose the greatest risks of gambling harm in New Zealand. The most harmful form of gambling in New Zealand is NCGMs at pubsclubs (defined in the Act as class ); this has been the case for many years. Most money spent on gambling in New Zealand comes from the relatively limited number of people who play NCGMs, and most clients accessing problem gambling intervention services cite pubclub pokies as a primary problem gambling mode. The National Gambling Study (NGS) found that atrisk and problem gamblers accounted for over half of total (estimated) electronic gaming machine (EGM) expenditure in (moderaterisk and problem gamblers ; lowrisk gamblers ). Similarly, the HLS found that almost half (; , ) of people who played NCGMs in pubs or clubs at least once a month had at least some level of gambling harm. Groups vulnerable to gambling harm Research shows that Mori and Pacific peoples, some Asian communities and people on lower incomes disproportionately experience gambling harm. The HLS found that gambling harm is experienced disproportionately by those living in areas with a high social deprivation index score ( or higher) , who were . times as likely to experience gamblingrelated arguments or money problems related to gambling. The study found that Mori and Pacific adults were more likely to develop problems from gambling (ie, to become a lowrisk, moderaterisk or problem gambler) than Europeanother New Zealanders. Asian people also experienced a slightly higher risk . Importantly, while inequalities between population groups by age, social deprivation, gender and ethnicity have reduced in absolute terms, in relative terms, disparities in exposure to gambling and experience of gamblingrelated harm persist, and have been relatively static over the past five years. Mori, Pacific peoples and Asian peoples are each more than twice as likely to experience moderate to severe gambling harm than the Europeanother population. Women and children Harmful gambling behaviour may impact significantly on women and children. There is a strong correlation between gambling and family , whnau or partner violence : percent of problem gamblers also experience family or whnau violence (Auckla nd University of Technology ). Women, who are common ly the primary caregivers within the ir family or whnau , are also particularly vulnerable to the economic strain caused by problem gambling. Primary prevention (public health action) Primary prevention services cover health promotion, increasing community action, raising community awareness about gambling and problem gambling, working with territorial authorities on their gambling venue policies and supporting the public health awareness and education programmes at a local and regional level. The Ministry will continue to fund dedicated Mori, Pacific and Asian providers to offer primary prevention services and explore further ways to reach those most at risk of gambling harm. The Ministry intends that service providers work across the five general domains listed below. However, it is clear that some behaviour change and innovation is required. The Ministry will undertake further advice and design work before it purchases services through a procurement process. . Policy development and implementation: The Ministry and service providers engage with other government agencies, social organisations and private industries and businesses to reduce gambling harm. . Safe gambling environment s: Environments that provide gambling opportunities are encouraged to actively minimise harm, and individuals are supported to recognise and seek support to minimise gambling harm. . Supportive communities: People live in communities that provide strong protective factors and that support individual and family resilience. . Aware and motivated communities: Agencies, communities, families and individuals are aware of the signs and range of harmful gambling arising from gambling and howwhere to seek suppor t. Estimated levy underrecovery or overrecovery, by sector (R) Section of the Gambling Amendment Act came into effect on March and requires the calculation of each sector s levy rate to take into account any underpayment or overpayment from that sector in previous levy periods. This change ended the previous system, deemed unfair, whereby all four gambling sectors were required to meet any net underpayment or overpayment of the levy amount across all sectors from the previous levy period. During the consultation process, views were expressed about the most appropriate way to calculate R, which the Gambling Commission commented on in its report to responsible Ministers. The Commission said R should be calculated by hindsight adjustment of earlier estimates of both C and D to produce (amend) the previously expected relative contribution from each sector to a corrected calculation of the actual cost of the strategy to the end of the previous levy period. The Commission considered this approach is consistent with the objective intent of the amendments to the Act and provide s a fair er allocation of any over or underpayment, as adjustments to each sector would be made in the same proportions as received (Gambling Commission ). Accordingly, the Ministry has calculated R by calculating its projected total spending for the period to by: STRATEGY TO PREVENT AND MI NIMISE GAMBLING HARM TO Proactively released b y the Minister of l A

e. Proposed disestablishment of the Strategy and Capability team The proposal to disestablish the Strategy and Capability team has not been made lightly. As mentioned previously, in the environment that we are in, deprioritising and stopping activities in areas where we have been able to operate beyond our core delivery responsibilities is required. Some of the mahi undertaken by this team is proposed to be split and redistributed within newly proposed and existing roles, such as the Practice Lead, Lead Regulator, Principal Advisor, Strategy and Business Planning, and Team Leader, Business Services. It is therefore proposed to disestablish the positions of National Manager, Strategy and Capability, four Senior Advisors, Business Advisor, Practice Lead Capability and Senior Capability and Training Advisor. Strategy, Intelligence and Risk The proposed establishment of the Strategy, Intelligence and Risk function will bring together the Strategy, Intelligence, Insights, Risk and Business Planning activities under one team. This function that will be responsible for maintenance of our regulatory strategy, turning our strategy into actionable business plan and utilising insights from intelligence and risk to help us focus our regulatory stewardship efforts. Given the resourcing constraints we face, it is critical that we target our effort to address known risks and plan our activities in areas that will have significant impact in our regulated sectors. i) Team Leader, Intelligence and Insights With the proposed disestablishment of the National Manager, Intelligence, Insights and Risk, the establishment of a new Team Leader, Intelligence and Insights is proposed to lead the Analysts and Senior Analysts in the team. This means a proposed change in reporting line for this team to the Head of Strategy, Intelligence and Risk. The new proposed Team Leader, Intelligence and Insights will be responsible for leading and managing the team, to ensure that intelligence, analysis, products and services are delivered consistently and to high quality standards. ii) Intelligence, Insights and Risk team The makeup of the team is also proposed to change, with a reduction in the number of Lead Intelligence Analysts from two to one, Senior Intelligence Analysts from four to three, Intelligence Analysts from four to two, and the disestablishment of the two Senior Data Analysts. The reduced capacity means that there will a strong focus on work that is commissioned for the team and the leadership team to work together to establish collective efforts. iii) Intelligence Coordinator To support the team with prioritisation of work, it is proposed to establish an Intelligence Coordinator. The proposed position would add valuable administrative support to the Intelligence team who, as they become busier and more embedded into our regulatory operating model, are finding themselves struggling to meet the administrative demands. The weights (W and W) The Act requires the Ministry to apply a weighting between current player expenditure (W) and presentations ( W) to help determine each sector s share of the cost ( C) that each sector is required to pay in levy. Table shows the proportion of expenditure ( A) and presentations ( B) attributed to each levypaying sector for , the most recent year comparative data is available for all four sectors. Table : Share of presentations and expenditure by sector, NCG Ms Casinos NZRB NZLC Presentations Expenditure Presentations Expenditure Presentations Expenditure Presentations Expenditure . . . . . . . . The top line of the levy formula determines the amount each sector shall pay. When a sector s proportion of expenditure is substantially different from its proportion of presentations ( W and W respectively), the weighting between expenditure and presentations is critical to determine how much each sector will be required to pay . . Levy rates Table sets out each sectors levy rate for to , expected payment amounts, and percent shares for the weighting. This is a change from previous levy periods that have used the weighting. The weighting reflects changing patterns of player expenditure and presentations, and recognises that too high a weighting on presentations alone does not adequately attribute to each sector its fair share of costs for low to moderate harm, or of strategy activities such as public health not covered by presentations to intervention services. The top row of the table shows the levy rate for each sector, as the percentage of player expenditure each sector must pay as a levy. For example, a rate of . means that the sector must pay . cents for each dollar of player expenditure from July to June . The second row shows the expected levy amount each sector would pay if actual player expenditure matches the forecasts. The third row shows this amount as a percentage of the total expected in levy payments (having adjusted for R). Engagement, Operational Policy and new Implementation team The proposed establishment of an Implementation function will bring our current Engagement and Operational Policy teams that currently sit in each regulatory system under a single function. The proposed establishment of this function is informed by feedback from workshops with kaimahi that there was insufficient support for regulator kaimahi to access to an upto, single source of truth on robust policies and business processes. This has resulted in a lack of confidence in regulatory operations and a broad inconsistency of practices across regions, and even across teams within regions. The bringing together of these teams under one function will ensure that the two teams that are responsible for the information and education of both our regulatory kaimahi and our sector work together closely and provide consistent guidance to endusers. Supporting our regulators and educating and supporting our regulated sector with sound, easily understood and digestible operational policy guidance is key to our role as effective regulatory stewards. A centralised Operational Policy team, under a broader Implementation function, will ensure that across the Group we are consistently applying best practice in the development and rollout of the necessary operational support to regulators, and guidance, support and clarity to the sector. Again, in this area it becomes imperative for us to scale back work beyond our core mahi, ensure that our regulators have the right information including policies and process to do their mahi and be sharp around planning our engagement with our sector and how we inform and educate them.

gaming convergence as discussed below) has steadily grown, and with it the risk of increased gambling harm. Gaming convergence For the purposes of the strategy, gaming convergence refers to the merging of gambling and gaming elements in a single product. The two main examples are where: gambling takes on the visual and aural queues associated with gaming; for example, virtual realityenabled Instant Kiwi tickets here in New Zealand. These forms of gambling are also an example of continuous gambling, which research shows poses an increased risk of harm video games include elements of what appears to be gambling (but does not currently meet the definition of gambling under the Act); for example, opening loot boxes and spinning wheels to unlock power ups . Gaming convergence, when coupled with associated increased levels of advertising and internetbased payment systems that make it easier to spend money on gambling products, represents the emergence of new levels of exposure to highrisk gambling products in New Zealand, and the associated probability of related gambling harm. Associated with gaming convergence is the potential harm from increasing opportunities to play games that simulate gambling; that is, they look and feel like gambling, but do not meet the definition under the Act (because there is no opportunity to stake, win or lose real money). For example, many online gambling websites promote their services with free toplay games that appear to be gambling , but do not involve real money These free toplay sites appear to avoid the Gambling Act prohibition on advertising as, by definition, no gambling is taking place on the site advertised. For example, SKYCITY launched a free toplay online gaming site in with virtual gaming machines (simulated pokies) and table games. Gambling providers in New Zealand, including SkyCity, have expressed interest in broadening their gambling products (eg, by moving online or increasing competitiveness with overseas markets). Submissions from service providers and health groups expressed concerns about gaming convergence, particularly in terms of the potential impact on vulnerable groups including Mori and Pacific youth. increased deprivation levels (Bellringer et al ). Pacific peoples make up percent of all people seeking treatment for gambling harm. There is evidence that children and young adults are exposed to considerable gambling messaging; for example, through advertising, which can help to normalise gambling behaviours (Signal et al ). As noted above , health group and service provider submissions on the draft strategy also raised concerns about the accessibility of online gambling and gaming convergence and these impacts on the wellbeing of children, youth and young adults. Comorbidities Harmful gambling typically presents with other health issues, and has been consistently associated with a range of coexisting health issues such as higher levels of smoking, hazardous alcohol consumption and other drug use, as well as higher levels of depression and poorer selfrated health. Comorbidity is an indication that a person may require holistic services (Auckland University of Technology ). . Intervention service data Every year, some of the people described abov e seek help from services funded by the Ministry of Health (the Ministry) for problems due to their own or someone else s gambling . In the year, over , people sought help from services funded by the Ministry of Health for problems due to their own or someone else s gambling. Most of these people were in crisis . If brief interventions in nonclinical settings were included in the analysis, the total would increase to more than ,. Over the last seven years gambling harm intervention services have seen approximately , clients per annum (including family , whnau and affected others). Of these, about , were for brief interventions. is an independent body established under the Films, Videos, and Publications Classification Act . Partnerships and Commissions Branch Performance teamm provide all secretariat and administrative functions to the Board. The Board does not report to, or receive direction from, the Department.
is an independent statutory body established by legislation. The Commission has specific statutory responsibilities under several statutes. These include the Local Government Act , relating to the provision of information and good practice about local government, as well as the local government reorganisation process, and the Local Electoral Act relating to local government representation arrangements. The Local Government Commission does not report to, or receive direction from, the Department.
is an independent statutory decisionmaking body established under the Gambling Act . The Gambling Commission hears casino licensing applications and appeals on licensing and enforcement decisions made by the Secretary for Internal Affairs in relation to gaming machines and other noncasino gambling activities. The Gambling Commission has the powers of a Commission of Inquiry and does not report to, or receive direction from, the Department.

not tell tracers everywhere they have been (wilful deception); and accurate contact details for close contacts are unavailable. The degree to which contact tracing and the isolation of potentially infected close contacts helps break a chain of transmission depends on the time elapsed between the index case being infected and the isolation of contacts. The key levers to speeding this up are based on: The time elapsed before someone is tested. The time to return a test result. The time taken to complete contact tracing. For technology to augment and accelerate manual contact tracing, it needs to more rapidly identify close contacts (known and unknown) and provide contact tracers with contact details as fast as practicable. Technology may also enable systems to automatically message probable close contacts, instructing them to selfisolate while awaiting contact from contact tracers. .. Manual contact tracing cannot stop COVID Ferretti et al determined that controlling the epidemic by manual contact tracing is infeasible. This is reinforced by a number of other modelling studies (Plank ; Hinch, ; Vaithianathan ) and the realities of countries around the world opting for economically crippling lockdowns, even those with more mature contact tracing systems public health capacity and pandemic preparedness than New Zealand. A strategy that relies solely on New Zealands ability to rapidly test and trace, absent enforced social distancing is simply not a credible strategy to prevent the spread of the virus. Between and of infections are understood to occur before symptom onset and inefficiencies in the manual contact tracing system result from a number of delays from the onset of symptoms: A delay from the onset of symptoms to access to a test ( days). A delay from access to a test to receiving test results ( days). A delay from notification of positive test to informing close contacts ( days). A delay from notification to isolate to full isolation ( day). The combined impact of these delays mean that the secondary cases have already both become infectious and, in most cases, finished their virus shedding cycle before isolation.

The promise of digital contact tracing Many countries are investigating and deploying technology solutions to augment and accelerate manual contact tracing. For the purposes of this paper, digital contact tracing refers to a smartphone app or device that is able to detect and record close contacts through detecting the corresponding app or device of the close contact using Bluetooth LE technology. Discussion of other possible means to locate people and their close contacts (GPS, cell towers, WiFi networks, etc) are not in scope of this paper, but generally considered not particularly effective in the New Zealand context. Digital contact tracing technology can accelerate contact tracing because a list of close contacts and their contact details can be made available immediately following a positive test result. This data can be used to notify potentially exposed persons immediately (with a text message) and to make the job of manual contact tracers much faster, more efficient and scalable. Presently, close contacts only consist of those persons that the interviewee is able (and willing) to recall. Our own trials, and wider literature (see section on Health Case, later in this document), shows significant inaccuracies in the recall of encounters, including their nature (touch or no touch) and duration. Three technology approaches, all based on Bluetooth LE technology, are emerging: Apps built on top of the Apple Google Exposure Notification API. Apps that are custombuilt, typically by Governments, such as Singapores TraceTogether. Dedicated hardware devices: CovidCard . By far the most important metric is the level of compliant adoption of any of these technologies. This is covered separately further in this document. Compliant adoption is defined as a user having the technology on their person and operating as designed. There are many barriers to compliant use, particularly with apps. Apps dont work if Bluetooth is disabled (by the user or the operating system to conserve battery) or if the app is not loaded by the user following a restart of their phone, for example. The clinical definition of which (in New Zealand) is defined as being within metres for minutes.

problems, typically in a nonclinical environment. This should not be confused with brief clinical interventions; for example, via telephone. During this period, the Ministry intends to add residential care and peer support to the service mix with pilot services (see Section . ). The Ministry is committed to improving access to services for all people adversely affected by gambling. Services and activities designed to identify people who are experiencing harm are crucial in providing early prevention and intervention treatment. This approach enables the Ministry to work actively to minimise the impact harmful gambling has on individuals, their families and whnau and others. Many people of all ethnicities will access mainstream services rather than culturally specific services. Given the long standing inequities Mori have experienced, and the Crown s responsibilities under Te Tiriti o Waitangi, the Ministry will consider how it can ensure tha t mainstream services go beyond cultural competence, and actively embed te ao Mori concepts into their clinical interventions. In addition, the Ministry notes that submissions called for more culturally accessible services. The Ministry intends to continue to work with dedicated Mori, Pacific and Asian service providers and consumer networks to explore ways to provide culturally appropriate interventions and support for those population groups. The Ministry expects all services to be clinically safe and effective. The Ministry considers it appropriate to pilot psychosocial interventions and support to address areas highlighted by the needs assessment and to test new service models: for example, to develop pilot services in areas that currently have limited access, and to explore innovation within those services. Data collection and reporting The Ministry largely carries out data collection and reporting internally. The small sum specifically budgeted each year for collecti ng and reporting on data allows for an external provider to address data collection issues that require institutional knowledge and to make small technical adjustments, if required. As of , intervention service providers are required to record and report clients National Health Index (NHI) numbers to the Ministry. These identifiers allow individual patients to be positively and uniquely identified for the purposes of treatment and care and for maintaining medical records. This will also help provide better data about services provided, treatment efficacy and outcomes. Workforce development (intervention) Workforce development will continue to be an important component to support psychosocial intervention services. programme seeks to control rates rises and I am looking broadly at options in four areas: decision making; systems and processes; funding and financing; and transparency and accountability. This paper updates you on the programme and describes my immediate next step, which is to introduce an omnibus bill that will lay the foundations for an improved local government system. I seek Cabinets agreement for me to issue drafting instructions for a Local Government System Improvements bill (the Bill) that will: . refocus the purpose of local government and reinstate a list of core services in the Local Government Act ; . improve council performance measurement and reporting standards so that ratepayers can more easily access consistent, comparable information; . improve systems for managing conflict between elected members, by enabling a standardised code of conduct to be issued; and . provide regulatory relief to councils and modernise outdated law. It is my intention for the Bill to be introduced in June and enacted in late , not long after the local elections. There is provision in the Legislation Programme for this Bill (Category priority). Policy development for other system improvements is continuing and I will report back to Cabinet in Quarter of seeking policy approval for a second tranche of measures for inclusion in the Bill. Collectively, the problems outlined above contribute to the current weaknesses in the three waters regulatory and service delivery system. Taken together , they mean that we cannot always be confident that drinking water will be safe to drink, and that accep table environmental outcomes are being achieved. . In addition, there will be broader national and local implications if performance improvements are not delivered across the three waters system, including: . housing infrastructure supply being unable to mee t demand in high growth areas; . failure to meet national and local environmental objectives for freshwater and the marine environment; . a constrained ability to plan and fund robust systems that can cope with climate change, emergencies, and natural hazards; . limitations on developing the regions, particularly for areas with declining rating bases, or small tourism centres with high seasonal demand. Additional challenges due to COVID . The situation caused by COVID means the local government sector is fa cing a series of additional issues and challenges, many of which relate to three waters services and infrastructure. COVID will have significant impacts on local government finances, with consequences for council service delivery and infrastructure inv estment . . The Department of Internal Affairs has worked with L ocal Government New Zealand , the Society of Local Government Manage rs, the New Zealand Local Government Funding Agency, and the Treasury to understand the impacts of COVID on local governme nt finances, and the potential implications of this for infrastructure investment and council services. reported that they rarely knew a close contacts phone number. Further, participants reported that it was extremely difficult to record t he specific hour in which they saw a close contact, and this question added a large amount of time to complete the daily diary A second amendment was submitted (and approved) to Otago Ethics, requesting permission to ask participants to record the first na me and first initial of the family name of the close contacts. With these improvements, we were able to distinguish between people included in the study and delete extraneous non participating close contacts. This process involved an added ste p of de identifying the raw data. .. Applications of the Bluetooth card We tested the inter card reliability to determine if contact events were being mutually recorded by a pair of cards involved in a contact event. That is, to confirm whether when card A re cords an interaction with card B, that card B also records the interaction with card A. Due to timestamps not being completely synced between cards, the analysis was conducted at the day level rather than the individual contact event level. We found that o n any given day, there were no instances of card A recording an interaction with card B and card B not recording the interaction with card A. Further, we found the mean difference of the recorded duration between cards involved in the contact event over th e day was only .mins. The detection of daily interactions and small average difference in recorded overall duration suggest there was a strong inter card reliability. Beyond technical adjustments, there were no adjustments made in Phase One with the Bluetooth card. An example timeline from one Bluetooth card over multiple days is presented in Figure . Each co lour represents a unique close contact detected by the card. This participant worked every day and had a role that required a high level of interaction with other staff members. .. Applications of the ultra wide band devices The distribution of the UWB devices was delayed due to the issues w ith the Bluetooth cards cited above in the Technical Challenges section (.). As such, all data before p m on Day was disregarded as human interaction. The UWB device was attached to a lanyard for participants as they generally do not wear belts to att ach them. As a result, most participants opted to carry the UWB device in the opposite pocket to the card ( if the card was in the pocket). Proactively Released by the Department of Internal Affairs

significant, at nearly percent of all gam bling harm. There are also well established inequities based on ethnicity and socioeconomic factors . People affected by gambling harm are more likely to be M ori, Pacific, or Asian, on a low income and or living in an isolated area. Most adults in New Zealand gamble at least occasionally and usually with out causing harm to themselves or others. However, most people participate only in lessharmful forms of gambling, such as occasional Lotto. By contrast, over half the money spent on gambling comes fro m a relatively limited number of people who play continuous forms of gambling such as gaming machines, which is the form of gambling most often associated with harm. Each year, some of these people seek help. For example, in , over , people sought help from Ministry funded services, for problems due to their own or someone elses gambling. Most of these people were in crisis. I f brief interventions in non clinical settings are included, the total of people seeking help is over , . The legislative context The Act provides the regulatory framework for gambling , primarily to control the growth of gambling and ensure that money from gambling benefits the community . The Act also recognises gambling can be harmful and includes a purpose to prevent and minimise harm from gambling, including problem gambling (section (b)). Several provisions are intended to help achieve this objective, including regulatory provisions administered by the Department of Internal Affairs (the Department), and an integrated problem gambling strategy focused on public health . The Act specifies the strategy must include: . measures to promote public health by preventing and minimising the harm from gamblin g; . services to treat and assist problem gamblers and their families and whnau ; . independent scientific research associated with gambling, including (for example) longitudinal research on the social and economic impacts of gambling, particularly the impacts on different cultural groups ; and . evaluation. The Ministry is funded through an appropriat ion to Vote: Health to develop and implement the Strategy . A problem gambling levy (the levy) is set by regulation at a different rate for each of the main gambling sectors , to reimburse the Crown the amount of t hat appropriation , ensuring the Strategy is broadly fiscally neutral over time. The levy is collected by Inland Revenue. The Act details a lengthy, three yearly process to refresh the Strategy and put in place a new levy. The Ministry consults gambling operators, problem gambling service providers and other affected groups on a needs assessment, draft strategy and costings, and estimated levy rates. After consulting, the Ministry revises its proposals and submit s them to the Ministers of Health and Internal Affairs, and the Gambling Commission. The Gambling Commission analyses the proposals, undertakes its own consultation and reports to the responsible Ministers. After considering advice from officials and the Gamb ling Commission, the relevant Associate Minister of Health and the Minister of Internal Affairs make recommendations on the Strategy and the levy. This will begin with Ministryled workshops to discuss the approach, scope and priorities for pilots, followed by an invitation for specific detailed proposals through a procurement process . Pilots may include both public health and intervention components, and the Ministry will evaluate them to inform future service provision. Budget for to The service plan outlines the services that the Ministry considers it will require for the period to make further progress towards the objectives in the strategy. It also sets out the estimated costs of providing these activities to prevent and minimise gambling harm. These costs cover the four nominal budget areas, plus a line item for new services and innovation pilots: public health services intervention services research and evaluation new services and innovation pilots Ministry operating costs. Table shows the budgeted costs for . The remaining sections discuss each of the line items in Table in more detail. The strategy provides for a total estimated cost of . million in Ministry spending over the ne xt threeyear levy period . This is a million increase in threeyear funding compared with the current levy period. This extra funding is required because: funding levels and appropriations have remained largely unchanged since , but the number of people affected has steadily increased in line with population growth the Ministry proposes to change the service focus and mix to address the matters and priorities noted above and also pilot new activities and technologies the pilots will enable innovative solutions to address areas of systemic, persistent gambling harm and vulnerable communities and to target the priority areas and vulnerable groups described above it will enable the Ministry to maintain baseline services while it pilot s new interventions and service models and undertak es further evaluations , to assess where to best direct resources in the long term. The Ministry will consider whether this increase in budget should be maintained in full or in part in future years based on what it learns during implementation. If a number of pilots are evaluated as successful, the Ministry is likely to seek an increase in the level of its overall funding accordingly for the levy period. Other data on gambling expenditure is available on DIA s website ( www.dia.govt.nz ). Presentations (B) The formula in the Act requires the levy rate calculation to take into account the latest, most reliable and most appropriate sources of information from the Ministry on client presentations to problem gambling sources. The Ministry the presentation figures used in the levy from data collected by its psychosocial intervention service providers. The figures relate to all clients who received a full, facilitation or followup intervention session during the months from July to June . The figures exclude brief screening interventions and primary problem gambli ng modes in gambling sectors that are not subject to the levy (although these are recorded). Brief interventions essentially means brief screenings carried out in non clinical settings. They are excluded mainly because they are considered unrepresentative of a sector. This is because a sectors share of brief interventions will vary depending on the settings in which service providers decide to undertake them. Table shows each gambling sector s share of player expenditure and presentations. The funding requirement (C) The funding requirement represented by C in the formula is the total cost of the strategy for , which the Ministry estimates as . million. The service plan in Section sets out details about the . millio n cost to provide and implement the strategy. The funding required may be comprised entirely of a new appropriation or a new appropriation and an expense transfer of any underspend from a previous levy period. Forecast player expenditure (D) The amounts represented by D in the formula are sector bysector forecasts of the amounts that DIA expects gamblers to spend on the gambling products of the four levypaying gambling sectors in the period . The higher the forecast expenditure is, the lower the levy rate necessary for a sector to pay its required contribution (as determined by the top line of the formula). As noted above, these forecasts by DIA took into account the latest, most reliable and most appropriate sources of information on player expenditure, including its NCGM electronic monitoring system (EMS), gambling operators annual and halfyearly The IRD provides gaming duty and problem gambling levy data to the DIA. The Tax Administration Act requires the IRD to use its best endeavours to protect the integrity of the tax system by (among other things) maintain ing the confidentiality of the affairs of taxpayers. temporal parameters and RSSI values. To accomplish these firmware improvements, extensive testing in a variety of controlled environments is re quired. Controlled field trials provide the opportunity to s tructure different scenarios with appropriate surveillance to detect the cause and effect of any discrepancies in card firmware. Further, they provide an opportunity to refine the close contact al gorithm using a controlled ground truth e.g. video surveil lance of close contacts. A larger field trial requires improvements in data uploading processes. The current average upload time of minutes is untenable for a study of , participants. These improvements could come in the form of improved softwa re, upgraded firmware or a process that enables uploads from multiple cards simultaneously. Recommendations: Improve card firmware. Refine the close contact algorithm. Improve data upload time and processes. . Recruitment and enrolment processes The curr ent word ofmouth approach was necessary as the research team and NMDHB did not want wide publicity of the trial. For a full scale trial, many aspects of the recruitment process will need improvin g and scaling. First, implemented an opt out consenting proc ess, whereby all participants are automatically enrolled in the study using their staff email address. Participants would be informed that the card was being introduced as a hospital wide contact tracing measure to protect healthcare workers. Second, more systematic promotion and information dissemination processes are required to support recruitment. Establishing a dedicated page on the NMDHB intranet with videos from the Chief Executive, lead res earchers and team leaders could help drive acceptance of the solution. Information sessions with unit team leaders (UTL), then all staff, via zoom could improve support for the initiative. Third, UTL should facilitate information and card distribution with in the hospital. Even though the CRC and the NMDHB Chief Exe cutive openly endorsed and promoted the project to prospective participants in Phase One, it was the endorsement of UTL, such as the lead charge nurse, that improved recruitment efforts. Further, UTL are also well placed to distribute the cards given their knowledge of the staff. Recommendations: Optout approach to improve participation rates. Establish multiple streams of communication to inform participants. Recruit unit team leaders to facil itate information and card distribution. The focus for the strategic plan is to increase uptake of a training programme to ensure that all the workforce can demonstrate those core competencies by and will have achieved, or be on a pathway to achieving, appropriate New Zealand Qualifications Authority level seven qualifications. The Ministry is currently reviewing Te Uru Kahikatea: The Public Health Workforce Development Plan (Ministry of Health ) . It will ensure that the strategic plan takes into account any changes resulting from that review. For the intervention workforce, the Ministry will prioritise new service models that address cultural barriers, such as the use of service codesign with community stakeholders, incorporating cultural models, and focus on training to ensure that all practitioners demonstrate the gambling harm competencies under the Addiction Intervention Competency Framework (DAPAANZ ). The Ministry s expectation is that all intervention practitioners will be: registered as a health practitioner permitted to practise within a relevant scope of practice under the Health Practitioners Competence Assurance Act , or registered or endorsed by the Addiction Practitioners Association Aotearoa New Zealand (DAPAANZ) as having demonstrated the relevant specific competencies, or equivalently registered with another relevant professional organisation ( eg, a counsellor registered with the New Zealand Association of Counsellors). The Ministry aims to increase the diversity of the workforce by introducing peer support in the short to medium term. While it will encourage the development of the peer support workforce, the peer support workers will not be subject to the same requirements listed above. Organisations can act once they are aware that the individual has died, such as beginning to pay out an entitlement to the deceased individuals estate, dealing with insurance, paying or changing social welfare or other benefits to or changing accounts for survivors. The Agreement will replace a series of other agreements : Agreement to provide birth and death information (Mortality Review Committe es); AIA Services NZ Limited Information Supply Agreement; Cigna Insurance Limited Information Sharing Agreement; Domain Name Commission Information Supply Agreement; Forsyth Barr Limited Information Supply Agreement; Government Superannuation Fund Inform ation Matching Agreement; Mori Trustee Te Tumu Paeroa Information Sharing Agreement; Massey University Information Sharing Agreement; MyTrove Information Sharing Agreement; National Provident Fund Information Matching Agreement; New Zealand Marketing Association Limited Information Sharing Agreement; University of Auckland Information Sharing Agreement; University of Waikato Information Sharing Agreement; and Westpac New Zeal and Limited Information Supply Agreement. The public services that this Agreement is intended to facilitate are: the accurate and efficient assessment of eligibility for and entitlement to receive public services; the accurate and efficient delivery of pu blic services by the Registrar General and the other public sector agencies that are Parties; the provision by the Registrar General of accurate Death Information and Overseas Death Information to Parties that are New Zealand Private Sector Agencies for th eir use as per Clauses to . Mortality Reviews and advice on how to reduce preventable deaths; and prevention, detection, investigation, and prosecution of offences, and the conduct of civil proceedings including judicial review The AISA is broad in t erms of the number and types of Parties , including broad classes of agencies and an intermediary class of agencies that may on share the information with other entities, including overseas entities, under a separate agreement death information fields the Parties can obtain, use, or on share , depending on the relevant purpose ; and purposes for which these Parties can obtain, use, or on share information. Given this AISAs breadth, m y focus during consultation s with DIA has been on the nature of the privacy protections built into it. ikudgtnr Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs
Privacy Commissioner CJ Te Mana Matapono Matatapu Classes mechanism and class es of intermediaries . The Privacy Act was amended to enable an authorised information sharing agreement to apply to classes of agency by members being added to a Schedule by the Lead Agency ( in this case , DIA), and the agreement applies to each member of the class as parties to the agreement . . This AISA will be the first agreement to apply s which allows an AISA to include classes of agencies. Under s ()(g), an AISA must specify with due particularity the class(es) of agency the agreement applies to. This ensures adequate public transparenc y concerning who may be obtaining, using, and on sharing individuals personal information, especially since classes can include private sector agencies and for whom DIA will be responsible for dealing with complaints if the private sector agency is unable to be held accountable . . Thirteen different classes of agencies are provided for under this AISA , including: Charitable entities under section () Charities Act ; Credit unions, friendly societies, incorporated societies, partnerships, registered limited partnerships and registered New Zealand companies; Crown entities listed in Schedule of the Crown Entities Act (other than specified organisations listed in secti on of the Privacy Act); Independent advisory committees and statutory supervisory authorities established under legislation to provide independent advice to a Minister or the Government on a matter relating to the implementation or operation of that legislation ; Independent statutory bodies established under legislation and having a regulatory or administrative role (other than a State services agency) ; Intermediaries New Zealand public sector or private sector agencies whose functions or activities i nclude the collection of death information to lawfully disclose that information to a New Zealand or overseas agency in accordance with an agreement ; Iwi organisations and other Mori organisations listed in the Schedule of the Electoral (Iwi Organisation and Other Mori Organisation) Regulations ; Local authorities named in Schedule to the Local Government Official Information and Meetings Act ; Mortality review committees appointed under section of the Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) Act ; Occu pational regulatory bodies established by or under legislation to license, register, approve, provide oversight of, or otherwise regulate individuals who belong to a particular profession, calling, trade, occupation, or industry ; Public tertiary institutio ns as defined in section () of the Education and Training Act . ; and The agreement has been reviewed on the basis of the proposed classes, however, the agreement has not yet been completed with the proposed members of each class as at the of review. ikudgtnr Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs
Privacy Commissioner CJ Te Mana Matapono Matatapu Privacy Commissioners submission on the proposed information sharing agreement facilitating access to information about deaths Introduction . Under s ()(a)(i) of the Privacy Act ( Privacy Act ), the Department of Internal Affairs ( DIA ), as the lead agency , has consulted me on a proposed information sharing agreement . The agreement seek to enable twelve public sector agencies and thirteen different classes of public and private sector agencies to collect, use, and share certain personal information about deaths of individuals (AISA ) to facilitate public services . . Section ()(a) provides that I must consider the privacy implications of the proposed agreement , and ss ()(b) further provides that I may make any submissions that I consider appropriate. In considering the privacy implications under ss (a) , I have regard to the AISAs required form and content , which is set out under s , including the specified safeguards that will apply to protect the privacy of individuals and will ensure that any interference with their privacy is minimised . Background . When a person dies in New Zealand, the Registrar General of Births, Deaths, and Marriages (Registrar General ) must register the persons death. This Agreement facilitates the sharing of death information the Registrar General holds to public and private agencies that have a role in updating individuals records when they die. Parties to this Agreement may take subsequent actions based on the update of records relating to the deceased individual or associa ted persons, such as granting benefits or entitlements. . This Agreement aims to ensure that personal information records held in organisations databases or lists in electronic formats are from information held by the Registrar General when the in dividual in question has died. The intended benefits are as follows: Organisations having ready access to an authoritative source of registered death information in New Zealand from the Death Register, avoiding the risk of services and communications to a living individual being incorrectly discontinued; Organisations not having to approach the survivors of the deceased individual to require them to provide information andor a death certificate and thus placing an additional burden on people already exp eriencing other complex issues; Avoiding the risk that incorrect or false information may be provided to an organisation; Organisations being aware of the death so that whnau of the deceased individual do not receive official correspondence, subscription reminders, or invoices for charges which may cause significant upset or distress to the deceaseds family; and ikudgtnr Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs
Privacy Commissioner CJ Te Mana Matapono Matatapu in the appropriate schedule and circulate the schedule to all Parties. This ensures further transparency for agencies and the public. Other safeguards . There are important l imits on sharing personal information under this agreement. Information may only be received under this Agreement where the Registrar General or DIA is either the providing or receiving Party. As identified, i ntermediaries can only on share information with Clients if they have a l egal basis to do so, other than this Agreement. Other Parties may not share personal information between themselves under this Agreement. This helps to ensure that once agencies receive personal information, there are protections to ensure that it is not unnecessarily diffused to other agencies. . The AISA also provides that n o Party is obliged to provide any of the requested information to be shared under this Agreement. This is an important privacy protection because it allows agencies to exercise discretion or judgement concerning personal information sharing in the interest s of an individuals privacy. An agency cannot be forced to share when they consider that sharing may constitute a breach of the agreement or a persons privacy more generally. . Another protection requires that c harities, registered New Zealand companies, partnerships, registered limited partnerships, friendly societies, credit unions, incorporated societies , and intermediaries may only offer andor commence products and services where the deceased individual had a prior relationship with the Party. I consider that this can prevent individuals personal information from being used in a way that could be considered potentially unethical during a time of distress for families. . The AISA also requires that p rocesses and procedures exist within each Party to ensure that information sent under this Agreement is transferred separately from information transferred under other agreements. This will help to ensure that p ersonal information is not inadvertently disclosed to the wrong agencies. It also means that agencies will be able to comply with privacy protective AISA obligations that apply to the information processed under this agreement, as agencies may have other r epositories of personal information outside of this agreement. Crucially, the AISA provides that p rocesses and procedures exist within each Party to ensure that the personal information received under this Agreement is only used for the purposes specified in this Agreement and remains protected. Review . This AISA provides that a joint review of this Agreement must be undertaken whenever any Party not included within a Class of Agencies believes a review is necessary. Furthermore, DIA shall conduct a review annually or at intervals specified by the Privacy Commissioner as specified in section of the Privacy Act . The report will be ikudgtnr Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs
Privacy Commissioner CJ Te Mana Matapono Matatapu Trustee corporations within the meaning of a trustee company the Trustee Companies Act and including the Public Trust . . On its face, the intermediaries class has the potent ial to be very broad. However, I am satisfied that the proposed AISA includes appropriate safeguards . . First, intermediaries are defined as A New Zealand Agency that is a public sector agency (other than a Department or a Specified Organisation) or a New Zealand private sector agency and whose functions or activities include the collection of death information for the purpose of lawfully discl osing that information to another New Zealand Agency or an Overseas Agency in accordance with an agreement between the Intermediary and that other agency. . Intermediaries may only on share information with their clients if they have a legal basis to do so. As New Zealand agencies, intermediaries will clearly fall within the scope of the Privacy Act and must comply with the information privacy principles , including principle (security of personal information) and principle (disclosure of personal information outside New Zealand) . Intermediaries are allowed to disclose information to overseas agencies. However, this can only be done in accordance with an ag reement between the intermediary and other agency governing the safeguar ds for the information before the intermediary shares information they receive under this AISA with the client. My Office and the Registrar General will review these written agreements before signing. . Moreover, I am pleased to see that prior to including a New Zealand Agency in the Intermediary class , DIA must consider the following : The nature of the Intermediarys undertaking or activity and whether the Intermediary has a genuine ne ed and lawful purpose to use the personal information in carrying out that undertaking or activity; The Intermediarys policies and practices in relation to the security of personal information and the privacy of individuals; and Any other matter that DIA considers to be relevant. . Further, DIA will have control over the specific data fields of death information to be shared with a particular intermediary that are appropriate for the intermediarys purpose and the permitted uses of that information when adding an intermediary party to the AISA. . Regarding classes other than intermediaries, while DIA may agree that an agency may become a member of a class and , therefore , a party to the AISA, DIA must obtain the Registrar Generals consent prior to approv ing the agencies inclusion . This will help to ensure that sufficient checks are occurring prior to the admission of an agency. Background The government has funded a post COVID recovery initiative across New Zealands library system, especially in public libraries. with a funding package of . million over years. The New Zealand Libraries Partnership Programme will support librarians a nd library services to be retained in New Zealand libraries and assist them to support community recovery. This will enable librarians and library services to play a key role in supporting their communities and people seeking jobs as part of the recovery from COVID. The Local Government COVI Response Unit signalled in its initial analysis that all councils expected a significant reduction in nonrate revenue in the fourthquarter of and well into . Councils that have large numbers of nonessential service businesses in their district are also more likely to face delayed collection from both commercial and residential property rates. The combined effect of lowerthanplanned rates and other revenue reductions means councils are likely to reduce some operationa l expenditure and capital expenditure , which will create job losses directly or indirectly. Although all local authorities provide public library services, such services are not a legislative requirement. The National Library has received clear signals from the library sector that reductions to public library services are expected as a direct result of councils reviewing their expenditure plans. Local governme nt collective ly is the biggest employer of librarians in New Zealand. Role reductions will likely mean a permanent loss of talent to the profession and a consequent deterioration of a valued community service that will be difficult to restore to former levels once skilled workers are lost. The tertiary education sector publicly signalled it is experiencing an impact that they expect will worsen over the next year. Deficits are likely to be addressed in the short term by cutting staff salaries. Library services that can be exited to reduce costs include collaborative services provided by the National Library that are likely to impact student access to knowledge and information. This initiative is designed to support the retention of librarians in employment by public libraries over the next two years, while councils position for recovery. The initiative will provide the opportunity to improve reading, literacy and wellbeing outcomes in communities. support building digital literacy among those who have been most excluded from online services and information during the pandemic or have lost jobs as a consequence . and create new digital resources to support online learning for students. This will primarily utilise and build the skills and experience of librarians currently employed in the local government sector. particularly where they otherwise risk losing their jobs. The programme also includes funding for specialist library services for schools and young people with the greatest need, and needs to consider where to from here for all elements of the programme. The opportunities this funding presents the libraries sector are immense. therefore a key focus of the programme is to assess both the current state of the New Zealand libraries system and define the desired future state, as well as develop a strategic roadmap on how to get there. Document Classification tPMG Confidenti .al Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs The intervention logic map for the programme as shown in the Programme Initiation Document describes the programme focus areas: Current state Intervention The programme had to be set up in a short timeframe to implement the business case and demonstrate how the National Library can help lead and support COVID recovery across New Zealands library system and public libraries. The programme has been setup with defined projects. These defined projects are supported by the central National Library project team that provide strategic direction and governance. According to the Programme Initiation Document, these projects include: Secondments Project: to evaluate and support the workforce capability of the seconded library staff. Evaluation and Monitoring Workstream: to support and monitor evaluation of secondments workstream and the programme to ensure they are meeting the defined outcomes. Workforce Capability Workstream: to build on the skills gap analysis and undertake a training provision analysis to understand what current training is available in the New Zealand market and where gaps exist. Document Classification KPMG Confidential Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs Maintaining of library seNices to the public during the time of community recovery. Skills enhancement in the community to support community recovery. . Focus on Matauranga Maori. . Support the communities most in need. . Leverage existing partnerships and initiatives. We understand from inteNiews that the National library wants to promote equitable outcomes for the sector and community. Rural and remote areas have a significant Maori population and an equity strategy is critical for the programme to achieve its strategic objectives in these areas. lnteNiews identified that the programme has limited Maori representat ion at the governance level and is struggling to hire Maori resources into the programme team. We did not see any evidence of a clear Maori and Pacific strategy that outlines how the programme plans to focus and help improve outcomes for Maori and Pacifica population in rural areas. We understand from the inteNiews that the library sector has a unique culture, operating model. and needs. This is accepted and recognised by the programme leadership . The programme team has limited resources with previous library sector experience which impacts the programmes ability to engage and relate with the public libraries effectively. Recommendations: The programme should accelerate and prioritise efforts to recruit Maori resources in the programme team and improve Maori representation at the governance level. The programme should leverage sector partnerships and relationships to hire resources with strong library experience . . Governance The NZLPP governance structure has been designed to cover both the programme governance and control, and sector reference group type approaches . The programme SRO is ultim ately accountable for the success of the programme and should ideally provide continuity of leadership throughout the programme. The SROs role is to: Ensure that the programme is focused on achieving its objectives and benefits. Ensure the programme gives value for money, ensuring a costconscious approach to the programme of work. Appoint the other members of relevant governance groups and programme management team. Secure funding for the programme. Hold the programme to account for the quality of the products created for any outputs created and realising the benefits, including undertaking benefits reviews. (LIAC) Other management groups or forums that support the Programme include: Governance Groups Responsibilities Frequency Training Advisory Group A small group of representatives from partners, public libraries and Monthly ITOs are available as an advisory group to the programme director and team. They will use their expertise across training, skills enhancement and the public library sector to support and guide the programme of initiatives. The responsibil ities of the Training Advisory Group are as follows: Provide input and advice to the programme team on training and capability uplift activities. Review and comment on training related documentat ion. Support the programme by sharing knowledge and helping connect the team to resources and the wider library sector. Provide an active and positive contribution to the programme. Programme Reference Group The Programme Reference Group are individuals brought together to Monthly discuss and deal with operational issues for the programme and the workstreams w ithin. They provide advice and guidance as subject matter experts to support programme delivery. The Reference Group will: Provide input and advice to the programme team. Review and comment on draft programme documents. Ensure that the views and interests of other stakeholders are represented . Provide an active and positive contribution to the programme. NZLPP Working Group The NZLPP Working Group is made up of internal National Library and Weekly programme team members. It is an extension of the programme team and meets to discuss programme progress and seek feedback and input from relevant National library subject matter experts. We understand from our interviews and review of the NZLPP Governance Member Induction Pack that the programme has a governance structure with the defined accountabilities for the Steering Group and supporting groups (Assurance Groups, Reference Group and Training Advisory Group) described above. However, a number of responsibilities of the Assurance Group and Steering Group overlap. The stakeholders indicated that the governan ce structure could be simplified for more robust decision making and that critical feedback received from the governance is limited. Documen t Oassrhcatk,n Client Confld,ntla l Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs Executive summary The results of NZLPP IOA Round Two indicate an uplift in programme management and governance since IQA Round One conduct ed in May which focused on the assessme nt of Programme Scope, Documentation, Sustainability and Programme Controls. This is primarily reflected in the stakeholders interviews conducted during the review, during which senior programme leadership expressed a strong level of comfort in overall programme management and reporting. KPMG notes positive changes have been made to the change control process and an improved programme governance structure. In addition. the Programme has also established clear tolerance levels around time, cost, scope and risk to remain in place until April . From that the Programme will be in the final weeks of programme closure activities and will adopt a zerotolerance change threshold i.e. anyall proposed changes need to have programme board visibility. While KPMG endorses the tolerance levels being implemented, the Programme should consider reassessing the baseline April ) for the time threshold to an earier to allow sufficient runway for implementation of any changes required. The library sector is diverse with different types of libraries such as medical, law and public etc. Public libraries have been a primary focus for the Programme. Although the Programme has had a positive impact in terms of creating benefits for the broader sector, t has an important role going forward to manage sector expectations around funding and the ongoing role of the National library, post the life of the Programme. Several benefits and positive community stories created by the Programme have been shared with KPMG during our review. However, these benefits and stories need to be shared more broadly w ith the sector. governmen t bodies and NZ public more proactively to gain and demonstrate sector buy in and to demonstrate the developed capabilities within the libraries to demonstrate what has been achieved over the lifetime of the Programme. Notwithstanding positive shifts in respect of the programme management and governance. we believe risk management across the Programme has been light and requires manageme nt attention. In particular, project delivery and postdelivery risks e.g. reputational risk for National library and partners if they are unable to demonstrate a lasting positive impact from NZLPP, needs to be appropriately tracked and managed. We have raised a recommendation associated with risk management in section . of the report. Whilst a review of the Programmes transition or wind down planning has not been a focus for this review period the Programme is at a critical juncture where it must move foiward with certainty and complete all inflight projectswo rkstreams by June and develop a clear plan for the Programmes transition into business as usual (BAU) post the end . The Programme should consider its future resourcing requirements to include specialist resources with strategy, change manageme nt and policy backgrounds to support management w ith effective w ind down planning. Scope The Client Services Order (CSO) dated November outlines the IQA scope as a formal programme level IOA Round Two. This is Round Two of three tranches of IOAs is planned to provide assurance over the overall health of the Programme, confirming appropriate controls, governance, and structure is in place to ensure success of the projects within it. This will certify that the sponsor receives independent feedback that the appropriate structure is in place across the Programme . Focus areas for IQA Round Two as agreed with NZLPP include: Programme Manageme nt Programme Governance Councils Progress Reporting Risk Manageme nt Sustainability . Approach Planning Before we commenced the review, we undertook a planning phase where we agreed the Programme stakeholders to be interviewed for the review to assess the Programmes progress in focus areas listed above. Fieldwork KPMG has achieved the scope through reviewing project documentat ion and interviewing relevant project stakeholders. The scope and approach form a broad review of project processes against accepted project management practices and the New Zealand Government guidelines for managing major project investments. Detailed analysis and collation of the programme data was undertaken by information gathering into specific themesa reas highlighted for validation, to ensure facts were confirmed and the context is fully understood to determine if the programme has adequately assessed the impact and likelihood of risks and identified appropriate responses to mitigate risks. Background The government has funded a post COVID recovery initiative across New Zealands library system. especially in public libraries. with a funding package of . million over years. The New Zealand Libraries Partnership Programme will support librarians and library seNices to be retained in New Zealand libraries and assist them to support community recovery. This will enable librarians and library services to play a key role in supporting their communities and people seeking jobs as part of the recovery from COVID. The Local Governmen t COVID Response Unit signalled in its initial analysis that all councils expected a significant reduction in nonrate revenue in the fourth quarter of and well into . Councils that have large numbers of nonessent ial seNice businesses in their district are also more likely to face delayed collection. from both commerc ial and residential property rates. The combined effect of lowerthanplanned rates and other revenue reductions means councils are likely to reduce some operational expenditure and capital expenditure. which will create job losses directly or indirectly. Although all local authorities provide public library seNices, such seNices are not a legislative requirement. The National Library has received clear signals from the library sector that reductions to public library seNices are expected as a direct result of councils reviewing their expenditure plans. Local government collectively is the biggest employer of librarians in New Zealand. Role reductions will likely mean a permanent loss of talent to the profession and a conseque nt deteriorat ion of a valued community service that will be difficult to restore to former levels once skilled workers are lost. The tertiary education sector publicly signalled it is experiencing an impact that they expect will worsen over the next year. Deficits are likely to be addressed in the short term by cutting staff salaries. Library seNices that can be exited to reduce costs include collaborat ive services provided by the National Library that are likely to impact student access to knowledge and information. This initiative is designed to support the retention of librarians in employment by public libraries over the next two years, while councils position for recovery. The initiative will provide the opportunity to improve reading, literacy and wellbeing outcomes in communi ties, support building digital literacy among those who have been most excluded from online services and information during the pandemic or have lost jobs as a consequence and create new digital resources to support online learning for students. This will primarily utilise and build the skills and exper ience of librarians currently employed in the local government sector. particular ly where they otherwise risk losing their jobs. The Programme also includes funding for specialist library services for schools and young people with the greatest need and needs to consider where to from here for all elements of the Programme. The opportunities this funding presents the libraries sector are immense, therefore a key focus of the Programme is to assess both the current state of the New Zealand libraries system and define the desired future state. as well as develop a strategic roadmap on how to get there. Programme Management NZLPP has made good progress with uplifting its programme management, documentation maintenance and addressing recommendatio ns around programme management made in IOA Round One. Senior programme stakeholders interviewed during the review expressed overall satisfaction and comfort in programme reporting, the quality of governance papers and procurement management. As indicated in Management Response to IOA Round One Recommendatio ns, the programme has developed and maintained a Programme Execution Plan (PEP) as a core programme document which provides an overview of programme operations, managemen t, scope and contractual requirements. Since the programme was rebaselined, a change control process has also been introduced which is positive. A Change Request form (template) has been developed which requires information about change request type, description. impact analysis and cost of change etc. All change requests require SRO and Business Owner approvals. KPMG has no recomme ndations in relation to Programme Management during the IQA Round Two. . Programme Governance We understand from the Project Execution Plan that NZLPP governance structure has been established to cater for programme management, governance, delivery, and ongoing quality assurance. The Senior Responsible Officer (SRO) has the overall financial accountability and responsibility for the strategic direction of the Programme . The SRO also has the accountability for programme success and continuity of leadership througho ut the Programme. Since IQA Round One. the Programm e has also changed responsibilities between the Programme Director and SRO. The former Programme SRO has moved to focus on the National Librarian role and the Programme Director has taken up SRO responsibilities. This has allowed the SRO role to be completely focused on the programme delivery and enabling the National Librarian to focus their attention on sector engagement and programme governance . Governance on the Programme has improved with the development of a clear Terms of Reference (ToR) for the Sector Reference Group and Programme Board that clearly outlines members roles and responsibilities. frequency of meetings and other forum details. We understand that Sector Reference Group has been established as a central forum with sector wide representation from various organisations e.g. LIANZA, Te RopO Whakahau, Public Libraries New Zealand and Local Governmen t New Zealand. to provide input and advice to the Programme. The benefits and engagemen t from the Sector Reference Group are recognised by the sector and we understand from stakeholders interviewed that there is a desire for it to continue beyond the Programme life and help sustain some of the benefits created by the Programme in the library sector. Given the broad library sector needs. expectations from National Library and varying operating models of different library types. dividing responsibility between two primary governance forums Sector Reference Group and Programme Board) should enable more effective managemen t of the Programme. Notwithstanding the enhancemen ts noted above we understand at times governance members might have competing sector interests. funding expectations and lose sight of expectations and forums purpose which is to provide advice and guidance as subject matter experts to support programme delivery. While stakeholders interviewed acknowledged that governance forums are held monthly as intended. attendance at these forums varies at times and in some instances. there is not sufficient time allocated to discuss significant programme decisions or agenda items.
