Councils Progress Reporting Since IQA Round One. NZLPP has introduced a consistent progress reporting template for reporting on quarterly progress across various councils which is positive. The template provides clear guidance on how to report on Action Statements and Delivery Objectives. We understand that definition of success is different for each library given different internal systems, processes and delivery objectives. Due to this how libraries wanted to use the funding and improve the libraries was quite varied which has resulted in variances in the level of detail reported by councils on action statements and delivery objectives. An overall view of councils performance over the length of the Programme and risks or issues are also missing, and we were unable to see evidence of an overarching reporting framework or mechanism being used to ensure consistency in the completion percentage being reported. Recommendation ..: The Programme should setup an ongoing reporting framework for councils. This is particularly important to ensure consistent and accurate sector reporting to Sector Reference Group as it is likely to continue beyond the Programmes life. The Programme Manager should challenge Councils on reporting to ensure there is a sufficient level of detail included in reports to ensure the Programmes qualitative and quantitative benefits are captured. Recommendation ..: The quarterly reporting template should be to include an overview of the councils performance to and any risks and issues. . Risk Management In the IQA Round One, KPMG made a recommendation in relation to programme controls, that the Programme should review the risk register to ensure that any longstanding risks are revaluated and mitigated in a timely manner. We understand that in response, NZLPP was going to hold a delivery phase risk workshop and maintain risk registers with a clear escalation path to the Programme Board as required. Our testing indicated however that this process has not been adhered to in all cases. Examples of this include: We did not see evidence of some of the key programme risks such as; potential reputationa l risk to National Library if the Programme is unable to demonstrate a lasting positive impact and loss of benefits to sector after the Programme ends being appropriately tracked or managed . There was no evidence of mitigations or treatment plans being consistently or managed. Most risks are owned by the Programme Manager. Risks have been open for a significant amount of time e.g. R Sector Engagement raised on October . According to some stakeholders interviewed, the Programme has internal processes to manage risks however, the risks are not robustly discussed at governance or strategic meetings. Recommendation ..: Additional focus on the Programme risk management is required. All programme risks should be captured and included within the risk register. The risks should be reviewed regularly and validated and if required, escalated to issues that are required to be managed by the Programme or an appropriate owner. Critical risk management should be prioritised ahead of the regular governance forums with Treatment Plans being adequate ly documented and . High () Mid () Low () as of June as of June as of June as of June as of June as of June as of June Source: Department of Internal Affairs How do inequities come about Inequities are not random; they are typically due to structural factors present in society and the local community that cannot be explained by biomedical differences between population groups. This means their causes are often complex and multifaceted and are outside the scope of the health system to address on its own. For example, income inequality (poverty) has been shown to be strongly associated with differences in health outcomes, including gambling (Canale et al ; KolandaiMatchett et al ; Rintoul et al ; Tu et al ; van der Maas ). This means that achieving equity in gambling harm minimisation requires a strong evidence base and a strategic, integrated approach from the health sector and other sectors. The Ministry will use strategies and frameworks such as He Korowai Oranga (Ministry of Health c); Equity of Health Care for Mori: A framework (Ministry of Health b); Ala Moui: Pathways to Pacific Health and Wellbeing (Ministry of Health a) and the New Zealand Health Strategy (Minister of Health ) to focus on minimising gamblingharmrelated inequities. It will support this focus through health literacy activities. The Ministry s health literacy framework and guide aim to improve the quality of services delivered to individuals, families , whnau and communities by raising awareness of issues such as the importance of screening and the presence of inequities and harm in service use (Ministry of Health ). It has applied the approach in gambling harm minimisation services; more broadly to promote screening in drug, alcohol and mental health services; and in the navigator approach to accessing health services. INCONFIDENCE Page of Office of the Minister for Government Digital Service s Office of the Minister of Internal Affairs Chair, Cabinet Economic Development Committee Progressing Digital Identity: Establishing a Trust Framework Proposal . Digital identity can deliver significant economic and social benefits to public and private sector organisations. The Covid pandemic has highlighted the role of digital identity as a foundation for accessing services and entitlements online. This paper recommends the creation of a Digital Identity Trust Framework (Trust Framework) to accelerate the development and uptake of digital identity services that are secure, trusted and intero perable. . This paper seeks approval for operating funding of . million in total for and to establish an interim Trust Framework and develop legislation to create a statutory Trust Framework. . The Trust Framework will align with trust frameworks in Australia, Canada and the United Kingdom, and is the basis for delivering on the Prime Ministers commitment under the Single Economic Market agenda for mutual recognition of digital identity services with Australia. Executive summary . Digital identity is the user consented sharing of personal and organisational information online to access services and complete transactions. Digital identity services are delivered by both public and private sector providers and rely on trusted information from sources such as government agencies and financial institutions. There is the potential for digital identity to play a larger role in New Zealands economy by improving service delivery and reducing inefficiencies, security risks and privacy breaches. Ther e is wide support in both the public and private sectors to ensure that digital identity services are trusted, coherent and sustainable. . Digital identity is a foundational element for enabling the integration of services and digital transformation across g overnment, as identified in Rautaki m ttahi Rngai Kwanatanga Matihiko , the Strategy for a Digital Public Service. . New Zealand has the opportunity to be a leader in digital identity. This includes delivering on the New Zealand and Australian Prime Min isters commitment to mutual recognition of identity services between Australia and New Zealand. It also includes ongoing alignment with Canada and the United Kingdom with each of these countries developing their own Trust Frameworks to clarify rules and enable interoperability. . The Covid pandemic has highlighted the importance of trusted digital identity for providing services in situations where face toface contact is difficult. This is one of the

Priority Routine Internal Affairs briefing Hon Brooke van Velden Minister of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua Internal Affairs Title: Options for making Class gambling online payments permanent June Key issues A temporary exemption allowing Class operators of largescale lotteries to take online or remote payments expires in October this year. On Thursday, June you are meeting with the Chief Executives of the Heart Foundation, Coastguard, and Auckland Rescue Helicopter Trust. They will likely ask you to make the exemption permanent to make fundraising easier. These organisations are reliant on largescale lotteries to raise money for their work in the community. Reverting to inperson or postal sales will severely hamper their fundraising efforts, especially when facing increased costs. We support making the exemption permanent , but it has been challenging to find a suitable legislative vehicle. There are essentially choices to make the exemption permanent. The first is to adopt Hon Barbara Edmonds yettodra wn Gambling (Enabling Remote Interactive Gambling for Class Operator s) Amendment Members Bill, or the second is to seek Cabinet approval prior to the expiry to make the exemption permanent when a suitable legislative vehicle becomes available. The likely legislation within the Internal Affairs portfolio would be the Regulatory Systems Amendment Bill or the online casino gambling legislation. Adopting the Members Bill and passing under urgency would ensure the permanent exemption is made before October . If you were to decide on a preferred option before the meeting next week, you could communicate this to the Class operators at the meeting. Action sought I Timeframe Read this briefing ahead of your meeting with the Chief Executives of the Heart Foundation, Coastguar d and Auckland Rescue Helicopter Trust on Thursday, June . By June Direct officials to draft a Cabinet paper based on your preferred option. This briefing provides options for you r consider ation , to make the exemption allowing Class operators of large scale lotteries to take online and remote payments permanent . In , a temporary exemption was given to Class operators What is Class gambling . Class gambling includes large scale lotteri es, housie (otherwise known as bingo) , instant games and other forms of gambling run by incorporated societies . It is used to raise money for an authorised purpose , where p rizes offered exceed ,. Organisations that hold Class licences are mostly registered charities and faith based organisations . . Under section of the Gambling Act (the Act), Class lotteries cannot be run online or by phone . This limit s operators to selling lottery tickets via post or in person and receiving payment by ca sh or cheque . However, New Zealanders are using cash less often to purchase goods and services and c heques are no longer an option as they have been phased out by banks. There is also a security risk of sending cash or credit card details in the mail. A temporary exemption allowing online payments expires in October . In , a s part of the COVID response , Class operators were permitted to sell their tickets online and remotely . This is because in person sales were difficult during lockdown . Due to the emergency related nature of the COVID related legislation, all amendments had an expiry in this case, October . . Since then, w e have tried to find a suitable legislative vehicle to make this exemption permanent. In March , the Department proposed an amendment for the next Statut es Amendment Bill. However, the Ministry of Justice concluded it was not suitable for inclusion as, in its view, the proposal did not meet the criteria of being non controversial. Another option was for the online g ambling legislative process to be utilised but that has not been progressed in time to address this issue before the temporary exemption expires. . Class operators have been contacting us, your office, and other Ministers advocating for the change to be come permanent. They are understandably concerned about the prospect of returning to non digital sales or being in breach of the law if they do not . . we do not expect the proposal to be controversial exce pt to the extent that any changes to gambling provisions always attract some attention from those concerned about gambling harm, even from low risk activities . Digital payments are the norm for most New Zealanders now and this change simply brings Class into line with that . There is no evidence that the exemption caused an increase in gambling harm or additional workload for the regulator . Class organisations rely on lottery sales for their operations . Organisations , such as the Heart Foundation and Coastguard, rely on large scale lotteries to raise money for their work in the community . For the Coastguard, its lottery programme is its second largest fundraising stream . It runs lotteries per year which generates ar ound .m per annum (around of its annual income in FY). Last year, . This was only possible because of the temporary exemption . . These organisations are concerned that removing digital or remote sales will result in: a loss of customers, both existing and new, because purchasing lottery tickets will become too hard under the old rules ,

Objective : Gambling environments are designed to prevent and minimise gambling harm There is compelling evidence that certain types of gambling are more likely to be associated with harm than others. The Ministry will continue to advocate for technological andor environmental changes to gambling environments that are likely to have a positive effect on reducing harmful gambling behaviour and be costeffective. It intends to focus on greater use of technology to monitor and manage gambling environments and gambling behaviours over the course of th is strategic plan, and has set aside resources to pilot new and innovative uses of technology that may include: technologybased support for people at risk of or affected by harmful gambling, such as online selfhelp and support services tools to support gamblers and host venues to monitor for signs of harmful gambling and enable gamblers to set limits on their gambling activity STRATEGY TO PREVENT AND MI NIMISE GAMBLING HARM TO Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs
Contact event was defined as contact that we would intend a contact tracing card to record by Ministry of Health contact definition , such as hugging, touching, and talking facetoface. For example, two people standing within two metres backtoback would be scored , but facetoface would be scored as the transmission risk is different even though the relative distance is the same. Minutes where two contacts were outofrange (m) from each other were left blank. Minutes where we were unable to determine distance were scored and both card and ground truth events for those minutes were removed before evaluation. Distances were verified by using floor plans as well as physically measured space between reference points such as walls and furniture.

However, recognising that some councils may want to move quickly to start shifting the delivery of water services into more financially sustainable models, Cabinet has agreed that new legislation will include provisions that help streamline the process for establishing water services council controlled organisations as currently provided for under the Local Government Act . Since becoming Minister of Local Government I have heard that the current legislative requirements make it challenging for councils in different districts to explore joint arrangements for service delivery. ()(g)(i) ()(g)(i) Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua Department of Internal Affairs INCONFIDENCE Page of The Bill will contain a bespoke set of consultation and decision making arrangements that will enable councils to streamline this process while continuing to provide the opportunity for community input. These streamlined arrangements are voluntary for councils to choose to use, as an alternativ e to some of the standard requirements in the Local Government Act. The arrangements include provisions that: o Clarify that councils can set up joint committees that can consult on a proposal across multiple districts (instead of each council carrying out separate consultation), and to make recommendations to participating councils o Set minimum consultation and information requirements one round of consultation, and information only needs to be provided on the analysis of two options (status quo preferred option) o Enable councils to consider the collective benefitsimpacts of a proposal (across multiple districts), in addition to the interests of their individual districts and to factor in the view of other participating councils This is just the first step in giving councils the flexibility to identify and use the service delivery models and financing tools that are right for them and their communities.

It would bring consistency into the digital identity ecosystem in New Zealand , enabling a high trust environment for all participants . Unlike Option , which would also enable a high trust envi ronment, it can be established in the near term and at a lower cost. It is sufficiently flexible and responsive enough to grow and develop into a larger and more complex model, if required. Government would maintain control over compliance process, ensuring consistency across the trusted digital identity ecosy stem. RealMe , or parts of it, could be incorporated into the Trust Framework . Mori representation at the governance level will ensure Mori concerns and approaches to personal information (e.g. prioritising iwi affiliation over other attributes) are given appropriate consideration . It would meet stakeholder requirements. Evidence gathered through The Departments engagement process indicated stakeholders generally wanted a government led intervention, that combined rules, compliance testing and legal enforceability, and could be established in a timely manner. The digital identity ecosystem is not at a level of maturity to allow for Option . Option would involve the establishment of a larger and more complex Trust Framework regime than Option . Similar to Option , the Trust Framework would be overseen by a governance body and supported by an accreditation regime , and it would bring trust and consistency to the digital identity ecosystem . Additionally, Option would allow for greater autonomy fr om government. It would still have clear lines of accountability and could react quickly to changes in industry standards. However, it could not be established in a timely fashion. Th is option could not be operationalised until a new entity had been created and resourced to support it, and until such time as a new Trust Framework Bill had been introduced, all of which will take years. Furthermore , there is a realistic possibility that it may not be fit for purpose when it does come on line. The size and complexit y of this option may be out of proportion with the market and requirements, especially as there will only likely be a small number of participants authorised to operate under the Trust Framework when it first comes online. As suc h, the cost of establishing a large and complex regime from the outset outweigh the benefits of such a regime. Approving Option does not preclude the possibility to moving to an Option model in the future, if the uptake and size of the ecosystem warrants such an approach. Option is preferred over Option as it enables responsive scalability. Options and will not achieve the objective of bringing trust and consistency into the digital identity ecosystem in New Zealand. Under Option , the digital identity ecosystem will continue to be afflicted by inefficiency and a lack of consumer control over their information. Phase two: the formal establishment of the Trust Framework ( ). In this phase, the Trust Framework is established in legislation and becomes legally enforceable. The governance board becomes formalised with its powe rs and parameters formally established in legislation. The compliance process in phase one transitions into a formal accreditation regime, where systems can be tested against legally enforceable rules, and compliance can be formally recognised. The limitat ions on the number of entities being assessed against the rules are relaxed and any entity wishing to participate in the trusted digital identity ecosystem can apply to undergo assessment. The Bill will provide the accreditation body with the power to impl ement a cost recovery model and charge for accreditation. The anticipated cost of this phase is . million . The outyear costs of running the Trust Framework will be confirmed once cost recovery policy is confirmed . Through the Water Service Delivery Plans, councils will be asked to provide baseline information about their water services operations, assets, revenue, expenditure, pricing, and capital. This is not a regulatory information gathering exercise, but is a useful first step to build the capability of councils and prepare the Commerce Commission ahead of the full economic regulation regime being introduced from the middle of next year. All councils that have water service delivery responsibilities (either directly or through existing council controlled organisations) will be subject to these requirements. As well as the Plans being , information collected through them will be shared with the Commerce Commission, to help them with the development of the future regulatory regime. ()(g)(i) Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua Department of Internal Affairs INCONFIDENCE Page of The Bill will also provide for some councils to be subject to an early form of information disclosure by the Commerce Commission, prior to the full economic regulation regime. This will build on the information collected through the Plans, and is intended to be for larger councils that have more advanced assetfinancial management practices, or those moved quickly to establish new organisations and are ready for a faster track t oward more detailed oversight. there is likely to be a reduction in revenue for sports and racing codes from the POCC removal and reductions in BI UC payments (the racing codes collected approximately million f rom POCC in the financial year and . million the financial year from BIUC agreements). The Department considers the risks of these costs outweighing the increased benefits of the monopoly are unlikely, it is not guaranteed. We also note that the racing codes support the monopoly despite these losses ; there is likely to be a reduction in GST as noted, the proposals will see a fall in GST paid as offshore operators exit the market. Officials estimate the amount of GST collected in from offshore operators that related to income from sports and racing wagering to be approximately . million. However much of the GST loss will be offset by increased TAB NZ GST revenue through the monopoly or gamblers shifting their spending to other GST registered gambling operators (e.g. casinos or pokies) or spending a similar amount of funds on other goods and services such as entertainment which are subject to GST. In addition, the payments from Entain NZ to TAB NZ that are conditional on an online mon opoly (m upfront should lead to additional spending in the New Zealand economy which would contribute to tax revenues. This positive impact of additional spending in the New Zealand economy could outweigh any GST losses from some NZ gamblers shifting to non compliant offshore operators. It is therefore assumed the impact will be minimal, but this will depend on the amount of customer s returning to TAB which is difficult to estimate ; customers may not automatically return to TAB NZ if the monopoly is established while Entain taking o ver the day today operations has resulted in improved odds and betting options, TAB NZ still offers less variety than most other online sports and racing wagering and there is a risk that a lack of competition could lower likelihood of TAB providing competitive odds and newinnovative products in future . a black market will likely remain while reputable operators are likely to prevent customers from New Zealand from accessing their sites, this is easy to circumvent using a VPN. Customers may also choose to bet with less reputable operators to access different products or more range, increasing the risk of gambling harm if they are using sites without adequate consumer protections and harm minimisation practices; there is a risk that the proposed interim enforcement regime will not be sufficient for TAB NZ to receive the payments from Entain provided. TAB NZ have advised us that they consider this risk to be minimal but as the payment is to be released it the discretion of Entain, we cannot be certain ; there is risk the that the online reforms will stall , leaving the interim regulator arrangement in place for a longer time than intended ; the monopoly favour s Entain as TAB NZ partner which some may consider inappropriate .

identified that when situations call for deliberation in the absence of high levels of emotion (cold cognition), such as voting, granting consent for research participation, and making autonomous medical decisions, the ability of an individual to reason and consider alternative courses of action reaches adult levels during the mid teen years. When situations that involve emotionally charged situations where time for deliberation and self restraint is unlikely or difficult (hot cognition), such as driving, co nsuming alcohol, and criminal behaviour, impulse choices are more likely and mental processes are slower to develop, reaching adult levels into adulthood.

Custom Bluetooth apps. Users would download and run such an app which would broadcast out unique keys to others in the area. If each phone is aware of other phones it has been close to for a defined time a view of close contacts can be formed. When an app user tests positive, the unique codes stored on their phone allows close contacts (normally defined as contacts within metres for minutes or more) to be quickly notified, contacted, and quarantined, faster than manual contact tracing might otherwise allow.

PHUs and the newly established National Close Contact Service hub required additional resources to cope with the existing level of tracing under Level .
Provide public health management advice (i e. direction to isolate), education, and identify welfare or cultural needs. Information from interviews is predominantly paperbased. A case report form is submitted for every case to the national ESR EpiSurv platform and some PHUs have their own IT solutions to manage the investigation of cases and contacts. Following the interview, the PHU traces close contacts, provides selfisolation advice and monitors these persons regularly for symptoms. The PHU also provides advice to institutions and the public in higher risk situations around management of casual contacts (e.g. flights). Since COVID there have been some modifications to this process, including establishment of the National Close Contact Service (NCCS) and the National Contact Tracing Solution an IT platform that can be used by PHUs (although is not mandatory and some PHUs have chosen not to use it) and the Ministry of Health to manage cases and contacts. The NCCS is a Ministry of Health service that aims to help find the contact details of close contacts and highrisk casual contacts (e.g. flights). The NCCS is available at the request of PHUs for the management of individuals or clusters. These two initiatives were necessitated by rapidly increasing COVID cases and multiple complex clusters, which rapidly exceeded the capacity of PHUs. Service delivery in to This section discusses service delivery during the to period in terms of public health activity, intervention activity, accessibility for and responsiveness to the needs of Mori and Pacific peoples, and research and evaluation. Public health Effective health promotion is central to the Ministry s national public health activity. In the context of gambling, the Ministry s public health promotion aims are to rais e awareness of the signs of harmful gambling and encourage more atrisk people to check whether their gambling is OK before harm escalates in severity, and to motivate those who are at risk to get help earlier (or change their behaviour through selfhelp). HPAs health promotion programme focuses on encouraging positive behaviour change among atrisk gamblers and raising awareness about the signs of harmful gambling and risky gambling behaviours. H PAled developments have included enhancing national awarenessraising campaigns, developing and implementing host responsibility policies and practices, and increasing staff knowledge of gambling harm minimisation. Over , HPA continued to promote the Gambling Helpline, Choice Not Chance and face toface support services. National and regional service providers delivered a variety of health promotion activities to minimise gamblingrelated harm in communities, including advocating and supporting hundreds of organisations and workplaces to adopt reducing gambling harm policies, run workshops and presentations on recognising gambling harm and learn how to support someone who wants help to stop gambling, and thousands of awarenessraising activities in communities. A regionally led campaign to Turn Off the Pokies was well supported by class venues. Many service providers also provided a community perspective into the reviews of local gambling venue policies undertaken by territorial authorities. Currently about percent of local authorities have either gaming machine caps or sinkinglid policies in their areas. In line with the objectives of th e strategy, the Ministry funded dedicated Mori, Pacific and Asian public health services to provide appropriate and relevant services within their communities. The national Multi Venue Exclusion Advisory Group led a review of MVE processes for gamblers who want to be stopped from entering gambling venues. As a result of the review, a pilot national standardised process for supporting this process is under way. www.choicenotchance.org.nzthelatestcampaign (accessed April ). This was calculated by totalling actual payments from each sector made to IRD up to June , together with the estimates of sector payments up to June . The Ministry then calculated the amount of levy that each sector was expected to pay by: referring to the relevant Cabinetapproved strategy before the start of each levy period, to identify each sectors expected share of the levy requirement for each threeyear period using those shares to calculate the amount each sector was expected to pay as its contribution to the Ministrys spending in each levy period . totalling these amounts across all levy periods to arrive at the amount each sector was expected to pay up to June . Functions of the strategy The strategy comprises a rolling sixyear strategic plan and a threeyear service plan and is refreshed every three years. Together, the strategic and service plans set out the Ministry s approach and the range of activities it plans to undertake to minimise gambling harm from to . The strategy sets out the statutory requirements for an integrated problem gambling strategy and the aim for gambling harm minimisation, and specifies strategic objectives. It reflects the Ministry s public health approach to gambling harm minimisation and its relationship to the complementary responsibility of DIA in regulati ng gambling activity. Other key Ministry strategic documents inform the strategy and align with it. The strategic plan provides the strategic context and direction for the threeyear service plan. The Ministry has made some changes to the strategic plan to reflect changes in the minimising gambling harm and wider addiction and mental health sector landscape . Section outlines more substantial changes for the next three years of the service plan, to address areas highlighted by the needs assessment and outcomes monitoring summarised below. Gambling venues are one of the best environments in which to observe, identify and intervene in potentially harmful gambling. The Ministry, DIA and HPA are committed to working with operators to maximise venues potential for offering safe gambling environments and detecting harmful gambling at an early stage. The Ministry will also support DIA to judicious ly and effective ly use its regulatory tools to deal with operators or venues that do not meet legal requirements. The location of EGMs in highrisk areas (most notably areas of high deprivation) is a longstanding area of concern. The Ministry will continue to support promoting awareness of safe gambling environments , to improve access to gambling harm prevention services in highrisk areas and to work with DIA on its riskbased regulatory approach that guides where regulatory actions should be applied. A particular focus in the next levy period will be NCGM locations and guidance to local authorities and other regulators. Host responsibility training will continue to be an important part of work under this objective. There will be a renewed emphasis on materials related to cultural competence, and how to effectively and appropriately engage with gamblers and their family and whnau from diverse cultural backgrounds. . hours will be claimed as Hours ECE hours and . hours claimed as Plus ECE hours.
Hours ECE Hours are the fully subsidised hours that the child receives.
Hours ECE enables services to provide early childhood education to yearolds, yearolds and yearolds for up to a maximum of hours per child per day and hours per child per week without charging fees.
Hours ECE funding can only be claimed for children who fill a childplace and are , or years of age.
Hours ECE funding includes both the Hours ECE hours and the Plus ECE hours.
Hours ECE funding is based on the child rather than the place they occupy in the service.
Hours ECE funding is paid three times a year, along with the ECE Funding Subsidy.
Hours ECE hours are funded at a higher level because they are intended to meet the full average cost of providing ECE for each service type.
Hours ECE hours are funded at a higher level to cover the full cost of providing ECE.
Hours ECE hours are the funded child hours that services can claim per eligible child for the provision of Hours ECE.
Hours ECE hours are the hours you would claim for yearolds, yearolds and yearolds. The signed attestation part of the enrolment agreement must be completed for each child.
Hours ECE hours claimed
Hours ECE hours may be claimed for the first . hours. Services must claim Plus ECE hours for the remaining half hour.
Hours ECE hours must only be claimed for up to hours per week for each child.
Hours ECE is a higher rate of funding than the ECE Funding Subsidy for threeyearolds, fouryearolds and fiveyearolds for up to a maximum of six hours per child per day and hours per week.
Hours Early Childhood Education (ECE) is a higher rate of funding for services to cover the average full cost of providing early childhood education.
Hours Early Childhood Education (ECE) is a higher rate of funding than the ECE Subsidy.

Active supervision of children can be achieved in a number of ways including:
Active supervision takes advantage of all available learning opportunities and means never leaving children unattended. It means being able to monitor (see or hear) all children at all times, including indoors, outdoors and when sleeping. Educators should use their professional judgment and common sense when deciding when it is appropriate to have any children out of their direct line of sight. For example, for older children who want to use the toilet with some privacy, it is appropriate to supervise by remaining in hearing distance.

Although it is important there is a place for people at the centre to go to when a fire breaks out or in another emergency such as an earthquake, it is just as important to ensure that this place does not put children or adults in further danger from other hazards. This can be a challenge for some centres because of the layout of their premises and proximity to main roads, car parks, waterways and so on. Young children often behave erratically when scared or distressed, and adults need to reduce stress (for themselves, as well as for the children) in these situations as much as possible.

Centres are required to keep a record of each emergency drill. At a minimum, this should record:
Centres have indoor and outdoor areas. The outdoor play areas are open all year, including in winter. The indoor spaces may be separated into activity areas such as dressup clothes, books, building blocks, or musical instruments.
Centres have to use clean sheets and blankets that are not shared between children. They must also provide safe bedding. An example is no pillows for children under .
Centres in rural or isolated areas that are not on a town water supply and use bores or water tanks must meet the Drinking Water Standards for New Zealand.
Centres must ensure that children who sit or stand when they wake have room to do so. Children who can pull themselves to a standing position should not be placed in the top cot for safety reasons.
Centres must ensure that during cooking activities children are closely supervised if they are to have access to the fridge and, if possible, any medicines are stored out of the reach of children.
Centres must have a child protection policy that meets the Childrens Acts requirements.
Centres must make the policy and information about its practices available to parents as required by criterion GMA Parent access to information.
Centres need adequate facilities to cater for occasions when an older child needs to rest or sleep. How a service provides these facilities depends on what suits their particular centre layout and operation.
Centres need to be designed and laid out so the physical environment supports the way the curriculum can be provided. Activity spaces need to be configured to allow for a range of learning experiences, as well as meeting the minimum space per child requirement. Centres must have sufficient indoor space for group learning, and outdoor space must be of a size and shape that does not restrict different kinds of physical activity.
Centres need to decide who provides any infant formula and bottles. If formula is provided, parental approval of the brandtype is required before it is used. If the usual brandtype is unavailable, parental approval of any substitute is also required prior to use.
Centres need to ensure there is adequate hygienic storage for this purpose such as wall hooks for linen bags. A cupboard or area which children cannot access is useful.
Centres need to first determine which emergency drills are relevant to their location and carry out each type of drill with children (as appropriate) on an, at least, monthly basis.
Centres need to first determine which emergency drills are relevant to their location, and then carry each of these drills out with children at least every months.
Centres should consider children with additional needs.
Centres should consider the age of the children at the service and ensure there are sufficient lowlevel cots for them to move into as they grow.
Centres should have a policy and procedure in regard to alcohol and other substances for staff, volunteers, parents and visitors to the centre.
Centres should take all reasonable steps to ensure equipment is kept in good repair and maintained regularly. A regular inspection programme to ensure equipment and surfacing are properly maintained is advised. This will ensure any necessary repairs and maintenance can be completed promptly.
Centres should talk with regional Ministry of Education ECE licensing staff and Fire and Emergency New Zealand personnel about the best options for their particular situation.

Educators must never smoke or vape in the home while children are attending the service at any time including while children are asleep. In addition, they must never smoke or vape whilst on an excursion with the children.
Educators must notify parents as soon as possible of the event and be able to provide as much detail as possible about what happened, when, and what actions they took. Educators must also notify their coordinator or the service provider.
Educators must think about the possible emergency situations they might encounter in the home. Preparing for an emergency situation is an important part of the induction process that the coordinator carries out with each educator.
Educators need to consider the time, place, and space to develop these relationships through informal and formal opportunities. Formal opportunities will include times where communication is planned, and may involve preparation, for example, a parent interview when the child is admitted to hospital. Enrolment schemes are used in New Zealand schools to manage roll growth and provide priority access to students who live within a defined geographical area, known as the school zone.
Enrolment schemes at state schools set out a geographical area around the school called a home zone. The scheme also outlines any special programmes that a school might run. If you live within a schools home zone, your child automatically qualifies to enrol.

Infants are learning to anticipate events, make sense of their worlds and communicate their needs in these early months of life. They learn through touch, sight, sound, smell, and taste in exploration of their everyday environments, and through interactions with adults and other children in environments that are safe yet provide sensory stimulation.

It is recommended that ECE services use bleach as a disinfectant when responding to recent outbreaks of diseases caused by microorganisms (germs) such as giardia, cryptosporidium and salmonella. Many of these germs are resistant to most disinfectants. Bleaches contain sodium hypochlorite, the chemical which kills bacteria and viruses. Bleach used must be at least hypochlorite. Supermarket bleach is labelled between and sodium hypochlorite. Bleach solutions must be made fresh daily to remain effective.

Multilevel cots (also known as bunk cots or stacker cots) are those where (usually) cots are fixed on top of each other.
Multilevel cots are only acceptable if the following can be assured:
Multilevel cots must have no gaps or protrusions that could trap an infant or catch their clothing and have no sharp edges. The sides must be high enough to stop an infant climbing out and there should be no footholds.
Multilevel cots must only be able to be opened from the outside by an adult to place a child in or remove a child.

Outdoor activity space is:
Outdoor space should enable children to experience natural settings (for example, wind, sky, sun, rain) and enable children to undertake activities that would generally not be allowed inside a building (for example, running, kicking a ball). Plastic equipment, while cheap, easily accessible and attractive to children, is often poor imitations of real objects. For example, a plastic hammer, plastic spanner and plastic carpentry bench have little educational value for carpentry play. By using a real hammer or spanner successfully, a child can learn a lot of carpentry skills as well as gain useful knowledge about these objects and their uses. With adult support, children will also learn about important issues relating to the safe use of real equipment.

Playcentres are licensed and must meet the same standards for education and care as teacherled services, but have different qualification requirements.
Playcentres cater for children from birth to school age. They are run cooperatively by parents and
Playcentres choosing to take up Hours ECE cannot claim initial advance funding for Hours ECE.
Playcentres choosing to take up Hours ECE in their centres cannot claim initial advance funding for Hours ECE.
Playcentres meeting the group supervision requirements for standard funding (as specified in section C) can access quality funding if one more adult with the Playcentre Introductory Award is on duty on the session. This adult would be in addition to those required by the group supervision requirements for standard funding. So, the number of required adults on session effectively increases by one.
Playcentres should contact their relevant Ministry regional office as early as possible to discuss their situation. It is important to note that if a playcentre does not meet the conditions on any provisional licence then the licence must be cancelled.
Playcentres that cannot meet the person responsible or minimum qualifications for group supervision may be eligible for discretionary funding for up to sessions per funding period. All other supervision and licensing requirements must be met including adult:child ratios and first aid qualification requirements.

Playgroup operational funding: a general grant available to all eligible playgroups to assist with ongoing operational costs.

Playgroup special grant: a discretionary grant available to assist playgroups to meet large costs that cannot be met from other funding.
Playgroups are certificated in accordance with the Education and Training Act under the Education (Playgroups) Regulations , which prescribe minimum standards that each certificated playgroup must meet. Certification criteria are used to assess how playgroups meet the minimum standards required by the regulations.
Playgroups are communitybased groups run by parent and
Playgroups are expected to have emergency drills at least every months. Evacuation drills should be organised to test a variety of emergency situations and scenarios. For example, practising both earthquake drills and fire evacuation drills, and practising evacuation via alternative exits if these are available. You should aim to hold your trial evacuations at times when you have typical numbers of children, of varying ages, and adults at the playgroup. Consider also the timing of evacuations and whether or not attending parents will be notified in advance. Holding unannounced evacuations at challenging times (for example during morning teatime) may be inconvenient but will give you greater assurance that your procedures are effective.
Playgroups are not licensed. To receive government funding and support, they need to be certified. Parents and
Playgroups are required to document a plan outlining the learning experiences and play opportunities they will provide. A plan provides a starting point for playgroups. It provides a summary of the experiences and opportunities available to children during sessions.
Playgroups are required to review the experiences and opportunities planned for and provided at playgroup at least every months. Reviewing these will help you to make sure they are consistent with the curriculum framework.
Playgroups do not receive the same level of funding as licensed ECE services.
Playgroups give children of all ages the chance to work and play together.
Playgroups have access to a range of organisations that support families, like Plunket, Barnardos, Ministry of Social Development (MSD), Rural Education Activities Programmes (REAP), local schools, councils and community networks such as churches. Information from these organisations could be made available to parents and caregivers.

Playgroups must meet the Education (Playgroups) Regulations to be certified and receive government funding.
Playgroups must provide the Ministry of Education with name and address for a funding contact person and keep them informed when changes occur. This is the person that funding claim forms and other information are sent to.
Playgroups recognised as Licenceexempt prior to December must continue to meet the definition of a playgroup in the Education Gazette on February to remain eligible for funding. Playgroups established after December must hold a current interim or full certificate to be eligible for funding.

Progression of certificated
Progression of certificated staff through the salary steps described in this section is only a required funding condition while a service attests to meeting the requirements of the full salary scale. If a service chooses not to attest, at any point, the condition does not apply. However, legal agreements that specify salary progression may still apply (eg employment contracts).
Progression of certificated teachers through the allowance steps described in this section is only a required funding condition while a service attests to meeting the requirements of the allowance level that the service has attested to. If a service chooses not to attest, at any point, the condition does not apply. However, legal agreements that specify allowance entitlements may still apply (e.g., employment contracts).

Risk is the likelihood that death, injury or illness might occur when a person is exposed to a hazard. Risks must be managed by taking action to eliminate them, and if that is not reasonably practicable, minimising or isolating them. Eliminating a hazard will also eliminate any risks associated with that hazard.

Some services are in lowlying coastal areas and therefore would be required to evacuate if there was a tsunami warning. Some of these services may have an evacuation procedure that requires the use of vehicles to get as many children as possible to high ground quickly. It is not expected that these services practice the tsunami drill to the full extent by overloading vehicles with children and travelling to the designated safe space as this is illegal in normal circumstances and poses unnecessary risk to children. These services should still practice their tsunami drill and include children as far as practicably possible, for example, drill may include a process that facilitates the movement of children to the proposed exit point as quickly as possible in preparation for getting children into planned evacuation vehicles.

Stateintegrated schools annual financial statements guidance
Stateintegrated schools are schools that have a special character. They generally have a philosophical or religious belief as part of their school programme. If your child attends one of these, it must be the closest school of its type for them to qualify for transport assistance. For example, the closest Catholic school if Catholic education is chosen.
Stateintegrated schools are schools with a special character. They are funded by the government and teach the national curriculum. They have their own sets of aims and objectives to reflect their own particular values and are set within a specific philosophy or religion. You will pay compulsory attendance dues.
Stateintegrated schools have to make specific disclosures in their financial statements. Read our guidance for the details.

Surfaces need to be constructed from or sealed with moistureimpervious materials and designed in a way that minimises a buildup of dirt, food particles and bacteria, for example in corners and joins. The annual plan describes and guides what the service will do in its operation in the next months. It is detailed enough to cover daytoday events, for example, excursions, staff appraisals or professional development, but is also a schedule of planned strategic opportunities, including for selfreview and internal evaluation (GMA). When a July roll is used, the adjustment is worked at as fiveeighteenths of the Year roll, rounded up to the nearest whole number.
When a March roll is used, the adjustment is worked out as eleventwelfths of the Year roll, rounded up to the nearest whole number.
When a centre takes some children on an excursion and some children remain at the centre, the first aid qualification ratio must be met both on the excursion and at the centre.
When a child becomes ill at a centre, the sooner they can be taken home, the better. The centre is not usually set up to deal with sick children for long periods of time, although an area away from other children at the centre where sick children can rest comfortably under supervision, while waiting to be taken home is required. For more information see PF Isolation area.
When a child becomes ill at a home that is not their own, the sooner they can be taken home, the better. In order for them to be kept at a safe distance from other children at the home the educator will need a separate area for them that can be easily supervised whilst looking after other children attending. For more information see the guidance for PF Isolation area.
When a child becomes unexpectedly ill at a centre, there needs to be somewhere for their care to make the sick child feel comfortable, as well as to keep other children from becoming ill until the sick child can be collected and taken home. The child must be able to be supervised. If the child is isolated in a separate room with an adult, the service must maintain adult to child ratios.
When a child becomes unexpectedly ill attending the homebased service, there needs to be somewhere for their care to make the sick child feel comfortable, as well as to keep other children from becoming ill until the sick child or other children at the home can be collected and taken home. The child must be able to be supervised. If the child is isolated in a separate room the educator should carry out regular checks every to minutes, as they would do with a sleeping child.

When children of different ages are together in the same space, it is very important that the environment is set up to allow infants and toddlers to explore and play safely. This can be done in ways that let them be part of the playgroup community and learn alongside other children while making sure they are safe and able to move without restrictions or limitations.
When children of varying levels of ability and mobility are together in the same activity space, it is very important the environment is designed with infants and toddlers in mind so they can safely play and explore, both indoors and outdoors. This does not mean that infants and toddlers cannot move throughout the centre, learning alongside older children.

When you are thinking about the type of outdoor equipment to provide for children, keep in mind that the outdoor area at your playgroup does not serve the same function as a public playground. Equipment will need to engage and challenge children for greater periods of time and be flexible enough for children to construct their own learning. Flexible, moveable equipment allows children choice and control over how their learning environment is set up. Moveable equipment also encourages cooperation between children and provides opportunities for problem solving.
When you can, try to fasten objects near the top rather than at the bottom. If you cannot, then the fastenings at the bottom will need to be very strong. This is because of the leverage effect when something topples (a fridge for example).

You should aim to hold your emergency drills at times when you have typical numbers of children, of varying ages, and adults at the centre. Holding unannounced emergency drills at challenging times (for example, during lunch time or sleep time) may be inconvenient but will give greater assurance that procedures are effective. The RegistrarGeneral can investigate complaints that a marriage or civil union celebrant has not fulfilled their obligations under the Marriage Act , the Civil Union Act , or the Births, Deaths, Marriages, and Relationships Registration Act .
The RegistrarGeneral will keep any personal information in the complaint private and confidential. Only authorised people will be able to view your information. They will not share your personal information with the celebrant, church or approved organisation unless they have your consent. However, due to the nature of the complaint, the celebrant may work out who made it.
The RegistrarGeneral will let you know the next steps in the process. They may also ask you for additional information.
The RegistrarGeneral will make a preliminary assessment to see if it is a valid complaint and within their jurisdiction to investigate.

This draft operational statement explains the income tax treatment of amounts societies, clubs and other associations receive from members, other than amounts subject to a specific tax exemption such as for charities or sports clubs. It explains that the mutual association provisions override the mutuality principle for trading stock and services supplied to members. It also explains that subscriptions and levies will not be covered by the mutuality principle if the association is not able to distribute to members. Such amounts may be business income or income under ordinary concepts, depending on the circumstances. The statement will be prospective in application when finalised.

I n Cabinet agreed that AL payments would be based on the greater of three rates: Ordinary Leave Pay (OLP) (a new calculation to replace the current Ordinary Weekly Pay (OWP) which has been problematic ), Average Weekly Earnings ( AWE ) of the last weeks or AWE over the last weeks. The short run A WE adds a third calculation to the methodology in the Act . Confidential advice to Government Confidential advice to Government T he complexity of the rules for determining the use of AL entitlement . One of the most problematic areas of the Act is determining the amount of the fourweek AL entitlement an employee uses when they take time away from work. Employers and employees must agree on this based on what genuinely constitutes a working week for the employee. The lack of prescription and extent of flexibility means that, in the case of employees with work cycles different to seven days (for example shift cycles or nine day fortnights) or variable hours of work, discretion and judgement must be app lied.

MINISTRY OF BUSINESS, l NOVATION EMPLOYMENT HIKINA WHAKATUTUKI BRIEFING Interim Report from the Holidays Act Taskforce December Priority: Medium I Security classificat ion: In Confidence Tracking number: Action sought Action sought Deadline Hon lain LeesGalloway Agree to the proposed twomonth January Minister for Workplace extension to the timeframe with the Relations and Safety Taskforce reporting to you in July Contact for telephone discussion (if required) Name Position Telephone st contact Gerard Clark Employment Standards Policy Manager Principal Analyst, Jon Saunders Employment Standards The following departme ntsagencies have been consulted Ministers office to complete: Comments D Approved D Noted Seen D See Ministers Notes D Declined D Needs change D Overtaken by Events D Withdrawn BRIEFING MINISTRY OF BUSINESS, INNOVATION EMPLOYMENT HIKINA WHAKATUTUKI Interim Report from the Holidays Act Taskforce December Priority: Medium Security In Confidence Tracking classification: number: I Purpose . This is the Interim Report from the Holidays Act Review Taskforce (the Taskforce) which you established in May to review the Holidays Act (the Act) and make recommendations for change. Executive summary . The Taskforce is making good progress and is currently identifying and developing possible solutions to address the issues with the current Act. The Taskforce expects to be in a position to report back to you with recommendations for change that have been robustly tested in July . This is a slight extension to the anticipated report back of May to allow the Taskforce to conduct some additional targeted consultation on its recommendations prior to reporting to you. . To , the Taskforce has an Issues Paper and received almost submissions on issues with the Act and ideas for change. The Taskforce has considered a number of options for change and has identified two main alternative options for determining and paying leave entitlements. It now intends to test these options with an independent payroll advisor. . In addition to its detailed testing with a specialist payroll advisor, the Taskforce also intends to conduct targeted confidential consultation with key stakeholders including a broader group of payroll providers in the first half of . This will ensure that the Taskforce can be confident that its final recommendations are credible, implementable and will meet the objectives of the review ( outlined in Annex One). MBIE view on the proposed extended timeframe . MBIE supports the Taskforces request for a twomonth extension to the timeframe and recommends that you agree to it. The additional consultation that the extension would allow for will mean that the Taskforces recommendations are better informed, better understood by key stakeholders and more likely to resolve current issues without creating any unintended consequences. . If the Taskforce did not undertake this additional consultation it is likely that MBIE would seek to do so after the Taskforce reported. The impact on the overall timeframe for making policy decisions on changes to the Act is therefore likely to be minimal. MBIE considers that the twomonth extension to the timeframe is justified. Recommended action The Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment recommends that you: a Note the attached interim report from the Holidays Act Taskforce Noted In Confidence b Agree to a twomonth extension to the review timeframe to allow for additional targeted consultation with the Holidays Act Taskforce reporting to you with its final recommendations in July .
