Refining the scope and process for speed limit reversals The scope of roads to be considered for reversal has been narrowed from all roads that had speed limits reduced since the Land Transport Rule: Setting of Speed Limits came into effect, to certain roads with speed limits reduced since Road to Zero came into effect ( January ). The documents now propose to reverse speed limits reduced since January in the following areas: . Local streets with permanent kmh due to the presence of a school . Urban connectors (arterial roads) . rural State highways. The stretch of road outside a school gate will need to meet the new variable speed limit requirements and the streets in the surrounding area will need to reverse to their previous speed limit. Reduced speed limits on arterial roads and rural State highways can only be retained if the Road Controlling Authority (RCA) can demonstrate public support for the lower speed limit. For urban connectors the speed limit for the whole corridor will either be reversed or retained. For rural State highways, the RCA would be able to segment the corridor to consult on retaining reduced speed limits on sections where the topography changes, i.e. segmenting a cor ridor by straight segments and windy, hilly segments . Regarding State highways, we understand your concerns are primarily around speed limits being reduced from kmh to kmh (or lower) . To capture this we have referred to rural State highways in the draft Rule. This will exclude State highways in urban environments or passing through town centres. The ability to segment rural State highways is not in the draft Rule as it currently stands. We will ensure it is covered off in the Rule prior to lodgement. The RCA will need to undertake consultation in line with the new consultation requirements in the draft Rule. As part of obtaining public support, RCAs can present economic and safety analysis to inform the consultation process, but this is not mandatory (this is not explicitly covered in the Rule, but can be covered in guidance) . The narrowed scope is expected to deliver the reversals that you are expecting. It is also expected to be a less onerous task for RCAs as they will need to identify fewer roads to be considered for reversal . To retain lower speed limits, RCAs will only need PROACTIVELY RELEASED BY MINISTRY OF TRANSPORT TE MANAT WAKA UNCLASSIFIED UNCLASSIFIED Page of to demonstrate public support rather than the previously proposed criteria of public support, positive economic analysis and a high rate of compliance. Changes to the proposed Ministerial Speed Direction Following our discussion with you, we propose renaming the Ministerial Speed Direction to the Ministerial Speed Objective. This is to reflect our conversation with you about the role of this tool, where you indicated that RCAs should have regard to it, rat her than give effect to. Therefore, the draft Rule requires RCAs to have regard to the Ministerial Speed Objective (alongside the Government Policy Statement on land transport) when considering speed limit changes. The change in scope provides more flexibility for RCAs to respond to safety concerns on their network beyond what may be included in the Objective . Any proposed speed limit changes would have to align with the new speed limit classifications in the draft Rule, and be subject to cost benefit analysis and public consultation . Variable speed limits outside marae You asked for more information on speed limit reductions around marae. NZTA has advised there are two marae (Mahimaru and Karepnia marae) on the State highway network with variable speed limits outside them. They are both on State highway near Awanui i n Northland with a posted speed limit of kmh. In both cases, the electronic variable speed limit signs are activated automatically through sensor pads embedded in the highway and the marae driveways. The sensors can detect when a vehicle is slowing down to turn into the marae. Once activated , the variable speed limit sign will display a kmh speed limit so vehicles can turn in and out of the marae safely. The speed limit returns to kmh five seconds after a vehicle has left the sensor. Karep nia marae also has a manual SMS solution that can be used when people are walking along the road from the marae to the urupa (cemetery) . A designated person can send an SMS to activate the speed limit sign and reduce the speed to kmh for minutes. There are limits to who can use this system and how often. This information is set out in a memorandum of understanding between NZTA and t he marae , including : . Only three users hav e access to the SMS system . Only six activations per hour period, each activation lasting ten minutes . Access to system can be r evoke d if used inappropriately . NZTA contact details if the system is not working as intended. We have included an image at A nnex One showing where the variable speed limits apply. PROACTIVELY RELEASED BY MINISTRY OF TRANSPORT TE MANAT WAKA UNCLASSIFIED UNCLASSIFIED Page of Static variable speed limit signs outside school gates NZTAs manual of traffic signs and marking contains minimum legibility requirements for road signs to ensure drivers can read, comprehend and react to the information at a given speed. The static variable speed limit signs (static signs) contain quite a lot of information the variable speed limit, times, school days and schoolkura. For this reason, the Land Transport Rule: Traffic Control Devices (TCD Rule) only allows static signs to be used on side roads adjacent to a main road with electronic signs. This is because vehicles are generally slowing down for a give way or stop sign on the side road and can read it. An amendment is required to allow them on the main road without an accompanying electronic sign. To meet the legibility requirements for a main road, the font on the static sign would need to increase. The increased font would substantially increase the size of the sign to the point that it would require two poles and would not be practical in many instances. To enable RCAs to use the existing static sign (not the large signs) we propose to consult on an amendment to introduce default variable speed limit times into the Land Transport Rule (Road User) . The standard drop off and pick up times will be in the Rule and reflected in the Road Code. Drivers will be expected to know the school travel times and slow down when they see the school sign, even if they cannot read and comprehend all the information on the sign. Any amendments to the Land Transport ( Road User ) Rule (the Road User Rule) need to be drafted by the Parliamentary Counsel Office (PCO) . We are discussing the proposed change with PCO . The consultation document will consult on the proposal, rather than the amendments to the Road User Rule. We will work with PCO during and post the consultation to draft the required amendments. Attached at Annex Two are examples of the static variable speed limit signs that will be outside schools. Key p oints You are due to sign a new Setting of Speed Limits Rule by September , as set out in the Governments Q Action Plan . We have prepared a Cabinet paper that summarises the feedback received on the draft Rule through consultation and seeks Cabinets agreement to key changes , which are : othe introduction of the requirement to consult on a cost benefit disclos ure statement. This will include information on travel time and safety impacts of the proposed change, as well as the rationale for the change ; othe requirements for variable speed limits outside schools will be amended by removing standardised times for drop off and pick up (when lower speed limits will apply) and allowing RCAs to set these times for each school ; othe Ministerial Speed Objective, speed management committee and regional speed management plans will be removed from the Rule; oa speed limit of kmh will be enabled on roads built and maintained to a standard to safely support this speed. The Cabinet paper attaches an Regulatory Impact Statement. A draft summary of submissions is attached to this briefing . We have included a timeline below with the steps required to meet the Governments Q Action Plan deadline of having the Rule signed by September . Subject to your approval of the documents, we recommend ministerial and departmental consultation commences on September for one week. PROACTIVELY RELEASED BY TE MANAT WAKA MINISTRY OF TRANSPORT PROACTIVELY RELEASED BY TE MANAT WAKA MINISTRY OF TRANSPORT PROACTIVELY RELEASED BY TE MANAT WAKA MINISTRY OF TRANSPORT RESTRICTED To support achievement of these outcomes, within the context of advancing New Zealands national interests, I am proposing a revised Cabinet mandate for our negotiators at the IMO . I am also proposing that Cabinet delegates authority to the Associate Minister of Transport, the Minister for Climate Change, the Minister of Foreign Affairs, and the Minister of Trade to take any final decisions on issues in the negotiations. This would allow Ministers to provide further direction to officials on New Zealands position in the negotiations . Should the negotiations move outside the bounds of the revised Cabinet mandate, any final decisions with regards to New Zealands position would, where possible, be considered by Cabinet. However, where there are fast moving developments in the negotiations and time constraints, it may not be possible to convene Cabinet to take final decisions. Therefore, I propose that Cabinet authorises, the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance, the Associate Minister of Transport, the Minister for Climate Change, the Minister of Foreign Affairs, and the Minister of Trade, to take together any final decisions on other issues in the negotiations. This paper is seeking Cabinet agreement to a principles based negotiating mandate that identifies New Zealands interests and priorities, consistent with the Governments Climate Change Strategy . It gives delegated Ministers power to act to provide further direction on the detailed design of measures as the negotiations develop.

PROACTIVELY RELEASED BY TE MANAT WAKA MINISTRY OF TRANSPORT PROACTIVELY RELEASED BY TE MANAT WAKA MINISTRY OF TRANSPORT The Government intends to appoint a skills based board (the ALR Board) to transition from the current representative board. The ALR Board will drive the detailed planning phase and transition the project through to a formal legal entity by the end of . That entity will be responsible for overseeing the completion of the detailed planning and the delivery of the project following a final investment decision. The ALR Board will endure through the phases of the project, continuing to be the responsible board once the new legal entity is created. As Sponsors, we have agreed in principle that the ALR Board will consist of between five and seven members including a Chair . It also enables a quorum for decision making, which will then be finalised in the Terms of Reference that Sponsoring Ministers have received delegat ion to approve through Cabinets decisions in December . Details about these appointments We intend to make three priority appointments at this stage, with the remaining appointments appointed in the third quarter of . These appointments were prioritised to ensure continuity of knowledge exists, and key leadership roles were identified early , and allow the incoming Chair to shape the direction of the Board. The Chair will have a very demanding role which will be different and, in many respects, more demanding than other Crown Chairs. The Chair will be the public face of the ALR Project in local communi ties and will need to confidently fro nt and navigate issues in the three very different political environments of central government, Auckland, and iwi in Tmaki Makaurau. Their ability to personally demonstrate leadership and accountability for the impacts of the ALR Boards decisions will be necessary to maintain the Projects credibility and social license throughout its lifecycle. In addition, the Chair must be able to demonstrate an appreciation of the types of financial, technical, commercial or legal issues, which could be expected to arise from designing and delivering a project of this nature. They will also hold the role of Senior Responsible Officer for the Project at this stage until the final Delivery Entity is formed. Members of the ALR Board n eed to have a range of technical, policy, commercial and social attributes. Required competencies include significant governance experience of projects of scale and complexity, deep understanding of Te ao Mori, Te Tiriti o Waitangi and engagement with man a whenua and mataawaka in Tmaki Makaurau, and the ability to operate collaboratively and navigate a politicised environment. Candidate for appointment Hon Dame Fran Wilde We intend to appoint Hon Dame Wilde as Chair of the ALR Board. Hon Dame Wilde is a highly experienced director who has served as a Cabinet Minister, Mayor, and in senior governance roles on many significant central and local g overnment boards. Hon Dame Wi ldes diverse range of experiences in governance, politics, community involvement, working with iwi, and delivering transport and urban development outcomes meet the requirements we are seeking from the ALR Board Chair.

PROACTIVELY RELEASED BY THE MINISTRY OF TRANSPORT TE MANAT WAKA Page of Updates Northwest Rapid Transit Update A targeted social media campaign is underway to promote the community information sessions being held at venues across the northwest between Wednesday August and Wednesday September . This includes Facebook posts about the events as well as promoting a project video on Facebook and LinkedIn. The level of detail provided at the events will be similar to what was in your media release on the project on July and involves an update on the project and talking through the indicative alignment and station locations. SH Papakura to Drury Stage A open ahead of programme As of Thursday August , SH Papakura to Drury Stage A is now fully open with three lanes open in both directions. The project team scheduled to open southbound on the evening of Sunday August , however great progress was made over the past few weeks and the third lane was opened ahead of programme. The project is now open at kph with all lanes running on final design geometry. The team is on track with quality assurance documentation to submit the application for Practical Completion this week two weeks ahead of the contract completion . The final running surface layer will be laid in OctoberNovember. It has an epoxy component requiring warmer and dryer conditions than asphalt only. Page of IN CONFIDENCE Key updates Atlas Wind update Atlas Wind is an internationally flagged vessel which carries dangerous goods like ammonia within its cargo. We, and the Australian Maritime Safety Authority (AMSA), have had significant ongoing safety concerns with this vessel, with numerous deficiencies identified, and the vessel being detained on a number of occasions. Our latest detention of the vessel was on July during a Port State Control (PSC) Inspection in Dunedin and AMSA detained the vessel on Wednesday August . The Vanuatu registered Atlas Wind is owned by MOVe Oceans Singapore, which is a wholly owned subsidiary of the New Zealand based company, MOVe Logistics. We have also been discussing our concerns with MOVe. We are pleased to hear that after all of this work the vessel is scheduled to discharge import cargo and then is scheduled to proceed directly to Singapore , around Monday September , to be sold. MOVe is then looking to charter a safer vessel. This shows the importance of maritime inspections and good engagement with other regulators, like AMSA, in managing poor quality vessels round our coast. KiwiRail update Maritime NZ is preparing for an additional I nternational Safety Management verification of KiwiRails safety management system , scheduled for the week of Monday September . This audit will look at KiwiRails processes, procedures, training, risk management and how it brings on new equipment and familiarises staff. KiwiRail advised that the Aratere was out of service from Saturday August Tuesday August for the installation of a new gearbox part, and that the ships Classification Society was involved throughout this process. Once the gearbox is fixed this is likely to result in KiwiRail seeking to resume passage through the Tory Channel before the school holidays. The Kaitaki is currently in Singapore for a routine dry dock to carry out scheduled checks and repairs, and is due to return in early October . This means that the Kaiarahi was the only KiwiRail vessel in operation from Saturday August Tuesday August .
Page of IN CONFIDENCE Key updates MV Connemara Maritime NZ is continuing to make enquiries about the Cook Strait ferry, MV Connemara , losing power late Thursday September , south of Wellington. The Strait NZ operated ferry is currently under a detention notice. Over the weekend of September , it moved under its own steam between wharves to unload cargo. It is now located at Glasgow Wharf. The ferry will remain under detention until all conditions are satisfied and Maritime NZ, as the regulator, has assurance about the vessel. To be released from det ention the cause of the power loss must be identified , all repairs need to be made, assurances need to be given by the vessels Flag State (Bahamas) and Classification society and these need to be passed on to Maritime NZ , and Maritime NZ will carry out a Port State Control Inspection.

Page of IN CONFIDENCE Key updates Public consultation on recovering the costs of goods management activities at the border Following Cabinet Economic Policy Committee and Cabinet agreement in August , Customs and the Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI) are now consulting on cost recovery proposals for goods management at New Zealands borders. As noted previously, the proposals will lead to some significant cost increases for the maritime sector. Customs and MPI met with representatives of Shipping New Zealand on Monday September , who represent the majority of international shipping companies coming to New Zealand ports. A Maritime NZ representative attended as an observer. The Shipping New Zealand representatives expressed strong opposition to the proposals at the meeting. A particular focus was the proposed new , fee for commercial ships. Concerns included the potential for New Zealand to become an unattractive destination for major shippers due to rising costs, potentially resulting in a reduction of services with longer periods for getting goods to markets, and the prospect of some of the costs arising from the new fee being passed on to consumers. A further, follow up meeting with Shipping New Zealand in early October is planned. Customs and MPI are currently planning to provide policy advice to Ministers on the fee proposals in the first quarter of . MyMNZ We are developing MyMNZ, an online interface to enable far greater, and more efficient, digital interaction with the sector for services and activities we undertake. As a regulator, notifications and enquiries are important sources of information used to inform the delivery of our proactive and reactive work. A key milestone was achieved with a new online event notification form launched in support of the new HSWA designation on ports from July . We are continuing this work to address feedback our stakeholders provided about using our digital channels and services. This includes the need for a consistent and coordinated system to provide a single place to submit or apply for notifications , certifications and licences, provide more transparency about where they are in a process, and reduce the time spent repeating information. We are currently working on the requirements for creating another online form for specific types of notifications, and requirements for making more of our services for recreational craft departing for overseas available onl ine. Having these tools in place will enable a more efficient and effective use of our resources. High quality digital information will both reduce the time spent following up with applicants, and lead to better insights and decision making. Connemara Incident The Connemara lost power at approximately .pm on Thursday September , near Sinclair Head. It was towed back to Pipitea Wharf by the tugs Tapuhi and Tiaki. Maritime NZ will be making preliminary enquiries on Friday September into what caused the vessel to lose power. Those enquiries will determine its next steps. The vessel will remain alongside until its deemed safe to resume operations. In this instance, due to the location of the Connemara, towage vessels out of Wellington were able to assist and bring the vessel back to port. s ()(f)(iv)
Page of RESTRICTED Key updates Inaugural New Zealand Seafarer Welfare Council The inaugural New Zealand Seafarer Welfare Council (The Council) meeting was held Monday August with all member representatives present. The Council is an equal participation of member organisations from government, industry, unions, and service delivery within the seafarer sector. A planning day will be held in November to develop a strategy and associated action plan. This will look at transforming seafarer welfare service delivery and outcomes, in compliance with the Maritime Labour Convention (MLC) requirements. New Zealand Cruise Association Conference On Thursday August , the Director of Maritime NZ attended and presented at the N ew Zealand Cruise Association conference . The focus of her presentation was on the wide range of work Maritime NZ does with and in support of the cruise sector. Areas of interest from participants included work being done to facilitate the availability of alternative fuels and shore power, safety and security. A strong theme of the conference was concern about rising costs with short timelines that make it impossible to build the costs into tickets already sold, increasing debt on a sector already holding high debt from COVID . In particular , the current consultation processes proposing increased levies across a range of agencies was having cumulative impact. Customs has recently written to submitters indicating, post consultation, that because of lowered projections of cruise visits, and higher aviation visits, that levies will have to rise further than originally proposed on cruises. This will likely incr ease frustration markedly, as the sector argue that lower cruise activity in New Zealand is a direct result of high costs. Biofouling also was a concern; not so much that it was required, but that there was a need for the sector and government to urgently find ways to safely clean the vessels. Winter cruise has been cancelled this year and cruise is down on last year. The sector is forecasting a further reduction in . New Zealand was seen as a safe and high interest location to visit, and there are ships available and more being built, but there was a real sense that the cost and difficulty of doing business here was too high and ships were being directed to other places in the Asia Pacific. Maritime in the Media Sadly there was another fatal incident after a vessel capsized on Saturday August while crossing the Catlins River bar. One person died as a result of the capsizing, and the other person on the vessel made it safely ashore. Our partners in the water safety sector publicly commented on bar safety risks and skipper responsibilities. Our previously agreed content was used as talking points by Coastguard when they spoke on the capsizing.
Page of IN CONFIDENCE Key updates Maritime NZ Board Stakeholder day in Auckland The Maritime NZ Board (the Board), and Executive Leadership team (ELT) stakeholder engagement day was held in Auckland on Monday August . This initiative is part of the Boards regular engagement programme, which includes meet ing with stakeholders three times a year in conjunction with the Boards routine business meetings. Engagement included a breakfast session with senior leaders from the maritime community discussing The future of maritime activity in New Zealand and our collective responsibilities in ensuring a safe, secure, clean, and sustainable maritime sector , a me eting with the Port of Auckland to discuss their strategy and their plans , and a visit to the Auckland Marine Rescue Centre (AMRC), with briefings from Coastguar d NZ, Surf Lifesaving NZ and three recreational craft community grant recipients about their work . We have received extremely positive feedback from stakeholders about the value of these cross sector discussions. Southern Tiare Detention On Wednesday August , during a Port State Control (PSC) Inspection in Timaru, Maritime NZ detained the vessel Southern Tiare. The inspection identified concerns with environmental protection, safety equipment, watch keeping, machinery, general maintenance and failure to effectively implement the Safety Management System. The vessel was released from detention on Sunday September , however, one deficiency concerning watch keeping arrangements remains outstanding and is required to be addressed to the satisfaction of the Flag State (Cook Islands) and Maritime NZ before the vessel can depart. Maritime NZ are currently waiting on information from the vessels management regarding this unresolved deficiency. The Southern Tiare is operated by Chatham Islands Shipping Ltd, serving as a vital transport link between the Chatham Islands and New Zealand. The detention and eventual departure delay may disrupt the import and export of goods including fuel and livestock. Manahau Update Tugs commissioned by the operator, Westland Mineral Sands, for the salvage operation, MMA Vision and smaller Kurutai, are now in Westport and the operator and crews are preparing for a salvage attempt over the next few days, as conditions permit. The operators plan is for the Manahau to be towed to Nelson Port for repairs. Maritime NZ is actively engaging with the operator to encourage them to update the public about salvage plans and to understand crew welfare needs. We will continue to engage with stakeholders to support the operation. Maritime NZs team on the ground in Westport include investigators, public information management, legal and a National On Scene Commander, supported by a Maritime NZ response team in Wellington. Once the Manahau is in a safe port, we will move quickly from a response role to a regulatory role. We continue to publish regular media updates about the Manahau as interest in the barge continues to be high, particularly from West Coast media outlets.

Page of IN CONFIDENCE Aviation Project: Consultations with the aviation sector Cabinet paper: New Zealand Air Services Agreement and Protocol (Associate Minister) To lodge: Thursday September To Committee: Wednesday September To Cabinet: Monday September On Time Performance (OTP) We met with Air New Zealand, Qantas, Jetstar and BARNZ to discuss our approach to OTP following our discussion at the officials meeting on Monday September. The airlines noted that they already publish their OTPs on their websites and were curious about the purpose of the Ministrys reporting. The meeting provided an opportunity to work through the revised scope of the initial reporting, and to discuss what data is required. We have asked the airlines to supply the data directly, as this should be the most accurate source (and is consistent with Australian practice to source the data direct). However, we are continuing to explore sourcing data from Airport Coordination Limited (ACL), the company responsible for airport slot co ordination. We informed the airlines that if we are unable to source data from either the airlines or ACL, we will use the Cirium data (which they are opposed to, because of concerns about its accuracy) to meet our September timeframe. We also discussed the intention to build out the reporting to cover regional and international OTP. We expect to provide you with the revised draft report next week so that it can be in September. s ()(f)(iv)

Project: Airports (Cost Recovery for Processing of International Passengers) Act Officials have now concluded the analysis of submissions from the consultation on the establishment of cost recovery regulations under the Airports (Cost Recovery for Processing of International Travellers Act) . The Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI), in consultation with the Ministry of Transport, New Zealand Customs Service (Customs) and the Civil Aviation Authority, are now finalising advice to the Minister for Biosecurity, which will include a summary of the submissions received. This advice is expected to be sent to the Minister for Biosecurity on Tuesday September and will be forwarded to the Ministers of Transport and Customs. Almost all submitters opposed the development of cost recovery regulations, preferring the establishment and ongoing costs for new and restarting airports be funded from MPI and Customs respective Border Processing Levies. However, some submitters indicated that if cost recovery regulations were to be developed, their preference is for these to recover establishment costs only (Option B of the consultation). Option B is the preferred option for officials. s ()(f)(iv)

Other portfolio Cabinet papers with transport implications Committees Cabinet Economic Policy Committee (ECO) Wednesday September Recovering the cost of border processing services for travellers The Ministers of Customs and Biosecurity are proposing to present a Cabinet Paper and Cost Recovery Impact Statement (CRIS) on amendments to the Customs and Excise (Border Processing Levy) for consideration at ECO on Wednesday September and Cabinet on Monday September . The paper contains proposals for amendments to levy rates for recovering the costs of processing international travellers. The proposals include a substantial increase in the levy on arriving cruise ship passengers to recover Customs costs incurred in their processing. We have provided comment to Customs that the paper and CRIS would benefit from more evidence on the harms or risks associated with arriving cruise ship passengers, and the effectiveness of the Customs interventions to address those harms or risks, to make a stronger case for the increase in the levy. The C abinet Paper and CRIS note that the cruise industry is opposed to the increase and has expressed concerns regarding the cumulative impact of recent increases in Government fees and levies on their businesses. We can confirm that this was a strong theme at the recent New Zealand Cruise Association Conference held on August . Since the initial consultation, Customs have written to submitters on the levy proposals, indicating that because of lowered projections of cruise visits, levies on arriving cruise ship passengers will need to rise further than what was initially proposed in the consultation process. This is likely to increase cruise sector frustration markedly, as the sector is already on record as saying that the lower cruise visit activity is a direct result of high costs. Wednesday September Biosecurity System Strategy Minister Hoggard has begun Ministerial consultation on the Biosecurity System Strategy package. Consultation will run until Friday August , before proposed ECO lodgement on Thursday September , for consideration on Wednesday September . The strategy aims to address the policy, operational, and participatory challenges in the functioning of the biosecurity system, and is connected to the Biosecurity Act Amendment Bill proposals. While the proposal does not contain any obvious concerns for the maritime transport system, Maritime NZ has asked the Ministry for Primary Industries to involve us in any future work that touches on our functions such as: our current approach to Ballast Water Management the role of Regional CouncilsHarbourmasters; and vessels and those on board (particularly with regard to safety).
Page of IN CONFIDENCE Manahau response After being refloated on Friday September , the Manahau was towed from Westport to Port Nelson on Sunday September . The barge was towed into Tasman Bay by the offshore vessel MMA Vision with the tug Kurutai in support. The Kurutai and Port Nelson harbour tugs then towed the barge into port. Maritime NZ placed the vessel under detention for safety reasons. Maritime NZ was the lead Government agency for the response. Our role included engaging with the vessel owner and operator, the salvage team, councils and Nelson Harbourmaster to provide expertise and support, and monitor plans for safety and compliance. We were also responsible for implementing the restricted public access areas. Our involvement was misreported in media on several occasions and we wrote to editors to have the record corrected. The cause of the grounding has yet to be identified and Maritime NZ and TAIC are each running separate investigations. The operator has also hired an independent investigator. The Manahaus repairs will need to be certified by its Classification Society and Flag State (Niue) before it can be released from detention. Maritime NZ will also inspect the vessel and require that any deficiencies found have been repaired satisfactorily before it is released. Maritime NZ maintained reduced restricted access areas around the site where the Manahau grounded for public safety, while the area was remediated. We will formally lift the restrictions once we are advised it is safe to do so. Chatham Islands: supply vessel and Harbourmasters Direction An outstanding deficiency on the vessel Southern Tiare (non compliance with revised watch keeping requirements) , caused the operator, Chatham Islands Shipping Ltd, to raise concerns about the impact of this on vessel operations and the movement of livestock from the I slands. As the Southern Tiare is a foreign flagged vessel Maritime NZ has no jurisdiction in this case and these questions can only be addressed by the Flag State, the Cook Islands . It is the responsibility of the ship owner and operator to ensure that ship, crew, and equipment on board meet the flag state and international requirements that all shipping companies must adhere to. Maritime NZ met with a representative of the Cook Islands to discuss the possibility of a limited transition period to allow the vessel to operate whilst providing the operator time to find the additional crew required. Maritime NZ is now awaiting confirmation from the ship that they are able to meet the flag states requirements. Maritime NZ is also seeking a meeting with the Chatham Islands H arbourmaster about a Harbourmasters Direction he has issued that places restrictions on vessels of more than metres length seeking to dock at the main wharf. We are seeking to understand the underpinning risk assessment behind the direction and whether a national control, like a pilotage area, might be more appropriate. We note that, as it stands, the Direction could make it difficult for vessels currently planning to transport livestock from the Islands to do so.

Page of IN CONFIDENCE Maritime NZ media escalation process Maritime NZ maintains a duty team, which includes a duty media officer. The duty team is in frequent contact with the Rescue Coordination Centre NZ (RCCNZ), which is staffed , and has established ways of contacting harbourmasters, councils and emergency services as required. The duty media officer will provide a heads up to your or Minister Browns Press Sec retary or Private Sec retary when we are responding to a significant event. This will include information about the event, response, media queries we have received and our approved replies. Examples of when we would do this include major search and rescue incidents coordinated by RCCNZ, high profile recreational craft events , commercial shipping incidents and major pollution spills . We note that Minister Brown retains delegation for Cook Strait ferry issues. Your O ffice can ask Maritime NZ to assist with reactive media lines for queries the Minister might receive. In many cases the work of Maritime NZ is operational in nature and responding to maritime incidents is business as usual for the agency. The Ministers media role would likely be to acknowledge victims and public concerns, confirm they are being kept informed, provide assurance to the public, state the Governments established position if there is one, and refer operational questions to Maritime NZ. . Sector Engagement Engagement with the Fishing Health Safety Forum On Thursday September , Maritime NZ met with the New Zealand Fishing Health and Safety Forum , with which we have a long standing collaborative relationship. The Forum brings together commercial fishing operators and representative organisations to discuss health and safety issues and collaboration opportunities. The Forum also provides Maritime NZ with feedback around the operational impacts of policy and regulatory changes being considered. We had a constructive session with Forum attendees. Two particular topics discussed were how we might further support the sector to provide feedback to us on regulatory proposals, and some new potential collaboration opportunities to address risk. The industry, for example, is concerned about recreational vessels on the West Coast reportedly chasing Bluefin Tuna attracted by large Hoki trawlers. The potential risks with this behaviour is that recreational craft may voyage beyond thei r limits or capabilities and may get too close to the commercial vessel creating risks to themselves, their craft (and the commercial crew and vessel as well in some inst ances) . We are meeting again with members of the Forum to discuss how we might raise awareness of the risks in this area. Engagement with Bay of Plenty regional Council Senior Maritime NZ staff attended the Bay of Plenty Regional Council Monitoring and Operations Committee meeting on Wednesday September , to outline progress made in national and local maritime incident preparedness since the MV Rena grounding and oil spill in . Deputy Chief Executive for Response, Security and Safety Systems, Graham MacLean, presented councillors with an update on key focus areas that Maritime NZ has worked on to enhance its capabilities for managing complex incidents, particularly in the Bay of Plenty. These included: readiness and response strategies and plans capability development, including targeted training development and implementation ensuring fit forpurpose appropriately maintained equipment Iwi and community and volunteer partnerships establishment of enhanced specialist support arrangements with both New Zealand and international parties The Council expressed assurance that Maritime NZ has implemented the recommendations of the Simon Murdoch report () and that New Zealand was in a much better position to manage maritime incidents, large and small, into the future.

Other portfolio Cabinet papers with transport implications Committees Cabinet Economic Policy Committee (ECO) Wednesday September Recovering the cost of border processing services for travellers The Ministers of Customs and Biosecurity are proposing to present a Cabinet Paper and Cost Recovery Impact Statement (CRIS) on amendments to the Customs and Excise (Border Processing Levy) for consideration at ECO on Wednesday September and Cabinet on Monday September . The paper contains proposals for amendments to levy rates for recovering the costs of processing international travellers. The proposals include a substantial increase in the levy on arriving cruise ship passengers to recover Customs costs incurred in their processing. We have provided comment to Customs that the paper and CRIS would benefit from more evidence on the harms or risks associated with arriving cruise ship passengers, and the effectiveness of the Customs interventions to address those harms or risks, to make a stronger case for the increase in the levy. The C abinet Paper and CRIS note that the cruise industry is opposed to the increase and has expressed concerns regarding the cumulative impact of recent increases in Government fees and levies on their businesses. We can confirm that this was a strong theme at the recent New Zealand Cruise Association Conference held on August . Since the initial consultation, Customs have written to submitters on the levy proposals, indicating that because of lowered projections of cruise visits, levies on arriving cruise ship passengers will need to rise further than what was initially proposed in the consultation process. This is likely to increase cruise sector frustration markedly, as the sector is already on record as saying that the lower cruise visit activity is a direct result of high costs.

Page of Annex : Foundation outcomes The masterplan (Blueprint Report) for the Maungawhau and Karanga aHape development programme was approved by the project sponsors in . It set out the vision and key strategic choices for the programme . The vision for the programme set out in this masterplan was: Our vision is for each precinct to become one of the best quality, high density urban villages in the country, which is highly accessible to all parts of the Auckland region. It will be a high ly sought after, contemporary, sustainable, residential led, mixed use urban village The strategic choices for the programme were housing affordability , employment diversity and a s ustainable futur e. The foundation outcomes for the Maungawhau (Mt Eden) an d Karanga aHape station development s ites that the Eke Pnuku and Kinga Ora propose will guide delivery of the development programme and achieve the vision and choices are : Environmental vitality and climate action: An exemplar net zero carbon urban regeneration development that is resilient to climate change and focuses on the prioritisation of sustainable modes of transport and environmental vitality. Mana whenua partnership: Partner with mana whenua to integrate their mtauranga and reflect their ident ity in the precinct. Homes: Provide healthy homes with a mix of typologies and accessible homes to cater for a diverse community. Affordable homes: Provide an adequate supply of quality, affordable homes in the precinct to make the most of the location b eing adjacent to a significant transport connection. Accessibility: Create an accessible precinct that encourages the use of public transport and provides a safe and connected neighbourhood. Economic social well being (Community well being): Provide am enities that enhances the existing community and enables people to thrive. Value realisation: Creating enduring investments for the community and realise value over time. As well as achieving the stated vision and choices for the work, and progressing the Governments Urban Growth Agenda and General Policy Statement Housing and Urban Development , and Auckland Councils Development Strategy, these outcomes closely align with Eke Panukus focus on urban regeneration and Kinga Oras goal to deliver quality urban developments that connect homes with jobs, transport, open spaces and the facilities tha t communities need. The foundation outcomes also support the investment objectives for the development programme agreed by stakeholder s in , namely: Transforming Maungawhau and Karanga aHape station precinct into exemplar net zero transit oriented ur ban neighbourhoods RELEASED UNDER THE OFFICIAL INFORMATION ACT

Page of Your early feedback on these indicative priorities, and feedback received during the formal public consultation on the full draft of the GPS later this year will help in the development of the final version of GPS. The GPS is planned to be finalised by mid (a year ahead of Waka Kotahi adopting the next National Land Transport Programme). The National Land Transport Programme is a three year programme that allocates the National Land Transport Fund to national and regional activities in a way that gives effect to the GPS priorities. How can we ensure we maintain acceptable levels of service with the available funding The land transport funding system is facing significant pressures due to rising demands and costs. In the shorter term it will be necessary to prioritise effectively and strengthen the focus on value for money. For the longer term, work is underway on the Future of the Revenue System that will consider how we pay for transport to years into the future. The project is a first principles approach on how the land transport revenue system, might be configured in future to make it more sustainable in our changing context of climate change and increasing cost pressures. This project will take time , and we expect to undertake substantive stakeholder and public engagement . In the meantime, officials will continue to advise Ministers on current land transport revenue settings (including petrol excise duty, road user charges, and Crown contributions) to support delivery of the GPS and the National Land Transport Programme (NLTP) .

Page of Annex : Business case evaluation The business case has detailed strategic, economic, commercial, financial and management cases. Key aspects are summarised below. A wide range of options were considered for the regeneration of Maungawhau and Karanga aHape. Under the Auckland Unitary Plan, the development sites have a capacity for approximately homes. Maximising development to the view shaft height controls would increase this capacity to . It is recommended that this be undertaken through resource consents by d evelopers. The wider precinct has a capacity for , homes to be developed under the Auckland Unitary Plan. Maximising development to the view shaft height controls increases this capacity to ,. Eke Panuku and Kinga Ora have been working alongside C RLL, Auckland Councils Development Programme Office (DPO), Auckland Transport and utilities providers to better understand the infrastructure requirements around the CRLL sites. They note that m uch of the local infrastructure for the development sites wil l be funded and delivered by CRLL as part of its scope which de risks the short term development. Some of the larger precinct projects are already underwa y such as Watercares trunk sewer connection to Western Springs. The development aligns with the Auckl and Plan () , the Newtown and Eden Terrace Plan , and the Karangahape Road Plan The Karangahape Road P lan notes that the new CRL station on Karangahape Road ridge will be a significant catalyst for revitalising the area, opening oppo rtunities for private development, encouraging new business and residential growth, and providing a high level of public transport access for all. The opportunity to accommodate high quality growth and integrate the CRL station, while protecting and enhanc ing Karangahape Roads heritage and keeping the edge and grit, which the area is known for, is the key challenge for Karangahape Road in the future . Benefits from the wider precinct programme are described, and will be used to inform phase of the CRL Benefits Realisation Plan (BRP), which is currently being developed. A formal Benefits Realisation Plan for the Maungawhau and Karanga a Hape development precinct programme will also be developed The benefits analysis in the proposal looks at benefits out to , and highlights a range of financial and non financial benefits including economic development (including commercial and retail sites), urban renewal, social, sustainability and climate change benefits. Risks result from uncertain events that impro ve or undermine the achievement of benefits. The main risks that might create, enhance, prevent, degrade, accelerate or delay the achievement of the Foundation Outcomes are reflected in the project schedule and it is proposed they will be reported monthly to the Executive Steering Group to ensure that the assigned risk owners take the necessary steps to implement the mitigation response at the appropriate time during the schedule. The proposal notes that it is important to recognise that development projec ts will be subject to market and economic forces that will govern investment decisions. Any adverse market conditions will limit both public sector and private sector ability to invest. The current economic climate already presents a number of challenges i n the next three years; the impact of Covid and the pace of the recovery and return to normal presents a number of uncertainties that will need to be proactively managed. Page of Project governance The proposal recommends Eke Panuku Board be the lead agency t o take the programme development sites to market. This would include negotiating, managing and concluding a development agreement(s) on behalf of CRLL and receipt of sale payment back to CRLL shareholders. This would be subject to the parameters agreed in advance with the shareholders. This requires formal delegations be provided to the Eke Panuku Board. A Joint Executive Steering Group representing Eke Panuku, CRLL , Auckland Council, and Kinga Ora is proposed to manage this programme delivery as it moves to the implementation phase. The Joint Executive Steering Group will ensure alignment with the foundation outcomes which give effect to Sponsors vision and strategic objectives. As an extra layer of assurance the proposal recommends an independent r eviewer shadow the development process to have oversight of the key process decisions and approvals. This would provide assurance to the CRL Sponsors around the market approach and decision making. The alignment of the programme with Eke P anukus strategic focus and the Councils wider strategy, and the leadership it has demonstrated in the development of the programme business , suggest Eke Panuku are well placed to lead the project. The business case also outlines the process for property where a right of first refusal (RFR) exists under the Ng Mana Whenua o Tmaki Collective Redress Act . Programme activities will align with the requirements of the Act where RFR areas overlap with proposed development blocks.

Page of IN CONFIDENCE Appointments in Confidence Transport Accident Investigation Commission: Jane Mearess retirement At her meeting with Minister Doocey on Tuesday August , Jane Meares, Chief Commissioner of the Transport Accident Investigation Commission (TAIC), advised that she intends to retire on September . As a result of this decision, she has tendered her resignation from TAIC. TAIC staff were informed on Wednesday August . We understand TAIC will look to make a public announcement in due course, and will liaise with Minister Dooceys Office on timing and content. We understand Minister Doocey is considering the Chief Commissioners recommendation to elevate David Clarke, currently a Commissioner at TAIC, to Chief Commissioner. Should this be the preferred option, this can be done quite quickly as the Responsible Mi nister has the power to appoint a Chief Commissioner from within the Board. In order for the appointment to be completed before Ms Meares leaves the Commission, we have advised that we would appreciate confirmation by the end of August . A new appointment would take a lot longer and would likely be completed near the end of the calendar year at the earliest. T he Crown Entities Act allows the Deputy Chief Commissioner to exercise the functions of the Chief Commissioner if no Chief Commissioner is appointed by the time Ms Meares leaves the Commission.

Updates on other matters Second Asia Pacific Ministerial Conference on Civil Aviation The second International Civil Aviation Organisation ( ICAO) Asia Pacific Ministerial Conference on Civil Aviation is in India between September. The first conference was held in China in , however due to the Covid pandemic this will be the first since then. ICAO Member States are in the Asia Pacific region and expected to participate. New Zealand will be represented by the High Commissioner to India, Mr Patrick Rata. We understand Ministers (or Associate Ministers) from Singapore, Japan, Republic of Korea, Solomon Islands, Micronesia, Fiji, Tonga, Samoa and PNG will be attending. The Conference will discuss issues on regional collaboration, safety and security initiatives, sustainability in the aviation industry, and aviation connectivity. India has emerged as one of the fastest growing aviation markets globally and Indian PM Modi will deliver a keynote address to the conference, signalling that India has elevated this conference in importance. Officials will report back on any significant outcomes from the meeting.

Page of IN CONFIDENCE Updates on other matters Department of Internal Affairs Regulatory Systems Amendment Bill Amendments The Department of Internal Affairs (the Department) is developing a Regulatory Systems Amendment Bill (RSAB). An RSAB is a vehicle for non controversial policy changes that improve regulatory systems, and typically includes amendments to several Acts. The Department administers the Commissions of Inquiry Act (the Act) and is proposing to remove redundant references to the Act through the RSAB. This includes removing the redundant references to the Act in section () of the Waitara Harbour Act . The Department also proposes to remove the Shipping Act from Schedule of the Inquiries Act , as the relevant clause in the Shipping Act has been repealed. The Department has assessed the proposals as minor, non controversial, and contributing to maintaining the regulatory system. The Ministry agrees with this assessment and recommends these references be removed from the legislation. The Department will provide you with a Cabinet paper seeking Cabinet policy decisions in October , with the Bill expected to be introduced into the House in mid .

Page of IN CONFIDENCE Transport stakeholder updates Stakeholder Update CAA Aviation Industry Meeting On Monday August , officials attended the Civil Aviation Authoritys quarterly Aviation Industry Meeting. Meeting attendees included the Tier airports, Air New Zealand and Qantas, industry associations, Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment, Police and Ministry of Health. A key focus of discussion was on the economic importance of the aviation sector, and the challenges the industry is currently facing with reducing traveller volumes and rising costs. The industry was positive about the work being undertaken by the CAA and AvSec but is feeling under pressure responding to the number and breadth of government consultations. Civil Aviation Rules engagement The Civil Aviation Act requires all civil aviation rules to be remade to carry over settings in place under the Act, with any necessary updates to reflect the Act and other technical changes. Draft revision of all civil aviation rules has been completed. Sector engagement on the realigned rules will be undertaken for eight weeks, from the week starting September until October . We expect to provide the suite of rules for your approval and signature by December . Local Government CEOs Invitation to Address Local Government CEOs on transport policy You received an invitation from Auckland Council CEO Phil Wilson to address a group of local government CEOs (just over half of all regional, city and district council CEs) in Auckland on Wednesday September . We understand you were unable to accept the invitation. Mr Wilson has queried whether a senior executive from the Ministry can attend instead. The theme suggested by Mr Wilson is Government policy direction with transport policy, funding and delivery, though he has indicated flexibility over the topics that are covered. He has noted the intention to release the CityRegional deal framework shortly, and expects the CEOs to participate in a broader discussion about economic development, jobs growth and alignment of infrastructure investment. DCE David Wood has capacity to accept the invitation. As you will appreciate officials can explain government policy, but are bound by convention not to promote policy. If the Ministry does participate in the proceedings, we will provide the Office with an advance draft of the presentation for review and feedback. Page Chapter Best value for money spent This chapter provides an overview of how procurement ensures that best value for money spent can be obtained when purchasing goods or services to deliver activities approved under s of the Land Transport Management Act (LTMA). This chapter provides guidelines on the: Identify best value for money at the activity selection stage Maintain or enhance value for money spent through the procurement process Financial and nonfinancial attributes that are appropriate to value during the procurement process Page Chapter Strategic approach to procurement This chapter sets out how a strategic approach to procurement will enable an approved organisation more likely to obtain best value for money. The strategic approach has the following steps: . Document the policy context (strategic objectives and outcomes, procurement objectives and outcomes, compliance with other relevant policies) . Document the procurement programme . Document the approved organisations understanding of the procurement environment . Develop an approach to delivering the work programme . Implement the procurement strategy Page Chapter Supplier selection process The supplier selection process is the means of obtaining the preferred supplier to deliver the outputs based on best value for money principles.

Page of As signalled in the Decarbonising Transport Action Plan , the draft GPS will include a high threshold for investments that are inconsistent with emission reduction objectives . More work (led by the Ministry of Transport) is underway to confirm how this threshold will operate. We are open to feedback on how the emissions reduction focus is incorporated and communicated to drive the right incentives and outcomes and avoid any unintended consequences. The release of the draft GPS (anticipated in April ) will provide another opportunity to provide feedback on this. While the overarching foc us on emissions reduction signals a clear intent from the Government, in practice, it does not mean that every individual investment must reduce emissions. It means that the suite of investments covered by the GPS will reduce emissions as a whole.

Page What is a business case approach The business case approach seeks at the earliest stage of the process, to clearly define the problems and contextual state of the district, with engagement of key partners and stakeholders where necessary. The business case approach also seeks to make sure during the lifecycle of a programme or project that the reason for doing it are still sound, and that it has a clear link back to organisational priorities and issues.

Page We will apply the intervention hierarchy to shape the appropriate mix of interventions for any opportunity or challenges. With our coplanning and investment partners we need to consider the full range of options to implement the right combination of responses. Our priority will always be to get the most from existing infrastructure and different travel options that are available and avoiding or delaying the need to invest in new infrastructure. The intervention hierarchy is to consider first: Integrated planning Plan and develop an integrated landuse and transport pattern that maximises use of existing network capacity, reduces travel demand and supports transport choice Then managing demand Keep people and freight moving and reduce the adverse impacts of transport, such as congestion and emissions at peak times, through demandside measures eg supporting mode shift or road pricing Then make best use of the existing system through optimised levels of service across networks and public transport services, and allocation of network capacity Then invest in new infrastructure Consider investment in new infrastructure, matching the levels of service provided against affordability and realistic need

It was attended by several developers and a number of senior central and local government agency officials. Mill Road and SH Drury to Bombay were mentioned as examples of projects that the private sector would like brought forward. Reminder notices have started to be sent to those that have received an infringement but have not paid within days. The next step if the infringement is not paid after the reminder is sent is to transfer the outstanding notice to Ministry of Justice for further action.

Page of IN CONFIDENCE Driver Licensing wait times Update on interventions of note: Following completion of the recent surge DTO training, internal NZTA staff who were supporting the training have been redeployed to progress the review of the Driver Testing Officer Manual (DTOM) and Driver Testing Officer Certification process. The review is focused on assessing the DTOM and the certification process for potential effectiveness and efficiency gains that would support managing the wait time challenges. We are working closely with Vehicle Testing New Zealand (VTNZ) on this. They have provided several initial suggested changes, two of which have already been implemented. We are updating plans for implementing the extension to the time period for conversion of overseas licences, following the change in announcement (from Monday September to late October ). We have withheld any communications on the matter and will be liaising with your office in the coming weeks to manage briefing the Automobile Association and VTNZ appropriately in preparation for these changes. This week the NZTA contact centre begins an outbound call campaign to speak with individuals who have repeatedly failed to attend their booked practical test time. Page of IN CONFIDENCE Updates NZTA determination made on legality of e scooter remote operation function This update confirms the verbal update on this matter that we provided to your Office on Monday August . Escooter company Ario was recently given approval by Auckland Council to operate remotely controllable e scooters in and around the suburb of New Lynn, Auckland. Globally, these Ario e scooters are the first share scheme devices to have remote operation functionality (a person physically removed from the device can drive it via on board cameras and sensors). NZTA has obtained external legal advice on this matter and has determined that the remote operation of e scooters without a rider does not fall within the ES cooter (Declaration Not to be Motor Vehicles) Notice , or the Land Transport (Road User) Rule . The law specifies that on such devices (which are defined as a wheeled recreational device), the motors are auxiliary propulsion motors. When operated remotely the motors are the only source of propulsion, so cannot be considered auxiliary. The effect of the determination is that the remote operation function must be deactivated or simply not used. The devices are otherwise legally compliant and can continue to be used. NZTA is working with officials at Auckland Council and Christchurch City Council, who are c urrently assessing future e scooter contract providers to ensure a joined up approach and smooth implementation of the NZTA determination. NZTA does not see this as meaning that this sort of technology could not be considered or used in New Zealand in the future. A wider piece of work will need to be done to ensure safe operations and understand risks and benefits. Ario has written to you seeking a review of this decision. The Ministry of Transport will provide you with further advice. Supporting Motorcycle Awareness Month NZTA is supporting ACCs Motorcycle Awareness Month in September by promoting the annual injury prevention campaign and sharing relevant safety reminders for riders and drivers via our own internal external communication channels at no cost. Our latest motorcycling safety advertising is relaunching during the month, and this is funded as part of our National Road Safety Promotion Programme. The activities are planned to take place in September as people on motorcycles are significantly over represented in deaths and serious injuries on the roads, with a spike in September each year , when many riders return to the roads after winter. Speed Management Plan certifications Under the Land Transport Rule: Setting of Speed Limits (the current Rule), the Director of Land Transport has a role to approve anomalies in speed limits and specific speed limit decisions made by Road Controlling Authorities (RCAs), as well as to certify speed management plans. Over recent months, the Director has received requests from RCAs to certify speed management plans under the current Rule. Currently any request made by an RCA must be considered and determined by the Director in accordance with the current Rule. With each request NZTA first confirmed with the RCA that it wished to proceed under the current Rule, noting the progress of the proposed Rule and impacts that may have on them when the new rule comes into effect. Page of IN CONFIDENCE The total standard hours for one FTE are hours (this is a standard hour working week minus breaks) . o Over hours per DTO FTE indicates overtime or longer operational hours have been used. o Under hours per DTO FTE indicates operational shrinkage (the time when DTOs are not actively testing). This can be caused for example by DTOs taking holiday or sick leave, DTO training time, or travel time to complete tests outside of a DTOs home site. NZTA uses a standard rate for anticipated operational productivity shrinkage of percent . This results in a standard productive range of or higher hours of tests completed per DTO per week.

Page of IN CONFIDENCE Release of Quarter Public Attitudes to Road Safety survey The Quarter Public Attitudes to Road Safety survey (covering the period April June ) will be to the NZTA website on Thursday September . The survey details the results of responses to a broad range of questions focussed on specific road safety topics, including attitudes to enforcement, speed, vehicle safety, impaired driving, distraction, driver fatigue and personal safety. Key findings include: Public sentiment is in favour of greater Police presence (, down on the last survey) and more effort being put into catching people breaking road safety laws (), with the latter down on the previous quarterly survey. A total of of those surveyed think that penalties for breaking road safety laws should increase, down on the last survey. A increase in agreement to the statement someone who drinks and drives is likely to get caught, up from to . Most New Zealanders () support lower speed limits (kmh or lower) around schools in urban areas. Three in five () support lowering speed limits in highrisk areas, with supporting kmh speed limits in urban areas generally (not necessarily with schools nearby). These figures are unchanged from the previous survey. A total of support compulsory roadside drug testing of drivers (down on the previous survey). Just under half () think safety cameras help to reduce road deaths (up on previous survey); support more safety cameras (down three percent on previous survey); while at least somewhat agree that safety cameras are effective for reducing the number of people driving over the speed limit (down ). The quarterly report has a margin of error of around plus or minus . based on a sample size of , (slightly up on the previous quarter of , respondents). This will be the last quarterly survey, with the frequency now moving to annual. Civil Aviation Authority funding review Release of documents for public consultation The Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) funding review consultation will commence from Tuesday August . Two documents are being released: the public consultation document titled Civil Aviation Authority Pricing Review and the Cost Recovery Impact Statement (CRIS). CAA costs have not been met by income from fees, levies and charges since due to a decrease in domestic and international passengers, as well as inflation, changing security standards and other cost pressures. This pricing review focuses on returning CAA to financial self sustainability by July . The quantum of increases will be a contentious issue for airlines. This concern is likely to be compounded by recent immigration visa fees increases, an increase to the International Visitor Conservation and Tourism Levy, and airport instigated increases to charges for airlines. The Aviation Industry Associations Letter on Friday August mentioned the CAA review directly when talking about Immigration NZ. INZ, like the CAA, largely works on a cost recovery model but it could be argued increases on the scale proposed by Erica Stanford are an over correction. This is why we must be on guard for the upcoming Funding Review of CAA. Appendix of the CRIS contains a Ministry provided price elasticity analysis that indicates that the proposed increase in passenger safety and security levies could lead to a decrease in travel. Specifically, it suggests a drop of approximately . in international travel and a drop of at least . in domestic travel based on the low scenario. Page of How should we integrate VKT (Vehicle Kilometr es Travel led) reduction into the development of our Regional Land Transport Plan (RLTP) The ERP sets a target to reduce total vehicle kilometres travelled (VKT) by our light vehicle fleet by percent (relative to projected growth) by through improved urban form and providing better travel options, particularly in our largest cities. This target applies to all light vehicles, not j ust those directly powered by fossil fuels. This represents about a one percent reduction in VKT compared to levels, assuming ongoing population growth and urban development. Later this year, the Government will publish sub national VKT reduction targets for Tier and urban areas. These proposed targets have been calculated based on each urban areas ability to reduce VKT, and will add up to ensure we meet the national target. Later in , Waka Kotahi will publish a national plan to outline wha t it will take to reduce VKT by light vehicles in ways that create better cities for people. This will provide a framework for Waka Kotahi to work with councils, i wi, and communities to develop programmes for reducing car dependency and use by improving al ternatives. These programmes for Tier and Tier urban areas will need to be integrated with the RLTPs. While this work is underway, you should consider how any proposed activities in your RLTP could affect VKT by light vehicles. Projects that reduce VK T by light vehicles are more likely to be funded than projects that significantly increase VKT. As signalled through the Indicative Strategic Priorities, GPS is likely to support councils to invest in activities that reduce car dependency and use, by allocating funding to activities such as improvements to public transport and active travel networks. What does this mean for funding These indicative priorities signal the overall direction for land transport investment. As with any GPS, any funding of projects or services from the NLTF must be consistent with the direction set through the Strategic Priorities. GPS will also need to cover other sources of funding that t he Crown may decide to contribute. This includes, for example, Crown contributions to rail, the Climate Emergency Response Fund and the New Zealand Upgrade Programme. This document does not set out projections about available transport investment, including the National Land Transport Fund. This information will be included in the draft GPS.

Page of IN CONFIDENCE Update on interventions of note: Overseas conversion testing continues to drive high demand within the system; interventions to reduce this demand are expected to have positive impacts on wait times. We are prioritising work with the Ministry to finalise Cabinet papers to progress legislation changes that enable the extension of the period for drivers on overseas licences from to months before requiring conversion. A VTNZ trial for those converting overseas licences (OVC) commenced on Thursday August and an additional trial led by the Driving Change Network (DCN) is being scoped. The DCN proposal is for a more intensive support model. Both trials will help understand impactful interventions that can help move people through the system and to inform potential more substantial changes to the graduated driver licencing system in the future. VTNZ have noted that the numbers being referred to the OVC trial are slowly ramping up. Diverting people to the trial is a manual process at the front counter and is a voluntary referral for additional support. Further feedback on the progress of the trial is expected in September . Page of IN CONFIDENCE Updates State Highway (SH) Hydro Road planned maintenance closure State Highway (SH) between Mangorei and Kent Roads will be under a single lane closure for weeks from Monday September to allow for this km stretch of the road to be rebuilt. This will be the first major site of the Taranaki maintenance and operations summer maintenance season. This section of road has proven challenging to work o n safely, despite having a passing lane, due to its narrow width and high traffic volume. NZTA is unable to run the site under contraflow controls due to the width of the road, nor are we able to run stopgo traffic controls during the day due to the high volume of traffic. As a result, we will alternate the single lane closure between both northbound and southbound traffic to accommodate peak traffic flows, being particularly mindful of work commuters and public transport schedules. The road will be closed to southbound traffic between midnight and midday and closed to northbound traffic between midday and midnight. The closures will be clearly signposted so that road users can take alternative routes easily in advance of approaching the site. The alternative state highways are SHA or SH. The timeframe for works includes contingency for poor weather and other delays outside our control (such as staff sickness or plant breakdowns). This plan has been developed in consultation with freight and is currently being communicated with key stakeholders and the wider public. Seatbelts advertising campaign NZTA has launched a new road safety campaign focused on encouraging people to wear seatbelts. In , there were deaths and serious injuries (DSIs) in light vehicles (e.g. everyday cars) where people werent wearing a seatbelt, and there has been a steady increase in seatbelt related deaths on our roads since . The campaign has been launched across digital and social channels (TVNZ, TikTok, Instagram, Facebook) as well as promoted on radio. This is a tactical education campaign for target audiences e.g. yearold males, living in rural areas, aimed at reminding them why they should always wear their seatbelts. The approach is in line with the Governments new set of objectives and intended actions for road safety that will focus on safer roads, safer drivers and safer vehicles .

Driver Licensing wait times Summary for week ending Friday August July Wait times for practical testing (restricted and full testing) have increased compared to last week. full tests up by days ( days) restricted tests up by days ( days) At an individual site level, of full test sites and of restricted test sites met the days or less target last week. While the monthly backlog increased steadily from October , it has remained consistently at K ( ) since the end of June . Demand for testing has been steady compared to last week, however the increase in wait time metric was due to fewer future testing hours being loaded into the scheduling system and D river Testing Officer (DTO) illness. The amount of scheduled testing varies day to day for several reasons, such as driver testing officer illness and scheduled customer care and staff training. None of these individually are impactful on wait times, but they are, in combination, impactful. V TNZ is continuing to confirm staffing availability and increase available hours where possible (more testing slots were being opened for booking on Tuesday August which should help mitigate the current issue). Our demand forecasting shows that high wait times will continue, until practical test capacity increases (through meaningful increases to the DTO workforce) to meet demand. We expect to see improvements in early September as the current cohorts of trainees are certified and begin testing. Page How is cost benefit information used in budget decision making CBAx informs value for money advice when considering different options for investment. The initiatives are not ranked and prioritised exclusively on the Return on Inves tment (RoI). The RoIs are considered in the context of the assumptions and the evident base, as well as unmonetised impacts. For example, an initiative with a lower RoI and a solid evidence base may be considered better value for money than a high RoI init iative with optimistic assumptions and limited evidence based. In the budget context, the CBAx analysis is used primarily by the Treasury vote team in developing value for money advice. Direct text f The Treasury Gateway Reviews https:treasury.govt.nzinformati onandservicesstate sector leadershipinvestment managementgateway review sprocess planning Gateway is an assurance methodology for major investments which was developed by the United Kingdoms Office of Government Commerce (OGC) in . It is an independent and confidential peer review process that examines projects and programmes at key points in their lifecycles to assess their progress and to rate the likelihood of successful delivery of their outcomes. A Ga teway review takes one week.
Page Specifying the performance expected in return for funding Reporting expectations Linkage should ensure the reporting of information shows or can be used to show value of money. Appropriation and reporting systems are most useful when they produce needed va luefor money information. The Government can use such information to channel the funding for services that under delivered into services that improves lives of citizens in more cost effective ways.
