Page of REGIONAL CONSIDERATIONS FOR IMPLEMENTING COMMUNITY CONNECT EXTENSIONS Government has provided initial direction on the intent of the Community Connect funding Cabinet agreed to establish Community Connect (a half price subsidy on adult public transport fares) for Community Service Card (CSC) holders through Budget . Com munity Connect for CSC holders is on track to start on July at the end of universal half price fares . Many public transport authorities (PTAs) have opened digital portals to enable concession registrations. Through Budget , the Community Connec t programme was expanded to make funding available from July to deliver: . half price fares for yearolds (under s) . half price Total Mobility fares for Total Mobility card holders . free public transport fares for yearolds (under s). This briefing focuses on the Community Connect extension as noted in paras . and .. In advance of Budget announcements, we provided initial implementation advice OC refers. Through this advice and subsequent weekly reports , Minister Wood confirmed that: . halfprice fares for under s should result in a passenger paying half the price of any age based fare they are currently eligible for (e.g., a child andor youth fares, and adult fares), and noted the subsidy will not apply to existing Tertiary fares. . smartcard implementation is preferable but interim options, can be explored. . Crown funding can contribute towards the establishment of age verification processes and PTA administrative costs (including customer support, scheme set up, and application programming interface or portal maintenance) . . Crown funding be provided on the b asis of existing fare products and fare levels as of May (i.e., in advance of Budget announcements) This advice also noted that some decisions may need to be revisited following engagement with PTAs to understand regional feasibility. PTAs have developed interim options to enable delivery of Community Connect in July PTAs are responsible for setting public transport fares and adopting fare concessions. Page of RESTRICTED Appointments in Confidence Transport Accident Investigation Commission: Jane Mearess retirement At her meeting with you on Tuesday August , Jane Meares, Chief Commissioner of the Transport Accident Investigation Commission (TAIC), advised you of her intention to retire on September . As a result of this decision, she has tendered her resignation from TAIC. TAIC staff were informed on Wednesday August . We understand TAIC will look to make a public announcement in due course, and will liaise with your Office on timing and content. Transport sector Chairs and Chief Executives will also be informed in advance of a public announcement. We understand you are considering the Chief Commissioners recommendation to elevate David Clarke, currently a Commissioner at TAIC, to Chief Commissioner. If you would like to do so, this can be done quite quickly as the responsible Minister has the power to appoint a Chief Commissioner from within the Board (rather than the Governor General, who appoints Commissioners on your recommendation). A timeline outlining steps that need to be taken for the appointment to take effect by October is listed below. If your preference is to elevate Mr Clarke, we would appreciate your confirmation by the end of this month. A new appointment would take a lot longer and would likely be completed near the end of the calendar year at the earliest. Officials note that the Deputy Chief Commissioner can exercise the functions of the Chief Commissioner under clause of schedule of the Crown Entities Act if no Chief Commissioner has been appointed by the time Ms Meares leaves the Commission on September . Time period Action for September APH meeting Action for September APH meeting Week August Minister Doocey to advise Ministry of preferred action.

Page of There is likely to be substantial pressure on the availability of funding from the National Land Transport Fund. As in the past, there will be the need to prioritise investments and make difficult trade offs, including deferring andor scaling co funding commitments to prioritise those projects, activities or services that can best support the strategic priorities in GPS . Strengthening partnership with Mori The Government has highlighted in the Indicative Strategic Priorities that those involved in the transport sector have responsibilities to work in a way that is consistent with te Tiriti o Waitangi and section H of the Land Transport Management Act . This involves building enduring partnerships with whnau, hap and iwi, and national organisations to reflect Mori aspirations in future transport initiatives. Does this affect the current National Land Transport Programme No. The current GPS applies until the end of this NLTP period ().

Page of IN CONFIDENCE Key updates Inaugural New Zealand Seafarer Welfare Council The inaugural New Zealand Seafarer Welfare Council (The Council) meeting was held Monday August with all member representatives present. The Council is an equal participation of member organisations from government, industry, unions, and service delivery within the seafarer sector. A planning day will be held in November to develop a strategy and associated action plan. This will look at transforming seafarer welfare service delivery and outcomes, in compliance with the Maritime Labour Convention (MLC) requirements. New Zealand Cruise Association Conference On Thursday August , the Director of Maritime NZ attended and presented at the N ew Zealand Cruise Association conference . The focus of her presentation was on the wide range of work Maritime NZ does with and in support of the cruise sector. Areas of interest from participants included work being done to facilitate the availability of alternative fuels and shore power, safety and security. A strong theme of the conference was concern about rising costs with short timelines that make it impossible to build the costs into tickets already sold, increasing debt on a sector already holding high debt from COVID . In particular , the current consultation processes proposing increased levies across a range of agencies was having cumulative impact. Customs has recently written to submitters indicating, post consultation, that because of lowered projections of cruise visits, and higher aviation visits , that levies will have to rise further than originally proposed on cruises . This will likely increase frustration markedly, as the sector argue that lower cruise activity in New Zealand is a direct result of high costs. Biofouling also was a concern; not so much that it was required, but that there was a need for the sector and government to urgently find ways to safely clean the vessels. Winter cruise has been cancelled this year and cruise is down on last year. The sector is forecasting a further reduction in . New Zealand was seen as a safe and high interest location to visit, and there are ships available and more being built, but there was a real sense that the cost and difficulty of doing business here was too high and ships were being directed to other places in the Asia Pacific. Maritime in the Media Sadly there was another fatal incident after a vessel capsized on Saturday August while crossing the Catlins River bar. One person died as a result of the capsizing, and the other person on the vessel made it safely ashore. Our partners in the water safety sector publicly commented on bar safety risks and skipper responsibilities. Our previously agreed content was used as talking points by Coastguard when they spoke on the capsizing.

Page of IN CONFIDENCE Key updates Minister engagement on RMS Niagara with the Hauraki Gulf Forum Minister Doocey has received an invitation to meet with Lucy Baragwanath, Executive Officer of the Hauraki Gulf Forum (the Forum). The wreck of RMS Niagara is a frequent agenda item for the Forum as the risk it presents has the potential to impact the Hauraki Gulf. Maritime NZ has previously engaged with the Forum to discuss the wreck, and has a positive and productive relationship with them. Any advice provided to the Forum has been consistent with advice to Ministers. We recommend Minister Doocey visits the Maritime NZ, Maritime Response Team in Te Atatu Auckland prior to meeting with Lucy Baragwanath. The Oil Spill Response capabilities and people that Maritime NZ employs, equips, trains and maintains through the Oil Pollution Fund (financed through the Oil Pollution Levy) would be the responder to a significant oil spillrelease from the RMS Niagara . This will give Minister Doocey a clearer understanding of the condition and risk associated with the RMS Niagara and Mar itime NZs capabilities and readiness generally to respond to marine oil spills. The team is also meeting with Iwi and members of the Forum in the week ending Friday August , so will be able to provide more information on what the Forum may be seeki ng. Maritime Digital Transformation Maritime in the Media KiwiRail is due to be sentenced on September for Kaitakis loss of propulsion incident in January . We are currently working through our external communications approach. Due to the ongoing investigation into KiwiRail following the grounding of the Aratere in June , we will be taking a short media statement only approach. Once the sentence is delivered we will proactively update both your Office and Minister Dooceys of the sentence. We are developing our approach around recreational craft safety for the springsummerautumn. Already this year we have seen some major events in the recreational craft sector. We will be working to have a people focused approach to our recreational craft free media harm prevention approach.

Page of IN CONFIDENCE Key updates Atlas Wind update Atlas Wind is an internationally flagged vessel which carries dangerous goods like ammonia within its cargo. We, and the Australian Maritime Safety Authority (AMSA), have had significant ongoing safety concerns with this vessel, with numerous deficiencies identified, and the vessel being detained on a number of occasions. Our latest detention of the vessel was on July during a Port State Control (PSC) Inspection in Dunedin and AMSA detained the vessel on Wednesday August . The Vanuatu registered Atlas Wind is owned by MOVe Oceans Singapore, which is a wholly owned subsidiary of the New Zealand based company, MOVe Logistics. We have also been discussing our concerns with MOVe. We are pleased to hear that after all of this work the vessel is scheduled to discharge import cargo and then is scheduled to proceed directly to Singapore, around Monday September , to be sold. MOVe is then looking to charter a safer vessel. This shows the importance of maritime inspections and good engagement with other regulators, like AMSA, in managing poor quality vessels round our coast. KiwiRail update Maritime NZ is preparing for an additional I nternational Safety Management verification of KiwiRails safety management system , scheduled for the week of Monday September . This audit will look at KiwiRails processes, procedures, training, risk management and how it brings on new equipment and familiarises staff. KiwiRail advised that the Aratere was out of service from Saturday August Tuesday August for the installation of a new gearbox part, and that the ships Classification Society was involved throughout this process. Once the gearbox is fixed this is likely to result in KiwiRail seeking to resume passage through the Tory Channel before the school holidays. The Kaitaki is currently in Singapore for a routine dry dock to carry out scheduled checks and repairs, and is due to return in early October . This means that the Kaiarahi was the only KiwiRail vessel in operation from Saturday August Tuesday August .

Page of IN CONFIDENCE Key updates Public consultation on recovering the costs of goods management activities at the border Following Cabinet Economic Policy Committee and Cabinet agreement in August , Customs and the Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI) are now consulting on cost recovery proposals for goods management at New Zealands borders. As noted previously, the pr oposals will lead to some significant cost increases for the maritime sector. Customs and MPI met with representatives of Shipping New Zealand on Monday September , who represent the majority of international shipping companies coming to New Zealand ports. A Maritime NZ representative attended as an observer. The Shipping New Zealand representatives expressed strong opposition to the proposals at the meeting. A particular focus was the proposed new , fee for commercial ships. Concerns included the potential for New Zealand to become an unattractive destina tion for major shippers due to rising costs, potentially resulting in a reduction of services with longer periods for getting goods to markets, and the prospect of some of the costs arising from the new fee being passed on to consumers. A further, follow up meeting with Shipping New Zealand in early October is planned. Customs and MPI are currently planning to provide policy advice to Ministers on the fee proposals in the first quarter of . MyMNZ We are developing MyMNZ, an online interface to enable far greater, and more efficient, digital interaction with the sector for services and activities we undertake. As a regulator, notifications and enquiries are important sources of information used to inform the delivery of our proactive and reactive work. A key milestone was achieved with a new online event notification form launched in support of the new HSWA designation on ports from July . We are continuing this work to address feedback our stakeholders provided about using our digital channels and services. This includes the need for a consistent and coordinated system to provide a single place to submit or apply for notifications , certifications and licences, provide more transparency about where they are in a process, and reduce the time spent repeating information. We are currently working on the requirements for creating another online form for specific types of notifications, and requir ements for making more of our services for recreational craft departing for overseas available online. Having these tools in place will enable a more efficient and effective use of our resources. High quality digital information will both reduce the time spent following up with applicants, and lead to better insights and decision making.

International Maritime Organization Reducing Greenhouse Gass Emissions from International Shipping Member states of the International Maritime Organization (IMO) will be meeting between Monday September and Friday October to negotiate the design of measures to reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions in international shipping and meet the agreed targets in the IMOs Strategy to reduce GHG emissions in shipping. The New Zealand delegation in attendance may seek decisions from Ministers with the Power to Act . If decisions are sought from Ministers with Power to Act, a briefing will be provided at the end of the week of Monday September, or the beginning of the week of Monday September (with the timing dependent on how the discussions progress). We expect the turnaround time for decisions will be very tight, in order to provide directions to the delegation in time (we would most likely need a unanimous decision from Ministers within or working days).

Page of IN CONFIDENCE Media heads up General comments On Saturday August there was a fatal recreational boating accident at Riverton. A recreational vessel carrying people overturned when crossing the bar, resulting in the loss of lives. The Commission determined not to open an inquiry into this incident as it was unlikely to result in any new systemic safety issues being identified. In May , the Commission issued a report into a similar accident at Manukau Bar (MO ). In that accident, which occurred on October , a recreational boat carrying four people overturned while crossing the bar, resulting in the deaths of persons. TAIC identified the following safety issues: In New Zealand there is little regulation of the recreational boating sector. There is no registration or licensing system, there are no minimum standards for the design and construction of pleasure boats and there is no minimum requirement for assessments and licensing of recreational skippers to ensure a minimum standard of competency.

Page of IN CONFIDENCE Manahau response After being refloated on Friday September , the Manahau was towed from Westport to Port Nelson on Sunday September . The barge was towed into Tasman Bay by the offshore vessel MMA Vision with the tug Kurutai in support. The Kurutai and Port Nelson harbour tugs then towed the barge into port. Maritime NZ placed the vessel under detention for safety reasons. Maritime NZ was the lead Government agency for the response. Our role included engaging with the vessel owner and operator, the salvage team, councils and Nelson Harbourmaster to provide expertise and support, and monitor plans for safety and compliance. We were also responsible for implementing the restricted public access areas. Our involvement was misreported in media on several occasions and we wrote to editors to have the record corrected. The cause of the grounding has yet to be identified and Maritime NZ and TAIC are each running separate investigations. The operator has also hired an independent investigator. The Manahaus repairs will need to be certified by its Classification Society and Flag State (Niue) before it can be released from detention. Maritime NZ will also inspect the vessel and require that any deficiencies found have been repaired satisfactorily before it is released. Maritime NZ maintained reduced restricted access areas around the site where the Manahau grounded for public safety, while the area was remediated. We will formally lift the restrictions once we are advised it is safe to do so. Chatham Islands: supply vessel and Harbourmasters Direction An outstanding deficiency on the vessel Southern Tiare (non compliance with revised watch keeping requirements) , caused the operator, Chatham Islands Shipping Ltd, to raise concerns about the impact of this on vessel operations and the movement of livestock from the I slands. As the Southern Tiare is a foreign flagged vessel Maritime NZ has no jurisdiction in this case and these questions can only be addressed by the Flag State, the Cook Islands . It is the responsibility of the ship owner and operator to ensure that ship, crew, and equipment on board meet the flag state and international requirements that all shipping companies must adhere to. Maritime NZ met with a representative of the Cook Islands to discuss the possibility of a limited transition period to allow the vessel to operate whilst providing the operator time to find the additional crew required. Maritime NZ is now awaiting confirmation from the ship that they are able to meet the flag states requirements. Maritime NZ is also seeking a meeting with the Chatham Islands H arbourmaster about a Harbourmasters Direction he has issued that places restrictions on vessels of more than metres length seeking to dock at the main wharf. We are seeking to understand the underpinning risk assessment behind the direction and whether a national control, like a pilotage area, might be more appropriate. We note that, as it stands, the Direction could make it difficult for vessels currently planning to transport livestock fro m the Islands to do so.

Page of IN CONFIDENCE Engagement with the Fishing Health Safety Forum On Thursday September , Maritime NZ met with the New Zealand Fishing Health and Safety Forum , with which we have a long standing collaborative relationship. The Forum brings together commercial fishing operators and representative organisations to discuss health and safety issues and collaboration opportunities. The Forum also provides Maritime NZ with feedback around the operational impacts of policy and regulatory changes being considered. We had a constructive session with Forum attendees. Two particular topics discussed were how we might further support the sector to provide feedback to us on regulatory proposals, and some new potential collaboration opportunities to address risk. The industry, for example, is concerned about recreational vessels on the West Coast reportedly chasing Bluefin Tuna attracted by large Hoki trawlers. The potential risks with this behaviour is that recreational craft may voyage beyond thei r limits or capabilities and may get too close to the commercial vessel creating risks to themselves, their craft (and the commercial crew and vessel as well in some inst ances) . We are m eeting again with members of the Forum to discuss how we might raise awareness of the risks in this area. Maritime NZ media escalation process Maritime NZ maintains a duty team, which includes a duty media officer. The duty team is in frequent contact with the Rescue Coordination Centre NZ (RCCNZ), which is staffed , and has established ways of contacting harbourmasters, councils and eme rgency services as required. The duty media officer will provide a heads up to your or Minister Dooceys Press Sec retary or Private Sec retary when we are responding to a significant event. This will include information about the event, response, media queries we have received and our approved replies. Examples of when we would do this include major search and rescue incidents coordinated by RCCNZ, high profile recreational craft events , commercial shipping incidents and major pollution spills . We note that you retain delegation for Cook Strait ferry issues. Your O ffice can ask Maritime NZ to assist with reactive media lines for queries you might receive. In many cases the work of Maritime NZ is operational in nature and responding to maritime incidents is business as usual for the agency. Your teams media role would likely be to acknowledge victims and public concerns, confirm they are being kept informed, provide assurance to the public, state the Governments established position if there is one, and refer operational questions to Mari time NZ. Engagement with Bay of Plenty regional Council Senior Maritime NZ staff attended the Bay of Plenty Regional Council Monitoring and Operations Committee meeting on Wednesday September , to outline progress made in national and local maritime incident preparedness since the MV Rena grounding and oil spill in . Deputy Chief Executive for Response, Security and Safety Systems, Graham MacLean, presented councillors with an update on key focus areas that Maritime NZ has worked on to enhance its capabilities for managing complex incidents, particularly in the Bay of Plenty. These included: readiness and response strategies and plans capability development, including targeted training development and implementation ensuring fit forpurpose appropriately maintained equipment Iwi and community and volunteer partnerships establishment of enhanced specialist support arrangements with both New Zealand and international parties The Council expressed assurance that Maritime NZ has implemented the recommendations of the Simon Murdoch report () and that New Zealand was in a much better position to manage maritime incidents, large and small, into the future.

Page of IN CONFIDENCE Other portfolio Cabinet papers with transport implications Committees Cabinet Economic Policy Committee (ECO) Wednesday September Recovering the cost of border processing services for travellers The Ministers of Customs and Biosecurity are proposing to present a Cabinet Paper and Cost Recovery Impact Statement (CRIS) on amendments to the Customs and Excise (Border Processing Levy) for consideration at ECO on Wednesday September and Cabinet on Monday September . The paper contains proposals for amendments to levy rates for recovering the costs of processing international travellers. The proposals include a substantial increase in the levy on arriving cruise ship passengers to recover Customs costs incurred in their processing. We have provided comment to Customs that the paper and CRIS would benefit from more evidence on the harms or risks associated with arriving cruise ship passengers, and the effectiveness of the Customs interventions to address those harms or risks, to make a stronger case for the increase in the levy. The C abinet Paper and CRIS note that the cruise industry is opposed to the increase and has expressed concerns regarding the cumulative impact of recent increases in Government fees and levies on their businesses. We can confirm that this was a strong theme at the recent New Zealand Cruise Association Conference held on August . Since the initial consultation, Customs have written to submitters on the levy proposals, indicating that because of lowered projections of cruise visits, levies on arriving cruise ship passengers will need to rise further than what was initially proposed in the consultation process. This is likely to increase cruise sector frustration markedly, as the sector is already on record as saying that the lower cruise visit activity is a direct result of high costs.

Page of IN CONFIDENCE Key updates Maritime NZ Board Stakeholder day in Auckland The Maritime NZ Board (the Board), and Executive Leadership team (ELT) stakeholder engagement day was held in Auckland on Monday August . This initiative is part of the Boards regular engagement programme, which includes meet ing with stakeholders three times a year in conjunction with the Boards routine business meetings. Engagement included a breakfast session with senior leaders from the maritime community discussing The future of maritime activity in New Zealand and our collective responsibilities in ensuring a safe, secure, clean, and sustainable maritime sector ; a me eting with the Port of Auckland to discuss their strategy and their plans, and a visit to the Auckland Marine Rescue Centre (AMRC) , with briefings from Coastguard NZ, Surf Lifesaving NZ and three recreational craft community grant recipients about their work . We have received extremely positive feedback from stakeholders about the value of these cross sector discussions. Southern Tiare Detention On Wednesday August , during a Port State Control (PSC) Inspection in Timaru, Maritime NZ detained the vessel Southern Tiare. The inspection identified concerns with environmental protection, safety equipment, watch keeping, machinery, general maintenance and failure to effectively implement the Safety Management System. The vessel was released from detention on Sunday September , however, one deficiency concerning watch keeping arrangements remains outstanding and is required to be addressed to the satisfaction of the Flag State (Cook Islands) and Maritime NZ before the vessel can depart. Maritime NZ are currently waiting on information from the vessels management regarding this unresolved deficiency. The Southern Tiare is operated by Chatham Islands Shipping Ltd, serving as a vital transport link between the Chatham Islands and New Zealand. The detention and eventual departure delay may disrupt the import and export of goods including fuel and livestock. Manahau update Tugs commissioned by the operator, Westland Mineral Sands, for the salvage operation, MMA Vision and smaller Kurutai, are now in Westport and the operator and crews are preparing for a salvage attempt over the next few days, as conditions permit. The operators plan is for the Manahau to be towed to Nelson Port for repairs. Maritime NZ is actively engaging with the operator to encourage them to update the public about salvage plans and to understand crew welfare needs. We will continue to engage with stakeholders to support the operation. Maritime NZs team on the ground in Westport include investigators, public information management, legal and a National On Scene Commander, supported by a Maritime NZ response team in Wellington. Once the Manahau is in a safe port, we will move quickly from a response role to a regulatory role. We continue to publish regular media updates about the Manahau as interest in the barge continues to be high, particularly from West Coast media outlets.

Page of IN CONFIDENCE Cabinet Economic Policy Committee (ECO) Wednesday September Biosecurity System Strategy Minister Hoggard has begun Ministerial consultation on the Biosecurity System Strategy package. Consultation will run until August , before proposed ECO lodgement on Thursday September , for consideration on Wednesday September . The strategy aims to address the policy, operational, and participatory challenges in the functioning of the biosecurity system, and is connected to the Biosecurity Act Amendment Bill proposals. While the proposal does not contain any obvious concerns for the maritime transport system, Maritime NZ has asked the Ministry for Primary Industries to involve us in any future work that touches on our functions such as: our current approach to Ballast Water Management the role of Regional CouncilsHarbourmasters; and vessels and those on board (particularly with regard to safety). Environment Canterbury has proposed to provide half price fares for under s until free fares can be implemented Given limitations of its ticketing system, Environment Canterbury ( ECAN ) can only implement one age related concession . ECAN officers have advised it propose s to apply halfprice fares to yearolds until changes to the ticketing system are implemented in August . This a pproach means under s will pay half price fares in July , with free fares implemented in August . As this interim solution is time bound (i.e. , one month) and aligns with the policy intent of Community Connect (to provide reduced fares for targe ted groups) , we recommend Crown funding is provided . ECAN also seeks confirmation that a reduced Crown reimbursement is available for on demand services Ondemand services are provided in Auckland, Wellington, Timaru, Waikato and Hawkes Bay. We have advised PTAs that they have discretion to apply the Community Connect concessions to on demand services (providing flexibility for implementation that works best for their networks). MyWay is the sole public transpo rt service in Timaru. ECAN has informed officials that: . For under s: it will not implement free fares . For yearolds: it will not implement half price fares . For under yearolds (existing adult fares): it can implement a percent fare reducti on given ticketing system limitations. ECAN is seeking confirmation that the Crown will fund the percent fare reduction . While Government has not signalled whether Community Connect funding is limited to provision of a percent discount, we have assum ed this is the preferred approach for permanent implementation options . We consider this is an acceptable interim solution as ECAN works to find a permanent ticketing system solution that offers the percent discount. We do not have an expected timeframe for this solution but anticipate this interim proposal could be in place for six months to one year. Officials will engage with ECAN as the work progresses and can keep you .

Page of IN CONFIDENCE Follow up from your recent meeting with the MetService CEO and Board Chair Following your recent quarterly meeting with the MetService CEO and Board Chair you asked for the following advice: How you can support the MetService through the implementation of the Hau Nuku review The Hau Nuku review is being led by MBIE and Treasury with Ministers Paul Goldsmith and Judith Collins as decision making Ministers. As per your delegation, you hold the contract between the Minister of Transport and the MetService. Your interests in the Hau Nuku review will be in ensuring the MetService continues to deliver the weather forecasting services in scope of this contract. You can influence decisions about the MetService and NIWA through conversations with your colleagues, especially with Ministers Goldsmith and Collins. We recommend that you focus these discussions with your colleagues on matters that impact on the MetServices ability to deliver its contracted services. Performance reporting provided by the MetService As per the contract, the service provider ( the MetService) must report to the Minister on performance of the Operational Services each quarter by email to the Ministry. The current process is that the Ministry, on your behalf, receives and summarises the quarterly report then provides it to you in a Weekly Report entry. The indicators that must be included in the MetServices quarterly report are listed below (Schedule of the contract refers): a) The timeliness of the issue of routinely issued weather forecasts b) Accuracy measures, expressed as Probability of Detection (POD) and False Alarm Ratio (FAR) of routinely issued marine wind warnings for coastal areas and advice of broad scale severe weather c) The number of forecasts, watches, and warnings issued for severe weather events d) The availability of key elements of the observing network e) Participation of MetService personnel at World Metrological Organisation (WMO) meetings.

Page of IN CONFIDENCE Media heads up General comments On Saturday August there was a fatal recreational boating accident at Riverton. A recreational vessel carrying people overturned when crossing the bar, resulting in the loss of lives. The Commission determined not to open an inquiry into this incident as it was unlikely to result in any new systemic safety issues being identified. In May , the Commission issued a report into a similar accident at Manukau Bar (MO ). In that accident, which occurred on October , a recreational boat carrying four people overturned while crossing the bar, resulting in the deaths of persons. TAIC identified the following safety issues: In New Zealand there is little regulation of the recreational boating sector. There is no registration or licensing system, there are no minimum standards for the design and construction of pleasure boats and there is no minimum requirement for assessments and licensing of recreational skippers to ensure a minimum standard of competency.

Part Direction to require screening . Authorised aviation security service providers must use their aviation security o icers to search for substances at international screening points Authorised Aviation Security Service Providers must ensure that, at every international screening point at which they are operating, aviation security o icers employed by them use all or any of the powers in section of the Act to undertake searches for () inorganic powders () liquids, aerosols, and gels, including (but not limited to): a. water and other drinks, soups, syrups, jams, stews, sauces, and pastes (including toothpaste); and b. foods in sauces or containing a high liquid content; and c. creams, lotions, cosmetics, and oils; and d. gels (including hair and shower gels); and e. contents of pressurised containers (including shaving foam, other foam, and deodorants); and f. waxy substances (including hair wax); and g. mascara, lipstick, lip gloss, and lip balm; and h. any item of similar consistency at room temperature to the items specied in paragraphs (a) to (g). Clause : amended on April by clause of the Civil Aviation (Direction to Require Searching for Inorganic Powders, Liquids, Aerosols, and Gels) Amendment Notice . Made at Wellington on March Hon James Meager, Acting Minister of Transport Civil Aviation (Direction to Require Searching for Inorganic Powders, Liquids, Aerosols, and Gels) Notice Explanatory Note This note is not part of the Notice but is intended to indicate its general e ect. This notice, which comes into force on April , replaces the Direction to Require Screening Notice (SR ) and the Civil Aviation (Direction to Require Screening and Searching) Notice (), which are revoked by section of the Civil Aviation Act . This notice is secondary legislation and is by the Ministry of Transport on its website and notied in the Gazette as required by the Legislation Act . It sets out the direction given by the Acting Minister of Transport to authorised aviation security service providers that all or any of the powers conferred on aviation security o icers under this subpart be used by its aviation security oicers to detect the items or substances specied in the direction. The notice is consistent with recommended security control guidelines for screening inorganic powders, liquids aerosols, and gels, including those issued by the International Civil Aviation Organization.

Part Two: Mode neutrality Mode neutrality involves two important aspects: . Making sure all modes and options are considered and evaluated to find the best system solution. . Making users and decision makers more aware of the benefits and costs of transport choices, to incentivise robust decision making and smart travel choices.
Part of this system from the beginning was that road user revenue would subsidise public transport fares to a reasonable level, as public transport benefited motorists if it reduced congestion, and this fun ding cou d be planned for and delivered without c ompromising the principles above referred to by the Ministry of Transport as the social contract . Road user revenue for major nonroad capital projects GPS introduced the use of road user revenue to fund rail capital and rapid transit infrastructure but implementing this change has proven more challenging than was envi saged. GPS proposes even more funding for these purposes, including incorporating the Rail Plan into the National Land Transpo rt Programme . In actual National Land Transport Fund spending was substantially under budget (by ) . Most of the under spend was in activity classes relating to rapid transit, rail and p ublic transport infrastructure. This meant the increases to F ED and RUC provided additional revenue that was not spent. Fuel taxes should not be increased as a means of raising and saving money to deliver projects in the longer term raising transport taxes in advance of needing the revenue is inconsistent with the payasyougo principle of the land transport funding system. In addition, GPS reduced funding for state highway improvements by .B over years to fund these new uses , meaning projects Waka Kotahi NZ Transport Agency (the Agency) previously as sessed of high value for communities and New Zealanders all around the country stopped . The NZ Upgrade Programme (NZUP) has largely replaced this funding with .B for road projects , which we support. However, this approach has: delayed shovel ready proj ects decreased infrastructure capacity we compete in a global market for capital and when improvements allocations were dialled down, capital and skills moved offshore, and are not immediately available again, which further delays these shovel ready proj ects.
Part of your request was transferred to the New Zealand Transport Agency, and you will hear directly from them on the Hill Street Intersection and T he Strand Optimisation project .
Participants also talked about the limits of the activity classes for getting funding for long term, network wide, urban form projects which were identified as essential to achieving significant mode shift. The importa nce of the NLTF for achieving large scale change In bigger cities, the NLTF was seen as an end that the council was already working towards and the changes in GPS mainly made it easier for them to sell their case. Participants from smaller councils discussed the need to unlock funding from the NLTF by packaging mode shift promoting projects with other work. Many projects were seen as having a mode shift promoting aspect which could be used to support a funding request. In almost all cases, the realit y of a co funding model was that if a project were not funded through the NLTF, it would not proceed. A common point discussed by all participants was that they observed it being easier to get piecemeal projects through and harder to get more complex, long er term projects through (such as a network wide programme). It is not surprising that simpler projects are easier to get approval for. However, many participants felt it would be easier to see substantive change with a greater focus on more ambitious mode shift initiatives. Changing priorities Getting mode shift projects prioritised Participants recognised that the NLTF could not cover all requests and that a process for prioritising was needed. Some also reflected on changes in prioritising activities ove r the three GPS periods, with implications for activities included in the NLTP. Following Ministerial concerns with implementing the GPS changes to the investment decision making process developed with the sector, participants talked about the increas ed emphasis on the business case process in . The Investment Prioritisation Method (IPM) used to prioritise projects was referred to several times as more focused on evidence, in contrast to the more strategic approaches used previously (such as the In vestment Assessment Framework used for the NLTP). While recognising that not everything could be funded, most participants discussed the difficulty in gathering sufficient evidence to make a case for prioritising mode shift promoting projects. It was felt that the high evidence requirements of the IPM tend to favour larger councils and certain types of projects where evidence is more readily available. The shift away from a more strategic approach to relying on business cases and the IPM was seen by ma ny as inflexible and unresponsive to projects leading to mode shift. Interviewees provided Place making and Travel Demand Management (TDM) as two comprehensive initiatives considered effective for mode shift but for which evidence was difficult to obtain f or specific component projects. Discussion indicating a preference for a more strategic approach signals the difficulties councils face in getting the full range of projects needed to support mode shift funded. Evidence gathering in smaller councils was al so seen as more difficult because they need capacity, and there is less to see (for example, less foot traffic) compared to larger urban areas. Some participants raised the interpretation and application of the IPM in as an example of how the priori tising process limited what was eligible for funding in the mode shift promoting activities. For example, Low Cost, Low Risk (LCLR) funding was described as an important avenue for much of the work to maintain and improve walking and cycling infrastructure . However, in the previous cycle, this was considered primarily directed towards larger urban areas (as directed by GPS ). . STUDY PHASES

Value for money in GPS : increases the emphasis on value for money to maximise the impact of money spent to achieve the Governments outcomes indicates that deci sionmakers should take into account the full range of benefits and costs over the whole life of investments, and be cognisant of possible future changes and uncertainty, so that investment is made in options that perform best across a wide range of differ ent scenarios places greater emphasis on transparent investment decision making and on enhanced reporting on the outcomes achieved by investment.

This relies upon a robust and transpare nt prioritisation of investme nt. Summary d Literature Summary
Pg , section . Value for money in infrastructure is about delivering the right infrastructure and serv ices to the right level at the best cost. Decision makers should consider a range of options, the costs and benefits (both short and long term) and the GPS strat egic direction. They should also consider possible future changes and uncertainties so that inv estment can be made in options that perform best across different scenarios.

Preface Research, Economics and Evaluation The Research, Economics and Evaluation team operates within the System Performance and Governance Group of the Ministry of Transport. The team supports the Ministrys policy teams by providing the evidence base at each policy development stage. The team i s responsible for the following: Providing sector direction on establishing and using the Transport Evidence Base (see below) including the collection, use, and sharing of data, research and analytics across the transport sector and fostering the develop ment of sector research capabilities and ideas. Leading and undertaking economic analyses, appraisals and assessments, including providing economic input on business cases and funding requests. Performing the evaluation function for the Ministry, includin g designing monitoring and evaluation frameworks and approaches, developing performance metrics and indicators, and designing, conducting and procuring evaluations.
Preface Research, Economics and Evaluation The Research, Economics and Evaluation team operates within the System Performance and Governance Group of the Ministry of Transport. The team supports the Ministrys policy teams by providing the evidence base at each policy development stage. The team i s responsible for: Providing sector direction on establishing and using the Transport Evidence Base (see below) including the collection, use and sharing of data, research and analytics across the transport sector and fostering the development of sector research capabilities and ideas. Leading and undertaking economic analysis, appraisals and assessments, including providing economic input on business cases and funding requests. Providing the evaluation function for the Ministry, including designing monit oring and evaluation frameworks and approaches, developing performance metrics and indicators, and designing, conducting and procuring evaluations. The Transport Evidence Base The Transport Evidence Base Strategy creates an environment to ensure data, information, research and evaluation play a key role in shaping the policy landscape. Good, evidence based decisions also enhance the delivery of services provided by the public an d private sectors to support the delivery of transport outcomes and improve wellbeing and liveability in New Zealand. This report is listed on the Evaluation Programme, which forms part of the Transport Evidence Base implementation plan. Pressures Waka Kotahi has faced a range of pressures over the funding period including increasing demand on the network, a growing asset base, a more complex network, all whilst managing organisational restructures. This has been perpetuated by a range of other internal and external factors (outlined below) which have restricted the potential efficiency of the investment with the final spend reconciling nearer to the upper GPS band of .B, for example: o Greater focus on health and safety risk ma nagement associated with the Code of Practice for Temporary Traffic Management (CoPTTM) has resulted in increased costs over the period (and periods moving forward). Variations directly attributed to this were observed totalling .M over the three years . o Recovering from more severe emergency works over the period resulted in an additional M spend. The majority of this cost increase appears to be outside of the organisations control, however, more robust governance and adherence to more effective processes would further assist in managing these events. o Increased maintenance on new assets accounted for M (direct cost impacts). The ongoing costs of managing reinstatement of the network and costs associated with new assets installed following the Kaikoura earthquake and Manawatu Gorge was in the order of M over the funding period. o The significant amount of change and restructures Waka Kotahi have experienced since its formation may have led to a level of ambiguity in acc ountabilities and responsibilities that could have resulted in some level of duplication of some activities and functions and possibly contributed to a lower than desired level of efficiency and effectiveness in service delivery. Increasing administrative overheads may require some offsetting of service delivery spend in future investment periods if funding is constrained. o Heavy vehicle use and volumes on the network has grown by over the past years, with a increase in kilometres travelled by heavy vehicles experienced across the State highways during the funding period alone, compared to . Growth has been largest on Arterial and Primary Collector class roads. This may have resulted in Waka Kotahi changing its investment strategy to accommodate the greater wear andtear caused by trucks on those roads. o It was noted that the budget, forecasted a financial impact of M from external uncontrollable cost pressures for cost escalationinflation, traffic, and freight growt h that was realised. Asset investment sustainability The Review team assessed Asset Investment Sustainability and Consumption as a proxy measure to determine whether levels of investment were suitable to maintain assets.
Prevents threats by seeking opportunities to mitigate threats early
Previously, investment in New Zealands rail network lacked a longterm view about rails role in our transport system. This resulted in shortterm investment decisionmaking. We need a new approach to how we plan and fund our rail network.
Previously, owners were required to prove they had financial security of approximately NZ million. Modelling and comparisons with other jurisdictions suggested this level was too low to meet the potential costs of an offshore incident. We amended the regime in so that in the event of an oil spill, offshore installation owners have financial security in line with the amount that would be required if there was a spill from their installation.
Pricing and other economic instruments can be used to encourage more efficient use of the network and can be used by local government to drive travel choices and decisions. Such instruments include differential charging of public transport (e.g., reduced off peak fares), subsidised public transport fares, tolling, congestion charging, and parking fees. For example, tolling can contribute to the cost of building and maintaining new roads. You are the key decision maker and responsible for recommending to the Governor General that a road is tolled under the LTMA. The Ministry will provide advice on tolling proposals, liaise with the Road Controlling Authorities (RCAs), and advise on the legislative process to establish a tolling order. There are three existing toll roads: Northern Gateway, Tauranga Eastern Link, and Takitimu Drive . Penlink, which is scheduled to open by late has also been approved as a toll road. Information and education are used in road safety and can help to nudge people to make more informed travel decisions by communicating or consolidating information about their travel choices. Examples of educational instruments to influence travel choices and decisions include travel planning, social media marketing, information provision, mass media campaigns. The greatest benefits come from combining economic and educational instruments with compl ementary measures, such as infrastructure provision and legislative changes. In doing so, these measures can help to more effectively achieve the outcomes you want to see in the transport system, such as reduced congestion, reduced emissions and better health outcomes . Regulation You have a range of tools in the transport regulatory system to deliver durable transport outcomes Regulation is indispensable to the proper functioning of economies and societies. Regulation underpins markets, create an enabling environment for firms and individuals, protect the rights and safety of citizens , and ensure the delivery of public goods and services. The system is comprised of primary and secondary legislation (which includes regulations, rules, and other instruments ). Some transport regulation involves the direct prohibition or authorisation of some commercial activity. Foreign ships are explicitly prohibited from carrying coastal cargo, except in specified circumstances and with specific approval., Airlines operating scheduled international services require an international air services licence, issued within parameters set out in Air Services In , the total tolling revenue raised from these roads was . million, with million going to collection costs and . million to repay debt https:www.nzta.govt.nzassetsresourcesannual report nzt a waka kotahi annual report .pdf RELEASED UNDER THE OFFICIAL INFORMATION ACT THE FIVE TRANSPORT LEVERS
Primary legislation Temporary changes The intention is for agreement to be reached with owners to avoid the need for compulsory acquisition. Waka Kotahi will only be able to use the simplified land acquisition processes for temporary rights in land for access and occupation required while the recovery works are undertaken. It will need to rely on existing PWA processes if compulsory acquisition for freehold title is required for works undertaken under its proposed OiC. No modification to Te Ture Whenua Maori Act is proposed as part of these t emporary changes. Waka Kotahi and KiwiRail will need to comply with this Act as part of the repair and rebuild works.

Priorities . Continue to maximise efficiencies and value for money across the transport system.
Priority Minimise demand Manage the reasons why transport is needed and the context in which transport demand is derived, to deliver the same access to services and activities with less poweredmotorised transport. Priority Enable modal shift Enable the choice of transport modes with the lowest environmental impacts, and enable easier ch anges between modes. Priority Optimise system efficiency Increase all efficiency measures of transport modes and their use, particularly in terms of gCO km for passengers and gCO tkm for freight. Priority Increase capacity After optimisation of the first three steps, any capacity increases that are required should be prioritised to the most efficient and sustainable modes.

Independent Review Function for Aviation: Scope of Decisions and Review Fees Portfolio Transport On December , the Cabinet Economic Policy Committee: noted that the Civil Aviation Act (the Act), which comes into force on April , introduces a new independent review function (IRF) to enable applicants to seek expert independent reviews of decisions made by (or on behalf of) the Director of Civil Aviation (the Director); noted that the Act leaves the scope of decisions to be covered by the IRF to be specified in regulations, and that the Ministry of Transport has consulted publicly on options for setting the scope of the IRF ECOMIN; agreed that the scope of reviewable decisions will comprise: . the key relevant categories of decisions taken by (or on behalf of) the Director that are appealable to the District Court; . decisions taken by (or on behalf of) the Director on the granting of individual exemptions from regulations and the Civil Aviation Rules; noted that the Ministry of Transport has also publicly consulted on options to partially recover the costs of IRF reviews from applicants ECOMIN; agreed that a twotiered fixed fee be applied of , (excl. GST) per IRF review application for individuals, and , (excl. GST) per IRF review application for organisations; invited the Minister of Transport to issue drafting instructions to the Parliamentary Counsel Office to create new regulations to set: . the scope of reviewable decisions, as set out in paragraph above; . fees to partially recovery the costs of reviews, as set out in paragraph above; authorised the Minister of Transport to make final decisions on the detail of the regulations and to make changes, consistent with the policy intent of the paper under ECOSUB, in response to any issues that arise during the drafting of the regulations; I N C O N F I D E N C E gmtqxxq Document PROACTIVELY RELEASED BY THE MINISTRY OF TRANSPORT TE MANAT WAKA I N C O N F I D E N C E ECOMIN noted that the Minister of Transport intends to report back to the Cabinet Legislation Committee seeking approval of regulations setting the scope of the IRF and IRF review fees by the end of February . Rachel Clarke Committee Secretary Present: Officials present from: Rt Hon Winston Peters (Chair) Hon David Seymour Hon Shane Jones Hon Brooke van Velden Hon Chris Bishop Hon Simeon Brown Hon Erica Stanford Hon Louise Upston Hon Judith Collins KC Hon Todd McClay Hon Tama Potaka Hon Matt Doocey Hon Simon Watts Hon Melissa Lee Hon Penny Simmonds Hon Chris Penk Hon Nicola Grigg Hon Andrew Bayly Hon Andrew Hoggard Hon Mark PattersonOffice of the Prime Minister Office of Hon Chris Bishop Office of Hon Erica Stanford Office of Hon Simon Watts Officials Committee for ECO I N C O N F I D E N C E gmtqxxq PROACTIVELY RELEASED BY THE MINISTRY OF TRANSPORT TE MANAT WAKA IN CONFIDENCE IN CONFIDENCEIN CONFIDENCE Office of the Minister of Transport Cabinet Economic Policy Committee Independent review function for aviation: scope of decisions and review fees Proposal I seek the Committees agreement to create regulations to: set the scope of the new independent review function (IRF) established by the Civil Aviation Act (the Act) apply fees to partially recover the costs of IRF reviews from review applicants. Relation to government priorities The Government is committed to rebuilding the economy, easing the cost of living and delivering the frontline services New Zealanders need in an efficient way. The IRF will enhance the rights of aviation participants by providing them with an alternative avenue to challenge regulatory decisions, and support improvements in the performance of the civil aviation regulatory system over time. Executive summary I have considered the outcome of public consultation on the decisions to be covered by the IRF and propose that the scope of the IRF comprise: the key relevant categories of decisions taken by (or on behalf of) the Director of Civil Aviation (the Director) that are appealable to the District Court decisions taken by (or on behalf of) the Director on the granting of individual exemptions from regulations and the Civil Aviation Rules (the Rules). Following public consultation on options to partially recover the costs of IRF reviews from applicants, I propose that fixed fees be set at , (excl. GST) per review for individuals, and , (excl. GST) per review for organisations. I seek Cabinets authorisation to issue drafting instructions to the Parliamentary Counsel Office (PCO) to create new regulations to bring these proposals into effect . I intend to ask the Cabinet Legislation Committee (LEG) to approve regulations setting the scope of the IRF and IRF review fees by the end of February . Background The IRF will carry out reviews of specified decisions made by (or on behalf of) the Director from April when the Act comes into force. The function was created in response to stakeholder concerns expressed in submissions on the Civil Aviation Bill about the time and costs of appealing decisions made by the Director through the courts, and the court systems lack of expertise on civil aviation matters. The IRF will provide an expert independent review option that is faster and less costly than the court system. It will also promote transparency, timeliness and accountability, and support improvements in decision making over time. The final decision in response to each IRF review rests with the Director. This is to ensure that the Director retains the ultimate responsibility for the safe and secure operation of the civil aviation system. gmtqxxq Document PROACTIVELY RELEASED BY THE MINISTRY OF TRANSPORT TE MANAT WAKA IN CONFIDENCE IN CONFIDENCEThe Act requires that regulations specify the scope of the function The Act leaves the categories of decisions to be covered by the IRF to be specified in regulations. The IRF will not c over medical certification decisions, as these are already reviewable through the medical convener procedure that the Act continues . In July , Cabinet agreed that the Ministry of Transport (the Ministry) release a consultation document and seek stakeholder feedback on three options to set the scope of the IRF ECO MIN refers. The consultation was undertaken over four weeks to September . The three IRF scope options consulted on were: . Option includes the relevant categories of Director decisions that are appealable to the District Court . This option focuses reviews primarily on decisions centred on aviation documents that affect the ability of individualsentities to operate within the civil aviation system . Around , decisions within this scope are made annually. . Option based on Option , with the addition of decisions on the granting of individual exemptions from regulations and Rules. Fewer than decisions on exemptions are made each year . . Option includes all regulatory Director decisions, except where inappropriate or inapplicable. Around , decisions a year are covered by this option. Submissions on the scope of the function expressed a range of views The Ministry received submissions on the options for the scope of the IRF three from individuals and from civil aviation organisations, including from the Civil Aviation Authority (C AA). The CAA indicated it strongly supports participants being able to challenge decisions that have a major bearing on their ability to participate in the sector in a way that is more accessible t han the court system . It submitt ed that the IRF scope should be limited to significant decisions that are appealable under the Act (effectively Option ) . It submitted that Option would not support the policy intent for the IRF because there is a significant risk that the function would be overloaded with the demand for reviews of more minor decisions, which would inhibit the timely reviews of more impactful decisions. The relevant categories of appealable decisions are set out in s ection of the Act. Some categories of Director decisions w ould be excluded from Option , as it would be inappropriate for the IRF to review them eg medical certification decisions section () (g) (k) given these are covered by the medical convener function; and decisions relating to investigation and enforcement section ( ) (e)(f) where there is a need for the CAA to act promptly to address public safety or security risks. Exemption decisions applying to any class of aviation participant, aeronautical product, aircraft, aerodrome, aviation related service or other thing section ()(b) of the Act would not be reviewable, as these class exemptions are deemed secondary legislation under section (), and thus they are effectively part of the settings of the regulatory framework. Any decisions on individual exem ptions from medical standards and certification Rule requirements would also be excluded under this option. In addition to the exclusion of the medical certification decisions and decisions relating to security, monitoring, investigation and enforcement, other exclusions under Option would include decisions governed by the Solicitor Generals prosecution guidelines or established Court processes (in the case of infringement offence notices) , and decisions on pecuniary matters relating to invoicing and payment of fees and charges . gmtqxxq PROACTIVELY RELEASED BY THE MINISTRY OF TRANSPORT TE MANAT WAKA IN CONFIDENCE IN CONFIDENCE Three organisations favoured Option on the grounds it would enable reviews of decisions on exemptions while ensuring the demand for reviews would be likely to be manageable. Five organisations indicated they favoured Option to ensure a wider range of decisions would be reviewable. Discussions officials later held with some of these submitters, however, clarified that many of the decisions they advocated for inclusion would in practice be covered under Option (for example because they were applications for exemptions to Rules, so would fall within the scope of Option ). The three submissions from individuals offered no comment relevant to the scope options. I consider O ption to be the most appropriate option to achieve the policy intent of the function Option most effectively meets the policy intent of providing fast and accessible reviews, while supporting impactful improvements in decision making in the aviation regulatory system over time. Like Option , Option provides a faster and less costly avenue to challenge appealable decisions than going through the courts. However, Option also includes decisions on individual exemptions a feature supported by many submitters and thereby provides more complete coverage of decisions that could have a significant impact on aviation participants. Option , with its broad scope including lower order decisions, is less likely to facilitate the faster review pathway that the IRF is intended to provide, as there are risks that the likely higher demand for reviews under this option would: limit the reviewers capacity to deliver timely reviews of the categories of decisions that have the most significant impact on applicants (this wasacknowledged by several submitters) im pose demands on CAA resources that intrude on the agencys day today regulatory operations, and limit the Directors ability to make final decisions on reviewers recommendations within the statutory time frame dilute the incentives for participants to resolve issues with the CAA beforeescalating them to the level of an IRF review. Implementing Option minimises the risks to managing the IRF within available resources. This will be especially important during the initial months of its operation, when the process is new and reviewers are settling into their respective roles. The risk of overwhelming the function might be mitigated to some extent by the intended introduction of partial cost recovery for reviews (see following section), but it could not be expected to significantly limit the prospect of numerous requests for reviews of more minor decisions. This is because IRF fees are to be set at a (partial cost recovery) level that does not present an undue barrier to applicants. Some submitters suggested introducing a materiality threshold to reduce the risk of applications for reviews under Option overwhelming the IRF. However, this would not be possible as reviewers have no powers under the Act to have the discretion to make judgements as to what decisions that have a material impact on an aviation participant (and therefore should be subject to an IRF review). gmtqxxq PROACTIVELY RELEASED BY THE MINISTRY OF TRANSPORT TE MANAT WAKA IN CONFIDENCE IN CONFIDENCEThe Ministry has also completed public consultation on cost recovery options In September , Cabinet agreed that the Ministry should publicly consult on options to partially recover the costs of the IRF through application fees for reviews. A partial cost recovery approach reflects that applicants are the primary beneficiaries of the review function, while enabling review fees to be kept at a relatively affordable level for sector participants. ECO MIN refers The consultation document set out three options and fee levels to partially recover the costs of IRF reviews: Option a single fixed fee for all participants, set at , (excl. GST) per application. Option a two tiered fixed fee of , (excl. GST) per application for individuals, and , (excl. GST) per application for organisations preferred option. Option an hourly fee up to a cap, comprising a base fee of (excl. GST), plus an hourly fee of (excl. GST), up to a cap of , (excl. GST) for individuals and , (excl. GST) for organisations. The Ministry undertook four weeks public consultation during October . Three submissions were received one in favour of each of Option and Option , while the third submission favoured a variable approach, based on the outcome of a review, with no fees being applied at all in cases where the review is successful and a Directors decision is reversed. I consider Option to be the most appropriate option for partial cost recovery I consider that the two tier fixed fee approach of Option is more appropriate than the uniform fee structure under Option as: decisions affecting organisations are likely to be more technically complex and therefore more time consuming to review than decisions affecting individuals organisations can generally be expected to have a greater capacity to paythan individuals. Option also utilises a fixed fee structure that is more straightforward to administer than the hourly fees under Option and would thus provide more certainty about potential costs for applicants. It would also likely raise (marginally) more revenue than either Option or Option . Next steps Subject to your agreement, I will issue drafting instructions for the P arliamentary Counsel Office (PCO) t o create regulations setting the scope of the IRF and review fees proposed in this paper . I also intend to bring a paper to the Cabinet Appointment s and Honours Committee (APH) on the appointment of IRF reviewers in February . gmtqxxq PROACTIVELY RELEASED BY THE MINISTRY OF TRANSPORT TE MANAT WAKA IN CONFIDENCE IN CONFIDENCECost ofliving Implications The scope of reviewable decisions for the IRF and the review fees proposed in this paper will not have a material impact on the cost ofliving. Financial Implications The residual costs of the operation of the IRF (not covered by review fees) will be met by the Ministry out of Crown funding approved in Budget for the implementation of the Act . Legislative Implications Section of the Act provides that the scope of decisions to be covered by the IRF is to be specified in regulations. Section () of the Act provides statutory authority for the Government to apply IRF review fees. PCO has been consulted on the upcoming work to deliver the regulations in February . Impact Analysis A Regulatory and Cost Recovery Impact Statement has been completed and is attached at Appendix . It has been reviewed by the Ministrys Regulatory Impact Analysis Review Panel. The panel considers that the information and analysis summarised in the statement meets the criteria necessary for Ministers to make informed decisions on the proposals in this paper. Climate Implications of Policy Assessment The Climate Implications of Policy Assessment (CIPA) team has confirmed that the CIPA requirements do not apply to these proposal s, as the threshold for significance is not met. Population Implications There are no population implications associated with this paper. Human Rights There are no human rights implications. Regulations developed to set the scope of decisions covered by the IRF and review fees will be consistent with the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act . I N C O N F I D E N C E I N C O N F I D E N C EIn Confidence Office of the Minister of Transport Cabinet Legislation Committee Land Transport (Clean Vehicle Standard) Amendment Regulations Proposal This paper seeks authorisation for submission to the Executive Council of the Land Transport (Clean Vehicle Standard) Amendment Regulations (the Regulations). Executive Summary The Regulations implement various changes to the Clean Vehicle Standard (the Standard), as decided by Cabinet on Monday July (CAB Min, CBC MIN refer). These changes result from a review of the Standard that I was required to undertake und er section A of the Land Transport Act (the Act) (the Review). A review of the achievability of the CO targets for vehicle importers under the Standard was also included in the National Partys manifesto commitments. The Regulations amend the Land Transport (Clean Vehicle Standard) Regulations (the Principal Regulations) to: . align the CO targets for vehicle importers under the Standard with Australia, . exclud e disability vehicles from the Standard and improve the definition of disability vehicle to limit fraudulent exemptions , . amend the weight adjusting formulae slopes for and , . amend the minimum and maximum weights for light commercial vehicles, and . correct an error relating to publication dates. A waiver of the day rule is sought relating to the changes for disability vehicles. No compliance issues have been identified, and I consider that the requirements in section C() of the Act are met . Policy The Standard reduces the average CO emissions of vehicles that are imported through annual CO targets that progressively decrease . Vehicle importers are required to meet the targets each year, on average, across the vehicles they import. The framework for the Standard is set out in the Principal Regulations and Part s and of the Act. xxfpyy PROACTIVELY RELEASED BY MINISTRY OF TRANSPORT TE MANAT WAKA I N C O N F I D E N C E I N C O N F I D E N C E The Government is committed to retaining the Standard to support us to achieve New Zealands net zero climate goal by accelerating the supply of low and zero emission vehicles. However, to better realise the potential of the Standard and to reduce mot oring costs for New Zealanders, the Government committed to the Review to ensure that the Standards targets are achievable. UNCLASSIFIED UNCLASSIFIED Page of December OC Hon Simeon Brown Action required by: Minister of Transport Friday, January SETTING OF SPEED LIMITS RULE REVIEW TERMS OF REFERENCE Purpose Seek your approval of the Terms of Reference for the review of the Land Transport Rule: Setting of Speed Limits . Key p oints The Ministry of Transport (the Ministry) has prepared a draft Terms of Reference for a review of the Land Transport Rule: Setting of Speed Limits (the Rule) for your approval . The Governments day plan includes a commitment to Stop blanket speed limit reductions and start work on replacing the Land Transport Rule: Setting of Speed Limits . On December you announced amendment s to the Rule , including revok ing the deadline for road controlling authorities (RCAs) and regional transport committees (RTCs) to submit their speed management plans to the NZ Transport Agency ( NZTA ). You have signalled your intention to draft a new rule t o ensure RCAs and RTCs take a more balanced approach to setting speed limits and consider economic impacts, travel times, and the views of road users and local communities alongside safety when making decisions. You have also signalled your preference for variable speed limits approaching schools at drop off and pick up times. The draft Terms of Reference and proposed timeline in Annex outline s a targeted review that considers the issues you have raised . We have also recommended considering some broader matters to achieve your outcomes, such as the roles and responsibilities under the rule, including in relation to the Speed Management Committee , the Director of Land Transport and the NZTAs guidance. The review is intended to result in a new rule and associated guidance. The Ministry will lead the policy development process and the NZTA will draft the rule and make associated changes to its guidance as required. Following your feedback on th e Terms of Reference , we can amend the scope of the work as required. We would also recommend publishing the Terms of Reference on the Ministry s website once approved. Productivity review There have been six new DTOs placed across Christchurch sites this year. The breakdown by site and recruitment round is: Site February recruitment round May recruitment round August recruitment round VTNZ Northwood VTNZ Jipcho Road VTNZ Lichfield Street VTNZ Rangiora Total Rangiora included as a Christchurch site due to proximity to the city and subsequent anticipated overflow to this site.
Productivity review approach and caveats NZTAs approach to reviewing productivity is being refined and enhanced. The current approach to review productivity involves converting the number of tests completed into total hours of tests completed (we do this because the number of tests completed isnt a highly accurate measure of productivity, due to the difference in time it takes to deliver a restricted vs. full licence test; this conversion equalises productivity where the proportion of full test may be higher than restricted tests). NZTA then averages the number of hours worked across the DTO Full Time Equivalents (FTE) to produce a baseline per FTE number of working hours. Average hours per DTO per week only represents a simplified indication of productivity. The analysis of FTE per location is based on where each DTO is contractually based, however DTOs do travel between sites. This is not accounted for here. (Continued over page)

Findings from this study will provide insights that support decisions across the projectprogramme life cycle, including evaluations and reviews of transport investments. Progress ion duration: Relationships to rider characteristics As with Class , to simplify the analysis of progression duration we focussed on a single cohort: those riders who obtained a learner licence in to and who progressed to subsequent stages by th e end of . Figure shows the distribution of progression durations for this cohort, overall and by gender (the labelled values are the lower quartile, median, and upper quartile of progression duration for each progression step and gender). For rider s who did progress from a learner to a full licence, there is virtually no difference in duration across genders. The median rider progressed from learner to full licence in around months, with half of riders progressing between around months and months. At the restricted stage, the median rider who progressed to a full licence took just over months.
Progress is measured against the strategic priorities: safety, access, environment and value for money, and their associated objectives.

Progression duration: Relationships to crash rates Figure shows a simple comparison of crash rates versus progression du ration, at each licence stage (see section .. of the Technical Report for further analysis). Given the complexities of progression duration, the results in this figure are based on drivers who obtained a learner licence in to (combined), were aged under at the time, and who progressed to a full licence by the end of in at least months (i.e. did not shorten their progression by being aged or older at the time of obtaining their full licence or by having an advanced certificate). In each case we compare the crash rate for drivers who progressed from a learner to a full licence in to months (i.e. within one year of the standard minimum time) with those who took longer to progress. At all licence stages there is some variation i n crash rates by progression duration, but the crash rates are similar and none of the differences in our analysis are statistically significant ( pvalues range from . to .). Thus, at a high level, it appears that progression duration for drivers who do progress is not strongly related to crash rates at any licence stage.

RCAs expressed concerns about overriding local decisions that went through robust consultation processes and overriding community wishes. Many queried why only NZTA has ability to retain lower speed limits if there is public support and suggested this is extended to other road types. Some technical submissions sought clarification about what the presence of a school means for the kmh speed limit reductions on local streets, e.g if a school was only one of a Retain as drafted. Enable all RCAs to be able to retain reduced speed limits with a new consultation and public support (in line with the State highway approach). If the school was only one reason for introducing kmh, clarify that reversal applies. Exempt roads where the land use has changed or there is a consent for a business that is subject to the reduced speed limit. PROACTIVELY RELEASED BY MINISTRY OF TRANSPORT TE MANAT WAKA
